doi:10.1002/1878-0261.70328.abstract: Impaired protein folding in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) causes ER stress and activates the unfolded protein response (UPR), which can induce apoptosis during prolonged ER stress. ER stress is therapeutically targeted in plasma cell malignancies, such as multiple myeloma (MM), but these treatments remain noncurative, and UPR signaling in B-cell malignancies is incompletely understood. A targeted CRISPR-Cas9 screen in RPMI-8226 cells exposed to thapsigargin identified known ER stress regulators (XBP1, IRE1, and calreticulin) and the translation factor eIF5A (eukaryotic translation initiation factor 5A), whose role in ER stress remains unclear. Competition assays showed that eIF5A depletion is detrimental under basal conditions but confers a proliferation advantage during thapsigargin treatment. Inducible EIF5A knockouts confirmed reduced sensitivity specifically to thapsigargin, loss of eIF5A had no or sensitizing effects on cell death induced by other ER stress drugs. Polysome profiling revealed that not general translation, but the translation of specific mRNA transcripts coding for UPR components and apoptotic proteins was affected by eIF5A depletion. Correspondingly, EIF5A KO cells showed reduced thapsigargin-induced UPR activation. In conclusion, these findings indicate that loss of eIF5A alters the stress response in MM cells.

doi:10.1002/1878-0261.70343.abstract: Angiogenesis is a major driver of tumor progression and a validated therapeutic target in highly vascularized cancers such as clear cell renal cell carcinoma. However, the clinical benefit of antivascular endothelial growth factor therapies is limited by the emergence of resistance. We identified a vascular endothelial growth factor A splice variant, termed Lymphatic and Vascular Resistance Factor (LVRF), which promotes both angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis and is upregulated following anti‐angiogenic treatment. To therapeutically target this pathway, we generated fully human monoclonal antibodies against LVRF. Lead antibodies displayed high specificity and nanomolar affinity and effectively inhibited LVRF‐driven biological activities. Anti‐LVRF antibodies reduced renal carcinoma cell invasion, inhibited vascular and lymphatic endothelial responses, and suppressed lymphatic endothelial cell sprouting. In vivo , treatment significantly reduced the growth of bevacizumab‐resistant renal carcinoma xenografts, induced regression of blood and lymphatic vessels, and decreased metastatic dissemination in zebrafish models. These findings identify LVRF as a mediator of resistance to anti‐angiogenic therapy and support therapeutic targeting of LVRF as a novel strategy for vascularized tumors resistant to current antivascular endothelial growth factor treatments.

doi:10.1002/1878-0261.70344.abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) are often considered undruggable due to their structural complexity. mRNA technologies can overcome this therapeutic limitation by enabling dynamic protein replacement therapies. Here, we explore the TF activity of LCOR (Ligand-dependent corepressor), which suppresses tumor growth, at least in part by inducing the antigen presentation machinery (APM) in tumor cells and constraining cellular plasticity. These effects facilitate tumor immune recognition and immune-mediated tumor eradication. We used poly β-(amino esters) (pBAE) nanoparticles (NPs) for local delivery of Lcor mRNA in multiple breast cancer models. pBAE-NPs efficiently encapsulate mRNA and facilitate cellular uptake, achieving optimal endosomal escape, resulting in high transfection efficiency in vitro and in vivo, restoring LCOR function in tumor cells and engaging their APM. In preclinical models, intratumoral delivery of Lcor mRNA reduced tumor growth. Importantly, the combination of Lcor mRNA-loaded RH-pBAE-NPs with anti-PDL1 or anti-CTLA4 immunotherapies eradicated most of the tumors in our preclinical TNBC model. Overall, our nanotherapeutic strategy emerges as an innovative TF-replacement therapy in a lock-in/wipe-out fashion, leveraging the immunogenic effects of LCOR to eradicate breast cancer tumors when combined with immunotherapy.

doi:10.1002/1878-0261.70345.abstract: Seminal extracellular vesicles (EVs) hold promise as a source of biomarkers for urogenital cancers. In this study, small seminal EVs were isolated from healthy donors by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) and three ultracentrifugation (UC) protocols, with or without filtration. EV samples prepared by UC had a higher abundance of typical EV-related molecules such as CD9, CD81, and Alix, compared to SEC preparations. However, ribosomal and ER-related proteins were more enriched in SEC samples. Furthermore, the level of several nonvesicular proteins and/or EV-corona proteins was higher in SEC samples. The addition of a filtration step in the UC protocols also reduced the abundance of these proteins. Finally, we found that the isolation protocol affected the presence of prostate cancer-specific proteins in the EV samples, with membrane proteins such as FOLH1, TMPRSS2, and PSCA enriched in samples prepared by UC. In conclusion, our results suggest that SEC and UC enrich for different EV populations, which should be considered when analyzing cancer biomarkers. Moreover, UC samples contained fewer nonvesicular proteins and/or EV-corona proteins, which may enable a more precise detection of EV-based cancer biomarkers.

doi:10.1002/1878-0261.70350.abstract: Signals emanating from the B cell receptor (BCR) are vital for driving cell survival and proliferation in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). BCR-mediated signals in CLL cells promote nuclear exclusion and inactivation of the transcription factor forkhead box protein O1 (FOXO1) and transient upregulation of FOXO1 expression. To investigate the mechanisms that regulate FOXO1 inactivation, we focused on the role of deubiquitinase (DUB) family proteins. Stratifying expression of individual DUB proteins, we established that ubiquitin-specific protease 7 (USP7), USP8, USP9x, USP10 and USP14 are significantly upregulated compared to healthy B cells. USP7 interacts with FOXO1 in primary CLL cells, suggesting that modulation of USP7 activity may impact FOXO1 function. Using selective USP7 inhibitors, P5091 and HBX19818, or USP7 knockdown, combined with ibrutinib, we demonstrated enhanced FOXO1 nuclear localisation over ibrutinib alone and increased FOXO1 activity, leading to modulation of selected FOXO target genes. This resulted in reduced CLL cell viability and enhanced cell cycle arrest in MEC1 cells, largely reversed by FOXO1 knockdown. These findings suggest that dual targeting of BCR signalling and USP7 activity can harness FOXO1-mediated anti-tumour activity and may represent a novel therapeutic approach for CLL treatment.

doi:10.1002/1878-0261.70351.abstract: Ovarian cancer diagnosis is often delayed due to poorly defined clinical symptoms, underscoring the need for novel biomarkers that enable earlier detection. Protein biomarker discovery in blood samples is analytically challenging using mass spectrometry, as high‐abundance proteins can obscure detection of low‐abundance biomarkers. Ovarian vein (ovarian) and median cubital vein (peripheral) serum were collected from healthy women or patients with benign or malignant (majority stage I) serous ovarian tumours. Proteograph XT assay was employed as a protein enrichment methodology prior to LC–MS/MS analyses to obtain deeper proteome coverage in these samples. From an initial cohort of 53 samples, we identified 6603 proteins across all samples, including 3467 proteins uniquely identified in ovarian serum. Following exclusion of red blood cell–contaminated samples, differential abundance analysis identified 86 and 101 malignancy‐associated protein candidates in ovarian and peripheral samples, respectively. Notably, ANK1, CAND1 and GMPR2 were differentially abundant across both sample types. Using logistic regression with repeated cross‐validation and permutation testing, ANK1 demonstrated strong discriminatory performance [area under the curve (AUC) = 0.97] when combined with clinical CA125 measurements. These findings highlight the importance of ovarian vein sampling for enhanced access to tumour‐associated proteins and support further validation of these candidate biomarkers for early ovarian cancer detection.

doi:10.1002/1878-0261.70352.abstract: Circulating tumor DNA-based liquid biopsy is increasingly integrated into cancer care, particularly for detecting minimal residual disease, yet patient perspectives remain poorly understood. This single-center, cross-sectional, mixed-methods study assessed recall, knowledge, and attitudes toward liquid biopsy and circulating tumor DNA among 195 patients (median age 65 years; 63% female) undergoing cancer treatment or follow-up, supplemented by focus groups. Although 65% reported prior liquid biopsy, this was confirmed in only 44%, and only 10% had heard of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA). Correct recall and knowledge on ctDNA were higher among patients with neuroendocrine neoplasms and those with postgraduate education. In hypothetical scenarios assuming proven clinical validity and utility, 62-80% supported liquid biopsy-guided clinical action, 74% were comfortable with liquid biopsy replacing tissue biopsy, and 79% accepted its use to guide adjuvant treatment. Most patients anticipated reassurance rather than stress, and 85% expected improved quality of life with home- or general practitioner-based blood sampling. Overall, patients showed high acceptance of clinically actionable liquid biopsy use, driven by trust and perceived clinical benefit.

doi:10.1002/1878-0261.70355.abstract: The efficacy of immunotherapy is commonly increased by simultaneous anti‐angiogenesis treatment. An experimental breast cancer model exhibits vascular normalization with reduced vascular leakage when grown in mice with endothelial Shb deficiency. This mutant ablates the effects of vascular endothelial growth factor A on angiogenesis and leakage. Unexpectedly, the endothelial gene expression changes that were observed under these conditions suggested an immunosuppressive state. Comparison of healthy human breast endothelium with breast cancer endothelium revealed similar immune suppressive gene expression differences, and lung cancer and colorectal cancer showed analogous patterns of changes. These findings suggest that normalized or physiologically normal endothelium may have immunosuppressive features, with implications for the optimization of cancer immunotherapy regimens.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72087.abstract: Venetoclax (VEN)-based regimens improve remission in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but infectious toxicity remains a concern. We compared infection profiles under VEN-based versus conventional therapy in newly diagnosed, non-M3 AML at a single tertiary center (2015-2024; n = 358; VEN = 156; non-VEN = 202). After 1:1 propensity-score matching on nine baseline covariates (115 per group), we assessed infection rates and event density (events per 1000 person-days) by site and pathogen, time to first infection (120-day cumulative incidence), and landmark associations between early infections and progression-free survival (PFS). Baseline predictors of microbiologically documented infection (MDI) were modeled in the pre-matching cohort. VEN was associated with higher febrile-neutropenia (FN) event density (IRR, 1.77; 95% CI, 1.33-2.36; p < 0.001; 16.40 vs. 9.27 per 1000 person-days). Site-level patterns diverged: upper-respiratory and lung infections showed lower first-event incidence with VEN, whereas skin/soft-tissue and perianal sites showed higher event density without higher patient-level incidence. By pathogen, bacterial and fungal first events were fewer with VEN while event densities were comparable; viral infections occurred earlier and accrued higher cumulative incidence. Cumulatively, the first infection was lower with VEN at days 30, 60, and 90 but converged by day 120. In the pre-matching cohort, higher HCT-CI (1-2/≥ 3 vs. 0) and higher DBIL independently predicted MDI, while female sex predicted lower risk. MDIs within 90 days-bacterial/fungal-driven-were associated with inferior PFS at 100 and 365 days, whereas early viral infections showed no association.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72243.abstract: ABSTRACT The CD40 gene, a key immune regulatory molecule, has been implicated in tumorigenesis, and its functional polymorphism rs1883832 located in the Kozak sequence, may modulate cancer susceptibility by influencing CD40 expression. To clarify inconsistent epidemiological findings, a comprehensive meta‐analysis was conducted to evaluate the association between the CD40 rs1883832 polymorphism and overall cancer risk. Eligible case–control studies were systematically identified from PubMed, Web of Science and Cochrane Library up to August 15, 2025, and pooled odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated under five genetic models. Eight studies encompassing 3858 cancer cases and 4699 controls met the inclusion criteria. The results revealed a significant association between the rs1883832 T allele and elevated cancer risk in 4 multiple models, including the allele (T vs. C: OR = 1.26, 95% CI: 1.09–1.47, p < 0.01), homozygous (TT vs. CC: OR = 1.58, 95% CI: 1.16–2.16, p < 0.01), recessive (TT vs. TC + CC: OR = 1.43, 95% CI: 1.18–1.82, p < 0.01), and dominant (TT + TC vs. CC: OR = 1.29, 95% CI: 1.03–1.62, p = 0.03) models. Subgroup analyses revealed suggestive patterns of associations in lung cancer and Asian populations. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings, and no substantial publication bias was detected. In conclusion, this meta‐analysis provides compelling evidence that the CD40 rs1883832 T allele may confer increased susceptibility to cancer, thereby underscoring the potential influence of immune gene polymorphisms in carcinogenesis and their relevance for genetic risk assessment in oncology. doi:10.1002/cam4.72247.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancers (TNBCs) are associated with poor prognosis and chemoresistance. Recent reports indicate that extracellular matrix (ECM) molecules, such as integrins, could influence TNBC development. Integrins are adhesion macromolecules that modulate ECM characteristics such as stiffening of ECM and being associated with hypoxia. Therefore, dysregulation in integrins could compromise the efficient delivery of cancer treatments. Some peptides and aptamers can directly target integrins, and they are now being studied; however, most monoclonal antibodies and PARP inhibitors that are used for TNBC do not directly target integrins. Integrins and the ECM can change the way these treatments work. Currently, the efficacy of these candidates is still being evaluated, and the majority of studies are in the early phase of development. The present article reviews the role of integrins in cancer development and captures the state-of-the-art evidence on the therapeutic targeting of integrins in breast cancer. Also, solutions to overcome challenges in the field are suggested.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72260.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Non‐pathological complete response (non‐pCR) is common in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) patients after neoadjuvant therapy, yet evidence guiding long‐term outcomes and postoperative risk stratification in the immunotherapy era remains limited. Methods We retrospectively enrolled consecutive ESCC patients treated with neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (nICT) or chemotherapy alone (nCT) followed by esophagectomy and restricted analyses to non‐pCR cases. Primary endpoints were five‐year overall survival (OS) and event‐free survival (EFS). A 1:1 optimal propensity score matching (PSM) procedure and administrative censoring at 60 months were applied. Survival outcomes were assessed using Kaplan–Meier and Cox proportional hazards analyses. Results Among 366 patients with non‐pCR disease, 164 matched pairs were generated. After matching, nICT demonstrated a higher major pathological response (MPR) rate (19.5% vs. 6.1%), a lower ypT4 proportion (3.7% vs. 22.0%), and fewer recurrence/metastasis rate (40.2% vs. 58.5%), all p < 0.001. In the matched multivariable Cox model, nICT was independently associated with a lower risk of EFS events (HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.36–0.84; p = 0.005), whereas no independent association with OS was observed (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.70–1.27; p = 0.707). Open esophagectomy (OE), ypN2‐3 disease, and perineural invasion (PNI) were associated with worse EFS, whereas lower Ki‐67 expression and postoperative adjuvant treatment were associated with better EFS. PNI was associated with worse OS, and postoperative adjuvant treatment was associated with better OS. Conclusion Among non‐pCR ESCC patients after neoadjuvant therapy and surgery, nICT was associated with lower recurrence risk and improved five‐year EFS compared with nCT, whereas a significant OS advantage was not observed. Pathological factors (PNI, high Ki‐67, and residual nodal burden) and postoperative treatment may help inform risk stratification, although the observational treatment associations should be interpreted cautiously.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72269.abstract: Patients with metastatic cancer at initial diagnosis have the worst prognosis. Despite their involvement in initial assessment, the relationship between Primary Care Physician availability and metastatic cancer at initial diagnosis remains unexplored. Our objective was to determine whether Primary Care Physician availability is associated with patients having metastatic cancer at initial diagnosis. This was a cross-sectional study of patients aged ≥ 18 and diagnosed with breast, colorectal, liver, lung, ovarian, pancreatic, or prostate cancer from 2015 to 2019. Population-based Texas and California cancer registries were used for patient data. The main exposure was county-level Primary Care Physician density per 3500 individuals. Additional exposures included demographic factors, insurance, rural-urban continuum codes, county poverty rates, and US State at Diagnosis. The primary outcome was adjusted odds of metastatic cancer at initial diagnosis. Subgroup analyses based on insurance type, age group, and metropolitan residence were performed. Models were stratified by cancer type. Overall, 708,451 patients were included. On combined multivariable analysis, with each additional Primary Care Physician per 3500 individuals, the odds for primary outcome decreased by 2% to 6%. In a stratified analysis using Primary Care Physician density per 3500 individuals as a categorical variable, compared with counties with < 1 Primary Care Physician, counties with 3 or more Primary Care Physicians had reduced odds of primary outcome for multiple cancer types with no statistically significant difference for counties with 1-1.9 Primary Care Physicians. Increased Primary Care Physician availability was associated with a nonlinear decrease in odds for metastatic cancer at diagnosis. Thus, increasing physician density can possibly lower the likelihood of metastatic cancer at initial diagnosis.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72283.abstract: ABSTRACT Aim Previous studies have discussed the effectiveness of the Karnofsky Performance Scale (KPS), Palliative Performance Scale (PPS), Palliative Prognostic Index (PPI), and Delirium‐Palliative Prognostic Score (D‐PaP) in predicting the survival of patients with terminal‐stage tumors, but their effectiveness in the Chinese terminal‐stage tumor population still needs to be explored. Therefore, we conducted this prospective cohort study to investigate the applicability of KPS, PPS, PPI, and D‐PaP in predicting survival in Chinese patients with terminal‐stage tumors. Methods This is a prospective cohort study that collected data from 449 terminal‐stage tumor patients across four medical institutions in China from January to December 2024. The feasibility of using KPS, PPS, PPI, and D‐PaP to predict the 7‐day and 30‐day survival of terminal‐stage tumor patients was discussed through ROC curves. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were used to examine the survival differences of terminal‐stage tumor patients using four survival prediction tools with new cut‐off values. Results The study ultimately included 449 patients with terminal‐stage tumors. For the prediction of 30‐day survival, the area under the ROC curve of KPS, PPI, PPS, and D‐PaP was 0.842, 0.749, 0.778, and 0.898, respectively. In our study cohort, the optimal cut‐off values were 25, 3, 35, and 9.25. Their corresponding sensitivity was 86.3%, 92.3%, 77.7%, and 76.0%, while their specificity was 69.7%, 44.4%, 67.7%, and 93.9%, respectively. Conclusion The results of this multicenter cohort analysis reveal that in terminal‐stage tumor patients in China, KPS, PPS, PPI, and D‐PaP are all effective for predicting survival. Specifically, D‐PaP is more applicable for predicting 30‐day survival. Although D‐PaP showed the most significant predictive power, its accuracy in predicting 7‐day and 30‐day survival outcomes was not significantly superior to that of experienced palliative care professionals. Therefore, future research still needs to develop or update scoring tools with better predictive performance.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72292.abstract: Gynaecological malignancies account for over 1.4 million new diagnoses, with outcomes constrained by late-stage presentation and chemoresistance. Dysregulated redox homeostasis is a hallmark of tumourigenesis. Tumour cells maintain elevated basal reactive oxygen species (ROS), which support proliferative signalling but may also increase susceptibility to further oxidative stress. Vitamin D, acting through the vitamin D receptor (VDR), has antiproliferative and pro-apoptotic effects across cancer models, but its ability to amplify ROS beyond an apoptotic threshold in gynaecological malignancies remains unresolved. We conducted a narrative literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov and the Surveillance, Epidemiology and End Results databases, using terms related to vitamin D and its metabolites, ROS/oxidative stress, apoptosis and gynaecological malignancies. Preclinical evidence indicates that calcitriol and related compounds can induce ROS-mediated mitochondrial apoptosis, modulate autophagy and arrest the cell cycle. In ovarian cancer, non-HGSOC cell data suggest that mutant TP53 may alter calcitriol responses, requiring validation in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma models. In cervical cancer, calcitriol radiosensitises human papillomavirus-positive cell lines through autophagy suppression, whilst an in vivo calcitriol-cisplatin study reported improved survival. In endometrial cancer, thioredoxin-interacting protein induction is a candidate mechanism for selective ROS-mediated apoptosis, although this remains context-dependent. Clinical evidence is heterogeneous: higher 25-hydroxyvitamin D status has shown modest inverse associations with ovarian cancer mortality; small trials report regression or reduced recurrence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia; no randomised controlled trial evidence supports efficacy in invasive cervical cancer; and associations with endometrial cancer incidence are largely null. Current evidence does not support vitamin D supplementation as an oncology-specific intervention. Future research should prioritise biomarker-stratified trials incorporating VDR genotype, CYP24A1 profiling, pre-specified 25(OH)D targets and pharmacokinetically informed dosing.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72302.abstract: Active surveillance is recommended as the first-line management for desmoid-type fibromatosis (DF); however, data on DF of the head and neck (H&N) and shoulder regions are limited. We examined patients with DF located in the H&N and shoulder regions, comparing baseline characteristics and event-free survival (EFS). A subgroup analysis was performed among patients initially managed with active surveillance. H&N accounted for 4% of all DF cases, and shoulder accounted for 5%. Pain (62% vs. 53% and 33%, respectively; p = 0.01) and functional impairment (29% vs. 0% and 6%, respectively; p = 0.002) were significantly more frequent in shoulder DF compared with H&N DF and DF at other sites. Regardless of initial management, the 3-year EFS rates for H&N and shoulder were similar to those for other locations (p = 0.74). Among patients initially managed with active surveillance, the 3-year EFS rates for H&N and shoulder were similar to that for DF at other locations (p = 0.63). Pain and functional impairment differed significantly by location; however, the outcomes of both H&N and shoulder DF did not differ significantly from those of DF at other locations. This investigation was registered under the clinical trial registration number NCT02867033.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72306.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Pancreatic cancer is associated with a high risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), with approximately one in five patients developing VTE. Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that primary thromboprophylaxis is effective and safe in ambulatory patients with pancreatic cancer treated with chemotherapy. Despite international guideline recommendations, thromboprophylaxis appears underused in clinical practice. Objectives To assess clinical practice regarding VTE prevention in ambulatory patients with pancreatic cancer among medical oncologists in the Netherlands. Methods A nationwide online survey was conducted between March and June 2025 among Dutch medical oncologists involved in pancreatic cancer care. The questionnaire assessed VTE risk perception, use of risk assessment tools, use of thromboprophylaxis, and patient education regarding thrombosis. Results Thirty‐eight medical oncologists completed the survey. Most respondents (79%) classified the VTE risk in patients with pancreatic cancer as high or very high, yet 63% never prescribed thromboprophylaxis to ambulatory patients receiving chemotherapy. Lack of a national guideline recommendation was the most frequently reported reason for not prescribing thromboprophylaxis (74%). Only 11% of medical oncologists reported using the Khorana score, and only 3% always discussed VTE risk with patients. Conclusion Although medical oncologists recognize the high risk of VTE in patients with pancreatic cancer, thromboprophylaxis remains substantially underused in clinical practice in the Netherlands. Limited awareness of risk assessment tools and national guidance were prominent findings that may inform future implementation efforts. These findings provide a benchmark for assessing the impact of the recently updated Dutch guideline on thromboprophylaxis in this high‐risk population.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72308.abstract: ABSTRACT Joint modeling (JM) of longitudinal and time‐to‐event (TTE) data is a powerful statistical technique that elucidates how temporal changes in a biomarker relate to TTE outcomes while accounting for study confounders. The growing use of next‐generation sequencing (NGS) in precision oncology, particularly in capturing circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) methylation via liquid biopsy, offers new opportunities to apply JM for patient prognostication. In this study, we used JM to analyze a prospective cohort of 251 non‐small cell lung cancer patients receiving standard‐of‐care immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment regimens. The JM is comprised of two sub‐models—a hierarchical cubic spline random effects model for the longitudinal biomarker component and a Cox proportional hazards model for the TTE outcome component. Each sub‐model incorporated baseline factors of age, gender, smoking status, and cancer stage. The main objective was to establish whether the evolution of a methylation‐derived tumor fraction (TF) is associated with patient outcomes. Our investigation revealed that TF is strongly associated with both real‐world overall survival and real‐world progression‐free survival. These results enable the generation of various patient‐level predictions that capture the dynamic interplay between TF and patient outcomes, offering a path toward real‐time, personalized prognostication. Although validation in larger, multi‐center cohorts is needed before routine adoption, this work represents an important step toward integrating dynamic predictions into serial liquid biopsy monitoring. This approach demonstrates the potential of JM to provide more nuanced and adaptive disease evolution monitoring, offering better clinical decision guidance compared to static models or imaging alone.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72309.abstract: Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) frequently disseminates within the lipid-rich peritoneal cavity, where tumor progression is accompanied by metabolic adaptations involving lipid utilization and mitochondrial function. Although these metabolic alterations are increasingly recognized as important features of EOC progression and peritoneal metastasis, the molecular factors linking mitochondrial-lipid metabolic remodeling with aggressive tumor behavior remain incompletely characterized. We therefore integrated mitochondrial- and lipid metabolism-related transcriptomic analyses to identify candidate regulators and further investigated the clinical and biological features associated with CDS2. Seven key genes associated with mitochondrial and lipid metabolism were identified in EOC through comprehensive bioinformatic analyses and were used to construct the MALRS prognostic model. Further integration of FIGO stage, histologic grade, and MALRS scores yielded a nomogram whose calibration plots showed good agreement between predicted and observed 1-, 3-, and 5-year survival probabilities. Subsequent screening of these candidate genes in chemotherapy-resistant datasets identified CDP-diacylglycerol synthase 2 (CDS2) as the most consistently upregulated candidate gene. Clinical validation confirmed that CDS2 was significantly overexpressed in tumor tissues and was associated with advanced disease stage, and survival analysis showed that higher CDS2 expression was associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS) in stage III/IV patients. Functional characterization demonstrated that CDS2 overexpression promoted both lipid droplet accumulation and migratory capacity in ovarian cancer cells. Pathway analysis identified significant enrichment of PI3K/AKT signaling, and experimental validation confirmed CDS2-mediated hyperactivation of PI3K/AKT phosphorylation. Computational immune-deconvolution analyses further identified exploratory associations between CDS2 expression, estimated T-cell abundance, and immune-checkpoint transcripts. CDS2 is a lipid metabolism-associated candidate biomarker linked to aggressive clinicopathological features in EOC. Our findings associate CDS2 with disease progression, PI3K/AKT-related signaling, and immune-related transcriptomic features, supporting its further evaluation as a candidate prognostic marker.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72312.abstract: ABSTRACT Background This cross‐sectional study aimed to identify symptom profiles and their associated factors in Chinese patients with multiple myeloma, thereby providing an evidence‐based foundation for developing targeted symptom management strategies. Methods Patients with multiple myeloma were recruited via convenience sampling from the hematology departments of three tertiary general hospitals in Zhejiang Province, China, between January and March 2024. Data collection utilized a sociodemographic and clinical characteristics questionnaire and the Chinese version of the M.D. Anderson Symptom Inventory‐Multiple Myeloma Module (MDASI‐MM) scale. The research conducted a latent profile analysis of symptom characteristics, followed by univariate analysis and multivariable multinomial logistic regression to examine factors associated with profile membership. Results The study included 265 Chinese patients with multiple myeloma. Latent profile analysis identified three distinct symptom profiles: “Low Symptom Burden with Walking Distress” (46.7%), “Moderate Physical Symptoms with Daily Life Interference” (37.9%), and “High Global Symptom Burden” (15.4%). Multinomial logistic regression analysis demonstrated that age, marital status, combination chemotherapy status, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status were significantly associated with symptom profile membership ( p < 0.05). Specifically, patients of advanced age and those with higher ECOG scores were more likely to belong to the higher burden profiles, while patients receiving combination chemotherapy and those who were unmarried/divorced/widowed were more likely to belong to the low‐burden profile. Conclusions Patients with multiple myeloma exhibit heterogeneous symptom experiences, classifiable into three latent profiles. Our findings suggest that age, marital status, combination chemotherapy, and ECOG performance status may help identify patients at risk for higher symptom burden. Future longitudinal research is needed to evaluate whether profile‐based interventions reduce symptom burden and improve quality of life.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72313.abstract: Skin cancer is the most common type of cancer worldwide, categorized into melanoma and non-melanoma types. While genetics play a crucial role in the development of skin cancer, recent developments in metabolomics have revealed that circulating metabolites influence genetic risk profiles. In this study, we utilized a bidirectional two-sample Mendelian Randomization (MR) approach, analyzing metabolite datasets from the Canadian Longitudinal Study of Aging (CLSA) and skin cancer datasets from the UK Biobank. Replication analyses were performed with the 10th round of the FinnGen project. Instrumental variables (IVs) were chosen according to established MR criteria and assessed through the Wald ratio, IVW, MR-Egger, and weighted median methods. Various sensitivity analyses were conducted utilizing Cochrane's Q, Egger's intercept, MR-PRESSO, and leave-one-out (LOO) techniques. After meticulous analysis, we identified causal relationships between circulating metabolites and skin cancer risks. Specifically, levels of 1,2-dilinoleoyl-GPE (18:2/18:2), 1-palmitoyl-2-linoleoyl-gpc (16:0/18:2), 1-stearoyl-2-arachidonoyl-gpc (18:0/20:4), 1-stearoyl-2-linoleoyl-gpc (18:0/18:2), and Docosapentaenoate n3 DPA, the ratio of Arachidonate (20:4n6) to oleate to vaccenate (18:1), and Oleoyl-linoleoyl-glycerol (18:1 to 18:2) to linoleoyl-arachidonoyl-glycerol (18:2 to 20:4) were linked to non-melanoma skin cancer, whereas levels of trans-urocanate were causally linked to melanoma of skin, and S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) showed a putative association. It should be noted that docosapentaenoate n3 DPA and SAH were each supported by a single SNP and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive causal evidence. Reverse MR analysis highlighted robust causal relationships with 18 and 10 metabolites and non-melanoma skin cancer and melanoma of skin, respectively. These findings enhance our understanding of skin cancer etiology and risk factors, providing genetic evidence for hypothesis-generating associations that support the development of targeted therapies and aid in the identification of potential biomarkers.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72317.abstract: ABSTRACT The diagnostic landscape for the Philadelphia‐negative myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), particularly in distinguishing Essential Thrombocythemia (ET) from Polycythemia Vera (PV), is compromised. The gold standard for diagnosing PV—measurement of red cell mass (RCM) by radioisotope dilution—has been largely abandoned, leading to widespread misclassification. Thus, an estimated 30%–50% (varying by diagnostic center and testing practice) of JAK2V617F ‐positive ET patients may, in fact, have “hidden” PV, depriving them of the cornerstone PV therapy: phlebotomy. This diagnostic inaccuracy exposes a sizable patient population to an unfortunate high risk of life‐threatening thrombotic events. Concurrently, the management of established PV is suboptimal, often relying solely on hematocrit, a flawed parameter especially in iron‐deficient or hydroxyurea‐treated patients. This perspective calls for the revival and clinical implementation of the Carbon Monoxide (CO)‐rebreathing technique as a promising, rapid, and nonradioactive alternative for RCM assessment. Herein, we review the history of this methodology and discuss its potential to improve MPN care by ensuring precise diagnosis, guiding rational phlebotomy, and ultimately reducing thrombotic morbidity and mortality, while also candidly addressing the current evidentiary and practical limitations that must be resolved before clinical adoption, while also offering potential health‐economic benefits.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72320.abstract: Observational studies report an overall-survival advantage for postoperative radioactive iodine (RAI) in lymph node-positive papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), but such estimates are vulnerable to confounding by indication and to bias from immortal time and the healthy-user effect. We assessed the credibility of this apparent benefit rather than RAI efficacy itself. Using SEER (2010-2015), we assembled a cohort of N1b, M0, totally thyroidectomized PTC patients and applied a 3-month landmark analysis (sensitivity analyses at 1 and 6 months) with stabilized inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting. We estimated RAI effects on overall survival, cancer-specific survival, and relative survival, and on a negative-control outcome-non-thyroid-cancer death-that RAI cannot plausibly affect. Residual confounding was quantified with E-values. Among 4275 patients, RAI showed an apparent survival benefit in direction across all three endpoints. However, the negative-control outcome likewise showed an apparent benefit (IPTW hazard ratio 0.713, 95% CI 0.562-0.906), indicating residual confounding not removed by weighting. The apparent survival benefits therefore could not be distinguished from unmeasured confounding. In registry data lacking key confounders, a negative control identifies the apparent RAI survival benefit as a candidate artifact of unmeasured confounding. The findings neither support nor refute RAI efficacy.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72322.abstract: Cancer cells within a single pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are most often heterogeneous in their expression of the basal or classical transcriptional program. Predominance of the basal subtype has been associated with poorer patient outcomes and increased resistance to chemotherapy. Based on this, we predicted that basal subtype would be enriched in tumors previously treated with chemotherapy, and in metastases derived from primary PDAC tumors with a mixed basal/classical population. To create matched classical and basal cell lines, we stably transduced two classical PDAC cell lines (AsPC1 and HPAFII) with the basal program transcriptional driver ∆Np63α or an mCherry control and assessed their growth, metastasis, and response to chemotherapy both in vitro and in vivo. Forced expression of ∆Np63α successfully converted both cell lines to basal transcriptomic subtype, yet the basal program failed to drive increased cell growth or chemoresistance in culture and did not affect tumor growth of AsPC1 in the murine pancreas. In mice orthotopically engrafted with ∆Np63α-expressing cells, no statistically significant increase in spontaneous pulmonary metastases was observed for AsPC1 or HPAFII, however, pulmonary metastases were enriched for ∆Np63 expression as compared to established primary tumors, including expression of endogenous ∆Np63 in the mCherry control. Increased resistance to irinotecan chemotherapy was observed in ∆Np63α + HPAFII, yet treatment selected for ∆Np63-negative cells in both HPAFII and ASPC1. In summary, our data show that PDAC metastases are enriched for basal subtype, but chemotherapy treatment does not preferentially select for basal-type cells.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72324.abstract: ABSTRACT Background With this study, we aimed to investigate the longitudinal relationships between lifestyle behaviors and physical health in childhood, adolescent, or young adult (CAYA) cancer survivors attending the Long‐Term Survivor's Clinic (LTSC) in Calgary, Canada. Methods Survivors attended the LTSC once or twice a year and completed a questionnaire at each visit. Among survivors of any cancer diagnosis who were aged ≥ 11 years at the time of assessment, physical health was captured using two outcomes: the number of self‐reported physical health problems and the number of physical health‐related medications used. Self‐reported lifestyle behaviors, including physical activity, alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis use, and sleep quality were scored as healthy (1) or unhealthy (0), and combined into a sum score ranging from 0 to 5. Multivariable, generalized linear mixed models (GLMM) were estimated to assess the association between lifestyle behaviors (sum score and individual behaviors) and physical health outcomes, irrespective of time. To address our second research question, cross‐lagged GLMMs, incorporating a time component, were estimated to assess directionality between lifestyle sum score and the number of physical health problems. Results In total, 766 responses from 312 CAYA cancer survivors (median age at follow‐up 23.8 years; 49% male; 37% diagnosed with leukemia) were included. A healthier lifestyle sum score and sufficient physical activity were associated with fewer physical health problems (estimate −0.15, SE 0.06, p ‐value 0.02 and estimate −0.23, SE 0.11, p ‐value 0.04, respectively). No significant associations were found between lifestyle and the number of medications used. Lifestyle behaviors at an earlier time did not predict better physical health at a later time and vice versa. Conclusions Findings confirm an association between a healthy lifestyle and fewer physical health problems. Additional studies are warranted to further elucidate directional pathways between a survivor's lifestyle and physical health.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72331.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Estrogen receptor (ER)‐positive/HER2‐positive breast cancer demonstrates significantly lower rates of pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant HER2‐targeted therapies compared to ER‐negative/HER2‐positive disease. However, the optimal ER positivity cutoff for clinically meaningful patient stratification remains undefined. Methods We analyzed a retrospective cohort of 741 HER2‐positive breast cancer patients treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy plus dual HER2 blockade (trastuzumab and pertuzumab) at Sun Yat‐sen University Cancer Center. The optimal ER cutoff for predicting pCR was determined by ROC analysis with Youden index and validated by bootstrap resampling (1000 iterations). Transcriptomic data from TCGA and SCAN‐B cohorts were analyzed to characterize biological differences between ER subgroups. Drug response was predicted using the oncoPredict algorithm, and cancer dependency was assessed using DepMap CRISPR screening data. Results ER ≥ 50% positivity was identified as the optimal predictive cutoff (bootstrap 95% CI: 25.0%–77.5%) and was an independent predictor of significantly lower pCR rates in multivariate analysis (OR = 0.27; 95% CI: 0.19–0.40; p < 0.001). Transcriptomic analysis revealed that ER ≥ 50% tumors are characterized by activated estrogen response signaling, downregulated cell cycle and immune pathways. Predicted resistance to trastuzumab, T‐DM1, and T‐DXd was consistently enriched in this subgroup, consistent with lower HER2 and CD16A expression observed in ER ≥ 50% tumors. CCND1, a canonical transcriptional target of ESR1, was significantly upregulated in ER ≥ 50% tumors across both cohorts, and ER + /HER2 + cell lines exhibited significantly higher CCND1 and CDK4 dependency scores in DepMap CRISPR screening ( p < 0.05), supporting activation of the ESR1‐CCND1‐CDK4/6 axis in this subgroup. Conclusions ER ≥ 50% positivity defines a clinically and biologically distinct HER2‐positive subgroup with poor response to standard neoadjuvant therapy and predicted resistance to ADCs, consistent with lower HER2 and CD16A expression in this subgroup. The convergent transcriptomic and functional evidence for ESR1‐CCND1 axis activation provides mechanistic support for combining CDK4/6 inhibitors with endocrine and anti‐HER2 therapies to improve outcomes in this resistant subgroup.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72334.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is among the leading causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Previous treatment regimens often have limited efficacy due to drug resistance and recurrence. Metabolic reprogramming participates in the initiation and progression of NSCLC, with prominent changes in lipid metabolism. Mutations in specific driver genes directly remodel lipid metabolic reprogramming in NSCLC by rewiring lipid synthesis, uptake, and catabolism, which confers cancer cells with enhanced proliferative and metastatic capacity. On this basis, targeted lipid metabolism reprogramming has become a promising new direction for the treatment of NSCLC. In this review, we examined the alterations in lipid metabolism in NSCLC, explored the mechanisms by which driver gene mutations change lipid metabolism in NSCLC, and provided possible therapeutic strategies targeting key lipid metabolism pathways at the current stage, aiming to offer a theoretical basis and prospects for the development of novel therapies targeting specific gene mutation subtypes of NSCLC.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72335.abstract: Immunotherapy has transformed the treatment landscape for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet resistance mediated by the tumor microenvironment (TME) limits its efficacy in most patients. This review aims to synthesize the current understanding of the TME as an integrated network driving immunotherapy resistance and to evaluate emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at overcoming it. We conducted a comprehensive narrative review of key literature in the field, sourced from PubMed and major conference proceedings. The focus was on mechanistic studies elucidating immunosuppressive cell circuits, metabolic reprogramming, epigenetic regulation, spatial heterogeneity, and microbiome interactions within the lung cancer TME. Preclinical and clinical evidence for TME-targeted combination therapies and biomarker development was also critically analyzed. The TME orchestrates resistance through highly interconnected axes: (1) cellular circuits including myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), regulatory T cells (Tregs), and M2-polarized tumor-associated macrophages (M2-TAMs), (2) metabolic barriers (lactate acidosis, nutrient depletion), (3) epigenetic reprogramming, and (4) systemic communication via exosomes and the microbiome. Spatial transcriptomics reveals that driver mutations (e.g., EGFR, KRAS) shape distinct immune-excluded architectures. To disrupt this network, rational combination strategies-such as immune checkpoint inhibitors with metabolic modulators (LDHAi), epigenetic drugs, targeted agents (METi), or microbiome interventions-show synergistic potential in early-phase trials. Furthermore, a tiered biomarker system integrating spatial, metabolic, and microbial features is proposed to guide patient stratification. Overcoming immunotherapy resistance requires a paradigm shift from single-target to network-targeted therapy. This review provides an integrated framework for understanding TME-mediated resistance and translates these insights into a roadmap for clinical translation. Future efforts must prioritize biomarker-validated, rationally designed combination therapies to improve outcomes for patients with resistant NSCLC.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72336.abstract: ABSTRACT Cyclin E1 (CCNE1), a pivotal member of the cyclin family, governs the G1/S phase transition of the cell cycle by binding to and activating cyclin‐dependent kinase 2 (CDK2), thereby initiating DNA replication and driving S‐phase entry. In a broad spectrum of human malignancies—including breast, ovarian, gastric, and non‐small cell lung cancers—amplification or overexpression of CCNE1 disrupts the orderly regulation of cell cycle progression, leading to uncontrolled proliferation, impaired DNA damage repair, and genomic instability. These oncogenic consequences are intimately associated with increased tumor aggressiveness, poor patient prognosis, and diminished therapeutic efficacy. This review provides an integrated examination of CCNE1 biology, spanning its physiological regulation in the cell cycle, the molecular mechanisms by which its dysregulation drives tumorigenesis and drug resistance, the clinical implications of CCNE1 amplification as both a prognostic biomarker and a predictor of therapeutic response, and the emerging strategies to target CCNE1‐driven vulnerabilities. By synthesizing findings across diverse cancer types and regulatory layers, we evaluate the translational potential of CCNE1 as a diagnostic marker and therapeutic target, and highlight key challenges and opportunities for future investigation.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72337.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Immune‐related adverse events (irAEs) are complications associated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Hematologic irAEs (heme‐irAEs) are rare but potentially serious and may interfere with cancer treatment. However, their clinical characteristics remain insufficiently described. Methods We conducted a single‐center retrospective study using the National Cancer Center Hospital East medical database from April 1, 2014, to March 31, 2024. Potential heme‐irAE cases were identified using diagnostic name searches, bone marrow examination records, and positive DAT results and were followed by chart review to exclude alternative etiologies, such as chemotherapy‐related myelosuppression, marrow involvement, infection, and hematologic malignancy. Results Of the 3371 patients treated with ICI‐containing regimens, 40 patients developed heme‐irAEs, indicating an observed incidence of 1.2%. The most common heme‐irAE reported was immune thrombocytopenia, and 85.0% of these events were Grade 3 or higher. The median time from ICI initiation to heme‐irAE onset was 12 weeks. For all affected patients included in the regimen‐specific onset‐time comparison, the median time to heme‐irAE onset appeared shorter with dual ICI therapy without chemotherapy than with ICI monotherapy, although this descriptive comparison was based on a small number of cases. ICI‐containing regimens were interrupted or discontinued in most patients, and systemic corticosteroids were administered to 25 patients, 18 of whom achieved hematologic improvement. Cancer treatment was resumed or continued for 20 patients, with no recurrent heme‐irAEs observed during the follow‐up period. In an exploratory landmark analysis, hematologic response was associated with longer survival after heme‐irAE onset. Conclusion Heme‐irAEs were rare but frequently severe in this Japanese single‐center cohort. Their occurrence was associated with prolonged interruption of cancer treatment, underscoring the importance of early recognition, careful diagnostic evaluation, and multidisciplinary management of heme‐irAEs. Our findings regarding dual ICI therapy, survival, and subsequent ICI therapy after heme‐irAE onset should be interpreted as exploratory.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72339.abstract: ABSTRACT Bone marrow fibrosis (MF) reflects stromal remodeling and has been associated with treatment resistance and adverse outcomes in hematologic malignancies; however, its clinical significance in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) remains uncertain. We retrospectively analyzed 103 patients with newly diagnosed ALL and documented MF grades between 2018 and 2023, comparing patients with MF grades 0–1 and those with MF grades 2–3. Higher‐grade MF was present in 50 patients (48.5%). B‐ALL accounted for a greater proportion of cases in the MF 2–3 group than in the MF 0–1 group (94.0% vs. 69.8%; nominal p = 0.002), and this difference remained statistically significant after false discovery rate correction. No mutation‐level difference between the MF groups remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. In Cox regression, MF 2–3 was associated with a lower observed hazard of death compared with MF 0–1 (adjusted HR, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.12–0.55; p < 0.001). A similar association was observed in a sensitivity analysis restricted to patients with B‐ALL (adjusted HR, 0.30; 95% CI, 0.13–0.70; p = 0.005). Given the retrospective design, limited number of deaths, and potential residual confounding, this unexpected inverse association should be considered exploratory and should not be interpreted as evidence of a biologically protective effect of MF. In conclusion, higher‐grade MF was common in newly diagnosed ALL and was associated with B‐lineage disease. An unexpected inverse association between MF grade and observed mortality was identified in this cohort and persisted in the B‐ALL‐restricted sensitivity analysis. External validation is required before MF can be considered for prognostic stratification or treatment decision‐making.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72342.abstract: Existing deep learning models for predicting biochemical recurrence (BCR) after radical prostatectomy often ignore the biological context beyond the tumor. This study aims to develop and validate a transformer-based model combining multi-regional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features and clinical data to improve BCR prediction after radical prostatectomy in prostate cancer (PCa). We enrolled 232 Pca patients from three medical centers between 2013 and 2020. Multi-parametric MRI sequences, including T2-weighted fat-suppressed and diffusion-weighted imaging, were collected before surgery. Patients from centers 1 and 2 were assigned to a discovery cohort (training: n = 146; internal validation: n = 36), and patients from center 3 (n = 50) formed an external test cohort. A transformer-based deep learning (DL) model was developed using imaging features from intratumoral, peritumoral, and periprostatic regions, combined with clinical variables. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and prognostic value was assessed via Kaplan-Meier (K-M) survival analysis. The combined three-region MRI-based model demonstrated superior predictive performance for BCR risk across all sets, with an AUC of 0.801 (0.663-0.920) on the external test set and an AUC of 0.799 (0.715-0.872) on the validation set. Notably, the integrated DL model, which combined MRI data with clinical characteristics, outperformed the MRI-based and clinical models. The three-region with clinical combined model improved AUCs from 0.801 (95% CI: 0.663-0.920) to 0.863 (95% CI: 0.697-0.975) on the external test set and from 0.799 (95% CI: 0.715-0.872) to 0.832 (95% CI: 0.746-0.904) on the validation set. K-M curve analysis revealed that the integrated model provided significantly better predictions than the MRI-based and clinical models (p < 0.0001). By combining intratumoral, peritumoral, and periprostatic regions from multi-parametric MRI with clinical data, the transformer-based DL model provides a multimodal approach for predicting BCR in PCa patients.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72343.abstract: ABSTRACT Purpose To examine associations of body mass index (BMI) with sociodemographic, clinical, treatment‐related, psychosocial, and patient‐reported outcomes among women with non‐metastatic estrogen receptor‐positive (ER+) breast cancer receiving adjuvant endocrine therapy. Methods This multicenter cross‐sectional study included 557 women treated at 11 Brazilian public and private institutions from June 2021 to March 2024. Participants were classified as having normal weight, overweight, or obesity. Health‐related quality of life was assessed using the EORTC QLQ‐C30 and QLQ‐BR23. Characteristics were compared across BMI categories using chi‐square or Fisher's exact test and Kruskal–Wallis test. Multinomial logistic regression examined factors associated with BMI category, using normal weight as the reference. Results Of 557 participants, 172 had normal weight, 234 were overweight, and 151 had obesity. Education, comorbidities, hospital type, cancer stage, endocrine therapy, axillary dissection, prior chemotherapy, and radiotherapy differed across BMI categories. Participants with obesity had poorer physical functioning and greater pain. In the final model ( n = 554), axillary dissection (OR = 2.51; 95% CI = 1.37–4.59) and continuous medication use (OR = 2.92; 95% CI = 1.78–4.79) were associated with obesity versus normal weight. Tamoxifen was inversely associated with overweight (OR = 0.58; 95% CI = 0.36–0.91), whereas low treatment adherence (OR = 1.54; 95% CI = 1.01–2.35) and continuous medication use (OR = 1.68; 95% CI = 1.10–2.58) were positively associated. Conclusion Overweight and obesity were common and associated with sociodemographic, clinical, treatment‐related, and selected quality‐of‐life characteristics. These findings support integrated survivorship care addressing weight‐related health, comorbidities, functional limitations, and symptom burden. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal relationships.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72346.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Gastric cancer (GC) has posed a severe threat to human health. Metabolomics analysis has been applied in the context of multiple diseases, offering new perspectives for the development of non‐invasive detections. Objective We aimed to develop a diagnostic model for GC based on a serum bile acid (BA) panel. Methods A total of 632 participants were recruited for serum samples collection, and their clinical characteristics were recorded. Targeted BA profiling was conducted using ultra‐performance liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (UPLC–MS). Participants from Xi'an were randomly allocated into a training cohort and an internal tuning cohort at a 7:3 ratio. The key BAs were identified through the two‐step selection method, and nine machine learning (ML) models were constructed and optimized. The optimal model was further evaluated externally using an independent validation cohort from Lanzhou. Results A panel of 10 serum BAs was confirmed for the construction of a diagnostic model. The XGBoost model exhibited the best performance on the tuning cohort, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.858. It also exhibited robust performance on the external validation cohort (AUROC = 0.816), significantly outperforming tumor markers (with the highest AUROC of CA72‐4 = 0.68). The developed model also demonstrated satisfactory predictive performance for patients with resectable stage GC (Stage I–II) (average precision [AP] = 0.75). Conclusion GC patients exhibit BA metabolic disorders. The XGBoost model based on a 10‐BA panel exhibited superior efficacy in GC detection, indicating its promising potential for clinical application.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72348.abstract: Colorectal cancer remains a major global health burden, and although population-based screening is beneficial, current programs have notable limitations. Risk-stratified screening has been proposed, yet existing prediction models vary in performance and in the inclusion of predictors. Data-adaptive modeling (machine learning) may strengthen risk prediction but depends on high-quality input data. Expert consensus methods offer a structured way to identify clinically meaningful variables for future tools. To establish expert consensus on the selection of relevant variables and refinement of self-reported questionnaire items for next-generation colorectal cancer risk-prediction tools. A modified Delphi study was conducted with seventeen internationally recognized experts. The process consisted of anonymized, email-based rounds aimed at refining a questionnaire for colorectal cancer risk prediction. Across three iterative rounds, experts rated item relevance, proposed revisions, and identified missing domains while reviewing group-level summaries of ratings and comments. Items not meeting predefined thresholds were removed, and validated lifestyle-related items were incorporated. Consensus was defined as 15 of 17 experts rating an item within a similar three-point range. All seventeen experts completed all rounds. The final I-CRC-RISK Questionnaire comprises 23 items across seven categories: Demography, Health Status, Family Health History, Dietary Patterns, Physical Activity, Smoking, and Alcohol Consumption. Expert consensus was reached for 19 items. The I-CRC-RISK Questionnaire provides an expert-informed set of self-reported variables to support future risk prediction efforts. It offers a structured basis for further validation and psychometric testing before prospective data collection may be undertaken. This foundational work could enhance the predictive performance of both traditional and machine-learning approaches by improving the consistency and relevance of input data.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72350.abstract: ABSTRACT Neoadjuvant therapy has become an integral component of the multidisciplinary management of resectable non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The introduction of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has transformed the perioperative treatment landscape by improving pathological response rates, reducing the risk of recurrence, and offering the potential for durable survival benefits. In recent years, multiple neoadjuvant strategies, including ICI monotherapy, chemoimmunotherapy, dual immune checkpoint blockade, and combinations with radiotherapy, anti‐angiogenic agents, or targeted therapies, have been actively investigated to further optimize treatment efficacy. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are reshaping neoadjuvant strategies for resectable NSCLC. LCMC3 confirmed the feasibility of ICIs monotherapy, while CheckMate 816 and NADIM demonstrated that ICI–chemotherapy combinations markedly improve major pathological response and survival outcomes. Emerging perioperative studies, including CheckMate 77 T and AEGEAN, further support the integration of immunotherapy into standard treatment paradigms. Radiotherapy enhances tumor immunogenicity and shows synergy with ICIs, as highlighted in PACIFIC and KEYNOTE‐799. Although clinical evidence for ICI–anti‐angiogenic combinations remains preliminary, their mechanistic rationale is strong. In EGFR‐ or ALK‐altered NSCLC, emerging data suggest that neoadjuvant targeted therapy and carefully selected immunotherapy‐based strategies may further improve disease control while delaying recurrence. Despite these advances, several challenges remain, including the paucity of long‐term survival data, discordance between pathological responses and clinical benefit, treatment‐related toxicities, optimal treatment sequencing, biomarker‐guided patient selection, and mechanisms of primary or acquired resistance. Advances in predictive modeling based on PD‐L1 expression, tumor mutational burden (TMB), radiomics, nomograms, circulating tumor DNA, and multi‐omics biomarkers, together with a deeper understanding of metabolic–immune crosstalk, are expected to facilitate precision perioperative immunotherapy. This review comprehensively summarizes current evidence regarding neoadjuvant immunotherapy strategies for resectable NSCLC, highlights pivotal clinical trial findings, discusses emerging combination approaches and predictive biomarkers, and outlines future research directions aimed at improving personalized treatment and long‐term patient outcomes.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72351.abstract: ABSTRACT Objective To explore the perioperative changes in inflammatory–immune–nutritional indicators in patients with advanced gallbladder cancer (GBC), defined as American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) Stage III–IV, and to assess whether individual indicators provide incremental prognostic information beyond conventional clinicopathological factors. Methods Patients with pathologically confirmed advanced GBC who underwent surgery at the Department of Hepatobiliary Surgery, National Cancer Center/National Clinical Research Center for Cancer/Cancer Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College, between 2010 and 2022 were retrospectively enrolled. Preoperative and postoperative Day 7 values of the albumin‐to‐alkaline phosphatase ratio (AAPR), albumin‐to‐globulin ratio (AGR), albumin–bilirubin score (ALBI), advanced lung cancer inflammation index (ALI), monocyte‐to‐lymphocyte ratio (MLR), neutrophil‐to‐lymphocyte ratio (NLR), prognostic nutritional index (PNI), and systemic inflammation response index (SIRI) were calculated. Perioperative dynamic changes were compared, and Cox proportional hazards models were constructed to evaluate the incremental prognostic value of these indicators. Results Among 103 patients with advanced GBC, all eight inflammatory–immune–nutritional indicators showed significant changes between the preoperative period and postoperative Day 7. Several preoperative and postoperative indicators were associated with cancer‐specific survival (CSS) in cutoff‐based exploratory analyses. After the incorporation of these indicators into clinicopathological models, most extended models showed varying degrees of improvement in discrimination and goodness of fit. Conclusion In this single‐center cohort, perioperative inflammatory–immune–nutritional indicators exhibit significant dynamic changes in advanced GBC and can improve, to a certain extent, the prognostic performance of models based on conventional clinicopathological characteristics. These indicators may serve as useful supplementary tools for risk stratification and individualized prognostic assessment in patients with advanced GBC.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72352.abstract: Cysteine-rich angiogenic inducer 61 (CYR61), a matricellular protein, has been implicated in gastric cancer aggressiveness through activation of integrin-mediated NF-κB signaling; however, effective pharmacological strategies targeting this axis remain limited. Cyclopiane, a bioactive small-molecule compound, has shown potential anti-tumor activity, but its role and underlying mechanisms in gastric cancer have not been fully elucidated. This study aimed to investigate whether Cyclopiane suppresses gastric cancer invasion and angiogenesis via modulation of the CYR61/αvβ3 integrin/NF-κB signaling pathway. Human gastric cancer cell lines AGS and MKN45 were treated with increasing concentrations of Cyclopiane. Cell viability was assessed using MTT assays, while invasive capacity was evaluated using Matrigel-coated Transwell assays. TUNEL staining was used to assess changes in apoptosis in tumor cells. The expression of invasion-, angiogenesis-, and inflammation-related proteins was analyzed by Western blot (WB) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Transcriptomic profiling of AGS cells treated with Cyclopiane versus vehicle control was performed to identify differentially expressed genes and enriched signaling pathways. CYR61 overexpression was achieved via adeno-associated virus (AAV-CYR61), with its pathway involvement further validated using integrin αvβ3 antagonists. The conventional anticancer drug 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) was employed to compare Cyclopiane's therapeutic effects. In vivo experiments utilized a nude mouse xenograft model to evaluate changes in tumor growth, angiogenesis, and inflammatory responses following Cyclopiane treatment. We found that Cyclopiane significantly reduced cell viability, invasive capacity of AGS and MKN45 cells and promoted apoptosis in a dose-dependent manner, with its high-dose effects comparable to those of 5-FU. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that Cyclopiane downregulated CCN1/CYR61, ITGAV and ITGB3 expression, with pathway enrichment identifying integrin signaling, ECM-receptor interaction, focal adhesion and NF-κB pathways as the top modulated terms. In vivo experiments demonstrated that Cyclopiane significantly inhibited tumor growth and progression. Both in vivo and in vitro studies showed Cyclopiane significantly downregulated vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2), and MMP-9 expression while inhibiting integrin αvβ3 expression and NF-κB activation, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylation levels of p65 and IκBα. Overexpression of CYR61 partially reversed the inhibition of invasion, angiogenic factor production, and NF-κB signaling mediated by Cyclopiane. The αvβ3/αvβ5 integrin antagonist Cilengitide also exhibited tumor-suppressive effects, and the co-treatment of Cyclopiane with Cilengitide achieved the strongest tumor-suppressive effect. These findings suggest that modulation of the CYR61/integrin/NF-κB signaling axis contributes, at least in part, to the anti-invasive and anti-angiogenic effects of Cyclopiane in preclinical gastric cancer models. Further studies are required to establish its molecular target specificity, safety, selectivity, and translational potential.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72355.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Advances in molecular and cell biology have led to a paradigm shift in cancer management. We implemented next‐generation sequencing (NGS) at our community‐based academic cancer center over a decade ago. We sought to optimize the use of genomics and understand its impact in identifying actionable genomic alterations to determine therapy options in patients with advanced solid tumors for whom standard therapies had been exhausted. Methods Through a prospective non‐randomized trial, patients with advanced solid tumors who had exhausted standard therapies and who did not qualify for routine guideline‐concordant NGS at the time of the study (the study excluded at least Stage 1B lung and Stage IV colorectal cancers) underwent in‐house NGS on tumor specimens to identify actionable alterations, and pharmacogenomic testing. Our in‐house‐developed/integrated bioinformatics pipeline (Flype) was used for structured reporting and served as a molecular knowledgebase. Patients were presented at a multidisciplinary molecular tumor board. Results 251 patients underwent somatic tissue NGS. 173 patients (68.9%) had alterations targetable with FDA‐approved or currently investigational drugs. 75 patients (29.9%) had alteration(s) qualifying them for FDA‐approved drug(s) for their tumor type. An additional 61 patients (24.3%) had alterations qualifying them for “off‐label” use of FDA‐approved drugs. 40 patients (15.9%) qualified for tumor‐agnostic therapies. Of the 224 patients (89.2%) who had RNA analysis, eight (3.6%) had targetable fusions. Of the 33 patients (19.1%) who received NGS‐guided targeted therapies, 19 (57.6%) were on treatment for longer than three months. 255 patients underwent pharmacogenomics testing, with over 40% having an alteration in typical response to opioids or antidepressants. Conclusions In this real‐world study, 54.2% of patients with advanced solid tumors were identified as candidates for FDA‐approved therapies (on‐ or off‐label), supporting the utility of in‐house NGS in providing genomics‐guided care for patients.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72356.abstract: Patients with chemotherapy- and androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI)-naïve metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) have generally shown worse overall survival (OS) with abiraterone versus enzalutamide in claims database studies. Given limitations of claims data, analysis using detailed electronic health records (EHRs) is needed to confirm this finding. This EHR-based analysis (2014-2023) of the Flatiron Health database included patients with chemotherapy- and ARPI-naïve mCRPC who initiated first-line ARPI (abiraterone or enzalutamide). OS, treatment duration, and time to subsequent therapy were assessed. A subgroup analysis evaluated patients who received first-line ARPI only with no subsequent treatments. Kaplan-Meier method and Cox proportional hazards models evaluated time-to-event outcomes. Stabilized inverse probability treatment weighting (sIPTW) adjusted for baseline differences. Among 2731 patients, 1316 received first-line abiraterone and 1415 enzalutamide (median follow-up: 21.8 and 23.2 months, respectively). sIPTW-adjusted median OS (24.6 vs. 25.8 months; hazard ratio [HR] 1.13; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.03-1.23), treatment duration (7.9 vs. 9.5 months; HR 1.21; 95% CI, 1.11-1.31), and time to subsequent therapy (14.7 vs. 17.9 months; HR 1.20; 95% CI, 1.08-1.32) were shorter with abiraterone versus enzalutamide. Among the 40% with no subsequent treatment (n = 1102), sIPTW-adjusted median OS (14.0 vs. 17.7 months; HR 1.32; 95% CI, 1.14-1.53), and treatment duration (7.5 vs. 10.6 months; HR 1.30; 95% CI, 1.12-1.50) were also shorter with abiraterone versus enzalutamide. Using more detailed data abstraction, these results confirm prior claims-based analyses showing that despite early use of subsequent therapy, first-line abiraterone is associated with shorter OS versus enzalutamide in ARPI- and chemotherapy-naïve mCRPC. Clinical Trial ID: NCT05968599.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72357.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are increasingly used in patients with gastrointestinal cancer (GIC). However, ICI-associated adverse event (AE) profiles in GIC remain poorly characterized, and whether AE incidence is associated with clinical outcomes is unclear. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified through February 2025. Primary outcomes included treatment-related AEs (TRAEs) and immune-related AEs (irAEs) (any grade/Grade 3+). Single-arm random-effects meta-analysis pooled AE incidences; risk ratios (RRs) compared toxicity across ICI regimens. Digitized Kaplan-Meier curves reconstructed survival data for pooled analysis and Cox models. Weighted Spearman's tests assessed correlations between AE incidences and median overall survival (OS)/progression-free survival (PFS). Forty RCTs enrolling 10,233 patients investigated ICI monotherapy, dual-ICI therapy, and ICI combination regimens. Pooled any-grade TRAE incidences were 68.0% (monotherapy, 95% CI: 60%-76%, I2 = 97.4%, p < 0.001), 87.0% (dual therapy, 95% CI: 73%-100%, I2 = 98.0%, p < 0.001), and 90.0% (combination therapy, 95% CI: 83%-96%, I2 = 94.6%, p < 0.001). IrAE incidences reached 24.0% (monotherapy, 95% CI: 18%-29%, I2 = 67.2%, p < 0.05) and 37.0% (combination therapy, 95% CI: 25%-49%, I2 = 98.8%, p < 0.001). Relative to monotherapy, dual-ICI therapy elevated any-grade (RR = 1.28, 95% CI: 1.05-1.55) and grade ≥ 3 TRAEs (RR = 2.71, 95% CI: 1.84-3.99); ICI combination therapy increased any-grade (RR = 1.32, 95% CI: 1.15-1.51) and grade ≥ 3 TRAEs (RR = 2.98, 95% CI: 2.30-3.87). Any-grade TRAEs moderately correlated with median OS (R = 0.46, p < 0.001) and PFS (R = 0.50, p < 0.001). Any-grade irAEs strongly correlated with median OS (R = 0.90, p < 0.001) and moderately with PFS (R = 0.57, p < 0.001). While AE incidence is high among GIC patients receiving ICIs, most events are low-grade. Dual-ICI and ICI-based combination therapies carry higher TRAE and irAE risks than monotherapy. At the trial level, higher non-severe irAE incidence correlated with favorable survival outcomes; this exploratory ecological association does not apply to individual patients. This study was registered on International Platform of Registered Systematic Review and Meta-analysis Protocols (INPLASY202230144).

doi:10.1002/cam4.72360.abstract: The objective of this study was to verify that a strategy involving prophylactic exposure of the inferior parathyroid glands and preservation of their venous blood flow-achieved through early identification and protection of their venous drainage-can enhance the success rate of maintaining glandular perfusion and effectively reduce the incidence of postoperative hypoparathyroidism. This study included 600 patients who underwent total thyroidectomy with concomitant bilateral central neck dissection between November 2019 and December 2025. Patients were divided into two groups based on the surgical technique: Group A (n = 244), in which a prophylactic approach was used to protect the venous drainage of the inferior parathyroid glands, and Group B (n = 356), which underwent conventional in situ preservation of the inferior parathyroid glands. A comparison was made between the two groups regarding both the percentage of inferior parathyroid glands successfully preserved in situ and the incidence of postoperative hypoparathyroidism. The rate of visualization of inferior parathyroid glands with optimal blood supply was significantly higher in Group A than in Group B (p < 0.001). Postoperation parathyroid hormone level in Group A was significantly higher than that in Group B (25.15 [19.39, 33.58] pg/mL vs. 19.12 [9.82, 28.85] pg/mL, p < 0.001). In Group A, the rates of postoperative hypoparathyroidism-encompassing both transient and permanent forms-were significantly lower than those in Group B (p < 0.001). The method of prophylactically exposing the inferior parathyroid glands and preserving their venous system-termed prophylactic preservation of inferior parathyroid venous blood flow-is achieved through early identification and protection of their venous drainage. This approach enhances the success rate of maintaining glandular blood supply and effectively reduces the incidence of postoperative hypoparathyroidism.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72365.abstract: Systemic metastasis remains the leading cause of mortality in patients with advanced prostate cancer, particularly in castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), for which effective systemic therapeutic options are limited. Gene therapy is a potential strategy for achieving selective tumor targeting and systemic disease control in metastatic settings. This study aimed to establish a systemic metastasis animal model for CRPC and evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of JC polyomavirus (JCPyV) virus-like particle (VLPs)-based gene therapy against metastatic disease. A near-infrared fluorescent protein (iRFP)-expressing CRPC cell line was used to establish a systemic metastasis model by tail-vein injection in mice. The therapeutic efficacy of JCPyV VLPs carrying a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) promoter-driven suicide gene (PSAtk-VLPs), administered in combination with ganciclovir (GCV), was evaluated longitudinally by fluorescence molecular tomography (FMT), with enzalutamide/leuprorelin acetate (ENZ/LEU) included as a clinical treatment comparator. CRPC metastases in the lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, and bones were detected by FMT in real time. Control mice exhibited exponential CRPC growth, whereas ENZ/LEU treatment delayed CRPC progression. PSAtk-VLPs/GCV significantly inhibited the growth of metastatic CRPC. However, no significant differences in survival were observed among the MOCK, ENZ/LEU, and PSAtk-VLP/GCV groups (log-rank test, p = 0.7351). These findings support that JCPyV-derived virus-like particles constitute a promising therapeutic approach for metastatic CRPC, enabling systemic delivery of suicide gene therapy with selective inhibition of tumor growth and translational relevance.
