doi:10.1002/cam4.72366.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Platinum‐doublet concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) for locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC) is frequently complicated by severe neutropenia. This Phase II trial investigated whether combining active bone marrow‐sparing (ABMS) radiotherapy with prophylactic pegylated recombinant human granulocyte colony‐stimulating factor (PEG‐rhG‐CSF) could reduce the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia below a prespecified historical benchmark of 30%. Methods Patients with FIGO 2018 stage IIA2–IVA LACC received SPECT‐guided ABMS radiotherapy (45 Gy external beam plus 30 Gy brachytherapy) concurrent with paclitaxel/carboplatin every 21 days for 4 cycles followed by prophylactic PEG‐rhG‐CSF. Using Simon's two‐stage design ( α = 0.05, β = 0.20), we tested whether grade ≥ 3 neutropenia could be reduced from a historical benchmark of 30% to ≤ 15%. The primary endpoint was grade ≥ 3 neutropenia incidence; secondary endpoints included other cytopenias, treatment completion, and survival outcomes. Results Fifty‐four patients were enrolled. Grade ≥ 3 neutropenia occurred in 13.0% (7/54; 95% CI: 5.4%–24.9%), meeting the prespecified success criterion (one‐sided exact binomial test, p = 0.003 versus the 30% benchmark). Other grade ≥ 3 toxicities included leukopenia (18.5%), anemia (3.7%), thrombocytopenia (5.6%), and febrile neutropenia (1.9%). Overall, 85.2% of patients completed all 4 planned chemotherapy cycles, and all completed radiotherapy within 8 weeks (median overall treatment time: 50 days). At a median follow‐up of 40 months, the 3‐year progression‐free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) rates were 88.8% and 88.9%, respectively (6 events each); the study was not powered for survival efficacy. Conclusions The combination of ABMS radiotherapy and prophylactic PEG‐rhG‐CSF was associated with a grade ≥ 3 neutropenia rate of 13.0% and a chemotherapy completion rate of 85.2% during platinum‐doublet CCRT for LACC. Because the single‐arm design and reliance on historical controls preclude causal inference, these findings are hypothesis‐generating and primarily establish the operational feasibility of this dual hematoprotection approach. Formal evaluation of safety and efficacy requires the ongoing randomized trial (ChiCTR2400087321). Trial Registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2100046911. Registered May 30, 2021

doi:10.1002/cam4.72367.abstract: Young breast cancer (YBC), defined as diagnosis at or before the age of 40 years, is characterized by an aggressive phenotype and poor prognosis. The tumor microenvironment (TME), comprising immune and stromal cells, plays a critical role in tumor initiation and progression and is closely associated with clinical outcomes. However, alterations in cell states and the organization of multicellular ecosystems within the YBC microenvironment remain poorly understood. We analyzed 7379 bulk transcriptome samples and spatial transcriptomic data from eight samples using EcoTyper and complementary spatial analyses. The abundance of CD4+ T cells (S07), fibroblasts (S05), monocytes/macrophages (S09), and epithelial cells (S05) was significantly lower in young than in older patients with breast cancer. CD4+ T cells (S07), fibroblasts (S05), and monocytes/macrophages (S09) formed a spatially organized multicellular ecosystem with putative interactions involving CDH1-PTPRF/ERBB3. Lower ecosystem abundance was associated with poorer prognosis, including among patients who did not achieve a pathological complete response after neoadjuvant therapy. These findings identify a distinct multicellular ecosystem within the YBC microenvironment, providing insights into the microenvironmental features associated with disease progression.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72368.abstract: We previously developed multiple machine-learning and regression-based risk prediction models using retrospective electronic health records (EHR) to estimate near-term risk of pancreatic cancer (PC). This pilot study aimed to assess the feasibility of an early detection strategy combining initial EHR-based risk prediction with downstream imaging and blood-based testing. This prospective study included adults aged 50-84 years with an estimated ≥ 1% 18-month risk of PC, identified between January 2021 and March 2023 using four previously validated models. Patients with a history or active suspicion of PC were excluded. Participants completed cross-sectional imaging and CA19-9 Labs at baseline and again at 18 months. Outcomes included enrollment rates, test completion rate, and burden of incidental findings. Of 1251 eligible patients, 102 (8.2%) enrolled (median age 69 years [IQR 62-75]; 58% women; 48% Hispanic, 34% White, 11% Black, and 7% Asian). At baseline, 89 (87%) completed imaging and 98 (96%) completed CA19-9. At 18 months, 79% completed both imaging and CA19-9. Ten (10%) participants underwent additional clinical evaluations triggered by imaging findings. Evaluations included an endoscopic ultrasound, renal imaging, and FibroScan. CA19-9 results were normal in most participants, though 18% had elevated levels at baseline. Real-time EHR-based ML algorithms can be combined with blood- and imaging-based surveillance for early detection of PC with acceptable burden of incidental findings. However, improved patient engagement is a key aspect that will need to be addressed in order to successfully scale an AI-guided strategy for early detection.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72369.abstract: Spatial heterogeneity in the colorectal cancer (CRC) tumor microenvironment (TME) is closely related to stromal organization and may influence treatment-related features. In this study, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic data from CRC tissues to examine cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF)-dominant spatial domains. GPC1 and CHPF were enriched in stromal regions and showed higher expression in CRC tissues than in normal tissues. In the analyzed cohorts, higher GPC1 and CHPF expression was associated with advanced clinicopathological features and poorer survival outcomes in univariate analyses. Single-cell analyses showed that GPC1 and CHPF were mainly expressed in fibroblasts and were enriched in an ADAM12-associated fibroblast subset with myofibroblast-like features, extracellular matrix-related genes, and hypoxia/glycolysis-related signatures. Cell-cell communication analysis suggested that this fibroblast subset was linked to higher inferred WNT signaling. Drug-response and immunotherapy-related analyses further showed that GPC1 and CHPF expression was associated with transcriptomic patterns related to treatment response. In mucinous adenocarcinoma (MA), the ADAM12-associated fibroblast program showed stronger inferred MIF-related signaling and was associated with macrophage M2-like features. Spatial mapping and multiplex immunofluorescence supported partial colocalization of GPC1, CHPF, and ADAM12 in CAF-rich stromal regions. In CAFs, GPC1 or CHPF knockdown reduced ADAM12, CAF activation markers, and WNT/MIF-related proteins, while ADAM12 knockdown weakened macrophage M2-like marker expression in a co-culture model. These findings suggest that GPC1 and CHPF mark an ADAM12-associated CAF program linked to stromal remodeling and immune-related features in CRC, especially in MA, but further studies are needed to define its functional role.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72370.abstract: ABSTRACT Objective To examine how the age distribution of radical prostatectomy and radical cystectomy changed in Japan during the period in which robot‐assisted surgery spread. Methods We used the National Database Open Data for fiscal years 2014 to 2024 (Japanese fiscal year, April to March). Procedures were identified by procedure code and classified as robot‐assisted or conventional. Rates per 100,000 population were calculated, and the rate in each age group was expressed relative to that in patients aged 70 to 74 years. Cells with fewer than 10 claims are suppressed in the source tables; sensitivity analyses imputed 0, 5 or 9 procedures into these cells. Results Radical prostatectomy increased from 20,222 to 29,239 procedures and radical cystectomy from 3545 to 4793. Rates in patients younger than 75 years rose only about 1.2‐fold. For prostatectomy, the rate ratio in men aged 75 to 79 years rose from 0.40 to 0.93, while that in men aged 80 to 84 years reached only 0.22. For cystectomy, the ratio in patients aged 80 to 84 years rose from 0.74 to 0.95, while no clear increase was seen in patients aged 85 years or older (0.18 to 0.20, p = 0.791). In men aged 80 years or older, robot‐assisted prostatectomy increased from 94 to 1239 procedures, whereas conventional surgery changed from 64 to 97. These findings were unchanged when suppressed cells were imputed as 5 or 9. Conclusions Between fiscal years 2014 and 2024, the age distribution of radical prostatectomy and radical cystectomy in Japan shifted toward older patients. The increase was concentrated in men aged 75 to 84 years for prostatectomy and in patients aged 80 to 84 years for cystectomy, and was accounted for mainly by robot‐assisted procedures.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72371.abstract: Healthcare services and data ecosystems remain fragmented, inequitable and misaligned with patient, clinician and public health needs. Three pathways to patient-centred Artificial Intelligence (AI) have emerged to address this: data collaboration, Whole System Approaches and digital inclusion. Each has advanced the field. However, none delivers the continuous, participatory and outcome-grounded learning that equitable AI demands. The populations whose data drives AI learning must also be the populations who benefit from it. This principle has not been structurally embedded in any existing pathway. This narrative review defines a framework for operationalising Adaptive Machine Learning (AML) as a fourth, integrative pathway to patient-centred AI. AML is defined as continuous learning from real-world individual-level data to generate personalised, population-level insights returning direct benefit to the communities who produce them. A narrative review of PubMed and Google Scholar (2018-2025) was conducted across five thematic domains: AI and machine learning in healthcare; real-world data and evidence; patient-centred care and digital health; data governance and AI regulation; and adaptive clinical trial design. Search terms covered healthcare AI applications and adaptive, continuously learning systems, emphasising prediction-oriented rather than static diagnostic approaches. Eligibility was determined through iterative thematic analysis. Eight systemic barriers to patient-centred AI are identified and the three existing pathways critically examined for limitations in addressing bias, validation and equitable implementation. AML is proposed as the mechanism that closes this gap, connecting systems medicine, personalised medicine and precision medicine through continuous, outcome-based learning, identifying three original conceptual contributions as enablers: Integrative Data Governance (IDG), Adaptive Clinical Trial (ACT) designs and Evidence Sandbox Facilities (ESFs). Progress requires globally standardised Healthcare Data Recycling frameworks, adaptive evaluation methodologies and ESFs enabling multi-stakeholder validation. Future research should address federated AML validation, collective consent mechanisms and alignment of regulatory frameworks with international AI governance standards.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72373.abstract: ABSTRACT The malignant progression of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is closely associated with the acquisition of ferroptosis resistance by tumor cells; however, the upstream regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study aims to elucidate the function and molecular mechanisms of the methyltransferase‐like 7B (METTL7B)/pleckstrin homology domain‐containing family A member 4 (PLEKHA4)/aurora kinase A (AURKA) signaling axis in ferroptosis resistance in PTC. Our results showed that PLEKHA4 was highly expressed in PTC. By binding to kelch‐like protein 12 (KLHL12), PLEKHA4 inhibited KLHL12‐mediated ubiquitination and degradation of AURKA, thereby stabilizing the AURKA protein and enhancing ferroptosis resistance in PTC cells. Upstream, METTL7B stabilized PLEKHA4 mRNA and upregulated its expression through N6‐methyladenosine (m6A) modification. Both in vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that knockdown of METTL7B increased ferroptosis sensitivity and suppressed PTC progression. This study reveals a novel paradigm in which PLEKHA4, as an effector of m6A modification, regulates ferroptosis by interfering with ubiquitin‐mediated degradation, providing a theoretical basis for targeting this pathway in the treatment of PTC.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72376.abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) mortality disparities are partly driven by unequal access to care. Transportation barriers may limit access to definitive treatment. We studied how driving travel time affects receipt of definitive PCa treatment. We conducted a cohort study of men with non-metastatic PCa (2000-2015; follow-up through 2018) across the metropolitan area cancer registries of seven US states. Travel time was estimated using Google Maps isochrones representing driving time thresholds to reach the hospital appended to geomasked residential addresses. Outcomes were "no treatment," "radical surgery," or "radiotherapy". Covariate-adjusted multinomial logistic regression with interaction terms assessed modification by sociodemographic factors. The study included 132,939 men, of whom 37.0% received no treatment, 41.0% underwent surgery, and 22.0% received radiotherapy. Longer driving time (≥ 90 min vs. < 30 min) was associated with higher radical prostatectomy (aOR: 1.08, 95% CI: 1.03, 1.12), but lower radiotherapy (0.72, 95% CI: 0.69-0.76). Subgroup analyses revealed higher surgery associated with longer driving times among those in nSES Q1 (aOR: 1.33, 95% CI: 1.21-1.45) vs. Q5 (aOR: 0.94, 95% CI: 0.86-1.04), those in low (aOR: 1.16, 95% CI: 1.09-1.24) vs. high (aOR: 1.03, 95% CI: 0.98-1.09) population density areas, and those with regional (aOR: 1.30, 95% CI: 1.14-1.48) vs. localized (aOR: 1.05, 95% CI: 1.00-1.09) disease. Longer driving time was mostly associated with lower odds of radiotherapy across sociodemographic subgroups. Higher travel time was associated with lower radiotherapy receipt, but higher surgery use in deprived and rural patients, warranting further investigation.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72377.abstract: Electronic patient-reported outcome (ePRO) systems support symptom monitoring after chemotherapy; however, their integration into structured nurse-led oncology workflows remains limited. In this study, we aimed to develop and evaluate the short-term feasibility and usability of a nurse-led ePRO system for home-based postchemotherapy symptom monitoring and structured nursing triage for cancer patients. This single-arm feasibility study was conducted at a cancer center in Taiwan between April and September 2024 among adult patients requiring home-based symptom monitoring after hospital-based chemotherapy care. The nurse-led digital system was designed to support weekly self-reporting of 12 chemotherapy-related symptoms using the Chemotherapy Toxicity Self-Assessment Questionnaire. The system incorporated rule-based triage categorization using green, orange, and red risk levels and predefined nurse response protocols. Feasibility outcomes included report adherence, triage alert management, and system performance. Usability was evaluated using the System Usability Scale. Forty-two patients submitted 306 symptom reports during the 8-week monitoring period, corresponding to an overall adherence rate of 91.1%. Among all reports, 16.3% generated orange alerts requiring nurse follow-up and 6.5% generated red alerts requiring urgent review. Fatigue, pain, and hand-foot syndrome were the most frequently reported abnormal symptoms. All orange and red alerts had documented nursing review. The system met the predefined technical performance indicators during simulated load testing, and achieved a mean System Usability Scale score of 92.6 ± 6.46. This nurse-led ePRO system demonstrated favorable short-term feasibility and usability for home-based postchemotherapy symptom monitoring and structured nursing triage. These findings support the practicality of integrating structured ePRO monitoring into postchemotherapy nursing care. Further multicenter and comparative studies are warranted to evaluate long-term engagement, scalability, and clinical outcomes.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72378.abstract: This study investigated relationships between the skeletal muscle index (SMI) and the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), peripheral immune phenotypes, and serum biomarkers in advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and evaluated the prognostic significance of these parameters. A retrospective analysis of 119 advanced PDAC patients was performed. Sarcopenia was diagnosed using sex-specific SMI cut-offs from baseline L3-level computed tomography (CT) images. The TIME was characterized by multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF; n = 31), peripheral immunity by flow cytometry, and serum biomarkers by routine testing. Associations with SMI were examined using Spearman correlation; prognostic relevance was assessed using Cox proportional hazards models. Sarcopenia (56/119, 47.1%) was associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS) (8.83 vs. 12.03 months, p = 0.016) and overall survival (OS) (10.20 vs. 17.33 months, p = 0.014). SMI correlated most strongly with stromal CD8+ T cells (ρ = 0.52), stromal total T cells (ρ = 0.52), and stromal M2 macrophages (ρ = 0.50) in the TIME; with circulating Th2-like cells (ρ = -0.58) and CD4+ memory T cells (ρ = 0.45) peripherally; and with hemoglobin (ρ = 0.32) among serum markers. In multivariable Cox regression, stromal CD4+ Treg percentage independently predicted OS (hazard ratio [HR] = 7.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.60-36.22, p = 0.011), stromal CD56dim natural killer (NK)-cell density predicted PFS (HR = 1.015, 95% CI 1.001-1.028, p = 0.031), and the lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR) predicted both PFS (HR = 0.86, p = 0.023) and OS (HR = 0.83, p = 0.009). No peripheral lymphocyte subset reached prognostic significance. SMI is broadly associated with local and systemic immune phenotypes in advanced PDAC. Stromal CD4+ regulatory T cells (Tregs), CD56dim NK cells, and LMR carry independent prognostic information and may complement body-composition assessment.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72380.abstract: New-onset diabetes (NOD) potentially associated with pancreatic cancer (PC) requires further investigation to assess its potential as a tool for PC screening. In this longitudinal nationwide register study, which includes 14,712 PC patients and 18 years of follow-up time (2000-2018), we aimed to assess the prevalence of diabetes by using a large national registry. Survival was analyzed according to diabetes status and duration (long-term diabetes, i.e., DM diagnosed > 3 years prior to PC, NOD, i.e., DM diagnosed 0-3 years prior to PC, or DM diagnosed after PC diagnosis) and treatment status (curative intent vs. palliative) using multivariable Cox regression analysis. Overall, 18% of PC patients had diabetes. The median time interval between DM and PC diagnoses was 4.8 months. In the multivariable Cox regression analysis, only DM diagnosed after PC was associated with worse survival, both in the palliative intent treatment group (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.03-1.23, p = 0.011) and in the curative intent treatment group (HR 1.44, 95% CI 1.14-1.81, p = 0.002). Among patients diagnosed with diabetes prior to PC, neither long-term nor NOD significantly affected survival. Most of the diabetic PC-patients have been diagnosed with DM within a close proximity of cancer diagnosis. The progression from diabetes to clinically detectable cancer seems to be rapid-less than 6 months. Given the aggressive nature of PC and the fact that NOD can be an early sign, screening may need to begin at the time of diabetes diagnosis. The fact that a DM diagnosis made after a PC diagnosis is associated with worse survival may suggest that pancreatic tumors that cause hyperglycemia are particularly aggressive.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72382.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Rehabilitation is increasingly recognized as an essential component of oncology care, but there remains limited evidence regarding its broader impact on patient outcomes. This study examined the associations of inpatient cancer rehabilitation with survival and post–discharge healthcare utilization among patients with diverse cancer types. Methods We conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study using cancer registry–linked claims data from designated cancer care hospitals in Osaka Prefecture, Japan. The study cohort comprised adults newly diagnosed with cancer from 2020 to 2022. The exposure was receipt of inpatient cancer rehabilitation during the initial cancer treatment hospitalization. The primary outcome was all–cause mortality within 1 year of diagnosis, and the secondary outcomes were unplanned readmissions and out–of–hours outpatient visits within 28 days of discharge. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards and Fine–Gray subdistribution hazards models were used, adjusting for demographic and clinical factors. Results Among 123,955 patients from 69 hospitals, 20,561 (16.6%) underwent inpatient cancer rehabilitation. Rehabilitation was associated with a lower risk of mortality (hazard ratio, 0.83; 95% confidence interval, 0.79–0.87). Lower mortality risks were also observed for the following cancer types: lung, upper gastrointestinal, colorectal, hepato–biliary–pancreatic, breast, and hematologic cancers. Among 115,046 patients included in the post–discharge healthcare utilization analyses, rehabilitation was associated with lower risks of unplanned readmissions (subdistribution hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% confidence interval, 0.73–0.85) and out–of–hours visits (0.92; 0.84–0.999). Conclusions Inpatient cancer rehabilitation was associated with lower mortality and reduced post–discharge healthcare utilization. These findings support the further integration of rehabilitation into routine oncology practice.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72385.abstract: Household size and composition may be associated with health-related quality of life (HRQoL), yet these associations remain poorly characterized among cancer survivors. We examined how household adult composition and presence of children were associated with HRQoL among U.S. cancer survivors. Adult (aged ≥ 18 years) cancer survivors were included from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) 2017-2024. Household composition was defined by number of adults (1, 2, or ≥ 3) and presence of children (none vs. ≥ 1). Outcomes included poor physical health (PPH), poor mental health (PMH; each defined as ≥ 14 days/month), and fair/poor general health. Multivariable Poisson regression was used to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) with 95% confidence intervals. Among 138,360 cancer survivors, 45.2% (n = 62,605) resided in single-adult households, 47.1% (n = 65,132) in two-adult households, and 7.7% (n = 10,623) in households with ≥ 3 adults; children were present in 5.1% (n = 7063) of households. After adjustment, two-adult household residence was associated with lower prevalence of poor physical health (adjusted prevalence ratio [aPR] 0.93, 95% CI 0.87-0.99), poor mental health (aPR 0.90, 95% CI 0.82-0.98), and fair/poor general health (aPR 0.92, 95% CI 0.88-0.97; all p ≤ 0.019) compared with single-adult households. Residence with ≥ 3 adults and child presence was not associated with any examined HRQoL outcome after adjustment. Exploratory stratified analyses identified associations within several sociodemographic subgroups. Two-adult household residence was consistently associated with better HRQoL. Single-adult household status may represent a simple social risk marker to inform survivorship assessment.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72386.abstract: TP53 mutations are linked to poor prognoses in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL), indicating that specific p53 target genes may contribute to drug resistance. Although the impact of specific genetic alterations on drug sensitivity has been reported in BCP-ALL, the effects of TP53 mutations on sensitivity to individual agents remain poorly defined in the clinical setting because of the use of combination chemotherapy regimens. In the present study, we addressed this issue through two complementary analyses using a large panel of BCP-ALL cell lines. Initially, 30 cell lines harboring TP53 mutations demonstrated significantly greater resistance to daunorubicin (DNR), mafosfamide (MAF; an active analog of cyclophosphamide), 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), and prednisolone compared to 46 cell lines without mutations. Second, 11 CRISPR/Cas9-mediated TP53-knockout sublines derived from cell lines with wild-type TP53 recapitulated resistance to DNR, MAF, and 6-MP, as well as to vincristine (VCR) and cytarabine (Ara-C). Consistent with these findings, re-evaluation of genome-wide CRISPR screening datasets revealed significant enrichment of TP53 gRNAs in cells treated with DNR, MAF, 6-MP, Ara-C, and VCR. Furthermore, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of p53 target genes in the two cell line models, along with re-evaluation of genome-wide CRISPR screening datasets, identified BAX, BBC3, and FDXR as key p53 target genes associated with multidrug resistance. These results highlight the potential value of targeting these p53 downstream pathways to improve outcomes in TP53-mutated BCP-ALL cases.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72388.abstract: Radiotherapy efficacy is constrained by tumor radioresistance, which arises in part from the interplay between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and epigenetic regulation. This review systematically synthesizes the bidirectional "epigenetics-ROS interactive network" that governs tumor radiosensitivity. We propose that this network operates through three core principles: stress adaptation (acute ROS triggers transient epigenetic adjustments for redox recovery), malignant reinforcement (chronic ROS drives stable epigenetic reprogramming toward therapy resistance), and contextual determinacy (cellular outcomes depend on integrated ROS-epigenetic patterns rather than individual signals). Mechanistically, we delineate four regulatory layers including DNA methylation, histone modifications, non-coding RNAs, and chromatin remodeling, through which the epigenetic machinery controls ROS homeostasis, and conversely, how radiation-induced ROS reshape the epigenetic landscape via oxidative modification of epigenetic enzymes and signaling pathways. These bidirectional interactions form feedback circuits that ultimately dictate whether cells undergo repair, senescence, apoptosis, or ferroptosis. Based on this mechanism, we propose a context-dependent decision framework that matches four distinct combination strategies (ROS amplification, epigenetic priming, hypoxia relief, and multi-pathway cell death induction) with four tumor subtypes defined by their oxidative and epigenetic profiles. We also identify five translational roadblocks including toxicity, delivery inefficiency, manufacturing scalability, regulatory uncertainty, and preclinical-clinical discordance. Resolving these barriers is essential for unlocking the therapeutic potential of this regulatory axis. Strategically targeting the epigenetics-ROS network offers a transformative paradigm for overcoming radioresistance and personalizing cancer radiotherapy.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72389.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Patients undergoing treatment for cutaneous melanoma are generally considered cured after a period of 5 years, since most recurrences manifest within three to 5 years. However, some patients can present with a delayed recurrence of melanoma beyond a 10‐year timeframe. Objective To identify clinicopathologic factors associated with survival in patients with cutaneous melanoma who developed metastatic recurrence at least 5 years after primary diagnosis. Methods We conducted a retrospective single‐center cohort study of 30 patients with cutaneous melanoma developing metastatic recurrence at least 5 years post‐diagnosis. The cohort contained 18 women and 12 men (mean age 50.2; range 25–76). Variables included age, sex, BRAF status, site, melanoma subtype, Breslow thickness, ulceration, Clark level, regression, and recurrence localization. Overall survival (OS), progression‐free survival (PFS), and post‐recurrence survival (PRS) were evaluated via Cox proportional hazards models. Results Mean OS, PFS, and PRS were 168.7, 130.4, and 43.7 months, respectively. Eight patients (27%) died. Tumors averaged 2.61 mm Breslow thickness; 50.0% were BRAF‐mutant, 53.3% ulcerated, and 50.0% truncal. Recurrences were locoregional (cutaneous, subcutaneous, in‐transit, nodal) in eight (26.7%) and distant in 21 (70.0%); one lacked data. Female sex predicted better univariate OS (HR 0.055, 95% CI 0.01–0.47; p = 0.008) and multivariate PFS (HR 0.364, 95% CI 0.14–0.93; p = 0.035). Increasing age predicted shorter multivariate PFS (HR 1.072, 95% CI 1.03–1.12; p = 0.001). Histologic regression (HR 3.557, 95% CI 1.04–12.17; p = 0.043) and BRAF status (HR 0.413, 95% CI 0.18–0.94; p = 0.034) independently impacted PFS. Kaplan–Meier showed longer OS and PFS in women, and longer PFS in patients younger than 50 years. Conclusions Delayed recurrence can manifest over a decade post‐diagnosis. Female sex and younger age correlate with favorable survival. These findings underscore the necessity of continued clinical vigilance and patient counseling beyond 10 years, although larger cohorts are needed to validate late‐recurrence risk stratification.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72391.abstract: ABSTRACT Alterations in the composition of the gut microbiota have been associated with colorectal cancer (CRC), with growing evidence indicating that specific microbes can have an impact on the tumour microenvironment. In this study, we investigated the associations of an oral pathobiont consortium comprising P. stomatis , F. nucleatum sensu lato and P. micra with the tumour immune microenvironment and the clinical presentation of CRC patients. Bacterial levels were quantified in fresh frozen tumour tissues using qPCR and the tumour immune environment was analysed using multiplex immunohistochemistry and multispectral imaging, profiling cytotoxic T cells, T‐helper 1 cells, regulatory T cells, B cells, macrophages and regulatory immune checkpoint molecules (CTLA‐4, PD‐1 and PD‐L1). Tumours with polymicrobial intratumoural co‐occurrence were more frequently right‐sided and exhibited microsatellite instability compared with tumours containing low bacterial levels or high levels of F. nucleatum sensu lato alone. Furthermore, polymicrobial tumours exhibited an altered tumour immune microenvironment, with decreased infiltration of FOXP3 + T regulatory cells and CD68 + macrophages, and increased tumour cell expression of PD‐L1 in the tumour centre. Polymicrobial tumours were also associated with poorer patient survival. In conclusion, our findings suggest a link between the co‐occurrence of P. stomatis , F. nucleatum sensu lato and P. micra and an altered tumour immune microenvironment in CRC. Elucidating the relationship between bacterial species and immune marker expression may enable the development of improved prognostic and predictive biomarkers, as well as new possibilities for therapeutic intervention.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72393.abstract: The global burden of liver cancer has been increasing over recent decades, whereas the incidence in Switzerland has remained relatively stable. This study assessed long-term trends in incidence, mortality, and 1- and 5-year relative survival of primary liver cancer in the Swiss canton of Zurich from 1980 to 2022, stratified by sex and age. This population-based retrospective analysis included all primary liver cancer cases diagnosed in the canton of Zurich and registered in the Cancer Registry of the cantons of Zurich, Zug, Schaffhausen and Schwyz between 1980 and 2022. Mortality data were obtained from the Federal Statistical Office. Cases were classified according to ICD-O-3 topography and morphology and, from 2003 onward, TNM stage. Age-standardised incidence and mortality rates were calculated using the 1976 European standard population. Temporal trends were analysed using Joinpoint regression and reported as Average Annual Percentage Changes (AAPCs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Relative survival was estimated using the Ederer II method and standardised according to international standards. Among 3866 incident cases, 71.3% were hepatocellular carcinomas and 70.7% occurred in men. Overall age-standardised incidence remained stable in both men (AAPC -0.1%, 95% CI -0.6 to 0.3%) and women (-0.2%, -0.9% to 0.4%). However, incidence increased significantly among individuals younger than 65 years, particularly in women (AAPC 2.3%, 1.3%-3.3%) and men (1.2%, 0.6%-1.9%). Mortality remained broadly stable in men and increased modestly in women. One- and five-year relative survival improved substantially, from 13.8% and 3.5% in 1980-1999 to 53.9% and 25.8% in 2016-2022, respectively. Improvements were greater in men than women. These findings reflect major advances in liver cancer diagnosis and treatment over the past four decades. Continued prevention, targeted screening of high-risk groups, and epidemiological monitoring remain important.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72394.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Component C1q binding protein (C1QBP) is known as an important regulator of mitochondrial plasticity and is involved in antitumor immune response in cancers. Nevertheless, its role in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) still remains largely unknown. Methods C1QBP expression in LUAD and adjacent normal samples was compared by Wilcoxon test, and the corresponding receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was used to estimate its diagnostic value. Associations between C1QBP expression levels and different clinical traits were analyzed by chi‐square test; K‐M curves were applied for analyzing survival differences, and univariate and multivariate Cox analysis were employed to construct the C1QBP ‐related nomogram model. Furthermore, GSEA and immune analysis were performed to explore the mechanism. Finally, rhC1QBP was applied to cultured mast cells in vivo to investigate its regulatory effect on mast cell dysfunction, and sh‐C1QBP was injected into LUAD xenograft mice to explore the effect of C1QBP knockdown on tumor growth in vivo. Results The C1QBP expression level, with a preferable diagnosis effect, was significantly different between LUAD and normal samples, and was notably interrelated with gender, TNM stage, and Fustat in LUAD patients. LUAD patients with high C1QBP levels displayed lower survival rates. Our nomogram based on C1QBP expression and T stage displayed decent prediction capability. There was a significant difference in C1QBP expression in plasma cells, regulatory T cells (Tregs), activated CD4 memory T cells, resting mast cells, and eosinophils between LUAD patients and the controls. Upregulation of C1QBP with rhC1QBP treatment promoted mast cell ferroptosis through interacting with the Cullin3 protein. While Fer‐1, a ferroptosis inhibitor, counteracted rhC1QBP induced ferroptosis in mast cells. Knockdown of C1QBP inhibited tumor growth in xenograft mice. Conclusion C1QBP may be a promising potential prognostic biomarker in LUAD and a potential therapeutic target by affecting the immune microenvironment of LUAD patients.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72395.abstract: Relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (R/R B-ALL) patients exhibit heterogeneous responses to CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. However, current studies primarily focus on the CAR-T cells or the leukemia blasts, and the patient's intrinsic molecular characteristics before treatment remain poorly understood. Fifteen R/R B-ALL patients enrolled in a phase II, single-arm clinical trial (NCT04684147) were stratified at a three-month landmark into 8 good responders and 7 poor responders. Clinical characteristics, genetic alterations and pre-treatment bone marrow transcriptomics were compared between groups, and an exploratory gene-expression score was derived. Differential expression and enrichment analyses identified a myeloid-like signature and upregulation of myeloid-related genes in poor responders. Seven myeloid-related genes were examined in independent patient cohorts, in B-ALL cell lines and at single-cell resolution in one patient; three were expressed by the leukemic cells themselves and four predominantly by monocytes and macrophages. A separate, variance-derived seven-gene least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) score separated response groups in the discovery cohort (apparent area under the curve, AUC 1.00), with bias-corrected and external estimates of approximately 0.57-0.59 (external cohort AUC 0.592, 95% confidence interval 0.356-0.828). Pre-treatment transcriptomic profiling revealed a myeloid-like signature in R/R B-ALL patients with poor CD19 CAR-T response, warranting further investigation as a candidate correlate of treatment outcome.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72396.abstract: Rurality is one of many disparities leading to lower cancer screening rates, as well as higher cancer incidence and mortality. Our study was designed to evaluate rural-urban disparities in incidence and cancer-specific mortality for the leading cancers in the State of Michigan from January 1, 2017, through December 31, 2021. Data was obtained for the 10 leading cancers in both incidence and cancer-specific mortality from the Michigan Department of Health and Human Service. Rural-urban comparisons were made for incidence, incidence by SEER stage, and cancer-specific mortality and reported as rate ratios. Combining the 10 leading cancers in Michigan during our study period, the age-adjusted incidence rate was significantly lower (IRR 0.95, 95% CI 0.94-0.96, p < 0.001), whereas the age-adjusted cancer-specific mortality rate was significantly higher (MRR 1.05, 95% CI 1.03-1.07, p = 0.023) in our rural study population. Regarding cancers with proven screening benefits, age-adjusted incidence rates and cancer-specific mortality rates for female breast (IRR 0.87; 95% CI 0.85-0.89; p < 0.001 and MRR 0.87; 95% CI 0.81-0.98; p = 0.012) and prostate (IRR 0.86; 95% CI 0.83-0.88; p < 0.001 and MRR 0.92; 95% CI 0.86-0.98; p = 0.012) cancer were significantly lower in rural Michigan. Lung and bronchus cancer had significantly higher age-adjusted incidence rates and cancer-specific mortality rates in our rural study population (IRR 1.07; 95% CI 1.05-1.10; p < 0.001 and MRR 1.17; 95% CI 1.14-1.20; p < 0.001). Our rural Michigan population had significantly lower incidence rates for the 10 leading cancers in incidence, female breast cancer, and prostate cancer in our study period. However, rurality was associated with higher age-adjusted cancer-specific mortality for the 10 leading cancers regarding mortality and for lung and bronchus cancer. Continued focus on Michigan's existing public health programs may further bridge rural disparity gaps.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72400.abstract: Most patients with hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (HPSCC) achieve partial response (PR) after induction chemotherapy. However, optimal post-induction management remains controversial. We compared survival outcomes of post-induction strategies for PR-HPSCC, with emphasis on advanced post-induction tumor stage (ycT) using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW-ATO) to mitigate confounding by indication. This retrospective study included 149 patients with PR-HPSCC after induction chemotherapy who subsequently received surgery-based therapy (SBT; n = 71) or definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT; n = 78). IPTW-ATO was used to address covariate imbalances between groups. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were evaluated using weighted Kaplan-Meier analyses and IPTW-ATO-adjusted Cox proportional hazards models. Sensitivity analyses compared findings across unadjusted, multivariable, and propensity score-weighted models. In unadjusted analyses, OS and PFS did not differ significantly between groups. After IPTW-ATO adjustment, SBT was associated with improved OS and PFS versus CRT. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested a potential differential treatment effect across ycT strata; however, interaction tests were not statistically significant, and no significant survival difference was observed in patients with early ycT disease. In multivariable analyses, thyroid invasion was independently associated with worse OS, whereas anti-PD-1 therapy was associated with improved OS. Outcomes among patients with PR-HPSCC are heterogeneous. After adjustment for covariate imbalances, SBT was associated with favorable survival. These findings suggest that PR should not be treated as a uniform entity and that post-induction ycT classification may help stratify patients for future prospective evaluation.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72402.abstract: Tissue biomarkers may improve risk stratification in locally advanced cervical cancer before definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT). We evaluated pretreatment expression of chromobox 4 (CBX4), NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4), specificity protein 1 (SP1), and copper transporter 1 (CTR1) in relation to CCRT response and overall survival. In this retrospective 1:1 matched case-control study, pretreatment biopsies from 40 patients with locally advanced cervical squamous cell carcinoma (20 CCRT-resistant, 20 CCRT-sensitive) were quantified by AI-assisted digital pathology using H-scores. A parsimonious CBX4 + NOX4 logistic model was evaluated by apparent ROC, leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV), repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation, and bootstrap optimism correction. Overall survival analyses were exploratory. CBX4 and NOX4 expression was lower in CCRT-resistant tumors (median H-score: CBX4, 40.47 vs. 79.62; NOX4, 7.00 vs. 53.93; both p < 0.001), whereas SP1 and CTR1 did not differ. Apparent AUCs were 0.840 for CBX4 and 0.843 for NOX4. The two-marker model had an apparent AUC of 0.903, LOOCV AUC 0.845, repeated 5-fold CV AUC 0.854 ± 0.022, and bootstrap-corrected AUC 0.883. High CBX4 and NOX4 expression was associated with better 5-year overall survival; in joint Cox models, hazard ratios per 1-SD increase were 0.31 (95% CI 0.13-0.74) for CBX4 and 0.48 (0.26-0.90) for NOX4. No histochemically detectable copper deposits were observed. Lower pretreatment CBX4 and NOX4 expression was associated with a CCRT-resistant phenotype and poorer overall survival in this small, response-enriched cohort. Internal resampling suggested discrimination, but same-dataset marker selection may introduce residual optimism and does not establish generalizability. Independent validation in a consecutively recruited cohort is required before clinical application. No mechanisms involving DNA repair, ROS, or chemoradiotherapy sensitivity were established.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72403.abstract: The use of evidence in clinical practice is essential for the provision of best practice care in psychosocial oncology. However, research demonstrates gaps in the implementation of evidence-based interventions and important resource barriers for clinicians. Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) are designed to translate the latest evidence into recommendations applicable within various clinical domains. A recent study identified 23 English-language, up-to-date psychosocial oncology CPGs. The present study sought to systematically assess the quality of these tools. CPGs were independently evaluated by four trained appraisers using the AGREE II tool, consisting of 23 items across six domains. Quality was determined using aggregate and consensus domain scores (0%-100%), with an acceptability cut-off score of 60%. Findings revealed that 20 of the 23 CPGs (87%) met the acceptability threshold (M = 76.45, SD = 12.35). The highest average domain scores were observed for Clarity of Presentation (M = 96.26, SD = 6.25) and Scope and Purpose (M = 87.38, SD = 19.55) while Applicability received the lowest score (M = 33.83, SD = 10.72). Rigor of Development scores (M = 71.17, SD = 17.46) demonstrated substantial variations across CPGs. Findings indicate that psychosocial oncology CPGs are specific and clear but may benefit from more transparency in reporting procedures and greater consideration of applicability and implementation strategies. These findings may help illuminate guideline developers on gaps in current tools and serve to inform clinicians on the strengths and shortcomings of these tools prior to selecting which ones to integrate within their clinical practice.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72404.abstract: ABSTRACT Metastasis of malignant tumors arising from epithelial organs to sentinel lymph nodes has important implications for prognosis, staging, and therapeutic decision‐making. Recent insights into anatomic pathways, pathogenesis, molecular interactions, and genetic factors have encouraged scientists and clinicians to develop drugs that target mechanisms of lymph node metastasis. We summarize important aspects of the vast literature that pertains to these mechanisms, focusing on five phases that implicate invasion through the epithelial basement membrane and tumor microenvironment, into initial lymphatics, and, after flow through lymphatic trunks, into the sentinel lymph node. Valuable information regarding tumor cell‐directed motility, lymphangiogenesis, host cells that enhance metastasis, immune responses to tumor antigens, and tumor‐induced changes in sentinel lymph node(s) provides a promising avenue for the continued development of new therapeutic approaches to prevent and treat metastasis. This article reviews these aspects by synthesizing current scientific and clinical advances and translating them for medical professionals.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72408.abstract: Chemoimmunotherapy (CIT) had long been used to treat chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) until 2014 when the first novel agent, ibrutinib, was approved in the United States. Numerous novel therapies have since become available. Nevertheless, as novel therapies have largely replaced CIT in CLL/SLL, its impact on survival has yet to be examined on the population level. In this study, we used the SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results) database to compare survival in patients with CLL/SLL before and after the approval of the first novel therapy. We included 9913 patients who started treatment within 2 years of CLL/SLL diagnosis. In the multivariable analyses, the overall survival improved significantly (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.86, 95% confidence interval: 0.81, 0.92), and death from CLL/SLL and other cancer (subdistribution-HR: 0.69 and 0.77) also decreased significantly. Nevertheless, CLL/SLL remains the main cause of death during the novel agent era.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72410.abstract: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) frequently occur during combination immune checkpoint inhibition. However, their prognostic impact may vary according to organ involvement and severity. In this study, we exploratorily evaluated whether severe non-endocrine irAEs represent a temporally distinct and prognostically unfavorable clinical phenotype in patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC) treated with ipilimumab plus nivolumab. We analyzed 63 patients with mRCC treated with ipilimumab plus nivolumab who were followed for at least 5 years. Patients were categorized into non-irAE, non-severe + severe endocrine irAE, and severe non-endocrine irAE groups. Overall survival (OS) was assessed. Multistate modeling was used to evaluate the transitions between treatment, irAE occurrence, and death. Landmark analyses were performed at 8 and 12 weeks to address immortal time bias. The severe non-endocrine irAE group was associated with inferior OS. The multistate analysis revealed a potentially increased risk of direct transition from ipilimumab plus nivolumab to death in the severe non-endocrine irAE group. A significantly higher proportion of patients in the severe non-endocrine irAE group experienced irAEs within 30 days. No significant association was observed in the 8- and 12-week landmark analyses. In this exploratory retrospective study, severe non-endocrine irAEs showed an association with early onset and potentially unfavorable clinical outcomes in patients with mRCC receiving ipilimumab plus nivolumab. Given the limited sample size, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and require confirmation in larger independent cohorts.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72411.abstract: Somatic alterations in the RAS-RAF-MAPK and PI3K pathways are key in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet their distribution, co-occurrence patterns, and clinical significance remain incompletely defined. We characterized RAS/MAPK- and PI3K-pathway alterations in a large cohort and assessed their prognostic implications. We analyzed whole-exome sequencing data from 1243 paired samples from patients with CRC. Somatic variants in KRAS, NRAS, HRAS, BRAF, and PIK3CA were analyzed to quantify frequencies, codon-level distributions, and co-occurrence patterns. Descriptive somatic mutation status and demographic and clinical characteristics were evaluated using chi-square or Fisher exact tests, and associations with overall survival (OS) were evaluated using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models. Any RAS-family mutation was detected in 507 tumors (40.8%); KRAS, NRAS, and HRAS mutations occurred in 35.3%, 5.4%, and 0.6%, respectively. BRAF V600E was detected in 85 tumors (6.8%), PIK3CA in 221 (17.8%), and KRAS G12C in 38 (3.1%). KRAS codon 12 was the dominant RAS hotspot. KRAS-PIK3CA co-mutations occurred in 126 tumors (10.1% overall; 28.7% of KRAS-mutant tumors), whereas KRAS-BRAF and KRAS-NRAS co-mutations were uncommon, consistent with MAPK pathway mutual exclusivity. RAS-mutant tumors were enriched in right-sided and microsatellite-stable disease (p < 0.001 for both). KRAS, BRAF V600E, and PIK3CA mutation frequencies were higher in right-sided than left-sided tumors. In unadjusted analyses, Hispanic patients had lower KRAS, BRAF V600E, and PIK3CA mutation frequencies than non-Hispanic patients. After adjustment for age, sex, tumor location, and MSI status, the associations with KRAS and PIK3CA were attenuated, whereas the lower frequency of BRAF V600E among Hispanic patients persisted (p < 0.01). Mutation status was not significantly associated with 5-year overall survival. RAS/MAPK and PI3K pathway alterations in CRC varied primarily by tumor subtype and molecular context, with clinically relevant co-mutation patterns and a targetable KRAS G12C subset. These findings may support future clinical trials targeting the BRAF-RAS axis.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72413.abstract: As cancer survival improves, cardiovascular disease (CVD) has emerged as a major competing cause of death. However, population-level evidence on the burden of pre-existing and post-cancer CVD remains limited. This study aims to quantify pre-existing and post-cancer newly documented major CVD and their association with mortality outcomes among people with cancer. Major CVD was identified using linked hospital records among 344,336 adults registered with primary invasive cancer in the New South Wales Cancer Registry from 2006 to 2016. The cohort was followed up until 31 December 2021. Fine-Grey modelling estimated sub-distributional hazard ratios (sHR) for cancer and cardiovascular mortality, and Cox proportional hazard modelling estimated hazard ratio for mortality from any cause across 20 common cancers. Overall, 18% (n = 62,675) of participants had pre-existing CVD within 5 years before cancer diagnosis, varying by age (3% for age < 50 vs. 40% for ≥ 80). Of those without pre-existing CVD (n = 281,661), 27% (n = 76,924) had post-cancer newly documented CVD, with the highest age-standardised incidence rates in pancreatic cancer (716 per 10,000 person-years), followed by lung (657). The median follow-up period was 6.8 years with an interquartile range: 2.1-10.3 The sHR of pre-existing CVD for cancer mortality ranged from 0.99 (95% CI: 0.85-1.13) in cancer of kidney to 1.81 (95% CI = 1.71-1.91) in lymphoma, and for cardiovascular mortality, 1.98 (1.78-2.18) in lymphoma to 4.74 (4.39-5.09) in pancreatic cancer. The sHR of post-cancer newly documented CVD for cancer mortality, ranging from 0.87 (95% CI: 0.69-1.05) in liver cancer to 2.33 (95% CI = 2.04-2.62) in cervical cancer and cardiovascular mortality, ranging from 1.45 (95% CI: 1.18-1.72) in myeloma to 3.39 (95% CI = 2.90-3.88) in liver cancer. CVD is prevalent both before and after cancer diagnosis, with strong relations to increased cancer, cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. Population-based strategies to strengthen holistic survivorship care and address key risk factors are essential to improve both cancer and cardiovascular outcomes.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72414.abstract: University students with cancer in Italy face major barriers in maintaining their academic pathways despite existing disability legislation. This brief communication combines an overview of the Italian legal and institutional context with findings from a community-led qualitative descriptive needs-assessment. Following a national social media call, the analysis included semi-structured interviews with 69 eligible participants. Interviews were documented through contemporaneous written notes and analyzed manually using descriptive content analysis, combining domains from the interview guide with recurrent categories identified in open-ended responses. Participants described administrative burdens, inconsistent recognition of cancer-related needs, limited access to remote learning and flexible examinations, marked variability in university support, emotional distress, and social isolation. These findings provide preliminary real-world evidence of how existing arrangements are experienced by Italian university students affected by cancer. Although specific interventions were not evaluated, the findings may inform the development and prospective assessment of more consistent academic accommodations, accessible information, individualized support, and integrated psychosocial services.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72416.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Cancer care is burdensome, but patient experience with time and administrative burdens is variable. Our objective was to assess the association between daily administrative tasks, time spent, and reported burden and identify demographic and clinical predictors. Methods Participants ( n = 122) from two longitudinal studies of individuals receiving cancer treatment utilized a mobile application (Daynamica) to track time spent on cancer care tasks over 28 days. Participants reported distress levels (NCCN Distress Thermometer) and time spent on three administrative tasks daily: scheduling appointments, managing medical bills/claims, and arranging support/transportation. Relationships between distress and tasks were assessed using generalized linear mixed models. Results Most participants (91.8%) performed at least one administrative task during the study. Participants were more likely to report clinically significant distress (score 4+) on days involving administrative tasks (scheduling [OR = 1.92, 95% CI: 1.40–2.64], managing bills [OR = 2.10, 95% CI: 1.34–3.29], or arranging support [OR = 3.56, 95% CI: 2.19–5.79]) compared to days without these tasks. While the median time spent was low (14 min per week; Q1–Q3: 3–39), the top quartile spent an average of 83 min per week on these tasks. Lack of reliable transportation was the only factor significantly associated with increased time spent on administrative tasks (median 57 vs. 10 min/week, p = 0.01); no other demographic or clinical factors were associated with higher workload. Conclusion Administrative burden is a distinct psychological stressor for individuals with cancer, regardless of the actual time required for administrative tasks. Interventions should focus on streamlining insurance, care coordination, and administrative processes to reduce patient distress. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05708703, NCT06322992

doi:10.1002/cam4.72419.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Cancer‐related psychological distress remains underaddressed globally. Virtual interventions offer promising alternatives but lack evidence for enhancing Psychological Capital (PsyCap) in chemotherapy patients. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of a virtual social interaction intervention on PsyCap in patients undergoing chemotherapy. Methods This single‐blind randomized controlled trial (RCT) enrolled 76 chemotherapy patients hospitalized in the oncology ward of Imam Sajjad Hospital, Ramsar, Mazandaran, Iran. Participants were selected via convenience sampling and then allocated to intervention or control groups using an odd–even (alternating) assignment method. The intervention group participated in 6 weeks of virtual social interactions, consisting of asynchronous materials (recorded audio, short videos, images, PDF, and PowerPoint files) uploaded weekly to Iranian messaging platforms (Eitaa), as well as live synchronous group sessions conducted on the Skyroom platform with a minimum of 10 participants per session. The control group received standard care. The PsyCap was measured using Luthans' Psychological Capital Questionnaire at both baseline and post‐intervention. The Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) models (A/B) were adjusted for baseline scores and age. Results The intervention group showed improvements across all outcomes, with the total PsyCap score increasing by 23.6 points. Components significantly increased: self‐efficacy by 5.8 points, resilience by 5.8, hope by 5.5, and optimism by 6.5 ( p < 0.0001). ANCOVA models confirmed robust effects after adjusting for baseline scores and age (Δ SMD > 1). Conclusions Virtual social interactions significantly enhance PsyCap in chemotherapy patients. However, to confidently generalize these findings and make recommendations, similar studies need to be conducted and replicated in larger, multicenter trials.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72422.abstract: Combination therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (IO-TKI) is a key treatment option for metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC), but distinguishing immune-related adverse events (irAEs) from TKI-related adverse events (TKI-AEs) is challenging because of overlapping clinical features. We aimed to evaluate whether eosinophil counts can help differentiate between them. In this retrospective multicenter study, 123 patients with mRCC treated with IO-TKI therapy were analyzed. Patients were classified into an irAE group (n = 64) and a TKI-AE group (n = 59). Changes in eosinophil counts from baseline to the start of the second treatment cycle were compared. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and logistic regression analyses were performed to assess associations with irAE occurrence. Baseline eosinophil counts did not differ between groups. Eosinophil counts at the start of the second treatment cycle were higher in the irAE group than those in the TKI-AE group (269.6 vs. 189.6 eosinophils/μL; p < 0.05). No significant differences were observed in other blood parameters, including neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, and platelet counts, the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, or the platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio. Although the overall discriminatory performance was modest (area under the ROC curve = 0.57, sensitivity = 0.30, specificity = 0.94), eosinophil counts ≥ 380/μL were associated with irAEs in both univariate (odds ratio = 7.21) and multivariable (odds ratio = 8.39; p < 0.05) analyses. Early increases in eosinophil counts were associated with irAEs and may help distinguish irAEs from TKI-AEs during IO-TKI therapy. Given their high specificity but limited sensitivity, eosinophil counts may have utility as an adjunctive rather than stand-alone marker, and prospective validation is warranted.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72422.title: Eosinophil Dynamics May Help Differentiate Immune-Related From TKI-Related Adverse Events During IO-TKI Therapy for Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72423.abstract: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in cancer patients. The AVERT trial showed apixaban thromboprophylaxis reduced VTE in intermediate-to-high-risk patients initiating chemotherapy. However, the efficacy and safety of apixaban according to baseline chemotherapy class remain incompletely characterized. We conducted a post hoc analysis stratified by chemotherapy class of the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled AVERT trial comparing apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) with placebo in ambulatory cancer patients initiating chemotherapy. The primary efficacy outcome was VTE, and the primary safety outcome was clinically relevant bleeding (major or clinically relevant non major bleeding (CRNMB)) per ISTH criteria. A subgroup analysis compared platinum-based with non-platinum chemotherapy. Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CI), adjusted for age, sex, and study site. Treatment-by-platinum interaction terms were used to assess effect modification by platinum exposure. A total of 563 patients were included and categorized by one or more chemotherapy classes at randomization. Compared with placebo, apixaban appeared to reduce VTE in patients on platinum (HR 0.30, 95% CI 0.16-0.57), taxane (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.23-0.75), taxane-platinum (HR 0.28, 95% CI 0.12-0.68), topoisomerase inhibitor (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.19-0.53), and antimetabolite regimens (HR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12-0.54), without increased bleeding. Among placebo-treated patients, platinum-based chemotherapy was associated with a higher risk of VTE compared with non-platinum regimens (HR 2.25, 95% CI 1.48-3.42), whereas no statistically significant difference was observed among apixaban-treated patients. Treatment-by-platinum interaction testing did not demonstrate significant effect modification by platinum exposure. In this exploratory, hypothesis-generating analysis, apixaban thromboprophylaxis was associated with reduced VTE across several chemotherapy regimens with generally acceptable safety outcomes. Patients receiving platinum-based chemotherapy may derive greater absolute benefit from thromboprophylaxis in the setting of higher underlying thrombotic risk.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72425.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Endometrial carcinoma (EC) is one of the most common gynecological malignancies. Aberrant DNA methylation (DNAm) is an important epigenetic alteration involved in cancer progression. Long non‐coding RNAs (LncRNAs) play critical roles in gene regulation and pathological processes. However, the biological and prognostic significance of lncRNA‐mRNA pairs associated with methylation remains unclear. Methods Transcriptomic, DNA methylation, and clinical data from The Cancer Genome Atlas were integrated to construct a differentially methylated sites (DMSs)‐lncRNA‐mRNA network. After mapping DMSs to their corresponding differentially methylated genes (DMGs), the DMS‐mediated network was further represented as a DMG‐lncRNA‐mRNA tripartite network. After removal of DMG nodes, a DMG‐associated lncRNA‐mRNA background network was constructed, and key lncRNA‐mRNA pairs were prioritized according to their topological importance using weighted shortest‐path calculation and PageRank‐based random walk algorithms. The methylation‐associated lncRNA‐ mRNA pair (MLMP) model was then established based on univariate Cox, LASSO Cox, and multivariate Cox regression analyses. Results Eight DMG‐associated lncRNA‐mRNA pairs were selected to construct the MLMP model. Under a common analysis framework, the MLMP model achieved higher area under the curve (AUC) values than 17 previously published prognostic signatures for overall survival prediction. Patients in the low‐MLMP group had significantly better overall survival than those in the high‐MLMP group. Functional enrichment and immune microenvironment analyses indicated that the MLMP model was associated with immune‐related pathways and distinct tumor immune microenvironment characteristics. Predictive analyses suggested that patients in the low‐MLMP group exhibited higher predicted responsiveness to CTLA‐4/PD‐1 blockade and differential predicted sensitivity to several therapeutic agents. Conclusions The MLMP model may serve as a potential tool for prognostic stratification in EC and provide insights into methylation‐associated lncRNA‐mRNA interactions. The predicted associations with immunotherapy response and therapeutic sensitivity may generate hypotheses for future treatment‐related studies. These findings require further validation in independent clinical cohorts and experimental studies before clinical application.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72426.abstract: Sleep problems are common among cancer survivors and are linked to poorer quality of life. In the general United States (US) population, socioeconomic status (SES) is strongly associated with sleep health, but emerging evidence suggests that these benefits may be diminished among non-White racial/ethnic groups. Whether such patterns extend to cancer survivors is unknown. We analyzed data on 25,732 adult cancer survivors from National Health Interview Surveys. Sleep duration (normal 6-8 h; short ≤ 5 h; long ≥ 9 h) and troubled sleep (≥ 3 days/week of difficulty falling or staying asleep) were assessed via self-report. SES indicators included educational attainment and family income. Poisson regression models with race/ethnicity-by-SES interaction terms were used to estimate racial/ethnic differences in SES-sleep associations. Among non-Hispanic (NH) White survivors, higher education and income were consistently associated with lower prevalence of short sleep and troubled sleep. These SES gradients were muted or reversed among NH Black and Hispanic survivors. For example, NH White survivors with a bachelor's degree had substantially lower odds of short sleep compared with those with ≤ high school education, whereas no such association was observed among NH Black or Hispanic survivors. When stratifying by both education and income, income showed more consistent associations with sleep across all groups, while additional benefits of higher education were observed only among NH White survivors. SES-sleep gradients differ markedly across racial/ethnic groups among US cancer survivors. Tailored interventions addressing structural and socioeconomic inequities may be needed to improve sleep health and reduce disparities in survivorship.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72427.abstract: ABSTRACT Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC) exhibits substantial molecular and morphological heterogeneity, yet current morphology‐based prognostic models often lack biological interpretability. We developed a transformer‐based computational framework (CTransPath) to virtually predict gene expression directly from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole‐slide images. Morphology‐associated genes were identified from the TCGA‐HNSC cohort, and a 32‐gene morphology‐guided prognostic signature (MGP_HNSC32) based on H&E‐derived predicted gene expression was developed using Random Survival Forest and multivariable Cox regression modeling. In TCGA‐HNSC, the MGP_HNSC32 risk score significantly stratified patients by progression‐free interval (PFI; HR = 4.13, 95% CI: 2.84–6.02), overall survival (OS; HR = 2.42, 95% CI: 1.78–3.29), and disease‐specific survival (DSS; HR = 4.88, 95% CI: 2.95–8.06; all p < 0.001), and remained independently associated with prognosis after multivariable adjustment. High‐risk tumors were enriched for cell cycle, E2F, MYC, and epithelial‐mesenchymal transition pathways and displayed poorly differentiated histology with nuclear atypia and stromal desmoplasia. In contrast, low‐risk tumors showed keratinizing morphology and immune‐rich stroma, corresponding to differentiation‐ and metabolism‐related transcriptional programs. In the independent HANCOCK cohort ( n = 701), risk scores calculated entirely from H&E‐derived predicted gene expression using the TCGA‐derived coefficients and prespecified cutoff were associated with progression‐free survival (HR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.03–1.90, p = 0.034). However, the continuous risk score was not significantly associated with progression‐free survival (HR = 1.001, 95% CI: 0.999–1.003, p = 0.328). MGP_HNSC32 links histomorphology to transcriptional programs and demonstrates preliminary prognostic associations using routine H&E images. The H&E‐based gene‐expression prediction component should be considered proof‐of‐concept, and further independent and prospective validation is required before clinical implementation.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72430.abstract: The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) staging system for advanced ovarian cancer has remained largely static since 2014, with stage IV subdivided into IVA and IVB without further stratification. Emerging evidence suggests substantial prognostic heterogeneity within stage IV, yet large-scale validation remains limited. We analyzed 28,010 patients from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database (2010-2022) and 1175 from the Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (SYSUCC) (2010-2026). Propensity score matching (1:1) balanced baseline characteristics. Overall survival (OS) was compared across subgroups. We defined IVA-T1a as patients meeting FIGO IVA criteria with intra-abdominal disease limited to one ovary (intact capsule). We defined IVB-ILNT2 as stage IVB with metastasis confined to a single extra-abdominal lymph node station and intra-abdominal disease ≤ T2. IVB patients were stratified by metastatic pattern and surgical outcome. In SEER, IVA-T1a patients (n = 49) showed no OS difference versus stage II (HR 1.08, 95% CI: 0.95-1.23, p = 0.250), but significantly better survival than stage IIIA (HR 1.35, 95% CI: 1.08-1.62, p = 0.024). Findings were validated in SYSUCC (IVA-T1a n = 15; vs. stage II p = 0.638, vs. IIIA p = 0.026). Among IVB patients, those with single-station lymph node metastases achieving R0/R1 resection (n = 152) had median OS of 29.0 months, comparable to stage IIIC patients (HR 1.08, p = 0.872). In SYSUCC, IVB-ILNT2 subgroup (n = 65) demonstrated survival comparable to stage II (p = 4e-04 vs. other IVB) and significantly better than stage IIIA. These findings suggest that such patients may have a more favorable prognosis than implied by their current stage designation and underscore the need for prospective validation to determine whether treatment de-escalation could be considered in these specific subsets without compromising outcomes. Future FIGO revisions should consider refined classification incorporating intra-abdominal tumor burden and metastatic pattern, pending consistent validation across multiple independent populations.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72431.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the relationship between the systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) and prognosis in patients with oesophageal cancer undergoing radiotherapy, and to evaluate the incremental prognostic value of combining SII with clinical TNM stage. A retrospective analysis was performed on 159 patients with locally advanced oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma who received radiotherapy. The optimal cut-off value for pre-radiotherapy SII was determined using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, and patients were stratified into low- and high-SII groups accordingly. Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses were employed to identify independent prognostic factors. The predictive performance of SII alone, TNM stage alone, and their combination was compared. Primary endpoints were overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). The optimal pre-radiotherapy SII cut-off was 506.63. SII showed a tendency to increase during the course of radiotherapy. Short-term efficacy in the low-SII group was significantly better than that in the high-SII group (p = 0.042). Significant differences were observed between the two groups in 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year OS and PFS rates (all p < 0.05). Multivariate Cox regression analysis identified tumour location, TNM stage, gross tumour volume, and pre-radiotherapy SII as independent prognostic factors (all p < 0.05). The area under the curve (AUC) for the combination of SII and TNM stage in predicting survival was significantly larger than that of SII or TNM stage alone. The combined SII-TNM model demonstrated superior predictive performance compared with either parameter individually (both p < 0.05). Pre-radiotherapy SII serves as an independent prognostic factor in oesophageal cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy, with higher SII values associated with poorer survival outcomes. Integrating SII with TNM stage provides enhanced predictive accuracy for prognosis in this patient population.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72434.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Phosphatidylinositol 3‐kinase catalytic subunit type 3 (PIK3C3) is central to autophagy, which supports cancer adaptation to environmental stresses and may contribute to drug resistance. KRAS ‐mutant cancers have been reported to require autophagy for survival. We investigated the influence of KRAS mutation status on the roles of PIK3C3 in colorectal cancer (CRC) cell viability and chemosensitivity in vitro, as well as its association with patient prognosis. Methods The clinical significance of PIK3C3 expression in relation to KRAS mutation status was evaluated by immunohistochemistry in patients with advanced CRC. Cell viability, colony formation, and spheroid formation assays were performed using CRC cell lines. Results In KRAS ‐wild‐type ( KRAS ‐WT) Caco‐2 and Colo320 cells, PIK3C3 and the KRAS/ERK pathway appeared to positively regulate each other. In contrast, PIK3C3 inhibition did not reduce p‐ERK levels or induce significant p62 accumulation in KRAS ‐mutant SW480 and HCT116 cells. PIK3C3 knockdown reduced cell viability but increased resistance to 5‐fluorouracil (5‐FU) in Caco‐2 and Colo320 cells, whereas the opposite effect was observed in SW480 and HCT116 cells. Transfection with a KRAS ‐mutant plasmid sensitized Caco‐2 cells to 5‐FU accompanied by reduced thymidylate synthase (TS) and β‐catenin levels following PIK3C3 inhibition. Clinically, high PIK3C3 expression was associated with KRAS mutation and poorer survival in patients with advanced CRC. Its adverse short‐term prognostic association was more pronounced in KRAS ‐mutant CRC than in KRAS ‐WT CRC. Conclusion Based on preclinical in vitro findings, PIK3C3 appears to support KRAS ‐WT and KRAS ‐mutant CRCs in different ways. Notably, PIK3C3 inhibition enhances 5‐FU sensitivity in KRAS ‐mutant CRC cells, potentially through TS regulation, and warrants further investigation as a therapeutic strategy.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72435.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Cancer incidence in Africa is projected to reach 2.1 million new cases annually by 2040. Current treatment guidelines remain largely based on pharmacogenomic data predominantly from European and Asian genetic profiles, potentially compromising safety and efficacy in African patients. However, limited clinical validation data, extreme intra‐population genetic diversity, and significant healthcare infrastructure barriers constrain the translational application of pharmacogenomics in Africa. Objective This review critically examines pharmacogenomic variants with established clinical actionability in cancer treatment, focusing on those with differential frequencies or African‐specific alleles, and evaluates the evidence base for their implementation in African healthcare settings. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, PharmGKB, dbSNP, and Google Scholar for peer‐reviewed studies reporting pharmacogenomic variants in African or African‐ancestry populations relevant to cancer therapeutics. We synthesised evidence from recent African and global studies on pharmacogenomic variants affecting commonly used chemotherapy agents. Results Several variants show marked frequency differences between African‐ancestry reference populations and European populations, including DPYD rs115232898 (2.06% vs. 0.00%), CYP2D6 * 17 ( 18.76% vs. 0% ), and CYP3A5 *6 (12.82% vs. 0%). However, many of these estimates derive primarily from African‐American datasets and should not be interpreted as representative of continental African populations. African‐specific variants such as CYP2D6 * 17 and DPYD rs115232898 are underrepresented in guideline development datasets. Intra‐African genetic diversity is the highest globally, with Khoi‐San populations harbouring extensive private variation, suggesting that no single pharmacogenomic panel will be universally applicable across the continent. Conclusion While pharmacogenomics holds substantial promise for personalising cancer treatment in Africa, its current translational readiness is limited by a critical lack of African‐specific clinical validation data. Priorities include multi‐site validation studies, development of African‐enriched genotyping panels, and integration of pharmacogenomic education into oncology practice. Implementation must be accompanied by ethical frameworks ensuring data sovereignty and equitable benefit‐sharing.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72440.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Prostate‐specific antigen (PSA) and PSA density (PSAD) are widely used for prostate cancer (PCa) screening, but their diagnostic thresholds have not been differentially adjusted for ethnic groups in clinical practice. This multicenter study aimed to establish the distribution of PSA and PSAD in Chinese men without PCa and compare these values with published data from African American (AA) and Caucasian American (CA) men to assess potential racial disparities. Methods We analyzed 528 biopsy‐negative Chinese men from two tertiary centers, comparing their age‐adjusted PSA/PSAD with published AA/CA data. Additionally, we compared PSA/PSAD distributions and the proportion of men exceeding the conventional PSA cutoff (4 ng/mL) across racial groups. Results PSA levels showed a weak but significant positive correlation with age ( r = 0.121, p = 0.005), whereas PSAD did not ( r = −0.032, p = 0.465). Notably, Chinese men without PCa exhibited significantly higher mean PSA and PSAD than AA and CA men (PSA: 17.28 vs. 7.97 vs. 4.30 ng/mL, p < 0.001; PSAD: 0.28 vs. 0.19 vs. 0.11 ng/mL/mL, p < 0.001). Using a PSA cutoff of 4 ng/mL, the specificity for PCa detection was substantially lower in Chinese men than in AA and CA men at matched sensitivity levels. Conclusions This study reveals striking racial differences in baseline PSA and PSAD among men without PCa, with Chinese men demonstrating markedly higher values than AA and CA counterparts. These findings challenge the universal application of current PSA thresholds and underscore the need for race‐specific adjustments to optimize PCa screening accuracy.
