doi:10.1002/cam4.72441.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Pulmonary carcinoids (PCs) are rare, well‐differentiated, neuroendocrine lung tumors with limited treatment options for advanced disease, underscoring the need for targeted therapies. PCs typically exhibit a low mutational burden. Although MEN1 and chromatin‐modifier mutations are known contributors, potentially actionable alterations remain poorly characterized. To better define therapeutic opportunities, we evaluated oncogenic fusions and variants across 17 cancer‐associated genes in a large retrospective PC cohort. Methods Formalin‐fixed, paraffin‐embedded primary tumors from Helsinki University Hospital ( n = 119, collected between 1990 and 2020) were subjected to targeted RNA‐based fusion and variant analysis using the Archer FusionPlex Lung v2 assay. Results The most frequent recurrent genetic rearrangements involved ALK ( n = 5), BRAF ( n = 3), FGFR2 ( n = 3), and NTRK3 ( n = 2), each featuring diverse fusion partners. Variant analysis identified BRAF , EGFR , FGFR1 , and FGFR3 as the most frequently mutated genes, although only 2.2% ( n = 4) of all detected variants were classified as oncogenic. Notably, 66.7% of all oncogenic or likely oncogenic variants occurred in BRAF and EGFR . Oncogenic variants were identified in ALK , BRAF , EGFR , and ERBB2 . Although all FGFR1–3 variants were of uncertain significance, their frequency (34.1% of all detected variants), together with the three FGFR2 fusions, suggested that FGFR alterations may be biologically relevant in PCs. Conclusion Despite the typically muted genomic landscape of PCs, our study revealed a small yet therapeutically relevant subset of alterations. The findings further characterized the molecular profile of PCs and identified potentially actionable molecular subgroups. While these alterations were not associated with disease‐specific survival or metastatic status, they support consideration of molecular profiling in selected patients with advanced disease.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72443.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Around 90% of children with cancer live in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs), with the majority dying of their disease. Despite the need for quality end‐of‐life (EoL) care in LMICs, access and integration remain limited. Quality indicators (QIs) can assess and provide standards for high‐quality care. The aim of this study was to develop QIs for EoL care for children diagnosed with cancer in LMICs. Methods The QIs were identified and prioritized through a multi‐phase process: (1) literature review identified potential QIs from existing guidelines, standards, and published studies; (2) modified Delphi approach engaged global experts to assess the importance and feasibility of QIs; and (3) prioritization conducted using a Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) with experts and dot voting prioritization exercise with bereaved family members. Results From the literature review, 73 potential QIs were identified. Fifty‐six global experts from 27 countries participated in the modified Delphi. Sixty‐four indicators across seven domains were deemed important with 25 identified as both important and feasible. Forty‐one global experts from 23 countries participated in the DCE prioritization and 12 bereaved family members from nine countries participated in the dot voting prioritization. While experts and family members prioritized some indicators similarly (i.e., symptom management), family members placed higher priority on QIs addressing communication and anticipatory guidance. Conclusion This study describes a robust, context‐specific process which identified QIs for pediatric EoL care in LMICs. Future efforts will pilot and refine the QIs to demonstrate feasibility, sustainability, and impact on care quality. Precis This study assessed potential quality indicators (QIs) for pediatric end‐of‐life (EoL) care in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs) through a multi‐phase process involving global experts and bereaved families. The findings provide a set of potential QIs to evaluate and improve EoL care for children with cancer in LMICs.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72444.abstract: ABSTRACT Background As populations age, older adults represent a growing proportion of patients with cancer nearing the end of life. However, age‐related differences in treatment decision‐making and patterns of end‐of‐life care in routine cancer practice remain insufficiently described. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with cancer who received palliative care consultations at a tertiary hospital in Korea between 2018 and 2022. Clinical data were linked with national health insurance claims. Patients were categorized into five age groups (18–44, 45–64, 65–74, 75–84, and ≥ 85 years), and age‐related differences in referral timing, decision‐making roles, and end‐of‐life care patterns were examined. Results Among 6151 patients, 54.3% were aged ≥ 65 years, including 3.3% who were aged ≥ 85 years. Older patients were referred earlier. Advance statements were completed by 59.2% overall, with the lowest completion (52.2%) and fewer patient‐determined decisions to withhold or withdraw life‐sustaining treatment (62.0%) in the oldest group. Intensive care unit admission rates were similar across age groups, while cardiopulmonary resuscitation and ventilation were less frequent among patients aged ≥ 85 years. Hospice use declined with age. Total medical costs during the last 6 months of life decreased with age yet remained considerable among older patients. Most deaths occurred in tertiary hospitals (26.9%–31.9%), while deaths in nursing care facilities increased with advancing age. Conclusions Although older adults were referred earlier to palliative care, they were less likely to make their own treatment decisions, and aggressive care remained common. These findings indicate a need for age‐sensitive approaches to improve end‐of‐life care.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72445.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The partial volume effect influences the results of volumetrics performed on MRI sequences with different slice thicknesses. Although a standardized brain tumor imaging protocol with high‐quality 1 mm slices is recommended, segmentation is still commonly performed on thicker slices, especially in retrospective studies. We aimed to quantify the impact of different slice thicknesses on volumetric measurements of brain tumors, using treatment‐naive glioblastoma as a representative example. Methods Volumes were measured on T1‐weighted contrast‐enhanced (CE) sequences using semiautomatic segmentation across three predefined slice thicknesses: 1 mm (“thin”; reference measurement), 3 mm (“intermediate”), and 5 mm (“thick”). Data from 46 patients with the availability of all three slice thicknesses were statistically analyzed, including repeated‐measures ANOVA with post hoc comparisons, Bland–Altman analysis, correlations, and linear regression. Results The tumor volumes measured increased with slice thickness, with mean values of 36.4 cm 3 (“thin”), 38.6 cm 3 (“intermediate”), and 41.0 cm 3 (“thick”). Repeated measures ANOVA showed significant differences between groups ( p < 0.01). The mean deviation of the tumor volumes on “thick” relative to “thin” slices was 16% (±10%). Bland–Altman analysis and linear regression confirmed systematically higher measured volumes on “thick” slices. Tumor size on “thin” slices correlated negatively with the percentage deviation on “thick” slices ( r = −0.56; p < 0.01). Conclusion Volumetric measurements obtained from “thick” slices showed systematically higher tumor volumes and greater variability relative to the 1 mm reference. Volumetric data obtained from different slice thicknesses should not be combined, or concepts for adjustment should be considered to maintain methodological consistency and reliability in volumetric studies. We advocate the use of high‐quality 3D 1 mm imaging for volumetric analysis whenever possible.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72448.abstract: ABSTRACT Precision oncology is based on comprehensive molecular characterization of a patient's tumor. This is mostly realized by next‐generation sequencing panels or exome sequencing. Data on the value of genome sequencing from formalin‐fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) material in a clinical setting is still scarce. In this pilot, we generated datasets of matched exome and genome sequencing of FFPE tumor samples from 15 cancer patients to benchmark quality metrics, clinical feasibility, and added value for a molecular tumor board. Despite the reduced sequencing depth, diagnostic detection of small nucleotide variations, copy number variations, and complex biomarkers was maintained in genome sequencing compared to exome sequencing with the exception of hard‐to‐sequence regions. Evaluation by the local molecular tumor board identified additional treatment recommendations with high priority in 20% (3/15) of patients and additional molecular markers to support existing treatment recommendations in another 20% (3/15) of patients. Our work underscores the diagnostic superiority of genome sequencing even for FFPE samples and therefore supports its integration into clinical practice.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72451.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Polygenic risk scores (PRS) and lifestyle factors are associated with colorectal cancer (CRC), but whether their associations and joint effects vary according to age at CRC onset remains unclear. We evaluated age‐related heterogeneity in the associations of genetic risk and lifestyle with CRC and examined their additive interaction in early‐ and late‐onset CRC. Methods We analyzed data from 405,453 cancer‐free participants aged 38–73 years at baseline in the UK Biobank. PRS and a healthy lifestyle score (based on eight modifiable factors) were assessed. Age‐scale Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) for CRC risk by age at onset. Heterogeneity across age intervals was assessed using likelihood ratio tests. Additive interaction was assessed using the relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI), and differences in standardized incidence rates were evaluated. Results During a median follow‐up of 13.65 years, 6620 CRC cases were identified. Compared with low genetic risk, high genetic risk was associated with HRs of 3.72, 3.32, 2.80, and 2.01 for CRC occurring at ages < 55, 55–64, 65–74, and ≥ 75 years, respectively, with significant heterogeneity across age intervals ( p for heterogeneity < 0.001). Compared with a favorable lifestyle, the corresponding HRs for an unfavorable lifestyle were 1.10, 1.50, 1.58, and 1.28, respectively, with evidence of overall heterogeneity ( p for heterogeneity = 0.015). For late‐onset CRC, positive additive interactions were observed for an unfavorable lifestyle combined with intermediate or high genetic risk, whereas no such interaction was detected for early‐onset CRC. Conclusions The associations of genetic susceptibility and baseline lifestyle with CRC varied according to age at onset. Positive additive interaction between genetic risk and an unfavorable lifestyle was observed for late‐onset but not early‐onset CRC. These findings provide further evidence that the relative and joint associations of genetic and lifestyle factors with CRC vary across the life course.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72453.abstract: ABSTRACT Relapse occurs in 10%–20% of children with hepatoblastoma and is associated with inferior outcomes, yet standardized management remains limited. Defining risk factors and relapse patterns, as well as the role of surgery, particularly transplantation, is critical to optimizing survival. A retrospective review was performed of patients aged 0–18 years diagnosed with hepatoblastoma from 2007 to 2024. Demographics, tumor characteristics, treatment course, relapse patterns, and outcomes were collected. Analyses included univariable and multivariable logistic regression, Kaplan–Meier survival estimation, and log‐rank testing. Among 135 patients, 98 (72.6%) achieved remission without relapse, 32 (23.7%) relapsed, and 5 (3.7%) experienced primary progression without remission. Older age, PRETEXT (pretreatment extent of disease) IV, metastatic disease at diagnosis, and macrovascular invasion were associated with relapse on univariable analysis, but only older age remained independently associated with relapse (adjusted odds ratio 1.27 per year, 95% confidence interval 1.05–1.53); PRETEXT IV and metastatic disease were not significantly associated with overall survival. Lung‐only relapse demonstrated favorable survival (100% alive), whereas combined liver and lung or extrahepatic relapse had poorer outcomes (40%–44% alive), although survival did not differ significantly across relapse sites ( p = 0.15). Of 54 liver transplant recipients, 44 underwent upfront transplantation, and 10 underwent salvage transplantation, with no significant difference in overall survival ( p = 0.90), although the salvage group was small. Relapse or progression after upfront transplantation occurred in 27% of recipients; lung‐only relapse again conferred favorable survival. Long‐term survival is achievable in relapsed hepatoblastoma, particularly for isolated pulmonary relapse. Older age, likely a surrogate for adverse tumor biology, was associated with relapse but did not preclude survival when aggressive multimodal therapy was used. Salvage transplantation achieved durable survival in selected patients and should be considered for unresectable intrahepatic relapse when extrahepatic disease is absent or controlled.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72459.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP CDM) is a data standard that enables multicenter research. Primary objective was to describe the magnitude of healthcare utilization in pediatric cancer versus non‐cancer patients. Secondary objective was to compare 6‐month clinical outcomes related to abnormal lab tests and mortality. Methods In this multicenter retrospective study, we included pediatric patients 0–18 years at first medication administration. Cancer patients had a malignant neoplastic disease diagnosis and received chemotherapy. Index date was the first chemotherapy date. Non‐cancer patients were assigned analogous index dates based on randomly sampled first medication to chemotherapy intervals. Outcomes were measured within 6 months of index date. Healthcare utilization included encounters, procedures, radiology, lab tests, and medications. Results Among 2810 cancer and 11,240 non‐cancer patients, all evaluated healthcare utilization measures were significantly more common in cancer patients. The largest relative differences were observed for long inpatient stay (risk ratio [RR] 26.32, 95% confidence interval [CI] 15.00–46.17), computed tomography (RR 23.59, 95% CI 19.24–28.92), blood culture (RR 37.04, 95% CI 9.58–143.14), and intravenous medication (RR 17.69, 95% CI 8.75–35.75). Death within 6 months was higher for cancer versus non‐cancer patients (RR 38.37, 95% CI 12.91–114.04). Conclusions Using the OMOP CDM, we found greater healthcare utilization and worse clinical outcomes among pediatric cancer patients than non‐cancer patients, with the largest relative differences observed for inpatient stay, computed tomography, blood culture, and intravenous medication. These findings provide insight into resource utilization patterns and illustrate the OMOP CDM research potential for multicenter studies.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70848.abstract: Cuproptosis arises from mitochondrial copper overload, yet how tumour cells evade this metabolic vulnerability remains unclear. We identify ATP7B as the central barrier to cuproptosis in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). ATP7B is aberrantly upregulated in PDAC and predicts poor prognosis. Its depletion increases intracellular copper, activates FDX1, DLAT/DLST lipoylation, disrupts tricarboxylic acid (TCA) metabolism, and reinstates cuproptosis in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, ATP7B undergoes ZBTB10-driven K63-linked ubiquitination, recognized by NBR1 for selective autophagic degradation. Leveraging this, we developed an ATP7B-targeting autophagy-targeting chimera (ATAUTAC) that promotes ATP7B clearance, amplifies copper-driven mitochondrial metabolic perturbations, triggers cuproptosis, and inhibits tumour growth with favourable tolerability. Notably, ATAUTAC sensitizes PDAC to gemcitabine, overcoming resistance by exposing latent metabolic fragility. These findings establish ATP7B as a mechanistic hub of cuproptosis tolerance and demonstrate that autophagy-based ATP7B degradation is a druggable strategy for copper-dependent tumour eradication. ATAUTAC offers a promising avenue for precision therapy in PDAC and other refractory malignancies.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70852.abstract: Thoracic radiotherapy can cause delayed cardiac fibrosis, but the immune mechanisms linking radiation injury to fibroblast activation remain unclear. We investigated whether CCR2+ monocytes contribute to radiation-induced cardiac fibrosis and whether AXL regulates their fibroblast-activating activity. C57BL/6 mice received 20 Gy whole-thorax irradiation, and remodelling was assessed from IR_D0 to IR_D60. Bulk RNA sequencing was integrated with single-cell datasets and CIBERSORTx deconvolution, lineage tracing, and tissue staining. CCR2+ monocyte function was examined by CCR2 neutralisation, and circulating CCR2+Ly6Cʰi monocytes were quantified by flow cytometry. AXL was investigated using inducible myeloid Axl deletion and bemcentinib (R428). MAPK signalling was assessed by transcriptomic analysis and immunoblotting of sorted CCR2+Ly6Cʰi monocytes. Conditioned medium from sorted monocytes after Axl deletion, AXL inhibition with R428, or MEK1/2 inhibition with U0126 was applied to cardiac fibroblasts. Cardiac fibrosis was established by IR_D30, while leukocyte infiltration and apoptotic signals remained above baseline. Transcriptomic analyses and lineage tracing showed increased cardiac accumulation of CCR2+ monocytes. CCR2 neutralisation reduced circulating CCR2+Ly6Cʰi monocytes and attenuated interstitial collagen deposition and fibrotic marker expression. Axl was enriched in the CCR2+ monocyte compartment. Myeloid Axl deletion and R428 reduced cardiac fibrosis. Axl deletion suppressed MAPK-related transcriptional programs, whereas genetic or pharmacological AXL targeting reduced MEK and ERK phosphorylation in sorted monocytes. Conditioned medium from IR_D30 monocytes induced COL1A1 and α-SMA expression in fibroblasts, and this effect was reduced by Axl deletion, R428, or U0126 treatment of donor monocytes. AXL signalling contributes to the fibroblast-activating paracrine activity of cardiac CCR2+ monocytes after irradiation, at least in part through MEK/ERK signalling. Radiation exposure induces cardiac fibrosis through immunestromal interactions. CCR2+ monocytes promote fibroblast activation during radiation-induced cardiac fibrosis. AXL regulates monocyte-mediated fibroblast activation through MEK/ERK signaling. Targeting the AXL-MEK/ERK pathway may provide a potential strategy for preventing radiation-induced cardiac fibrosis.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70853.abstract: Abstract Background Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most aggressive malignancies and is characterized by a high degree of heterogeneity. However, HCC treatment remains difficult, highlighting the need to better define molecular subgroups of HCC and understand their potential relationships with therapeutic response. Methods In this study, we established 20 patient‐derived organoids and 12 patient‐derived cell lines from 20 individuals diagnosed with HCC. These models were comprehensively characterized using whole‐exome sequencing, RNA sequencing, drug screening, and hepatitis B virus (HBV)‐targeting PCR with a focus on HBV‐related HCC. Results Based on transcriptomic profiling, this study classified HCC into two molecular subtypes, aligning with previously reported classifications. Drug screening revealed that the greater enrichment of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling pathway was associated with increased sensitivity to everolimus and lenvatinib. Integrated transcriptomic and drug‐response analyses further identified candidate genes associated with lenvatinib response. In addition, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis targeting the HBV surface, core, and X genes demonstrated noticeable discrepancies relative to the clinically reported HBV infection status. Notably, HBV DNA detection was associated with activation of the calcium signalling pathway and oxaliplatin response. Conclusions This study provides a valuable resource for investigating the biology and pharmacological characteristics of HCC, particularly in the context of molecular subtypes and HBV‐associated mechanisms. Ultimately, these findings offer additional insights into HCC heterogeneity and drug response and may serve as a basis for further investigation of molecular determinants of therapeutic response.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70854.abstract: Allergic rhinitis (AR) remains a global health challenge. However, the transcriptional and epigenetic features associated with seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR) and perennial allergic rhinitis (PAR) relative to non-allergic rhinitis (NAR) remain poorly characterised at single-cell resolution. We performed integrated single-cell transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of nasal mucosal tissues from 22 patients, including NAR (n = 8), SAR (n = 6), and PAR (n = 8), to characterise transcriptional and epigenetic patterns associated with immune cell heterogeneity. We identified eight major immune cell types and 29 immune cell subsets across the nasal mucosa. Comparisons with NAR revealed distinct transcriptional and epigenetic features in SAR and PAR across both myeloid and T-cell compartments. In Macro_CCL3 cells, SAR showed enrichment of inflammation-associated programs, whereas PAR showed greater enrichment of antigen-presentation-related features. CD4_Tcm cells exhibited subtype-associated epigenetic differences, with IL-1β/IL-17-related features enriched in SAR and eosinophil- and Th2-associated programs enriched in PAR. CD8_Trm cells in both AR groups showed cytotoxicity-related features, including increased accessibility near GZMB and PRF1, while distinct inferred regulatory patterns were observed across the two AR groups. In addition, T-cell co-expression modules identified by hdWGCNA showed distinct associations with NAR, SAR, and PAR. sLDSC analysis revealed significant enrichment of pollinosis-associated heritability in CD8 T-cell open chromatin regions. Our study characterises distinct immune regulatory features associated with SAR and PAR relative to NAR across innate and adaptive immune compartments, providing a multi-omic framework for characterising AR heterogeneity and identifying subtype-associated molecular features for further investigation.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70856.abstract: Early identification of vulnerable carotid plaques is crucial for stroke prevention, but the upstream metabolic processes linked to endothelial transition and immune recruitment remain poorly defined. We characterised lactate metabolism in ACKR1+ endothelial cells (ECs) in human carotid plaques and derived a machine-learning signature for discriminating plaque vulnerability. Internal and external (GSE253903) single-cell datasets were integrated to identify endothelial subpopulations, and bulk transcriptomic (GSE163154) and in-house proteomic data were used to assess metabolism-immune correlations. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression selected core features for a logistic model, which was locked and applied to three independent cohorts: GSE43292 (Stary stage ≥ IV vs. I-II), GSE28829 (early vs. advanced lesions) and GSE100927 (normal vs. atherosclerotic arteries). Key molecules were validated in situ by immunohistochemistry (IHC) and spatial transcriptomics in independent plaques (five stable, five unstable). An ACKR1+ EC subpopulation linked to neovascularisation showed hyperactive glycolysis and enhanced lactate metabolism. Computational inference linked lactate accumulation to HIF-1α stability, CXCL12 release and CD8+ T-cell infiltration via the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis, and the monocarboxylate transporters SLC16A3 and SLC16A4 emerged as quantitative readouts of this 'lactate-immune' state. In unstable plaques, IHC confirmed higher atypical chemokine receptor 1 (ACKR1; geometric mean ratio [GMR] = 6.82), CD8+ T-cell density (GMR = 4.63), SLC16A3 (GMR = 4.74) and HIF-1α (GMR = 4.02; all q < .05), with lactylation elevated in the lipid core. A four-feature model (ACKR1, SLC16A3, SLC16A4, CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity score) performed well in training and retained discrimination in the progression-stratified cohorts, while in GSE100927 it showed high disease-identification performance across three arterial beds. Lactate metabolic reprogramming under hypoxia is associated with ACKR1+ EC-related CD8+ T-cell recruitment and plaque instability. This chain is an association-based hypothesis requiring functional confirmation. The signature discriminates robustly at both the vulnerability-stratification and disease-identification levels, providing a quantifiable framework for molecular classification of atherosclerotic plaques.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70857.abstract: Mitochondrial transplantation is built on a simple idea: failing cells might be rescued by healthy mitochondria. The approach has entered early clinical testing, and encapsulation and cell-type targeting have improved uptake in selected systems. Better delivery, however, does not explain the therapy. Internalised donor mitochondria encounter an established network, quality-control machinery and sensors for mitochondrial material. Donor material may remain in the endolysosomal system or reach the cytosol. Cytosolic fates include network integration, clearance and a candidate functional contribution without fusion. Intracellular processing may also generate bioactive cargo. These fates imply different mechanisms and evidence requirements. This Review examines how recipient cells shape the contribution of internalised mitochondria, while recognising extracellular routes to benefit. We distinguish direct transplantation evidence from mechanistic support drawn from endogenous mitochondrial biology and natural intercellular transfer. The required donor fate and duration depend on the therapeutic task. Transient rescue may rely on short-term donor function or productive processing in specific models; sustained support may depend on continued donor function, recipient adaptation or redosing. Durable mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) correction requires donor-mtDNA retention and replication. Linking these tasks to product design, safety assessment and clinical endpoints shifts the question from how many mitochondria enter cells to what they accomplish after arrival. Recipient-cell handling shapes what transplanted mitochondria do after uptake. Uptake, structural integration and donor mitochondrial DNA retention require distinct evidence. Transient rescue, sustained support and durable mitochondrial DNA correction impose different requirements. Therapeutic goals should guide donor selection, product testing and clinical endpoints.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70858.abstract: Spatiotemporal transcriptomics (STT) integrates spatially resolved gene expression with temporal information derived from staged samples, paired treatment specimens, or computational inference, providing a framework for reconstructing tissue-level dynamics. In the tumour microenvironment (TME), STT extends static molecular and cellular maps by revealing how cellular neighbourhoods and functional niches are reorganised during tumour evolution. This review examines how STT characterises TME remodelling during malignant transformation, invasion, metastasis, ageing, and treatment response. We discuss strategies for resolving temporal dynamics, including stage-stratified sampling, paired or serial specimens, pseudotime and trajectory inference, and complementary intravital imaging. We further consider how spatiotemporal analyses can connect changes in cellular states, spatial organisation, and intercellular interactions with clinically relevant tumour phenotypes. By linking the spatial organisation of the TME with stage- and treatment-associated molecular changes, STT may improve the prioritisation of candidate targets, treatment stratification, and the development of precision oncology strategies.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70861.abstract: Recent studies have established that the nervous system is not merely a bystander in tumour progression but can actively remodel the tumour microenvironment through the neuro-tumour axis, thereby promoting tumour invasion, metastasis and survival. Semaphorin 3C (SEMA3C) has been reported to regulate tumour migration, angiogenesis and immune suppression, highlighting its potential role in tumour progression. Although the neuro-tumour axis has been identified in multiple cancer types, its role and underlying mechanisms in gastric cancer peritoneal metastasis (GCPM) remain unclear. We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) of GCPM tissues to profile tumour cell heterogeneity and identify tumour cell populations associated with neural-related signalling. Candidate tumour-microenvironmental interactions were further investigated using patient-derived organoids and co-culture models, and the identified signalling axis was validated using corresponding in vivo models. SnRNA-seq identified a distinct subpopulation of poorly differentiated tumour cells with pronounced stem-like properties and high SEMA3C expression. This subpopulation was associated with neural-related features and interacted with tumour-associated endothelial cells, thereby contributing to remodelling of the metastatic microenvironment. Furthermore, these cells enhanced tumour-endothelial communication by activating the fibroblast growth factor receptor-associated signalling pathway. The transcription factor early B-cell factor 2 (EBF2) regulates the expression of FGF7 within this subpopulation, thereby strengthening FGF7-FGFR2 signalling and promoting tumour progression. Functional validation further demonstrated that SEMA3C depletion impaired organoid growth and tumour-endothelial interactions, whereas disruption of the SEMA3C-EBF2-FGF7-FGFR2 signalling axis attenuated tumour growth and peritoneal tumour burden in vivo. Additional experimental validation supported the potential involvement of neural-related signalling in the SEMA3C-associated tumour cell state. Our findings identify a SEMA3C+ tumour cell subpopulation associated with neural-related signalling and suggest that SEMA3C promotes tumour-endothelial interactions through the EBF2-FGF7-FGFR2 signalling axis, providing a potential mechanistic link between neural regulation and microenvironmental remodelling in peritoneal metastasis of gastric cancer.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70863.abstract: Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) is a pivotal lipid-sensing receptor that governs the functional plasticity and metabolic fitness of mononuclear phagocytes, including microglia, osteoclasts, dendritic cells and tissue-resident macrophages. While originally identified as a genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), TREM2 functions as a context-dependent immunometabolic checkpoint rather than a uniform phenotypic driver, exerting divergent biological outputs dictated by distinct tissue microenvironments and ligand repertoires. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of TREM2 immunobiology, detailing how ligand engagement-including cell-surface phospholipids and apolipoprotein E (ApoE)-activates the DAP12/DAP10-SYK-PI3K-mTOR signalling axis. This coordinated intracellular cascade instructively drives myeloid adaptation towards metabolically competent disease-associated microglia (DAM) and lipid-associated macrophage (LAM) states, sustaining bioenergetics and debris clearance under pathological stress. Across neurodegenerative proteinopathies and acute cerebral ischemia, TREM2 signalling is predominantly neuroprotective by promoting aggregate compaction and mitigating secondary excitotoxicity, although chronic dysregulated activation may drive stage-dependent neuroinflammation. In peripheral inflammatory pathologies such as rheumatoid arthritis and sepsis, TREM2 fine-tunes macrophage efferocytosis and systemic metabolic thresholds. In oncology, TREM2 displays a complex, microenvironment-dependent divergence: in central nervous system malignancies such as glioblastoma (GBM), TREM2 exerts controversial, stage-dependent effects, spanning microglial tumour containment in early stages versus pro-tumoural myelin recycling and immunosuppression by monocyte-derived macrophages in post-treatment recurrence; conversely, in peripheral solid tumours, monocyte-derived TREM2+ tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) predominantly orchestrate an immunosuppressive, nutrient-deprived niche that impairs cytotoxic T-cell function. Furthermore, we synthesise emerging paradigms along the bidirectional microbiome-gut-brain-tumour axis, elucidating how commensal and intra-tumoural microbial cues dynamically calibrate myeloid signalling tone and therapeutic susceptibility. We address translation bottlenecks-including blood-brain barrier (BBB) shuttles, human trial scarcity and soluble TREM2 (sTREM2) biomarker harmonisation-outlining a biomarker-guided, context-tailored precision therapeutic framework for targeting the TREM2 axis.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70864.abstract: Pulmonary endarterectomy (PEA) remains one of potentially curative options for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). The operation can remove proximal thromboembolic materials and their secondary branches. However, the cellular landscape and pathological features across different anatomical regions remain limited understood. Ten patients with CTEPH undergoing PEA surgery and six reference distal pulmonary arteries were conducted single-cell transcriptomics to profile the cellular composition of the main and its bifurcate portion. Pronounced muscularised and fibrotic thrombi organisation were presented in the main portion, and the proportion of mononuclear phagocytes was significantly increased. Inflammatory response and pro-inflammatory activity were attributed to CD8+ effector T cells and nature killer cells subsets and a M1-like (high IL1B and TNF, minimal IL6) phenotypic macrophage subcluster. The colander-like lesions were dominant in the bifurcate portion, and the percentage of plasma cells was markedly increased. Immune dysregulation was induced from CD4 naïve T cells, and a downregulation of M2-like macrophage infiltration into the vascular wall. The expression of plasminogen activator, urokinase receptor, urokinase receptor (PLAUR; plasminogen activator) were observed in M2-like (high MRC1 and CD163, virtually no IL1B or TNF) macrophage in bifurcate portion. Notably, one of smooth muscle cells (SMCs) subclusters in the bifurcate portion gained more significantly myofibroblast markers than those in the main portion, and other subclusters remained the function of SMCs. The regions with colander-like lesions changes had more obviously T cell and macrophages driving immune-inflammatory response and SMCs differentiation, suggesting that combining therapeutic interventions after surgical removal of accessible thrombus may be beneficial. This study reveals the comprehensive cellular composition in main/lobar and bifurcate pulmonary endarterectomy (PEA) specimens at the single-cell level. The bifurcate regions with colander had more obviously T cell and macrophages driving immune-inflammatory response and smooth muscle cells (SMCs) differentiation, however, the remodelling of distal or micro-vessels still remained.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70865.abstract: Acute allograft rejection is largely dependent on T cell-driven immune responses; however, the molecular programs that establish and maintain effector T cell states during rejection remain incompletely defined. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis was conducted to characterize the activation of signalling pathways in T cells during acute allograft rejection. The function of MEK1/2 signalling was evaluated both in vitro and in vivo using mice with targeted deletion of Mek1/2 in T cells and pharmacological inhibition. Phosphoproteomic analysis, immunofluorescence staining, and western blotting were conducted to investigate downstream signalling mechanisms, particularly those involving SMAD4. Effector CD4 and CD8 T cells exhibited enhanced MEK/ERK pathway activation throughout the rejection process. MEK1/2 inhibition, either via genetic deletion or pharmacological blockade, attenuated T cell activation and effector activity, leading to reduced rejection and prolonged graft survival. Phosphoproteomic analysis identified SMAD4 as a key downstream effector of MEK1/2 signalling. Mechanistically, MEK1/2 deficiency reduced SMAD4 nuclear translocation in activated T cells, accompanied by diminished effector T cell responses. MEK1/2 signalling regulates T cell activation and effector phenotypes via SMAD4 nuclear translocation in heart transplant rejection. Therapeutic intervention targeting this pathway may contribute to alloimmune response regulation and improve transplant outcomes.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70866.abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease worldwide. However, albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), which define and stage DKD, report established injury and do not resolve the cellular heterogeneity underlying variable progression. Urine, the only biofluid to traverse every nephron segment, carries shed cells, extracellular vesicles (EVs) and cell-free DNA (cfDNA), each retaining information about its cell of origin. This review develops the concept of a digital urinary biopsy, in which the three compartments are read together against spatial single-cell kidney atlases to infer non-invasively which cell states are active and whether niche-associated programs are engaged, an approach we term atlas-anchored molecular profiling. For each compartment, we tabulate study population, sample size, processing, assay, performance and validation status. Because shed-cell RNA, selectively sorted vesicle cargo and cfDNA methylation differ in origin, measurement scale and bias, each requires its own reference matrix, sampling function and background terms. All three carry renal information in feasibility studies, yet none is a validated clinical assay in DKD. Moreover, a cfDNA methylation reference at the required resolution is lacking, and no named computational method has been tested on urine. We therefore present the framework as a structured research hypothesis and define the required validation, from analytical and clinical validity to prospective demonstration of utility, with non-albuminuric DKD, which albuminuria-based screening misses, as the index use case. It offers a testable route to cell-resolved, non-invasive staging of DKD rather than a demonstrated capability.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70871.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) ranks among the most prevalent malignant tumours worldwide, accounting for approximately 90% of primary liver cancer cases, with the highest incidence observed in Asia. Activating Transcription Factor 6 (ATF6) is an endoplasmic reticulum stress-responsive transcription factor. Our previous studies have demonstrated that ATF6 contributes to HCC tumourigenesis and progression through signalling pathways such as ATF6-CTH-Keap1-mTORC1 and ATF6-PPM1H-RPS6KB1. RNA sequencing identified ATF6 transcriptional targets, with Ras homolog family member Q (RHOQ) validation via chromatin immunoprecipitation and electrophoretic mobility shift assay. RHOQ expression and clinical significance were analysed in HCC cohorts. Functional assays assessed proliferation, migration, invasion and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Tumour growth was evaluated in orthotopic (NOG mice) and subcutaneous (nude mice) models. Mechanistic analyses were performed to characterise RHOQ-mediated regulation of p21-activated kinase 1 (PAK1) signalling and metabolic remodelling. Furthermore, therapeutic synergy between PAK1 inhibitor IPA-3 and Glypican-3 (GPC3)-CAR T cells was tested. We identified RHOQ as a direct transcriptional target of ATF6. Clinically, elevated RHOQ expression correlated with poorer progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with HCC. Functionally, RHOQ promoted the proliferation and metastasis of liver tumour cells. Correspondingly, RHOQ knockdown markedly suppressed tumour growth in xenograft models, with consistent results observed in a hydrodynamic tail vein injection(HTVi) model. Mechanistic investigations revealed that RHOQ directly bound to PAK1, promoted its phosphorylation and activation and thereby drove aerobic glycolysis in liver tumour cells. Furthermore, combined treatment with the PAK1-specific inhibitor IPA-3 and GPC3-targeted CAR T-cell therapy produced a significant synergistic anti-tumour effect. In summary, this study systematically delineated the importance of the ATF6-RHOQ-PAK1 signalling cascade in driving liver cancer progression and provided a rationale for the design of targeted combination therapies. RHOQ is a novel direct transcriptional target of ATF6 in HCC. High RHOQ expression is associated with unfavourable clinicopathological features and poorer PFS. RHOQ drives HCC progression via PAK1 activation and aerobic glycolysis. Combining the PAK1-specific inhibitor IPA-3 with GPC3-targeted CAR T-cell therapy produces a potent synergistic anti-tumour effect.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70873.abstract: Acquired resistance to sorafenib in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is accompanied by coordinated changes in oxidative-stress handling and regulated cell-death pathways, yet how membrane organisation connects these adaptations is not fully resolved. We therefore examined whether B4GALNT1, a ganglioside biosynthetic glycosyltransferase, couples changes in ganglioside composition and lipid-raft architecture to ferroptosis regulation and caspase-1/GSDMD-associated signalling in sorafenib-resistant HCC. We combined TCGA-LIHC analysis, single-cell transcriptomics, pathway-level analyses, and graph attention network modelling with a treatment-annotated local cohort of 92 patients with HCC who received sorafenib. Functional experiments were conducted in Huh7/Huh7-SR cells and additional liver-tumour models using B4GALNT1 gain- and loss-of-function, an independent second-sgRNA knockout clone, GM1 rescue, and re-expression of either wild-type B4GALNT1 or the catalytic-loss D358A variant. Validation included ganglioside profiling, detergent-resistant membrane isolation, lipid-raft disruption/repletion, ferroptosis-directed pharmacology, cell-death measurements, and xenograft studies. B4GALNT1 was enriched in tumour-associated hepatocyte populations and was upregulated in Huh7-SR cells. In the local cohort, higher B4GALNT1 protein abundance tracked with less favourable response to sorafenib and poorer survival outcomes. Increasing B4GALNT1 shifted ganglioside abundance toward GM2/GM1/GD2 and increased GM1-enriched raft-associated fractions, whereas knockout produced reciprocal changes. B4GALNT1-high cells showed increased GPX4 and SLC7A11, reduced lipid peroxidation and labile Fe2 +, and lower ferroptotic injury. At the same time, caspase-1/GSDMD-associated signalling and IL-1β/IL-18 release increased without widespread terminal membrane lysis. Exogenous GM1 partially rescued knockout-associated changes, and wild-type B4GALNT1 restored the phenotype more effectively than the D358A mutant. Concordant directional effects were observed in additional cell models and in xenografts. The data are consistent with a model in which B4GALNT1 reshapes ganglioside composition and GM1-enriched membrane microdomains, thereby supporting a drug-adapted state that combines greater ferroptosis resistance with restricted caspase-1/GSDMD-associated membrane permeabilisation. This integrated phenotype accompanies reduced sorafenib responsiveness and offers a mechanistic basis for acquired resistance in HCC. B4GALNT1 is associated with sorafenib resistance and poorer outcomes in treated HCC. B4GALNT1 remodels gangliosides and lipid rafts, limiting ferroptotic injury. Caspase-1/GSDMD signalling increases without widespread terminal membrane lysis. Genetic rescue and cross-model studies support B4GALNT1 specificity.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70876.abstract: Mitophagy is essential for mitochondrial quality control during myocardial ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury. Lysosomal protein transmembrane 5 (LAPTM5) has been implicated in cardiovascular disease and autophagy, but its role in cardiac mitophagy remains unclear. LAPTM5 knockout mice and cardiomyocyte-targeted AAV9-cTnT-LAPTM5 were used to determine the role of LAPTM5 in myocardial I/R injury. Cardiomyocyte hypoxia/reoxygenation models, mt-Keima imaging, mitochondrial fractionation, LC3-mitochondrial colocalization, co-immunoprecipitation, molecular docking, site-directed mutagenesis, NEDD4 gain- and loss-of-function, and p62 ubiquitination assays were used to investigate the underlying mechanism. Depending on data distribution and group number, appropriate parametric or non-parametric statistics were applied together with correction for multiple testing. LAPTM5 expression progressively decreased following I/R or H/R stress. LAPTM5 deficiency aggravated myocardial injury, cardiac dysfunction, and mitochondrial structural and functional damage, whereas LAPTM5 overexpression attenuated these abnormalities. LAPTM5 promoted mitophagy by enhancing LC3 recruitment to mitochondria. Mechanistically, LAPTM5 recruited NEDD4 to mitochondria through its PY3 motif and facilitated NEDD4-LC3 complex formation. NEDD4 depletion abolished LAPTM5-mediated mitophagy and cytoprotection, whereas re-expression of NEDD4-WT, but not the E3-inactive NEDD4-CS mutant, restored these effects. NEDD4-WT also increased p62 ubiquitination. AAV9-mediated LAPTM5 re-expression reduced infarct size, improved cardiac function, and preserved mitochondrial integrity in LAPTM5-deficient hearts. LAPTM5 protects against myocardial I/R injury by promoting mitophagy through the NEDD4-LC3 axis. PY3-dependent recruitment of NEDD4 and its E3 ubiquitin ligase activity facilitate LC3-associated mitochondrial clearance, accompanied by enhanced p62 ubiquitination, thereby preserving mitochondrial homeostasis during reperfusion.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70878.abstract: Functional assays can assist individualised selection of treatment regimens by evaluating the ex vivo response of tumour cells to anticancer therapeutics. However, the two major strategies used to assess responses to targeted drugs, target-based profiling and phenotypic profiling, have inherent limitations. Target-based profiling does not directly capture downstream cell-fate outcomes, whereas phenotypic profiling provides limited mechanistic information on drug action. Live-cell fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) microscopy was used to integrate the interaction between EGFRL858R and GRB2 with cellular phenotypic features, thereby predicting the efficacy of EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) at the single-cell level. The target-based drug score (T-score), derived from the interaction between EGFRL858R and GRB2 in living cells co-expressing CFP-EGFRL858R and YFP-GRB2, enabled evaluation of the on-target activity of EGFR-TKIs against EGFRL858R. The phenotype drug score (P-score), constructed from cellular phenotype features, characterised the phenotypic responses induced by EGFR-TKIs. The TP-score, integrating the T- and P-scores, accurately predicted the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs. In living H3255 cells, the TP-score of osimertinib (OSI) was higher than that of gefitinib (GEF). Notably, in H3255 cell-derived xenograft (CDX) mouse models, OSI showed superior in vivo antitumour efficacy compared with GEF. Furthermore, live-cell TP scoring revealed that primary tumour cells from a patient with NSCLC did not respond to OSI, a finding consistent with the absence of actionable EGFR mutations in this patient. This study demonstrates the clinical feasibility of predicting EGFR-TKI efficacy by integrating EGFRL858R-GRB2 interactions with cellular phenotypic features in single living cells.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70880.abstract: How PTEN function is impaired in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) without detectable genomic alterations remains unresolved. We investigated whether the long isoform of fatty acid-binding protein 6 (FABP6L) contributes to this process. Analyses that distinguished FABP6 isoforms identified FABP6L as the principal tumour-upregulated variant, whereas the short isoform, FABP6S, did not show a comparable increase. SHOX2 depletion preferentially reduced FABP6L expression. Biochemical experiments linked FABP6L to increased association between PTEN and the E3 ligase WWP2, enhanced PTEN polyubiquitination, and reduced PTEN protein stability. These changes were accompanied by increased AKT/mTOR signalling. Gain- and loss-of-function experiments supported a growth-promoting role for FABP6L in cultured ccRCC cells and xenografts, while genetic rescue experiments indicated a major contribution of PTEN to the signalling and growth phenotypes. In preclinical models with reduced everolimus sensitivity, FABP6L depletion increased PTEN abundance and enhanced the response to mTOR inhibition. The findings support an isoform-specific mechanism connecting FABP6L to PTEN turnover and ccRCC growth. They also provide a basis for investigating FABP6L-directed approaches to improve everolimus response, although their clinical relevance requires further validation.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70882.abstract: Epigenetic silencing of tumour suppressor genes is a pivotal early event in colorectal cancer (CRC) pathogenesis. PDZ and LIM Domain 4 (PDLIM4) is a member of the PDZ-LIM family with context-dependent roles in tumour progression across different malignancies. However, its specific role and epigenetic regulation in colorectal cancer (CRC) remain elusive. We integrated multi-omics datasets and clinical cohorts to evaluate PDLIM4 expression and promoter methylation. Stool DNA was analyzed to assess the feasibility of non-invasive detection of PDLIM4 promoter methylation. PDLIM4 knockout and overexpression cell lines were constructed to perform functional assays including proliferation, apoptosis, and stemness. In vivo experiments were validated utilizing xenograft mice or an azoxymethane (AOM)/ dextran sulphate sodium salt (DSS) CRC mouse model with intestinal epithelial cell-specific overexpression of PDLIM4. Mechanistic investigations were conducted using coimmunoprecipitation coupled with mass spectrometry, RNA sequencing, ChIP-qPCR and pharmacological rescue experiments. We identified a progressive loss of PDLIM4 protein along the normal-adenoma-carcinoma sequence, driven by DNMT3A-mediated promoter hypermethylation, and lower PDLIM4 expression was associated with adverse patient prognosis. PDLIM4 methylation was also significantly increased in stool DNA from CRC patients compared with healthy controls. Mechanistically, genetic ablation of PDLIM4 significantly blunted the therapeutic efficacy of the DNA demethylating agent 5-Azacytidine against CRC. Functionally, PDLIM4 restoration suppressed CRC cell proliferation and stemness while enhancing apoptosis in vitro, and reduced tumour growth in both AOM/DSS and xenograft models in vivo. At the molecular level, PDLIM4 interacted with BTF3 and promoted its autophagic-lysosomal degradation, thereby limiting PI3K/Akt signalling, with NTRK2 identified as a potential transcriptional target linking BTF3 to PI3K/Akt activation. DNMT3A-mediated silencing of PDLIM4 is an early epigenetic event that facilitates CRC progression. PDLIM4 suppresses tumour growth by promoting BTF3 degradation, thereby restricting PI3K/Akt signalling. Thus, PDLIM4 methylation may have potential as a biomarker for early CRC detection. DNMT3A-mediated PDLIM4 promoter hypermethylation is an early event in colorectal tumorigenesis. Restoring PDLIM4 suppresses CRC proliferation and stemness while promoting apoptosis in vitro and in vivo. PDLIM4 promotes the autophagic-lysosomal degradation of BTF3 and restrains PI3K/Akt signalling. Stool DNA analysis supports the potential of PDLIM4 methylation as a non-invasive CRC biomarker.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70886.abstract: Our previous study revealed that Piezo1 in colonic goblet cells senses mechanical stimuli to regulate the production and secretion of MUC2, but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Altered endoplasmic reticulum function and the unfolded protein response (UPR), which are critical for MUC2 protein folding and secretion, were observed in goblet cell-specific Piezo1 knockout mice. This study aimed to investigate whether and how Piezo1 in goblet cells modulates mucus barrier function by regulating the UPR. In vitro, LS174T cells were subjected to orbital shaking to simulate fluid shear stress (FSS) stimulation. The expression of UPR-related molecules and MUC2 was detected using real-time PCR, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence staining in the presence or absence of Piezo1 and UPR inhibition. In vivo, goblet cell-specific Piezo1 knockout (cKO) mice were treated with dextran sulphate sodium (DSS) and water avoidance stress (WAS). We analysed changes in goblet cell morphology, mucus layer thickness, UPR-related protein expression and ER structure. In addition, DSS-induced colitis mice were intraperitoneally injected with Yoda1 to activate Piezo1, and alterations in pathological structures and mucus layer thickness were subsequently evaluated. Compared with PERK or ATF6, FSS activated PIEZO1 and promoted calcium influx, thereby maintaining ER calcium homeostasis and selectively activating the IRE1α-XBP1 signalling pathway. This cascade facilitated MUC2 production, whereas pharmacological inhibition of PIEZO1 or IRE1α expression significantly abolished these effects. Compared with WT mice, cKO mice exhibited aggravated mucus barrier impairment, downregulated IRE1α-XBP1 and aggravated ER swelling under DSS and WAS. In contrast, pharmacological activation of Piezo1 via Yoda1 treatment restored intestinal mucus layer thickness and ameliorated colitis in DSS mice. Piezo1 senses mechanical stimulation to maintain ER calcium homeostasis and modulates the UPR via the IRE1α-XBP1 pathway, thereby facilitating MUC2 production in goblet cells and maintaining intestinal mucosal barrier homeostasis. Piezo1 in colonic goblet cells senses intestinal mechanical stimulation and modulates endoplasmic reticulum calcium homeostasis via Ca2+ influx. The Piezo1-Ca2+-IRE1α-XBP1 signaling axis controls Mucin2 synthesis and production to maintain intestinal mucus barrier integrity. Pharmacological activation of Piezo1 by Yoda1 rescues mucus barrier defects, providing a potential therapeutic strategy for gastrointestinal mucosal injury.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70889.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death among peritoneal dialysis (PD) patients, yet PD-specific biomarkers and prediction models remain limited. This study aimed to identify glycated peptide biomarkers associated with CVD in PD patients and develop a prediction model integrating glycated proteomics and clinical indicators using machine learning. In Phase I, a matched discovery cohort (48 PD patients with CVD and 48 without CVD) was used to identify glycated peptides by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), with glmnet used to prioritise candidate biomarkers. In Phase II, candidate biomarkers were quantified in a prospective internal derivation cohort (n = 240) and a multicentre external validation cohort (n = 102). The combined model was developed using F-test feature selection and elastic-net logistic regression. Its predictive performance was compared with three published cardiovascular risk models. Patients were stratified using a training-derived Youden cutoff. In the discovery cohort, 257 glycated peptides were differentially abundant between groups. Four candidate biomarkers were prioritised, and two peptides, GEAFTLK(g)ATVLNYLPK and K(g)QHLFVK, were retained in the final model together with six clinical indicators: phosphate, diabetes, total Kt/V, albumin, cardiac troponin T, and glycated albumin. The combined model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.784 in the training set, 0.781 in the internal testing set, and 0.822 in the external validation cohort, respectively. Using the training-derived cutoff of 0.373, higher 1-year CVD incidence was observed in the high-risk group in both validation cohorts. The combined model also achieved higher ROC-AUCs than the published cardiovascular risk models. We developed and externally validated a PD-specific CVD prediction model by integrating glycated peptide biomarkers with clinical indicators, which may facilitate earlier risk stratification and targeted prevention.

doi:10.1002/hon.3153.abstract: Abstract CD19‐targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T‐cells have revolutionized the treatment of lymphoid malignancies, including large B cell lymphoma (LBCL). Following seminal early phase multicenter clinical trials published between 2017 and 2020, three CD19‐CAR T‐cell products received FDA and EMA approval designations in lymphoma in the third‐line setting, paving the way for follow‐up studies in the second‐line. Meanwhile, investigations into the applications of CAR T‐cell therapy have further broadened to treating high‐risk patients even prior to completion of first‐line conventional chemo‐immunotherapy. Furthermore, as early trials excluded patients with central nervous system involvement with lymphoma, several studies have recently shown promising efficacy of CD19‐CAR T‐cells in primary and secondary CNS lymphoma. Here we provide a detailed overview on clinical data supporting the use of CAR T‐cells in patients with LBCL.

doi:10.1002/hon.70244.abstract: ABSTRACT Autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) with thiotepa‐based conditioning has replaced whole‐brain radiotherapy as consolidation for primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL), providing improved efficacy and reduced neurotoxicity. However, the optimal thiotepa‐containing regimen remains undefined. We retrospectively analyzed patients aged ≤ 60 years who underwent ASCT with thiotepa–busulfan–cyclophosphamide (TBC) or busulfan–thiotepa (BuTT) conditioning after high‐dose methotrexate–based induction at two Korean institutions between 2015 and 2023. Propensity score matching (PSM; n = 20 per group) was performed to adjust for baseline differences. Sixty‐seven patients were included (TBC, n = 30; BuTT, n = 37). TBC was associated with significantly longer progression‐free survival (PFS) from induction (3‐year: 89.9% vs. 72.1%, p = 0.034) and from transplantation (89.9% vs. 69.2%, p = 0.032); overall survival did not differ significantly. In multivariable Cox regression adjusted for pre‐transplant response and cumulative MTX exposure, BuTT was independently associated with inferior PFS (HR 4.09, 95% CI 1.27–13.18, p = 0.019). After PSM, TBC retained superior PFS (84.7% vs. 73.3%, p = 0.035), with a non‐significant trend in Cox analysis (HR 0.22, 95% CI 0.05–1.03, p = 0.054). TBC was associated with delayed engraftment and more grade ≥ 3 non‐hematologic toxicities, but no treatment‐related mortality occurred. In younger patients with PCNSL, TBC demonstrated a trend toward more durable disease control than BuTT, with manageable toxicity. As the thiotepa dose represents the major distinction between regimens, dose‐intensified thiotepa strategies with adjusted partner agents merit further prospective investigation.

doi:10.1002/hon.70245.abstract: ABSTRACT Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a hematological malignancy of mature clonal B‐cells commonly affecting elderly patients. Novel targeted therapies have improved survival, with 5‐year overall survival (OS) approaching that of the general population. However, data from Sub‐Saharan Africa, including Tanzania, remain scarce, and the epidemiology, clinical presentation, and treatment outcomes are poorly defined. We conducted a retrospective review of all patients diagnosed with hematological malignancies at the National Referral Hospital in Tanzania between January 2010 and December 2022, based on morphological assessment of peripheral blood or bone marrow aspirates. Data were analyzed using STATA v17. Descriptive statistics summarized patient characteristics. Trends in diagnosis were assessed using chi‐square and linear regression. Survival was estimated by Kaplan–Meier and predictors of mortality analyzed using Cox regression. Of 2751 patients diagnosed with hematological malignancies, 174 (6.3%) had CLL. CLL diagnoses increased significantly over time, with an average annual rise of 0.9% ( p = 0.001). Median age at diagnosis was 65 years (IQR 58–72), with a male‐to‐female ratio of 1.3:1. Most patients (71.9%) presented with advanced disease (Rai stage III/IV). Of the 174 patients, 144 received treatment, predominantly chlorambucil plus prednisolone (70.1%). Median OS was 3 years, with a 5‐year OS of 32.7% (95% CI 22.9–42.9), and 62% of patients died within 5 years. Untreated patients had a 2.5‐fold higher hazard of death compared to the treated patients. CLL is an uncommon hematological malignancy in Tanzania, presenting at a slightly younger age and predominantly with advanced disease. Outcomes remain poor with chlorambucil‐based therapy, underscoring the urgent need to strengthen diagnostics and expand access to effective targeted therapies.

doi:10.1002/hon.70246.abstract: ABSTRACT Multiple targeted agents are available for first‐line treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), yet the absence of mature head‐to‐head comparisons makes treatment selection challenging. The prospective, multicenter FIRST‐CLL study evaluated real‐world treatment allocation, and the contribution of biological, clinical, logistical and patient‐related factors to first‐line regimen choice in Italy. 285 consecutive patients with CLL/small lymphocytic lymphoma initiating first‐line therapy across 13 Centers were included. Treating physicians rated predefined variables guiding treatment selection using the 5‐point relevance score . Overall, 116 patients (41%) received continuous Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors (BTKi), 114 (40%) ibrutinib plus venetoclax (IV), and 55 (19%) venetoclax plus obinutuzumab (VO). Continuous BTKi were more frequently prescribed in older and comorbid patients, whereas IV was preferentially used in younger individuals. TP53 disruption was associated with BTKi use, while mutated immunoglobulin heavy chain status was common in patients receiving VO. According to relevance scores , age, treatment duration and administration route, and patient preference were the most influential determinants of treatment selection. Comorbidity burden additionally guided BTKi prescription, whereas molecular features were more relevant in the selection of fixed‐duration regimens. This study offers a real‐world quantitative assessment of treatment decision drivers in frontline CLL, offering a data‐driven framework to interpret clinical decision‐making.

doi:10.1002/hon.70247.abstract: ABSTRACT Philadelphia‐negative myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN), a spectrum of blood malignancies characterized by uncontrolled myeloid proliferation, persist as a key challenge in onco‐hematology due to their intricate molecular background, heterogeneous clinical phenotypes, and variable prognoses. Although generally accepted as indolent disorders, a considerable fraction of MPN patients exhibit progressive, and sometimes accelerated, bone marrow fibrosis, reflecting a critical shift toward a more debilitating condition marked by an increased symptom burden. As marrow scarring advances, hematopoietic capacity declines, severely compromising both patients' quality of life and survival. Increasing evidence highlights the crucial involvement of multiple players and mechanisms orchestrating marrow fibrotic transformation, thereby reflecting the multifaceted nature of this pathogenetic process. In this review, we untangle the pro‐fibrotic programs underlying fibrosis progression in MPN, critically analyzing the available scientific literature. We explore the potential impact of the mutational landscape on the fibrotic transformation risk and examine the role of dysfunctional megakaryocytes as principal catalysts of fibrotic remodeling. Additionally, we provide insight into the influence of the bone marrow microenvironment, examining the contribution of both soluble factors and direct cell‐cell communication in sustaining and exacerbating the fibrotic signature. The urgent need for earlier diagnoses, tailored prognoses, and more effective therapeutic strategies stresses the importance of investigating the pathological basis of fibrotic progression from a deeper perspective.

doi:10.1002/hon.70248.abstract: ABSTRACT In this hypothesis‐generating study, we integrated histopathology and transcriptomics in six patients with relapsed/refractory diffuse large B‐cell lymphoma (R/R DLBCL) receiving anti‐CD19 CAR‐T therapy, stratified into CAR‐T‐responsive and CAR‐T‐resistant cohorts by clinical response. Resistant tumors exhibited diffuse growth patterns with cohesive blast sheets, centroblastic morphology, tumor necrosis, and an immune‐desert tumor microenvironment. Transcriptomics revealed three transcriptional programs that may correlate with CAR‐T resistance: pro‐fibrotic/extracellular matrix remodeling, proliferative and pro‐survival traits, and immune dysfunction. Exploratory integrative analysis indicated associations between morphological features and pre‐existing pathway dysregulation in CAR‐T‐resistant patients, such as hyperactivated PI3K–Akt–mTOR and impaired antigen presentation. Collectively, these observations imply CAR‐T resistance in R/R DLBCL may stem from synergistic interplay among morphological aberrations, dysregulated proliferative/stromal pathways, and local immunosuppression. Pending prospective validation in larger independent cohorts, the candidate biomarkers observed herein may aid outcome prediction and combinatorial regimen design for R/R DLBCL.

doi:10.1002/hon.70249.abstract: ABSTRACT The therapeutic landscape for older adults with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) has undergone a major paradigm shift with the advent of lower‐intensity targeted regimens, particularly hypomethylating agents combined with venetoclax. As treatment transitions from acute induction to prolonged, multi‐cycle administration, clinical success increasingly depends on the patient's capacity to sustain repeated cycles, manage cytopenias and infections, and maintain functional independence. Current precision oncology models excel at characterizing the leukemic clone via cytogenetics, genomics, and measurable residual disease (MRD); however, they provide limited insight into the patient's underlying biological reserve. In this perspective, we propose host fitness as a critical, complementary dimension of precision medicine in older AML. Host fitness is a dynamic, multidimensional construct encompassing functional reserve, body composition, nutritional status, immune competence, inflammatory burden, and metabolic resilience. Moving beyond traditional performance status and simplistic metrics like body mass index, longitudinal assessment of host fitness aims to identify actionable vulnerabilities, guide targeted supportive interventions, and optimize treatment persistence. Integrating continuous host‐fitness evaluation with clonal profiling establishes a dual host–tumor precision‐medicine framework designed to maximize therapeutic efficacy while preserving patient resilience and quality of life.

doi:10.1002/hon.70251.abstract: ABSTRACT The craniofacial region represents a distinct yet poorly understood pattern of extranodal involvement in diffuse large B‐cell lymphoma (DLBCL). However, the prognostic significance and molecular characteristics of craniofacial involvement in extranodal DLBCL (EN‐DLBCL) remain unclear. This study included 164 patients with EN‐DLBCL, comprising 98 with craniofacial involvement (CFI) and 66 without. Prognostic factors and survival, as well as relapse and other clinical factors, were analyzed. Targeted next‐generation sequencing was performed in 87 cases. Patients with CFI had significantly inferior 5‐year progression‐free survival ( p = 0.0097) and overall survival ( p = 0.0088), and CFI remained an independent adverse prognostic factor after adjustment for International Prognostic Index (IPI). Sequencing showed that MYD88 , TMSB4X , and PCLO mutations were more frequent in the CFI group. Among the recurrently mutated genes in patients with CFI, only BTG2 mutation was associated with both inferior PFS and OS, whereas no significant prognostic effect was observed in patients without CFI. Immunohistochemistry further demonstrated significantly lower BTG2 expression in BTG2 ‐mutant samples than in wild‐type samples ( p = 0.008). These findings indicate that CFI defines a clinically unfavorable subset of EN‐DLBCL with distinct molecular features and that BTG2 alteration may serve as a candidate biomarker for risk stratification in this setting.

doi:10.1002/hon.70253.abstract: ABSTRACT In recent years the addition of the oral BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax to hypomethylating agents (HMAs) has emerged as the standard‐of‐care for patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) who are not fit for intensive chemotherapy, significantly improving survival and quality‐of‐life. Venetoclax is metabolized mainly by cytochrome P450 3A4 enzymes and serves as a P‐glycoprotein substrate, which make it largely affected by interactions with drugs. Dose reductions are needed to allow mold active antifungal prophylaxis, but there is no consensus on the exact venetoclax target dose concomitantly with posaconazole. We report on efficacy and safety of venetoclax combinations in 38 first‐line (FL) and 51 relapsed‐refractory (R/R) AML patients. Although complete remission (CR) rate was lower in R/R than in FL (49% vs. 68%; p = 0.08), achievement of this status was associated with comparable median overall survival (OS) in R/R and FL (13.67 vs. 13.72 months). Eighteen (20%) patients underwent allogenic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) with a 2‐year OS probability of 66.7%. Although antifungal prophylaxis was associated with a lower rate of grade 3–4 fungal infections (6% vs. 24%, p 0.044), patients treated with venetoclax daily dose of 50 mg with posaconazole had significantly shorter mOS in multivariate analysis (16.5 vs. 4.5 months; p 0.011). We conclude that AML patients in remission with venetoclax combinations may still be consolidated, and potentially cured, by HSCT, even after failure of intensive chemotherapy. Posaconazole prophylaxis effectively reduces risk of severe fungal infections, but a concomitant venetoclax dose of 50 mg may be sub‐optimal.

doi:10.1002/hon.70254.abstract: ABSTRACT The SH2B3 gene, also known as LNK , encodes an adaptor protein that negatively regulates key hematopoietic signaling pathways, including JAK–STAT, MAPK, and PI3K/AKT, thereby maintaining hematopoietic homeostasis. SH2B3 interacts with major signaling regulators such as JAK2, MPL, FLT3, and KIT. Loss‐of‐function alterations have been reported in several hematologic malignancies, supporting its role as a leukemia predisposition gene. We previously identified a germline start‐loss mutation (c.3G > A) in SH2B3 in a family with early‐onset myeloproliferative neoplasm, demonstrating that this variant causes SH2B3 haploinsufficiency. In the present study, next‐generation sequencing of 149 de novo AML patients identified a frequent intronic polymorphism (rs111340708), located within intron 6 (IVS6) of SH2B3 . Although this variant has a reported minor allele frequency (MAF) of approximately 12% in European populations, it was enriched in our AML cohort, reaching 34.2% in Core Binding Factor leukemias (CBFLs). The presence of the rs111340708 variant was associated with inferior overall survival, whereas no significant association with progression‐free survival was observed. Functional analyses demonstrated that this polymorphism promotes aberrant IVS6 intron retention in AML cells, resulting in reduced abundance of correctly spliced SH2B3 transcripts and predicted generation of truncated peptides and/or nonsense‐mediated decay. Consistently, immunoblot analyses of AML patient samples and hematologic cell lines revealed heterogeneous SH2B3 protein expression, including additional SH2B3‐immunoreactive species in variant carriers, together with reduced levels of the canonical SH2B3 protein. Collectively, these findings identify a common germline splicing polymorphism as a novel mechanism contributing to SH2B3 functional impairment in AML and highlight the potential relevance of non‐coding variants in leukemia pathogenesis, with possible implications for risk stratification and future therapeutic strategies.

doi:10.1002/hon.70256.abstract: ABSTRACT Natural killer/T‐cell lymphoma (NKTCL) is an aggressive lymphoma subtype with limited treatment options, especially for relapsed or refractory patients. Chidamide, a histone deacetylase inhibitor, and linperlisib, a phosphatidylinositol‐3‐kinase (PI3K) inhibitor, have shown promise in treating peripheral T‐cell lymphoma, but their effects on NKTCL are less explored. In this study, the therapeutic efficacy and mechanisms of combining chidamide and linperlisib in the treatment of NKTCL were investigated. Three human NKTCL cell lines (NKYS, KHYG1, and YT) were used to assess the effects of chidamide and linperlisib on cell proliferation, apoptosis, and the cell cycle. RNA‐seq and Western blot assays were employed to uncover the underlying mechanisms, and a YT xenograft mouse model was used for in vivo validation. Both chidamide and linperlisib exhibited dose‐ and time‐dependent anti‐tumor effects, and their combination enhanced efficacy, reduced cell viability, and increased apoptosis. This combination induced G2/M cell cycle arrest. Transcriptomic, Western blot, and immunohistochemical analysis revealed significant inhibition of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, which correlated with upregulation of the tumor suppressor PRDM1 . These findings were confirmed in the YT xenograft model. In conclusion, the combination of chidamide and linperlisib has synergistic anti‐tumor effects on NKTCL, which are mediated through inhibition of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, suggesting a promising therapeutic strategy for NKTCL management.

doi:10.1002/hon.70257.abstract: ABSTRACT Older or medically unfit patients with newly diagnosed FLT3‐mutated acute myeloid leukemia (AML) have poor outcomes with hypomethylating agent (HMA) monotherapy. Venetoclax plus HMA is a modern lower‐intensity standard, but FLT3‐mutated AML remains biologically heterogeneous, and triplet regimens combining HMA, venetoclax, and a FLT3 inhibitor are increasingly used despite limited randomized comparative evidence. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science, Scopus, and major hematology/oncology conference proceedings were searched from inception to 12 June 2026 in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and MOOSE guidance. Eligible studies reported primary clinical outcomes for newly diagnosed FLT3‐ITD and/or FLT3‐TKD AML treated with frontline lower‐intensity HMA alone, VEN‐HMA doublet, HMA/LIC plus FLT3 inhibitor, or HMA/LIC plus VEN plus FLT3 inhibitor therapy. Comparative effect estimates and single‐arm proportions were synthesized only when clinical and statistical assumptions were defensible. Thirteen eligible records were retained. Direct VEN + AZA versus AZA evidence came from one FLT3‐mutated pooled subgroup comparison (42 vs. 22 patients), showing CRc 67% versus 36%, RR 1.83 (95% CI 1.01–3.32), and median OS 12.5 versus 8.6 months. The randomized non‐venetoclax LACEWING trial showed higher CRc with gilteritinib + AZA than AZA (58.1% vs. 26.5%; HR for OS 0.916; p = 0.753), illustrating that improved remission does not guarantee survival benefit. The principal comparative triplet evidence was one retrospective study: CR/CRi 93% versus 70%, RR 1.32 (95% CI 1.09–1.61), with median OS not reached versus 9.5 months. Prospective and long‐term triplet reports described CR/CRi rates of 93%–96%, deep FLT3‐ITD MRD negativity, and median OS up to 38.5 months; several reports derive from overlapping institutional series and non‐randomized designs, limiting independent corroboration and causal inference. VEN + AZA improves remission compared with AZA in the FLT3‐mutated subgroup, but the evidence base is underpowered for FLT3‐specific survival conclusions. Triplet therapy produces the strongest remission‐depth and MRD signals but has not shown superiority over VEN‐HMA in a randomized frontline comparison. On current evidence, triplets are a promising biologically rational strategy requiring direct randomized validation against the contemporary VEN‐HMA standard.

doi:10.1002/hon.70258.abstract: ABSTRACT Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are clonal disorders with high risk of progression to acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo‐HSCT), including haploidentical HSCT (haplo‐HSCT), is the only curative option. Age‐stratified selection of conditioning regimens based on organ reserve and comorbidity burdens has been routine clinical practice for many years. However, recent developments warrant a critical re‐examination: the incorporation of hypomethylating agents and targeted therapies (decitabine, venetoclax), the introduction of the quantitative Transplant Conditioning Intensity (TCI) score, and emerging data in patients aged ≥ 70 years. This review summarizes age‐stratified regimens: myeloablative (MAC), reduced‐intensity (RIC), and reduced‐toxicity (RTC). In younger patients (< 50 years), MAC achieves 3‐year overall survival (OS) > 70% and non‐relapse mortality (NRM) < 15%. In middle‐aged (50–60 years) and elderly (> 60 years) patients, RIC/RTC yield OS of 60%–70% with NRM < 20%, though these estimates derive largely from retrospective or single‐center studies. Adding targeted/hypomethylating agents (e.g., decitabine, venetoclax) has shown promise in reducing relapse in high‐risk patients. Age‐stratified conditioning combined with these agents forms the core of individualized transplant strategies, reducing NRM and improving efficacy. Prospective, MDS‐specific randomized trials are urgently needed to transform these preliminary observations into evidence‐based standards.
