doi:10.1007/s00540-026-03923-5.abstract: The primary objective was to evaluate the influence of needle tip positioning during suprazygomatic maxillary nerve block on bupivacaine concentration within the pterygopalatine fossa (PPF). The secondary objective was to correlate early injectate spread on computed tomography (CT) with PPF bupivacaine concentrations. Suprazygomatic maxillary nerve block attempts (n=34) were performed on 17 human cadaveric heads with different needle tip positions. Each attempt involved injection of 5 mL containing 0.4% bupivacaine, iohexol, and methylene blue. Computed tomography was used to determine needle tip location and early injectate spread. PPF samples were harvested via a transmaxillary approach for bupivacaine quantification by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. The highest median [Q1-Q3] bupivacaine concentrations were observed when needle tip was positioned within pterygomaxillary fissure or PPF, with 829.3 [728.1-1015.7] µg/g, and when positioned directly against maxillary tuberosity, with 535.3 [355.7-820.7] µg/g. Concentrations were highly variable with off-bone infratemporal placements (range, 0.1-335.8 µg/g). Lateral needle displacement was associated with lower bupivacaine concentrations (β=-0.193, 95% CI -0.301 to -0.086; P<0.001), whereas anterior (β=0.107, 95% CI 0.018-0.196; P=0.020) and cranial displacement (β=0.079, 95% CI 0.017-0.141; P=0.014) were associated with higher concentrations. CT contrast spread between temporalis and lateral pterygoid muscles was not associated with higher PPF bupivacaine concentrations (P=0.117). Needle tip position influenced bupivacaine concentration within PPF, with concentrations generally increasing as the needle approached PPF and with more anterior positioning, including placement at the maxillary tuberosity. More superficial or posterior infratemporal placements yielded lower and more variable concentrations. Moreover, infratemporal contrast spread on early CT imaging was not associated with higher PPF bupivacaine concentrations.

doi:10.1007/s00540-026-03926-2.abstract: Pain during propofol injection is common, yet little is known about how often patients remember this experience after anesthesia or which perioperative factors influence memory formation during induction. In this prospective single-center observational cohort study, English-speaking adults (≥ 18 years) receiving propofol under general anesthesia (GA) or monitored anesthesia care (MAC) were enrolled. Perioperative characteristics, intravenous access details, anesthetic medications and clinician-observed injection pain were recorded. On postoperative day 1, patients were interviewed using a standardized questionnaire assessing recall of discomfort during induction. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses calculated adjusted odds ratios (aOR) and identified factors associated with recall. Of the 1,699 enrolled patients, 1,319 completed the postoperative day 1 assessment; 8.1% reported recall of injection discomfort. Multivariate analysis indicated that younger age (aOR = 1.03; 95% CI = 1.01-1.04; p < 0.001), female gender (aOR = 1.69; 95% CI = 1.02-2.82; p = 0.044), hand IV placement (aOR = 2.164; CI 95% = 1.287-3.636; p = 0.004), and absence of midazolam premedication (aOR = 2.62; 95% CI = 1.44-4.78; p = 0.002) were associated with increased recall. Approximately one in twelve patients recalled discomfort during propofol injection. Patient characteristics and modifiable anesthetic practices, particularly premedication and intravenous access site, were associated with memory of propofol injection discomfort. These findings highlight that memory formation during induction represents a distinct and clinically relevant patient-centered outcome.

doi:10.1007/s00540-026-03927-1.abstract: Anesthetic management in general surgery poses substantial risks in elderly patients because age-related physiologic decline and preexisting comorbidities increase vulnerability to peri-operative complications. Older adults have reduced physiological reserve, impaired organ function, and slower recovery from surgical and anesthetic stress, placing them at increased risk for postoperative delirium and early postoperative cognitive impairment. Dexmedetomidine, a selective α2-adrenergic receptor agonist, has sedative, anti-inflammatory, and opioid-sparing properties that may influence early postoperative cognitive outcomes without significant respiratory depression. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the association between dexmedetomidine and 24-h postoperative delirium/early postoperative cognitive impairment in elderly patients undergoing general surgery. Four studies involving 479 patients met the inclusion criteria. Across the included studies, dexmedetomidine was generally administered as a 1 µg/kg loading dose followed by continuous intraoperative maintenance infusion of 0.2-0.7 µg/kg/h. Pooled analysis showed that dexmedetomidine was associated with significantly lower odds of 24-h postoperative delirium/early postoperative cognitive impairment compared with control treatment (pooled OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.24-0.61; p < 0.001). These findings suggest that dexmedetomidine is associated with lower odds of early postoperative cognitive outcomes in elderly surgical patients compared with control treatment. Larger, long-term studies are needed to confirm these findings and establish standardized dosing protocols.

doi:10.1007/s00540-026-03935-1.abstract: Some parturients experience discomfort, pain, and nausea/vomiting during cesarean delivery under neuraxial anesthesia. We evaluated whether intravenous dexmedetomidine administered after fetal delivery and cord clamping improved maternal intraoperative experience. In this prospective, triple-blind, placebo-controlled trial, women aged 20-45 years undergoing elective cesarean delivery under combined spinal-epidural anesthesia were randomized 1:1 to dexmedetomidine or saline. Dexmedetomidine was administered after cord clamping as a loading dose of 1 μg/kg over 10 min, followed by 0.4 μg/kg/hr until peritoneal closure; controls received equivalent-volume saline. The primary outcome was satisfaction with intraoperative sedation/analgesia, assessed on postoperative day 1 using a 7-point verbal rating scale. Secondary outcomes were Quality of Recovery-40 score, maximum intraoperative pain score, intraoperative nausea/vomiting, and motor recovery time. Eighty-three participants were randomized; 81 contributed to the available-case analysis. Satisfaction scores were higher with dexmedetomidine than saline (Hodges-Lehmann location shift, 1.0 point; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.0 to 2.0; P < 0.001). In ordinal logistic regression, dexmedetomidine was associated with higher satisfaction scores (common odds ratio, 13.4; 95% CI 4.6 to 39.0). Dexmedetomidine reduced intraoperative pain and intraoperative nausea/vomiting, but did not improve 24-h Quality of Recovery-40 scores and modestly prolonged motor recovery. Post-delivery intravenous dexmedetomidine improved patient-reported satisfaction with intraoperative sedation and analgesia. Exploratory findings suggested reduced pain and nausea/vomiting without improved 24-h recovery. These findings support further evaluation of dexmedetomidine as a selective adjunct rather than for routine sedation. doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08094-1.abstract: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the potential impact of a Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-cleared artificial intelligence (AI)-based decision support tool for breast ultrasound in reducing benign biopsies. This study was conducted at two academic medical centers from March to May 2025 following the clinical implementation of an FDA-cleared AI-based decision support tool for breast ultrasound interpretation (Koios DS; New York, NY). Fourteen breast imaging radiologists documented BI-RADS 4 (suspicious) cases, along with the corresponding AI output. AI assessments were compared with biopsy pathology results to characterize AI classification within this selected cohort. Overall, 271 lesions in 253 women (mean age, 54 years; range, 24-92 years) were categorized as BI-RADS 4 and were biopsied, aspirated, and/or surgically excised. Of these, 23.2% (63/271) yielded malignant pathology, while 76.8% (208/271) were benign. The AI tool classified 90.5% (57/63) of malignant lesions as BI-RADS 4 and 9.5% (6/63) as BI-RADS 2 or 3. Among benign cases, the AI tool assigned 41.8% (87/208) as BI-RADS 2 (benign), 18.8% (39/208) as BI-RADS 3 (probably benign), and 39.4% (82/208) as BI-RADS 4 (suspicious). Retrospective application of the AI output to biopsy triage decisions suggests the potential for reduction in benign biopsy recommendations, with 60.6% (126/208) of benign lesions classified by the AI tool as BI-RADS 2 or 3. AI may help reduce benign biopsy recommendations among lesions assessed as BI-RADS 4 by radiologists; however, careful integration with radiologist judgment and clinical history is essential to ensure timely cancer diagnosis.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08095-0.abstract: Various social determinants of health (SDOH) have been shown to negatively impact breast cancer outcomes. Though there are recommendations for comprehensive SDOH assessment, little is known about the optimal frequency of reassessments and change in health-related social needs (HRSN) over time for specific patient populations. We sought to characterize SDOH screening and HRSN patterns among patients with breast cancer in a safety-net system. A retrospective study was conducted to evaluate SDOH survey responses in the electronic medical records and screening frequency from patients diagnosed with breast cancer between January 2021 to January 2024 at Parkland Health. There were 566 patients diagnosed with breast cancer with a mean age at diagnosis of 55.0 (standard deviation, SD: 11.4) years. There were 54 (9.5%) with Stage IV breast cancer. Patients were initially at risk for 1.36 (SD: 1.39) out of the 11 HRSN domains. Patients completed an average 17.3 (SD: 8.9) out of 28 questions on initial survey. The most common risk domains identified were Alcohol Use and Food Insecurity. No patients were screened for Interpersonal Violence. The median time from initial survey to first change in risk level for any domain was 8.7 months. Patients with Stage IV disease underwent fewer SDOH re-screenings compared to patients with Stage I, II, and III disease (p < 0.001). Within our system, greater attention should be placed towards fully assessing patients' HRSN and screening for interpersonal violence. SDOH screening at 6-month intervals may help to capture changes in HSRNs and assess the impact of resource interventions.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08096-z.abstract: Endocrine therapy for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer is associated with adverse metabolic effects - including increased fat mass, decreased lean muscle mass, and insulin resistance - that may attenuate the efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). This study evaluated GLP-1 RA-associated weight loss outcomes in breast cancer patients receiving concurrent endocrine therapy. We conducted a retrospective cohort analysis of 269 breast cancer patients at a single academic center receiving concurrent GLP-1 RA and adjuvant endocrine therapy. GLP-1 RA and endocrine therapy data were obtained from electronic medication reconciliation lists and pharmacy dispense reports. Patients were required to have initiated GLP-1 therapy during the study period and to have received concurrent GLP-1 RA and endocrine therapy for at least one year. The primary outcome was percentage weight change from GLP-1 initiation to 12 months (± 2 months). Secondary outcomes included proportions achieving ≥ 5%, ≥ 10%, and ≥ 15% weight loss. Mean one-year percentage weight loss was - 4.5% (95% CI: -6.0% to - 3.0%; -3.9 kg; 95% CI: -4.96 to - 2.93 kg), significantly below the 10-20% observed in postmenopausal subgroups of GLP-1 randomized trials (all p < 0.001). Only 21.3% achieved ≥ 10% and 10.4% achieved ≥ 15% weight loss. Weight loss differed significantly by GLP-1 agent (p = 0.003); semaglutide (- 5.8%) and tirzepatide (- 4.7%) outperformed dulaglutide (+ 0.1%), which is approved for type 2 diabetes only. Higher baseline weight was associated with greater absolute loss (r = - 0.19, p = 0.002), though percentage weight loss did not differ significantly by baseline BMI category (p = 0.303). PR-negative patients lost more than PR-positive patients (- 8.2% vs. -4.2%; p = 0.021, d = 0.46). Type 2 diabetes was present in 70.6% of patients; T2DM status was not significantly associated with weight loss on t-test (p = 0.288), though patients without T2DM were numerically more likely to achieve ≥ 15% loss (21.5% vs. 5.8%). GLP-1 RAs produce statistically significant but substantially attenuated weight loss in breast cancer patients on concurrent endocrine therapy. GLP-1 agent selection significantly influences outcomes. Given emerging evidence of oncologic benefit, prospective trials are needed.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08097-y.abstract: Breast conservation for invasive breast cancer is associated with better survival and fewer complications than mastectomy, which is especially relevant for older patients. It is unclear whether this can be extrapolated to ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). This population-based cohort study used data from the Breast Cancer Database Sweden (BCBaSe 3.0) to compare overall survival (OS), breast cancer-specific survival (BCSS) and local recurrence (LR) probabilities in three different age groups (< 60, 60-69, 70 + years) of women with primary DCIS undergoing breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy (BCS + RT), mastectomy without radiotherapy (Mx-RT), or breast-conserving surgery without radiotherapy (BCS-RT) during 2008-2019. Complete cases (CC) and multiple imputation (MI) analyses were applied. In 7165 women, treatment was BCS + RT (53.3%), BCS-RT (13.4%), or Mx-RT (33.2%). Estimated 10-year OS was 90.4% (95% CI 89.3-91.5) and BCSS 98.8% (98.3-99.2). After adjustments for patient and tumour factors, including socioeconomic status and comorbidity, Mx-RT was associated with a higher overall mortality than BCS + RT in CC (HR 2.10; 95% CI 1.20-3.67) but not in MI analyses (HR 1.29; 0.95-1.76). In age 70 + years, however, the overall mortality was consistently increased (CC: HR 2.48; 1.09-5.62, MI: HR 1.89; 1.23-2.90). Also BCS-RT was associated with a higher overall mortality than BCS + RT (CC: HR 2.68; 1.34-5.34, and MI: HR 1.72; 1.23-2.39). The 10-year LR probability was low (7.2%, 95% CI 6.3-8.0). Compared to BCS + RT, Mx-RT was associated with a lower (HR 0.18, 95% CI 0.11-0.28) and BCS-RT with a higher LR risk (HR 1.79; 1.31-2.46), especially among ages 70+. BCS + RT in DCIS appears safe. Acknowledging potential selection bias, BCS + RT may be associated with favourable overall survival outcomes in older women despite a higher risk of local recurrence.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08098-x.abstract: To compare late toxicities, cosmetic outcomes, and reconstruction failure in patients undergoing immediate autologous reconstruction (AR) versus implant-based reconstruction (IBR) followed by postmastectomy radiotherapy (PMRT). A multi-institutional retrospective cohort study (2013-2024) assessed patients undergoing mastectomy with immediate reconstruction and PMRT. Primary endpoints were reconstruction failure (loss or replacement of the index implant reconstruction, or total flap loss) and late toxicities, including contracture, fat necrosis, and cosmesis (Kroll scale). 113 patients were included (68 AR, 45 IBR). AR utilised deep inferior epigastric perforator flaps; IBR cohort consisted of 41 direct-to-implant procedures and four latissimus dorsi flaps combined with implants. Among available baseline variables, cohorts were broadly similar except that AR patients were slightly older. Reconstruction failure was analysed in all IBR patients; four IBR patients were not evaluable for subsequent capsular contracture and cosmetic assessment because of implant removal before late assessment. Reconstruction failure occurred exclusively in IBR (28.9% [13 of 45] vs. 0% [0/68] in AR; P < 0.001). Clinically significant firmness was observed in 46.3% (19/41) of IBR versus 14.7% (10/68) of AR patients (P < 0.001). Fat necrosis occurred in 16.2% of AR patients without flap loss. Good/Excellent physician-assessed cosmesis was more frequent after AR (83.8% vs. 36.6%; P < 0.001). Recurrence rates were comparable between cohorts. AR was associated with higher reconstruction survival and more favourable physician-assessed cosmetic outcomes compared with predominantly direct-to-implant, subpectoral IBR after PMRT. For patients with a high probability of requiring PMRT, AR should be discussed early and strongly considered when clinically feasible.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08100-6.abstract: Podany et al. examined associations between Area Deprivation Index (ADI) and tumor genomics, PI3K inhibitor use, and survival in 1,127 patients with metastatic breast cancer. While their multi-institutional, genomically annotated dataset is a valuable contribution, several methodological issues warrant scrutiny. We critically reviewed the study's statistical approach, focusing on multiple-comparison handling, potential confounding from ctDNA shedding variability, and the reliability of subgroup survival estimates. Key findings (TP53, AKT1, overall survival, PI3Ki-use disparity, and Black patient survival disadvantage) relied on borderline p-values from uncorrected multiple comparisons across 19 supplementary tables. Lower visceral, nodal, and soft-tissue metastasis rates in high-deprivation patients suggest reduced ctDNA shedding, which could confound reported mutation-frequency differences, particularly for AKT1. The AKT1 subgroup hazard ratio (6.27) derived from roughly five events, far below recommended events-per-variable thresholds, raising concerns about estimate stability. Addressing multiplicity correction, ctDNA shedding assessment, and transparent event-count reporting would strengthen confidence in the study's conclusions and better inform future prospective research.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08101-5.abstract: Drug resistance is a major cause of treatment failure in breast cancer patients. Numerous genetic and epigenetic markers have been proposed to influence Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy (NACT) response, and genes that regulate the effectiveness of chemotherapeutic agents undergo expression regulation via methylation. In this study, we aimed to investigate the methylation levels of KDM5A, KDM5B, and KDM5C, as well as their associated genes, EZH2, TFAP2C, ZMYND8, and SIN3B (Exon 1-2 and 19-20), in blood samples collected from patients before and after NACT treatment. Besides, we also examined potential variations in the KDM5A, KDM5B, and KDM5C gene regions. Twenty patients were diagnosed with breast cancer, and 30 healthy control individuals were included in the study. Blood samples were taken from the patients twice, before and after NACT. Methylation levels of KDM5 family genes and related genes were analyzed using Methylation-specific PCR (MSP). Additionally, potential variants in the KDM5A, KDM5B, and KDM5C gene regions were identified using Sanger sequencing. According to the methylation analysis results, the SIN3B (Exon 19-20), KDM5C, EZH2, and TFAP2C genes were prominent in patients with pathological partial response, while the KDM5A, KDM5B, KDM5C, EZH2, TFAP2C, and SIN3B (Exon 19-20) genes were prominent in patients with pathological complete response. According to genotyping results, rs41308616 and rs971896841 variants were detected as heterozygous in the KDM5C gene region in two patients, respectively. The methylation percentages and genetic variations in the KDM5 family and related gene regions identified in this study may serve as potential biomarkers for developing treatment strategies for breast cancer patients.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08102-4.abstract: Idiopathic granulomatous mastitis (IGM) is a benign inflammatory breast condition that can resemble mastitis or malignancy clinically and radiographically. We aimed to develop a quantitative scoring system, based off the Komen Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC) scoring system [1], evaluating clinical and radiologic features to distinguish IGM from benign and malignant breast conditions. We conducted a retrospective chart review of biopsy-proven IGM patients diagnosed from 2014 to 2025 via institutional electronic medical records. Clinical symptom onset, features, and diagnostic imaging were analyzed. A continuous scoring scale (1-50) was created, encompassing three categories: symptom onset, clinical features, and radiographic findings. Scores of IGM patients were compared with those of patients diagnosed with IBC, mastitis (lactational and non-lactational), and locally advanced breast cancer (LABC). Welch's two-sample t-test assessed statistical differences, and Youden index identified the optimal score threshold for predicting IGM. Among 148 IGM patients, predominantly Hispanic (56.8%) and Asian (26.7%), the mean age was 37.2 years, older than mastitis patients and younger than IBC patients. Key clinical features included pain or painful breast mass (100%), fistula or draining wound (77.7%), erythema (94.6%), and phlegmon (87.8%). Imaging revealed mass with collection in 84.6% and multiple masses/collections in 38.9%. The mean IGM score (35.5) was significantly higher than scores for IBC, mastitis, and LABC groups (14.4, 18, and 15.2, respectively; p ≤ 0.05). A score ≥ 24.5 predicted IGM with 93% sensitivity and 95% specificity. This novel scoring system provides an objective framework to differentiate IGM from similar breast conditions, facilitating early diagnosis and guiding appropriate management. not applicable.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08103-3.abstract: When a radial sclerosing lesion (RSL) with associated epithelial atypia is diagnosed on image-guided core needle biopsy, current guidelines recommend complete excision to exclude malignancy. Prior studies have reported that a substantial proportion of such lesions will be 'upgraded' to malignancy when surgical excision is undertaken. More personalized management may be possible if subgroups with lower risk of harboring malignancy are identified. Following a systematic review of existing studies, we conducted an observational cohort study including all RSLs with associated atypia diagnosed on image-guided needle biopsy performed at our institution from 2020 to 2025. We estimated the cumulative incidence of malignancy at the RSL site in subgroups defined by the type of epithelial atypia and whether the atypia involved the RSL or was in the adjacent tissue. A total of 105 RSLs with associated atypia were included. Surgical excision was performed following biopsy diagnosis for 22 of 24 (91.7%) with atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) involving the RSL, 17 of 35 (48.6%) with ADH in the adjacent tissue, 16 of 20 (80.0%) with lobular neoplasia or other atypia involving the RSL, and 7 of 26 (26.9%) with lobular neoplasia or other atypia in the adjacent tissue. The remaining lesions underwent imaging surveillance. The cumulative incidence of malignancy at 3 years was 29.2% (95% CI: 15.1, 51.6%) for lesions with ADH involving the RSL; 8.6% (95% CI: 2.8, 24.3%) for lesions with ADH in the adjacent tissue; and 2.2% (95% CI: 0.3, 14.4%) for lesions with lobular neoplasia or other atypia. Lesions with ADH involving a RSL are likely to harbor malignancy. For other subgroups, the risk of malignancy is lower. These findings provide evidence that may be used to inform shared decision-making around imaging surveillance for selected patients with RSL and atypia on core needle biopsy.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08104-2.abstract: Germline genetic testing is increasing. While testing barriers are well characterized, less is known about post-testing needs and utilization of screening and prevention resources by women with pathogenic variants (PVs) in breast cancer susceptibility genes. A 38-question online survey was developed by Facing Our Risk of Cancer Empowered (FORCE), a patient advocacy group, and administered electronically to subscribers from February-May 2024. Study eligibility criteria included female sex and a germline PV conferring elevated lifetime risk of breast cancer (ATM, BARD1, BRCA1, BRCA2, CDH1, CHEK2, PALB2, PTEN, RAD51C, RAD51D, STK11, or TP53). Of 1,025 respondents who initiated the survey, 937 were women. Most were non-Hispanic White (91.7%) and from the United States (81.6%). The most common PVs were BRCA2 (31.4%), BRCA1 (25.5%) and CHEK2 (9.2%). The most frequently used resources were education and information services about medical options (39.3%) and peer support (28.1%). Few respondents used financial navigation (4.0%) or financial support (5.3%), but up to 45% reported needing these services. Among breast screening users (53.8% used mammogram, 42.2% magnetic resonance imaging, 19.4% ultrasound), 37.8% found it hard to prepare emotionally for results and 14% found it hard to pay for screening. One-third (37.1%) of respondents found deciding whether to have risk-reducing mastectomy hard; two-thirds (64.0%) found physical recovery hard, more than half (60.2%) found emotional recovery hard, and one-quarter (24.7%) found paying for risk-reducing mastectomy hard. In this contemporary sample of women at elevated risk of breast cancer, more than one-third had unmet financial needs and up to two-thirds had difficulty with screening or risk-reducing surgery. Closing these gaps will be essential to improve outcomes for women with hereditary breast cancer.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08105-1.abstract: High-volume hospitals deliver improved outcomes for patients with breast cancer, supporting referrals for breast cancer surgical care to high-volume regional facilities. This retrospective cohort study investigated how multidisciplinary cancer care trajectories and patient care experiences varied by surgical facility classification (regional vs. community as a proxy for high- vs. low-volume) and whether effects differed by rural-residence. We used Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results-Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems (SEER-CAHPS) data for Medicare beneficiaries who received surgery for non-metastatic breast cancer from 2009 to 2019. We mapped cancer care trajectories using facility classification and oncologist specialty and performed state sequence analysis to identify care trajectory clusters. We used linear mixed-effects models to examine associations of surgical facility classification with patient-reported experience measures and assessed effect modification by rurality. Of the 3,327 patients in our cohort, 15.4% were rural-residing and 68.8% received surgery at a regional facility. Care trajectories indicated that patients tended to receive adjuvant care from the same type of facility as their surgical treatment. Patients who received surgery at community facilities (vs. regional) were significantly more likely to report better experiences with getting needed care (Est. (95%CI) = 3.5 (0.10,6.9), p = 0.043), with no significant differences for getting care quickly, care coordination, or doctor communication. Rural-residence was not a significant effect modifier. Receiving surgery at community facilities is associated with better patient-reported experiences for getting needed care. Moreover, surgical facility classification appears to influence the setting for subsequent cancer care, which may impact patient experiences in getting needed care. Not applicable.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08106-0.abstract: De-escalation has become standard across breast cancer management. Many early-stage HR+/HER2-negative breast cancers are eligible for both SLNB omission and accelerated partial breast irradiation (APBI). However, the oncologic safety of dual de-escalation has not been evaluated except in patients ≥ 70 years. We sought to characterize national practice patterns and factors associated with adoption of this dual de-escalation approach. Women aged 50-69 years with clinical T1-T2N0 breast cancer who underwent upfront breast-conserving surgery between (2012 - 2022) were identified from the National Cancer Database. Patients were categorized by axillary surgery and by adjuvant radiation modality (WBI, APBI, or none). We assessed trends and factors associated with de-escalation. 316,324 patients met inclusion criteria, of whom 98% underwent SLNB. Among patients who underwent SLNB, 83% received WBI, 11% received APBI, and 6% received no radiation. In contrast, among patients in whom SLNB was omitted, 63% received WBI, 8% received APBI, and 30% received no radiation. SLNB omission remained low throughout the study period at < 3%, while APBI use increased from 8% to 16.5%. Dual de-escalation was rarely performed throughout the study period remaining < 0.30%. Shared predictors of de-escalation included cT1 tumors, ductal histology, low grade, and treatment at academic/research programs. These findings highlight the need for prospective studies to define the safety, outcomes, and patient selection criteria for combined de-escalation strategies. Until these data are available, patient-centered discussions are essential to determine the most appropriate strategy for patients with low-risk disease.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08107-z.abstract: The interval between breast cancer diagnosis and surgery is psychologically demanding, and meeting the Swedish standardised care pathway target has remained challenging. We examined whether diagnosis-to-surgery lead time is associated with patient-reported psychological outcomes. We conducted a longitudinal cohort study using Swedish National Quality Register for Breast Cancer data (2020-2024). The cohort comprised 2,906 women with primary invasive breast cancer undergoing surgery, with patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) data at baseline (n = 2,906), 6 months (n = 2,638), and 12 months (n = 2,678). Lead time from biopsy to surgery was modelled continuously (per 1 SD ≈ 19 days). The primary outcome was worry about future health (EORTC QLQ-BR23 item 43); secondary outcomes were general worry, tension, depressed mood, and overall quality of life. Associations were estimated using mixed-effects cumulative link models adjusted for clinical and tumour factors, pandemic era, patient, and healthcare region. Median lead time was 32 days (IQR 23-42). Longer lead time was associated with greater worry about future health (adjusted OR 1.15 per SD, 95% CI 1.04-1.27), while associations with the secondary outcomes were smaller and not statistically significant. At baseline, high future-health worry was more common with lead times > 35 vs. ≤ 35 days (42.2% vs. 35.1%). Longer diagnosis-to-surgery lead time was associated with greater future-health worry, with smaller, non-significant associations for general distress and quality of life. The findings highlight the preoperative waiting period as a potential context for improved communication about expected timelines and reasons for delay.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08108-y.abstract: Advancements in human epidermal growth factor (HER)-targeted therapy have significantly improved survival in patients with de novo metastatic HER-2 positive (HER2+) breast cancer (dnMBC). The role of breast surgery is debated. We examined which HER2 + dnMBC patients undergo surgery and compared outcomes to systemic therapy alone. We performed a single institution retrospective review of patients with HER2 + dnMBC diagnosed 2011-2023. Data included demographics, clinicopathologic details, treatment information, local and distant disease progression, and survival outcomes. Analyses included logistic regression, Kaplan Meier, and Cox proportional hazards models. The study included 103 patients. Of these, 42.7% underwent breast surgery (70.5% mastectomy, 29.5% lumpectomy). Of these, 72.7% underwent axillary surgery (38.6% axillary lymph node dissection, 27.3% sentinel lymph node biopsy, 6.8% targeted axillary dissection). The median age at diagnosis was 48 years (surgery) and 56 years (no surgery) (p = 0.10). The surgery group had lower number of metastatic sites (1.3 vs. 1.9, p = 0.003) and exhibited higher rates of local disease progression pre-operatively (39% vs. 23.5%, p = 0.05). Post-operatively, there was no significant difference in local disease progression (17.1% vs. 23.5%, p = 0.42). After adjusting for age, sites of metastases, and number of metastatic sites, those who underwent surgery had improved overall survival (HR 0.33 (0.14-0.77), p = 0.02). Patients with HER2 + dnMBC with lower metastatic disease burden and local disease progression were more likely to undergo breast surgery. There was no significant difference in local disease control post-operatively. The significant association between surgery and improved survival must be interpreted with caution due selection bias in this retrospective study.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08110-4.abstract: Race and ethnicity play an important role in breast cancer disparities; however, these variables are not consistently reported in research articles. Our study evaluates contemporary trends in racial and ethnic demographic reporting in clinical breast surgery research over a six-year period. PubMed search engine was queried for breast surgery related clinical research articles published from January 2017 to June 2023. The four breast journals with the highest impact factors were evaluated: Annals of Surgical Oncology, Breast Cancer Research and Treatment, Clinical Breast Cancer, and The Breast Journal. Statistical analyses were conducted using chi-square, Fisher's exact tests, or Cochran-Armitage Trend Test. Among 288 studies included, 181 (62.9%) reported any race/ethnicity. Studies were divided based on year of publication into three study periods: 2017-2018 (n = 108), 2019-2020 (n = 87), 2021-2023 (n = 93). Studies consistently reported White race across all time periods (100% vs. 96.4% vs. 100.0%) (p = 0.09), along with Black race (79.3% vs. 76.4% vs. 88.2%, p = 0.20), Asian race (50.0% vs. 45.5% vs. 60.3%, p = 0.24), Hispanic ethnicity (46.6% vs. 47.3 vs. 48.5%, p = 0.97), and "Other" race (55.2% vs. 61.8% vs. 66.2%, p = 0.45). Reporting of any race/ethnicity was found to have increased in recent years (53.7% vs. 63.2% vs. 73.1%, p < 0.01), only up to 73.1% in 2021-2023. Race reporting in high-impact breast surgery journals has increased significantly from 2017 to 2023, although only reaching 73.1% in 2021-2023. Specific populations, including Hispanics and Asian-Americans, remain underrepresented. While increasing, race reporting remains limited in clinical breast research, underscoring the need for more consistent and comprehensive research standards.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08111-3.abstract: Infiltrating lobular carcinoma (ILC) accounts for ~ 10% of all invasive breast cancer histologies. ILC is associated with worse prognosis than infiltrating ductal cancer. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are commonly elevated in metastatic breast cancer (mBC) and elevated levels of CTCs are associated with worse prognosis in breast cancers. We investigated CTC incidence in ILC in two patient cohorts. Data from electronic medical records at the University of Michigan were identified using the EMERSE search engine to assess CTC levels in patients with mBC, using CellSearch®. Findings were validated in a separate cohort of mBC patients who participated in a research protocol where CTC were analyzed. Within the EMERSE cohort of 218, 38 (17%), 29 (13%) and 151 (69%) patients, had lobular, mixed, and ductal mBC subtype, respectively. Overall, 101/218 (46%) patients had elevated CTC (≥ 5/7.5 ml whole blood). In this cohort, patients with ILC were more likely to have elevated CTCs (28/38; 74%) compared to those with mixed (14/29; 48%) or ductal (59/151; 39%) mBC (p = 0.001). In multivariate regression, patients with ILC were seven times more likely than ductal mBC to have elevated CTCs. These data were validated in 146 separate mBC patients in the research cohort. Elevated CTCs were detected in 79%, 31%, and 36% of patients with lobular, mixed and ductal mBC, respectively. CTC are more commonly elevated and tend to be higher in magnitude in patients with lobular compared to ductal mBC. CTC levels in mixed ductal-lobular morphology numerically more resemble ductal mBC.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08112-2.abstract: Chemotherapy and pembrolizumab treatment can improve survival in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), but data are limited in older adults. We examined treatment patterns, efficacy, and safety for older patients on pembrolizumab for early-stage (eTNBC) and metastatic TNBC (mTNBC). Through medical record review, we collected tumor, treatment, and outcome data for patients ≥ 65 years receiving pembrolizumab-containing therapy for TNBC between 2021 and 2024. For all, we examined immune related adverse events (irAEs) and hospitalizations. For eTNBC, we examined percent ideal dose, treatment discontinuation, and factors associated with pathologic complete response (pCR). Among patients with mTNBC, progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier methods. Among 136 included patients, median age was 71 (range 63-91); 85 had eTNBC, of whom 42% received the neoadjuvant KEYNOTE-522 regimen. There were 51 with mTNBC who received a variety of regimens. In eTNBC, mean ideal dose was 82%, 43% had a pCR, 41% were hospitalized, 39% experienced irAEs, and 4% had treatment-related deaths. Patients aged > 70 had more irAEs, and lower % ideal dose. No clinical or treatment variables were associated with pCR. In mTNBC, 43% were hospitalized, 18% were admitted to the ICU, and 41% experienced irAEs. With a median follow-up of 29 months, median PFS was 5.45 months (95% CI, 3.8-7.8), and median OS was 23.1 months (95% CI, 18.6-35.4). In this cohort of older adults with TNBC receiving pembrolizumab-containing treatment, we observed high rates of serious toxicity, with lower-than-expected pCR rates in eTNBC, and short OS in mTNBC. Not applicable.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08113-1.abstract: Evidence is inconsistent regarding an association between alcohol consumption and survival following a breast cancer diagnosis; therefore, we examined how change in alcohol consumption affects all-cause mortality (ACM) in a population of breast cancer survivors. We prospectively assessed pre-diagnosis, pre- to post-diagnosis, and post-diagnosis change in alcohol consumption among 1,558 postmenopausal women (mean age-at-diagnosis: 71 years) diagnosed with non-metastatic invasive breast cancer from the American Cancer Society Cancer Prevention Study-II Nutrition Cohort (baseline: 1992-1993). Five categories of alcohol intake were determined at each assessment; change in alcohol consumption was categorized as stable, quit, reduced, and increased. Change occurred at a median of two years before (pre-diagnosis) and two years after (post-diagnosis) diagnosis. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to estimate adjusted hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the associations between change groups and ACM. Over a median follow-up of 12.6 years, 750 women died (130 breast cancer deaths). Compared to stable consumption, the association between cessation and ACM varied by change interval: pre-diagnosis (HR:0.91, CI:0.69-1.21), pre- to post-diagnosis: (HR:1.39, CI:1.12-1.73), post-diagnosis: (HR:0.98, CI:0.70-1.35). Alcohol reduction was not associated with ACM. Among women consuming ≥ 1 drink/day pre-diagnosis, increasing consumption elevated ACM risk (HR:1.83, 95%CI:1.02-3.31). Alcohol reduction or cessation was not associated with a decrease in ACM among older breast cancer survivors. Among those drinking ≥ 1 drink/day, an increase in consumption pre-diagnosis was associated with higher mortality. Findings may be limited by uncontrolled confounding, a low prevalence of heavy drinking, or an insufficient duration of sustained change.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08114-0.abstract: Trastuzumab-emtansine (T-DM1), an antibody drug conjugate, is approved in the adjuvant (residual disease post-neoadjuvant chemotherapy) and metastatic settings for HER2-positive breast cancer. Real-world evidence on T-DM1 biosimilar from India remains sparse. During October 2021-July 2025, 101 cases treated with T-DM1 biosimilar - UJVIRA ®, across seven oncology centers in India were retrospectively analyzed. The adjuvant cohort (n = 19), had patients with residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy and surgery, and the metastatic cohort (n = 82), comprised patients progressing on trastuzumab-chemo regimens. Primary endpoints were invasive Disease-Free Survival (iDFS) and Progression Free Survival (PFS) in the adjuvant and metastatic cohort respectively. Overall Survival (OS) and safety were secondary endpoints. In the adjuvant cohort (median follow-up 19 months), median iDFS was not reached (mean 14.6 months), with 2 events (10.5%). In the metastatic cohort (median follow-up 8 months), median PFS was 7.5 months (mean 8.3 months; 61 events, 74.4%). PFS was longer when T-DM1 was administered earlier: 28 months in first-line, 9 months in second-line, and 8 months in third- and fourth-line (p = 0.06). Median OS in the metastatic cohort was 15.5 months and 36 months with 1st line T-DM1. In 14.6% of metastatic patients, grade 3 thrombocytopenia occurred; there were no grade 3/4 events in the adjuvant cohort. UJVIRA® demonstrated real-world clinical effectiveness and an acceptable safety profile in both adjuvant and metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer, with outcomes similar to landmark clinical trials supporting its role as a cost-effective biosimilar in India.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08115-z.abstract: Abstract Purpose To characterize clinicopathologic, treatment-related, and sociodemographic factors associated with rapid versus late relapse in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), and to evaluate how relapse timing influences metastatic patterns and survival outcomes. Methods Using linked Swedish population-based registers, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of women diagnosed with non-metastatic TNBC between 2007 and 2021. Patients were classified into three groups based on time to distant relapse or death: rapid relapse (rrTNBC; ≤24 months), late relapse (lrTNBC; >24 months), or event-free at last follow-up. Tumor characteristics, comorbidity, treatments, and sociodemographic variables were compared across groups. Multivariable logistic regression and survival outcomes were assessed. Sensitivity analyses restricted to healthcare regions with complete relapse data were performed. Results Among 8,298 patients, 15% experienced rrTNBC, 18% lrTNBC, and 67% remained event-free. rrTNBC was associated with older age, larger tumors, nodal involvement, advanced stage, and a higher frequency of visceral and multi-organ metastases. Patients with rrTNBC were less likely to receive adjuvant systemic therapy or radiotherapy and more likely to undergo mastectomy. Sociodemographic disparities were observed, with rrTNBC more frequent among patients who were single or widowed, lower educated, or had lower household income. Survival outcomes were substantially worse for rrTNBC compared with lrTNBC and event-free patients. Conclusions Rapid relapse defines a particularly vulnerable TNBC population characterized by aggressive tumor biology, early dissemination, inferior survival, and sociodemographic disadvantage, while lrTNBC represents an intermediate phenotype with delayed disease progression. Distinguishing rrTNBC from lrTNBC may improve risk stratification, guide treatment decisions, and support more personalized follow-up strategies.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05774-2.abstract: Outcome prediction in neuro-oncology remains challenging due to heterogeneity in tumor biology, imaging characteristics, treatment response, and patient-specific clinical factors. Although molecular databases have advanced understanding of brain tumor biology, many datasets lack broader data necessary for generalizable predictive modeling. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly being explored to integrate these heterogeneous data sources and support precision neuro-oncology. A narrative review was performed using PubMed and Embase to identify studies evaluating oncology databases, ML models, multimodal data integration, and AI applications relevant to neuro-oncology. Studies published between 2020 and 2026 were preferentially reviewed, with additional landmark studies included when relevant. Traditional ML approaches including regression-based models, random forests, support vector machines, and gradient boosting algorithms have been applied to survival prediction, recurrence classification, treatment response estimation, and molecular biomarker prediction using clinical, imaging, molecular, and population-level datasets. More advanced architectures including natural language processing, large language models, vision transformers, geometric deep learning, and graph neural networks have expanded the ability to analyze unstructured and multimodal data sources including radiology reports, histopathology slides, MRI volumes, molecular datasets, and electronic health records. Multimodal AI systems integrating imaging, molecular, histopathologic, clinical, and socioeconomic data frequently demonstrated improved predictive performance compared with single-modality models. However, widespread clinical implementation remains limited by dataset heterogeneity, limited external validation, interpretability concerns, and inconsistent representation across patient populations. AI and ML approaches are increasingly capable of integrating complex neuro-oncology datasets in ways that more closely reflect real-world clinical decision-making. Although most current models remain investigational, multimodal AI frameworks may ultimately improve prognostic assessment, treatment stratification, and precision neuro-oncology care. Continued progress will require larger representative datasets, improved data harmonization, external validation, and clinically interpretable models.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05821-y.abstract: MGMT promoter methylation (MGMTpm) is a well-established molecular biomarker in neuro-oncology. We review current practices, challenges, and future directions for MGMTpm as a biomarker in central nervous system (CNS) tumors. The literature on MGMT function, and MGMTpm clinical significance and testing in CNS tumors was reviewed. We discuss the biological role of MGMT in DNA repair and the mechanisms by which MGMTpm leads to increased tumor sensitivity to alkylating agents. We summarize the clinical significance of MGMTpm in glioblastoma and its emerging relevance in other CNS tumors. Testing practices using methylation-specific PCR, pyrosequencing, and genome-wide methylation array-based approaches are discussed, along with challenges related to testing variability and "gray-zone" methylation, and emerging technologies such as nanopore sequencing. Despite ongoing technical and interpretative challenges, MGMTpm remains a robust and clinically valuable biomarker in neuro-oncology.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05822-x.abstract: To characterize the weekly trajectory of hippocampal diffusion during fractionated partial-brain radiation therapy (RT) for high-grade glioma and determine whether the magnitude of change is associated with planned hippocampal dose. Forty-five adults enrolled in a prospective observational imaging study and treated with 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concurrent temozolomide underwent diffusion MRI before RT and weekly during treatment. Relative bilateral hippocampal apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) change and fractional anisotropy (FA) were evaluated longitudinally. Linear mixed-effects models included treatment week and planned mean bilateral hippocampal dose as fixed main effects. A secondary laterally-specific analysis evaluated baseline-to-Week-6 ADC change separately in the hippocampi ipsilateral and contralateral to the tumor. Hippocampal ADC increased progressively from a median relative change of 0.5% at Week 1 to 12% (IQR, 6%-18%) at Week 6. The ADC time coefficient was + 2.2% points per week (95% CI, 1.8-2.5; P < 0.001). After accounting for week, higher planned mean bilateral hippocampal dose was associated with greater ADC change (+ 0.81% points/Gy; 95% CI, 0.76-0.93; P < 0.001). In the secondary laterally-specific analysis, higher dose was associated with greater Week-6 ADC change in both the ipsilateral hippocampus (β = 0.83% points/Gy; 95% CI, 0.52-1.26; P = 0.013) and the contralateral hippocampus (β = 0.36% points/Gy; 95% CI, 0.05-0.712; P = 0.046). FA remained stable through Week 3 and declined during Weeks 4-6. Weekly diffusion MRI demonstrates a progressive, dose-associated hippocampal response during fractionated RT. The laterality-specific findings further support an association between local radiation exposure and ADC change and support hippocampal ADC as a candidate treatment-phase imaging phenotype for prospective validation.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05825-8.abstract: Central neurocytomas (CNs) are rare, WHO grade 2 brain tumors that have relatively high recurrence rates following resection. The present collaboration between Northwestern University and the Mayo Clinic describes long-term outcomes of CN as it relates to potential prognostic variables that entail recurrence risk, such as RT timing, tumor proliferation index (Ki-67), and age at diagnosis. Patients established between 1990 and 2025 with a tissue diagnosis of CN were reviewed. Recurrence free survival (RFS) and overall survival (OS) were calculated according to the Kaplan Meier-method. Multivariate cox regression analysis was performed with pre-planned variables. Fifty-one patients with CN with a median age of 26 years and 9.7 years median follow-up were included. OS at 10 years for the cohort was 94%. Without adjuvant RT, 5-year RFS for post-GTR was 61% versus 46% for post-STR (P value = 0.18). Multivariate analysis found omission of adjuvant RT (HR: 9.0, P = 0.003), subtotal resection (HR:5.7, P = 0.017), younger age at diagnosis (HR3.1, P = 0.002), and higher Ki-67 (HR 1.13, P = 0.017) were associated with worse RFS. Salvage RT after first recurrence (n = 17) had a 5-year RFS of 83%, with a median follow-up of 4.8 years. We report one of the largest and most comprehensive cohorts of CN with long-term follow-up. Contrary to previous reports, recurrences were frequent after GTR. Higher Ki-67 and age at diagnosis were associated with worse RFS in our cohort. Salvage RT at recurrence achieved durable long-term tumor control, and 10-year mortality was low.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05827-6.abstract: The objective of this study was to develop and externally validate complementary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based models and their stacked combinations for preoperative World Health Organization (WHO) grading of intracranial meningioma. This retrospective multicenter study included 455 histopathologically confirmed meningiomas: a four-center development cohort (n = 346) with leave-one-center-out cross-validation and an external cohort (n = 109). Four base models used contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI: tumor + peritumoral radiomics, an nnU-Net segmentation-based classifier, frozen DINOv3 transfer-learning features, and clinical variables. All 15 combinations were prespecified and stacked using a linear meta-learner trained on development out-of-fold predictions. Frozen models were externally evaluated without modification. WHO 2-3 tumors comprised 24.6% overall (112/455; development 20.5%; external 37.6%). External AUCs were 0.732 for nnU-Net, 0.703 for DINOv3, 0.645 for clinical, 0.628 for radiomics. The multimodal ensemble (nnU-Net+DINOv3+Clinical) achieved the highest external AUC (0.742), exceeding radiomics (ΔAUC +0.114, p = 0.008) but not nnU-Net (ΔAUC +0.011, p = 0.737). Compared with the clinical model, discrimination was higher but nonsignificant at the prespecified threshold (ΔAUC +0.098, p = 0.050), while reclassification improved (IDI +0.109, p < 0.001). Radiomics-containing combinations performed strongly in development but lost most discrimination externally. The multimodal ensemble had an external calibration slope of 1.32 (Brier 0.190) and net benefit above default strategies at thresholds ≥ 0.23. The multimodal ensemble achieved the highest external AUC but did not significantly exceed nnU-Net, which was the most transportable single predictor of meningioma grade. Clinical variables did not improve discrimination but enabled interpretable feature-level attribution. Handcrafted radiomics lacked external transportability.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05828-5.abstract: Despite significant advances in glioma surgery, early postoperative neuroimaging frequently reveals signs of surgical brain injury (SBI). This prospective observational study aimed to investigate the incidence, radiological characteristics, neurological outcomes and risk factors of SBI following glioma resection. Patients with newly diagnosed supratentorial gliomas who undergo tumor resection were prospectively enrolled. Serial MRI examinations were administrated early postoperative (≤ 72 h) and on postoperative days 7, 14 and 28 to assess the characteristics of infarction, edema and microhemorrhage. Neurological outcomes were evaluated using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at postoperative day 28. A total of 64 patients was included. Postoperative infarction was identified in 14 patients (21.9%), with all anatomically localized to the basal ganglia, thalamus, or insular regions. Intraoperative blood loss ≥ 300 mL was independently associated with postoperative infarction (Odd Ratio [OR]: 4.62, p = 0.035). Microhemorrhage was observed in 53.8% of patients. Peritumoral edema occurred in all cases and exhibited two distinct patterns: residual tumor-associated edema (n = 42) and de novo surgery-induced edema (n = 22). The average volume of tumor-associated edema decreased, whereas that of surgery-induced edema increased over time. Among the 53 patients who completed neurological outcome assessments, 13 developed disability (mRS ≥ 2). Risk factors were higher intraoperative blood loss (OR: 8.88, p = 0.013) and postoperative infarction (OR: 6.33, p = 0.031). SBI, including infarction and edema, is common following glioma surgery and associated with adverse neurological outcomes. Meticulous intraoperative hemostatic management is essential to prevent postoperative infarction and even disability outcome.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05829-4.abstract: Despite the high risk of postoperative motor dysfunction from corticospinal tract (CST) involvement, no preoperative system integrates CST-tumor interactions to stratify the prognosis in brainstem gliomas (BSGs). We enrolled 180 BSG patients who underwent craniotomy between 2020 and 2023. Preoperative DTI tractography classified CST-tumor relationships as displacement, infiltration, and traverse types. Clinical, pathological, and follow-up data (KPS, mRS, MRC, OS) were systematically collected at predefined intervals. Longitudinal outcomes were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models; survival was assessed by Kaplan-Meier. The cohort comprised 51 displacement (28.3%), 83 infiltration (46.1%), and 46 traverse (25.6%) cases, with excellent inter-rater reliability (κ = 0.93). Tumor biology, CST fractional anisotropy (FA), and preoperative functional status demonstrated clear gradients across subtypes. The traverse type was predominantly high-grade (97.8%), exhibited the lowest FA (0.424 ± 0.055), and had the poorest preoperative KPS/mRS (all P < 0.001). Conversely, the displacement type was mostly low-grade (74.5%), showed the highest FA (0.45 ± 0.038), and had superior functional status; infiltration was intermediate. FA correlated positively with preoperative muscle strength (ρ = 0.238, P = 0.001). Longitudinal trajectories differed significantly (P_FDR < 0.05): displacement patients recovered rapidly, traverse patients showed minimal recovery with late decline, and infiltration was intermediate. Median OS was not reached for displacement, versus 15.3 months for infiltration and 12.0 months for traverse; all pairwise comparisons were significant. This DTI-based CST-tumor classification system effectively stratifies BSG patients preoperatively and is associated with distinct recovery trajectories, providing a hypothesis-generating framework for surgical planning.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05830-x.abstract: Routine blood counts may capture treatment-related host immune perturbation in glioblastoma, but most studies rely on static pretreatment values. We investigated whether the intra-individual preservation of circulating monocytes during chemoradiotherapy provides prognostic information beyond established clinical factors and other hematologic trajectories. We retrospectively analyzed adults with histologically confirmed IDH-wildtype glioblastoma treated with radiotherapy and concurrent temozolomide. Absolute monocyte counts obtained before and at the end of chemoradiotherapy were used to define monocytic resilience as log2(post-treatment/pre-treatment monocyte ratio). Overall survival (OS) was the primary endpoint. Cox models adjusted for MGMT promoter methylation, gross total resection, Karnofsky Performance Status, and age. The ratio was analyzed continuously for primary inference. A post/pre ratio of 0.75 was additionally evaluated as an exploratory, clinically interpretable threshold for two-group Kaplan-Meier visualization and sensitivity analysis. Among 127 patients, 115 had complete monocyte trajectories and OS data. The primary adjusted model included 102 patients and 86 deaths. The continuous monocyte post/pre ratio was independently associated with OS (HR 0.53 per doubling, 95% CI 0.37-0.76; p = 0.00051). Using the exploratory 0.75 threshold, 52 patients had low resilience (< 0.75) and 63 had preserved resilience (≥ 0.75), with median OS of 10.2 and 17.3 months, respectively (log-rank p = 0.00064). Preserved resilience was associated with lower mortality in univariable Cox analysis (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.34-0.75; p = 0.00080). Bootstrap resampling showed that outcome-optimized cut-points clustered around this region (median 0.74; IQR 0.70-0.81), although the threshold remains exploratory and requires external validation. Preservation or recovery of circulating monocytes during chemoradiotherapy was associated with a favorable host-response phenotype in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma. This dynamic signal remained associated with survival after adjustment for established clinical factors, baseline monocyte burden, lymphocyte change, systemic inflammatory imbalance, and measured corticosteroid exposure. External prospective validation, medication-level confounder assessment, and immune phenotyping are required before clinical use.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05831-w.abstract: High-grade gliomas carry a poor prognosis, and MRI-based radiotherapy (RT) planning may inadequately capture metabolically active tumor infiltration. ¹⁸F-fluoroethyl-tyrosine (FET) PET provides superior tumor delineation, yet prospective North American evidence supporting integration with RT planning remains limited. FETSMaRT enrolled 30 patients with WHO grade 3 or 4 high-grade glioma receiving post-operative RT. FET-PET/MRI was acquired before RT with the radiation oncologist blinded to PET, enabling retrospective quantification of discordance between MRI-based and FET-PET/MRI-derived gross tumor (GTV), clinical target (CTV), and planning target (PTV) volumes. In the glioblastoma subgroup (n = 23), Kaplan-Meier and Cox analyses related GTV and CTV discordance to time to progression. Median age was 60 years; 77% had glioblastoma and 60% MGMT promoter methylation. GTV discordance occurred in 17/30 patients (56.7%) and CTV discordance in 15/30 (50.0%). FET-PET/MRI-derived volumes significantly exceeded MRI-based volumes for GTV (43.6 vs. 38.6 cc; p < 0.0001), CTV (119.2 vs. 110.8 cc; p = 0.0045), and PTV (171.1 vs. 159.6 cc; p = 0.0003). Larger GTV∆ and CTV∆ change values were associated with numerically shorter median time to progression, but neither association was statistically significant. Radiation treatment failures were predominantly central (60.0%). FET-PET/MRI-derived target volumes were significantly larger than MRI-based volumes, confirming systematic underestimation of metabolically active tumor extent by anatomical MRI. While not meeting significance in this pilot study, directional CTV and GTV discordance suggests a possible association with progression; the hypothesis generating exploratory pilot data nonetheless justify a prospective trial of FET-PET-guided RT in high-grade glioma. NCT06499831.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05832-9.abstract: Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) are critical tools for measuring how patients experience their illness and treatment. Neuropsychiatric symptoms, headaches, seizures, and neurological deficits evolve over time and impact quality of life. In this narrative review, we summarize current literature on PROs in neuro-oncology, extant artificial intelligence (AI) tools for PRO analysis, considerations for real-world application, and ethical implications. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Google Scholar for English-language articles published from January 2015 through April 2026, supplemented by reference-list reviews. Four themes were agreed upon, and authors were assigned to each theme. Authors conducted a literature review, selected articles, and synthesized the information under each of these themes. An initial 78 articles were narrowed down to 53 confirming eligibility if they reported PRO or symptom data in people with brain tumors or computational/AI methods were applied to PRO or symptom monitoring in oncology. Article selection was verified by two senior authors (L.V.Y, A.S.). Older, foundational studies were retained where they remain the primary evidence. The growing volume and complexity of PRO data present challenges for traditional analysis methods. Integrating AI, including machine learning (ML) and large language models (LLMs), may help model longitudinal symptom trajectories to predict deterioration, extract symptoms from free-text clinical notes, and embed outputs in clinical decision support tools. Autonomy, informed consent, data security, bias, access, transparency and accountability should be considered. Successful translation will require interpretable, electronic health record-integrated, bias-mitigating tools that allow for actionable insights and preserve patient consent, privacy, and autonomy in this highly vulnerable population. Not applicable.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05833-8.abstract: For over a century, the pathologist's interpretation at the microscope was the final word on a brain tumor's identity. The 2021 World Health Organization (WHO) classification of central nervous system (CNS) tumors, 5th edition, changed that hierarchy by introducing a layered, integrated diagnosis in which molecular findings take precedence over histology when the two conflict. Artificial intelligence (AI) applied to digitized slides adds a computational layer to this framework and marks a fundamental change in diagnostic workflow. This review examines the role of AI and digital pathology in adult CNS tumors and discusses the opportunities and challenges in clinical, neuro-oncology implementation. We conducted a narrative review of relevant literature indexed in PubMed before and after the 2021 WHO classification, covering digital pathology, whole-slide imaging (WSI), and AI applications in adult neuro-oncology. We synthesized evidence on diagnostic performance, molecular prediction, prognostic modeling, workflow integration, and ethical considerations. AI and digital pathology show potential to improve diagnostic consistency, shorten turnaround time, and integrate histopathological, molecular, and radiological information. AI models may support glioma grading, prediction of molecular alterations from routine histology, survival stratification, prediction of brain metastasis, and intraoperative decisions. Barriers to clinical adoption include limited generalizability, lack of transparency, data privacy, and evolving regulatory oversight. AI and digital pathology are transforming adult CNS tumor diagnostics and could improve precision, efficiency, and multidisciplinary decision-making. Successful implementation will require rigorous multi-institutional clinical validation, transparent governance, equitable access, and collaboration among patients and health care professionals.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05834-7.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being developed across the Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) workflow, but its current applications and readiness for clinical integration remain underutilized. This narrative review examines the emerging role of AI in GKRS, with emphasis on treatment planning, outcome prediction, and post-treatment assessment. A structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus was conducted through September 20, 2026 to identify studies applying learning-based AI approaches specifically to GKRS. Eligible studies evaluated AI models using GKRS clinical, imaging, or treatment-planning data, while non-GKRS and non-learning-based studies were excluded. Included studies were synthesized according to major stages of the GKRS workflow. AI applications were identified across tumor segmentation, isocenter selection and treatment planning, prescription and dose-distribution prediction, synthetic computed tomography generation, and plan-quality assessment. Post-treatment applications include longitudinal tumor monitoring and prediction of response, functional outcomes, and toxicity including peritumoral edema and radiation necrosis. Several models demonstrate promising performance, but the evidence remains predominantly retrospective and task-specific, with frequent reliance on single-center or small datasets and limited external or prospective validation. AI has the potential to improve the consistency, efficiency, and personalization of GKRS by supporting specific technical and clinical decisions. Further multicenter validation, prospective evaluation, workflow integration, and demonstration of meaningful clinical benefit are required before routine adoption. AI currently remains a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for radiosurgical expertise.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05835-6.abstract: NF1-associated high-grade gliomas (HGGs) are rare, biologically heterogeneous tumors with poor outcomes. Although MEK inhibitors (MEKis) are established options for selected NF1-associated low-grade gliomas, their role in NF1-associated HGG remains undefined. We describe clinical and radiographic outcomes with MEKis, including mirdametinib. We retrospectively reviewed adult patients with NF1-associated HGG treated at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who initiated selumetinib, mirdametinib, or dabrafenib plus trametinib from December 1, 2019, to January 31, 2026. Outcomes included radiographic response and Kaplan-Meier estimates of progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) from MEKi initiation. Progression was defined as the earliest documented radiographic or clinical evidence of progression. Nine patients were included. Median age at HGG onset was 34 years (range, 22-58), and median Karnofsky Performance Status at MEKi initiation was 60 (range, 50-90). Diagnoses were high-grade astrocytoma with piloid features (n = 6), IDH-wildtype glioblastoma (n = 2), and IDH-wildtype HGG/not otherwise specified (n = 1). Most patients received MEKi after prior local and/or systemic therapy. Among three patients treated with mirdametinib, two evaluable patients achieved partial response by Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology criteria. Six patients received selumetinib for 1-7 cycles, and one patient received dabrafenib/trametinib for 2 cycles. Stable disease was the best response among the remaining evaluable patients. Median PFS and OS from MEKi initiation were 2.9 and 9.4 months, respectively. Radiographic partial responses were observed in two patients with NF1-associated HGG treated with mirdametinib, but durability of benefit was limited. The best response with selumetinib and dabrafenib/trametinib was stable disease in evaluable patients. Larger prospective studies are needed to define the role of MEK inhibition in this population.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05837-4.abstract: To assess whether the association between postoperative diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and neurological worsening after eloquent-area glioma surgery differs according to lesion morphology. We retrospectively analyzed 139 consecutive patients undergoing resection of eloquent-area supratentorial gliomas (WHO 2-4). Postoperative MRI (< 48 h) classified lesions as sector- or rim-shaped. Neurological status was assessed at discharge and 4-6 months. DWI lesions occurred in 44/139 patients (31.7%; 31 sector-shaped, 13 rim-shaped); 59 (42.4%) worsened at discharge. Overall, DWI positivity alone was not associated with worsening. Sector-shaped DWI lesions were associated with neurological worsening (positive predictive value, PPV of 58.1%) and remained associated after multivariable adjustment (OR 3.83, 95% CI 1.30-11.29), although the confidence interval was wide and the unadjusted association was borderline. Rim-shaped lesions carried a PPV of 38.5%, comparable to the risk in DWI-negative patients (37.9%), and the two morphologies did not differ significantly in direct comparison. Awake craniotomy was also independently associated with worsening, and frontal site with a lower risk. 61% of worsening occurred with negative DWI. A deficit was present at the 4-6 month follow-up in 9 patients (6.5%), all with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, and was associated with a ≥ 50% evoked-potential decrease. In this cohort, postoperative DWI positivity was associated with neurological worsening mainly when the lesion was sector-shaped, a finding that requires confirmation in larger series. Rim-shaped lesions showed a risk of worsening similar to that of a negative scan. Most worsening occurs without DWI ischemia, suggesting non-ischemic mechanisms of function-guided surgery. A deficit at follow-up occurred only in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma and was associated with intraoperative neurophysiological changes.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05838-3.abstract: Elderly patients with spinal metastases are often considered poor candidates for aggressive local therapy, due in part to medical comorbidity and limited evidence to guide treatment selection. This study evaluated outcomes following spine stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) in this patient population and examined predictors of local failure (LF) and vertebral compression fracture (VCF). A prospectively maintained database of consecutive patients aged ≥ 70 years with available imaging who underwent spine SBRT at a quaternary referral center from 2002 to 2024 was analyzed. The median single-fraction dose was 16 Gy (range: 12-18 Gy), and multi-fraction regimens ranged from 18 to 35 Gy in 2-5 fractions. Of 208 metastases in 161 patients (median age: 75 years, range: 70-94 years), 72% had prior conventional radiotherapy and 76% received a single fraction. The 6-, 12-, 24-, and 36-month cumulative incidence rates were 6%, 9%, 9%, and 10% for LF and 4%, 7%, 8%, and 9% for VCF (median follow-up: 9 months, range: 1-132 months). Gross tumor volume > 37 cc (subdistribution hazard ratio [sHR]: 6.27, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.48-26.63, P = 0.013) and Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS, per-point sHR: 1.23, 95% CI: 1.07-1.42, P = 0.005) were independently associated with LF; only SINS was independently associated with VCF (per-point sHR: 1.19, 95% CI: 1.06-1.34, P = 0.003), and 11 of 17 VCFs required cement augmentation or surgery. Age was associated with overall survival (hazard ratio: 1.05 per year, 95% CI: 1.01-1.09, P = 0.018); no statistically significant association was detected with LF or VCF when age was analyzed continuously, at thresholds of 75 or 80 years, or by exploratory maximally selected rank statistical analysis. Complete or partial pain response followed 61 of 148 evaluable treatments (41%) among 186 symptomatic metastases, and 18% of patients had grade 1-2 radiation toxicity. Spine SBRT, predominantly single-fraction reirradiation, was associated with low rates of LF and VCF; chronologic age alone should not preclude its use in appropriately selected elderly patients.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05840-9.abstract: Distant recurrence (DR) represents a distinct and lethal trajectory in glioblastoma (GBM), characterized by the colonization of spatially isolated neural niches. The mechanisms by which disseminated tumor cells remodel the microenvironment to overcome anatomical and immunological barriers remain poorly understood. This study aimed to decode the immune ecosystem of DR and elucidate the intercellular crosstalk driving this lethal dissemination. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on paired primary and DR tumor specimens from GBM patients, alongside an independent local recurrence (LR) control cohort, to map dynamic cellular shifts. Bioinformatic analyses, including differential abundance testing (Milo), cell-cell communication inference (CellChat), and copy number variation (CNV) analysis, were integrated with clinical co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) validation, bidirectional in vitro co-culture assays, and an orthotopic xenograft mouse model. Our high-resolution atlas revealed a profound remodeling of the microenvironment in DR lesions, characterized by a specific expansion of anti-inflammatory monocyte-derived tumor-associated macrophages (Anti_infl-TAM) and a paradoxical co-enrichment of CD8 + T cells and Tregs. Mechanistically, an OPC-like subpopulation of PTN+ tumor cells acted as a "paracrine architect," promoting Anti_infl-TAM polarization through the interaction between PTN and NCL. Co-IP assays confirmed direct physical binding of these two proteins in human DR tissues. Functional and bidirectional knockdown assays demonstrated that decoupling this cellular communication, achieved by targeting either PTN in tumor cells or NCL in macrophages, significantly attenuated glioma cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and macrophage polarization. In vivo, silencing PTN markedly reduced Anti_infl-TAM infiltration, suppressed intracranial tumor burden, and prolonged overall survival in tumor-bearing mice. This study establishes that DR GBM is defined by a reconfigured immune niche rather than mere genetic drift. The paracrine crosstalk between PTN+ tumor cells and Anti_infl-TAM serves as a critical engine of this permissive soil, offering a promising therapeutic target to disrupt the supportive microenvironment in distant recurrent GBM.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05840-9.title: A PTN+ glioblastoma subclone orchestrates immune reprogramming to drive distant recurrence.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05841-8.abstract: Patients with high-grade glioma reach surgery during the initial, index hospitalization (urgent), or through scheduled/outpatient pathways. There is a paucity of literature examining what patients require expedited versus elective surgery. This single-center retrospective study describes complications, utilization, and survival by pathway. Adults with WHO grade 3-4 gliomas undergoing primary resection (2021-2026) were classified as urgent (admitted without a planned resection date) or scheduled (discharged and readmitted for planned surgery, or managed exclusively as an outpatient). Primary outcomes were 30-day complications and days alive at home within 30 days of admission for resection (DAH-30). Secondary outcomes were progression free and overall survival. Survival was analyzed with propensity-score overlap weighting and Cox regression. Of 166 patients, 122 underwent urgent resection and 44 scheduled resections; 40 of 44 (91%) proceeded as planned. Urgent patients more often had midline shift (62% vs. 32%), less often seizure (15% vs. 39%), and lower Karnofsky scores (70 vs. 80); all p ≤ 0.002. They had longer index hospitalizations (median 8 vs. 3 days, p < 0.001) and fewer days at home (median 15 vs. 27; adjusted difference - 8.9 days, 95% CI - 12.9 to - 4.8). Complication rates (36% vs. 30%; adjusted OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.52-2.62) and overall survival (median 15.4 vs. 19.0 months, p = 0.758) did not differ detectably. Scheduled resection identified a distinct population, recognizable at initial evaluation by preserved performance status and the absence of midline shift. These patients spent more days at home and required shorter hospitalizations; no harm signal was observed. These data suggest that a substantial proportion of patients with newly diagnosed presumed high grade gliomas can be managed effectively in an expedited, outpatient basis.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05842-7.abstract: Brain metastases (BM) incidence and characteristics remain poorly defined due to registry data being often incomplete, recording only primary tumors or unspecified metastases. The objective of this study was to examine BM incidence rates and characteristics confirmed by MRI in North Savo, Finland. In this retrospective study, North Savo residents with first MRI diagnosis of BM between 1 January 2004 and 31 December 2023 were identified through the radiology information system, irrespective of primary cancer diagnosis date. Medical and histopathological records were reviewed. Population person-years were estimated by summing annual end-year counts of all North Savo residents obtained from Statistics Finland. Crude incidence rates and age-standardized incidence rates (ASIRs), standardized to the 2013 European Standard population, were calculated. Temporal trends were assessed using age-adjusted Poisson regression. Among 516 patients, 474 had histopathological verification. Cancers originating from lung and breast tissue accounted for 56.8% of BM cases. Overall crude incidence was 10.22 (95% CI 9.36-11.15) and ASIR was 9.20 (95% CI 8.42-10.04) per 100,000 person years. ASIR increased from 5.8 in 2004-2008 to 11.8 in 2019-2023. Age-adjusted Poisson regression estimated a 24% increase in incidence per five-year period (incidence rate ratio 1.24; 95% CI 1.14-1.34; P < 0.001). Age-specific incidence peaked at 33.1 per 100,000 person years among patients aged 70-74 years. MRI-confirmed BM incidence increased over 20 years, despite age standardization. Incidence was highest among older adults. These findings provide contemporary population-based epidemiological data of BM incidence.
