doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05843-6.abstract: To examine the association between neighborhood material deprivation and days at home (DAH) after glioblastoma diagnosis. This population-based retrospective cohort study used linked administrative data from Ontario, Canada, for adults diagnosed with glioblastoma during 2003-2023. Material deprivation was assigned using Ontario Marginalization Index quintiles (Q1, least deprived; Q5, most deprived). The primary outcome was DAH within 365 days, defined as days alive outside acute hospitals, inpatient rehabilitation, and continuing or complex care. The primary analysis included diagnoses through 2022. Median quantile regression adjusted for age, sex, comorbidity, frailty, rurality, and diagnosis year. Secondary outcomes included other DAH horizons and overall survival. Among 9172 adults, 4491 (49.0%) were younger than 65 years and 5435 (59.3%) were male. Median DAH-365 was 249 days (interquartile range, 67-350) in Q1 and 138 (27-332) in Q5. In 8234 complete cases, adjusted median differences versus Q1 were - 8.8 days for Q2 (95% confidence interval [CI], - 19.6 to 2.0), - 14.8 for Q3 (- 27.0 to - 2.6), - 18.3 for Q4 (- 29.4 to - 7.2), and - 36.2 for Q5 (- 51.5 to - 20.9). Median survival was 324 days (95% CI, 306-343) in Q1 and 225 (211-244) in Q5. Greater neighborhood material deprivation was associated with substantially fewer DAH after glioblastoma diagnosis. The adjusted gap exceeding 5 weeks supports investigation of treatment access and supportive care pathways to inform efforts to improve equity.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05844-5.abstract: Craniospinal irradiation (CSI) is used for leptomeningeal carcinomatosis (LMC), yet comparative data between proton CSI (pCSI) and photon volumetric modulated arc therapy CSI (xCSI) are limited. We evaluated clinical outcomes and longitudinal toxicity profiles following pCSI versus xCSI in patients with solid tumor LMC. We retrospectively identified adults with solid tumor LMC treated with CSI at a single institution from 2020 to 2025. Toxicities were graded per CTCAE v5.0 at baseline, during treatment, and at 1, 3, and 6 months post-CSI. Overall survival (OS) and central nervous system progression-free survival (CNS-PFS) were estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods; Cox models evaluated OS associations. 45 patients initiated CSI (18 xCSI, 27 pCSI). Grade ≥ 3 lymphopenia during treatment was similar (75% xCSI versus 56% pCSI; p = 0.43), whereas Grade ≥ 3 thrombocytopenia occurred only with xCSI (29% versus 0%; p = 0.04). At 3 months, Grade ≥ 3 lymphopenia was higher with pCSI (79% versus 17%; p = 0.02). Non-hematologic Grade ≥ 3 toxicities were rare. OS did not significantly differ (median 8.5 months pCSI versus 4.8 months xCSI; p = 0.50), nor did CNS-PFS (5.9 versus 3.0 months; p = 0.20). On multivariable analysis, worse OS was associated with higher extracranial tumor burden (HR 2.77, 95% CI, 1.20-6.40) and performance status (HR 2.88, 95% CI, 1.01-8.23), but not modality. No statistically significant modality differences in OS or CNS-PFS were detected; baseline performance status and extracranial burden were associated with OS. VMAT-based CSI represents a practical alternative in settings without protons, with careful monitoring of acute hematologic toxicity.

doi:10.1007/s12630-026-03204-5.abstract: Tracheal intubation is a physically and mentally demanding for anesthesiologists because it requires fine motor control, technical precision, rapid decision-making, situational awareness, and error avoidance. While videolaryngoscopes reduce muscle strain in normal airways, their ergonomic impact during difficult airway management remains poorly established. We aimed to compare upper limb muscle activity using dynamic surface electromyography during intubation via direct laryngoscopy (DL) vs videolaryngoscopy (VL) in simulated difficult airway scenarios. We conducted a randomized crossover trial involving 35 experienced anesthesiologists who performed tracheal intubation on a high-fidelity manikin with a normal airway, locked jaw, and rigid neck, respectively, using a Macintosh direct laryngoscope, a C-MAC® videolaryngoscope (C blade), and a King Vision® channeled videolaryngoscope. The primary outcome was upper limb muscle activity, measured by surface electromyography. Secondary outcomes included intubation time, force on upper incisors, first-attempt success rate, and perceived workload (National Aeronautics and Space Administration Task Load Index [NASA-TLX] score). Direct laryngoscopy produced significantly higher brachioradialis muscle activity than C-MAC VL in the simulated normal airway (16 vs 13 µV; median difference [MD], 3 µV; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0 to 5; P = 0.04), locked jaw (18 vs 12 µV; MD, 6 µV; 95% CI, 1 to 11; P = 0.02), and rigid neck (16 vs 13 µV; MD, 4 µV; 95% CI, 0 to 9; P = 0.03) scenarios. Direct laryngoscopy was the fastest method but exerted the highest force on the incisors (P < 0.001). King Vision VL was associated with the highest NASA-TLX workload score (P < 0.001 compared with DL), whereas C-MAC VL was least demanding. In simulated difficult airways, VL reduced upper limb muscle activity compared with DL. Nevertheless, perceived workload was higher with King Vision VL than with DL, whereas it was lower with C-MAC VL. Among the devices tested, C-MAC VL provided the most favorable ergonomic balance, combining reduced muscle strain, lower perceived workload, and highest first-attempt success rate across all airway scenarios. Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI/2021/11/038305); first submitted on 26 November 2021.

doi:10.1007/s12630-026-03207-2.abstract: Intraoperative hypotension (IOH) has been increasingly linked to postoperative complications and adverse outcomes. Nevertheless, the association between preoperative hemoglobin levels and the risk of IOH has not been investigated. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 2,060 patients aged ≥ 18 yr who underwent general anesthesia between 2019 and 2023. We defined intraoperative hypotension as any mean blood pressure (MBP) < 65, 60, 55, 50, or 45 mm Hg, based on 5-min interval recordings. We assessed the association between preoperative hemoglobin levels and IOH using multivariable logistic regression with restricted cubic spline modeling. We also evaluated the association between preoperative hemoglobin levels and postoperative length of hospital stay using a generalized additive model. We found no significant association between preoperative hemoglobin levels and IOH risk at MBP < 65 and < 45 mm Hg (P = 0.13 and 0.12, respectively). Nevertheless, at MBP < 60 mm Hg, patients with lower preoperative hemoglobin levels had a significantly higher risk of IOH (P = 0.03). We observed similar trends at more severe hypotension thresholds (< 55 mm Hg and < 50 mm Hg), with P values of 0.02 and 0.03, respectively. Lower hemoglobin levels were associated with more frequent IOH episodes and higher odds ratios. We also found a significant association between lower preoperative hemoglobin levels and a longer postoperative length of hospital stay. Lower preoperative hemoglobin levels were significantly associated with an increased risk of IOH and longer postoperative length of hospital stay. These findings highlight the potential value of incorporating hemoglobin level assessments into IOH risk stratification and may help improve patient outcomes.

doi:10.1007/s12630-026-03213-4.abstract: Indigenous Peoples in Canada are disproportionately burdened with a spectrum of health issues and consistently report lower satisfaction with their health care; nevertheless, little is known about their experiences with critical care and the support received during critical illness. We aimed to describe the current scope of critical-care-specific resources available to Indigenous patients and their families across Alberta to identify gaps and opportunities to implement actionable change to realize more equitable and culturally safe care. We conducted a two-phase environmental scan. Phase 1 entailed searching websites for information to support Indigenous patients, their families, and health care workers. Phase 2 facilitated 21 interviews with intensive care unit (ICU) stakeholders from across Alberta to further describe site-specific resources, services, tools, or initiatives to support Indigenous Peoples. Indigenous partners were engaged through all aspects of the project. Our environmental scan identified a paucity of ICU-specific resources, programs, or policies to support Indigenous patients and families' navigation with critical care. We identified two national resources aimed at clinicians, rather than patients or families. Interviews with ICU stakeholders confirmed the paucity of Indigenous-specific resources. Stakeholders cited numerous barriers, including inadequate culture training, staff time constraints and burnout, physical space limits, and insufficient personnel, such as Indigenous liaisons and social workers. Multiple gaps exist in the availability of critical-care-focused resources and supports for Indigenous Peoples experiencing critical illness in Alberta, Canada. Addressing these care gaps may improve health equity, access, and the experience for Indigenous patients and families during critical illness and further build trust and strengthen relationships with health care workers.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101931.abstract: This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate whether intraoperative hemoadsorption during cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) improves postoperative outcomes compared with the standard of care. We systematically searched EMBASE, PubMed, and the Cochrane Library for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing hemoadsorption versus standard care in patients undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB. Data were analyzed using a frequentist approach and trial sequential analysis (TSA). The primary outcome was the incidence of cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury (CSA-AKI) within 7 days after surgery. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD42025634991). A total of six RCTs comprising 798 patients were included. Four RCTs (n = 723; 355 hemoadsorption, 368 control) reported CSA-AKI incidence, which did not significantly differ between groups (RR = 0.93 [95% CI: 0.71-1.21], p = 0.57; I² = 42.0%). Hemoadsorption was not associated with significant differences in secondary outcomes: interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor, 28-day mortality, SOFA score, and ICU length of stay. Hemoadsorption during CPB was not associated with a reduction in CSA-AKI or with improvement in secondary clinical outcomes in elective patients undergoing cardiac surgery. However, the accrued sample represented only 48% of the heterogeneity-adjusted required information size (1,491 patients), and the cumulative Z-curve crossed neither the monitoring nor the futility boundary. PROSPERO International Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42025634991; January 31, 2025).

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101934.abstract: Lung-protective ventilation in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remains under-applied at the bedside, partly due to the absence of integrated, context-aware decision-support tools. Large language models (LLMs) with advanced code generation capabilities have created a new possibility: physicians can now build the bedside tools they need without depending on software vendors or programming expertise. This practice, broadly termed "vibe coding", has entered medical discourse but has not been formally evaluated as a clinical competency. We report the development of VentiProtect ARDS, a real-time ventilator titration assistant built by a single physician in a single session of 4 minutes 25 seconds, as a proof-of-concept for physician prompt engineering: the structured translation of clinical knowledge into a natural-language specification that constrains LLM code generation. A structured eight-block prompt was developed through an iterative pre-prompt reasoning process and submitted to Claude Opus 4.6 via the Antigravity agentic development environment. The generated application computes predicted body weight, tidal volume, driving pressure, respiratory system compliance, mechanical power, and oxygenation index, with real-time colour-coded alerts and an active suggestion engine that calculates exact corrective ventilator settings. Formula accuracy was verified using an independent automated test suite of 100 scenarios (1,400 individual checks) with no computational errors identified. The tool runs locally with no installation, network dependency, or patient data transmission. This proof-of-concept suggests that physician prompt engineering may represent a potential clinical competency that does not require programming experience, although a single self-performed case cannot establish it across physicians. The LLM generates syntax. The physician generates medicine.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101937.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping anaesthesiology and critical care, enhancing physiological monitoring, perioperative risk prediction, and clinical decision-making. As its adoption accelerates, attention has increasingly turned to the environmental consequences of digital healthcare, raising important questions regarding the energy consumption and carbon footprint associated with clinical AI. This study examines the environmental implications of AI in anaesthesiology and critical care by placing computational emissions within the broader context of healthcare sustainability. Current evidence indicates that, although AI systems generate measurable greenhouse gas emissions, their operational carbon footprint remains several orders of magnitude lower than that of established sources of emissions, including volatile anaesthetic agents, intensive care, and surgical care. Quantitative comparisons, complemented by an illustrative environmental break-even analysis, suggest that even modest improvements in healthcare efficiency may be sufficient to offset the operational emissions of current clinical AI applications. These findings indicate that the sustainability of clinical AI should not be judged solely by its computational footprint, but by its overall environmental value. The relevant question is not simply how much AI emits, but whether its implementation reduces resource utilisation, avoids unnecessary healthcare activities, and generates environmental savings that outweigh its own operational costs. Achieving this objective will require computationally efficient model design, low-carbon digital infrastructures, lifecycle assessment, and the routine integration of environmental metrics into AI evaluation. Rather than representing a major new source of healthcare emissions, clinical AI should be viewed as an opportunity to advance both digital innovation and environmental stewardship. By integrating sustainability alongside clinical effectiveness, anaesthesiologists are uniquely positioned to guide the responsible development and implementation of AI technologies that benefit both patients and the healthcare systems in which they are delivered.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101947.abstract: This technical note is meant to be complementary to the recently published Professional Practice Guidelines of the SFAR-ADARPEF. The limits of using blood pressure as a surrogate for changes in cardiac output and the variable accuracy of its non-invasive measurement are reminded. As clearcut population-based threshold values based on measurements obtained in awake or anaesthetised children cannot be provided, an adaptation based on the child's baseline blood pressure, comorbidity and surgical context is necessary to prevent unnecessary treatment of an acceptable low blood pressure or tolerating a too low blood pressure. The measurement of a baseline awake blood pressure, although often difficult to achieve in children, is therefore very helpful. If a low intraoperative MAP is measured, the presence of hypotension should be confirmed by repeat measurement and the simultaneous evaluation of clinical and paraclinical signs, and the observation of the surgical field. The treatment should then be adapted to the cause: anaesthetic overdose, hypovolaemia, positioning, surgical action, anaphylaxis, etc.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101948.abstract: Data are lacking regarding current ventilatory settings during abdominal surgery. Expert recommendations emphasize the need for protective ventilation, and several tools are now available to individualize positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP). We conducted a nationwide cross-sectional survey among French anesthesiologists and nurse anesthetists in November 2025 to assess ventilatory settings during abdominal surgery, both for laparotomy and laparoscopy. Protective ventilation was defined as the combination of low tidal volume (6-8 mL/kg predicted body weight), low-to-moderate PEEP (5-8 cm H2O), and recruitment maneuvers. Individualization of PEEP was defined as the use of driving pressure, mechanical power, or compliance to titrate PEEP. Among 1091 anesthesiologists and nurse anesthetists, female responders accounted for 46% (497/1084), the median age of anesthesia providers was 39 (33-47) years, and most responders (77%, 839/1090) had an adult-based main field of activity. Main ventilatory settings used during laparotomy were 6 to 8 ml/kg of predicted body weight (93%, 1013/1084), a respiratory rate set according to EtCO2 in 53% of responders (579/1084), and a PEEP set between 5 and 8 cmH20 for 87% of responders (950/1091). Most participants performed recruitment maneuvers (98%, 1065/1091). Overall, protective ventilation was used in 70% (763/1090), and individualization of PEEP in 45% (479/1054). Similar ventilatory settings were reported for laparoscopy. In this nationwide survey, expert consensus-based recommendations for protective ventilation during abdominal surgery appeared widely implemented in France. In contrast, individualized PEEP strategies were reported in fewer than half of cases, reflecting ongoing uncertainty and variability regarding PEEP titration in routine perioperative practice.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101949.abstract: Women with cardiogenic shock (CS) under VA-ECMO face excess mortality, yet the pharmacological basis of this disparity remains poorly understood. Arginine vasopressin (AVP) is increasingly used as a non-adrenergic vasopressor in this setting, but whether sex modifies the hemodynamic response to AVP is unknown. In this multicenter retrospective cohort of VA-ECMO-supported CS patients, we assessed whether sex was independently associated with successful vasopressor de-escalation at 48 hours (norepinephrine equivalent dose [NEE] <0.25 µg/kg/min) after AVP initiation. Multivariable logistic regression and linear mixed-effects models were used to evaluate sex differences in treatment response and NEE trajectories over time. Among 193 eligible patients, 32% of women achieved successful de-escalation versus 49% of men (p = 0.023). Male sex was independently associated with treatment success (aOR 2.08, 95% CI 1.07-4.15, p = 0.033). A significant sex-by-time interaction was observed in NEE trajectories (p = 0.041), with divergence emerging at 48 hours (NEE 0.24 vs. 0.01 µg/kg/min, p = 0.008). The excess failure risk was confined to postmenopausal women aged ≥55 years (aOR 2.75, 95% CI 1.32-5.93, p = 0.008). Female sex, particularly in a postmenopausal context, was independently associated with impaired vasopressor de-escalation following AVP in CS on VA-ECMO. These hypothesis-generating findings suggest that hormonal status may modulate vascular responsiveness to AVP and support the need for prospective studies incorporating hormonal profiling.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101950.abstract: Apnea testing is mandatory for brain death determination but may induce hypoxemia despite standard preoxygenation procedures. High-flow oxygen (HFO) systems may improve apneic oxygenation during the procedure, although clinical data remain limited. We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study including consecutive adult patients undergoing apnea testing for brain death determination between January 2023 and May 2026. Standard oxygen insufflation (6-15 L/min) was compared with HFO delivered through the Opt970® interface (Fisher & Paykel) at 50 L/min and FiO2 1.0. The primary outcome was longitudinal pulse oximetry saturation (SpO2) evolution during apnea testing. Secondary outcomes included desaturation events and arterial blood gas parameters. Repeated SpO2 measurements were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model. A total of 144 apnea tests were analyzed, including 78 using standard oxygen insufflation and 66 using HFO. Baseline characteristics and ventilatory parameters were comparable between groups. Lowest SpO2 during apnea testing was significantly higher with HFO (100 [98-100] vs. 99 [95-99]; p = 0.003), while desaturation below 94% occurred less frequently (9.1% vs. 21.8%; p = 0.04). Post-test PaCO2 was slightly higher in the HFO group (73 [67-81] vs. 70 [62-77] mmHg; p = 0.04). Longitudinal mixed-effects analysis demonstrated a significant decrease in SpO2 over time in both groups (p < 0.0001). However, HFO was associated with overall higher SpO2 values throughout the procedure (β=+1.38; standard error 0.69; p = 0.047), without significant group-by-time interaction (p = 0.578). HFO delivered through the Opt970® device was associated with modestly higher oxygen saturation during apnea testing compared with standard oxygen insufflation. Further prospective studies are required to confirm these findings.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101951.abstract: Anesthesiologists play a central role in optimizing perioperative care and improving outcomes for patients with hip fractures (HF). Standardized care bundles are essential to guide clinicians, enhance expertise, and improve overall quality of care. We conducted a nationwide modified Delphi study to establish French expert consensus on key components of a standardized care bundle for patients over 75 years old with HF. A two-round modified Delphi process was conducted with 30 multidisciplinary experts representative of major French academic societies to assess consensus on perioperative care practices for HF in patients over 75. Experts rated 34 clinically relevant items using a 9-point Likert scale, with consensus defined as ≥70% rating ranging from 7 to 9 for agreement or 1 to 3 for disagreement. The process was conducted via the REDCap platform and adhered to ethical and data protection standards. The expert panel included 11 (36.7%) anesthesiologists, 9 (30%) geriatricians, 6 (20%) orthopedic surgeons, and 4 (13.3%) hospital pharmacists. Agreement consensus was reached for 29 out of 34 proposed items. A shortlist of 12 items that achieved over 90% consensus was identified, comprising 2 organizational, 7 perioperative, and 3 surgical items. The bundle of care for HF elaborated in this study provides perioperative teams with clear, actionable objectives to improve care quality and equity. Its impact on patient outcomes warrants further evaluation.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101953.abstract: The supraglottic airway device i-gelTM Plus (Intersurgical Ltd., Berkshire, UK) may provide more secure ventilation than the original i-gelTM (Intersurgical Ltd., Berkshire, UK). This prospective randomized trial was conducted to evaluate the performance of i-gelTM Plus compared with the original i-gelTM in patients in the lateral decubitus position under general anesthesia with a neuromuscular blocking drug. We inserted two types of i-gelTM in the supine position in adult patients undergoing general anesthesia with 0.6 mg/kg IV rocuronium. The primary outcome was oropharyngeal leak pressure in the lateral position. Secondary outcomes included expiratory tidal volume and glottic view in that position. We analyzed 84 surgical patients in the i-gelTM Plus [n = 42] and original i-gelTM [n = 42] groups. The oropharyngeal leak pressure and expiratory tidal volume at the oropharyngeal leak pressure in the supine position were similar between the two groups. The lateral decubitus position demonstrated higher oropharyngeal leak pressure (P < 0.001) and expiratory tidal volume at oropharyngeal leak pressure (P < 0.001) in the i-gelTM Plus group (median [interquartile range], 22 [20-25] cmH2O and 694 [602-750] ml, respectively) than in the original i-gelTM group (15 [14-18] cmH2O and 470 [420-634] ml, respectively). However, fiberoptic glottis view grade scores did not differ between the two groups. The i-gelTM Plus implements higher oropharyngeal leak pressure in the lateral decubitus position than the original i-gelTM. Our results indicate that the i-gelTM Plus may be a better choice as a supraglottic airway device in the lateral decubitus position than the original i-gelTM in paralyzed patients. University Hospital Medical Information Network (UMIN000061937).

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101954.abstract: Pre-emptive antibiotic therapy is frequently prescribed after pancreaticoduodenectomy when intraoperative bile cultures are positive, despite the absence of clinical infection. Evidence supporting this practice remains limited. We assessed the association between withholding pre-emptive antibiotics and postoperative outcomes in patients with biliary colonization. This multicenter retrospective cohort study included 301 consecutive adults undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy with positive intraoperative bile cultures in four French tertiary centers between January 2014 and December 2024. Overall, 89 patients received PE-ATB, and 212 did not. Propensity score matching at a 1:2 ratio yielded 138 patients, including 46 treated patients and 92 controls. The primary outcome was 5-year overall survival. Secondary postoperative outcomes were examined using prespecified exploratory non-inferiority margins. Preoperative biliary stenting independently predicted PE-ATB use (odds ratio, 4.11; 95% confidence interval, 1.26-13.40;P = 0.019). In the matched cohort, withholding PE-ATB was compatible with the non-inferiority margin for intra-abdominal abscess, pancreatic fistula, transfusion requirements, and antibiotic duration. Overall postoperative infection did not differ significantly between groups (odds ratio, 1.42; 95% confidence interval, 0.66-3.07; P = 0.376). Five-year mortality was higher in the group without PE-ATB in the matched cohort (hazard ratio, 2.02; 95% confidence interval, 1.01-4.04; P = 0.048), whereas no survival difference was observed in the overall unmatched cohort. Withholding PE-ATB was not associated with worse early postoperative outcomes and was associated with reduced antibiotic exposure. The survival difference observed only after matching should be considered cautiously and may reflect residual confounding. Prospective randomized trials are needed.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101956.abstract: Spontaneous breathing trials (SBT) guide extubation decisions in intensive care unit (ICU), predicting the respiratory effort required by the patient after extubation. Different SBTs exist and should be adapted to critical illness. Viral pneumonias such as COVID-19 combine lung injury, sepsis-induced systemic inflammation, and encephalopathy, making classification challenging. The objective was to assess which SBT could be used to reproduce postextubation respiratory effort in COVID-19-related acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) patients. In this multicenter randomized crossover study, COVID-19-related ARDS patients mechanically ventilated at least 24 hours and ready for extubation underwent 3 different 15-minute SBT at random order: pressure support ventilation of 7-cmH2O with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 0-cmH2O (PSV7PEEP0), PSV 0-cmH2O with PEEP 0-cmH2O (PSV0PEEP0) and T-piece trial. At baseline, end of each SBT, and 20 minutes after extubation, surrogates of respiratory effort were measured: esophageal pressure-time-product (PTPes), PTPes per minute (PTPes.min), swing esophageal pressure (SwingPes), and SwingPes per minute (SwingPes.min). Sixty measurements of respiratory effort from 12 patients were analyzed. Median PTPes.min increased from 193.8 [170.8-227.2] cmH2O.s/min at baseline to 236.6 [192.1-313.6] after extubation, with no significant differences between SBTs and postextubation. SwingPes and SwingPes.min were lower during PSV7-PEEP0 than after extubation, with median paired differences of 4.7 (95% CI 0.6-9.8) and 115.3 (95% CI 4.8-297.8), but these differences did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons. No SBT modality differed significantly from post-extubation respiratory effort, suggesting that none could be excluded in COVID-19-related ARDS patients.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101957.abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is an important postoperative neurocognitive complication, and cumulative anticholinergic drug burden (ADB) may increase its risk by impairing central cholinergic neurotransmission. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to clarify the overall association between ADB scores and POD risk in adult surgical patients. We searched major databases and trial registries through February 2026 for studies that assessed ADB using validated scales and reported POD outcomes in adult surgical patients. Random-effects models pooled SMDs and ORs. Prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses explored heterogeneity and robustness. Risk of bias was assessed using NOS, and evidence certainty was rated using GRADE. Ten reports from nine independent cohorts comprising 10,457 participants were included. Patients with POD had higher ADB scores than those without POD (SMD = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.20-0.43). Each one-point increase in continuous ADB was associated with 22% higher odds of POD (OR = 1.22, 95% CI: 1.09-1.37). Both low-to-moderate and high burden were associated with increased POD risk. In scale-specific analyses, the association was significant for ACB. The association was attenuated in studies that excluded patients with cognitive impairment. Methodological quality ranged from moderate to high, and certainty of evidence was low. Higher ADB is significantly associated with higher odds of POD, with a graded increase in risk across burden levels. Baseline cognitive impairment appears to amplify this association. These findings support preoperative ADB assessment and medication optimization in vulnerable surgical patients, while highlighting the need for prospective head-to-head comparisons of anticholinergic burden scales. PROSPERO (CRD420261294941).

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101961.abstract: Non-pharmacological techniques have recently been developed to decrease preoperative anxiety, and music or video may be combined, as in children. This study aims to compare two additional preoperative strategies in adult outpatients. This before-after trial was approved by the ethics committee and included adults undergoing ambulatory procedures under general anaesthesia. It compared usual care before surgery and another period with a video of the expected local journey combined with a relaxing music session. After consent, the level of anxiety was measured via the APAIS score, a repeated visual analogue scale for anxiety, and investigators collected preoperative fears. The main objective was to reduce the number of patients with significant preoperative anxiety. Secondary outcomes compared anxiety during the journey, pain, and quality of recovery after surgery. A P-value < 0.05 was considered significant. 99 patients were included in each period, and 194 completed the study. The intervention group showed a significant reduction in the rate of patients with significant anxiety at admission in the operating room: 23/95 (24.2%, 95%CI [16.7-33.7]) vs. 43/99 (43.4%, 95%CI [34.1-53.3]) with P = 0.005. Secondary outcomes showed no difference in anxiety after surgery, neither in length of stay nor incidence of PONV. The postoperative level of pain was also statistically reduced (P = 0.033). The study suggests that a combined video and music strategy decreases the rate of significant anxiety in patients undergoing outpatient procedures. This low-cost strategy showed a high level of satisfaction and should be encouraged in adults. Clinicaltrials.gov: NCT06461052.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101962.abstract: Periprocedural anticoagulant management requires balancing thrombotic risk against procedure-specific bleeding risk. Existing procedure bleeding risk classifications are fragmented across specialties, inconsistent in methodology, and rarely extend beyond a few procedural domains, limiting their clinical applicability. To develop a comprehensive, standardized, procedure-specific bleeding risk classification to accompany the 2026 GIHP-SFAR periprocedural anticoagulant management guidelines. A formal multidisciplinary consensus was conducted under the auspices of GIHP and SFAR, in collaboration with 24 surgical and interventional specialty societies. For each procedural domain, a working group performed a systematic literature review. Procedures were classified into four tiers: no bleeding risk, low bleeding risk, high bleeding risk, and very high bleeding risk. A specific category was created for procedures carrying particular contextual risk (e.g., anatomical site, patient factors, or need for reversible anticoagulation). Consensus was reached by the full expert panel. Twenty-four procedural domains were classified, ranging from regional anaesthesia and digestive endoscopy to cardiac surgery, neurosurgery, and ophthalmology. Each domain provides a procedure-specific bleeding risk table, with narrative supporting evidence. Procedures warranting delayed resumption of anticoagulation (≥72 hours) or use of short-acting/reversible anticoagulants are identified. The classification covers common and complex surgical scenarios, including those with limited published evidence where structured expert opinion was applied. This companion document provides clinicians with a standardized, evidence-based, procedure-specific bleeding risk framework across 24 domains to support individualized periprocedural anticoagulant decisions in daily practice.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101964.abstract: State Entropy (SE) and Surgical Pleth Index (SPI) parameters aim to optimise anaesthetic depth and intraoperative opioid administration, but their impact on postoperative complications remains unclear. Insufficient training and limited decision support may contribute to inconsistent findings. Thus, we evaluated whether tailored training to improve SE and SPI compliance reduced major postoperative complications. Adult inpatients undergoing intermediate- to high-risk noncardiac surgery were included in this prospective single-centre before-after study in France. The educational intervention and outcomes were based on the Kirkpatrick framework. All anaesthesia providers were invited to participate voluntarily in lectures and bedside training on SE and SPI monitoring. Training impact was assessed using a composite of major postoperative complications within 28 days as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included changes in monitoring practices. Among 1,623 eligible patients, 1,025 were included over a 13-month period (517 before and 508 after training). Of 202 eligible providers, 91 participated in the one-month training programme (45%). After training, simultaneous SE and SPI sensor use increased from 26% to 42% (P < 0.001), and combined SE-SPI compliance increased from 23% to 39% (P < 0.001). Major postoperative complications occurred in 66/517 patients (13%) before and 71/508 patients (14%) after training (P = 0.6). Multivariable and propensity score analyses showed no significant association between the intervention and the primary outcome. This training did not reduce the incidence of major postoperative complications, despite improvements in intraoperative monitoring practices. Future educational strategies should strengthen provider engagement and reinforcement to translate improved monitoring practices into clinical benefit. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06111248.

doi:10.1016/j.accpm.2026.101965.abstract: Dysnatremia is common in critically ill patients and has been linked to poor outcomes and renal prognosis. Burn patients are particularly vulnerable, but the prognostic significance of dysnatremia in this population remains unclear. We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 1,758 burn patients admitted to a French burn center between 2011 and 2023. Dysnatremia was defined as at least one episode of hyponatremia ( 145 mmol/L) during intensive care unit (ICU) stay. The primary endpoint was the incidence of dysnatremia; secondary endpoints included major adverse kidney events (MAKE) at ICU discharge and acute kidney injury (AKI) occurrence and severity. Dysnatremia occurred in 56.3% of patients (n = 990), with hyponatremia in 50.5% (n = 888) and hypernatremia in 23.8% (n = 418). MAKE at ICU discharge did not differ between hyponatremic and normonatremic patients (12.6% vs. 10.9%, p = 0.304) but was sixfold higher with hypernatremia (32.3% vs. 5.4%, p < 0.001). After adjustment for age and burned total body surface area, hypernatremia was independently associated with MAKE at ICU discharge (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 4.03; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.92-5.56; p < 0.001), whereas hyponatremia was not (aHR 1.15; 95% CI: 0.85-1.55; p = 0.377). Clustering analysis identified three phenotypes: Cluster B (severe burns, worst outcomes), Cluster A (older patients, mostly hyponatremic, intermediate outcomes), and Cluster C (younger patients, mild burns, best outcomes). Dysnatremia affects over half of burn patients. Sodium disturbances should be viewed as markers of systemic severity, warranting close monitoring and preventive strategies.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.07.047.abstract: Fibrinogen concentrate (FC) has a well-established safety profile and is recommended for treating acquired fibrinogen deficiency. However, its comparative effectiveness vs other treatments regarding transfusions and patient outcomes remains uncertain. Comparative studies from a range of clinical settings in which patients received FC for acquired hypofibrinogenaemia and that evaluated blood product needs, mortality, thromboembolic events, or hospital length of stay were included in a systematic literature review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO: CRD42024602804). Meta-analyses used pooled data to provide an estimate of the difference in outcome between FC and all other treatments; separate analyses were conducted for adult and paediatric patients. Overall, 58 studies (N=13 530 patients) were analysed. Adult FC recipients received significantly fewer red blood cell, fresh frozen plasma, and platelet units than with other treatments: 28% (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0.72; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.59-0.89; P=0.002), 31% (IRR 0.69; 95% CI 0.54-0.89; P=0.004), and 44% less (IRR 0.56; 95% CI 0.33-0.95; P=0.03), respectively. These results were largely driven by cardiac surgery studies. In an RCT subanalysis, the use and quantity of blood products were significantly reduced with FC. No significant difference in mortality or thromboembolic events was found between treatments in adult patients or in any outcomes analysed in paediatric patients. This meta-analysis suggests FC administered for acquired hypofibrinogenaemia can reduce blood product transfusions in adults, with no obvious safety concerns, compared with other treatments.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.08.007.abstract: Frailty is an established predictor of adverse postoperative outcomes, yet preoperative frailty assessment remains inconsistently implemented despite guideline recommendations. Early identification of frailty enables targeted perioperative assessment and optimisation, and has been associated with improved postoperative outcomes, including a reduction in 1-yr mortality. Asking patients to report their own frailty status before a preoperative assessment could play an important role in improving the assessment of frailty. In this context, the study by Alkadri and colleagues addresses an important practical question: can older surgical patients reliably assess their own frailty status using the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS)? They report a substudy of a prospective cohort examining agreement between self-rated and clinician-rated preoperative CFS scores in patients aged 65 yr and older undergoing elective noncardiac surgery. Their findings suggest moderate agreement between patient and trained assessor ratings, but patient-rated CFS had insufficient sensitivity to replace clinician-led frailty assessment in routine practice.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.08.014.abstract: In-hospital diabetes mellitus management currently relies on intermittent glucose monitoring with point-of-care (POC) testing, rather than continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). Most studies on CGM have focused on its benefits and accuracy in the outpatient setting, in contrast to the hospital setting, where the accuracy may be different. In this prospective observational study (NCT06297850), we assessed the accuracy of CGM (Dexcom G7, Dexcom Inc.) compared with POC monitors in people with diabetes mellitus requiring glucose-lowering medication undergoing surgery or admission to the ICU. The primary outcome was agreement between CGM and POC measurements, defined as median absolute relative difference (MARD). Clarke error grid (CEG) and Bland-Altman analyses were used to quantify the accuracy. Secondary analyses assessed agreement during periods of hypoperfusion, defined as a mean arterial pressure of <65 mm Hg, infusions with vasopressors, or reduced peripheral perfusion index. In 58 participants (mean [standard deviation] age 71 [11]yr; 34% female), the median MARD was 10.9% (5.1-19.4%); 1186 of 1212 paired POC and CGM measurements (98%) were within clinically acceptable ranges (CEG zones A and B). MARD was 4.5% higher (95% confidence interval 2.3-6.7%) during periods of hypoperfusion. Given that hypoglycaemia (<4 mM) did not occur, no paired readings were obtained. Bland-Altman analysis showed similar CGM and POC measurements, with a mean difference of -1 mM (95% limits of agreement -5.6 to 3.4 mM). For the vast majority of interstitial glucose measurements, CGM was accurate in people with diabetes mellitus. Although overall performance was good, caution may be warranted when interpreting CGM data during periods of impaired peripheral perfusion. NCT06297850.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.08.039.abstract: Chronic postsurgical pain after thoracoscopic surgery remains common. We investigated whether perioperative low-dose esketamine infusion would reduce chronic pain after video-assisted thoracoscopic lung resection. In this multicentre, randomised controlled trial, 914 adults were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either esketamine or normal saline. Esketamine was administered as a 0.1 mg kg-1 bolus at induction, followed by continuous intraoperative infusion (0.1 mg kg-1 h-1) and postoperative infusion (0.015 mg kg-1 h-1) for 48 h. The primary outcome was chronic pain at 3 months, defined as persistent pain with a numeric rating scale score ≥1 during coughing in the surgical region. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain, supplemental analgesics use, recovery of bowel function, in-hospital adverse events, and esketamine-related side-effects. We analysed 873 patients (median age, 55 yr; 63% female). The incidence of 3 month chronic pain was lower in the esketamine group than in the control group (14.7% vs 21.2%; adjusted odds ratio, 0.62; 95% confidence interval, 0.43-0.90; P=0.013). A reduction was also observed when using a post hoc outcome definition of a numeric rating scale pain score ≥3 during coughing at 3 months (adjusted odds ratio, 0.39; 95% confidence interval, 0.19-0.84; P=0.015). Esketamine also reduced overall pain scores at rest and during coughing within the first 48 h, and decreased supplemental analgesic requirements within 48 h and 3 months. Perioperative low-dose esketamine infusion significantly reduced 3 month chronic pain after thoracoscopic lung resection without increasing adverse effects. ChiCTR2000040012. This trial was registered on the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (Identifier: ChiCTR2000040012; principal investigator: Fu-hai Ji; dated November 18, 2020; https://www.chictr.org.cn/showprojEN.html?proj=62319).

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.08.040.abstract: Inflammation is widely viewed as a driver of pain, yet clinical and transcriptomic studies report conflicting associations. A clearer understanding of how inflammatory processes relate to pain across clinical contexts is essential for improving diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of chronic pain. We analysed whole-blood RNA sequencing from seven human cohorts spanning four pain conditions, including acute, postoperative, chronic localised, and chronic widespread pain in almost 500 blood samples with corresponding pain intensity scores. Using gene-level meta-analyses, pathway enrichment, and immune cell-specific gene ontologies, we tested how inflammatory responses relate to current pain, future pain trajectories, and within-person changes over time. Inflammation emerged as one of the strongest biological correlates of pain across all cohorts, yet its association direction depended on the pain state. In acute musculoskeletal and postoperative pain, higher inflammatory activation, which correlated with enhanced neutrophil and macrophage function, was associated with greater pain intensity but also correlated with better subsequent recovery, consistent with an adaptive inflammatory response. In chronic localised pain, this relationship was disrupted and inverted: higher inflammatory activity was linked to lower pain intensity and associated with worse long-term outcomes. In chronic widespread pain, macrophage-related inflammatory activity remained positively associated with both pain severity and persistence, suggesting progression toward a maladaptive immune state. These findings indicate that inflammation is not uniformly detrimental in pain but plays distinct roles depending on disease stage and context. Inflammation might support resolution during acute injury yet become dysregulated in chronic and nociplastic pain. Recognising these context-dependent roles could help explain conflicting findings in the literature and guide more precise use of anti-inflammatory therapies.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.08.052.abstract: Exercise is the most common approach to prehabilitation; the optimal exercise interventions to improve postoperative outcomes are unknown. This was a systematic review with network meta-analysis that followed a prespecified protocol (CRD420251034396). Peer-reviewed search strategies were applied from inception to 4 April 2025, to Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), without language restrictions. We included all RCTs of prehabilitation that included at least one exercise intervention (aerobic, strength, pulmonary, or functional exercises) and that reported at least one critical outcome (postoperative complications, length of stay, health-related quality of life, or physical recovery). P-scores were used to rank interventions by their probability of being most beneficial. Best practices, including duplicate review, were followed. Confidence in network meta-analysis informed certainty ratings. We screened 7660 citations, reviewed 1480 full-text articles, and included 96 unique RCTs (N=7396). Combined aerobic, pulmonary, and functional exercise were most likely to reduce complications (P-score 0.94, odds ratio 0.16, 95% CI 0.05-0.60; very low certainty) and length of stay (P-score 0.97, mean difference -3.4 days, 95% CI -5.7 to -1.0; moderate certainty). Combined aerobic and strength exercise was most likely to improve health-related quality of life (P-score 0.93, standardised mean difference 0.67, 95% CI 0.07-1.27; low certainty). No exercise interventions significantly improved physical recovery. The efficacy of exercise prehabilitation interventions may be outcome-specific. Implementation of aerobic and pulmonary exercise prehabilitation may be warranted. Low-risk-of-bias trials are required to confirm or refute available data, which are mostly low certainty.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.08.053.abstract: Intraoperative noise is an occupational hazard with the potential to compromise anaesthetist performance and patient safety. The WHO recommends hospital sound exposure ≤ 35 dB LAeq (A-weighted equivalent continuous sound level), yet noise levels routinely exceed this level. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine intraoperative noise levels worldwide. Five databases were searched from inception to May 2026, in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Studies were eligible for inclusion if they included surgical specialty and a measure of noise sampled recorded with validated sound metres. Studies were eligible for meta-analysis if they included a mean time-weighted average. Two authors undertook searches and risk-of-bias assessment. Meta-regression estimated pooled means, heterogeneity, and variance. Fifty studies met the inclusion criteria in the systematic review, with 28 studies providing 43 unique datasets subclassified by type of surgical procedure for analysis. The pooled random-effects mean intraoperative noise level was 70.7 A-weighted dB [dB(A)] (95% CI 69.0-72.3). Subgroup analysis demonstrated the highest exposures in otolaryngology at 78.8 dB(A) (95% CI 72.8-84.7) and orthopaedics at 73.3 dB(A) (95% CI 68.9-77.8). Meta-regression confirmed surgical specialty as a significant predictor of mean exposure (Q=25.8, degrees of freedom=6, P=0.0002). Anaesthetists are consistently exposed to intraoperative sound levels exceeding WHO guidelines, particularly in high-intensity specialties such as orthopaedics and otolaryngology. These findings provide a specialty-specific synthesis of noise exposure and highlight the need for targeted interventions, standardised measurement, and research linking exposure to clinical outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.08.054.abstract: Diaphragmatic dysfunction contributes to perioperative respiratory morbidity. Point-of-care ultrasound enables noninvasive bedside assessment of diaphragmatic structure and motion and is increasingly used in perioperative practice. However, its diagnostic performance and measurement reliability in this setting have not been systematically evaluated. This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence, with emphasis on reliability, reproducibility, and agreement with reference standards. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported as per Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews. A protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework. MEDLINE, MEDLINE ePubs and In-Process Citations, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane databases were searched. Eligible studies included adult or paediatric surgical patients undergoing perioperative diaphragmatic ultrasound. Data were charted on study characteristics, ultrasound techniques, reference standards, and measures of diagnostic accuracy and inter- and intra-observer agreement. Nineteen studies (712 patients) were included, most being prospective observational and published after 2015. In adults, diaphragmatic ultrasound showed generally positive, although variable, correlations with spirometry, transdiaphragmatic pressure, electrophysiological measures, neuromuscular recovery, and arterial blood gas-based weaning criteria. Thresholds for excursion and thickening varied across studies. Inter- and intra-observer agreement was generally good to excellent, including among operators with limited training. In paediatric populations, ultrasound demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy and strong agreement with fluoroscopy, with excellent interobserver reliability. Perioperative diaphragmatic ultrasound shows acceptable reliability and agreement with reference standards. Heterogeneity in techniques and outcomes limits comparability. Standardisation and outcome-linked studies are needed to define its role.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.08.055.abstract: Postoperative increases in plasma total tau (t-tau) protein have raised concerns that surgery can cause CNS injury. Brain-derived tau (BD-tau) is a novel biomarker that quantifies CNS-derived tau. We assessed BD-tau concentrations in plasma and CSF after surgery to investigate neuronal injury and mechanisms driving increases in plasma t-tau. This was a substudy of a previous prospective cohort study enrolling adult patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty. We measured plasma and CSF BD-tau and t-tau before neuraxial anaesthesia (baseline) and at 4, 8, 24, 32, and 48 h after surgery and assessed cognitive performance at baseline and 3 months. Biomarker concentrations are reported as median (IQR) percentage change from baseline. Plasma BD-tau peaked at 4 h with a 254% increase (137-382%, P<0.001) and remained elevated by 31% (6-75%, P<0.001) at 48 h. CSF BD-tau was unchanged at 4 h but increased by 51% (21-82%, P=0.004) at 48 h. Plasma BD-tau was associated with plasma t-tau (β=1.09, 95% CI 0.95-1.23, P<0.001), whereas plasma BD-tau and CSF BD-tau were inversely associated (β=-0.71, -0.97 to -0.45, P<0.001). Higher postoperative plasma BD-tau was associated with both higher CSF albumin and worse cognitive performance at 3 months. Early postoperative increases in plasma t-tau are consistent with a CNS origin but not concomitant neuronal injury. Instead, the early plasma BD-tau increase and the inverse association between CSF and plasma BD-tau could indicate a redistribution of tau from the CNS to plasma.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.08.059.abstract: Some women receiving epidural labour analgesia become hyperthermic. Assuming a causal mechanism, denser and more extensive sympathetic blocks might promote hyperthermia by inhibiting sweating. We therefore tested the hypothesis that hyperthermia is most common when epidural blocks are particularly effective, as indicated by excellent analgesia. In this multicentre prospective observational study, we enrolled nulliparous women with term cephalic singleton pregnancies who planned vaginal delivery with epidural analgesia. Pain intensity was assessed using an 11-point numerical rating scale (0-10) during uterine contractions before analgesia, at 10, 30, and 60 min after initiating analgesia, and then hourly until the end of the third stage, and calculated as time-weighted average, average, area under the curve, and peak scores. Our primary endpoint was intrapartum hyperthermia (≥38°C). Intrapartum hyperthermia occurred in 13% (124/952) of participants (median age 29 yr). After adjustment for confounding factors, lower pain intensity was associated with higher odds of intrapartum hyperthermia across all four measures: time-weighted average (odds ratio 1.64; 95% CI 1.40-1.91; P<0.001), average (1.56; 1.35-1.81; P<0.001), area under the curve (1.05; 1.03-1.07; P<0.001), and peak scores (1.19; 1.09-1.30; P<0.001). The identified inflection points were a time-weighted average score ≤3 points (odds ratio 8.67; 95% CI 4.19-17.9; P<0.001), average score ≤3 points (6.63; 3.56-12.3; P<0.001), area under the curve ≤30 point⋅h (13.0; 3.75-45.0; P<0.001), and peak score ≤4 points (2.53; 1.65-3.89; P<0.001), all of which were associated with increased intrapartum hyperthermia. Among nulliparous women receiving epidural analgesia for labour, lower pain scores were associated with higher odds of hyperthermia. Extensive sympathetic blockade may promote maternal hyperthermia. NCT04940091.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.09.002.abstract: Patients from more deprived backgrounds experience poorer postoperative outcomes. We analysed preoperative characteristics in UK Perioperative Quality Improvement Programme participants according to socioeconomic position to explore opportunities for targeted interventions. Participants were adults aged ≥18 yr undergoing major elective surgery at UK Perioperative Quality Improvement Programme sites. Socioeconomic position was determined using postcode data and the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) standardised aggregate scale of area-level deprivation. Associations between IMD position and patient characteristics, health behaviours, and comorbidities were analysed using descriptive statistics with appropriate parametric and nonparametric testing. Of 55 938 participants included, quintile 1 (most deprived) represented the smallest subgroup (14.2%), with recruitment varying by region and site. Median age was 66 yr with IMD 1 participants 5 yr younger (62 yr) than IMD 5 (67 yr). Deprivation gradients (IMD 5 to 1) were seen for home ownership, occupation, and educational attainment. Prevalences of smoking, inactivity, and obesity increased from IMD 5 to 1. Higher prevalences of major long-term conditions including diabetes mellitus, heart failure, stroke, and ASA physical status 3-4 were observed in more deprived quintiles. Prevalence rates of dementia and renal impairment were similar across quintiles despite the age gradient. Notably, the proportions of patients living with frailty and disability increased with deprivation. Patients presenting for major surgery from more deprived backgrounds do so in poorer overall health. They can encounter barriers to both research participation and available preoperative support. Addressing this unmet need to prevent widening perioperative health inequalities requires interventions tailored to the patient's socioeconomic context.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.09.012.abstract: Adverse neurocognitive and functional outcomes are common after cardiac surgery. Cerebral near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) monitors regional cerebral oxygen saturation, allowing clinicians to detect and reverse cerebral desaturation. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs to evaluate whether intraoperative NIRS monitoring improves neurocognitive outcomes after cardiac surgery. We searched CENTRAL, CINAHL, Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science for RCTs comparing NIRS-guided intraoperative management with usual care in adults undergoing on-pump cardiac surgery, assessing the outcomes of postoperative cognitive decline, delirium, stroke, mortality, and functional recovery. We pooled data using random-effects meta-analysis and assessed certainty of evidence using GRADE methodology. We included 17 RCTs (N=2288). NIRS-guided management probably reduces early postoperative cognitive decline (risk ratio [RR] 0.65, 95% CI 0.42-0.99; I2=65%, moderate certainty), may have little or no effect on stroke (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.42-1.91; low certainty) or mortality (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.47-1.52; low certainty), and may have no effect on delirium (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.56-1.09; I2=32%, low certainty). Findings were primarily derived from small, single-centre trials with heterogenous NIRS thresholds and intervention algorithms. Few studies evaluated outcomes beyond 30 days, and none evaluated validated measures of quality of life or function. Although NIRS-guided intraoperative care shows promise for reducing early postoperative cognitive decline after cardiac surgery, evidence of benefit for other neurocognitive or clinical outcomes remains limited. Large multicentre studies are needed to confirm its utility, refine intervention thresholds, and determine its impact on long-term cognition, function, and quality of life. Systematic review protocol. PROSPERO (CRD42022336468).

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.09.015.abstract: Acute respiratory acid-base changes induce pH-dependent electrolyte redistribution. Although this response has been characterised in vitro, the in vivo changes depend on multicompartment buffering and remain poorly defined. We conducted a multicentre retrospective study of patients undergoing apnoea testing for organ donation after determination of brain death, a clinical model allowing in vivo study of acute ventilatory changes. The primary outcome was the pH-dependent change in strong ion difference (SID). Secondary analyses examined individual electrolytes, pH-SID effect modification by physiological variables, and how well the derived model agreed with observed SID changes compared with a simple bedside pH-correction method (ΔSID=-15×ΔpH). In 263 participants, pH decreased from 7.40 (0.07) to 7.23 (0.07) and returned to 7.40 (0.08). Per pH unit increase, SID changed by -11.7 meq L-1 (95% CI -13.1 to -10.3; P<0.001), driven primarily by sodium ion (Na) (52% of change -7.2 mM; P<0.001) and chloride ion (Cl) (36% of change +3.7 mM; P<0.001). Higher haemoglobin concentration was associated with a higher pH-dependent SID change, together explaining 53% of within-patient variability. Agreement between predicted and observed SID changes was only modestly improved by using the derived model vs a simplified pH-correction model (sd of differences 1.74 vs 1.92 meq L-1). Acute respiratory acid-base disturbances produce in vivo Na and Cl redistribution associated with pH change that are modulated by haemoglobin concentration. The observed pH-dependent electrolyte redistribution is consistent with physiological buffering and can be reasonably approximated using a simple bedside pH-correction model.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.09.016.abstract: Pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg positioning during laparoscopic colorectal surgery promote atelectasis and increase the risk of postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs). Electrical impedance tomography (EIT) enables individualised PEEP titration by visualising regional lung collapse, facilitating lung-protective ventilation. However, evidence of its effect on clinical PPCs remains limited. In this single-centre, parallel-group RCT, adults with intermediate to high risk for PPCs (ARISCAT score ≥26) who underwent laparoscopic colorectal surgery were randomly assigned to receive intraoperative PEEP titration guided by EIT or a conventional fixed PEEP of 5 cm H2O. The primary outcome was PPCs incidence within 30 days, as determined by a multidisciplinary adjudication team using standardised criteria. Among the 117 randomised participants (mean [range] age: 62 [37-80] yr; 37% female), EIT-guided PEEP (n=59) resulted in lower driving pressure (16 [15-18] cm H2O) compared with fixed PEEP (n=58; 19 [17-22] cm H2O; P<0.0001). The incidence of 30 day PPCs was lower among participants randomised to EIT-guided PEEP (29/59 [49.2%]) than those in the fixed-PEEP group (42/58 [72.4%]; hazard ratio: 0.53; 95% CI, 0.33-0.85; P=0.009). PPCs including atelectasis and pneumonia occurred less frequently among participants randomised to EIT-guided PEEP. Compared with conventional fixed PEEP of 5 cm H2O, EIT-guided PEEP was associated with a lower incidence of PPCs among patients at intermediate to high PPCs risk undergoing laparoscopic colorectal surgery, suggesting a role for EIT in intraoperative lung protection. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2300076677.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.09.018.abstract: Pain after kidney transplantation is often severe, and graft function constrains the use of systemic analgesia. Previous syntheses of regional techniques pooled them as a class, combined donors with recipients, and did not use a minimal clinically important difference (MCID). We searched PubMed, Embase, and CENTRAL through 5 September 2026 for randomised trials of regional analgesia in adult kidney transplant recipients (PROSPERO CRD420261478933); a trial-registry search and network meta-analysis were added post hoc. Bayesian random-effects models with MCID-scaled priors yielded posterior probabilities of benefit and of exceeding the MCID, and certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. Fourteen trials (903 participants) were included. Only quadratus lumborum (QL) and transversus abdominis plane (TAP) blocks could be pooled against control. Both yielded lower pain at every pooled time point, but no pairwise pain comparison reached 80% probability of exceeding the 1.0 point MCID. Opioid consumption at 24 h was lower with the QL block (-15.5 morphine milligram equivalents; 95% credible interval -23.6 to -6.7) and the TAP block (-10.5; -14.4 to -5.5), with each reduction exceeding the 5 mg MCID with a probability >97%. In the network meta-analysis, no difference between QL and TAP blocks in pain or opioid consumption reached 80% probability of exceeding the MCID. Graft function and safety data were too sparse to pool. Twelve eligible registered trials were unpublished; certainty of evidence was very low. Quadrtus lumborum and transversus abdominus plane blocks reduce pain and opioid consumption at 24 h, but only the reduction in opioid consumption has a high probability of being clinically important. Certainty of evidence is very low; no technique is preferred, and effects on graft function are unknown.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.09.021.abstract: Propofol-based total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) is commonly used in neurovascular surgery, in which intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring limits inhalation anaesthetic use. However, propofol causes hypotension, and prolonged infusions can delay emergence. Remimazolam, a benzodiazepine whose effects are reversible with flumazenil, has been associated with less intraoperative hypotension than propofol, but its use raises concerns about postoperative delirium (POD). We tested whether remimazolam-based TIVA is noninferior to propofol-based TIVA for POD. In this single-centre, double-blind, randomised noninferiority trial, adults undergoing elective intracranial aneurysm clipping, arteriovenous malformation resection, microvascular decompression, or superficial temporal artery-middle cerebral artery bypass received remimazolam-based TIVA with flumazenil reversal at emergence, or propofol-based TIVA, both with remifentanil. The primary outcome was the cumulative incidence of POD within 5 days, assessed twice daily with the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the 3-Minute Diagnostic Interview for CAM-defined delirium (3D-CAM). The prespecified noninferiority margin was 10 percentage points. Among 686 patients in the modified intention-to-treat analysis, POD occurred in 44 of 344 (12.8%) with remimazolam and 37 of 342 (10.8%) with propofol (risk difference, 1.97 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.85 to 6.80; one-sided P<0.001 for noninferiority); per-protocol results were consistent. Hypotensive burden below a mean arterial pressure threshold of 65 mm Hg was lower in the remimazolam group (median, 0 vs 7.5 mm Hg min; P<0.001), and tracheal extubation in the operating room was more frequent (85.2% vs 67.3%). Remimazolam-based TIVA met the prespecified criterion for noninferiority to propofol-based TIVA with respect to postoperative delirium after elective neurovascular surgery. Interpretation should take into account that the observed incidence of postoperative delirium was lower than anticipated when the noninferiority margin was defined. NCT06115031 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.09.022.abstract: Fluid accumulation in surgical patients is associated with worse outcomes. Lung ultrasound (LUS) and venous excess ultrasound (VExUS) grading can assess congestion and thereby fluid tolerance. However, evidence regarding epidemiology, feasibility, and associations of reduced fluid tolerance with outcomes in surgical patients is lacking. This was a prospective single-centre observational cohort study in patients undergoing major gastrointestinal surgery. LUS and VExUS were performed before surgery and daily for up to 5 days after surgery. Reduced fluid tolerance was defined as pulmonary congestion (B profile on LUS), systemic congestion (VExUS ≥2), or both. The primary outcome was the prevalence of reduced fluid tolerance. Secondary outcomes were feasibility of ultrasound assessments, Clavien-Dindo grade ≥3 complications, and length of stay (LOS). Of the 200 participants included, 73 (37%) exhibited signs of reduced fluid tolerance, most commonly on postoperative day 4 (n=28; 14%). Reduced fluid tolerance was primarily driven by pulmonary congestion (n=69; 95%), whereas systemic congestion was rare. In most affected patients (47 of 73; 64%), reduced fluid tolerance was limited to 1 day. Of 1200 planned assessments, 146 (12%) were missing: 123 because participants declined, mostly owing to the burden of repeated assessments, and 23 (2%) because of incomplete views. Reduced fluid tolerance was associated with LOS of >7 days (odds ratio 3.29; 95% CI 1.03-10.70), but not with major postoperative complications (hazard ratio 1.18; 95% CI 0.49-2.86). Reduced fluid tolerance detected by ultrasound is common after major gastrointestinal surgery and associated with increased LOS. Ultrasound assessments were technically feasible, but repeated assessments were perceived as a burden by a substantial proportion of patients. NCT06166719 (principal investigator: A.P.J. Vlaar; first registered: 04-12-2023).

doi:10.1016/j.bjao.2026.100857.abstract: Scientific satire occupies an unusual place in medical publishing. This editorial discusses the role of medical satire by highlighting an article that poses as a retrospective observational trial using a large database, and compares a clinically relevant outcome between two arbitrary, physiologically meaningless groups. The differences between the groups are statistically significant, but physiologically nonsensical. The editorial explores epistemology as it applies to the practice of medicine. The greatest value of the satire may be medical education and its teaching of clinical reasoning. It reminds clinicians that cognitive heuristics, arbitrary categorisation, and large datasets can combine to produce statistically convincing, yet clinically meaningless, associations.

doi:10.1016/j.bjao.2026.100864.abstract: Patients with obesity are at an increased risk of postoperative pulmonary complications and impaired lung function after general anaesthesia. Although higher levels of PEEP combined with recruitment manoeuvres may improve intraoperative respiratory mechanics, their effect on postoperative lung function remains uncertain. We evaluated whether high PEEP with recruitment manoeuvres improves postoperative spirometry in obese patients undergoing abdominal surgery. This single-centre substudy of the Protective Ventilation in Obese Patients randomised controlled trial was conducted at Ghent University Hospital, Belgium. Adults with a BMI of ≥35 kg·m-2 undergoing abdominal surgery were randomised to high PEEP (12 cm H2O) with recruitment manoeuvres or low PEEP (4 cm H2O) without routine recruitment manoeuvres. Both groups received low tidal volume ventilation (7 mL·kg-1 predicted body weight). The primary outcome was the change in forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) from baseline to postoperative day 1. Secondary outcomes included changes in spirometry variables and oxygen saturation. Postoperative spirometry data were available for 44 patients (23 low PEEP, 21 high PEEP). Postoperative lung function declined in all patients. The change in FEV1 from baseline to postoperative day 1 did not differ between the low- and high-PEEP groups (-0.90 [0.68] L vs -0.93 [0.66] L; between-group effect 0.0 L; 95% confidence interval -0.4 to 0.4 L; P=0.89). No differences were observed in secondary outcomes. In obese patients undergoing abdominal surgery with low tidal volume ventilation, high PEEP with recruitment manoeuvers did not improve postoperative spirometric outcomes or oxygen saturation compared with low PEEP without routine recruitment manoeuvres. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02148692.

doi:10.1016/j.bjao.2026.100865.abstract: Acute pain management is shifting away from traditional paternalistic models towards more collaborative, patient-centred approaches that emphasise shared decision making and the use of digital health technologies. Here, we review recent advances in digital health technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) that support shared decision making, including interactive decision aids, video narratives, and AI-assisted tools. These innovations have the potential to optimise analgesia, reduce the risks associated with opioids and opioid-related harms, and enhance patient autonomy across surgical, emergency, and primary care settings. Although emerging evidence shows promise in improving prescribing efficiency and increasing patient satisfaction, there are still significant barriers to implementation. These include resource limitations, challenges in selecting appropriate tools, and the necessity for robust validation of AI systems. Herein, we critically evaluate the current evidence, discuss practical strategies for implementation, and provide recommendations for integrating these technologies into routine clinical practice.

doi:10.1016/j.bjao.2026.100868.abstract: Prehabilitation optimises patients' physical, nutritional, and psychological readiness before major surgery, but remains largely absent from Austrian clinical practice. We aimed to identify stakeholder-perceived barriers to prehabilitation implementation and assess the readiness of the healthcare system. An exploratory qualitative study using semi-structured interviews was conducted with eight purposively sampled stakeholders representing anaesthesiology (n=2), surgery (n=2), outpatient cardiology (n=1), clinical psychology (n=1), physiotherapy (n=1), and health insurance administration (n=1). Interviews conducted between February and March 2024 were analysed using descriptive thematic content analysis and mapped to the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. Six themes emerged: attitudes towards prehabilitation, work environment, healthcare system structure, economic factors, cultural factors, and politics, evidence, and guidelines. Despite unanimous recognition of clinical value, knowledge of prehabilitation varied widely. Critical barriers included the structural and financial separation between inpatient and outpatient sectors, the absence of reimbursement mechanisms, workforce shortages, organisational inertia, and limited advocacy by professional societies. Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research mapping identified barriers across all five domains, with outer setting barriers-particularly fragmented financing and the absence of national guidelines-being the most prominent. These exploratory findings reveal conceptual, systemic, and cultural barriers to prehabilitation in Austria. The simultaneous absence of integrated financing, professional society advocacy, and coordinated governance may explain Austria's particularly limited uptake compared to that in the UK and the Netherlands. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation through larger-scale qualitative studies, quantitative surveys, and pilot implementation trials that include patient perspectives and economic modelling.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103250.abstract: Cancer incidence is rising among young adults in several high-income countries, yet comprehensive data from Southern Europe, particularly Portugal, remain limited. We characterized temporal trends in cancer incidence among young adults (20-49 years) in Portugal between 2001 and 2022, comparing them with older adults (≥50 years). This nationwide population-based cohort study included 1,102,774 incident cancer cases recorded by the Portuguese National Cancer Registry. Age-standardized incidence rates (ASIR) per 100,000 inhabitants were calculated using the European Standard Population. Temporal trends were analysed using joinpoint regression, estimating annual percentage changes (APC) and average annual percentage changes (AAPC) by sex, age group, and cancer type. Cancer cases increased from 36,604 in 2001 to 60,926 in 2022. Young adults accounted for 13.0% of all cases. Among young women, ASIR increased by 31.6% (from 156.2 to 205.6; AAPC: +1.48%), driven largely by breast cancer (+50.0%), thyroid (+94.1%), melanoma (+84.1%), and lung cancer (+78.7%). In contrast, young men showed stable overall ASIR (AAPC: -0.05%), with a biphasic pattern of increase (2001-2010) followed by decline (2010-2022). However, young men experienced substantial rises in colorectal (+56.6%), thyroid (+185.1%), and melanoma (+70.1%) incidence, alongside declines in stomach (-67.0%), oesophageal (-56.8%), and lung (-45.8%) cancers. Older adults demonstrated significant ASIR increases driven by trends before 2011, with subsequent stabilization or decline. Cancer incidence among young Portuguese adults is increasing, particularly among women, with sex-specific and site-specific patterns. While declines in tobacco-related cancers reflect successful prevention efforts, rising rates of breast, colorectal, thyroid, and melanoma in young adults signal the need for enhanced targeted prevention strategies and continued etiological research.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103251.abstract: The five-year relative survival (RS) for cervical cancer in Puerto Rico and the United States (US) is less than 70%. To assess survival trends in the past decades, we compared the five-year RS of cervical cancer in Puerto Rico and in the US. Data was obtained from the Puerto Rico Central Cancer Registry and the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program. We included microscopically confirmed cases of cervical carcinoma between 2000 and 2021. The five-year RS trends were analyzed with Joinpoint regression models using the JPSurv software, which estimated the Average Absolute Change in Survival (AAC_S). Puerto Rico showed a lower five-year RS than US overall across the study period. In the US, the AAC_S was -0.78 for patients diagnosed between 2000 and 2003 (95%CI: -1.32 to -0.23), -0.22 for 2003-2013 (95%CI: -0.36 to -0.08), and 0.25 for 2013-2021 (95%CI: 0.01-0.49). In Puerto Rico, the AAC_S was -0.03 for 2000-2011 (95%CI: -0.56-0.51), 1.71 for 2011-2016 (95%CI: 0.60-2.83), and -1.10 for 2016-2021 (95%CI: -3.12-0.92). Puerto Rico shows poorer cervical cancer five-year RS than the US. Increased five-year RS was observed in the US overall population after 2013. In Puerto Rico, improvements in five-year RS were observed after 2011, but these were halted after 2016. This finding may suggest that barriers to accessing care during periods of extreme events, such as the convergence of the 2017 hurricanes and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic challenges, likely affected survival trends from 2016 to 2021. Future research should further characterize barriers to improve cervical cancer survival.
