doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2026.10.001.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has revolutionized treatment of hematological malignancies, but cytokine release syndrome (CRS) remains a major toxicity. Fever-a hallmark of CRS-has been understudied as a modifier of therapeutic efficacy. In a retrospective cohort of patients with B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia treated with CD22-directed CAR T cells (NCT02315612), sustained high-grade fever inversely correlated with clinical response. Mechanistically, experimental hyperthermia impaired proximal CAR signaling, reduced cytotoxicity, and compromised metabolic fitness through dysregulated arginine metabolism. Arginine supplementation restored CAR T cell function following hyperthermic stress and enhanced cytotoxicity under normothermic conditions. This effect required mTOR-dependent recruitment of the eIF4F translation-initiation complex and downstream c-MYC-driven metabolic reprogramming. Importantly, arginine enhanced good manufacturing practice (GMP)-manufactured CAR T cell function under normothermia, while oral supplementation improved in vivo efficacy. These findings identify metabolic control of translation as a fever-sensitive checkpoint and establish arginine supplementation as a tractable strategy to enhance CAR T cell efficacy.

doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2026.10.010.abstract: This phase 2 trial included 211 Chinese participants with type 2 diabetes mellitus (mean age 48.4 years; 131 participants were male). Participants received once-weekly subcutaneous UBT251 (2 mg, 4 mg [initial dose 0.5 mg], 4 mg [initial dose 1 mg], or 6 mg), 1 mg semaglutide, or placebo for 24 weeks. At week 24, UBT251 achieved least-squares mean changes in glycated hemoglobin of -2.16% (95% CI, -2.39 to -1.92) to -1.98% (95% CI, -2.31 to -1.64), versus -1.77% (95% CI, -1.99 to -1.54) for semaglutide and -0.66% (95% CI, -0.90 to -0.41) for placebo (placebo-adjusted differences: -1.50% to -1.32%; all p < 0.001). UBT251 significantly reduced fasting blood glucose, 2-h postprandial glucose, and waist circumference versus placebo (all p < 0.001). Weight reduction with UBT251 was significantly greater than both placebo and semaglutide (all p < 0.05). Gastrointestinal events were the most common treatment-emergent adverse events. These findings support further phase 3 evaluation of UBT251. Registration: CTR20250029; NCT07163624.

doi:10.1016/j.ctrv.2026.103219.abstract: Pathological response (pR) has increasingly been used as a surrogate marker of neoadjuvant treatment efficacy in soft tissue sarcoma (STS), yet evidence linking it to improved survival remains inconsistent. This review evaluates the prognostic value of pR in neoadjuvant-treated STS. A systematic literature review identified clinical trials, observational studies, and retrospective studies assessing survival outcomes associated with pR, defined by residual viable tumour cells (RVT), necrosis, or fibrosis/hyalinization, in STS treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or chemoradiotherapy. Results were reported narratively given substantial heterogeneity between studies. Twenty-seven studies comprising 3961 patients (median 112, range 50-496) were included. Twenty-five reported RVT, eight necrosis, and seven fibrosis/hyalinization. Considerable variability was observed in the prognostic value of pR across studies. Low RVT predicted improved survival in 36% (9/25), high necrosis predicted decreased survival in 75% (6/8), and fibrosis/hyalinization was inconsistent (43% favourable, 29% unfavourable). Cut-off values, histological parameters and definitions, and patient and treatment characteristics varied widely. Analyses were predominantly unadjusted for confounders, including tumour grade, histological subtype, and resection margin. Current evidence is insufficient to support pR as a reliable prognostic predictor. The prognostic value of RVT, necrosis, and fibrosis/hyalinization varies substantially across studies, likely reflecting differences in histological subtype, tumour biology, treatment heterogeneity, and methodological inconsistencies in pR assessment. Standardisation of histological parameters assessed, their definitions, and pR categorisation criteria is required to determine the prognostic relevance of pR in STS. The proposed CHIRE framework provides a practical foundation for harmonising pR assessment and reporting in future STS studies.

doi:10.1016/j.ctrv.2026.103222.abstract: Research over the past two decades has repositioned exercise from a general lifestyle recommendation to a potential anticancer intervention. Pooled analyses of more than 1.4 million participants link regular physical activity with lower incidence of at least 13 tumour types, and prospective cohort data report cancer-specific mortality 24-31% lower among the most active patients with breast, colorectal, prostate and lung cancer, although these estimates derive from observational designs using self-reported activity. In 2025, a phase III trial in stage III colon cancer provided the first randomised evidence that a structured exercise and behaviour-change programme improves disease-free and overall survival after adjuvant chemotherapy; a randomised trial in ovarian cancer subsequently did not show a progression-free survival benefit. Candidate mechanisms include insulin and growth-factor signalling, myokine secretion, immune mobilisation, reduced chronic inflammation and gut microbiome remodelling, although these rest on evidence ranging from cell culture to human trials and are rarely distinguished by level. Despite this evidence, structural, educational and economic barriers prevent integration of exercise into routine oncology care. This Review synthesises the available evidence and identifies the steps required for clinical adoption.

doi:10.1016/j.ctrv.2026.103223.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into pharmaceutical discovery, yet the extent to which AI-enabled assets have translated into clinical-stage programs remains incompletely characterized. We performed a cross-sectional descriptive analysis of therapeutic assets discovered or developed using AI approaches that had entered at least one interventional human clinical trial through March 1, 2026. We identified 129 AI-enabled therapeutic assets across 69 companies. Oncology was the dominant therapeutic area (74 assets, 57.3%), and small molecules accounted for the majority of the pipeline (103 assets, 79.8%). Among these assets, 72 (55.8%) had completed Phase 1 and 24 (18.9%) had completed Phase 2; only five had entered or completed Phase 3. The observed probability of success was 77.8% for Phase 1 and 19.5% for Phase 2. Forty-eight assets (37.2%) were classified as targeting a novel biological target. Among companies with available data, the median time from founding to Phase 1 entry was 6.5 years (IQR 4.0-9.2), median total funding raised was $186.7 million (IQR $48.1-$595.0 million), and the median employee count at clinical entry was 73 (IQR 32-129), with a median operational intensity of $2.72 million per employee. AI-enabled therapeutics are entering clinical testing at increasing scale, but most programs remain early in development, with few having advanced beyond Phase 2. This dataset provides a baseline for future evaluation of whether AI-enabled discovery ultimately improves regulatory approval rates and clinical outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.ctrv.2026.103225.abstract: Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (HDGC) caused by germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in CDH1 remains a difficult hereditary cancer syndrome to manage. Prophylactic total gastrectomy has long been considered the most definitive preventive strategy, but recent penetrance estimates, expert endoscopic surveillance cohorts, and better characterization of early signet-ring cell lesions have challenged a uniform approach for all carriers. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on CDH1-associated gastric cancer risk, testing criteria, mechanisms of carcinogenesis, prophylactic gastrectomy, endoscopic surveillance, and emerging biomarkers for risk stratification. The available data support a more individualized discussion that integrates family history, age, comorbidity, sex-specific cancer risks, patient preferences, and access to expert surveillance. However, current biomarkers remain investigational, and no blood-, stool-, gastric-fluid-, or tissue-based assay is validated to replace surgery or endoscopic surveillance in routine care. At present, personalized management is best understood as structured shared decision-making within specialist centers, rather than fully biomarker-driven prevention. Future progress will require prospective registries, standardized surveillance protocols, molecular endpoints linked to clinical progression, and careful evaluation of quality of life after both surveillance and gastrectomy.

doi:10.1016/j.ctrv.2026.103234.abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) remains one of the most lethal thoracic malignancies, characterized by rapid progression, early metastasis, and limited durable responses to conventional therapy. Delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3), a Notch pathway inhibitory ligand aberrantly overexpressed on the surface of approximately 70-85% of SCLC tumor cells but largely absent from normal adult tissue, has emerged as a compelling and therapeutically actionable target. Early efforts to exploit DLL3 through the antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) rovalpituzumab tesirine (Rova-T) yielded important mechanistic insights despite failing to demonstrate survival benefit in phase III trials and have since catalyzed a new generation of more refined DLL3-directed strategies. This review critically examines the evolving portfolio of DLL3-targeted therapies across three principal modalities: T-cell engagers, ADCs, and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapies. In parallel, we examine emerging non-DLL3 therapeutic strategies reshaping the broader SCLC landscape. We additionally discuss the translational science underpinning DLL3 as a biomarker, including the emerging roles of circulating tumor cell-based liquid biopsy and DLL3-directed immunoPET-CT imaging in patient selection and treatment monitoring.

doi:10.1016/j.ctrv.2026.103237.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the treatment landscape of several malignancies; however, their efficacy in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer (PROC) remains limited. The immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) in ovarian cancer constitutes a major barrier to effective antitumor immunity, prompting the development of various strategies to enhance responsiveness to ICIs. This narrative review examines current therapeutic approaches targeting the TME to overcome resistance to ICIs in PROC, with a focus on angiogenesis, innate immunity, and adaptive immune pathways. Despite a strong biological rationale, most chemotherapy-free ICI-based combinations targeting specific immune or stromal components have shown limited and inconsistent clinical benefit. The most notable clinical activity has been observed when ICIs are combined with chemotherapy, particularly in regimens that include anti-angiogenic agents. Recent positive results from a single phase 3 trial evaluating pembrolizumab in combination with weekly paclitaxel, with or without bevacizumab, mark a notable deviation from the predominantly negative outcomes of earlier studies. Nevertheless, it remains uncertain whether this result represents a true paradigm shift or a context-specific effect. Currently, no validated predictive biomarkers exist to reliably identify patients most likely to benefit from ICI-based strategies. The discrepancy between the isolated success of chemo-immunotherapy combinations and the failure of most previous trials highlights the need for further investigation into TME biology. A more comprehensive understanding of TME dynamics and the development of biomarker-driven patient selection strategies will be essential to define the role of ICIs in this challenging clinical context.

doi:10.1016/j.ctrv.2026.103239.abstract: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) is associated with chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV), yet the incidence, severity, and optimal antiemetic prophylaxis remain uncertain. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to quantify T-DXd-related nausea and vomiting and evaluate the effectiveness of triplet vs doublet prophylaxis. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched Ovid MEDLINE® ALL, Embase, and the Cochrane Library (1946 to June 2025) for studies reporting nausea and vomiting outcomes with T-DXd. The primary endpoint was pooled incidence of nausea and vomiting. Secondary endpoints included relative risk compared with standard therapies and comparative effectiveness of triplet vs doublet antiemetic prophylaxis. Thirty-two studies including 5365 patients (4224 T-DXd recipients) met inclusion. At the 5.4 mg/kg dose, pooled incidence was 65% for any-grade nausea and 31% for any-grade vomiting, with ≥ grade 3 events ≤4%. Incidence rates were similar at 6.4 mg/kg, with no significant dose-dependent increase in gastrointestinal toxicity (RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.83-1.11). Across five randomized trials, T-DXd significantly increased the risk of any-grade nausea 70.8% vs 28.4% (RR 2.29; 95% CI 1.74-3.02) and vomiting (RR 3.49; 95% CI 2.78-4.38) compared with standard therapies, while high-grade events remained uncommon (≤4%). Triplet antiemetic prophylaxis significantly improved delayed-phase nausea control (RR 1.27; 95% CI 1.03-1.58). Nausea and vomiting, particularly delayed nausea, are common with T-DXd, representing a major unmet supportive-care need. Triplet antiemetic prophylaxis improves delayed nausea control and should be considered. Future prospective studies incorporating patient-reported outcomes are needed to optimize prophylactic strategies. None.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106499.abstract: Valvular heart disease (VHD) lacks disease-modifying pharmacological therapies. Drug repurposing guided by human genetics may help identify therapeutic opportunities. We aimed to integrate human genetic associations, drug-target information, and clinical evidence to identify repurposing opportunities and prioritise potentially druggable targets across the VHD spectrum. We retrieved VHD-associated genetic variants from the NHGRI-EBI Genome-Wide Association Studies Catalogue and Ensembl, interrogated annotated genes in the Open Targets Platform, and evaluated linked drugs through structured searches of MEDLINE and ClinicalTrials.gov. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251071741). We identified 1464 genetic associations corresponding to 844 unique variants and 582 candidate genes. Of these genes, 431 had tractability information and 51 had linked compounds, comprising 388 distinct pharmacological agents, 273 in phase 3 or 4 of clinical development. Drug-linked targets were concentrated in aortic stenosis. Clinical evidence supported therapeutic potential for 14 drugs, with preclinical or mechanistic cardiovascular support for eight additional drugs and adverse cardiovascular signals for four. An exploratory evidence-weighted framework prioritised targets according to genetic-functional evidence, tissue and mechanistic context, and translational tractability. This genetics-informed evidence synthesis identifies drug-repurposing opportunities and a substantial gap between genetically supported targets and available therapies. The findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework for mechanistic validation and future valve-focused studies. doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106502.abstract: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a complex autoimmune disease with distinct clinical and serological subtypes. Previous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified several susceptibility loci, particularly within the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), but the broader genetic architecture and causal variants underlying AAV remain incompletely defined. We conducted a genome-wide association study including 2068 individuals with AAV and 3258 controls of European ancestry. The discovery cohort comprised a previously published GWAS dataset supplemented with newly recruited cases. Analyses were stratified by clinical (granulomatosis with polyangiitis [GPA] and microscopic polyangiitis [MPA]) and serological (proteinase 3-ANCA [PR3] and myeloperoxidase-ANCA [MPO]) subtypes. Findings were evaluated in an independent case cohort of 465 individuals. We performed conditional and joint analyses of the HLA region, functional fine-mapping, linkage disequilibrium score regression, and integrative multi-omics analyses to prioritise candidate causal variants and assess genetic correlations. We identified eight previously unreported loci and replicated four known loci associated with AAV at genome-wide significance. Within the HLA region, HLA-DPB1∗04 showed the strongest association with AAV, GPA, and PR3 subtypes, whereas HLA-DRB1∗04 was most strongly associated with MPO and MPA. Conditional analyses identified additional independent effects, including amino acid variation in HLA-DQA1. SNP-based heritability estimates indicated a substantial genetic contribution to AAV (h2 = 0·40). Genetic correlation analyses revealed shared heritability with multiple traits, including celiac disease and hypothyroidism. Integrative analyses highlighted candidate genes, including HCG9 and PRTN3, and implicated protein interaction networks involving genes related to neutrophil biology. Protein-protein interaction analysis identified networks involving genes implicated in AAV risk, including PRTN3, AZU1, ELANE, and SERPINA1. These findings expand the genetic landscape of AAV and support a complex and heterogeneous genetic architecture involving both MHC and non-MHC loci. The integration of genetic association, functional annotation, and network analyses suggests that disease susceptibility is mediated through multiple biological pathways, including immune regulation and neutrophil function. These insights may inform future mechanistic studies, improved disease stratification, and the development of targeted therapeutic strategies. doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106506.abstract: Canopy FGF signalling regulator 3 (CNPY3) is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident chaperone essential for toll-like receptor (TLR) folding, trafficking and inflammasome activation. In rare paediatric cases, biallelic CNPY3 variants have been associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), but available data remain sparse. 50 individuals from 38 unrelated families with biallelic CNPY3 variants and DEE were evaluated for exome and genome findings, standardised clinical phenotype descriptions, EEG results, and neuroimaging data. A selection of variants underwent functional analysis focussing on protein stability and localisation, TLR2 function, NLPR3 inflammasome activation, and structural conformation. Disease onset occurred in early infancy (median age at onset 68 days), with a clinical phenotype comprising global developmental delay (100%) and intractable epilepsy (86%), accompanied by microcephaly (70%), spasticity (77%), growth faltering (63%), stridor (48%), and early mortality (38%). Epileptic spasms and tonic seizures (46% each) were the most frequent seizure types, and EEG findings included suppression-burst (37%) and hypsarrhythmia (28%). Phenotypic severity varied substantially, with most patients being severely affected (median score 16, range 2-20). Most variants occurred in the homozygous state (95%), including 13 missense changes and 7 truncating alleles. Variants were classified as of uncertain significance (71%), followed by likely pathogenic (23%) and pathogenic (6%) according to ACMG/AMP criteria. Genotype-phenotype correlation showed that individuals with truncating variants were, on average, more severely affected than those with non-truncating variants (median score 18 vs 14.5). Protein modelling predicted conformational effects for most missense variants. In cells, frameshift alleles abolished CNPY3 protein expression, whereas nonsense alleles markedly reduced protein levels. ER localisation of CNPY3 remained preserved across tested genotypes; however, capacity to support TLR2 maturation and processing varied substantially. Remarkably, some missense variants permitted TLR2 surface expression but impaired downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, uncoupling trafficking from signal transduction. CNPY3-associated DEE is a severe early-onset disorder with genotype-dependent phenotypic severity, accompanied by allele-specific disruption of innate immune pathways. Our findings reveal separable effects on TLR trafficking, downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, identifying CNPY3 as a key regulator of multiple cellular pathways involved in inflammatory responses and neurodevelopment. doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106508.abstract: Although antigenemia is associated with poor outcomes in respiratory viral infections, the underlying mechanisms driving viral bloodstream dissemination remain not fully understood. Herein, we aimed to characterise SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N)-antigenemia kinetics in patients with severe COVID-19. We also sought to identify host and viral determinants associated with viral dissemination through a multiparametric integrated analysis and assess the associated risk of death. This observational study included hospitalised patients with severe COVID-19 across three independent cohorts (discovery, n = 66; confirmation, n = 137; validation, n = 27), used respectively for identification, replication, and validation of findings, along with patients with mild COVID-19 and with severe influenza infection, as a disease severity and non-COVID-19 control group. From blood and nasal samples, N-antigenemia levels were analysed in relation to 45 host/viral parameters. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to assess the association with in-hospital mortality. Single-cell RNA sequencing was used to identify host determinants, and in vitro primary human airway epithelial models were used to assess epithelial barrier integrity and viral translocation. Across cohorts, we observed a significantly higher detection rate and concentration of N-antigenemia in patients with severe COVID-19 at admission compared to those with mild COVID-19 or controls (fold change [FC] >54.7, p < 0.001 [Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn post-hoc]). Type-I interferon (IFN-I) activity was the strongest correlate of N-antigenemia (ρ = 0.72, p.adj < 0.001 [Spearman, Benjamini-Hochberg]), and longitudinal analyses revealed a strong positive sigmoidal relationship (p < 0.001 [approximate Wald test]). Patients with severe COVID-19 with neutralising autoantibodies against IFN-I lacked detectable N-antigenemia, further supporting a link between systemic viral dissemination and IFN-I activity. Single-cell RNA sequencing showed higher expression of interferon-stimulated genes in monocytes and dendritic cells in patients with a high N-antigenemia level. Furthermore, high N-antigenemia at hospital admission was independently associated with an increased risk of death (aOR 2.6, 95% CI 1.0-6.7; p = 0.042 [Wald test]). Finally, we demonstrated that prolonged IFN-I exposure in vitro appears to impair epithelial barrier integrity. These findings suggest that sustained IFN-I activity is associated with systemic viral dissemination and epithelial barrier dysfunction in patient with severe COVID-19. The concordance between clinical observations and in vitro data supports a potential link between prolonged IFN-I responses and these processes, although causality remains to be established. These results highlight the potential importance of the timing and duration of IFN-I immunity and warrant further investigation of its clinical relevance. doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106510.abstract: Early antiretroviral therapy (ART) after perinatal HIV infection can restrict reservoir size and diversity, offering potential for remission. We evaluated HIV-1 DNA dynamics up to four years of age and predictors of reservoir size in early-treated African children. In this prospective, multicentre cohort study, infants with perinatal HIV from South Africa, Mozambique, and Mali who initiated ART before 6 months of age and within 3 months of diagnosis were enrolled. Children were followed at 2, 6, 12, and 24 weeks, then biannually for 4 years. Total HIV-1 DNA in PBMCs was quantified longitudinally by droplet digital PCR in 207 children. The main outcomes were HIV-1 DNA reservoir size at year 3 (log10 copies/million PBMC) and longitudinal HIV-1 DNA decay. Multivariable models were developed to identify predictors of reservoir size using generalised additive regression models, and decay dynamics were evaluated using mixed-effects Poisson models including random intercepts and viral load slopes. Of 207 children, 155 (75%) had >12 months of follow-up. HIV was diagnosed at a median age of 31 days (IQR: 0, 47) and ART started at 33 days (IQR: 23.5, 69.5). Nineteen of 155 (12.3%) had undetectable HIV-1 DNA at year 4. Median decay rate was -0.020 log10 copies/million cells/month (-0.212/year). Smaller reservoirs at year 3 were associated with lower pre-ART viral load (β = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.09, 0.43) and faster first-year HIV-1 DNA decay rate (β = 1.09, 95% CI: 0.02, 2.19), with trends toward smaller reservoirs among females (β = -0.41, 95% CI: -0.87, 0.04) and larger reservoirs among children whose mothers reported social challenges (β = 0.42, 95% CI: -0.04, 0.87). Faster decay correlated with longer time on ART, lower serial viral loads, sustained viral suppression >12 months, earlier ART initiation, and region (Mali). Maternal health issues correlated with slower decay. Eleven "excellent controllers" maintained durable viral suppression, immunological control, and undetectable total HIV-1 DNA at last follow-up. Early virological parameters may help identify children likely to develop smaller HIV reservoirs. Early ART is key to faster reservoir reduction. Maternal health issues influence reservoir decay, reflecting a parental legacy effect. Sex differences should be further explored to understand mechanisms of reservoir control. Children with sustained virological suppression, preserved immune status, and undetectable total HIV-1 DNA may represent candidates with favourable characteristics for HIV remission strategies, as these factors have been associated with a reduced burden of persistent HIV infection and have been observed in rare cases of post-treatment control. EPIICAL consortium through ViiV Healthcare and Penta Foundation.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106511.abstract: Neurofilament light chain (NfL) is an established biomarker for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, it remains unclear whether biomarkers reflecting amyloid-β metabolism (Aβ), tau (phosphorylated tau, pTau), and astrogliosis (glial fibrillary acidic protein, GFAP) can complement NfL in clinical applications. It is also unclear how Alzheimer's disease (AD) co-pathology affects disease progression in ALS. We studied 264 patients with ALS and 164 disease-control participants, analysing baseline cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) NfL, Aβ peptides, pTau181, pTau217, and GFAP. A two-step diagnostic strategy was examined in individuals with intermediate NfL values, using machine-learning models. Prognostic associations were evaluated using linear mixed-effects and Cox models adjusted for established predictors; survival was additionally examined in pooled analyses including an external ALS cohort (n = 153). Patients with ALS exhibited higher CSF NfL, Aβ38, Aβ40, Aβ42, pTau181, and pTau217 than controls, even within Aβ-negative subgroups. NfL discriminated ALS from controls with an AUC of 0.85 (0.82-0.88), which increased to 0.90 (0.88-0.92) in machine-learning models incorporating additional biomarkers. The machine-learning models maintained a high positive predictive value (0.90) for classifying cases with intermediate NfL values. Significant Aβ × NfL interactions were observed for longitudinal functional decline, and pooled survival analyses showed stronger associations between NfL and survival in the Aβ-positive ALS subgroup (14%) than in the Aβ-negative ALS subgroup (HR 4.02 [2.17-7.45] vs 1.62 [1.36-1.92]). Multiple biomarker assessments can reduce misclassification of individuals with intermediate NfL values. CSF Aβ positivity modified the association between baseline NfL and disease progression. Personalised diagnosis and prognosis based on fine-grained co-pathology evaluation may enhance clinical management of ALS. This study was primarily supported by JST SPRING (JPMJSP2125). doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106512.abstract: Disease features in resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTHβ), caused by THRB mutations, arise from insensitivity to thyroid hormone in tissues expressing thyroid hormone receptor (TR)β and from lifelong thyrotoxic effects in TRα1-expressing tissues, posing substantial cardiovascular morbidity/mortality. The T3-analogue triiodothyroacetic acid (Triac) holds potential as an effective treatment. Systematic data on Triac therapy in RTHβ are lacking, and the mechanisms through which Triac acts are unclear. This study aims to elucidate these knowledge gaps. Clinical and biochemical data were obtained through an, international retrospective cohort study in patients with RTHβ. Transcriptional activity of all TRβ mutants, on the background of the pituitary-expressed β2 receptor isoform and positively (DR+4-TRE) or negatively (TSHα-TRE) regulated reporter genes plus T3 or Triac, was studied. Thyroid function and TSH responses to T3 and Triac were tested in zebrafish expressing TRβ mutants. We collected data from 28 patients with RTHβ (range: 0.4-73.1 years) with 18 unique mutations treated with Triac in 6 centres. Triac reduced TSH (by 43%) and FT4 (by 37%) concentrations in all heterozygous patients, supported by consistent findings in zebrafish. Our functional studies showed that TRβ2 mutants exhibited reduced (all) or absent (G432del) T3-dependent transcriptional activity, with similar EC50 and IC50 values for T3 and Triac, except for R316H, which showed a 5-times lower EC50/IC50 value for Triac compared to T3. In this international, multicentre study we have documented that Triac lowers elevated FT4 concentrations in patients with RTHβ effectively. Integrating our clinical and molecular observations we suggest that Triac can act via different modes of action, with activation of the wild-type receptor being a relevant mechanism. Our study may inform clinical management and could shape future interventional studies in patients with RTHβ. doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106515.abstract: rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP vaccine is recommended for prevention of Ebola virus (EBOV) infection and disease (EVD). However, breakthrough EBOV infections have been observed in vaccinees. Currently available diagnostic and research assays cannot reliably distinguish individuals vaccinated against Ebola virus from those previously infected with the virus. This limitation complicates interpretation of vaccine-effectiveness studies, seroepidemiologic investigations, and estimates of infection or attack rates. The ability to differentiate vaccine-induced immune responses from those resulting from natural infection remains an important unmet public health and research need. We developed a multiplex sero-diagnostic assay simultaneously detecting IgA, IgG, and IgM antibodies against vesicular stomatitis Indiana virus nucleoprotein (VSV-N), a vaccine-specific marker absent in natural infection, and EBOV-GP, the vaccine's target antigen. We evaluated longitudinal samples from 30 individuals after vaccination and 30 placebo (saline) recipients, as well as 8 participants from a long-term vaccination follow-up study. We detected increase in all antibodies against both protein antigens in vaccinated individuals. Critically, the assay reveals that anti-VSV-N IgA responses emerge earlier and more robustly than anti-GP responses in vaccinees, establishing anti-N IgA as a definitive, early, and durable biomarker of rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP vaccination with high sensitivity and specificity. The assay enables rapid, accurate identification of vaccine recipients and supports real-time assessment of vaccine effectiveness during outbreaks. Furthermore, the assay's adaptability to the expanding pipeline of VSV-vectored vaccines positions it as a transformative diagnostic platform for accelerating preparedness for future infectious disease threats and outbreak response strategies. Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The National Cancer Institute (NCI) and the Divisions of Intramural Research (DIR) and Clinical Research (DCR) of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) at the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH).

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106516.abstract: Adverse drug events (ADEs) are a critical indicator of patient safety but are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. The potential of recent advances in natural language processing (NLP), particularly generative large language models (LLMs), to identify ADEs remains understudied. This study aimed to compare the performance of multiple LLMs in identifying ADE-Drug relationships in inpatient and ambulatory clinical notes. We used clinical notes from the 2018 National NLP Clinical Challenge (n2c2) ADE dataset (inpatient; n = 505) and from outpatient encounters (n = 2555) between October 1, 2018, and December 31, 2019, at a large academic medical center based in New England. Notes were pre-processed into snippets for model input. Evaluated Models included: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.2-3B and their instruction fine-tuned variants (including low-rank adapters for Llama). Performance was assessed using both strict and relaxed evaluations (precision, recall, and F1) for all models, followed by manual evaluation (exact semantic match, partial match, missing ADE, drug mention only, not a drug, or wrong) of the two best-performing models. Of the 1048 notes in the local test split, 450 (42.9%) contained at least one ADE. The n2c2 test set included 202 notes, of which 155 (76.7%) contained at least one ADE. GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini were the top-performing models among those evaluated. GPT-4o consistently outperformed GPT-4o-mini in ADE extraction across both datasets, with higher F1-scores (0.524 vs. 0.381) and a more balanced precision-recall profile. Both models captured ADEs effectively in explicit and complex clinical contexts, although limitations included misclassification of pre-existing allergies and occasional conflation of therapeutic indications with adverse effects. GPT-4o achieved higher exact match coverage and fewer errors across clinical notes, indicating more reliable performance in both inpatient and ambulatory settings. This work establishes a foundation for integrating LLM methods into real-world drug safety surveillance, with direct implications for improving patient safety. None.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106517.abstract: Placental foetal vascular malperfusion (PFVM) is a chronic disorder characterised by impaired blood flow and abnormal vascular development, inducing adverse neonatal outcomes. Long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LC-PUFAs) play a crucial role in placenta health. We aimed to explore the role of genetic variation in LC-PUFA metabolism in PFVM risk as well as underlying mechanisms. Associations were examined between two functional polymorphisms (rs174538 and rs174556) of the fatty acid desaturase 1 (FADS1) gene encoding the rate-limiting enzyme for LC-PUFA metabolism and PFVM among pregnant women (n = 646). Placental transcriptomes were correlated with PFVM and FADS1 genotypes. Various assays were performed in human umbilical vein endothelial cells and trophoblasts with FADS1 inhibitor and LC-PUFA interventions to characterise their function changes. Low-function alleles of both polymorphisms were significantly associated with increased PFVM risk and decreased placental FADS1 transcription level. In placenta tissue, lower FADS1 expression is also associated with PFVM. PFVM-associated genes are enriched to pathways related to immune responses, apoptosis, and angiogenesis, which overlap with the genes and pathways associated with the risk alleles and demonstrate a cell-type enrichment to endothelial cells. In vitro, FADS1 inhibition impairs multiple functions of and interactions between endothelial and trophoblast cells. These impairments are reversed by LC-PUFA supplementation. These findings highlight the impact of maternal LC-PUFA homoeostasis in placenta health and suggest that maternal FADS1 variants can potentially be an early diagnostic marker for PFVM. Our data supports PUFA metabolism as a precision therapeutic or preventive target to reduce placental dysfunction risk. NIH, Wayne State University and Michigan State University.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106518.abstract: Adenomyosis has been shown to reduce live birth rates and increase the risk of pregnancy loss. The diagnosis is often established by ultrasonographic assessment using the revised Morphological Uterus Sonographic Assessment (MUSA) criteria. However, the reproductive impact of specific sonographic features remains unclear. A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted to investigate whether individual ultrasonographic adenomyosis features influence pregnancy outcomes in women with infertility or pregnancy loss. We searched MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase, Cochrane Library (CENTRAL), Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar (most recent 200 records) from inception to May 11th, 2026. Observational and interventional studies reporting specific ultrasonographic features of adenomyosis in women with infertility and/or pregnancy loss were included. Primary outcomes were clinical pregnancy, live birth, and pregnancy loss. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools, as appropriate by study design. Meta-analyses were performed using random-effects models, with common-effects models applied where appropriate; remaining evidence was synthesised narratively. Certainty of evidence was assessed by GRADE. The protocol was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251077005). Of 2322 records screened, 29 studies comprising 19,510 patients (7569 with adenomyosis) were included. Diffuse adenomyosis was associated with lower odds of live birth compared with no adenomyosis (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.34-0.79; I2 = 63%), as well as internal adenomyosis compared with no adenomyosis (OR 0.49 95% CI 0.42-0.57 I2 = 0%). Narrative synthesis suggested poorer reproductive outcomes with adenomyosis features located near the endometrium and with larger uterine volume. The overall certainty was low or very low for 20 out of 21 outcomes, and moderate for one, primarily driven by imprecision and indirectness related to variation in diagnostic criteria across studies. Reproductive outcomes in adenomyosis vary according to specific ultrasonographic features, supporting feature-based reporting beyond a binary diagnosis. Substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, including inconsistent ultrasonographic diagnostic criteria, variable application of MUSA definitions, and differences in fertility treatment protocols, warrants cautious interpretation of pooled estimates. Standardised definitions and reporting of adenomyosis features are needed to improve evidence synthesis and clinical translation. The Novo Nordisk Foundation and the Danish Research Council.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106523.abstract: Yersinia pestis (Y. pestis), the bacterial pathogen responsible for plague in humans, remains a public health threat, particularly in light of the recent emergence of antibiotic resistance strains. To better understand the immune response against plague and to identify potential targets for immunointervention, we performed an epitope mapping study of the IgG response against a library of peptides representing 18 Y. pestis proteins. The study included sera from 51 individuals who had recovered from plague, 26 uninfected human controls, and 20 sera from mice protected by a live-attenuated vaccine. Analysis of human sera revealed 32 reactive peptides distributed across eight protein antigens, whereas analysis of mouse sera identified 187 reactive peptides spanning all 18 proteins. Combined analysis of the human and mouse IgG responses to the 32 human-reactive peptides identified 27 B-cell epitopes located within YopD, YopB, LcrV, FyuA, Pla, Ail, Caf1, and PsaA. Of these, one epitope had previously been described as protective and another as immunodominant, whereas the remaining 25 represent immunodominant epitopes identified in this study. Interestingly, IgG antibody responses to selected YopD and YopB peptides were significantly stronger in pneumonic plague than in bubonic plague, suggesting that the distinct clinical manifestations of the disease may be associated with distinct underlying pathophysiological and molecular mechanisms. Our comprehensive mapping of linear IgG epitopes recognised by convalescent human sera, combined with prioritisation based on their predicted neutralising potential, provides a resource for future studies evaluating peptide-based diagnostics, vaccines, and monoclonal antibody therapies against plague. The project was supported by a grant from Agence Nationale de la Recherche (ANR).

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106525.abstract: Reactivation of human herpesviruses (HHVs), particularly EBV, is associated with more severe acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and the development of Long COVID (LC). Reactivation of HHVs has been previously implicated in hormonal dysregulation, which has also been observed in LC, suggesting a potential link. This study aims to examine the relationship between LC symptoms and salivary HHV DNA, cortisol, testosterone, and oestradiol levels. Our cross-sectional, case-control study enrolled 45 participants with LC, and 45 age-sex-matched controls. Surveys and validated health questionnaires were used to collect demographics, medical history, and symptom profiles. Saliva was self-collected at waking, 15, 30, and 45 min, and 8 and 16 h after waking, across two consecutive days. Salivary cortisol, testosterone and oestradiol were measured, and extracted nucleic acid was tested for EBV, HSV 1/2, HCMV and HHV-6 A/B using multiplex qPCR, and for SARS-CoV-2 and RNaseP using RT-qPCR. Detection of salivary EBV and HHV-6 DNA copies was highest early in the morning. There were no significant differences in salivary cortisol, testosterone, or oestradiol, or in EBV or HHV-6 DNA between the LC and control groups. However, salivary HHV-6 DNA levels were positively associated with a greater aggregated LC propensity score (r = 0.24, 95% CI = 0.02-0.44, p = 0.015, adj. p = 0.030), as well as anxiety (β = 0.69, 95% CI = 0.02-1.36, p = 0.045) and depression (β = 0.24, 95% CI = 0.05-0.42, p = 0.013) scores. The observed correlation between salivary HHV-6 DNA and symptom severity suggests HHV-6 may contribute to post-acute disease, though mechanisms remain unclear. While we did not identify a relationship between salivary EBV DNA and LC, EBV may still play a role at earlier time points in the disease course, or in compartments not sampled in this study. These findings highlight the potential importance of HHV-6 in LC pathophysiology and underscore the need for longitudinal, multi-compartment studies of herpesvirus reactivation in LC. This work was supported in part by the Else Kröner Fresenius Prize for Medical Research 2023 (to AI), the Howard Hughes Medical Institute Collaborative COVID-19 Initiative (to AI), and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (to AI), the Polybio Research Foundation (to AI and DP) and the Steven and Alexandra Cohen Foundation (to DP). National Institutes for Health (NIH) funding sources supported AT, SB and CM.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106526.abstract: Tecovirimat was developed as an antiviral countermeasure against orthopoxviruses and approved by the US Food and Drug Administration Animal Rule based on efficacy in preclinical studies and clinical pharmacokinetic and safety trials. However, recent randomised clinical trials in patients with mpox who initiated tecovirimat an average of 6-9 days after onset of symptoms did not show improvement in time to resolution of skin lesions. Here, we evaluated whether timing of tecovirimat initiation influenced antiviral efficacy following mpox infection in nonhuman primates and defined the therapeutic window for treatment initiation. In this randomised preclinical study, 32 cynomolgus macaques were challenged intravenously with 1 × 106 TCID50 mpox clade IIb virus. Oral tecovirimat (10 mg/kg, once daily for 14 days) treatment was initiated on Day 2 (post-exposure and pre-symptomatic), Day 5 (early symptomatic), or Day 9 (peak symptomatic) after mpox challenge, or no treatment was given as a control group. The primary study endpoint was area under the curve (AUC) and peak numbers of progressive skin lesions. The secondary endpoint was AUC and peak levels of plasma viral loads. Additional analyses included total skin lesions, adaptive immune responses, and transcriptomic signatures. Treatment adherence was 100%. All tecovirimat-treated animals survived to study completion on Day 28, whereas two untreated control animals required early euthanisation on Days 16 and 17. Tecovirimat efficacy was time-dependent. Progressive skin lesion AUC was significantly lower when treatment was initiated on Day 2 (P 0.99). In this randomised preclinical study, tecovirimat demonstrated antiviral therapeutic efficacy but only when initiated early prior to peak viraemia. These findings emphasise the importance of early initiation of treatment and define the therapeutic window for optimal tecovirimat treatment in nonhuman primates. This study was supported by SIGA Technologies.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106528.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) ranks among the deadliest malignancies, with limited survival benefits despite recent therapeutic advances. Few prognostic biomarkers are available for PDAC monitoring in clinical practice. We conducted a meta-analysis to evaluate and synthesise evidence on the prognostic significance of miRNA expression in PDAC. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023463542). We conducted a systematic search in PubMed, CENTRAL, and Embase on January 27, 2026, to identify studies assessing miRNA expression levels in patients with PDAC with reported overall survival (OS) or progression-free survival (PFS) outcomes. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using a random-effects model. Prediction intervals (PI) were reported if feasible. Separate analyses were performed by miRNA functional categories: oncogenic, tumour suppressor, chemoresistance-related, metastasis-related, and dual-role miRNAs. A total of 142 studies, including 13,824 patients, were included. High expression of oncogenic miRNAs was associated with worse univariate OS (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.38-2.10; 95% PI 0.63-4.57) and PFS (HR 2.25, 95% CI 1.63-3.10; 95% PI 1.11-4.55). High expression of chemoresistance-related miRNAs was associated with worse multivariate OS (HR 2.11, 95% CI 1.68-2.66; 95% PI 0.96-4.68) and PFS (HR 2.51, 95% CI 1.89-3.33; 95% PI 1.58-3.97). Between-study heterogeneity varied substantially across pooled analyses (I2 range 0-94%). miRNA-21 was the most frequently studied individual biomarker and showed a consistent association with worse multivariate OS (HR 2.24, 95% CI 1.95-2.57; 95% PI 1.92-2.61). Elevated expression of oncogenic and chemoresistance-related miRNAs is associated with worse survival outcomes in PDAC. However, substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction intervals observed in several pooled analyses indicate variability in effect sizes across studies. Among the investigated biomarkers, miRNA-21 has shown the most consistent prognostic association and may represent the strongest candidate for future clinical implementation. Further validation and standardisation are required before miRNA profiling can be integrated into routine clinical practice. None to declare.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106531.abstract: Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a highly pathogenic, tick-borne orthonairovirus responsible for severe human disease, yet no approved vaccines or therapeutics exist. The glycoprotein precursor (GPC), including its GP38, Gn, and Gc components, and the nucleoprotein (NP) have been explored as vaccine targets with varying success. A chimpanzee adenoviral vector (ChAdOx) vaccine encoding full-length GPC previously conferred complete protection in mice, supporting Phase I evaluation. However, the essential protective components and mechanisms of vaccine-induced immunity remain unclear. We evaluated ChAdOx2 vaccines encoding individual GPC subunits (GP38, Gn, or Gc), full-length GPC, or NP in a lethal interferon receptor-deficient mouse model. Protective efficacy and immune responses were assessed to define protective immunogens and mechanisms. Single-dose vaccination with ChAdOx2-GP38 or ChAdOx2-Gc conferred complete survival (6/6 per group; both p = 0.0005 vs PBS), with minimal histopathology and viral RNA burden at the 21-day study endpoint, comparable to full-length GPC (6/6; p = 0.0005 vs PBS). ChAdOx2-NP likewise conferred complete survival (6/6; p = 0.0008 vs PBS) and elicited robust NP-specific immune responses. In contrast, ChAdOx2-Gn conferred partial survival (2/6; p = 0.0101 vs PBS), while low-dose GPC vaccination provided limited protection (1/6; p = 0.0617 vs PBS) with impaired IgG responses while preserving T-cell responses. Immunological analyses showed that GP38, Gc, and full-length GPC constructs induced robust antibody responses with similar Fcγ receptor engagement and limited neutralising activity. These findings identify GP38 and Gc as individually protective immunogens while reinforcing GPC and NP as effective vaccine targets. Together, these data support roles for non-neutralising antibodies and T-cell responses in protection against CCHFV and continued development of ChAdOx-vectored vaccines for clinical use. This research was supported by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106532.abstract: CD30+ T cell lymphoproliferative disorders (CD30+ T LPD) with cutaneous involvement comprise a diverse group of neoplasms with variable clinical outcomes. The molecular mechanisms underlying the prognostic differences in these diseases are poorly understood. In this multi-institutional retrospective study, 79 patients with CD30+ T LPD were evaluated. DNA and RNA sequencing were performed on skin biopsy samples to characterise molecular features. Patients were assigned to low- and high-risk groups based on treatment recommendations in clinical records. Pathogenic pathways, immune microenvironments, transcriptomic profiles, driver mutations, and mutation signatures were compared between the risk groups. Across risk groups, there was high mutational recurrence in genes involved in epigenetic regulation and intracellular signalling pathways. Mutational signature analysis revealed a shared prevalence of 5-methylcytosine deamination, UV exposure, defective mismatch repair, and POLE-associated proofreading deficiency. In contrast, gene set enrichment analysis showed that the high-risk group was enriched in pathways governing cell cycle progression, DNA damage response, and immune activation compared to the low-risk group. Furthermore, immune microenvironment deconvolution showed a higher abundance of resting dendritic cells in the low-risk group. Finally, high-risk patients exhibited significant overexpression of clinically relevant proteins, highlighting potential alternative treatment approaches for this population. Mutation analyses suggest diverse pathogenesis in these diseases. The high-risk and low-risk groups diverge in gene expression profiles and immune microenvironment, suggesting that these biological differences hold prognostic significance. Molecularly informed therapeutic strategies should be investigated prospectively through clinical trials. doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106533.abstract: Early life is a critical window for co-development of the brain and gut microbiome (GM). Evidence supports a role for the GM in brain development, but longitudinal human data remain limited, particularly regarding the influence of social disadvantage (SD), a powerful determinant of child mental health and neurodevelopment. Here, we examine longitudinal relationships between the GM and neurodevelopmental outcomes over the first three years of life, and the impact of SD on them. We sequenced and analysed stool samples of 187 children, collected at 5 timepoints over 4-36 months of life (MOL; 905 samples) using a whole-metagenome sequencing approach. Associations between GM-derived Gut-Brain Modules (GBM) and neuroactive potential were assessed using generalised linear mixed models, adjusting for covariates. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were evaluated by Bayley-III (cognitive, language, and motor), and neurobehavioural dysregulation and externalising/internalising-behaviour by the Infant-Toddler Social and Emotional Assessment (ITSEA) and Preschool Age Psychiatric Assessment (PAPA). Temporal changes were observed in GBMs, including glutamate/GABA synthesis and degradation pathways, as well as short-chain fatty acids. GM community structure and GBMs were significantly associated with concurrent and later Bayley-III outcomes, most consistently for cognition and language (FDR < 0.10). Several GBMs were associated with both neurobehavioural outcomes and SD, including S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) synthesis, butyrate synthesis, and glutamate and GABA synthesis II (FDR < 0.10). A partial mediating effect between SD and 36 MOL language outcomes was observed using SAM synthesis at 4 MOL (β = -0.042, P = 0.048). This longitudinal cohort study of GM neuroactive metabolic capacity across early transitional developmental windows reveals a dynamic pattern of GM-derived neuroactive metabolic pathways and identifies specific pathways associated with later neurodevelopmental (cognitive, language) and neurobehavioural outcomes, even after controlling for important covariates. These pathways are shaped by the socioeconomic status of mothers, starting with in-utero exposure, and GBMs partially mediated this effect. The study identifies microbial pathways associated with both SD and neurodevelopmental outcomes, highlighting potential biological processes that may contribute to neurodevelopmental risk and warrant further investigation. This work was supported by the National Institute of Mental Health, March of Dimes, Children's Discovery Institute, National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, and National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106534.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) drives intestinal barrier dysfunction, endotoxemia, and liver injury, yet the epithelial mechanisms remain undefined. Autophagy and lysosomes maintain intestinal epithelial homoeostasis and barrier integrity, but their response to chronic alcohol exposure is unclear. Human intestinal tissues from individuals with and without AUD were analysed alongside human intestinal organoids. Wild-type, CAG-RFP-EGFP-LC3, GFP-LC3B, and Atg16l1 hypomorphic mice underwent chronic-binge ethanol feeding. Organoids and Caco-2 cells were exposed to ethanol (50 mM) with or without bafilomycin A1 or Torin-2. Autophagy-lysosome pathways were assessed using transcriptomics, immunofluorescence, biochemical fractionation, and flux reporters. Alcohol induced heterogeneous autophagy-lysosome responses characterised by lysosomal stress/adaptive remodelling. These changes occurred with limited autophagosome formation and maturation, resulting in impaired autophagic throughput. These responses differed along the crypt-villus axis and between intestinal regions. Disrupted autophagy was associated with altered trafficking and accumulation of claudin-2. Atg16l1 hypomorphic mice exhibited increased baseline intestinal permeability vs wild-type controls (p = 0.03). Following ethanol exposure, Atg16l1 hypomorphic mice showed greater intestinal permeability (p = 0.003), circulating and hepatic endotoxin (p = 0.002), hepatic triglycerides (p = 0.01), and serum ALT (p = 0.02) vs ethanol-fed wild-type mice. Alcohol disrupts intestinal autophagy-lysosome homoeostasis in a spatially heterogeneous manner, accompanied by defective epithelial proteostasis and tight junction dysregulation. Impaired autophagosome formation exacerbates gut permeability and liver injury, supporting intestinal autophagy as a potential therapeutic target in alcohol-associated disease. Broader applicability of the human findings requires validation in larger cohorts. This study was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106535.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) causes severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and is uniquely capable of person-to-person transmission, with no licenced vaccines or therapeutics available. A Phase 1 trial (NCT03682107) demonstrated that an ANDV DNA vaccine targeting Gn/Gc envelope proteins elicits neutralising antibodies in humans. We evaluated whether these human antibodies protect against lethal disease in an animal model. Day 197 sera from vaccinated human subjects were pooled, purified, and passively transferred to female Syrian hamsters one day prior to lethal ANDV challenge across two independent experiments. Controls included normal human IgG, PBS (negative controls), and SAB-400 (positive control). Neutralising antibody levels were quantified using pseudovirion neutralisation assays (PsVNA) and plaque reduction neutralisation tests (PRNT) to determine exploratory cutoff titres predicting survival. Human antibodies from DNA-vaccinated subjects-unlike normal IgG-conferred significant protection against lethal ANDV challenge in both experiments. The exploratory cutoff titres predicting protection were determined to be 31-184 for PsVNA50 and 20-80 for PRNT50, depending on the analysis population and model parameters. Vaccine-induced human antibodies are sufficient to protect against lethal ANDV infection in an established animal model. If confirmed, these results indicate that neutralising antibody titres could serve as a surrogate endpoint and correlate of protection for future hantavirus Gn/Gc-targeted vaccines. doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106536.abstract: Management of drug-resistant bacterial pneumonia has become increasingly precise, but early precision does not remove the need to reinterpret the patient's course during illness. Active and appropriate empirical therapy, informed by local epidemiology, remains essential, yet treatment often begins before the definitive microbiological profile is available or adequate drug exposure can be confirmed. While rapid diagnostics and pharmacological optimisation can narrow this initial uncertainty, the harder problem arises when antimicrobial treatment appears plausible but the patient shows delayed improvement, clinical deterioration, or incomplete recovery. These trajectories should not be treated as a single form of antibiotic failure. Instead, they require reassessment of whether the dominant limitation is persistent infection, inadequate drug exposure, dysregulated host response, a non-infectious mimic, or repair-limited recovery. In this Review, we propose a trajectory-guided conceptual framework that links management to the process most likely to limit recovery and distinguishes clinically implementable interventions from emerging translational concepts.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106539.abstract: The 2024 McDonald criteria broaden the definition of multiple sclerosis (MS), enabling diagnosis in individuals with asymptomatic MRI findings or clinical presentations not meeting the 2017 criteria. We assessed whether these criteria identify such cases using independent laboratory/imaging biomarkers and whether these biomarkers predict subsequent disease activity. Participants with asymptomatic MRI findings or clinical presentations not meeting the 2017 criteria were included and stratified according to the 2024 criteria. Serum neurofilament light chain (sNfL) and 3T brain MRI measures-including normalised brain volumes, T2 lesion load (T2LL), cortical lesion (CL) and paramagnetic rim lesion (PRL)-were compared between McDonald2024-positive and McDonald2024-negative groups, and with age/sex matched McDonald2017-positive cases according to the 2017 criteria; predictors of disease activity were assessed using penalised-Cox regression. A total of 141 participants were included: 95 not meeting the 2017 criteria (n = 64 asymptomatic MRI findings; n = 31 clinical presentations), stratified as McDonald2024-positive (n = 46) or McDonald2024-negative (n = 49), and 46 McDonald2017-positive cases. McDonald2024-positive vs. McDonald2024-negative cases showed higher age-corrected sNfL Z-scores (median 0.28[IQR 0.76] vs. -0.12[0.82], p = 0.003/pFDR = 0.006), reduced normalised thalamic volume (mean 0.009±[SD]0.0007 vs. 0.010 ± 0.0007, p = 0.003/pFDR = 0.006), and higher CL (1[4] vs. 0[0], p < 0.001/pFDR < 0.001) and PRL (1[1] vs. 0[0], p < 0.001/pFDR = 0.003) counts (differences remaining significant after age/sex, disease duration and T2LL adjustments). Biomarker profiles were comparable between McDonald2024-positive and McDonald2017-positive cases. Penalised-Cox regression (n = 52) identified sNfL Z-score and PRL presence as the most consistently selected predictors of disease activity, with higher bootstrap stability for sNfL (0.84) than PRL (0.76), and good model discrimination (C-index = 0.71). The 2024 McDonald criteria identify individuals not meeting the 2017 criteria who already exhibit MS-like neuroinflammatory/neurodegenerative pathological changes. These are reflected by laboratory and imaging biomarkers, including sNfL, which may predict subsequent disease activity and complement current diagnostic frameworks to support early clinical decision-making. doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108365.abstract: The optimal salvage therapy for relapsed germ cell tumors (GCTs) remains undefined and the optimal timing for high-dose chemotherapy (HD-CT) is unclear. We analyzed data from the European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation registry to evaluate contemporary outcomes in patients treated with HD-CT across salvage lines. We extracted data of adult males with GCTs (excluding mediastinal primary) who received one or more courses of HD-CT with carboplatin and etoposide between 2000 and 2022. Patients treated within 3 months from diagnosis were excluded, as this was considered upfront therapy. Time from diagnosis to first HD-CT (TT) was categorized in 3-6, 6-12, and >12 months. A Cox model with restricted cubic splines was used to evaluate the nonlinear effect of TT on survival. Data from a total of 2204 patients were analyzed. Histology was available for 1074, of whom 69% had nonseminoma. Among 969 patients with primary site information, 69% had testicular GCT. International Prognostic Factors Study Group (IPFSG) categories were available for 500 patients: 17% very high, 38% high, 31% intermediate, 10% low, and 3.6% very low risk. TT was 3-6 months for 280 (13%), 6-12 months for 831 (38%), and >12 months for 1093 (50%). Of the patients, 1118 (51%) received three cycles of HD-CT. Median overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were 36.4 [95% confidence interval (CI) 30.3-58.7] and 9.9 months (95% CI 8.5-12.4), respectively. Spline analysis showed increasing hazard of progression and death with longer TT. No interaction was observed between TT and IPFSG risk for PFS (P = 0.62), whereas a significant interaction was found for OS (P = 0.04) in non-high-risk patients. In the largest contemporary series of salvage HD-carboplatin-etoposide in GCTs, HD-CT was effective regardless of TT as a surrogate of salvage line, with a significant interaction in non-high-risk patients, suggesting a nonlinear association between HD-CT timing and OS.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108533.abstract: The European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Clinical Practice Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of patients with early and locally advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) were published in August 2025 and were adapted in November 2025 according to previously established standard methodology to produce the Pan-Asian adapted ESMO consensus guidelines for the management of Asian patients with early and locally advanced NSCLC. The adapted guidelines presented in this article represent the consensus opinions reached by a panel of Asian experts on the treatment of patients with early and locally advanced NSCLC representing the oncological societies of China (Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology), Indonesia (Indonesian Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology), India (Indian Society of Medical and Paediatric Oncology), Japan [Japanese Society of Medical Oncology (JSMO)], South Korea (Korean Society of Medical Oncology), Malaysia (Malaysian Oncological Society), the Philippines (Philippine Society of Medical Oncology), Singapore (Singapore Society of Oncology), Taiwan (Taiwan Oncology Society) and Thailand (Thai Society of Clinical Oncology), coordinated by ESMO and JSMO. The voting was based on scientific evidence and was independent of the current treatment practices, drug access restrictions and reimbursement decisions in the different regions of Asia. The latter are discussed separately in the article. The aim is to provide guidance for the optimisation and harmonisation of the management of patients with early and locally advanced NSCLC across the different countries of Asia, drawing on the evidence provided by both Western and Asian trials. Attention is drawn to the disparity in the drug approvals and reimbursement strategies among the different regions.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108550.abstract: Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) is known to exhibit distinct metastatic patterns compared with carcinoma of no special type (NST); however, little is known about its specific propensity for central nervous system (CNS) and leptomeningeal (LM) involvement, particularly in estrogen receptor (ER)-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative subtype. We leveraged a multicenter study of 1710 patients with advanced breast cancer (BC). We recorded site of first metastatic recurrence and occurrence/type of the first CNS event. The study endpoints were CNS-free survival, LM-free survival, and post-LM survival. The risk of LM as the first CNS event across histological types was evaluated using a competing-risk framework. Among 1587 patients with known tumor histology, 15.5% had ILC. Within the ER-positive/HER2-negative BC cohort (n = 669), 31.5% of patients developed a CNS event. ILC and NST were associated with similar metastatic CNS-free survival [hazard ratio (HR) 1.30, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.95-1.77, P = 0.095]. In contrast, metastatic LM-free survival was significantly and independently shorter in ILC versus NST (multivariate analysis of LM events without concurrent brain metastases, adjusted HR 4.94, 95% CI 1.57-15.83, P = 0.006). Consistently, Fine-Gray competing-risk analysis confirmed a significantly higher risk of LM involvement as the first CNS event for ILC versus NST (adjusted subdistribution hazard ratio 5.07, 95% CI 1.57-16.41, P = 0.007). Among patients with ER-positive/HER2-negative BC and LM disease, ILC was associated with worse post-LM survival compared with NST (HR 2.79, 95% CI 1.03-4.17, P = 0.040). In patients with ILC presenting with extracranial metastatic disease, we observed similar LM-free survival between those treated with cyclin-dependent kinase 4 and 6 inhibitors and those who were not (P = 0.286). In patients with ER-positive/HER2-negative advanced BC, ILC was independently associated with a higher cumulative incidence of LM as the first CNS event than NST. Patients with ILC who developed LM also experienced poorer post-LM survival. These findings highlight the need for heightened clinical awareness and support prospective studies evaluating earlier LM detection in this population.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108584.abstract: We conducted a randomized phase II trial to evaluate whether adding erlotinib to platinum/docetaxel improves clinical outcomes in the first-line treatment of recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous-cell carcinomas, building on our previous single-arm phase II trial. This was a placebo-controlled, double-blind, single-center phase II study. Patients (N = 120) were randomly assigned (1 : 1) to receive platinum (carboplatin area under the curve 6 or cisplatin 75 mg/m2 every 21 days for six cycles) plus docetaxel (75 mg/m2 every 21 days for six cycles) with either erlotinib (150 mg/day orally until progression) or placebo. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included overall survival, response rates, duration of response, and correlations of erlotinib-induced rash/biomarkers with outcomes. Median PFS was 6.1 months with erlotinib versus 4.4 months with placebo [hazard ratio (HR) 0.63, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.42-0.95, P = 0.026]. Median overall survival was 17.0 months in the erlotinib arm compared with 13.7 months in the control arm (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.43-1.04, P = 0.0718), meeting the prespecified type I error threshold. Subgroup analyses demonstrated numerically favorable PFS HRs across most clinical subgroups, with a more pronounced benefit observed in patients with oropharyngeal and human papillomavirus-related tumors. Development of grade ≥2 rash during the first cycle of erlotinib was associated with significantly improved overall survival (HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.19-0.87, P = 0.021). The addition of erlotinib increased the incidence of grade 2-4 adverse events, particularly gastrointestinal toxicity, rash, fatigue, and dehydration but no unexpected safety signals were observed. The study met its primary endpoint, supporting the continued relevance of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibition in this disease. Although contemporary immunotherapy-based standards limit direct adoption of this regimen, these results provide clinically meaningful insight into EGFR biology and support further development of modernized, tyrosine kinase inhibitor-based EGFR strategies, including rational combinations and biomarker-driven approaches, to improve outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108596.abstract: Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) are associated with poor outcomes, with many patients never receiving any cancer-directed treatment. Population-based registries from England, France, Italy and Spain share a similar picture: emergency presentation, rather than planned referral, accounts for roughly half of diagnoses, and >50% of patients with cholangiocarcinoma in England received neither surgery, systemic therapy nor stenting. This attrition is not exclusive to real-world settings: in PROOF-301 and FIGHT-302, a considerable proportion of eligible or randomly assigned patients never started their allocated treatment. BTC is also no longer a disease confined to older adults, with ∼7% of cases diagnosed in individuals <50 years of age. On top of this, access to reimbursed therapies, molecular profiling and expert multidisciplinary discussion remains markedly uneven across Europe. "Our patients deserve better" and closing these gaps in diagnosis, access to treatment and care delivery is as urgent as developing new drugs for this disease.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108602.abstract: Whether intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) offers measurable clinical benefits over intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) for oropharyngeal cancer remains debated. We pooled data from two phase III randomized trials and one matched cohort study comparing IMPT with IMRT and analyzed disease-control, survival, acute toxicity, and nutritional outcomes. The hazard ratio for locoregional recurrence was 1.37 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.56-3.36, I2 = 0%]; for progression-free survival, 0.90 (95% CI 0.61-1.33, I2 = 0%); and for overall survival, 0.79 (95% CI 0.32-1.98, I2 = 47%). Acute grade 3 dysphagia occurred in 24% of patients receiving IMPT, compared with 40.9% receiving IMRT [risk ratio (RR) 0.65, 95% CI 0.51-0.84, I2 = 0%]. Grade 3 xerostomia or oral/pharyngeal dryness occurred in 19.9% and 32.5%, respectively (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.54-0.95, I2 = 0%). Exploratory nutritional outcomes showed no definitive benefit, including 12-month gastrostomy dependence (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.08-1.28, I2 = 0%), weight loss ≥20% (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.12-9.38, I2 = 85.7%), and composite nutritional endpoints (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.12-7.07, I2 = 87.7%). IMPT's primary advantage is reducing acute toxicity, not improving efficacy.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108604.abstract: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are established biomarkers of breast cancer immunogenicity and prognosis. Reproductive events induce durable immunological remodelling of the breast, but whether TIL levels at diagnosis reflect the immunological imprint of these events remains unclear. We included women diagnosed with invasive breast cancer between 1978 and 2012 in the Energy Balance and Breast Cancer Aspects throughout Life study, a substudy of the population-based Tromsø Study (Norway). Prediagnostic host factors were obtained. TILs were scored on an ordinal scale (1-4). Associations between host factors and the TIL score were analysed using ordinal logistic regression with interaction terms for hormone receptor (HR) status. Breast cancer-specific mortality was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox regression. A total of 425 women were included [median age at diagnosis 56.0 years, 360 (87.6%) parous], of whom 84 (19.8%) had HR-negative tumours. Among HR-negative cases, parity [odds ratio (OR) 10.14, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.97-52.22], longer breastfeeding duration [OR 1.87 per standard deviation (SD), 95% CI 1.10-3.17], and higher age at first birth (OR 1.79 per SD, 95% CI 1.06-3.01) were associated with higher TIL scores, whereas higher mean arterial pressure (OR 0.59 per SD, 95% CI 0.41-0.86) was inversely associated. Significant interactions with HR status were observed for parity and breastfeeding duration. No associations were observed in HR-positive tumours. High-TIL levels (scores 3-4 versus 1-2) were associated with lower breast cancer-specific mortality in HR-negative tumours (adjusted hazard ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.14-0.72) but not in HR-positive disease (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.58-1.68; Pinteraction = 0.023). These findings suggest that reproductive history and timing may shape the tumour immune microenvironment over the life course. If confirmed in larger studies, TILs may represent an intermediate phenotype linking upstream host characteristics to downstream clinical outcomes in breast cancer.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108605.abstract: Endometrial cancer with somatic POLE exonuclease domain mutations (EDMs) has a highly favorable prognosis; however, the clinical implications of non-hotspot EDMs in POLE remain unclear. In 793 patients with endometrial cancer enrolled at the National Cancer Center and Juntendo University Hospitals, 25 prespecified variants were screened using the Luminex assay. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was carried out to evaluate 54 patients with hotspot and non-hotspot EDMs. In patients with endometrial cancer (n = 4864) registered in Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange (GENIE), those harboring hotspot EDMs were matched with randomly sampled patients without EDMs, and a polymerase epsilon (POLE) score for gene panel testing was developed. In our cohort, POLE-EDMs, including hotspot (n = 91) and non-hotspot (n = 12) EDMs, were identified in 103 (12.9%) of 793 patients. The prevalence of grade 3 and advanced-stage endometrial cancer was higher in patients with non-hotspot EDMs than in those with hotspot EDMs. WES analysis of 54 patients revealed no significant differences in genomic mutations between the groups, and four non-hotspot EDMs were identified. A POLE-specific mutational signature was observed in tumors with EDM. In addition, the POLE score criteria were developed based on hotspot EDMs using the GENIE cohort, achieving a detection sensitivity of 0.94. Using the established POLE score, we identified nine non-hotspot EDMs. We identified 13 novel candidate non-hotspot EDMs using a newly established POLE score for gene panels and demonstrated an association between non-hotspot EDMs and favorable prognosis. The identification of additional non-hotspot EDMs will facilitate precise molecular classification of endometrial cancer.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108607.abstract: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) has demonstrated substantial clinical benefit in patients with advanced human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive and HER2-low breast cancer. However, treatment-related adverse events-particularly interstitial lung disease (ILD) or pneumonitis-represent a clinically relevant limitation. While UGT1A1 polymorphisms influence toxicity with other topoisomerase I inhibitor-based therapies, their role in T-DXd-related toxicity appears limited. The PROCURE project aimed to investigate germline pharmacogenetic variants beyond UGT1A1 associated with T-DXd-induced ILD. The PROCURE project is a multicenter translational study conducted across 26 Spanish institutions. Germline DNA from patients with advanced HER2-positive or HER2-low breast cancer treated with T-DXd was genotyped using the Infinium Global Diversity Array enriched for pharmacogenomic variants. A candidate gene approach was applied to 14 genes involved in drug metabolism, transport, pharmacodynamics, and immune-mediated drug hypersensitivity. Logistic regression models were used to evaluate associations with ILD/pneumonitis. A total of 290 patients with clinical and genotyping data were included in the analysis. The median age was 58 years (range, 34-94 years). After a median follow-up of 18.3 months [95% confidence interval (CI): 15.4-20.5], the cohort registered 33 ILD cases (incidence of 11.4%). The strongest association signals mapped to variants within the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region, with the top single nucleotide polymorphism near HLA-F (rs9258213; OR 6.8, 95% CI 2.6-17.9, P = 9.5 × 10-5). Additional associations were observed in SLCO1B1 and CYP3A4, genes involved in T-DXd transport and metabolism. This study identifies host genetic variation within the HLA locus and drug pharmacokinetic pathways as potential contributors to T-DXd-induced ILD in patients with advanced breast cancer. Although no definitive pharmacogenomic predictor was identified, these findings provide insights into the biological mechanisms underlying this toxicity and support further investigation of pharmacogenomic biomarkers to improve risk stratification and guide personalized T-DXd therapy.
