doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.003.abstract: To describe the current landscape of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) to treat surgical menopause following bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO) in individuals with hereditary ovarian cancer risk in British Columbia, Canada. We aimed to describe current use of HRT, identify factors associated with HRT use and identify potential barriers for uptake and access. Individuals with germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in an ovarian cancer susceptibility gene were identified through the BC Cancer Hereditary Cancer Program (HCP) Progeny database. A cross-sectional survey was administered to collect participant demographics, personal and family cancer history, and participant experiences with HRT. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize the sample and logistic regression used to explore associations between sociodemographic variables and reported HRT use. Open text fields were analyzed using inductive quantitative content analysis. In total, 374 responses were received from 1284 potential participants (29.1% response rate). Of participants who have had a BSO, 41% (101/245) report HRT use. In open-text responses, 22% of participants reported lack of support by healthcare professionals and 26% described gaps in counselling about HRT and surgical menopause. In the regression analysis, HRT use was less likely in individuals who: were of increasing age, reported a history of any cancer type and who reported receiving no counselling about HRT (all p < 0.0011 after Bonferroni correction). Barriers to HRT access and uptake exist for individuals at increased risk of ovarian cancer. Together this data indicates that patients require additional support in this area particularly as it relates to education and resources.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.004.abstract: Metformin is a potential anticancer agent; however, evidence of benefit in endometrial neoplasia is limited. We evaluated whether adding metformin improved the outcomes of progestin-based fertility-sparing treatment. In this multicenter, open-label, randomized, phase IIb trial using blinded central adjudication, women aged 18-42years with an institutional diagnosis of atypical endometrial hyperplasia (AEH) or presumed stage IA grade 1 endometrioid carcinoma were assigned (1:1:1) to medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) alone, MPA plus metformin 750mg/day, or MPA plus metformin 1500mg/day. Central pathological review reclassified baseline specimens according to the 2020 World Health Organization criteria and adjudicated remission and recurrence. The primary endpoint was the 3-year recurrence-free survival (RFS) rate from treatment initiation. Secondary endpoints included remission, pregnancy outcomes, and safety. Analysis included 154 patients. Median body mass index was 24.3 (range, 15.6-57.1) kg/m2. The Kaplan-Meier estimates of the 3-year RFS rate were 44.7% with MPA alone and 44.5% with the pooled metformin groups. The prespecified log-rank test showed no significant difference (P=0.825). Remission rates were 54.0%, 58.8%, and 50.9% in the MPA-alone, metformin 750mg, and metformin 1500mg groups, respectively. Among the 57 women who attempted to conceive, pregnancy occurred in 36.8%, 57.9%, and 42.1%, and live birth in 31.6%, 52.6%, and 31.6%, respectively. Metformin increased gastrointestinal adverse events and was associated with less MPA-associated weight gain; no new safety signals emerged. Adding metformin to MPA did not improve RFS or remission rates, suggesting limited benefit in fertility-sparing treatment of endometrial neoplasia.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.005.abstract: As immunotherapy (IO) is increasingly utilized for treatment of endometrial cancer (EC) and cervical cancer (CC), optimal treatment strategies after IO remains poorly defined. We evaluated clinical outcomes, treatment patterns, toxicity, and survival among patients with recurrent EC and CC who received IO after prior IO. An Institutional Review Board approved, single-institution retrospective cohort study was conducted among patients with recurrent EC or CC treated with subsequent IO between January 1, 2017, and January 1, 2025. Patients were included if they received at least one dose of IO after prior IO. Clinical characteristics, immune-related adverse events, response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS) were abstracted from the electronic medical record. Of fifty eligible patients, 36 had EC and 14 had CC. Pembrolizumab was the most common first IO agent in both cohorts. Second IO regimens differed by disease site, with pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib most common in EC and pembrolizumab alone most common in CC. Following second IO exposure, objective response rate was 27.8% for EC and 14.3% for CC, while disease control rate was 55.6% and 64.3%, respectively. Median PFS with second IO exposure was 8.1 months in EC and 9.7 months in CC. Grade 3/4 immune-related adverse events occurred in 20.0% during second IO. IO retreatment demonstrated clinical activity in selected patients with recurrent EC and CC after prior IO, with disease control achieved in more than half of patients. Prospective studies are needed to define optimal patient selection and post-IO treatments.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.006.abstract: The PERSONA-Ovary study evaluated germline pathogenic/likely-pathogenic variant prevalence, feasibility of unselected multigene testing integration in routine clinical care, and germline-somatic BRCA concordance in ovarian cancer patients. We conducted a prospective observational study of consecutive ovarian carcinoma patients treated at a tertiary-cancer care center, between July 2018 and September 2021. Germline multigene panel testing was performed using next-generation sequencing. Feasibility was assessed by informative rate and turnaround time. Germline-somatic concordance was assessed in patients with paired tumor BRCA results. Among 320 patients, pathogenic/likely-pathogenic variants were identified in 95 (29.7%, 95% CI 24.7-35.0); 81 (85.3%, 95% CI 76.5-91.7) carried mutations in ovarian cancer susceptibility genes, including 60 with BRCA alterations (63.2%, BRCA1 n=43, BRCA2 n=17). Germline testing was informative in all patients (100%). Median turnaround time was 221days (IQR 173-284), improving significantly across study periods (p<0.001). Tumor BRCA testing was available in 298 patients (93.1%), with germline-somatic concordance of 94.0% (κ=0.82, 95% CI 0.72-0.90). A germline-first strategy with reflex tumor testing achieved complete detection with fewer assays than parallel testing; a tumor-first strategy required the fewest assays (366 vs 596) but missed two germline BRCA carriers (detection rate of 96.3%). Unselected germline multigene panel testing was technically feasible and clinically informative in routine ovarian cancer care. Pathogenic/likely-pathogenic variants were identified in 29.7% of patients, supporting germline testing integration into contemporary ovarian cancer management. Although germline-first strategies maximize hereditary cancer detection, dedicated molecular workflows remain necessary to ensure clinically actionable turnaround times.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.007.abstract: To evaluate the impact of adjuvant chemotherapy on oncologic outcomes in patients with surgically staged 2009 FIGO stage I uterine serous carcinoma (USC) and to assess the prognostic significance of peritoneal cytology. We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent surgery at our institution for newly diagnosed, 2009 FIGO stage I USC. Outcomes were stratified by depth of myometrial invasion. We identified 327 patients: 185 (56.6%) with non-myoinvasive disease, 113 (34.6%) with <50% myometrial invasion, and 29 (8.9%) with ≥50% myometrial invasion. Among patients with any myoinvasion, the 5-year PFS was 54.4% (95% CI: 35%-70.2%) for no chemotherapy versus 62.6% (95% CI: 52.2%-71.3%) for chemotherapy (P = 0.10), and the 5-year OS was 52.3% (95% CI: 33.4%-68.2%) versus 79.9% (95% CI: 70.4%-86.6%), respectively (P = 0.008). Use of chemotherapy was independently associated with improved PFS (adjusted HR, 0.50 [95% CI: 0.26-0.96]) and OS (adjusted HR, 0.42 [95% CI: 0.23-0.78]). For patients with non-myoinvasive disease and negative cytology, the 5-year PFS was 89.5% (95% CI: 83.4%-93.5%), and for those with positive cytology, it was 48.8% (95% CI: 22.8%-70.6%; HR, 0.19 [95% CI: 0.08-0.44]). In this patient cohort, postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy was associated with improved survival when myoinvasion was present but did not appear to confer a survival benefit in the absence of myoinvasion. Malignant peritoneal cytology was strongly prognostic in non-myoinvasive disease, and these patients had outcomes resembling those with myoinvasive tumors. These findings support incorporating cytology status into adjuvant decision-making for stage I USC.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.009.abstract: The survival outcomes of advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer (EC) have not improved markedly despite the expanding therapeutic options. We performed molecular characterization of EC to identify therapeutic targets and prognostic biomarkers. Whole-exome sequencing (WES)-based somatic mutation profiling was performed in tumor samples obtained from 67 EC patients (41 early-stage and 26 advanced/recurrent cases). The frequencies of somatic mutations were compared between early and advanced/recurrent EC. Copy number variation analysis was also performed. Survival outcomes and recurrences according to mutational status were analyzed. TP53 and KRAS mutations tended to be more frequent in advanced/recurrent disease than early-stage EC. Deletions were also more common in advanced EC (42.3% vs. 17.1%). Among the advanced EC patients (n=26), 16 patients recurred. Recurrent cases had significantly higher TP53 mutation rates (56.3% versus 10%) and lower PTEN mutation rates (25% versus 80%) than non-recurrent cases. KRAS and CTNNB1 mutations also tended to be enriched. Although KRAS mutation alone only showed a trend of shorter OS (p=0.179) in advanced EC, KRAS-TP53 co-mutation exhibited the worst survival outcomes (p=0.011). KRAS-TP53 co-mutation was associated with chemoresistance: all the co-mutated cases were chemoresistant, whereas patients without either mutation were chemosensitive. Among copy-number low (CNL) and microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) tumors (n=46), KRAS-TP53 co-mutation was strongly associated with adverse survival outcomes (p=0.003). KRAS-TP53 co-mutation represents a potential molecular biomarker of poor prognosis and chemoresistance in advanced EC. It may enable refinement of TCGA classification, especially for CNL and MSI-H subgroups, and support investigation of KRAS-targeted therapeutic strategies.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.010.abstract: To examine temporal trends in immunotherapy (IO) adoption and identify factor-related disparities among older adults with advanced endometrial cancer (EC). We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the National Cancer Database (NCDB), including women aged ≥65 years diagnosed with stage III-IV EC between 2019 and 2023. Temporal trends of IO use were assessed, and multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of IO utilization. Among 38,931 patients with advanced EC, 21,272 (54.6%) were aged ≥65 years. IO utilization increased significantly over time across all age groups (P-trend <0.001). By 2023, 1851 older adults (40%) received IO, but utilization remained substantially lower among patients aged ≥85 years (55/255, 21.6%; P < 0.001). On multivariable analysis, patients aged ≥85 years were significantly less likely to receive IO compared with those aged 65-74 years (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.41; 95% CI, 0.32-0.52; P < 0.001). Non-Hispanic (NH)-Black (aOR 0.81; 95% CI, 0.73-0.90; P < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (aOR 0.84; 95% CI, 0.71-0.99; P = 0.034) were also less likely to receive IO compared with NH-White patients. After adjustment for socioeconomic factors, NH-Black was 12% less likely to receive IO (aOR 0.88; 95% CI, 0.77-0.99; P = 0.0034). Despite the proven clinical benefit of IO use for patients with advanced EC, substantial age-based disparities persist. A lower likelihood of IO receipt among NH-Black compared with NH-White patients was also observed even after adjustment for socioeconomic factors. These findings highlight the need for further investigation into clinical, socioeconomic, and structural barriers influencing treatment access in older and minoritized populations.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.011.abstract: Low-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (LGSOC) is a rare epithelial malignancy characterized by frequent mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway alterations, hormone receptor expression, relative resistance to cytotoxic chemotherapy, and a prolonged, relapsing clinical course. Since publication of the 2023 international expert consensus, significant advances have reshaped the management of both newly diagnosed and recurrent disease. The 2026 LGSOC Consensus Conference convened an international multidisciplinary panel of experts in the field to review emerging evidence and update recommendations across pathology, molecular testing, translational biology, frontline and recurrent treatment, imaging, treatment-associated toxicity, regulatory strategy, patient advocacy, and future research priorities. Recommendations were informed by contemporary clinical evidence, multidisciplinary discussion, and patient perspectives. The updated consensus incorporates practice-changing data from NRG-GY019 supporting chemotherapy-containing postoperative therapy as the current reference approach for stage II-IV disease while recognizing selected circumstances in which endocrine monotherapy may represent individualized de-escalation. It also integrates recent advances in recurrent disease, including the US Food and Drug Administration's accelerated approval of avutometinib in combination with defactinib for KRAS-mutated LGSOC, emerging evidence supporting endocrine therapy combined with CDK4/6 inhibition, and refined guidance for biomarker-directed treatment selection, imaging assessment, toxicity management, and patient-centered survivorship. The panel emphasizes treatment-specific biomarker interpretation, multidisciplinary care, central pathology review for clinical trials, and the continued need for prospective studies addressing treatment sequencing, predictive biomarkers, and quality-of-life outcomes. This updated international consensus provides an evidence-based framework for the diagnosis and management of LGSOC while identifying priorities for future clinical research and drug development.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.012.abstract: This study examined both National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guideline concordance and steroid taper duration with clinical outcomes in patients with gynecologic malignancies experiencing immune-related AEs. This single-institution retrospective cohort included patients with gynecologic malignancies treated with immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) from August 2016 to September 2025 who developed grade 3 or 4 immune-related AEs requiring systemic steroids. Clinical and steroid treatment data were abstracted. NCCN guideline concordance and outcomes were assessed. 63 patients contributing 73 steroid tapers were included. Most patients had endometrial (41.3%), cervical (27.0%), or ovarian cancer (23.8%), and pembrolizumab was the most used ICI (74.6%). 46 tapers (63.0%) were NCCN guideline concordant and 27 (37.0%) were NCCN guideline discordant, with discordance most often driven by taper length and premature initiation. 14 (19.2%) were < 28 days, and 59 (80.8%) were ≥ 28 days. NCCN discordant tapers were more likely to require additional supportive medications for irAE management (e.g. secondary steroids) than concordant tapers (81.5% vs 56.2%, p = 0.0300). NCCN concordance was associated with longer time to ICI restart (56 vs 21 days, p = 0.0241). Tapers <28 days were more likely to require additional supportive medications (100% vs 57.6%, p = 0.0027) and steroids (35.7% vs 8.4%, p = 0.0253) than tapers ≥28 days. Tapers ≥28 days were associated with higher rates of ICI discontinuation due to toxicity (59.3% vs 28.6%, p = 0.0381). Rates of hospitalization, ICU admission, and AE resolution did not differ by NCCN concordance or taper duration. Corticosteroid taper practices varied substantially in patients with gynecologic malignancies experiencing severe irAEs; shorter and guideline-discordant tapers were associated with greater treatment escalation and steroid reinitiation.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.013.abstract: The antiangiogenic pathway is an effective target for recurrent uterine cervical carcinoma (rCC). This study evaluated the safety and efficacy of cabozantinib monotherapy for rCC. This open-label phase II study (NCT04205799) enrolled patients with rCC who previously received platinum-based chemotherapy. Patients received oral cabozantinib (60 mg daily) until progression or discontinuation from any cause. The main objective was based on joint primary endpoint of efficacy (3-month disease control rate, DCR3) and safety (proportion of patients with grade ≥ 2 (CTCAE v5.0) gastro-intestinal (GI) perforation, GI-vaginal and/or genito-urinary (GU) fistula events) according to a Bryant-and-Day design. Key secondary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS), duration of response (DOR) and safety. Among 57 patients enrolled, 54 received cabozantinib: median age was 55.5 years, 18 patients (33.3%) had received more than two prior lines of treatment; 28 patients (51.9%) had been previously treated with bevacizumab. Median duration of follow-up was 8.9 months. DCR3 was 46.3% [95% CI, 32.8-60.3]. Fistula/perforation occurred in 5 (9.3%) patients. Objective response rate was 9.3%, with a median DOR of 2.5 months. Median PFS was 2.8 months (95% CI, 2.5-4.6). Grade ≥ 3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 51.9% of patients, most commonly asthenia (15%), hypertension (9%) and mucositis (6%). Dose reductions and treatment interruptions were reported in 26 (48%) and 24 (44%) patients, respectively. Cabozantinib demonstrates efficacy comparable to other anti-angiogenic monotherapy in rCC; however, modest benefit and toxicity do not support further monotherapy development.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.016.abstract: Chicago has a high degree of care fragmentation, with multiple large health systems and numerous safety-net systems. Fragmentation may be why the west and south areas of Chicago have high incidences of cervical cancer despite high self-reported screening rates. This study assesses utilization of cervical cancer screening-associated tests and procedures across seven health systems in Chicago between 2012 and 2022. This retrospective cohort study included females aged 15+ years enrolled in one or more health systems in the CAPriCORN network. Data were analyzed with descriptive statistics, geolocation, linear mixed-effects model, and Poisson regression. Proportions and trends in utilization by year of test modalities (cytology alone, cytology and human papillomavirus (HPV) test [cotest], HPV test alone, colposcopy, and cervical procedures [cone biopsy, loop electrosurgical excision procedure, and ablation]) were calculated and stratified by Chicago's six geographic zones. The time between screening utilization was compared by age, Chicago zone, and change in health system. Of 1.20 million in the study cohort, 53.6% had only 1 screening test during the 11-year study period; 22.9% had 2 tests, and 22.9% had 3 or more. Individuals in Chicago who changed health systems between two consecutive screening tests had a longer median interval between tests compared with those who did not change (34 versus 15.4 months). Over half of the cohort only had one screening test and may be underscreened. Switching health systems more than doubled the time interval between screening tests compared with patients who remained in the same system.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.018.abstract: Leiomodin 1 (LMOD1) was previously reported to be associated with longer survival in leiomyosarcoma (LMS) in analysis combining uterine and non-uterine tumors. The objective of the present study was to analyze the expression and prognostic role of LMOD1 in a large series of exclusively uterine LMS (uLMS). LMOD1 protein expression by immunohistochemistry was analyzed in tissue microarrays (TMAs) from 244 uLMS and whole sections from 203 uLMS, of which 134 were included in both series. Expression was assessed for association with clinicopathologic parameters and disease-specific survival (DSS). TMAs were informative in 221/244 (91%) tumors, of which 100 (45%) expressed LMOD1. No significant association with DSS was observed for 156 patients with clinical data. In the series stained using whole sections, LMOD1 was expressed in 142/203 (70%) tumors, and higher expression was associated with significantly longer survival (203 patients with survival data; p=0.007). Other parameters related to survival in the latter series were FIGO stage (p<0.001), tumor diameter (p<0.001), mitotic count (p<0.001), the degree of atypia (p=0.006) and lymphovascular invasion (LVSI; p=0.006). In Cox multivariate analysis, FIGO stage (p<0.001), mitotic count (p<0.001), tumor diameter (p=0.001) and LMOD1 expression (p=0.003) were independent prognosticators. LMOD1 expression in whole sections is a new candidate marker of longer survival in uLMS. This study additionally highlights the limitations associated with use of TMA sections compared to whole sections in biomarker studies.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.020.abstract: To evaluate the incidence, risk factors, and clinical outcomes associated with venous thromboembolism (VTE) in patients with gynecologic cancer treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). This retrospective cohort study included patients with gynecologic malignancies treated with ICI at a single institution between January 2017 and April 2026. The primary outcome was the development of VTE from ICI initiation through one month after the final cycle. Incidence, clinical characteristics, risk factors, and healthcare utilization were evaluated. Among 458 patients who received ICI therapy, 37 (8.1%) experienced a VTE. Deep vein thrombosis was the most common event (48.6%, n = 18), followed by pulmonary embolism (40.5%, n = 15). The median time from ICI initiation to VTE was 1.43 months (IQR, 0.70-2.93). Endometrial cancer was the most common disease site among patients with VTE (54.1%, n = 20). Smoking history differed significantly between groups (p < 0.01). ICI monotherapy was more common among patients who experienced VTE compared with those who did not (64.9% vs. 44.9%, p = 0.020), and patients with VTE had received fewer total lines of therapy (2.4 vs. 3.3, p = 0.008). Most events required emergency department evaluation (64.9%, n = 24) and hospitalization (59.5%, n = 22), and ICI therapy was delayed in 24.3% (n = 9) of cases. Breakthrough thrombosis was observed in 18.9% (n = 7) of patients receiving anticoagulation. VTE occurred in 8.1% of gynecologic cancer patients receiving ICI, was early in onset, and carried significant clinical burden. These data can guide provider awareness and patient counseling when initiating ICI in this population.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.024.abstract: Black women experience poor survival from epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) for all stages at diagnosis and histotypes. The contribution of an ancestry-related genotype in the Atypical Chemokine Receptor 1 (ACKR1) gene to mortality after an EOC diagnosis in Black women has not been previously reported. The relationship between the Duffy-null genotype (CC) in the ACKR1 gene and overall post-enrollment mortality in 408 Black women with EOC, including 275 with high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSC) was evaluated using Bayesian modeling approach to estimate hazard ratios (HR) and 95% credible intervals (CI) adjusting for stage, age at diagnosis, socioeconomic factors, and ovarian cancer family history. Tumor immune and genetic features were generated from sequencing assays on subsets of the HGSC cases. The CC genotype was associated with reduced all-cause mortality among EOC cases (adjusted HR = 0.60, 95% CI: 0.36-0.99). Among HGSC, the CC genotype was associated with higher African origin, lower ACKR1 expression (p = 0.049), lower cytotoxic T cell abundance (p = 0.062), and a higher frequency of homologous recombination deficient (HRD) tumors (p = 0.051). In this study, the Duffy-null CC genotype was associated with 40% lower EOC all-cause mortality in Black women. These are hypothesis-generating findings that require replication and further inquiry into mechanisms.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.025.abstract: To evaluate the prospective risk of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion or worse (HSIL+) in high-risk HPV (HR-HPV)positive women, assessing the independent and interactive effects of baseline HPV16-status, genotype multiplicity, and follow-up HPV persistence. A prospective cohort of 2562 HR-HPV-positive women referred for colposcopy were categorized into four groups: single non-HPV16, single HPV16, HPV16 plus other HR types, or multiple non-HPV16. HSIL+ risk was analysed using Cox-proportional-hazards-regression, restricted mean survival time (RMST) at 36months, and Fine-Gray competing-risk models. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated concurrent HSIL+ risk associated with follow-up HPV persistence. Overall, 691 women (27.0%) developed HSIL+. Infection with HPV16 plus other HR types carried the highest risk (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR]2.10, 95%CI: 1.69-2.62) and shorter median HSIL+-free survival than single non-HPV16 infection (24 vs. 54months), corresponding to 5.1 fewer HSIL+-free-months at 36months (p<0.001). Baseline HPV16 positivity and genotype multiplicity exerted independent, additive effects without multiplicative interaction (adjusted p=0.600). Incorporating multiplicity improved model discrimination beyond entry cytology and HPV16 status (concordance index 0.612 vs. 0.587, p<0.001). Results remained robust in competing-risk analyses (subdistribution HR2.03, 95%CI: 1.64-2.52) and after excluding early-treated women (aHR2.00, 95%CI: 1.52-2.62). Follow-up viral persistence strongly correlated with concurrent HSIL+ (aHR5.71-8.59, p<0.001), reflecting a cross-sectional risk correlation complementary to baseline prognostication. Baseline HPV16 positivity and genotype multiplicity are independent, additive risk factors for HSIL+, with HPV16 plus other HR types marking the highest-risk subgroup. Genotype multiplicity provides distinct clinical predictive value alongside HPV16 status, while follow-up HPV persistence offers complementary, non-redundant information for concurrent risk evaluation in risk-based management strategies.

doi:10.1016/s1470-2045(26)00281-0.abstract: National cancer control plans (NCCPs) vary in scope and comprehensiveness, yet expert-led review is resource intensive and limits cross-country comparability. We aimed to assess NCCP comprehensiveness across 50 countries using the policy reasoning integrated sequential model (PRISM), a validated multiagent artificial intelligence (AI) system. We identified the most recent national NCCP for each country from the International Cancer Control Partnership repository, the WHO Noncommunicable Disease Document Repository, and government websites; sub-national plans, broader non-communicable disease or health-sector strategies, drafts, and superseded versions were excluded. We developed an analytical framework of 12 elements and 76 sub-elements, aligned with WHO, International Cancer Control Partnership, and Union for International Cancer Control guidance and validated it through a modified two-stage Delphi process (online survey of 67 experts; triangulation workshop with 31 participants). PRISM comprised document ingestion (Qwen2.5-VL-72B), policy analysis with retrieval-augmented generation (Llama 4 Scout, 109B), and semantic quality assurance. PRISM was validated against masked dual-expert ratings for six purposely selected NCCPs, then applied to all NCCPs. Scores were normalised to 0-5 and medians compared across World Bank income group and WHO region. We identified 50 NCCPs that met the inclusion criteria. Median overall comprehensiveness was 2·78 (IQR 2·25-3·09), with high comprehensiveness classified as 4·0-5·0, moderate as 2·0-3·9, and low as 0-1·9. Europe (2·96; 2·78-3·35) and lower-middle-income countries (2·97; 2·48-3·15) had the highest medians; the western Pacific (2·21; 1·78-2·87) and low-income countries (2·05; 1·94-2·22) had the lowest. Element-level medians were highest for implementation (4·17; 3·54-4·38), health services (3·89; 2·63-4·19), and governance and organisation (3·67; 3·35-3·98), and lowest for financing (1·88; 1·00-2·69), outcomes (1·83; 1·33-2·33), and threats (2·19; 1·72-2·34). Financing showed the largest gaps-only five of eleven financing sub-elements had median scores of 1·0 or less. Our analysis suggests that NCCP comprehensiveness varies substantially between countries with consistent weaknesses in financing, outcome measurement, and contextual analysis. A shared health systems framework and scalable AI appraisal tools, such as PRISM, could support more complete, comparable, and actionable plans to strengthen cancer control globally by providing the possibility for rapid analysis of comprehensiveness of NCCPs and generation of timely, achievable, and evidence-informed, context-specific plans that use the latest data. doi:10.1016/s1470-2045(26)00290-1.abstract: Anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy is the standard second-line treatment for patients with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma. However, there is no evidence from randomised controlled trials in patients ineligible for transplantation. To address this gap, we compared zamtocabtagene autoleucel (zamto-cel), a CAR T-cell therapy directed at CD20 and CD19, with rituximab-gemcitabine-oxaliplatin (R-GemOx) chemoimmunotherapy in patients ineligible for transplantation with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma. DALY 2-EU is an open-label, multicentre, randomised, phase 2 trial conducted at 45 centres across 12 countries in Europe. Eligible patients were adults (aged ≥18 years) with second-line relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma confirmed histologically who were ineligible for transplantation and had received first-line chemoimmunotherapy containing a combination of an anthracycline-based regimen and an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status score of 2 or less. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to zamto-cel (single intravenous infusion of 2·5 × 106 fresh (ie, non-cryopreserved) CAR T-cells per kg, capped at 100 kg, produced in a closed automated system) or R-GemOx (rituximab [375 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1], gemcitabine [1000 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1 or 2], and oxaliplatin [100 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1 or 2] administered for up to eight 14-day cycles). Randomisation was done with an interactive web response system and stratified by age, gender, lactate dehydrogenase, International Prognostic Index, histology, time to relapse after the start of first-line therapy, and country. The primary endpoint was event-free survival assessed by a masked independent review committee and compared all patients randomly assigned to the zamto-cel and R-GemOx groups using a one-sided log-rank test. Safety was assessed in all patients who received study treatment. This ongoing trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04844866). Between Oct 14, 2021, and Jul 16, 2024, 219 patients were screened and 160 were randomly assigned to zamto-cel (n=82) and R-GemOx (n=78). The median age was 74·0 years (IQR 70·5-77·0). Patients were predominantly male (100 [63%] of 160 were men and 60 [38%] women) and White (91 [57%]), with race not reported for 64 (40%). Median vein-to-vein time for zamto-cel was 15 days (IQR 15-16). With a median follow-up of 17·0 months (IQR 9·0-22·8), event-free survival was longer in the zamto-cel group than in the R-GemOx group (6·21 months [95% CI 3·84-13·77] vs 2·53 months [1·97-3·35]; HR 0·39 [95% CI 0·27-0·58]; p<0·0001). Grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 63 (83%) of 76 with zamto-cel and in 65 (86%) of 76 with R-GemOx. The most common grade 3-4 adverse events were neutropenia (28 [37%] with zamto-cel and 17 [22%] with R-GemOx), anaemia (11 [14%] and 12 [16%]), and decreased neutrophil count (20 [26%] and seven [9%]). Serious adverse events occurred in 31 (41%) patients with zamto-cel and 50 (66%) with R-GemOx, most commonly malignant neoplasm progression (11 [14%] and 38 [50%]), cytokine release syndrome (CRS; six [8%] and none), and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (four [5%] and none). Treatment-related deaths occurred in two (3%) of 82 patients with zamto-cel (due to CRS and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis) and in one (1%) of 78 with R-GemOx (malignant lymphoma progression). The risk-benefit ratio observed in the DALY 2-EU study supports consideration of zamto-cel as a second-line standard treatment option for patients with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma who are ineligible for transplantation. doi:10.1016/s1470-2045(26)00340-2.abstract: Up to 12% of childhood cancer survivors have an underlying cancer predisposition syndrome (CPS). As a result, these childhood cancer survivors are at increased risk for developing and succumbing to subsequent malignant neoplasms. Identifying childhood cancer survivors with CPS is essential to improving overall outcomes by informing tailored approaches to cancer screening, treatment, and, for some, risk-reducing interventions. Despite these potential benefits, it is often unclear which childhood cancer survivors warrant referral for genetic counselling and germline genetic testing. Using an evidence-based approach, a standardised guideline for referral for cancer genetics evaluation of childhood cancer survivors at high risk of having a CPS was developed and incorporated into the Children's Oncology Group Long-Term Follow-Up Guidelines for Survivors of Childhood, Adolescent, and Young Adult Cancers. This Policy Review details the importance, development, and anticipated impact of this new guideline. Raising awareness of this guideline is crucial to enhancing the integration of genetics into survivorship care and improving health outcomes for childhood cancer survivors with CPS.

doi:10.1016/s1470-2045(26)00347-5.abstract: Patients with de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma were historically deemed incurable and treated with palliative intent. Emergence of potent systemic therapy in combination with local treatment for both locoregional and metastatic diseases has enabled long-term survival in some patients. This international guideline was developed through consensus-building by 54 experts from 46 centres across 18 countries or regions and endorsed by 17 oncology organisations. 32 recommendations across seven clinical domains were formulated, including 29 strong (≥80% agreement [consensus] or high quality of evidence) and three conditional recommendations (67-79% agreement). We recommend that curative-intent treatment should be offered to medically fit patients with no more than three metastatic lesions in two or fewer organs at baseline or following response to systemic therapy; multimodality treatment (comprising immunochemotherapy, locoregional radiotherapy, metastasis-directed therapy, and maintenance therapy) is recommended. This guideline provides a practical framework for standardisation of clinical management of de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma and identification of key evidence gaps for future research.

doi:10.1016/s1470-2045(26)00355-4.abstract: The TALAPRO-2 trial showed improved radiographic progression-free survival and overall survival with first-line talazoparib plus enzalutamide versus placebo plus enzalutamide in patients with metastatic androgen pathway modulator-resistant prostate cancer (APMR; also referred to as castration-resistant prostate cancer) unselected for homologous recombination repair (HRR) gene alterations treated. We aimed to assess HRR gene alteration status agreement between prospective solid tumour tissue and circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) testing, the potential complementary value of prospective and retrospective ctDNA testing, and the prognostic utility of baseline ctDNA burden, changes in ctDNA burden, and circulating tumour cell (CTC) reductions. In TALAPRO-2, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, men aged 18 years or older (≥20 years in Japan) with asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic metastatic APMR prostate cancer and no previous life-prolonging systemic therapy for APMR disease were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive once daily, oral talazoparib 0·5 mg plus enzalutamide 160 mg or placebo plus enzalutamide and stratified by HRR gene alteration status and previous treatment for androgen pathway modulator-naive/sensitive disease. The sponsor, patients, and investigators were masked to allocation of talazoparib or placebo; enzalutamide was open label. In this exploratory analysis, HRR gene alteration status agreement was evaluated in the unselected intention-to-treat cohort between solid tumour tissue prospectively tested using a clinical trial assay based on FoundationOne CDx and retrospectively tested ctDNA samples, collected at screening and assessed using an assay based on FoundationOne Liquid CDx. Tumour burden was categorised as positive or negative (ctDNA tumour fraction detectable or not detectable). Reductions in CTCs, enumerated using CELLSEARCH, were defined as conversion (from five or more cells per 7·5 mL of blood to four or fewer cells per 7·5 mL of blood) or CTC0 (from one or more cells per 7·5 mL of blood to zero). Radiographic progression-free survival was assessed for patients with baseline ctDNA positivity (positive vs negative) and for patients with ctDNA conversion and CTC conversion and CTC0 at week 9 (and week 17 for CTC conversion and CTC0) by treatment group. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrial.gov, NCT03395197 and is active, not recruiting. Between Jan 7, 2019, and Sept 17, 2020, 805 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned (402 to talazoparib plus enzalutamide; 403 to placebo plus enzalutamide); median follow-up for radiographic progression-free survival was 24·9 months (IQR 21·9-30·2) for the talazoparib group and 24·6 months (14·4-30·2) for the placebo group. A high concordance in HRR gene alteration status was observed between results from prospectively tested solid tumour tissue samples and retrospectively tested screening ctDNA samples (reported for 739 [92%] of 805 enrolled patients), with 84% (421 of 501) agreement in patients evaluable as either HRR-deficient or HRR-non-deficient by both tests. Median radiographic progression-free survival for positive versus negative ctDNA burden was 21·0 months (95% CI 16·5-not reached [NR]) versus NR (NR-NR), respectively (hazard ratio [HR] 2·46; 95% CI 1·68-3·60; p<0·0001) with talazoparib plus enzalutamide, and 11·0 months (8·4-13·8) versus 33·2 months (30·3-NR), respectively (HR 4·03; 2·85-5·72; p<0·0001) with placebo plus enzalutamide. In both groups, week 9 conversion from positive to negative ctDNA was prognostic of improved radiographic progression-free survival versus remaining ctDNA positive. Patients remaining ctDNA negative had more favourable radiographic progression-free survival versus conversion from positive to negative ctDNA. CTC conversion and CTC0 at week 9 were prognostic for radiographic progression-free survival benefit in both groups. Our results support broad prognostic utility of ctDNA burden and CTC enumeration in metastatic APMR prostate cancer, including in the context of poly(ADP) ribose polymerase inhibitor therapy. Pfizer.

doi:10.1016/s1470-2045(26)00394-3.abstract: VEGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are considered the backbone for the treatment of metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma. We hypothesise that the administration of bevacizumab during scheduled breaks in pazopanib (TKI) treatment can improve tolerability and prolong progression-free survival compared with historical controls. In this single-arm, phase 1/2 trial in five US academic cancer centres, patients (aged ≥18 years) with histologically confirmed metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 1 or less, and adequate organ functions were included. The phase 1 portion included patients with up to one previous therapy with high-dose IL-2 or an anti-PD-1 compound alone or in combination with a CTLA-4 inhibitor. The phase 2 portion enrolled only patients with treatment-naive metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma. The primary endpoint of phase 1 was to find the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D). We tested a novel regimen using four dose levels: oral pazopanib (600 or 800 mg daily on days 1-28, followed by a 7 day break) alternating with intravenous bevacizumab (5, 7·5, or 10 mg/kg, one on day 36 and one on day 50) on a 10-week cycle in patients with metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma naive to TKI treatment. The primary endpoint of phase 2 was median progression-free survival, assessed by a masked central statistician review. Dose selection (in patients who had completed 15 weeks) and activity (in patients who had completed one full 10-week cycle of the novel regimen) were analysed in the per-protocol population. Safety analyses included all patients who received any treatment. This trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01684397) and is ongoing but closed to new participants. Between Nov 21, 2012, and June 11, 2018, phase 1 enrolled 25 patients, with 18 patients evaluable for dose-limiting toxicity during the extended 15-week safety assessment period. The RP2D was established as pazopanib 800 mg daily (days 1-28) and bevacizumab 10 mg/kg on days 36 and 50 of a 10-week cycle. Between Jan 23, 2019, and Oct 19, 2023, phase 2 enrolled 53 patients, of whom 51 (including six from phase 1) were evaluable for activity and 59 were evaluable for safety. 36 (71%) patients were male and 15 (29%) were female, and 48 (94%) patients were White. 33 (65%) patients in phase 2 had favourable risk per the International Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Database Consortium categories. After a median follow-up of 63·7 months (IQR 16·2-73·5), median progression-free survival was 24·8 months (95% CI 17·2-34·3). The most common grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events were hypertension (20 [34%] of 59) and elevated aspartate aminotransferase (seven [12%]) and alanine aminotransferase (ten [17%]). Five (8%) patients discontinued the study for drug-related serious adverse events. No treatment-related deaths occurred. The phase 1 portion identified the safe RP2D. The phase 2 portion showed that this novel regimen has promising antitumour activity in patients with metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma in the predominantly favourable risk group who are naive to treatment. Phase 3 randomised controlled trial data are needed to confirm these findings. The Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center (RPCCC), US National Cancer Institute (NCI), Novartis.

doi:10.1016/s1470-2045(26)00446-8.abstract: To our knowledge, UNION is the first phase 3 trial to assess a neoadjuvant strategy incorporating radiotherapy, immunotherapy, and chemotherapy compared with standard care in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer, which reported positive results for the primary endpoint (blinded independent review committee [BIRC]-assessed pathological complete response rate; 39·8% vs 15·3%). Here, we present a prespecified interim analysis of event-free survival. This open-label, randomised, phase 3 trial was conducted at nine hospitals in China. Eligible patients were aged 18-75 years with untreated cT3-4 or N+ rectal adenocarcinoma (≤10 cm distance from the anal verge) and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1; stratified by clinical T stage and N stage), using permuted blocks, to receive neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy (25 Gy in five fractions) followed by two cycles of intravenous camrelizumab (200 mg on day 1) plus CAPOX (oral capecitabine 1000 mg/m2 twice daily on days 1-14 and intravenous oxaliplatin 130 mg/m2 on day 1; experimental group) or long-course chemoradiotherapy (50·4 Gy in 28 fractions with concurrent oral capecitabine 825 mg/m2 twice daily) followed by two cycles of CAPOX (standard-of-care group). After surgery, both groups received six cycles of adjuvant CAPOX, and the experimental group additionally received adjuvant camrelizumab for up to 15 cycles. The primary endpoint was BIRC-assessed pathological complete response rate in the intention-to-treat population, which has been previously reported. Here, we performed a prespecified interim analysis of investigator-assessed event-free survival (one of the key secondary endpoints, defined as time from randomisation to radiographic progression precluding surgery, local recurrence or distant metastasis, or death) in the intention-to-treat population (all randomly assigned patients) with a boundary of a two-sided p values less than 0·0102. Safety was evaluated in all patients who received at least one dose of the study treatment according to the assigned regimen. The study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04928807, and is active, but no longer recruiting. Between July 23, 2021, and March 1, 2023, 231 patients (153 [66%] males and 78 [34%] females; 227 [98%] were Han Chinese, and four [2%] were other ethnicity Chinese) were randomly assigned to the experimental group (n=113) and standard-of-care group (n=118). As of Oct 1, 2025, the median follow-up duration was 36·7 months (IQR 32·6-39·9) in the experimental group and 34·7 months (31·1-39·1) in the standard-of-care group. The 3-year investigator-assessed event-free survival rate was 91·3% (95% CI 83·9-95·4) in the experimental group versus 77·4% (67·9-84·4) in the standard-of-care group (stratified hazard ratio 0·33 [0·15-0·71]; two-sided log-rank p=0·0029). During the entire treatment period, the most common grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events were decreased lymphocyte count (23 [20%] of 115 in the experimental group vs 31 [28%] of 112 in the standard-of-care group), decreased white blood cell count (13 [11%] vs 16 [14%]), decreased neutrophil count (13 [11%] vs 13 [12%]), and decreased platelet count (seven [6%] vs 15 [13%]). Treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in 22 (19%) versus 15 (13%) patients, with the most common being decreased platelet count (one [1%] vs six [5%]), and radiation gastroenteritis (two [2%] vs four [4%]). Treatment-related deaths occurred in one patient in the experimental group (septic shock related to chemotherapy, but unrelated to camrelizumab) and none in the standard-of-care group. In this interim analysis, short-course radiotherapy followed by camrelizumab and CAPOX significantly improved 3-year event-free survival in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer, with a safety profile similar to long-course chemoradiotherapy followed by CAPOX. Comparison of this promising new treatment strategy with contemporary total neoadjuvant therapy strategies is warranted. doi:10.1016/s1470-2045(26)00532-2.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has poor outcomes and high rates of locoregional recurrence. MASTERPLAN evaluated whether stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) reduced locoregional recurrence in patients with high-risk, localised PDAC. MASTERPLAN was an open-label, randomised, phase 2 trial conducted across 14 hospitals in Australia and New Zealand. Eligible participants were aged 18 years or older with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0-1, and had previously untreated localised PDAC with at least one high-risk feature, including tumour size more than 4 cm, extrapancreatic extension, node-positive disease, borderline resectable disease, or locally advanced disease. Participants were randomly assigned (2:1) using the method of minimisation to investigator-choice chemotherapy, with or without SBRT, stratified by participant cohort (potentially operable vs inoperable), planned chemotherapy regimen, randomisation before or within the first 28 days of chemotherapy, and institution. Chemotherapy consisted of mFOLFIRINOX (day 1 oxaliplatin 85 mg/m2, irinotecan 150 mg/m2, leucovorin 50 mg, and fluorouracil 2400 mg/m2 over 46 h every 14 days for six cycles; all intravenous) or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (gemcitabine 1000 mg/m2 and nab-paclitaxel 125 mg/m2 on days 1, 8, and 15 every 28 days for three cycles; both intravenous). SBRT was delivered as 40 Gy in five fractions, with two to four fractions delivered per week, with real-time radiotherapy quality assurance. Surgical resection was considered following induction therapy, followed by a planned further 12 weeks of adjuvant chemotherapy with either mFOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus capecitabine (28-day cycles of 1000 mg/m2 intravenous gemcitabine administered on days 1, 8, and 15 with 830 mg/m2 oral capecitabine twice daily administered on days 1-21). Participants deemed not suitable for surgery continued the same chemotherapy for an additional 12 weeks with reassessment for surgical suitability permitted, for a total planned duration of chemotherapy of 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was 12-month locoregional recurrence in the intention-to-treat population, with safety endpoints analysed by treatment received. The trial planned to recruit 120 patients but due to slow accrual closed to recruitment early on Jan 6, 2025. Trial closure and database lock occurred on July 21, 2026. This trial was registered with the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trial Registry (ACTRN12619000409178) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04089150), and is complete. Between Feb 26, 2020, and Jan 6, 2025, 74 participants (43 [58%] male, 31 [42%] female) were randomly assigned to chemotherapy and SBRT (n=49) or chemotherapy alone (n=25). After a median follow-up of 3·2 years (IQR 1·9-4·3), 12-month locoregional recurrence was 20·2% (95% CI 9·9-33·1) in the SBRT group and 52·0% (30·3-69·9) in the chemotherapy alone group (subdistribution hazard ratio 0·44 [95% CI 0·22-0·88]; p=0·022). Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 33 (70%) of 47 participants in the SBRT group and 16 (64%) of 25 participants in the chemotherapy alone group (p=0·27), with one (4%) treatment-related death secondary to biliary tract infection in the chemotherapy alone group. The most common grade 3-4 adverse events were diarrhoea (seven [15%] in the SBRT group vs five [20%] in the chemotherapy alone group), and thromboembolic events (three [6%]) vs one [4%]). Overall grade 3 or higher serious adverse events occurred in 30 (64%) of 47 participants in the SBRT group, and 14 (56%) of 25 participants in the chemotherapy alone group (p=0·24). There were two serious adverse events attributable to SBRT; grade 2 small bowel obstruction and grade 3 pancreatitis. In patients with high-risk, localised PDAC, the addition of SBRT to chemotherapy was associated with significantly reduced locoregional recurrence without a significant increase in toxicity and warrants further investigation in larger studies. Medical Research Future Fund, Australasian Gastro-Intestinal Trials Group, National Health and Medical Research Council Clinical Trials Centre (University of Sydney), and Gut Cancer Foundation, New Zealand.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03144-5.abstract: Abstract Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are clonal hematologic malignancies characterized by the overproduction of mature myeloid lineage cells. Although JAK2 inhibitors, such as ruxolitinib, can alleviate constitutional symptoms, they typically fail to eradicate malignant clones or reverse bone marrow fibrosis. Moreover, treatment failure and drug intolerance often limit their long-term use. Recent studies have identified PIM1 kinase as an important mediator of MPN pathogenesis. PIM1 expression is upregulated in MPN hematopoietic progenitors, which may contribute to aberrant proliferation and disease progression by regulating key downstream effectors, including mTORC1, BAD, MYC, HIF-1α, and TGF-β. Notably, PIM1 contributes to JAK2 inhibitor-persistent cell growth, and its inhibition restores ruxolitinib sensitivity in JAK2 mutant cells. Preclinical studies using genetic ablation and pharmacological inhibition of PIM1 have shown significant attenuation of the myelofibrosis phenotype in mouse models, providing a strong rationale for targeting this kinase. PIM kinase inhibitors are currently being evaluated in clinical trials for patients with myelofibrosis. This review summarizes the current understanding of PIM1 biology in the context of MPNs, details the molecular mechanisms underlying its pathogenic contributions, and evaluates the translational potential of PIM1-targeted therapies for MPNs.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03157-0.abstract: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is driven by the constitutively active BCR::ABL1 kinase, which promotes uncontrolled cell proliferation. Although protein-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have revolutionized CML treatment, resistance remains a significant barrier to curative therapy, particularly due to BCR::ABL1 mutations and the persistence of leukemia stem cells (LSCs). New treatment strategies that directly inhibit BCR::ABL1 protein expression are needed to achieve more effective therapy. Using a high-content antibody microarray and bioinformatics analyses, we investigated differences in the proteome and phosphorylation landscape of Imatinib (IM)-resistant cells and identified highly activated members of the eukaryotic translation initiation complex (eIF4F), particularly eIF4G1, a core component of eIF4F. These eIF4F complex members are highly expressed and activated in CD34+ CML stem/progenitor cells and in IM-resistant cells. Genetic inhibition of eIF4G1 or pharmacological targeting with the small-molecule inhibitor SBI-756 diminished eIF4F complex assembly, reduced overall translation initiation, reduced BCR::ABL1 expression and key downstream targets, impaired the survival of nonresponder stem/progenitor cells, including BCR::ABL1-T315I mutant cells, and sensitized them to TKIs, with strong synergistic effects in vitro and in a PDX model. These findings underscore the potential of eIF4F complex inhibition as a new therapeutic strategy to overcome TKI resistance in CML and other BCR::ABL1+ malignancies.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03159-y.abstract: Abstract CD24 is highly expressed in aggressive B-cell malignancies and represents a novel immunologic vulnerability to overcome resistance to CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. We developed a CD24 × CD3 bispecific antibody (CD24 BsAb) and CXCR3-armed CD24 CAR-T cells, both exhibiting potent antitumor activity in lymphoma and leukemia models. CD24 BsAb and CD24 CAR-T overcome CD19 CAR-T resistance driven by antigen loss and apoptosis defects in vitro and in vivo. Beyond direct cytotoxicity, CD24-targeted T cells reprogram macrophages toward an M1-like phenotype and enhance phagocytic clearance. We further engineered a dual-specific, dual-functional CD19 CAR-T that secretes a CD24 bispecific T-cell engager (CD24 BiTE), enabling simultaneous targeting of CD19 and CD24 to address tumor heterogeneity and achieve superior efficacy. Collectively, our study demonstrates that CD24-directed adoptive T-cell therapies are warranted for B-cell malignancies through robust induction of both innate and adaptive immune responses.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03160-5.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells are highly dependent on mitochondrial activity for survival, with this metabolic reliance driven in part by BCL-2, which is therapeutically targeted by venetoclax-based therapies. The regulation of mitochondrial dynamics in leukemic cells is therefore essential for maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis. However, the mechanisms that enable selective degradation of damaged mitochondria (mitophagy) are still poorly understood in AML. In this study, we sought to elucidate the role of PTEN-induced putative kinase 1 (PINK1), a key sensor of mitochondrial stress, in regulating mitophagy in leukemic cells. Our results identified PINK1 as a central modulator of mitophagy. Genetic depletion of PINK1 reduced both basal and stress-induced mitophagy, leading to mitochondria accumulation and functional impairment. Additionally, we discovered that PINK1 stabilization during mitochondrial stress is regulated by Prohibitin 2 (PHB2), and that depletion or inhibition of PHB2 mirrored the biological effects of PINK1 loss. Notably, both genetic depletion of PINK1 or PHB2, as well as pharmacological inhibition of PHB2, significantly increased AML cell sensitivity to venetoclax both in vitro and in vivo. Together, these findings highlight the potential of targeting the PHB2/PINK1 signalling pathway to improve the efficacy of venetoclax-based therapies in AML by disrupting the mitophagy process.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03168-x.abstract: Abstract The hyperactive kinase FLT3-ITD causes acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and is a prognostic biomarker. We synthesized and characterized MA191 as a novel von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) E3 ubiquitin ligase-based proteolysis targeting chimera (PROTAC) for FLT3. MA191 induces apoptosis in cultured and primary AML patient cells harboring FLT3-ITD (IC 50 =9.6-11 nM; EC 50 =0.001-0.883 µM). Comparison with a VHL-binding-deficient stereoisomer of MA191 demonstrates that FLT3-ITD degradation is superior to kinase inhibition ( p < 0.03). Rapid depletion of FLT3-ITD by MA191 (DC 50 =10 nM) requires VHL, neddylation, proteasome activity, and the pro-apoptotic BH3-only protein BIM. MA191 reduces FLT3-ITD prior to apoptosis, uncovering apoptosis-independent roles of BIM for protein stability. Higher expression levels of FLT3 in leukemia cells than in healthy cells ( n = 3675/ n = 1249) are associated with worse AML patient survival ( p = 0.0099). MA191 does not harm healthy blood and bone marrow progenitor cells or myeloid cell differentiation. In Danio rerio larvae, MA191 halts AML cell proliferation without significant toxicity. Human stromal cell interactions and mutations in the tyrosine kinase domain of FLT3-ITD that confer resistance to FLT3 inhibitors do not abolish anti-leukemic effects of MA191. Accordingly, leukemia cells with acquired resistance to MA191 lack such mutations. We offer a framework for fast-acting next-generation FLT3 degraders that overcome resistance mechanisms to classical inhibitors.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03169-w.abstract: Aberrant expression of neoantigenic receptor ROR1 has been identified in diverse lymphomas, including mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) and in a broad spectrum of nonlymphoid malignancies. While ROR1 has emerged as an attractive therapeutic target, its oncogenic role and the underlying mechanisms remain rather poorly characterized. Focusing on MCL, we found that ROR1 expression is heterogeneous and it can be induced under environmental stress. Inhibition of ROR1 expression resulted in cell-cycle suppression and apoptotic cell death. The ROR1 loss affected expression of numerous genes and altered phosphorylation of many proteins, including those involved in cell-cycle progression. ROR1 also promotes the synthesis of pyrimidines and purines, including induction of phosphorylation of enzymes involved in pyrimidine synthesis. Finally, we found that ROR1 induced phosphorylation of DEK and that its depletion abrogates ROR1 expression. These results provide insights into the multi-faceted oncogenic role of ROR1, further justifying targeting ROR1 in MCL and other malignancies.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03176-x.abstract: Serine metabolism is of growing biologic and therapeutic interest in cancer. Upregulation of the serine synthesis pathway (SSP) can fuel tumor growth, and cancers with this phenotype are often sensitive to. SSP inhibitors. In parallel, dietary restriction of serine and glycine (SG) can suppress some cancers, but the determinants of sensitivity to. this approach are poorly understood. This is especially true in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where serine metabolism has been less explored. We report that a subset of human AML cell lines and primary samples are completely dependent on external serine, known as serine auxotrophy. These leukemias consistently suppressed the SSP enzyme PSAT1, failed to. synthesize serine, responded to. SG restriction in vivo, and were rescued by restoring PSAT1. We also found that SG restriction synergized with venetoclax in serine auxotrophic AML, and that MECOM rearrangement was strongly associated with PSAT1 suppression and serine auxotrophy. These findings define a metabolically distinct AML subtype and nominate it for targeting by SG restriction.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03177-w.abstract: We interrogated data from 217 subjects with primary myelofibrosis (PMF) diagnosed before 2001 to identify covariates at diagnosis associated with long-term survival. Forty-one survived more than 25 years. Long-term survivors were more often female, younger than 50 years and less likely to have anemia, splenomegaly, increased blood CD34-positive cells, a JAK2V617F variant, and more likely to have grade-0 bone marrow fibrosis and increased platelets. In multivariable logistic regression analyses, age 450 × 10⁹/L, and grade-0 bone marrow fibrosis independently predicted long-term survival. These co-variate associations were confirmed in Cox regression with landmark analyses. Long-term survivors had a lower cumulative incidence of anemia and thrombocytopenia during follow-up. Identifying long-term survivors at diagnosis provides clinically meaningful prognostic information in PMF and may influence therapy decisions.

doi:10.1038/s41388-024-02996-4.abstract: Abstract Colorectal cancer (CRC) has a high degree of heterogeneity and identifying the genetic information of individual tumor cells could help enhance our understanding of tumor biology and uncover potential therapeutic targets for CRC. In this study, we identified LPCAT2+ tumor cell populations with less malignancy than LPCAT2- tumor cells in human and mouse CRC tissues using scRNA-seq. Combining in vitro and in vivo experiments, we found that LPCAT2 could inhibit the proliferation of CRC cells by inducing ferroptosis. Mechanistically, LPCAT2 arrested PRMT1 in cytoplasm of CRC cells via regulating acetylation of PRMT1 at the K145 site. In turn, PRMT1 enhanced SLC7A11 promoter activity. Thus, LPCAT2 attenuated the positive regulatory effect of PRMT1 on SLC7A11 promoter. Notably, SLC7A11 acts as a ferroptosis regulator. Furthermore, in LPCAT2 knockout mice (LPCAT2−/−) colon cancer model, we found that LPCAT2−/− mice exhibited more severe lesions, while PRMT1 or SLC7A11 inhibitors delayed the progression. Altogether, we elucidated that LPCAT2 suppresses SLC7A11 expression by inhibiting PRMT1 nuclear translocation, thereby inducing ferroptosis in CRC cells. Moreover, inhibitors of the PRMT1/SLC7A11 axis could delay tumor progression in CRC with low LPCAT2 expression, making it a potentially effective treatment for CRC.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-03965-9.abstract: Cardia gastric adenocarcinoma (CGA) is an aggressive malignancy with rising incidence and poor prognosis, driven in part by significant molecular heterogeneity. Through integrated bioinformatics and clinical analyses, we identify Latent-Transforming Growth Factor Beta-Binding Protein 2 (LTBP2) as a key heterogeneously expressed protein markedly upregulated in CGA compared to non-cardia gastric adenocarcinoma (NCGA), correlating with advanced tumor stage and reduced survival. Mechanistically, we uncover a novel post-translational regulation of LTBP2 wherein SIRT1-mediated deacetylation stabilizes LTBP2 by attenuating its binding to the CUL3/SPOP E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, thereby reducing ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Functionally, stabilized LTBP2 activates the TGF-β/PI3K-AKT signaling axis, promoting tumor cell proliferation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and metastasis in vitro and in vivo. Genetic ablation of LTBP2 or SIRT1 impairs tumor growth and EMT, phenotypes rescued by LTBP2 reconstitution. Importantly, LTBP2 deficiency sensitizes tumors to 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) chemotherapy, both in cell models and murine xenografts. Collectively, our findings delineate a SIRT1-LTBP2-TGF-β regulatory axis critical for CGA progression and chemoresistance, nominating LTBP2 as a promising therapeutic target in this aggressive gastric cancer subtype.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-03997-1.abstract: Abstract Characterizing the genealogy of tumor cells and their population dynamics is central to our understanding of the evolution of cancer. While direct monitoring of the tumor evolutionary process is impractical, we leverage advances in phylogenetics and phylodynamics to explore the evolutionary dynamics of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) using single-cell whole exome sequencing data from 351 tumor cells across 11 NSCLC patients, predominantly focusing on the primary tumors and early stages of NSCLC. Our results reveal distinct phylogenetic tree shapes and evolutionary trajectories across different stages of NSCLC evolution. However, this intricate and multi-phase evolutionary process cannot be fully elucidated by current tumor models. Herein, we hypothesize that tumors progress through the following phases: (1) an initial rapid expansion through Big Bang-like growth, (2) a prolonged plateau period of non-progression with possible accumulation of neutral substitutions, (3) a subsequent phase where adaptive substitutions accumulate gradually, (4) a bottleneck event where selectively advantageous subclones acquire invasive capabilities (characterized by a pattern of punctuated evolution), and, potentially, a rapid expansion leading to metastasis. This work highlights the use of single-cell phylogenetics and phylodynamics for interpreting the evolution of NSCLC, with potential in predicting cancer progression, resistance mechanisms, and treatment response.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04008-z.abstract: T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains (TIGIT) is a key inhibitory receptor on cytotoxic lymphocytes, yet the mechanisms governing its context-dependent upregulation in tumors remain poorly defined. Here, we identify tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα) signaling as an upstream driver of TIGIT expression. Integrated analyses of patient transcriptomic datasets revealed a consistent positive association between TNFα pathway activity and TIGIT expression across multiple cancer types, with strong concordance in melanoma and prognostic relevance in kidney renal clear cell carcinoma. Mechanistically, TNFα directly induced TIGIT expression in natural killer cells via TNFR2 signaling, increasing chromatin accessibility at distal TIGIT enhancers and promoting NF-κB and AP-1 recruitment together with BRD4 and P300. Functionally, combined anti-TNFα and anti-TIGIT treatment suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival more effectively than either monotherapy in murine melanoma and colon cancer models. These findings define a TNFα-TNFR2-enhancer axis controlling TIGIT expression and provide a mechanistic rationale for dual TNFα and TIGIT targeting in inflamed tumors.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04013-2.abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is frequently associated with lymph node metastasis, which contributes to a poor prognosis; however, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. In this study, we identify the N6-methyladenosine (m⁶A) reader IGF2BP1 as a critical driver of lymphatic metastasis in GC. IGF2BP1 is significantly upregulated in GC tissues with lymph node metastasis and is correlated with adverse clinical outcomes. Mechanistically, IGF2BP1 binds to the m⁶A-modified 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of METTL21A mRNA, thereby enhancing its mRNA stability and expression levels. METTL21A, a non-histone lysine methyltransferase, interacts with and methylates the transcription factor SOX18, facilitating its nuclear translocation without altering protein stability. Once in the nucleus, SOX18 directly activates the transcription of CXCL12. Secreted CXCL12 promotes lymphangiogenesis and facilitates lymphatic metastasis through CXCR4 signaling. Functionally, both IGF2BP1 and METTL21A enhance tube formation and migration of lymphatic endothelial cells and promote lymphatic metastasis in GC. Notably, METTL21A knockout abolishes IGF2BP1-induced lymphangiogenesis, whereas SOX18 depletion eliminates the pro-lymphangiogenic effects of IGF2BP1. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized signaling axis-IGF2BP1-METTL21A-SOX18-CXCL12-that links m⁶A-dependent post-transcriptional regulation with methylation-dependent transcriptional activation, offering potential therapeutic targets for the prevention of lymphatic metastasis in gastric cancer.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04015-0.abstract: Lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) lacks effective targeted therapies despite frequent hyperactivation of the PI3K/AKT pathway, and the contribution of adaptor proteins to this process remains poorly defined. Here, we identify Insulin Receptor Substrate 4 (IRS4) as a common substrate of Src kinase and the phosphatase RPTPα, and uncover a previously unrecognized, conserved phosphorylation site at YY111/112 within the IRS4 PH domain. Src-mediated phosphorylation at this site is essential for IRS4-driven proliferation, anchorage-independent growth, and invasiveness in LUSC cells. Mechanistically, phosphorylation at YY111/112 induces conformational rearrangements in IRS4 that enhance the recruitment of the p85β SH2 domain to the YXXM motif of IRS4, thereby promoting AKT activation without altering IRS4 protein stability or subcellular distribution. An IRS4-derived cell-permeable phosphopeptide containing pYY111/112 disrupts the Src-IRS4 interaction and significantly suppresses tumor growth in vivo in a YY111/112-dependent manner. Consistently, YY111/112 phosphorylation is markedly elevated in human LUSC tissues and correlates with advanced disease stages. Collectively, these findings define a Src-IRS4-PI3K/AKT signaling axis and identify YY111/112 as a critical regulatory site of IRS4 and a potential therapeutic vulnerability in LUSC.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04017-y.abstract: KRAS is mutated in 30% of all human cancers. Small molecule inhibitors targeting KRAS with distinct mechanisms-of-action and variable specificities have entered the clinic, but their full effect on the RAS signaling network remains unclear. Here, we described the impact of RAS inhibition on the KRAS interactome using Proximity-dependent Biotin Identification. Two inhibitors were used: panRAS-ON, which forms a ternary complex between cyclophilin and RAS in the GTP-bound state; panKRAS-off, which binds to the KRAS switch II pocket. RAS inhibitors were found to significantly alter 16.5% of proteins in proximity to KRAS. Despite their distinct modality, the KRAS inhibitors induced highly correlated changes in the KRAS interactomes. Among KRAS-proximal proteins, Afadin was highly affected by RAS inhibition. AFDN is a key regulator of cell motility, invasion, and metastasis. Analysis of AFDN phosphorylation revealed that AKT only partially modulates p-Ser1718, while KRAS inhibition sufficiently abolished EGF-mediated AFDN phosphorylation. Silencing AFDN in a KRAS-driven non-small cell lung cancer model abolished chemotaxis and disrupted directional migration in an EGF-driven wound healing model. We demonstrated that KRAS is a central node in regulating growth factor-induced cell migration, and that KRAS inhibition plays a broader role than MAPK-mediated cell proliferation and survival.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04018-x.abstract: Therapeutic efficacy of temozolomide (TMZ) remains limited, and GBM patients generally experience poor outcomes due to the presence of multiple mechanisms of TMZ resistance. Previously, we developed two novel compounds: EPIC-1027, which targets HOTAIR/PRC2 complex, and EPIC-1042, which disrupts interaction between PTRF and CAV1. In this study, we aim to establish a novel combinatorial strategy for GBM by targeting mitochondrial function. Proteomics was employed to evaluate global protein alterations induced by EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042. Super-resolution microscopy and transmission electron microscopy were used to characterize changes in mitochondrial morphology. Metabolic flux analysis was performed to assess alterations in cellular energy metabolism following combined treatment. An intracranial GBM model was established to validate the anti-GBM efficacy of EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 in vivo. Combined treatment with EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 reduced the abundance of respiratory chain complex proteins by promoting p62-dependent protein degradation, resulting in severe mitochondrial damage. Both glycolytic activity and oxidative phosphorylation were markedly suppressed following EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 treatment. In vitro, EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 exerted a synergistic inhibitory effect on GBM cell proliferation and significantly induced apoptosis in an MGMT-independent manner. In vivo, combined treatment with EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 significantly attenuated tumor growth and prolonged survival in mice bearing orthotopic GBM. Our study demonstrates that combined treatment with EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 induces mitochondrial structural abnormalities and functional impairment, leading to suppressed proliferation and enhanced apoptosis. These findings identified a novel combinatorial therapeutic strategy targeting mitochondria for the treatment of glioblastoma.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04019-w.abstract: Endocytosis regulates receptor trafficking and signaling, yet its role in colorectal cancer (CRC) remains unclear. We analyzed transcriptomic data from 15,025 CRC tumors to evaluate gene expression in clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) and the endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT) pathway. Pathway-level signatures were compared across consensus molecular subtypes (CMS) and examined in relation to oncogenic signaling programs, while individual endocytosis-related genes were evaluated for associations with clinical outcomes in an independent randomized trial cohort. Expression of CME and ESCRT pathways varied by CMS, with the highest expression in CMS4 and the lowest in CMS3. Endocytosis signatures correlated with multiple oncogenic signaling pathways, including MAPK, TGF-β, WNT, PI3K, NOTCH, and angiogenesis, suggesting broad links between endocytic activity and tumor biology. In the randomized phase III CALGB/SWOG 80405 trial, low expression of AP2M1-a core adaptor in the CME complex-was significantly associated with longer overall survival and progression-free survival in patients treated with anti-EGFR agents, but not in those receiving anti-VEGF agents. These findings suggest that endocytic trafficking may be associated with oncogenic signaling and differential therapeutic benefit in patients with metastatic CRC. The endocytosis pathway reflects biologically relevant heterogeneity in CRC and may help guide therapeutic stratification.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04020-3.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by severe immunosuppression and metabolic reprogramming, yet the spatial dynamics of lipid flux between malignant and stromal cells remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a profound, type-specific metabolic rewiring in HCC driven by the widespread downregulation of fatty acid transport protein 5 (FATP5). FATP5 deficiency in malignant cells selectively attenuates the uptake of long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs), creating an extracellular lipid surplus that is passively sequestered by neighboring FATP3-expressing tumor-associated endothelial cells (TECs). Within TECs, accumulated LCFAs function as endogenous ligands that activate the nuclear receptor PPARγ, culminating in the robust transcriptional upregulation and paracrine secretion of the chemokine CXCL12. Endothelial-derived CXCL12 subsequently engages CXCR4 on infiltrating CD8+ T cells, inducing PD-1 expression and driving terminal T-cell exhaustion, thereby establishing an immunosuppressive niche that accelerates tumor progression. Importantly, our data suggest that HCC subtypes marked by FATP5 depletion and CXCL12+ TEC enrichment may possess potential therapeutic susceptibility to PPARγ antagonism or anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade. Besides affecting the secretory function of TECs, accumulated LCFAs can impair endothelial barrier function, thereby creating a microenvironment with hematogenous metastasis risk. Collectively, our findings delineate a novel tumor-promoting microenvironment cascade orchestrated by LCFA spatial redistribution, providing a promising mechanistic foundation to support the future development of targeted precision interventions for FATP5-low HCC.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04021-2.abstract: Fatty acid (FA)-induced internalization of the FA transporter CD36 normally functions as an intrinsic brake on FA uptake and lipid overload, but cancer cells can bypass this checkpoint to sustain lipid-fueled growth. The mechanism underlying this failure remains unclear. Here, we identify a FA 2-hydroxylase (FA2H)-CD36 signaling axis that operates as an endogenous brake on lipid fueling in gastric cancer cells. FA2H-derived (R)-2-hydroxy palmitic acid ((R)-2-OHPA) disrupts CD36 interaction with its palmitoyltransferase DHHC4, thereby limiting CD36 palmitoylation and trafficking to the plasma membrane. Loss of FA2H permits CD36 palmitoylation and establishes a feed-forward loop that amplifies FA uptake, lipid accumulation, and tumor growth. Restoring FA2H expression or supplementing cells with exogenous (R)-2-OHPA reinstates the lipid-sensing checkpoint. Moreover, FA2H activation sensitizes gastric cancer cells to inhibition of endogenous FA synthesis through blockade of FA synthase (FASN) or stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1). In vivo, (R)-2-OHPA treatment or expression of the palmitoylation-deficient CD36 AASS mutant attenuates FA2H deficiency-driven lipid accumulation and tumor growth, positioning CD36 palmitoylation as the critical effector in this metabolic circuit. Together, these findings establish FA 2-hydroxylation as a metabolic checkpoint that links FA structure to CD36 trafficking and FA utilization in gastric cancer, revealing a targetable vulnerability in lipid-driven tumor growth.
