doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adi0178.abstract: Perineural invasion (PNI) is a biological characteristic commonly observed in pancreatic cancer. Although PNI plays a key role in pancreatic cancer metastasis, recurrence, and poor postoperative survival, its mechanism is largely unclarified. Clinical sample analysis and endoscopic ultrasonographic elasticity scoring indicated that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) were closely related to the occurrence of PNI. Furthermore, CAF-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) were involved in PNI in dorsal root ganglion coculture and mouse sciatic nerve models. Next, we demonstrated that CAFs promoted PNI through extracellular vesicle transmission of PNI-associated transcript (PIAT). Mechanistically, PIAT specifically bound to YBX1 and blocked the YBX1-Nedd4l interaction to inhibit YBX1 ubiquitination and degradation. Furthermore, PIAT enhanced the binding of YBX1 and PNI-associated mRNAs in a 5-methylcytosine (m5C)–dependent manner. Mutation of m5C recognition motifs in YBX1 or m5C sites in downstream target genes reversed PIAT-mediated PNI. Consistent with these findings, analyses using a KPC mouse model demonstrated that the PIAT/YBX1 axis enhanced PNI through m5C modification. Clinical data suggested that the PIAT expression in the serum EVs of patients with pancreatic cancer was associated with the degree of neural invasion and prognosis. Our study revealed the important role of the PIAT/YBX1 signaling axis in the tumor microenvironment (TME) in promoting tumor cell PNI and provided a new target for precise interference with CAFs and RNA methylation in the TME to suppress PNI in pancreatic cancer.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adi3363.abstract: Candida causes an estimated half-billion cases of vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) every year. VVC is most commonly caused by Candida albicans , which, in this setting, triggers nonprotective neutrophil infiltration, aggressive local inflammation, and symptomatic disease. Despite its prevalence, little is known about the molecular mechanisms underpinning the immunopathology of this fungal infection. In this study, we describe the molecular determinant of VVC immunopathology and a potentially straightforward way to prevent disease. In response to zinc limitation, C. albicans releases a trace mineral binding molecule called Pra1 (pH-regulated antigen). Here, we show that the PRA1 gene is strongly up-regulated during vaginal infections and that its expression positively correlated with proinflammatory cytokine concentrations in women. Genetic deletion of PRA1 prevented vaginal inflammation in mice, and application of a zinc solution down-regulated expression of the gene and also blocked immunopathology. We also show that treatment of women suffering from recurrent VVC with a zinc gel prevented reinfections. We have therefore identified a key mediator of symptomatic VVC, giving us an opportunity to develop a range of preventative measures for combatting this disease.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adr0448.abstract: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) constitute the second most common type of intracranial vascular malformations. Cavernomas arise because of somatic or autosomal dominant inherited loss-of-function mutations in CCM genes, forming fragile mulberry-like malformed blood vessel structures that are prone to leak and break. Treatment is limited to surgical removal of solitary cavernomas, and because patients often present with multiple lesions, pharmacological alternatives to surgery are needed. We performed a high-throughput screen of 5200 bioactive molecules in programmed cell death 10 (PDCD10 or CCM3)-deficient mouse endothelial cells, coupled to automated image analysis. This screen identified dabrafenib, a clinically approved BRAF inhibitor, as a compound that restored cell-cell junctions and vascular barrier properties of CCM3-deficient endothelial cells. The potential translatability of dabrafenib was tested in acute and chronic CCM mouse models, where it reduced cerebral lesion burden and suppressed lesion permeability. Dabrafenib also rescued abnormal structural defects present in the developing retina vasculature in an acute CCM mouse model. Mechanistically, dabrafenib targeted extracellular regulated kinase (ERK)5-Krüppel-like factor (KLF)2/4 signaling and suppressed F-actin stress fiber formation in human brain endothelial cells, two potentially independent and central molecular processes involved in CCM pathology. Silencing BRAF did not prevent dabrafenib-induced KLF2/4 inhibition or restoration of cell-cell junctions, suggesting that its dual therapeutic outcome is independent of BRAF pathway inhibition. In conclusion, dabrafenib is a low-molecular weight compound that inhibits cavernoma pathogenesis, suggesting that CCMs could be treated with dabrafenib to block cavernoma growth and vascular leakage.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.ads0848.abstract: Cartilage lesions do not heal spontaneously and predispose to osteoarthritis. Functional cartilage tissues, engineered using autologous chondrocytes, have a therapeutic advantage over conventional cellular therapies in preclinical studies. Here, we tested whether ex vivo maturation of engineered grafts for cartilage repair leads to improved patient benefit. Using autologous nasal chondrocytes (NCs), we tested whether implantation of in vitro–matured NC-tissue-engineered cartilage (N-TEC) versus undifferentiated NC-cell-activated matrices (N-CAM) in focal cartilage lesions would result in a superior clinical outcome. The prospective, randomized, parallel, open-label phase-2 trial ( ClinicalTrials.gov , NCT02673905) enrolled 108 patients in five hospitals from four countries. Patients ranging in age from 30 to 46 years with full-thickness knee cartilage defects (size, 2.7 to 6.0 square centimeters) were equally randomized and treated with N-TEC or N-CAM. The primary preregistered outcome was the overall Knee Injury Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) at 24 months. N-TEC, which underwent a longer NC culture time, was phenotypically, structurally, and functionally more like hyaline cartilage than N-CAM. The overall KOOS increased with clinical relevance in both groups compared with preoperative values. KOOS was higher at 24 months for N-TEC [85; interquartile range (IQR), 74 to 91] than for N-CAM (79; IQR, 65 to 85). N-TEC, but not N-CAM, was similarly effective in patients with larger defects or revision surgery. Radiologically, N-TEC resulted in a superior composition of both repair tissue and surrounding cartilage, whereas structural scores were similar. This trial validates the clinical efficacy of NC-based grafts for articular cartilage repair and supports the clinical relevance of engineering mature tissues, even for patients with more challenging cartilage defects.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adv2106.abstract: Hepatocyte apoptosis is a key feature of metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH), but the fate of apoptotic hepatocytes in MASH is poorly understood. Here, we explore the hypotheses that clearance of dead hepatocytes by liver macrophages (efferocytosis) is impaired in MASH because of low expression of the efferocytosis receptor T cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain containing 4 (TIM4; gene Timd4 ) by MASH liver macrophages, which then drives liver fibrosis in MASH. We show that apoptotic hepatocytes accumulate in human and experimental MASH, using mice fed the fructose-palmitate-cholesterol (FPC) diet or the high-fat, choline-deficient amino acid–defined (HF-CDAA) diet. Apoptotic hepatocyte accumulation is associated with impaired efferocytosis and loss of TIM4. Administration of neutralizing anti-TIM4 antibodies or genetic deletion of Timd4 in Kupffer cells of FPC and HF-CDAA diet–fed mice decreased efferocytosis by liver macrophages, increased profibrotic activation of collagen-producing hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), and accelerated the progression to fibrotic MASH. Genetic restoration of macrophage Timd4 in FPC and HF-CDAA diet–fed MASH mice or cell therapy with TIM4 + macrophages enhanced apoptotic hepatocyte clearance and decreased HSC activation and liver fibrosis. Studies using an ex vivo macrophage HSC cross-talk model and the HF-CDAA MASH model revealed that inactivation of HSCs by efferocytosing macrophages involved macrophage reprogramming to secrete interleukin-10 (IL-10), which activated the IL-10 receptor on HSCs to dampen their profibrotic activation. These findings reveal a key process in the progression from hepatic steatosis to early MASH fibrosis and identify a mechanism-based therapeutic strategy to prevent fibrotic MASH progression.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adv7928.abstract: B cells are a critical arm of the adaptive immune system. However, the impact of B cells and antibody responses on overall cancer survival remains understudied. Here, we report results from a prospective randomized phase 2 trial of 106 patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and identify that B cell antibody responses are associated with exceptional complete responses to ICI in certain cancer types. To further dissect the impact of B cell subtypes, we generated a comprehensive single-cell RNA sequencing database of intratumoral B cells in 12 tumor types from 152 patients. We found a context-dependent role for B cells, in which they are beneficial in certain cancer types and potentially unfavorable in others, with germinal center and memory B cells enriched in favorable prognosis cohorts and immunoglobulin A-positive plasma cells enriched in unfavorable prognosis cohorts. Depletion of B cells using rituximab in patients before surgery affected intratumoral T cell frequency and diversity. Furthermore, we show that B cells improve long-term overall survival even when T cell infiltrates are already high, indicating that a coordinated dual-arm T cell and B cell adaptive immune response is key to long-term tumor control. Overall, these results demonstrate that B cells and antibody responses in the proper context play an important role in durable complete responses in multiple tumor types.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.ady4852.abstract: The incidence and mortality of high-grade endometrial cancers are increasing, and heterozygous hotspot mutations in PPP2R1A are drivers of the most aggressive forms of uterine cancer. PPP2R1A encodes the Aα scaffolding subunit of the heterotrimeric phosphatase PP2A. These recurrent mutations, specifically at the Pro179 and Ser256 residues, disrupt the binding of tumor-suppressive substrate-directing B56 and B55 subunits to the PP2A scaffolding subunit while maintaining binding to other regulatory subunits. Here, we identified a series of molecular glues that correct PP2A trimer formation in the context of the P179R (Pro179→Arg) and S256F (Ser256→Phe) mutants. A small-molecule library was designed to fit into the pocket at the binding interface of the Aα/B56α/C heterotrimer. The lead molecule, RPT04402, promoted B56α heterotrimerization to the AαP179R and AαS256F mutant scaffolds. In mice, RPT04402 treatment drove tumor regressions and extended median survival in multiple independent mutant cell lines and patient-derived xenografts, proving a robust single-agent activity. This activity was abrogated upon knockout of B56α. Combined, these data demonstrate that PP2A molecular glues are a promising first-in-class therapy that might benefit patients with PPP2R1A mutant uterine cancer by targeting a driver of this aggressive disease.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adz2015.abstract: Proliferative lupus nephritis (LN) is triggered by deposition of autoantibodies in glomeruli and paralleled by a T cell–rich kidney infiltrate. Although these T cells have been attributed to the propagation of tissue injury, it is unclear how they are activated and whether T cell autoreactivity drives local inflammation. Kidney-infiltrating T cells are also observed in urine, where they have high resemblance to interstitial T cells. Therefore, urinary T cells are a proxy for investigating tissue pathogenesis. Here, we analyzed urinary T cells to elucidate whether a kidney-specific T cell autoimmune reaction contributes to tubulointerstitial inflammation in LN. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we compared transcriptomes and clonotypes of T cells from the blood and urine of patients with active LN and showed that urinary T cells were mostly activated CD8 effector memory cells recruited from a circulating CX3CR1 + subset. Several urinary CD8 T cell clones were expanded. However, upon in vitro testing of their T cell receptors, we did not observe autoreactivity against autologous tubular epithelial cells. Instead, ~20% of expanded clonotypes were Epstein-Barr virus–specific or cytomegalovirus-specific, but respective viral antigens were undetectable in kidney biopsies or urine. Conversely, kidney-infiltrating T cells had access to interleukin-15 and interferon-β (IFN-β), and stimulation with these cytokines was sufficient to trigger degranulation and production of tumor necrosis factor, IFN-γ, and granzyme K. Together, these results show that CD8 + CX3CR1 + T cells are recruited into the kidney in LN, where they are activated by cytokines, enabling them to contribute to local inflammation.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adz2140.abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), also called Machado-Joseph disease, the most common form of autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia, is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in ATXN3. The mutant protein is prone to aggregation and exerts toxic gain-of-function effects, whereas the wild-type protein has important neuroprotective roles as a deubiquitinase. Current treatment strategies for SCA3 lack specificity for the mutant allele. Identifying genetic variants such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in linkage with the pathogenic CAG expansion offers a promising avenue to develop allele-specific therapeutic interventions, like antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs). To address this, we conducted allele-specific, targeted, multiplexed nanopore sequencing on 79 patients with SCA3 from Germany, UK, and Portugal. We identified almost 200 polymorphisms and grouped them into three haplotype blocks on the basis of linkage disequilibrium. These SNPs were strongly associated with the CAG expansion. Genotypic modeling of our subcohorts indicated that targeting only two SNPs from different blocks could enable allele-specific treatment of the majority of European patients with SCA3. We evaluated 17 candidate ASOs targeting SNPs from different haplotype blocks. Seven of these ASOs caused allele-preferential reduction of more than 65%. A single ASO application in two SCA3 iPSC-derived cortical neurons (AX1, AX2) achieved up to 90% reduction of mutant ATXN3. Toxicity assessments together with RNA sequencing analyses in AX1 did not indicate evidence of toxicity or widespread transcriptional perturbations. These findings highlight that characterizing heterozygosity rates offers valuable opportunities for selective ASO therapies. Our proof-of-principle targeting with ASOs demonstrates the feasibility of haplotype-informed allele-specific silencing in ATXN3.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adz4081.abstract: Synovitis is a central driver of osteoarthritis (OA) progression, yet the cellular and molecular mechanisms sustaining inflammatory circuits in the synovium remain incompletely understood. Through integrative analysis of time-resolved single-cell RNA sequencing in murine synovium and spatial transcriptomics of human OA tissues, we identified a pathogenic CD74+ macrophage subset that expands in OA and localizes at the synovial-cartilage interface. This subset exhibits a proinflammatory, nonclassical polarization and displays a metabolic dependency on glycolysis. Multiomics and mechanistic studies revealed that CD74 interacts with the glycolytic enzyme enolase 2 (ENO2). This interaction orchestrates a feed-forward signaling axis wherein CD74/ENO2 facilitates the nuclear translocation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1-α (HIF-1α)/β-catenin dimers, which coactivate glycolytic and inflammatory gene programs, thereby sustaining a metabolically driven inflammatory state. Genetic ablation of CD74 in myeloid cells or its pharmacological blockade mitigated synovitis and cartilage degradation in murine OA models. To translate this axis therapeutically, we developed synovium-targeted cationic lipid nanoparticles decorated with MIF-mimetic peptides (PcLNPs) for the delivery of CD74 siRNA. Intra-articular administration of PcLNPs efficiently targeted CD74+ macrophages, attenuated their inflammatory and glycolytic phenotypes, and ameliorated murine OA progression in vivo. Our findings establish the CD74/ENO2/HIF-1α/β-catenin axis as a critical integrator of metabolic reprogramming and inflammation in OA synovitis and present a potential targeted nanotherapeutic strategy for disease modification.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adz4815.abstract: Aging is characterized by progressive functional decline, yet metabolomic signatures across the human life span remain incompletely defined. Here, we profiled plasma metabolomes from 18,476 participants aged 1 to 96 years across six centers in China using nano-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry (LDI-MS) and identified 56 representative age-associated metabolites. In a healthy cohort, we developed a stacking ensemble model to estimate metabolomic age and quantified metabolomic age acceleration (mAA) as each individual's deviation from chronological age. Higher mAA was associated with health deterioration and unfavorable lifestyles. During follow-up from 2019 to 2025, individuals with accelerated mAA showed increased risk of incident chronic diseases, such as fatty liver disease, hypertension, and diabetes, as well as increased all-cause mortality. In a disease cohort, we further developed a mortality-linked metabolomic metric (age deviation) that quantified individualized departures from age-expected mortality risk inferred from plasma metabolites. Age deviation was associated with established composite health measures and increased with multisystem disease involvement and higher multimorbidity burden. Together, these findings support the potential of plasma metabolomic profiling as a scalable, life span-wide approach for deriving clinically interpretable metabolomic aging metrics associated with health status, chronic disease risk, and mortality.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aea4947.abstract: Choline kinase α (ChoKα) is a biomarker of lung cancer, is overexpressed in 60% of human pulmonary malignancies, and is associated with an aggressive phenotype and poor clinical outcome. Patients with lung cancer who undergo surgery have a recurrence rate of 30 to 50%, indicating a potential need for better tumor detection modalities. A near-infrared fluorescent ChoKα-targeting imaging agent, JAS239 (λex, λem: 745, 775 nanometers), was developed for intraoperative identification of tumors, their margins, and local metastases. In lung cancer cells, JAS239 inhibited phosphocholine production, reduced viability in a dose-dependent manner, and accumulated in the cytoplasm where ChoKα is active. JAS239 had favorable pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics for imaging metastatic lung lesions in mice. In situ and ex vivo fluorescence imaging of primary lung tumors in a canine clinical trial showed distinct tumor identification and margin delineation with a tumor-to-background ratio of 5.0 ± 0.6 and a contrast-to-variance ratio of 2.0 ± 0.2 at 0.5 milligram/kilogram. Fluorescence imaging identified a clinically significant event where an occult lesion was found after primary tumor resection. Fluorescence imaging also identified a close surgical margin, which prompted further investigation. Immunohistochemistry for ChoKα showed overexpression in canine lung tumors proportional to tumor fluorescence. Ex vivo human tumor painting demonstrated preferential JAS239 localization with a tumor-to-background ratio of 1.5 ± 0.1 and a contrast-to-variance ratio of 0.9 ± 0.1. These studies establish JAS239 as a safe and effective imaging agent for intraoperative lung tumor detection, warranting further evaluation for human patients with lung cancer.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aea7127.abstract: T cell-engaging bispecific antibodies (TCBs) have seen notable successes in hematologic malignancies, and emerging data demonstrate their potential for the treatment of solid tumors. Most oncology applications of TCBs have focused on targeting tumor cells via tumor-specific antigens; however, TCBs have been underutilized for strategic depletion of immunosuppressive cells in the TME. Regulatory T cells (Treg cells) play a crucial role in suppressing antitumor immune responses, making them an attractive target for immune-based therapies. Treg cells express several surface markers that can serve as potential targets for antibody-mediated depletion, including C-C chemokine receptor type 8 (CCR8), which is highly enriched on tumor-infiltrating Treg cells. Monoclonal antibody (mAb)-mediated Treg cell depletion relies on natural killer (NK) cells, which can be scarce in some solid tumors, whereas TCBs can broadly engage the T cell compartment by overwriting antigen specificity and redirecting potent T cell cytotoxicity against target cells. Here, we have developed a CCR8xCD3 TCB and show that it effectively depletes CCR8-expressing Treg cells in a T cell-mediated manner. CCR8xCD3 TCB led to the selective depletion of intratumoral Treg cells from human solid tumor samples in vitro and mediated inhibition of tumor growth in multiple syngeneic tumor models with variable levels of T cell infiltration alone or in combination with anti-PD-L1. In cynomolgus monkeys, CCR8xCD3 TCB was well tolerated without evidence of acute phase inflammation or cytokine release syndrome and led to effective and durable depletion of the CCR8-expressing subset of Treg cells.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aea7127.title: T cell-mediated depletion of intratumoral regulatory T cells using a CCR8xCD3 T cell-engaging bispecific antibody (TCB) promotes antitumor immunity in preclinical mouse models.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aea8738.abstract: Recent evidence implicates a metabolic switch in afferent spinal circuits as a key driver of the transition from acute pain– to chronic pain–related behaviors in mice after tissue injury, yet the cellular substrates and functional consequences remain incompletely defined. Using a combination of pharmacological and genetic approaches, we investigated whether metabolic reprogramming in spinal cord cell populations constitutes a causal mechanism linking peripheral injury to the progression to pain chronicity. After peripheral injury induced by a hindpaw formalin injection in mice, single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) revealed that spinal oligodendrocytes down-regulated transcripts for myelin protein synthesis and up-regulated transcripts important for lipid biosynthesis. Comparative lipidomics showed that this resource reallocation after peripheral injury was associated with disrupted spinal myelin composition. Moreover, axonal integrity was compromised, causing neuronal accumulation of amyloid precursor protein, enhanced β-site amyloid precursor protein–cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1) expression, and increased insoluble amyloid-β 42 (Aβ 42 ) during a critical temporal window for the transition to pain chronicity. Blocking Aβ 42 production by BACE1 inhibition or clearing Aβ 42 by intrathecal 4G8 monoclonal antibody injection prevented the emergence of persistent pain after hindpaw formalin injection. Oligodendrocyte-specific deletion of N -acylethanolamine acid amidase, a key regulator of cell metabolism and pain, prevented Aβ 42 release and chronic pain development induced by formalin injection or sciatic nerve ligation. These findings uncover an unexpected mechanistic link between chronic pain and amyloid pathology and identify the NAAA→Aβ 42 pathway as a target for disease-modifying intervention.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aec5740.abstract: Microglial dysfunction is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis, with loss-of-function variants in the microglial receptor TREM2 as major risk factors for late-onset AD. We report VG-3927, an oral, CNS-penetrant small-molecule TREM2 agonist that engages the transmembrane domains of TREM2 and its adaptor DAP12 to promote higher-order receptor complex formation and downstream signaling. VG-3927 and tool compound VG-3909 exhibited (sub)nanomolar potency, cooperated with endogenous ligands including amyloid-β (Aβ), and restored signaling in disease-associated TREM2 variants. In human iPSC-derived neuron-microglia-astrocyte cultures, VG-3927 reduced inflammatory cytokines and markers of neuronal damage. In 5xFAD amyloidosis mice expressing the common variant of hTREM2 (5xFAD;hTREM2CV), VG-3909 induced neuroprotective transcriptional reprogramming of microglia, particularly in the plaque niche; enhanced Aβ phagocytosis; and boosted brain glucose metabolism. By contrast, a TREM2 agonist antibody, which may be sequestered by soluble TREM2 (sTREM2), failed to engage plaque microglia. In a first-in-human, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 1 trial (NCT06343636, n = 115), VG-3927 was well tolerated across single and multiple ascending doses of up to 140 milligrams. Pharmacokinetics supported once-daily dosing with high CNS penetration (CSF-to-unbound plasma ratio of 0.91). VG-3927 induced dose-dependent reductions in CSF sTREM2, a biomarker of target engagement, consistent across healthy and elderly participants and participants with AD, supporting further clinical development in AD under the new designation SAR448851.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aec9689.abstract: The transition from acute kidney injury (AKI) to chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains a major clinical problem with unclear underlying mechanisms. Emerging evidence suggests that alterations in tryptophan metabolism, particularly in the production of downstream metabolites such as quinolinic acid (QA), play a role in renal pathophysiology. QA, an intermediate in de novo nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide biosynthesis, is metabolized by quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase (QPRT). We investigated whether QA contributes to kidney injury using models of folic acid-induced AKI-to-CKD transition and cisplatin-induced AKI, genetic and exogenous approaches to alter QA, and clinical observations. Untargeted kidney metabolomics identified QA as one of the most elevated metabolites after folic acid injury. After folic acid injury, Qprt haploinsufficiency exacerbated kidney injury and fibrosis-related gene expression; aged Qprt-haploinsufficient mice exhibited increased fibrosis-associated gene expression without overt renal dysfunction. Exogenous QA administration increased serum creatinine in uninjured mice and worsened renal dysfunction and fibrosis-related gene expression in the folic acid AKI-to-CKD model. Conversely, mice deficient in either 3-hydroxyanthranilate 3,4-dioxygenase (HAAO) or kynurenine 3-monooxygenase (KMO), which reduce flux toward QA, showed improved renal outcomes after folic acid injury and cisplatin-induced AKI. Multimodal spatial metabolomics analysis of kidney biopsies from patients with AKI revealed QA accumulation in regions of inflammatory infiltration. Last, children with CKD exhibited higher urinary QA compared with healthy individuals. These findings underscore QA as a potential mediator of kidney injury and a therapeutic target for preventing the progression from AKI to CKD.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aed4200.abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) bacteremia causes substantial morbidity, but tissue reservoirs that permit bacterial persistence remain poorly defined. Using intravenous USA300 MRSA infection in mice, multiplexed imaging, dual-species transcriptomics, host and bacterial genetics, and cell-based assays, we uncovered the renal inner medulla, the site of urine concentration, as an MRSA reservoir. In this hyperosmotic niche, MRSA evaded immune detection and co-opted tissue polyamines to sustain growth, enabling subsequent spread toward the renal cortex. Neutrophil recruitment to the inner medulla was profoundly delayed owing to osmotic inhibition of immune cell migration. Disruption of medullary osmolality with the loop diuretic furosemide accelerated neutrophil infiltration, limited bacterial spread, and improved renal outcomes. Mechanistically, polyamines promoted MRSA persistence through both extracellular and intracellular actions that depended on local osmolality and pH. In the medullary milieu, polyamines primarily associated with the bacterial surface and stabilized membranes against osmotic stress. Intracellular polyamines enhanced translation of guaB (inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase), the rate-limiting enzyme in bacterial de novo purine biosynthesis. The polyamine-catabolizing gene speG (spermidine acetyltransferase), uniquely present in epidemic USA300 MRSA strains, mitigated polyamine toxicity and conferred a selective advantage in the polyamine-rich kidney. These findings revealed the inner medulla as a physiologically immune-restricted MRSA reservoir and supported modulation of medullary osmolality and bacterial polyamine metabolism as candidate adjunctive strategies for limiting renal persistence and dissemination during MRSA bacteremia.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aed9994.abstract: Diffuse midline glioma (DMG) is a lethal pediatric brain tumor with limited therapeutic options and a poor prognosis. The success of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy requires both improving T cell tumor infiltration and persistence and reducing the risk of on-target/off-tumor toxicity. Here, we adapted and advanced a brain-restricted CAR T cell platform previously validated in glioblastoma to address the anatomical and biological challenges of DMG. We engineered a T cell circuit in which a brain-specific synthetic Notch (synNotch) receptor recognizing brevican (BCAN) induced CAR expression against EphA2 or IL-13Rα2 ("B-SYNC"), thereby restricting CAR expression to the central nervous system (CNS). In immunodeficient DMG models, a single infusion of intravenous (iv) or intracerebroventricular (icv) B-SYNC circuit T cells led to tumor infiltration, sustained persistence, antitumor activity, and extended survival. An alternative BCAN-primed CAR targeting B7-H3 or IL-13Rα2 ("B-SYNC-B/I") similarly improved therapeutic efficacy when delivered intravenously. However, icv administration triggered fatal neurotoxicity because of low-level B7-H3 expression in nontumor CNS regions, indicating that rapid CNS exposure via icv delivery can amplify off-tumor toxicity. In contrast, in an immunocompetent syngeneic DMG model, both iv and icv delivery of a murinized BCAN-gated B7-H3 CAR (mB-SYNC-B7-H3) achieved durable tumor clearance and resistance to rechallenge without any detectable neurotoxicity. Mechanistically, synNotch-primed CAR T cells exhibited reduced exhaustion, enhanced activation, and enrichment of naïve and stem cell memory-like subsets. These findings demonstrate that brain-sensing synNotch CAR T circuits represent a generalizable and translatable strategy for targeting multiple CNS malignancies, including DMG.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aee0680.abstract: ZIP12, a membrane-bound zinc importer, is up-regulated in the remodeled pulmonary arterioles of patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Genetic deletion of its encoding gene, Slc39a12, ameliorates the disease in rodent models. Here, we show that ZIP12 overexpression in human pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs) increased intracellular labile Zn2+ and promoted proliferation. ZIP12 siRNA knockdown attenuated pulmonary hypertension in rodent models. We developed a humanized anti-ZIP12 monoclonal antibody, APL-9796, that normalized intracellular Zn2+ concentration, suppressed proliferation in fibroblasts derived from patients with PAH and PDGF-stimulated PASMCs, and reduced PDGF-induced cytoskeletal remodeling in PASMCs and contractility in PASMCs and engineered pulmonary artery tissues. APL-9796 showed dose-dependent efficacy in humanized Slc39a12 rats, improving cardiopulmonary parameters after induction of pulmonary hypertension and was well tolerated in phase 1 clinical studies. Transcriptomic profiling revealed modulation of several molecular pathways, including those involving AMPK, PPAR, and PI3K-Akt. ZIP12-driven labile Zn2+ signaling underpins the pathogenesis of PAH. Targeting ZIP12 with APL-9796 offers a promising therapeutic strategy.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aee4629.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now enables the exploration of vast chemical and sequence spaces, the design of synthesizable antibiotics, and the prioritization of safe, mechanism-diverse candidates through integrated modeling and accelerated testing. Here, we survey recent advances in AI for both small-molecule and peptide antimicrobial drugs, highlight emerging data and reporting standards, and outline translational pathways and regulatory hurdles needed to bring these agents to patients.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aef3967.abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by hyperproliferative keratinocytes and a dysregulated cytokine milieu, perpetuating a self-reinforcing inflammatory cycle. Despite the key involvement of keratinocytes in this pathogenic loop, the molecular pathogenesis remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify chitinase-like protein CHI3L2 as a key mediator. Elevated CHI3L2 levels were detected in serum and lesional skin from patients with psoriasis, predominantly in keratinocytes, as also verified by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic analyses. In vitro stimulation of keratinocytes with M5 cytokine cocktail (IL-17A, IL-22, oncostatin M, IL-1α, and TNF-α) increased CHI3L2 expression, demonstrating that CHI3L2 is inducible under inflammatory conditions. Transgenic mice expressing human CHI3L2 exhibited aggravated psoriasis-like phenotypes in both imiquimod- and mannan-induced psoriasis models, characterized by epidermal hyperplasia and scaling. To dissect the role of CHI3L2, we used recombinant protein injection, parabiosis, and bone marrow transplantation, identifying keratinocytes as the primary source of pathogenic CHI3L2. This was further confirmed by keratinocyte-specific CHI3L2 knockin mice. CHI3L2 functions in the HaCaT cell line and primary keratinocytes were investigated by recombinant CHI3L2 administration or CHI3L2 knockout. CHI3L2 disrupted phospholipid homeostasis, leading to altered inflammatory responses, proliferation, and differentiation of keratinocytes. CHI3L2 activated secretory phospholipase A2, elevating lysophosphatidylcholine, thereby establishing an autocrine loop perpetuating keratinocyte inflammation and reshaping the immune microenvironment. Therapeutic neutralization of CHI3L2 with antibodies or intervention of phospholipid pathway ameliorated skin inflammation in mouse psoriasis models. Our findings reveal CHI3L2 as an important regulator of keratinocyte-driven lipid remodeling and inflammation in psoriasis, highlighting potential as a therapeutic target.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aef7406.abstract: Successful hematopoietic cell transplant requires immunosuppression to prevent graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), a lethal, T cell-mediated complication. The phase 3 BMT CTN 1703 trial demonstrated superior GVHD-free/relapse-free survival for posttransplant cyclophosphamide (PT-Cy)-based GVHD prophylaxis versus tacrolimus/methotrexate (Tac/MTX), but the T cell biology underpinning these outcomes remains unknown. To determine this, 324 patients were coenrolled onto BMT CTN 1801 to investigate the distinct T cell immune reconstitution pathways of these regimens, including extensive evaluation of T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire, via sequencing of 2359 longitudinal samples and 180,432,350 T cells. Multimodal T cell analysis revealed that PT-Cy was associated with pan-T cell deletion followed by delayed T cell expansion from a smaller founder population compared with Tac/MTX. This created a T cell diversity bottleneck, leading to reduced TCR repertoire diversity for 2 years posttransplant. Reduced TCR diversity, more common in patients receiving PT-Cy, was linked to protection against chronic GVHD when patients were analyzed without regard to study arm. Leveraging donor- and host-specific TCR clonal analysis, we determined that PT-Cy-mediated T cell depletion also depleted pathogen-specific TCRs, rendering PT-Cy patients more likely to lack detectable graft-derived pathogen-specific TCRs early after transplant, which was associated with an increased risk of severe infection. This study reveals how distinct immunosuppression strategies uniquely remodel T cell immunity and shape divergent transplant outcomes.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aef8416.abstract: Integrated strategies to combat antibiotic-resistant bacteria and fungi require innovative commercial models, new discovery platforms, standardized genomic surveillance, and streamlined clinical trials. Machine learning and other new technologies will accelerate the development of diagnostics and therapeutics (small molecules, antibodies, and vaccines) to combat antimicrobial resistance. Next-generation approaches should align societal impact with investment to ensure rapid global public health gains.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aef9466.abstract: Expanded CAG/CTG repeats cause more than 15 different diseases that all remain without a disease-modifying treatment. Because repeat length accounts for most of the variation in disease severity, contracting CAG/CTG repeats presents an attractive therapeutic avenue. Here, we show that the CRISPR-Cas9 nickase targeted to CAG/CTG repeats leads to efficient repeat contractions in Huntington's disease (HD) patient-derived neurons and astrocytes and in myotonic dystrophy type 1 patient-derived neurons. The approach was allele selective and free of detectable off-target mutations. Injection of the Cas9 nickase into the striatum of the R6/1 mouse model of HD using adeno-associated viral vectors led to repeat contractions in more than half of striatal neurons. Upon injection, we observed a reduction in the number of inclusion bodies, an improved gene expression profile, and amelioration of locomotion deficits in the open field test. The effects were greater than expected from the contractions induced, suggesting that non-cell autonomous mechanisms may be involved. Our results provide the proof of concept that correction of CAG/CTG repeats can improve HD phenotypes in a mouse disease model.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aeh0442.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) affects ∼20% of hospitalized patients and is traditionally viewed as a transient complication of acute illness. Evidence suggests that AKI can initiate long-term renal and cardiovascular disease, even when kidney function appears to recover. Survivors of AKI face increased risks of CKD, heart failure, myocardial infarction, and premature mortality, yet post-AKI care remains poorly defined. We synthesize emerging mechanistic and clinical evidence linking AKI to systemic cardiorenal disease and discuss how biomarkers, imaging, and clinical risk prediction may enable identification of high-risk patients and support translational strategies to prevent progression to chronic disease.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aeh1292.abstract: The continuous antigenic evolution of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has repeatedly undermined the effectiveness of monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapies, underscoring the need for innovative approaches that improve therapeutic mAb breadth and durability of protection. Here, we engineered messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA)-encoded bispecific antibodies (bsAbs) that, upon intravenous administration in lipid nanoparticles, achieved high serum concentrations, extended half-life, and serum neutralizing titers exceeding 1:10,000 in human neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)-expressing mice. To enhance resilience to viral escape, we used structure-guided computational design to introduce Fc modifications that promoted selective homodimerization, thereby enabling codelivery of multiple mRNA-encoded bsAbs with cognate heavy chain pairing. In vivo expression of a triple bsAb combination resulted in broad serum neutralization of historical and contemporary SARS-CoV-2 variants, including the highly mutated BA.3.2.2 lineage. Preexposure prophylaxis with the mRNA-delivered bsAb combination conferred protection against SARS-CoV-2 XBB.1.5 challenge, preventing weight loss and decreasing viral burden in the lungs compared with vehicle control treatment. Together, the results provide proof of principle for mRNA-based delivery of Fc-engineered bsAb combinations to combat SARS-CoV-2 and potentially other rapidly evolving pathogens.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aei2870.abstract: Innate immune signaling through inflammasome activation has been implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple sclerosis (MS). We previously demonstrated that nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), drugs approved to treat HIV and hepatitis B virus infections, and kamuvudines, safer NRTI derivatives, both inhibit inflammasome activation. Here, we report that in the experimental autoimmune encephalitis mouse model of MS, treatment with kamuvudine-9 (K-9), an NRTI derivative with an enhanced safety profile, prevented further neurological deficits and reversed preexisting paralysis and vision loss. K-9 promoted myelin and axonal preservation in the mouse spinal cord and abolished the increase in serum neurofilament light (NfL) chain. K-9 disrupted interactions between nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat (NLR) pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) and NIMA-related kinase 7 (NEK7) and between NLRP3 and NLR CARD domain containing 4 (NLRC4), inhibiting dual inflammasome activation. K-9 also exhibited appropriate safety and pharmacokinetic characteristics and biodistribution. In three distinct human cohorts, there was a lower incidence of MS in those individuals receiving NRTIs for HIV infection, preexposure prophylaxis for HIV, or hepatitis B virus infection. NRTI use was also associated with a reduction in relapse rate in individuals with MS. These findings provide a rationale for further investigating K-9 for treating MS.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aei5117.abstract: Dengue is the canonical viral disease for which immune history is a determinant of protective versus pathogenic responses and immunogenicity. Yet, because of limitations in animal models and clinical presentation after peak viremia, how preinfection and early immune responses affect dengue outcome is not confirmed. We conducted a phase 1 clinical trial with 45 healthy adults to test whether secondary infection challenge with a heterotypic, full-length, attenuated virus increases viremia and immunogenicity compared with primary and tertiary infection. Viremia was associated with more, but still mild, clinical signs and symptoms, and secondary infection resulted in greater viremia, neutralizing antibodies, and protective T cell responses. However, those whose baseline antibodies most efficiently increased dengue virus replication in an in vitro assay experienced delayed inflammatory and adaptive immune activation, the highest viremia, strong acute immune responses, and waning of potent CD8+ T cells and antibodies. In contrast, higher baseline antibodies against the nonstructural protein 1 of multiple serotypes predicted early interferon and balanced immune activation, viremia control, and development of enduring, potent B and T cells, revealing how vaccines can induce broad, long-lasting protection. Last, individuals with potent and neutralizing antibodies and IFN-γ+ T cells at baseline experienced minimal viral replication. Together, these findings demonstrate that controlled human challenge with dengue virus can delineate coordinated versus dysregulated acute immune responses and their effects on immunogenicity, informing therapeutic and vaccine strategies for dengue and other viral diseases.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aei5968.abstract: Amphotericin B remains the gold-standard therapy for invasive fungal infections, but its clinical utility is limited by toxicity arising from poor selectivity for fungal ergosterol over mammalian cholesterol, a challenge that decades of medicinal chemistry have failed to fully overcome. Here, we report mandimycin M16, a polyene macrolide engineered from a unique 5 + 1 polyene scaffold that uncouples antifungal potency from host toxicity. Mandimycin M16 exhibited potent, broad-spectrum activity against 11 tested World Health Organization (WHO) priority fungal pathogens. Unlike amphotericin B, which binds cholesterol, M16 exhibited no detectable cholesterol binding and showed no detectable hemolysis, cytotoxicity, or nephrotoxicity at concentrations up to 128 micrograms per milliliter in vitro and after up to seven daily intravenous doses in mice. Mechanistic studies revealed that mandimycin M16 exerted rapid fungicidal activity through selective recognition of the conjugated C5-C8 diene system present in ergosterol but absent in cholesterol, a mode of sterol discrimination fundamentally different from classical polyenes. In multiple disseminated murine infection models, M16 outperformed liposomal amphotericin B at equivalent doses, achieving up to 3.4 log reduction in fungal burden and 100% survival without detectable renal injury by biomarkers or histopathology. These findings establish that the 5 + 1 polyene architecture enables complete sterol selectivity and molecularly uncouples antifungal potency from host toxicity, providing a next-generation antifungal candidate for the treatment of invasive fungal infections.

doi:10.1136/gutjnl-2026-339304.abstract: Background Steatohepatitic hepatocellular carcinoma (SH-HCC) is a distinct subtype of hepatocellular carcinoma with poorly defined molecular features and limited diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. Objective This study aimed to delineate its multi-omics landscape, develop non-invasive diagnostic tools and identify actionable therapeutic targets. Design We integrated multimodal clinical and omics datasets from an overall cohort of 156 patients, including RNA-seq (n=69), spatial transcriptomics (n=36), spatial metabolomics (n=6), lipidomics (n=125) and serum proteomics (n=152), for comprehensive molecular profiling and diagnostic model construction. FABP4 was functionally validated in Sleeping Beauty-induced HCC mouse models. Results An SH-HCC index was established to reliably differentiate SH-HCC from conventional HCC. Drug response analysis suggested a potential reduction in responsiveness to sorafenib and immunotherapy-based regimens in SH-HCC, whereas transarterial chemoembolisation may remain an effective therapeutic option. Spatial transcriptomics revealed increased immune cell infiltration, a reinforced immune barrier and reduced tumour-immune cell communication. SH-HCC is characterised by a lipid-rich phenotype, and a diagnostic model based on 12 lipid species showed good performance in an independent cohort (area under the curve (AUC)=0.909). Serum proteomic model demonstrated good performance in the test cohort (AUC=0.828). Importantly, our preliminary findings suggest a potential therapeutic role for FABP4, as its genetic deletion suppressed tumour growth, reshaped the tumour immune microenvironment and enhanced the response to PD-1 blockade. Conclusion This study provides the first multi-omics characterisation of SH-HCC, highlighting the SH-HCC index and non-invasive diagnostic models, with FABP4 as a potential target.

doi:10.1136/gutjnl-2026-339637.abstract: Background Engineered bacterial therapeutics represent a promising strategy for sustained intestinal delivery of therapeutic molecules, but their efficacy is limited by inefficient colonisation, safety concerns and the need for repeated administration or auxiliary delivery systems. Objective To develop a safety-optimised native bacterial chassis capable of long-term gut colonisation and sustained therapeutic delivery for intestinal inflammatory and metabolic diseases. Design Native murine Escherichia coli isolates were screened for antibiotic susceptibility, genetic tractability and long-term intestinal colonisation. The selected strain, MEc30, was further optimised by deleting the putative virulence-associated clb and irp loci. MEc30 was then engineered to produce nicotinic acid (MEc30-NA) or deliver murine interleukin-10 (MEc30-mIL-10), and therapeutic efficacy was evaluated in a high-fat diet-induced metabolic dysfunction model as well as Il10 −/− and dextran sulphate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis models. Results MEc30 achieved stable lifelong colonisation of the murine intestine after a single oral administration, without antibiotic preconditioning or auxiliary delivery systems and did not detectably disturb host physiology or gut microbial ecology. Deletion of clb and irp abolished potential colibactin- and yersiniabactin-associated biosafety risks while preserving bacterial growth and colonisation capacity. MEc30-NA continuously produced nicotinic acid in the gut, activated epithelial GPR109a-associated barrier signalling, improved glucose and lipid metabolism, reduced systemic inflammation and avoided the sharp peak exposure associated with conventional nicotinic acid administration. MEc30-mIL-10 enabled sustained intestinal interleukin-10 delivery, suppressed inflammatory macrophage activation, improved barrier integrity and alleviated colitis in both Il10 − / − and DSS-induced mouse models. Conclusion This study identifies MEc30 as a durable and safety-optimised native E. coli chassis for sustained intestinal therapeutic delivery. Engineered native symbionts may provide a long-acting live biotherapeutic strategy for metabolic diseases and chronic intestinal inflammation.

doi:10.1136/rapm-2026-108180.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted nerve tracking facilitates real-time ultrasound-guided nerve identification, but its effect on independent nerve identification after AI support is removed remains uncertain. Methods In this prospective randomized trial, 80 ultrasound novices (60 medical students and 20 anesthesiology residents) were assigned to either a control group receiving B-mode ultrasound training without AI assistance or an AI-assisted group using a real-time nerve tracking system (NerveTrack). Following a standardized lecture and a 10-minute hands-on training session, participants underwent assessment with the AI function disabled. The primary outcome was first-attempt independent identification success for the median nerve and supraclavicular brachial plexus. Secondary outcomes included performance after additional training and self-reported confidence. Results 78 participants completed the study. First-attempt independent identification success rates did not differ significantly between the control and AI-assisted groups for the median nerve (57.5% vs 65.8%; RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.62; p=0.452) or the brachial plexus (35.0% vs 42.1%; RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.68 to 2.11; p=0.519). Following additional AI-assisted training, participants in the AI-assisted group reported greater confidence in identifying the brachial plexus than those in the control group (4.7±0.5 vs 4.4±0.9; p=0.046). No significant differences were observed in independent identification success after additional training. Conclusions Brief AI-assisted training did not improve immediate independent ultrasound identification of the median nerve or supraclavicular brachial plexus after AI support was removed. These findings do not establish long-term retention, transfer to unfamiliar anatomy, or clinical procedural performance. The registration number NCT05857787 .

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-2084.abstract: Growth-induced solid stress and fluid pressure contribute to tumor progression and drug resistance. Beyond tumor endogenous physical forces, cells in the tumor microenvironment may also experience external macroscopic mechanical stress, and some tumors preferentially develop in weight-bearing regions with higher focal pressure. Characterization of the impact of macroscopic mechanical stress on the tumor microenvironment could help uncover the mechanistic links between external mechanical forces and increased tumor incidence. Here, we showed that recurrent macroscopic mechanical stress disrupts nuclear envelope integrity, leading to spatial reorganization and fibroblast subtype changes at the tumor-stromal interface. In mouse models of plantar melanoma, exogenous mechanical stress induced nuclear envelope rupture in melanoma cells and increased LRRC15-positive myofibroblasts. Reduction of nuclear envelope integrity through inducible deletion of Lmna likewise increased LRRC15-positive myofibroblast generation. Co-culture with myofibroblasts promoted nuclear envelope rupture in melanoma cells in 3D culture, suggesting a positive feedback loop. In addition, mechanical stress-driven transcriptomic changes in tumor and stromal cells were observed alongside enhanced lymph node metastasis and immunotherapy resistance. Analysis of human melanoma samples revealed mechanical stress-associated stromal remodeling and a higher incidence of lymph node metastasis in tumors arising in mechanically stressed regions, although these features were not significantly associated with overall survival. Together, these findings suggest that macroscopic mechanical stress may influence cancer progression by inducing nuclear envelope damage and reshaping tumor-stromal interactions.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-2748.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a lethal malignancy 20% more likely to develop in Black African Americans (BAA) compared to Non-African Americans (NAA). Large-scale gene expression analysis of tumor subtypes and cellular microenvironments in a diverse PDAC cohort could help provide insights into cell and molecular differences in BAA cancer cells. Here, we conducted a multi-omics interrogation of BAA versus NAA PDAC using whole exome sequencing, spatial transcriptomics (ST), and spatial proteomics. Whole exome sequencing confirmed patient ancestry and showed no significant differences in driver mutations between race groups. BAA PDAC tumors had significantly fewer classical molecular subtype cells with no change in more aggressive basal-like cells. Instead, BAA patients showed a significant enrichment of the intermediate/hybrid subtype compared to NAA patients. BAA tumors also displayed increased B cell and reduced myeloid cell interactions compared to NAA tumors. Analysis of tertiary lymphoid structures in a validation cohort revealed that tumors in BAA patients displayed larger TLS size and number compared to NAA. In conclusion, these findings identify an increased intermediate molecular subtype signature in BAA tumors at the expense of cells with a classical subtype, accompanied by a distinct immune cell composition and spatial distribution. This study highlights that health disparities in patients of different ancestries may have a molecular basis that influences tumor aggressiveness and the immune response, which may inform therapeutic strategies.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-4071.abstract: Mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDHm) define a distinct molecular class of gliomas. IDHm converts α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2HG), which drives tumorigenesis. The IDHm inhibitor vorasidenib suppresses D-2HG production and prolongs progression-free survival in some, but not all, patients. Here, using patient-derived models, genetically engineered glioma cells, orthotopic xenografts, and patient tissue, we showed that phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH) mediates intrinsic resistance to vorasidenib by sustaining D-2HG production despite IDHm inhibition. Silencing PHGDH suppressed residual D-2HG synthesis and restored vorasidenib sensitivity in resistant models, whereas PHGDH overexpression restored D-2HG production and induced resistance in sensitive models. Importantly, restoration of intracellular D-2HG rescued growth despite continued vorasidenib treatment, demonstrating a causal role for residual D-2HG production in the resistant phenotype. Mechanistically, a permissive chromatin state characterized by increased H3K4me3, reduced H3K27me3, and enhanced ATF4 occupancy at the PHGDH promoter facilitated PHGDH upregulation in resistant models. Pharmacologic induction of this chromatin state induced PHGDH expression, restored D-2HG production, and conferred resistance to vorasidenib in sensitive models. Consistently, tumor tissue from patients with poor response to IDHm inhibitor treatment exhibited higher PHGDH expression, coupled with the ATF4-enriched permissive chromatin state observed in resistant models. Finally, deuterium metabolic imaging of D-2HG production from diethyl-[3,3'-2H]-α-KG provided an early, non-invasive readout of response and resistance to vorasidenib in vivo. Collectively, this study identifies a chromatin-regulated ATF4-PHGDH-D-2HG axis as a mechanism of intrinsic resistance to IDHm inhibition and establishes diethyl-[3,3'-2H]-α-KG as a metabolic imaging probe for interrogating treatment response in IDHm gliomas.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-4782.abstract: Abstract The Tn antigen, a truncated O-glycan, is frequently elevated in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Multiple therapeutic approaches targeting Tn have been developed, but they have not demonstrated clear efficacy signals in early-phase clinical studies. Improving Tn-targeted strategies in PDAC will require both overcoming the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and defining pathways by which truncated O-glycans promote growth and immune evasion. In this study, we show that Tn reshapes the tumor immune landscape of PDAC. Expression of Tn antigen on PDAC cells enhanced proliferation in vitro and tumor growth in vivo. Tn expression remodeled the immune microenvironment, skewing tumor-associated macrophages toward M2-like phenotypes, reducing cross-presenting dendritic cells, and expanding myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC). Single-cell RNA sequencing confirmed the expansion of MDSCs and downregulation of antigen processing and presentation in the immune cell infiltrate of Tn+ tumors. Tumor-intrinsic transcriptomic analyses revealed the activation of TNFα/NF-κB signaling and induction of IL34, a cytokine linked to monocyte survival and differentiation in Tn antigen–expressing tumors. Additionally, high Tn expression in both organoids derived from patients with pancreatic cancer and in PDAC mouse models was associated with increased IL34 expression. The genetic deletion of Il34 in PDAC cells attenuated Tn-driven tumorigenesis and reduced MDSC infiltration, whereas recombinant IL34 promoted myeloid cell differentiation and proliferation in vitro. Together, these findings establish a glyco–immune–cytokine axis in which truncated O-glycans contribute to IL34-mediated immunosuppression, providing mechanistic insights and potential therapeutic targets in PDAC. Significance: Altered glycosylation stimulates TNF-α/NF-κB signaling and induces IL-34-mediated accumulation of suppressive myeloid cells in pancreatic cancer, providing a myeloid-mediated mechanism of immunosuppression that could guide the development of therapies targeting glycosylation.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-5347.abstract: Lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) is an aggressive subtype of non-small cell lung cancer with limited targeted therapeutic options and incompletely defined immune-regulatory dependencies. Here, we identified atypical chemokine receptor 3 (ACKR3) as a squamous-enriched regulator that restrains malignant progression in LUSC. Integrative analyses of human LUSC datasets, autochthonous genetically engineered mouse models, and ex vivo organoid systems showed that ACKR3 loss accelerated tumor growth and remodeled the immune microenvironment, marked by reduced CD8⁺ T cell infiltration and increased T cell exhaustion. Mechanistically, ACKR3 limited activation of the MIF-CD74-PD-L1 axis, thereby constraining tumor-cell PD-L1 expression and preserving antitumor immune surveillance. In preclinical LUSC models, treatment with the ACKR3-directed PD-L1 degrader KineTAC, a bispecific molecule that co-engages ACKR3 and PD-L1 to promote lysosomal degradation of PD-L1, enhanced antitumor efficacy, particularly in combination with chemotherapy. Together, these findings define ACKR3 as a squamous-associated immune checkpoint regulator and nominate ACKR3-directed PD-L1 degradation as a tumor-selective therapeutic strategy for LUSC.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-5500.abstract: Hormone receptor positive (HR+) breast cancer is the most common breast cancer subtype globally and remains a leading cause of cancer-related death in women. Black women diagnosed HR+ breast cancer experience significantly worse outcomes than White women, a disparity that persists even after accounting for factors such as healthcare access and educational attainment. Understanding the biological mechanisms underlying these differences has been limited by the underrepresentation of Black patients in genomic datasets. To address this gap, we generated an HR+ breast cancer transcriptomic dataset enriched for Black patients while controlling for access to healthcare and education level. Tumors from Black women showed enrichment of tumor microenvironment-related signatures, including increased collagen deposition and prognostically unfavorable T-cell landscapes. Data from in vitro and in vivo experimental models showed that race-aligned collagen deposition patterns were driven, at least in part, by tumor cell-intrinsic signaling and promoted metastatic phenotypes associated with poorer outcomes. Further analysis of the patient transcriptomic dataset revealed that unfavorable T-cell signatures previously attributed to race or ancestry were more strongly associated with poverty burden. Across multiple independent datasets, STAT4 emerged as a potential master regulator of this poverty-associated immune phenotype. Collectively, these findings suggest that molecular features of breast tumors are shaped by both biological and structural factors linked to self-identified race and socioeconomic disadvantage. These results demonstrate that integrating social determinants of health with molecular analyses can reveal mechanisms contributing to cancer outcome disparities and provide a foundation for the development of more effective and equitable precision oncology approaches.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-5714.abstract: Gastric mixed neuroendocrine-non-neuroendocrine neoplasms (MiNENs) are aggressive malignancies that exhibit complex cellular heterogeneity driven by the dual lineages. The dismal patient survival rates highlight the need to elucidate the cellular origin of gastric MiNENs and the key regulatory mechanisms to develop improved treatment strategies. Here, we identified a gastric POU2F3+epithelial population as a potential cell of origin for gastric MiNENs. Lineage tracing and single-cell RNA sequencing further identified that POU2F3+ cells include three distinct subpopulations with divergent differentiation trajectories: progenitor cells (SOX2+SOX9+), tuft cells (POU2F3+DCLK1+), and neuroendocrine cells (SYP+CHGA+). Combined Rb1/Trp53 deletion and MYC overexpression in POU2F3+ epithelial cells (Pou2f3-CreERT; Rb1fl/fl; Trp53fl/fl; LSL-MycT58A) led to the rapid development of gastric MiNENs containing both neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine lesions, recapitulating human gastric MiNENs pathology. Transcription factor activity analysis and spatial transcriptomics revealed SOX2 and SOX9 as critical regulators driving subpopulation specification, with SOX2 and SOX9 being enriched in dysplasia and adenocarcinoma, respectively. Bulk RNA sequencing further showed increased expression of CXCL5 in gastric MiNENs, and inhibition of CXCL5 reduced the growth of tumor organoids and xenografts in mouse models. Together these findings offer a physiologically relevant model for studying gastric MiNENs and identify CXCL5 as a potential therapeutic target for this heterogeneous cancer.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-5766.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and deadly primary brain tumor in adults, characterized by diffuse infiltrative lesions, distinct oncogenic alterations, and a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). These traits, however, are not fully recapitulated in current syngeneic murine glioma models, thereby limiting the pre-clinical development of novel therapies. Here we developed murine GBM models with patient-specific mutations that shared striking resemblance with human disease. Mosaic analysis with dual-recombinase mediated cassette exchange (MADR) and CRISPR-Cas9 were leveraged to generate autochthonous tumor models with single-copy somatic transgenesis of murine epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (mEGFRvIII) and loss-of-function mutations commonly observed in GBM. Characterization of a model lacking Pten and Cdkn2a (mEGFRvIII-PC) via histopathologic analyses, functional assays, and single-cell RNA sequencing showed these tumors developed as diffuse, infiltrative lesions with ill-defined margins and a necrotic core. The TIME was primarily comprised of microglia with minimal lymphocyte infiltration, recapitulating patient tumors. Furthermore, these tumors displayed intrinsic resistance to immune checkpoint blockade, potentially due to poor myeloid cell antigen presentation and T cell priming. Additionally, mEGFRvIII-PC cells were the most resistant to antigen-specific T cell-induced cytotoxicity and simultaneously promoted T cell exhaustion, while murine interferon-γ (mIFN-γ) stimulation induced a greater response in vitro with enhanced upregulation of PD-L1 relative to MHC-I. In sum, these findings demonstrate the improved fidelity of the mEGFRvIII-PC model to patient tumors and support its use in developing and refining novel therapeutic paradigms for GBM.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-5866.abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is characterized by profound metabolic reprogramming and substantial inherited susceptibility. The molecular mechanisms linking germline risk variation to tumor metabolic reprogramming could potentially be exploited for precision interventions. Here, we aimed to delineate the germline regulatory architecture underlying ccRCC susceptibility and to determine how inherited noncoding variation influences mitochondrial metabolism and tumor progression. Whole-genome sequencing and transcriptomic profiling of matched ccRCC tumor and adjacent normal kidney tissues were integrated with cross-ancestry genome-wide association, cis-expression quantitative trait locus, transcriptome-wide association, and fine-mapping analyses. LINC02068 was identified as a genetically regulated tumor suppressor associated with inherited ccRCC susceptibility, and cross-ancestry fine-mapping prioritized rs234043 as a candidate causal variant. The rs234043 risk allele preferentially recruited HOXC8 and repressed LINC02068 transcription. Reduced LINC02068 expression promoted malignant cellular phenotypes and was associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Mechanistically, LINC02068 localized to mitochondria, interacted with the co-chaperone DNAJA3, and promoted DNAJA3 destabilization, thereby attenuating mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Allele-specific editing and genetic rescue experiments further supported a functional rs234043-HOXC8-LINC02068-DNAJA3 regulatory axis driving ccRCC progression. Pharmacologic impairment of mitochondrial complex I suppressed ccRCC cell migration and proliferation. These findings establish a mechanistic link between a germline noncoding variation and mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming in ccRCC and identify targeting oxidative phosphorylation as a potential avenue for precision therapy.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-26-0035.abstract: Vasculogenic mimicry (VM) is a process in which malignant cells acquire endothelial-like functions to generate perfusable vascular channels independent of endothelial cells. VM represents a major barrier to effective vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA)-targeted therapy in cancer. In this study, we used organ-scale vascular imaging that identified a mechanism of VM in glioblastoma (GBM) mediated by alpha-L-fucosidase 1 (FUCA1). FUCA1 was preferentially expressed in glioblastoma stem-like cells (GSCs) with high CD44 expression. FUCA1 functioned as a key regulator of GSC-mediated VM by stabilizing LDHA protein and promoting a metabolic shift toward glycolysis. Elevated glycolytic flux increased lactate production and enhanced histone H3 lysine 18 lactylation (H3K18la), which in turn activated SERPINF1 transcription and drove VM in GSCs. In preclinical models, the FUCA1 inhibitor deoxyfuconojirimycin hydrochloride (DFH) significantly reduced GSC tumorigenicity and VM in vivo and exhibited robust antitumor activity when combined with anti-VEGFA therapy. Collectively, these findings define a FUCA1-mediated histone lactylation pathway that enhances GSC VM and highlight a therapeutically targetable mechanism to improve the efficacy of current anti-angiogenic strategies in GBM.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-26-0507.abstract: Epigenetic dysregulation plays a vital role in the progression of endometrial cancer (EC), yet targeted treatment options remain limited. Here, we identified the histone acetyltransferase KAT5 as a therapeutic target in EC. KAT5 was significantly overexpressed in EC and correlated with poor patient outcome. Silencing KAT5 inhibited EC cell proliferation and tumor growth. KAT5-deficient EC cells exhibited impaired cytoskeletal dynamics, leading to heightened DNA damage and increased micronuclei formation. The release of micronuclear DNA into the cytoplasm activated the cGAS-STING pathway, thereby amplifying proinflammatory immune responses. Mechanistically, KAT5 acetylated H2A.Z to transcriptionally activate Arp2/3 complex genes, promoting actin polymerization and chromosomal stability. Inhibition of Arp2/3 or depletion of its subunit ARPC5 replicated the effects of KAT5 loss, whereas restoring ARPC5 mitigated chromosomal instability and cGAS activation. In transplantation models of EC cell lines and syngeneic murine Trp53-/-;Pten-/- EC organoids, pharmacological inhibition of KAT5 with NU9056 suppressed tumor progression and enhanced immune cell infiltration. NU9056 also induced Arp2/3 disruption, genomic instability, and cGAS-STING activation in patient-derived organoids from clinical endometrial cancer samples. Together, these findings highlight KAT5 as a promising therapeutic target in EC that influences chromatin remodeling, cytoskeletal dynamics, and immune modulation.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-26-0563.abstract: Metabolic reprogramming is a well-described hallmark of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). Gene copy number variation and altered gene expression data suggest enhanced branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) transamination and reduced BCAA oxidation are highly selected traits in ccRCC. Surprisingly, we found that genetic modulation of BCAA oxidation had little effect on experimental ccRCC cell growth in vitro and in vivo. In contrast, BCAA transamination in ccRCC cells was essential for the generation of glutamate-derived glutathione and cell viability when glutamine was limiting. Thus, BCAA transamination conferred resistance to states of low glutamine or treatment with the glutaminase inhibitor CB-839 by providing glutathione independent of glutamine breakdown. Targeting BCAA transamination in vitro and in vivo sensitized ccRCC to CB-839 mediated glutaminase inhibition by decreasing glutathione biosynthesis and redox homeostasis. These findings reveal that BCAA transamination maintains critical glutamate and glutathione levels in glutamine-deprived ccRCC, explaining why CB-839 treatment has been ineffective in ccRCC clinical trials and demonstrate an approach to treat ccRCC by targeting BCAA transamination to create a vulnerability to glutaminase inhibition.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-26-0860.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) driven by gain-of-function mutations in CTNNB1 (CTNNB1GOF) that stabilize β-catenin exhibits a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), rendering it resistant to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). Metabolic reprogramming is increasingly recognized as a crucial mediator of immune activity, highlighting the need to elucidate the specific metabolic mechanisms underlying immune exclusion in CTNNB1GOF HCC. Here, we identified a critical metabolic-immune network orchestrated by co-mutations of CTNNB1 and ARID2. Integrative analysis of HCC patient cohorts and a de novo MYC/CTNNB1GOF HCC mouse model revealed that tumors harboring concurrent CTNNB1 and ARID2 mutations exhibited a more immune-active TME and improved survival compared to tumors with CTNNB1 mutations alone. Mechanistically, β-catenin and ARID2 cooperatively enhanced the transcription of tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO2), leading to accelerated kynurenine production and activation of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) in myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). This metabolic axis established an immunosuppressive milieu characterized by MDSC accumulation and impaired T cell function. Genetic ablation of Arid2 in CTNNB1GOF HCC attenuated TDO2-dependent kynurenine synthesis, reduced MDSC infiltration, and enhanced CD8⁺ T cell cytotoxicity, thereby sensitizing tumors to anti-PD-1 therapy. Clinically, co-mutations of CTNNB1 and ARID2 correlated with elevated immune infiltration and favorable ICB responses across multiple human cancers, including HCC. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of AhR phenocopied the immunomodulatory effect of ARID2 loss and, when combined with anti-PD-1, robustly reversed the immune-cold phenotype of CTNNB1GOF HCC. These findings reveal TDO2-kynurenine-AhR signaling as a pivotal metabolic pathway enforcing immune evasion in CTNNB1-mutant HCC.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-26-1315.abstract: Abstract Activating mutations in KRAS drive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Although mutant-selective KRAS inhibitors and pan-RAS inhibitors provide clinical benefits, the development of resistance limits durable responses. In this study, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed that, despite effective suppression of mutant KRAS signaling, resistant cells sustain cell-cycle progression. Distinct orthogonal mitogenic pathways were engaged in a context-dependent manner to bypass KRAS inhibition. Although these pathways could be broadly inhibited using the pan–RAS-ON inhibitor RMC-6236, cells remained capable of developing acquired resistance, in which cell proliferation was uncoupled from RAS signaling. Combinatorial drug screens and genome-wide CRISPR–Cas9 screens showed that perturbing cell-cycle nodes via targeting cyclin-dependent kinases CDK4/6 and CDK2 restored sensitivity to KRAS/RAS inhibitors. Cotargeting CDK4/6 induced G1 arrest and suppressed E2F-regulated proteins across all resistant models. In contrast, cotargeting CDK2 exerted a broader effect by impairing DNA replication, inducing G2 arrest, preventing mitotic entry, and yielding a more durable cytostatic response that delayed cellular outgrowth after drug withdrawal. Finally, concurrent inhibition of KRAS with either CDK4/6 or CDK2 yielded durable tumor control in vivo in xenografts derived from models with acquired resistance. In conclusion, these findings identify sustained cell-cycle activity as a defining feature of resistance to KRAS-directed therapies and establish cell-cycle cotargeting as an effective strategy to overcome KRAS/RAS inhibitor resistance. Significance: Acquired resistance to KRAS/RAS inhibitors limits clinical benefit. We identify active cell cycle machinery as a defining feature of resistance and demonstrate distinct combinatorial strategies to target cell cycle progression.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-26-1323.abstract: Abstract Chemotherapy is a standard treatment for lung adenocarcinoma, yet the efficacy is often limited, highlighting the need to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of chemoresistance. Given the important role of the tumor microenvironment in lung adenocarcinoma progression, we established a biobank of patient-derived lung adenocarcinoma organoids (LCOs) paired with cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) from treatment-naïve tumors and found that coculture with CAFs reduced the drug sensitivity of LCOs. Plasminogen activator urokinase (PLAU) was identified as a specific marker of chemoresistance-associated CAFs linked with poor survival in patients with lung adenocarcinoma. Tumor cells induced polarization of fibroblasts toward a PLAU+ chemoresistant state that secreted C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 5 (CXCL5) to upregulate the endoplasmic reticulum chaperone calmegin (CLGN) in tumor cells. CLGN ablation restored drug sensitivity, whereas CLGN expression was elevated in chemotherapy-resistant lung adenocarcinoma and correlated with pathologic progression. Together, these findings identify the PLAU+ CAF–CXCL5–CLGN axis that drives lung adenocarcinoma chemoresistance and suggest that CLGN inhibition could be a promising therapeutic strategy to overcome chemoresistance in advanced lung adenocarcinoma. Significance: Development of a paired tumor organoid-stroma biobank enabled identification of a PLAU+ fibroblast-CXCL5-CLGN axis that mediates chemoresistance in lung adenocarcinoma, revealing a targetable stromal mechanism with promising therapeutic potential.
