doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-25-0942.abstract: Breast cancers with a stiff extracellular matrix (ECM) frequently evade immune surveillance through mechanisms that remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify a mechanosensitive immune-evasion pathway governed by the phosphorylation-dependent prolyl isomerase Pin1. We show that ECM rigidity stabilizes Pin1 and promotes its nuclear accumulation in cancer cells, where it preserves heterochromatin organization and nuclear envelope integrity by sustaining HP1α-Lamin interactions, thereby suppressing transposable element (TE) activity. Pin1 loss induces early heterochromatin relaxation and LINE1 reactivation, activating the cGAS/STING/type I interferon pathway. Pin1 depletion further promotes TE-derived neoantigen generation and broadly remodels the tumor immune microenvironment, eliciting innate and adaptive immune responses that enhance tumor clearance. Genetic Pin1 depletion, or pharmacological inhibition with clinically available drugs, sensitizes fibrotic, immune-cold tumors to immune checkpoint blockade. These findings uncover a mechano-genomic mechanism of immune evasion in breast cancer and establish Pin1 as a therapeutic target to restore tumor immunogenicity and improve immunotherapy efficacy.

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-25-2090.abstract: To evaluate the functional relevance of mutations newly detected in breast cancer metastases, we analyzed genomic data from 662 paired and ~6,000 unpaired primary and metastatic tumors. These analyses indicate that metastasis-specific mutations are frequently acquired post-dissemination, with a disproportionate contribution from APOBEC-mediated mutagenesis. Metastasis-specific mutations converged on a set of pathways that were highly recurrent, distinct from those altered in primary tumors, and dependent on metastatic site. 95% of patients harbored metastasis-specific mutations within a minimum set of 10 pathways. Remarkably, more than half the variation in metastatic latency across patients was explained by the relative timing of mutation acquisition within implicated pathways before versus after dissemination. These findings support a "mutability-dependent" model of metastasis in which functionally consequential mutations accumulate after primary tumor dissemination and contribute to metastatic outgrowth, with latency reflecting the time required for DTCs to acquire the remaining driver mutations needed to achieve metastatic competence.

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-25-2314.abstract: Abstract Small molecules that modulate protein complexes have transformed cell biology and oncology, yet few chemical starting points exist to probe protein–protein interactions. To expand this space, we developed molecular COvalent Protein Ligators (COUPLr), elaborated small molecules flanked by two cysteine-reactive warheads. Using COuplr NEtwork deteCTor (CONNECT), an integrated chemical proteomic platform that identifies proteins and complexes amenable to coupling, we revealed 171 targetable protein classes, including mutant-selective complexes and assemblies not traditionally addressed by small molecules. We then optimized a COUPLr against the oncogenic fusion EML4–ALK. This compound engages EML4–ALK by binding its EML4 domain, remodeling protein dynamics, disrupting downstream signaling, and inducing proteasome-mediated degradation of the fusion. Finally, we show that FDA-approved drugs can be converted into COUPLrs to degrade their targets, indicating that this modality can endow existing therapeutics with new functional properties. Overall, molecular COUPLrs offer an unbiased framework to discover, characterize, and pharmacologically exploit protein complexes. Significance: Developing drugs against multi-protein complexes is traditionally challenging. In this study, we develop molecular COUPLrs, dual cysteine-reactive small molecules, that can engage complexes across the proteome. As proof of concept, we designed COUPLrs targeting EML4–ALK and show that COUPLrs can reshape protein dynamics, drive degradation, and reprogram approved drugs.

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-26-0104.abstract: Mitigating on-target off-tumor toxicity remains a central challenge for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy for solid tumors. We developed a hypoxia-inducible CAR-T-cell product targeting carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) that restricts CAR activation to hypoxic tumor niches via oxygen-dependent expression control. In this first-in-human, phase I trial enrolling heavily pretreated patients with relapsed stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), a single infusion of the investigational product achieved an objective response rate of 47% and a disease control rate of 87%, with a manageable safety profile. Exploratory analyses showed that clinical outcomes were associated with baseline factors. Deep single-cell profiling indicated that the clinical response was associated with the expansion of hypoxia-adapted, tumor-reactive-like CD8+ T cells alongside coordinated functional maturation of natural killer (NK) cells. Collectively, these data provide clinical proof-of-concept for hypoxia-inducible CAR design and inform the rational development of strategies leveraging tumor microenvironmental features in solid tumor cellular immunotherapy.

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-26-0180.abstract: Non-genetic intratumor heterogeneity underlies therapeutic failure in cancer, yet how resistant tumor states are encoded in patients remains unclear. In this study, we show that chemoresistant evolution in high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) is prefigured by epigenetically primed tumor cell states present before therapy. Using multimodal single-nucleus approaches, we profile transcriptional programs and histone modifications from longitudinal frozen biopsies of 16 patients with HGSOC. Tumors comprise a limited set of functional states that evolve reproducibly under chemotherapy: proliferative and IFN-responsive states are depleted, whereas TNFα-associated and epithelial-mesenchymal transition-associated programs persist or expand. Chromatin profiling reveals that these resistant programs are broadly enriched for histone H3 lysine 4 monomethylation (H3K4me1) prior to treatment, indicating that features of resistance are epigenomically primed. Baseline tumor composition is associated with survival, and fibroblast remodeling accompanies malignant adaptation. Together, these findings identify epigenomic priming as a feature of chemoresistant tumor cell states and provide a scalable framework for anticipating resistance from biopsies. Using a clinically compatible multimodal single-nucleus approach, the authors show that chemoresistant evolution in HGSOC is prefigured by epigenetically primed tumor cell states present before therapy.

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-26-0187.abstract: Breast cancer that arises in the postpartum period often carries a poor prognosis and urgently requires chemoprevention strategies, particularly for women at elevated risk. Here, we report that a single post-lactation dose of cabergoline, a dopaminergic agonist that blocks prolactin secretion, delays the onset and reduces the incidence of postpartum mammary cancer in K14-Cre; Brca1F/F, Trp53F/F mice. In these mice, cabergoline treatment remodels the mammary gland by potentiating involution, reducing ductal area and proliferation, and reversing T cell exhaustion, potentially through modulation of ion channel expression. Notably, independent retrospective studies in two large cohorts of European women showed that cabergoline treatment was associated with a lower incidence of postpartum breast cancer, with a meta-analysis indicating an approximate 69% reduction in risk. Our work underscores the importance of targeting postlactational involution as a strategy for the prevention of postpartum breast cancer and positions cabergoline as a novel, low-risk chemoprevention strategy.

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-26-0255.abstract: T cell exhaustion within the tumor microenvironment poses a major barrier to effective cancer immunotherapy, yet the epigenetic mechanisms that preserve functional states of tumor-infiltrating T cells remain incompletely understood. Here, using an in vivo CRISPR screen, we identify heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein A2/B1 (hnRNPA2B1) as a regulator of CD8+ T cell fitness. Transcriptomic analyses of cancer patient cohorts reveal that hnRNPA2B1 is preferentially enriched in a proliferative, intermediate exhausted T cell subset associated with favorable clinical outcomes. Genetic ablation of hnRNPA2B1 in CD8+ T cells accelerates terminal exhaustion, impairs antitumor immunity, and diminishes responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade. Mechanistically, hnRNPA2B1 forms nuclear puncta and stabilizes RNAs involved in chromatin organization, thereby maintaining chromatin accessibility that restrains exhaustion-associated programs while preserving proliferative and cytotoxic potential. Together, these findings establish hnRNPA2B1 as an RNA-mediated epigenetic regulator sustaining functional exhausted T cell states in tumors.

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-26-1312.abstract: Neuroendocrine differentiation (NED) promotes lineage plasticity and therapy resistance in prostate and lung cancers. Here we identify NED as a route of treatment escape in breast cancer: neuroendocrine features emerged or increased in 22% of progressive cases, predominantly, but not exclusively, in HER2-positive subtype. Using patient-derived, epithelial/neuroendocrine organoid and xenograft models, we map the epigenetic and transcriptional divergence between epithelial and neuroendocrine states arising from a shared mutational background and define a breast cancer neuroendocrine signature. NED involves epigenetic silencing of EpCAM and amplified HER2, while NEUROD1 functions as a master transcriptional regulator of the neuroendocrine fate. NCAM-positive putative circulating tumor cells were detected in patients in whom EpCAM-based detection had failed. Neuroendocrine tumor cells exhibit an FGFR1 dependency associated with NCAM-FGFR1 interaction and mesenchymal FGFR1 splicing. Together, these findings establish NED as a mechanism of escape from HER2-targeted therapy in breast cancer, with implications for disease monitoring and intervention.

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-nw2026-0095.abstract: Both ARPA-H and the FDA recently launched programs to help accelerate clinical trials. ARPA-H announced the SURPASS program, which is intended to create faster clinical trials that are more cost-effective and have fewer participants than current studies. It is seeking ideas from cross-disciplinary teams in statistics, artificial intelligence, and clinical trial design, operations, and regulation. The FDA has created a pilot program for accelerating phase I clinical trials that pairs drug sponsors with research organizations.

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-nw2026-0096.abstract: BioNTech's HPV16 mRNA vaccine BNT113 failed to significantly delay progression of head and neck cancer in a phase II/III trial, the latest in a string of near-misses for off-the-shelf, shared-antigen cancer vaccines that reliably generate T cells but have struggled to improve patient outcomes. Researchers argue the vaccines themselves are working, and that success will depend on testing them in the right patients and settings and judging them by overall survival rather than tumor progression.

The data were presented at the ESMO Congress 2026, held October 23-27, in Madrid, Spain.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-14-0072.abstract: Abstract In the past few years, the field of cancer immunotherapy has made great progress and is finally starting to change the way cancer is treated. We are now learning that multiple negative checkpoint regulators (NCR) restrict the ability of T-cell responses to effectively attack tumors. Releasing these brakes through antibody blockade, first with anti-CTLA4 and now followed by anti-PD1 and anti-PDL1, has emerged as an exciting strategy for cancer treatment. More recently, a new NCR has surfaced called V-domain immunoglobulin (Ig)-containing suppressor of T-cell activation (VISTA). This NCR is predominantly expressed on hematopoietic cells, and in multiple murine cancer models is found at particularly high levels on myeloid cells that infiltrated the tumors. Preclinical studies with VISTA blockade have shown promising improvement in antitumor T-cell responses, leading to impeded tumor growth and improved survival. Clinical trials support combined anti-PD1 and anti-CTLA4 as safe and effective against late-stage melanoma. In the future, treatment may involve combination therapy to target the multiple cell types and stages at which NCRs, including VISTA, act during adaptive immune responses. Cancer Immunol Res; 2(6); 510–7. ©2014 AACR.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-18-0622.abstract: Abstract The remarkable clinical success of immune-checkpoint inhibitors for the treatment of a growing number of cancer types has sparked interest in the discovery of novel forms of immunotherapy, which may be used alone or in combination. In this context, cytokine-based therapeutics are well poised to play a role in modern cancer therapy. This article focuses on antibody–cytokine fusion proteins (also called “immunocytokines”) as one class of biopharmaceuticals that can substantially improve the therapeutic index and, thus, the applicability of cytokine products. In many preclinical settings, antibodies can be used to preferentially deliver many (but not all) types of cytokines to primary and metastatic tumor lesions. The antibody-based delivery of certain proinflammatory payloads (such as IL2, IL12, and TNF) to the tumor microenvironment can lead to a dramatic potentiation of their anticancer activity. However, although some fusion proteins have advanced to late-stage clinical trials, much work remains to be done in order to fully characterize the mechanism of action and the pharmaceutical potential of immunocytokines in the clinical setting. Various factors contribute to in vivo performance, including the target antigen, the antibody properties, the nature of the payload, the format of the fusion protein, the dose, and schedule, as well as their use in combination with other therapeutic modalities. Protein engineering opportunities and insights in cancer immunology are contributing to the development of next-generation immunocytokine products and of novel therapeutic concepts, with the goal to increase antitumor activity and reduce systemic toxicity (a common problem for cytokine-based biopharmaceuticals).

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-18-0658.abstract: Abstract T cells are central players in cancer immunotherapy. Despite much concentrated effort on the study of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL), such as T cells, a series of fundamental properties that include heterogeneity, clonal expansion, migration, and functional state transition remain elusive. Advances of single-cell sequencing have enabled the detailed characterization of immune cells in tumors and have vastly improved our understanding of less-defined cell subsets. Here, we discuss the current strategies for uncovering the heterogeneity of TILs, and how the deep transcriptome coupled with T-cell receptor analysis enhances the understanding of detailed properties of T-cell subsets. We further discuss the identification of novel T-cell markers with therapeutic or prognosis potentials, and highlight distinct T-cell properties among different cancer indications.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-24-0333.abstract: Abstract The optimal means to prime for effective antitumor immunity in a patient with cancer remain elusive in the current era of checkpoint blockade. Crafting a strategy to amplify the number and function of CD8+ T cells while blocking regulatory cells should increase immunotherapy efficacy. Biomaterial carriers have been demonstrated in preclinical studies to amplify the effects of immunomodulatory agents, synergistically integrate the effects of different agents, and concentrate and manipulate immune cells in vivo. Herein, we report data from a phase I trial in patients with metastatic melanoma who received the cytokine GM-CSF and the innate Toll-like receptor 9 agonist CpG oligonucleotide admixed with autologous tumor lysate onto a microporous poly-lactide-co-glycolide matrix polymer scaffold that achieves precise control over the spatial and temporal release of immunostimulatory agents in vivo. This materials system (WDVAX) served as a physical antigen-presenting structure to which dendritic cells and other immune-stimulating cells are recruited and activated. In this first clinical trial of a macroscale biomaterial–based vaccine, WDVAX treatment was found to be feasible and to induce immune activation in patients with melanoma.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-25-1399.abstract: Abstract To date, non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, underscoring the urgent need for new treatment options. The oncofetal carbohydrate CD176 is masked on healthy tissues but is present on a variety of cancer entities and is associated with cancer invasiveness and metastasis. In this study, we employed chimeric antigen receptor T cells (CAR-T) directed against CD176 for treatment of NSCLC. CD176-CAR-Ts were optimized with an additional inducible cassette encoding IL18 (CD176-iIL18-TRUCK) or IL12 (CD176-iIL12-TRUCK) to augment antitumor reactivity through autocrine and paracrine signaling. CD176-iIL18- and CD176-iIL12-TRUCKs eradicated NSCLC cells in a three-dimensional tumor spheroid model and tissue slices derived from patients with lung adenocarcinoma more potently than CD176-CAR-Ts. Administration of TRUCKs in a lung carcinoma xenograft mouse model resulted in partial or complete tumor eradication in all mice treated with CD176-iIL12-TRUCKs and in 50% of mice treated with CD176-iIL18-TRUCKs. This study highlights the potential of CD176 as a CAR T-cell target and suggests CD176-CAR-Ts armored with IL18 or IL12 as a promising new therapeutic approach for the treatment of NSCLC and several other CD176-positive cancer entities.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-25-1401.abstract: Abstract Histone lactylation is an epigenetic modification that connects lactate metabolism with protein function. Our study identified that lactate enhances the protein lactylation level not only in the myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC) of tumor-bearing mice but also in the tumor tissues of patients with lung cancer. This modification led to the upregulation of CD38 expression and enhanced the immunosuppressive function of MDSCs. Mechanistically, CD38 promoted immunosuppression by depleting NAD+, and treatment with a CD38 inhibitor or siRNA-mediated knockdown of CD38 in MDSCs delayed tumor progression. Histone H3 lysine 18 is enriched at the CD38 promoter region, with p300, histone deacetylases 1 to 3, and bromodomain-containing protein 4 identified as key epigenetic regulators in this process. Our findings reveal the critical role of the lactate–CD38–NAD+ axis in regulating MDSC immunosuppressive function and establish histone lactylation as an epigenetic mechanism controlling CD38 expression.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-25-1471.abstract: Abstract Despite the availability of various treatment modalities for liver cancer, its mortality rate remains high. Immunotherapy represents an emerging approach for liver cancer. However, the response rate to single-agent immune checkpoint blockade therapy is suboptimal. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) oxidoreductase 1-alpha (ERO1A), a potential therapeutic target associated with ER stress, is implicated in impeding protective antitumor immunity. In this study, we found that targeting ERO1A in liver cancer while activating the protein kinase R-like ER kinase/eukaryotic initiation factor 2 alpha subunit/activating transcription factor 4/C/EBP homologous protein–mediated apoptosis and autophagy signaling downregulated adenosine A1 receptor and inhibited the cyclic guanosine monophosphate–protein kinase G pathway, thereby promoting the expression and secretion of C-C chemokine ligand 4. This led to an increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells into the immune microenvironment, enhancing the antitumor immune response. Furthermore, targeting ERO1A in liver cancer also upregulated type I interferon synthesis, activated the Janus kinase–signal transducers and activators of transcription pathway, and promoted programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) and MHC-I expression. Using liver cancer animal models, we demonstrated that combination treatment with an ERO1A inhibitor and a PD-L1 inhibitor increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration and enhanced their function within the tumor microenvironment, resulting in synergistic antitumor effects. Therefore, ERO1A represents a promising therapeutic target in liver cancer, potentially suitable for combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors to improve patient outcomes.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-25-1508.abstract: Abstract Early-onset colorectal cancer (EOCRC), typically defined as colorectal cancer diagnosed before 50 years of age, is increasing in incidence worldwide and exhibits distinctive clinical, molecular, and environmental features compared with later-onset (LOCRC) disease. However, the tumor-immune microenvironment (TiME) of EOCRC and its implications for prevention and therapy remain poorly characterized. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on the TiME of EOCRC and contrast it with that of conventional LOCRC. We first discuss global features of the EOCRC immune landscape, including innate and adaptive immune composition, functional states, and spatial organization, highlighting areas where apparent age-related differences reflect true biology versus confounding by tumor site, stage, or mismatch repair (MMR) status. We then examine immunogenomic and epigenomic determinants—such as MMR deficiency distribution, microbial mutational signatures, chromosomal instability, and age-conditioned methylation programs—that shape neoantigen landscapes, antigen presentation, and immune evasion in younger patients. Next, we review microbiome-driven immunomodulation, focusing on dysbiosis, genotoxic bacteria, and early-life and young-adult exposures as joint modifiers of mucosal immunity and tumor development. Finally, we explore how these insights inform immune-based prevention (risk stratification, screening, diet and microbiome interventions, and chemoprevention) and immunotherapy strategies, including checkpoint blockade and rational combinations in the predominant microsatellite-stable EOCRC population.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0104.abstract: Abstract Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) have emerged as critical immune niches within the tumor microenvironment across various cancers. However, their structural organization and functional roles in non–muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) remain poorly characterized. In this study, we comprehensively characterized TLS in NMIBC using en bloc resected primary diagnostic specimens, which enabled high-resolution spatial mapping and quantitative histologic assessment across a large cohort of primary tumors (97 patients). Compared with TLS in inflammation-driven cystitis, tumor-associated TLS showed heterogeneous spatial organization, altered immune composition, and disrupted follicular dendritic cell (FDC) networks with reduced high endothelial venule density. TLS density increased with NMIBC grade and stage and correlated with higher recurrence risk and shorter progression-free survival in multivariable analysis. Paired analysis of primary and recurrent tumors showed a reduction in FDC density and a shift from M1 to M2 differentiation in tumor recurrences, suggesting the development of an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Single-nuclei RNA sequencing of TLS from NMIBC and cystitis samples revealed impaired germinal center activity in tumor-associated TLS, with asynchronous B-cell maturation and reduced B-cell interactions with both T follicular helper cells and FDC. Tumor-associated TLS also showed increased myeloid infiltration and altered dendritic cell function, including reduced MHC class II antigen presentation and downregulation of costimulatory (CD86–CD28) and migration-related (CD99) pathways compared with TLS from cystitis samples. Overall, we found that NMIBC-associated TLS are structurally and functionally impaired, which may limit effective local immune responses and suggests they may be relevant as biomarkers and targets for immunomodulatory therapy in bladder cancer.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0106.abstract: Abstract The spatial arrangement of immune cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME) varies widely, from dispersed to clustered and tumor-excluded to infiltrating. Multiplexed spatial profiling is an effective means of characterizing tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and immune complexes such as tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) in the TME. However, few approaches have been described for objectively parametrizing patterns of immune organization and assessing their association with biological or clinical variables. This makes it difficult to evaluate whether a set of tumors is relatively immunologically cold or hot. In this study, we describe an intuitive set of statistical tools (available in the R package, tlsR) for characterizing lymphocyte patterns in the TME of solid cancers. We applied tlsR to primary prostate cancer, which is often described as immunologically “cold.” Using a cohort of 29 radical prostatectomy specimens stratified into low Gleason grade (LGG; n = 15) and high Gleason grade (HGG; n = 14), we showed that HGG prostate cancer is significantly more infiltrated than LGG prostate cancer, with lymphocytes organized into B or T cell–enriched immune clusters (IC). A subset of these ICs had the B- and T-cell zonation and follicular dendritic cells characteristic of bona fide TLSs. HGGs were also enriched with ICs containing precursors of exhausted T cells and proliferating B cells, and their tumor compartments harbored granzyme B+ cytotoxic T cells in contact with cancer cells. Thus, far from being cold, a subset of HGG prostate cancer has features associated with active immune surveillance, a finding with implications for emerging prostate cancer immunotherapies.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0160.abstract: Abstract Occasional complete responses (CR) to immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy demonstrate that acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) can be immunosensitive when appropriately targeted. In this study, we analyzed patients with AML/MDS (n = 14) who were treated with the anti-TIM3 sabatolimab and the hypomethylating agent decitabine in a phase Ib clinical trial (NCT03066648) using single-cell RNA and T-cell receptor (TCR) sequencing (n = 6) and functional coculture assays. Unlike T cell–restricted CTLA4 and PD1, TIM3 was broadly expressed across natural killer (NK) cell, myeloid cell, and T-cell populations. Therapy induced the expansion of cytotoxic NK cell subsets and enhanced type I IFN signaling. Fewer than 1% of bone marrow CD8+ T cells displayed a canonical exhaustion phenotype, and treatment preferably expanded small CD8+ T-cell clones in responders. Responders exhibited greater expansion of cytotoxic CD4+ T cells and B cells, as exemplified by a patient with preexisting CD4+ T-cell large granular lymphocyte leukemia (T-LGLL) achieving an outstanding CR lasting 23 months. More than 20% of this patient’s lymphocytes were T-LGLL cells expressing a TCR capable of recognizing autologous blasts. Overall, our results suggest that anti-TIM3 combined with decitabine engages a distinct mechanism of immune activation compared with anti–PD-1 and anti-CTLA4, preferentially expanding NK cell and CD4+ T-cell populations.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0181.abstract: T-cell exhaustion limits durable antitumor responses and remains a barrier to adoptive cell therapies (ACT) in solid tumors. To identify regulators of T-cell persistence, we performed genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens in primary human CD8⁺ T cells expressing an NY-ESO-1-specific T-cell receptor and subjected them to repeated tumor cell rechallenge. These screens revealed enrichment of single-guide RNAs targeting components of Cullin-RING E3 ligases, particularly Cullin-5 (CRL5) assemblies comprising CUL5, RNF7, and ARIH2. Disruption of CRL5 genes in T cells preserved cytotoxic activity and enhanced cytokine production while sustaining effector-associated transcriptional programs and suppressing exhaustion-related signatures. Pharmacologic inhibition of cullin neddylation with the NEDD8-activating enzyme inhibitor MLN4924 recapitulated CRL5 loss and enhanced T-cell effector function in vitro. In a human melanoma xenograft model, ACT with CRL5-deficient T cells improved tumor control. Together, these findings identify CRL5 as a negative regulator of T-cell fitness and a potential therapeutic target to enhance ACT durability in solid tumors.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0236.abstract: Abstract Penile squamous cell carcinoma (PeSCC) is a rare malignancy with limited treatment options in advanced stages. The phase II PERICLES trial (NCT03686332) investigated atezolizumab with or without radiotherapy (RT) in advanced penile cancer. Here, we report mature overall survival (OS) and updated progression-free survival (PFS) outcomes and an in-depth biomarker analysis. Patients were treated with atezolizumab monotherapy (n = 12) or atezolizumab in combination with RT (n = 20, 33 fractions of 1.5–1.8 Gy) for locoregional disease control. Comprehensive analysis of baseline tumor tissue (n = 28/31) was performed using bulk RNA sequencing, immunohistochemistry, and multiplex immunofluorescence. Additionally, spatial transcriptomics (n = 9) was conducted to further explore functionality and (co-)localization of immune cell subsets. With extended follow-up (median: 38 months), landmark 2-year OS and PFS in the full study cohort was 18.8% [95% confidence interval (CI), 9.1–38.6] and 12.5% (95% CI, 5–31.3), respectively. High-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV)-positive tumors were enriched for IFNγ and IFNα signatures, potentially explaining the improved PFS and OS observed in this subgroup. Both stromal CD68+ myeloid cell density and intratumoral CD8+PD-1+ T-cell density were associated with nonprogression at 1 year. Increased intratumoral CD8+PD-1+ T-cell density was also associated with improved PFS and OS, with consistent findings in the hrHPV-positive subgroup. Spatial transcriptomics identified these CD8+ T cells as tissue-resident cytotoxic effector cells coexpressing checkpoint molecules (LAG3 and TIGIT), chemokines (CCL4 and CXCL13), and cytotoxic molecules (PRF1 and GZMB). Interrogation of the penile cancer immune microenvironment highlights CD8+PD-1+ T cells as candidate biomarkers in relation to clinical benefit from immune checkpoint blockade in advanced PeSCC.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0305.abstract: Malignant ascites provides a window into cancer-immune interactions in the peritoneal cavity. Using Cytometry by Time of Flight (CyTOF), we analyzed ascitic immune cells collected from patients with advanced gastrointestinal cancers, nonmalignant forms of hepatitis (NMH), and healthy control peripheral blood mononuclear cells (HC PBMCs). Compositionally, ascitic immune cells shared a myeloid-rich, B and naïve T cell-low signature relative to HC PBMCs. Underneath the shared ascitic compositional signature, three major functional immunophenotypes emerged in response to exogenous stimulation along a suppressive to cytotoxic axis, aligning with Luminex measurements of ascitic cytokine levels: IL-10 enriched, Nonpolarized, and Granzyme B (GZMB) enriched. In our cohort, the IL-10 enriched functional immunophenotype was exclusive to samples from patients with cancer while the GZMB enriched response was dominated by NMH samples. Ascites from patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) contained a persistent anti-cancer humoral response characterized by IgG that bound to autologous ascitic PDAC cells and multiple allogeneic PDAC cell lines.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0367.abstract: Despite advances in adoptive T cell therapy, therapeutic efficacy in solid tumors remains inconsistent, and the mechanistic determinants of treatment failure are incompletely understood. Increasing evidence suggests that effective antitumor responses depend not only on direct recognition of malignant cells but also on interactions with the tumor microenvironment, including non-malignant host cells that cross-present tumor antigens. Using an HLA-A2-transgenic syngeneic mouse cancer model that enables near-physiological presentation of human tumor antigens by both malignant and host cells, we investigated how TCR antigen sensitivity relates to therapeutic outcome. We compared T cell receptor-engineered (TCR-)T cells with different antigen sensitivities directed against the same HLA-A2-restricted melanoma antigen. Although high- and low-sensitivity TCR-T cells recognized tumor cells comparably in vitro, only high-sensitivity TCR-T cells mediated durable tumor regression in vivo. Improved tumor control correlated with enhanced recognition of cross-presented tumor antigen on tumor-associated CD11b+ myeloid cells and increased intratumoral effector activity. IFN-γ levels in tumor tissue and peripheral blood reflected intratumoral T cell activity and correlated with therapeutic response. Together, these findings identify host cell antigen recognition as a sensitivity-dependent functional correlate of TCR-T cell efficacy and provide a mechanistic explanation for the superior activity of higher-sensitivity TCRs in solid tumors.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0433.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the treatment of advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet a large proportion of patients do not respond. The lung microbiome is a key modulator of antitumor immunity, however, the functional contribution of active microbial communities and their interaction with host transcriptional programs in shaping ICI outcomes remain poorly defined. Here, we prospectively analyzed bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) samples from 71 NSCLC patients prior to ICI initiation. We profiled the microbiome and host transcriptome in the BAL to look for microbial and host signatures in the lower airways associated with treatment response. We found that enrichment of the lower airway microbiome with oral commensals was associated with disease progression and worse prognosis of patients treated with ICI. Metatranscriptomics-derived microbial clustering revealed distinct functional profiles. The microbial cluster enriched with oral commensals, which was only present among patients with poor response to ICI, had differential regulation of pathways involved in the metabolism of short-chain fatty acids, methane, and pyruvate. This cluster also correlated with host immune pathways including upregulation of interferon signaling, neutrophil degranulation, and mitophagy, all of which could contribute to the poor response to immunotherapy. In a preclinical murine model of lung cancer with dysbiosis, inoculating lung tumor-bearing mice with oral commensals increased intratumoral neutrophils and Th17 responses and impaired ICI efficacy. Our findings support the concept that microbial communities in the lower airways influence tumor-immune interactions via defined metabolic-immune axes.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0459.abstract: Abstract Cancer immunotherapies have achieved meaningful clinical benefits but remain limited by systemic toxicities that restrict the use of potent immune modulators. CD47-targeting antibodies promote tumor cell phagocytosis but are hindered by hematologic toxicity, whereas IL2 activates cytotoxic lymphocytes but induces broad, dose-limiting immune activation. In this study, we engineered a reciprocally masked antibody–cytokine fusion [CD47-specific antibody (aCD47)/IL2/IL2 receptor complex (IL2c)] designed for tumor-selective activation. In this construct, an aCD47 and an IL2c sterically and functionally suppress each other via protease-cleavable linkers, preventing CD47 blockade and IL2 receptor engagement in circulation while enabling protease-dependent unmasking within the tumor microenvironment. A human construct demonstrated masking and protease-dependent restoration of both CD47–signal regulatory protein alpha (SIRPα) blockade and IL2 signaling, with improved systemic tolerability in human CD47/SIRPα transgenic mice, supporting translational potential. A murine analog enabled mechanistic and efficacy studies in immunocompetent tumor models. The tolerability of mouse aCD47/IL2c was improved in comparison with individual components. Antitumor activity required both CD47 blockade and IL2 activity and resulted in robust antitumor efficacy, including in an immune checkpoint–resistant melanoma model. The robust antitumor efficacy was associated with inflammatory macrophage polarization and increased numbers of effector CD8+ T cells inside the tumor. Unlike conventional CD47 antibodies or IL2 therapies, this approach enabled coordinated, tumor-localized activation of innate and adaptive immunity while limiting systemic exposure. Together, these data highlight reciprocal masking as a clinically relevant strategy to expand the therapeutic index of immune modulators constrained by systemic toxicity.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0483.abstract: Adoptive T-cell therapies require T cells to sustain cytotoxic function for as long as tumor persists. In this issue, two independent studies converge on a ubiquitin-dependent pathway, centered on the cullin-5 (CUL5)-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase (CRL5) complex, as an intrinsic brake on T-cell function under repetitive antigen stimulation. Genetic disruption of individual CRL5 components preserves cytotoxicity during repeated tumor challenge. Saco and colleagues demonstrate similar benefits with pharmacologic inhibition of CRL5 and related ubiquitin ligase complexes, whereas Bachl and colleagues extend the genetic benefit across multiple antigens and receptor architectures. Targeting this pathway offers a strategy to improve T-cell functional persistence and therapeutic durability. See related article by Bachl et al., p. XXX . See related article by Saco et al., p. XXX .

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0497.abstract: Metabolic dysregulation in obesity reshapes immune function, but how lipid signals drive immune suppression remains unclear. Herein, we identify a FABP4-PD-L1 axis that links lipid metabolism to immune checkpoint regulation in myeloid cells. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed a distinct FABP4high immunosuppressive splenic macrophage subset enriched under high-fat diet (HFD) conditions, characterized by impaired antigen presentation and elevated PD-L1 expression. Mechanistically, palmitic acid (PA) was shown to induce FABP4 and promote PD-L1 palmitoylation, leading to its stabilization on the cell surface independent of transcriptional regulation. FABP4 was essential for this process, which enabled PD-L1 surface stabilization, immunosuppression and mammary tumor progression. In humans, a conserved CD14intCD16⁺ monocyte population exhibited elevated FABP4-PD-L1 signaling and correlated with obesity and invasive breast cancer. These findings establish PD-L1 as a metabolically regulated protein and reveal a mechanism by which lipid excess drives immune evasion, suggesting FABP4 as a potential therapeutic target in cancer immunotherapy.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0591.abstract: We conducted a phase I study to evaluate the safety, clinical activity, and immune correlates of autologous tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL) therapy LM103 in Chinese patients with refractory metastatic melanoma. Fourteen patients with refractory metastatic melanoma received lymphodepleting chemotherapy followed by LM103 infusion (3.58-19.47×10¹⁰ cells) and high-dose interleukin-2. Characteristics of baseline tumor, TIL products and pre-/post-infusion peripheral blood were analyzed. LM103 therapy demonstrated manageable safety and promising efficacy. TEAEs included myelosuppression (100%), capillary leak syndrome (100%), fever (85.7%), and rash (71.4%). Grade 3-4 TEAEs included leukopenia (85.7%), neutropenia (78.6%), lymphopenia (78.6%), fever (71.4%), and thrombocytopenia (57.1%). The objective response rate was 35.7% (95% confidence interval [CI], 12.76 to 64.86), and the disease control rate was 85.7% (95% CI, 57.19 to 98.22). Median progression-free survival was 4.52 months (95% CI, 2.07 to 14.31), and median overall survival was 16.58 months (95% CI, 5.16 to not estimable). Baseline tumor immune infiltration and mutational burden were not associated with clinical outcome. LM103 infusion induced marked peripheral T cell receptor repertoire remodeling, with more than 60% of infused TIL clones detectable in peripheral blood at 6 months. Patients with superior clinical outcomes demonstrated greater expansion and persistence of dominant TIL clones. In addition, genes favoring T cells tumor infiltration were upregulated in TILs of patients with longer PFS. LM103 showed manageable safety and encouraging antitumor activity. Clinical benefit was associated with sustained in vivo clonal persistence and upregulated genes favoring tumor re-infiltration of infused TILs. Trial registration number CTR20233999.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0608.abstract: Engineered T-cell therapies are limited by progressive dysfunction under chronic tumor antigen exposure, and genetic perturbation of negative regulators has emerged as a promising strategy to sustain effector activity. We reanalyzed a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen in primary human T cells under repetitive tumor stimulation; protein-protein interaction mapping revealed seven members of the Cullin-RING Ligase 5 (CRL5) complex as an enriched hit cluster. Knockout of any of these members (CUL5, ARIH2, RNF7, UBE2F, UBE2L3, CISH, DCUN1D3) enhanced tumor serial killing, and CUL5, the complex scaffold, emerged as the strongest target. CUL5 knockout T cells exhibited sustained cytotoxicity, elevated effector cytokine production, and fewer exhaustion marker-positive cells while retaining antigen specificity and cytokine dependence. Quantitative ubiquitylation proteomics in resting, and acutely and chronically stimulated T cells mapped CRL5-dependent candidate substrates beyond the canonical JAK/STAT axis, including nutrient transporters, receptor trafficking proteins, and TCR signaling components. The benefit of CUL5 knockout extended across CARs targeting CD19, BCMA, and HER2 with different costimulatory domains, and to 1XX-modified CAR and HLA-independent TCR architectures. Combining CUL5 ablation with a tumor-induced IL-2 circuit produced tumor control across nine rounds of repetitive stimulation, whereas either modification alone eventually failed. In vivo, CUL5 knockout BCMA CAR T cells were enriched in the bone marrow following repeated tumor rechallenge and exhibited enhanced ex vivo cytotoxicity after nearly 90 days in tumor-bearing mice. These findings position CUL5 perturbation as a strategy to improve T-cell persistence and the efficacy of adoptive cell therapies, potentially with engineered cytokine support.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0706.abstract: Concomitant chemoradiotherapy (CRT) is a standard-of-care treatment for unresectable locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA-SCCHN), but its immune effects, particularly relative to radiotherapy (RT) alone, remain incompletely understood. Using syngeneic murine models, we integrated Nr4a3-Tocky reporter analysis with single-cell transcriptomics and T cell receptor clonotyping to comprehensively profile intratumoural CD8⁺ T-cell responses following RT and CRT. We show that CRT uniquely drives robust clonal expansion of antigen-engaged CD8⁺ T-cells and biases differentiation toward progenitor-exhausted (TPEX) states, whereas RT favours terminal exhaustion (TEX). Single-cell analyses further reveal preferential clonal dominance within TPEX populations following CRT. In peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients treated with CRT, TEX populations predominated early after treatment, followed by delayed expansion of circulating TPEX-like populations at 3 months, suggesting phased recovery of progenitor-like T-cell states. Together, these findings demonstrate that CRT and RT induce distinct CD8⁺ T-cell differentiation trajectories and clonal architectures, providing insight into treatment-induced immune remodelling in LA-SCCHN.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0730.abstract: Abstract Neoadjuvant PD-1 blockade produces substantial tumor regression in mismatch repair-deficient or microsatellite instability-high (dMMR/MSI-H) locally advanced lower rectal cancer (LRC), but response assessment and the safety of watch-and-wait (W&W) remain uncertain. BASKET was an open-label, multicenter, single-arm, phase 2 study conducted at two Chinese centers (ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04643041). Patients with non-metastatic dMMR/MSI-H LRC received six cycles of neoadjuvant sintilimab (200 mg every 3 weeks), followed by multimodal assessment including endoscopy, digital rectal examination, CEA, MRI, CT, and transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy. Patients meeting protocol-defined clinical complete response (cCR) criteria entered W&W surveillance. Of 15 treated patients, 13 completed treatment and response assessment. All 13 per-protocol patients achieved cCR and entered W&W (13/13, 100%), corresponding to 13/15 (86.7%) in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population. Only 1 of 13 per-protocol patients (7.7%) achieved radiologic complete response on MRI; persistent radiographic abnormalities were adjudicated using the other response modalities. At a median follow-up of 37.7 months (range, 0.7–56.2) in the ITT population, one death occurred 0.7 months after treatment initiation, and no local recurrence or distant metastasis. The estimated 1-year disease-free and overall survival rates were both 93.3% (95% CI, 68.1%–99.8%). Among the 13 per-protocol patients no local recurrence, distant metastasis, or death was observed. No grade 3 or higher immune-related adverse events or biopsy-related complications occurred. These findings suggest that W&W may be feasible in carefully selected patients following rigorous multimodal response assessment and with close surveillance; however, the incremental value of biopsy and the oncologic equivalence of W&W to surgery remain unproven.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0770.abstract: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is a major dose-limiting toxicity of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, yet the upstream mechanisms driving macrophage activation remain incompletely understood. Here, we established a xenograft model of human CAR T-cell therapy that recapitulates key features of CRS and combined single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with pharmacological intervention to define the inflammatory programs underlying CRS. CAR T-cell treatment induced dose-dependent systemic inflammation and remodeled the host myeloid compartment, leading to the accumulation of a distinct population of CRS-associated macrophages. Analysis of clinical scRNA-seq datasets from CAR T cell-treated glioblastoma patients confirmed enrichment of the CRS-associated macrophage gene signature following therapy in patients, supporting the clinical relevance of our findings. Transcriptomic analyses identified marked upregulation of the chemokine receptors CCR1 and CCR2 together with activation of CCL3- and CCL2-associated signaling pathways. Pharmacological inhibition of CCR1 and CCR2 significantly reduced clinical CRS, inflammatory cytokine production, and macrophage activation while preserving CAR T-cell expansion, effector cytokine production, and in vivo antitumor efficacy. These findings identify CCR1/CCR2-dependent chemokine signaling as a critical regulator of macrophage-driven CRS and support chemokine receptor blockade as a promising strategy to improve the safety of CAR T-cell therapy without compromising therapeutic efficacy.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-1102.abstract: Abstract Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells can provide cures to patients affected by certain hematologic malignancies. Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is a major side effect of this treatment, yet its pathophysiology remains incompletely understood and selective therapeutic options are limited. In this issue, Li and colleagues identify the CCR1–CCR2 axis as a key mediator of inflammatory macrophage recruitment to sites of CAR T-cell activation, thereby contributing to CRS. In preclinical models, blockade of this axis prevented macrophage recruitment and substantially diminished CRS severity. This discovery could open a new avenue for targeted intervention against CRS, although further validation of the role of the CCR1/CCR2 axis, particularly in clinically relevant settings, is required. See related article by Li and colleagues et al., p. XX

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-1107.abstract: Abstract In this issue, Chen and colleagues show that MHC class II expression by pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) malignant cells is a robust biomarker of both local production of IFNγ from lymphocytes and intact IFNγ signaling. RAS pathway inhibition can restore malignant cell IFNγ responsiveness in some patients, and malignant cell MHC class II expression may indicate which patients could further benefit from immunotherapy. See related article by Chen et al., p. XX .

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-1127.abstract: High tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS) density predicts favorable outcomes in several solid tumors but worse outcomes in bladder cancer, and the basis for this discrepancy is unclear. In this issue, Péricart and colleagues leverage en bloc resection of non-muscle-invasive bladder tumors to show that TLS accumulate without acquiring the features of productive antitumor immunity. The work reframes TLS in this setting as structures for which functional state, not abundance, dictates their contribution to tumor control. See related article by Péricart et al., p. XX.

doi:10.1159/000546697.abstract: Background and Aims: We conducted an updated network meta-analysis to evaluate and identify the optimal first-line treatment for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) among all relevant interventional and targeted therapies. Methods: We analyzed 16 phase 2 or 3 randomized controlled trials involving 9,482 patients with metastatic or unresectable HCC published between 2018 and 2024. The trials evaluated 11 systemic agents and 5 interventional treatments in combination with systemic therapy, using either sorafenib or lenvatinib as the control. The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), and secondary outcomes included progression-free survival (PFS) and grade 3–4 adverse events. Subgroup analyses were conducted to assess individual treatment efficacies in specific clinical settings. Results: Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) combined with lenvatinib provided the greatest improvement in OS over sorafenib, with a hazard ratio of 0.41 (95% confidence interval, 0.30–0.58), followed by sintilimab + IBI305 (0.57; 0.43–0.75), camrelizumab + rivoceranib (0.62; 0.48–0.80), atezolizumab + bevacizumab (0.66; 0.51–0.85), lenvatinib + pembrolizumab (0.77; 0.62–0.97), and tremelimumab + durvalumab (0.78; 0.64–0.95). These combinations, except for tremelimumab + durvalumab, also showed significantly superior PFS to sorafenib. TACE + lenvatinib was ranked first in OS analyses with the other current standard-of-care regimens (lenvatinib, atezolizumab + bevacizumab, and tremelimumab + durvalumab) as controls. TACE + lenvatinib, sintilimab + IBI305, and atezolizumab + bevacizumab demonstrated consistently significant extension of OS over sorafenib in subsets with portal invasion, extrahepatic metastasis, and hepatitis B. All immunotherapy-based combinations were significantly associated with a higher risk of adverse events than sorafenib. Conclusions: For advanced HCC, our first-line analysis consistently scored TACE + lenvatinib the best for survival outcomes, followed by various immunotherapy-based combinations. However, the superior efficacy of TACE + lenvatinib should be interpreted with consideration of its derivation from a region with high hepatitis B virus prevalence.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag001.abstract: People with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) often have underlying comorbidities, which may impact prognosis and lead to safety challenges following treatment. This exploratory, post hoc analysis of the phase 3 HIMALAYA study (NCT03298451) assessed outcomes in participants with unresectable HCC and cardiovascular or metabolic comorbidities at baseline. Participants with unresectable HCC were randomized to STRIDE (Single Tremelimumab Regular Interval Durvalumab), durvalumab monotherapy, or sorafenib. Comorbidities were based on medical history assessed at baseline and qualified using preferred terms from cardiovascular or metabolic Standardised Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities Queries. Overall survival (OS) rates were evaluated in participants with or without cardiovascular or metabolic comorbidities within and by treatment group. The proportion of long-term survivors (alive ≥36 months post-randomization) and safety were assessed in participants with cardiovascular or metabolic comorbidities. Data cutoffs: August 27, 2021 (primary analysis); January 23, 2023 (4-year updated analysis, OS, and serious treatment-related adverse events). Hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus were the most common cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidities, respectively. The 48-month OS rates with STRIDE were 28.0% and 21.7% in participants with and without cardiovascular comorbidities and 20.4% and 28.5% in those with and without metabolic comorbidities, respectively. In total, 28.2% of participants with cardiovascular comorbidities and 22.6% of participants with metabolic comorbidities experienced long-term survival with STRIDE. Safety in participants with cardiovascular or metabolic comorbidities was generally consistent with all participants in the safety analysis set; no new safety signals were observed. OS benefits with STRIDE were similar in participants with vs. without cardiovascular or metabolic comorbidities, with manageable safety in participants with comorbidities. These results support the durable benefits of STRIDE in a broad population reflective of unresectable HCC globally.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag002.abstract: Radiological response dynamics may provide prognostic information beyond conventional response categories in patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) receiving atezolizumab plus bevacizumab. Building upon findings from the IMbrave150 trial, we evaluated the prognostic significance of depth of response (DpR), duration of response (DoR), and time to response (TTR) in a real-world cohort. This retrospective multicenter study included 183 treatment-naïve patients with unresectable HCC treated with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab between November 2020 and September 2024. Tumor response was assessed according to mRECIST. Associations of DpR, DoR, and TTR with overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were evaluated using landmark analyses and time-dependent Cox analyses. Deeper tumor response, longer DoR, and ≥50% reductions in serologic biomarker correlated with improved survival. Patients who achieved an early response (≤2 months) tended to have less favorable survival outcomes than those with a later response. Multivariate analysis confirmed DoR (HR = 0.40; 95% CI: 0.30-0.55; p < 0.001) and DpR (HR = 0.45; 95% CI: 0.38-0.55; p < 0.001) as independent predictors for improved OS, while early response independently predicted worse OS (HR = 1.64; 95% CI: 1.26-2.15; p < 0.001). Similar trends were observed for PFS. Exploratory analyses suggested a potential association between conversion surgery and prolonged OS. DpR and DoR were independently associated with survival outcomes in patients with unresectable HCC receiving atezolizumab plus bevacizumab, extending and validating previous findings from IMbrave150 in a real-world setting. The prognostic significance of TTR and conversion surgery warrants further prospective investigation.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag004.abstract: Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (Atezo-Bev) is a standard first-line systemic therapy for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). We aimed to explore the benefits of adding curative locoregional therapy (LRT) to patients who achieve a partial response (PR) to Atezo-Bev treatment. This multinational retrospective study enrolled patients who received Atezo-Bev as first-line systemic therapy for unresectable HCC and reached complete response (CR) or PR. Patients were categorized into three cohorts: patients who underwent curative LRT after PR, patients with PR but did not receive curative LRT, and patients achieving CR without LRT. Curative LRT included surgery, ablation, and definitive radiotherapy with imaging evidence showing disease-free status afterward. A total of 243 patients were enrolled from 8 countries or regions; 31 patients received curative LRT after PR, 180 patients obtained PR but did not receive curative LRT, and 32 patients achieved CR without LRT. The curative-LRT group, compared with patients who did not receive curative LRT after PR, exhibited significantly longer PFS (median, 44.4 months vs. 18.2 months, p = 0.004) and overall survival (OS) (median, not reached vs. 34.3 months, p < 0.001). The differences remained significant after inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) adjustment. By contrast, whether before or after IPTW adjustment, the curative-LRT group did not exhibit statistically significant difference in PFS, OS, and recurrence-free survival from patients who obtained CR without curative LRT. Curative LRT may consolidate the efficacy of Atezo-Bev in patients achieving a PR, potentially prolonging survival compared to systemic therapy alone.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag005.abstract: Early progressive disease (early PD) at the first imaging assessment during atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (Atezo/Bev) therapy may represent primary resistance and is associated with poor outcomes in unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (uHCC). This study aimed to quantify the frequency, prognostic impact, and baseline predictors of early PD in a large real-world cohort. Consecutive patients with uHCC who initiated Atezo/Bev therapy at 28 institutions in Japan (September 2020-August 2025) were retrospectively analyzed. Early PD was defined as PD at the first on-treatment imaging assessment, according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1. Overall survival (OS) was compared using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Baseline predictors were examined using prespecified multivariable logistic regression with multiple imputation: the primary multivariable model included Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) stage C and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) ≥400 ng/mL, while an alternative tumor-feature model including extrahepatic spread (EHS) and macrovascular invasion (MVI) was evaluated as a sensitivity analysis. Among 685 treated patients, 666 were evaluable at the first imaging assessment, of whom 148 (22.2%) had early PD. The median OS was 333 days in the early-PD group versus 768 days in the non-early-PD group (log-rank p < 0.001). In the primary multivariable model, AFP ≥ 400 ng/mL (OR 2.33, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.58-3.43) and BCLC-C (OR 1.76, 95% CI: 1.15-2.68) independently predicted early PD. In the alternative tumor-feature model, AFP ≥ 400 ng/mL (OR 2.50, 95% CI: 1.69-3.69) and EHS (OR 1.52, 95% CI: 1.03-2.23) remained significant predictors, whereas MVI did not. Two-point baseline scores (AFP ≥ 400 plus BCLC-C or EHS) stratified the risk of early PD in a stepwise manner, reaching approximately 40% in the highest-risk group (p for trend < 0.001). Early PD occurs in approximately one-fifth of patients with uHCC treated with Atezo/Bev and is associated with markedly poorer OS. AFP ≥ 400 ng/mL and BCLC-C provide a pragmatic baseline risk stratification approach that may help guide early monitoring and treatment sequencing.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag005.title: Baseline Predictors, Prognostic Impact, and Risk Stratification of Early Progressive Disease on Atezolizumab-Bevacizumab in Unresectable Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Multicenter Real-World Study.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag006.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) represents an increasing global health challenge, associated with poor prognosis and an epidemiological shift towards an aging and comorbid population. Frailty is a multidimensional syndrome of reduced physiological reserve. It is recognized as a robust predictor of clinical outcomes in chronic liver disease and some cancers but remains underexplored in HCC. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the clinical significance of frailty in HCC, focusing on its impact on outcomes, evidence for targeted interventions, and potential role in clinical decision-making. Frailty is associated with adverse outcomes in HCC, including increased healthcare utilization, reduced treatment tolerance, and decreased survival. However, heterogeneity in frailty assessment methods and limited prospective data preclude its clinical application. Early evidence suggests that structured exercise programs are safe, feasible, and may improve frailty measures, although larger prospective studies are required to determine whether these translate into meaningful clinical benefits. Frailty is an emerging prognostic marker and may inform supportive care in HCC. Standardized assessment and interventional trials are needed to support routine integration of frailty for more personalized HCC management.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag009.abstract: Although combining systemic and locoregional therapies has improved outcomes for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), identifying appropriate candidates remains challenging because no reliable tool predicts response. This retrospective multicenter study enrolled 334 HCC patients who received first-line locoregional-systemic therapy from nine centers in China. Following automated tumor segmentation using nnU-Net on pretreatment contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging, predefined radiomics features were computationally extracted, and deep learning features were obtained via a ResNet convolutional neural network. Three types of predictive models for tumor response (radiomics, deep learning, and combined) were developed and validated on the training cohort (n = 213), internal validation cohort (IVC, n = 53), and external validation cohort (EVC, n = 68). Performance was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and net reclassification improvement (NRI). Associations of model with progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were evaluated. Among the three models (multi-sequence radiomics, multi-sequence deep learning, and combined), the combined model showed the best predictive performance in both the training (AUC: 0.997, 95% CI: 0.994-1.000) and validation cohorts (AUC of IVC 0.900, 95% CI: 0.806-0.994; AUC of EVC: 0.871, 95% CI: 0.790-0.951). The combined model demonstrated significantly improved predictive performance compared with the multi-sequence radiomic model (training NRI = 43.9%, p < 0.001; IVC NRI = 38.7%, p = 0.038; EVC NRI = 3.2%, p = 0.806) and multi-sequence deep learning model (training NRI = 80.8%, IVC NRI = 72.7%, EVC NRI = 50.4%; all p < 0.05). Specifically, the combined model was significantly associated with both PFS and OS. The combined radiomics-deep learning model outperformed both single-modality models in predicting objective response and stratifying survival outcomes in unresectable HCC patients receiving combined systemic and locoregional therapy.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag010.abstract: Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (Atezo/Bev) has been recommended globally for patients with Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) stage C hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); however, this regimen has shown modest survival benefits. Therefore, this study aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of Atezo/Bev with or without transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) as first-line treatment for BCLC C HCC. This nationwide multicenter retrospective cohort study recruited patients with BCLC stage C HCC from 14 medical centres who received TACE combined with Atezo/Bev (TACE+Atezo/Bev) or Atezo/Bev alone as first-line treatment between October 2020 and January 2025. To mitigate potential confounding imbalances between groups, propensity score matching (PSM) and stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting (sIPTW) were applied. Overall survival (OS) was set as the primary endpoint, with progression-free survival (PFS), objective response rate (ORR), and safety assessed as the secondary endpoints. Of the 256 patients included in the analysis, 154 received TACE+Atezo/Bev and 102 received Atezo/Bev. After PSM, analysis of 96 patients per group showed that the TACE+Atezo/Bev group significantly extended the median OS (25.9 months vs. 15.2 months, p < 0.001) and PFS (15.8 months vs. 7.4 months, p < 0.001), compared with the Atezo/Bev group. Post-application of sIPTW, 154 patients were assigned to the TACE+Atezo/Bev group and 102 to the Atezo/Bev group, and the median OS (25.3 vs. 15.4 months, p < 0.001) and PFS (15.5 vs. 7.5 months, p < 0.001) were significantly longer in the TACE+Atezo/Bev group than in the Atezo/Bev group. A higher ORR was observed in the TACE+Atezo/Bev group compared with the Atezo/Bev group (primary cohort: 48.7% vs. 31.4%, p = 0.009; PSM cohort: 51.0% vs. 31.2%, p = 0.008; sIPTW cohort: 50.6% vs. 32.0%, p = 0.005). Moreover, Grade 3/4 adverse events (AEs) occurred in 60 patients (39.0%) in the TACE+Atezo/Bev group and 34 patients (33.3%) in the Atezo/Bev group. Compared with Atezo/Bev alone, TACE+Atezo/Bev may significantly improve ORR, PFS, and OS as first-line treatment for BCLC stage C HCC, while maintaining an acceptable safety profile.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag011.abstract: Portal vein tumor thrombus (PVTT) is the most common form of macrovascular invasion in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and is associated with poor prognosis, rapid intrahepatic dissemination, and limited responsiveness to systemic therapy. Increasing evidence indicates that PVTT is not merely an intravascular extension of the primary tumor, but rather a biologically distinct and highly adaptive immunosuppressive niche that contributes to immune escape and therapeutic resistance. This review summarizes current genomic, transcriptomic, single-cell, and spatially resolved evidence regarding the immune landscape of PVTT in HCC. We discuss how early clonal divergence, hypoxia-associated metabolic rewiring, and stromal-vascular remodeling cooperatively shape the PVTT microenvironment. PVTT is characterized by enrichment of suppressive myeloid populations, activation of cancer-associated fibroblast programs, extracellular matrix accumulation, endothelial barriers to immune-cell trafficking, and progressive dysfunction or exclusion of effector lymphocytes. Together, these features establish a strongly immune-excluded and immunosuppressive ecosystem, providing a mechanistic basis for the limited efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade in patients with HCC-PVTT. We further highlight the translational implications of this framework for biomarker development, patient stratification, and rational combination strategies targeting suppressive myeloid and stromal programs, vascular barriers, and metabolic-immune crosstalk. PVTT should be regarded as a distinct immunosuppressive niche rather than a passive vascular extension of the primary tumor. Its immune landscape is shaped by coordinated interactions among tumor evolution, metabolic adaptation, stromal remodeling, and immune dysfunction. A better mechanistic understanding of PVTT may support biomarker-guided stratification and the development of more effective precision therapies for HCC with macrovascular invasion.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag012.abstract: Hepatobiliary oncology is at an inflection point. Parallel advances in surgical technique, locoregional therapy, systemic treatment, and understanding of tumour biology have expanded the boundaries of curative-intent care yet have also exposed a critical reality that technical resectability is not synonymous with oncologic resectability. Technically successful resection or liver transplantation may be futile when tumour biology is aggressive, leading to early recurrence and limited survival benefit. Modern hepatobiliary surgical and transplant oncology must therefore move beyond anatomy-driven decision-making towards biologically informed strategies that incorporate tumour behaviour, treatment response, and temporal disease stability. The Asia-Pacific Transplant Oncology Symposium (APTOS) 2024 examined how Eastern and Western paradigms intersect across hepatocellular carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, and colorectal liver metastases, identifying pathways towards integration. Eastern and Western programmes have historically approached hepatobiliary oncology through distinct and longstanding philosophies. Eastern centres, frequently operating within living donor liver transplantation-dominant systems characterized by organ scarcity and the ethical principle of double equipoise, have traditionally leveraged high operative volume and technical expertise in complex resections. These environments have favoured surgery-first approaches when resection appears technically feasible, alongside response-driven conversion strategies aimed at expanding operability. Western centres, shaped by deceased-donor allocation frameworks and trial-oriented oncology models, have more consistently prioritized biological selection and longitudinal validation of disease control before proceeding to curative-intent intervention, particularly in borderline-resectable disease. These differences are driven by infrastructural and ethical factors, including donor availability, transplant systems, and biomarker integration, rather than surgical capability. This article is an expert statement reflecting the opinion of an international multidisciplinary faculty of hepatobiliary surgeons, transplant surgeons, hepatologists, and medical and clinical oncologists from Eastern and Western centres. It is a narrative expert perspective and not a formal consensus or guideline. This expert statement proposes that the next phase of hepatobiliary oncology requires harmonized, biology-driven definitions of resectability, transplantability, and futility. Comparative evaluation of regional strategies is essential to clarify how treatment sequencing affects recurrence and survival, an effort that is time-sensitive as advances in systemic therapy may soon obscure strategy-specific effects. Rather than competing models, Eastern procedural expertise and Western biology-centred frameworks should be viewed as complementary, supporting context-dependent or sequential approaches that integrate surgery with biology-guided systemic or locoregional therapy. Aligning these paradigms within ethical stewardship of donor organs can establish globally coherent, biology-driven standards that maximize durable survival while minimizing futile surgery and transplantation.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag013.abstract: Abstract Introduction Despite the availability of several approved therapies, continued investigation of novel treatment options is needed to further improve outcomes in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The phase 2 KEYSTEP-004 study evaluated the safety and efficacy of quavonlimab coformulated with pembrolizumab (quavonlimab/pembrolizumab) plus lenvatinib as first-line therapy for advanced HCC. Methods Adults with confirmed advanced HCC and no prior systemic therapy were enrolled. In the safety lead-in phase, participants received intravenous quavonlimab 25 mg coformulated with pembrolizumab 400 mg every 6 weeks plus oral lenvatinib 12 mg (body weight ≥60 kg) or 8 mg (body weight <60 kg) once daily (dose level 0 [DL0]). Allocation to the efficacy expansion phase was permitted if lenvatinib DL0 plus quavonlimab 25 mg coformulated with pembrolizumab 400 mg every 6 weeks was determined to be tolerable. Primary endpoints were objective response rate (ORR) per RECIST v1.1 by blinded independent central review (BICR) and safety. Secondary endpoints included duration of response (DOR) and progression-free survival (PFS) per RECIST v1.1 by BICR, and overall survival (OS). Results As of June 22, 2023, 116 participants were enrolled, and 115 were treated. No dose-limiting toxicities were observed in the safety lead-in phase. Lenvatinib DL0 in combination with quavonlimab 25 mg coformulated with pembrolizumab 400 mg every 6 weeks was determined to be tolerable. Median study follow-up was 18.0 months (range, 12.0–26.6). Confirmed ORR was 37.4% (95% CI: 28.5–46.9). Median DOR was 10.6 months (range, 1.2+ to 23.1+), median PFS was 8.2 months (95% CI: 6.2–10.2), and median OS was 22.1 months (95% CI: 15.5-not reached). Grade 3–5 treatment-related adverse events (AEs) occurred in 66 participants (57.4%); 14 (12.8%) required high-dose steroids for management of a treatment-related AE. Conclusion Quavonlimab coformulated with pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib is an active combination and has a manageable safety profile in advanced HCC.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag014.abstract: Vessel encapsulating tumor cluster (VETC) defines a distinct vascular phenotype of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), characterized by tumor nests fully encased within a continuous endothelial lining. This architecture correlates with poor prognosis and enhanced sensitivity to anti-angiogenic therapies. To dissect the morphological, phenotypical, molecular, and functional programs that define VETC-associated ECs in HCC and to identify endothelial pathways potentially driving VETC vascular organization and tumor progression. Biological samples (blood, plasma, Peripheral blood mononuclear cells, and tissue) were collected from VETC+ and VETC- HCCs. Quantitative tissue imaging was integrated with EC-specific molecular profiling. Vascular architecture was assessed on whole-slide images, and purified tumor ECs underwent targeted and transcriptome-wide gene expression analyses. ECs from both VETC+ and VETC- HCCs lacked pro-growth and anti-apoptotic features. VETC+ ECs show overexpression of pro-angiogenic and immune-modulatory factors, in particular vascular endothelial growth factor alpha, FGF and IL10, and a specific gene signature involved in metabolic reprogramming, increased trafficking and migratory capacity. VETC+ transcriptional phenotype is driven by a coordinated hepatic xenobiotic-sensing network in which HNF4A and HNF1A provide the dominant regulatory architecture, while NFE2L2 contributes a distinct regulatory layer governing the antioxidant response elements-dependent arm of the xenobiotic and oxidative-stress response. VETC+ ECs actively shape the HCC microenvironment through the release of angiogenic and immunomodulatory cues. These findings support the existence of a specialized angiocrine program in VETC+ HCC.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag025.abstract: Abstract Image-guided ablation has emerged as a potentially curative treatment for colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM), yet substantial heterogeneity persists in patient selection, technical execution, and perioperative management. To establish standardized, evidence-based guidance, a multidisciplinary panel of 68 experts including image-guided interventionalists, surgeons, and oncologists conducted a systematic review of literature from 2000 to 2025 and developed consensus recommendations through a modified two-round Delphi process. Evidence was graded using the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine framework, achieving at least conditional consensus (≥75% agreement) for all statements. Finally, twenty consensus recommendations were established addressing patient selection, imaging evaluation, image-guided techniques, ablation strategies, complication management, surveillance protocols, and combination therapies. This expert consensus provides a comprehensive framework for optimizing image-guided ablation as an integral component of multidisciplinary, personalized CRLM management.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag026.abstract: Abstract Background & Aims: Clinical responses to atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (AB) therapy can vary across hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) nodules among individual patients. This study aimed to derive and externally validate a non-invasive radiomics signature (ABRad) translated from a transcriptome signature for nodule-level prediction of AB response (ABS). Methods: We originally derived and validated ABS using 209 and 44 pre-treatment HCC samples from the IMbrave150 and GO30140 trials, respectively. ABS was then translated into ABRad using a machine-learning approach on 59 patients with paired genome-wide transcriptome and pre-resection computed tomography imaging from surgically resected HCC. Subsequently, ABRad was externally validated using 178 HCC nodules from 55 patients treated with AB therapy. Results: The 148-gene ABS predicted therapeutic response and progression-free survival (PFS) in the clinical trial cohorts. The final ABRad model, constructed using a random forest algorithm, was heavily weighted toward contrast-enhanced features. In the external validation cohort, ABRad demonstrated a significant positive association with the degree of therapeutic response (p <0.001). The areas under receiver operating characteristics curve for predicting complete response (CR), objective response (OR), and disease control (DC) were 0.71 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.61-0.80), 0.65 (95% CI, 0.56-0.73), and 0.69 (95% CI, 0.59-0.78), respectively. Nodule-level ABRad was independently associated with therapeutic response with adjusted odds ratios of 3.39 (95% CI, 1.40-8.21) for CR, 2.55 (95% CI, 1.19-5.67) for OR, and 2.60 (95% CI, 1.03-6.56) for DC. Patient-level ABRad was significantly associated with prolonged PFS (p = 0.005). Conclusions: ABRad successfully predicted nodule-level response to AB therapy in HCC.
