doi:10.1186/s13073-023-01230-2.abstract: Abstract Background Primary liver cancer has significant intratumor genetic heterogeneity (IGH), which drives cancer evolution and prevents effective cancer treatment. CRISPR/Cas9-induced mouse liver cancer models can be used to elucidate how IGH is developed. However, as CRISPR/Cas9 could induce chromothripsis and extrachromosomal DNA in cells in addition to targeted mutations, we wondered whether this effect contributes to the development of IGH in CRISPR/Cas9-induced mouse liver cancer. Methods CRISPR/Cas9-based targeted somatic multiplex-mutagenesis was used to target 34 tumor suppressor genes (TSGs) for induction of primary liver tumors in mice. Target site mutations in tumor cells were analyzed and compared between single-cell clones and their subclones, between different time points of cell proliferation, and between parental clones and single-cell clones derived from mouse subcutaneous allografts. Genomic instability and generation of extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA) was explored as a potential mechanism underlying the oscillation of target site mutations in these liver tumor cells. Results After efficiently inducing autochthonous liver tumors in mice within 30–60 days, analyses of CRISPR/Cas9-induced tumors and single-cell clones derived from tumor nodules revealed multiplexed and heterogeneous mutations at target sites. Many target sites frequently displayed more than two types of allelic variations with varying frequencies in single-cell clones, indicating increased copy number of these target sites. The types and frequencies of targeted TSG mutations continued to change at some target sites between single-cell clones and their subclones. Even the proliferation of a subclone in cell culture and in mouse subcutaneous graft altered the types and frequencies of targeted TSG mutations in the absence of continuing CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, indicating a new source outside primary chromosomes for the development of IGH in these liver tumors. Karyotyping of tumor cells revealed genomic instability in these cells manifested by high levels of micronuclei and chromosomal aberrations including chromosomal fragments and chromosomal breaks. Sequencing analysis further demonstrated the generation of eccDNA harboring targeted TSG mutations in these tumor cells. Conclusions Small eccDNAs carrying TSG mutations may serve as an important source supporting intratumor heterogeneity and tumor evolution in mouse liver cancer induced by multiplexed CRISPR/Cas9.

doi:10.1186/s13073-024-01388-3.abstract: Abstract Background Neoantigen vaccines can induce or enhance highly specific antitumor immune responses with minimal risk of autoimmunity. We have developed a neoantigen DNA vaccine platform capable of efficiently presenting both HLA class I and II epitopes and performed a phase 1 clinical trial in triple-negative breast cancer patients with persistent disease on surgical pathology following neoadjuvant chemotherapy, a patient population at high risk of disease recurrence. Methods Expressed somatic mutations were identified by tumor/normal exome sequencing and tumor RNA sequencing. The pVACtools software suite of neoantigen prediction algorithms was used to identify and prioritize cancer neoantigens and facilitate vaccine design for manufacture in an academic GMP facility. Neoantigen DNA vaccines were administered via electroporation in the adjuvant setting (i.e., following surgical removal of the primary tumor and completion of standard of care therapy). Vaccines were monitored for safety and immune responses via ELISpot, intracellular cytokine production via flow cytometry, and TCR sequencing. Results Eighteen subjects received three doses of a neoantigen DNA vaccine encoding on average 11 neoantigens per patient (range 4–20). The vaccinations were well tolerated with relatively few adverse events. Neoantigen-specific T cell responses were induced in 14/18 patients as measured by ELISpot and flow cytometry. At a median follow-up of 36 months, recurrence-free survival was 87.5% (95% CI: 72.7–100%) in the cohort of vaccinated patients. Conclusion Our study demonstrates neoantigen DNA vaccines are safe, feasible, and capable of inducing neoantigen-specific immune responses. Clinical trial registration number NCT02348320.

doi:10.1186/s13073-024-01417-1.abstract: Abstract Background The occurrence of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) following a traumatic event is associated with biological differences that can represent the susceptibility to PTSD, the impact of trauma, or the sequelae of PTSD itself. These effects include differences in DNA methylation (DNAm), an important form of epigenetic gene regulation, at multiple CpG loci across the genome. Moreover, these effects can be shared or specific to both central and peripheral tissues. Here, we aim to identify blood DNAm differences associated with PTSD and characterize the underlying biological mechanisms by examining the extent to which they mirror associations across multiple brain regions. Methods As the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium (PGC) PTSD Epigenetics Workgroup, we conducted the largest cross-sectional meta-analysis of epigenome-wide association studies (EWASs) of PTSD to date, involving 5077 participants (2156 PTSD cases and 2921 trauma-exposed controls) from 23 civilian and military studies. PTSD diagnosis assessments were harmonized following the standardized guidelines established by the PGC-PTSD Workgroup. DNAm was assayed from blood using Illumina HumanMethylation450 or MethylationEPIC (850 K) BeadChips. Within each cohort, DNA methylation was regressed on PTSD, sex (if applicable), age, blood cell proportions, and ancestry. An inverse variance-weighted meta-analysis was performed. We conducted replication analyses in tissue from multiple brain regions, neuronal nuclei, and a cellular model of prolonged stress. Results We identified 11 CpG sites associated with PTSD in the overall meta-analysis (1.44e − 09 < p < 5.30e − 08), as well as 14 associated in analyses of specific strata (military vs civilian cohort, sex, and ancestry), including CpGs in AHRR and CDC42BPB . Many of these loci exhibit blood–brain correlation in methylation levels and cross-tissue associations with PTSD in multiple brain regions. Out of 9 CpGs annotated to a gene expressed in blood, methylation levels at 5 CpGs showed significant correlations with the expression levels of their respective annotated genes. Conclusions This study identifies 11 PTSD-associated CpGs and leverages data from postmortem brain samples, GWAS, and genome-wide expression data to interpret the biology underlying these associations and prioritize genes whose regulation differs in those with PTSD.

doi:10.1186/s13073-025-01479-9.abstract: Abstract Background Transcriptional activation of otherwise repressed retrotransposable elements (RTEs) is a hallmark of cancer, shaping tumour progression and immunogenicity by multifaceted, yet incompletely understood, mechanisms. Methods We used an extended pan-cancer transcriptome assembly to identify potential effects of RTEs on the genes within which they have integrated or those in proximity. These were subsequently verified in test cases by further analysis of transcriptional profiles in cancer patient data, and by in vitro studies involving restoration of gene activity, and proliferation and migration assays in cancer cell lines. Results We report that cancer-specific transcriptional activation of RTEs causes frequent reduction or loss of gene function. Exonisation and alternative splicing of RTEs creates non-functional RNA and protein isoforms and derepressed RTE promoter activity initiates antisense transcription, both at the expense of the canonical isoforms. Contrary to theoretical expectation, transcriptionally activated RTEs affect genes with established tumour-promoting functions, including the common essential RNGTT and the lung cancer-promoting CHRNA5 genes. Furthermore, the disruptive effect of RTE activation on adjacent tumour-promoting genes is associated with slower disease progression in clinical data, whereas experimental restoration of gene activity enhances tumour cell growth and invasiveness in vitro. Conclusions These findings underscore the gene-disruptive potential of seemingly innocuous germline RTE integrations, unleashed only by their transcriptional utilisation in cancer. They further suggest that such metastable RTE integrations are co-opted as sensors of the epigenetic and transcriptional changes occurring during cellular transformation and as executors that disrupt the function of tumour-promoting genes.

doi:10.1186/s13073-025-01514-9.abstract: Abstract Background The FDA approval of T cell receptor-engineered T cells (TCR-T) for synovial sarcoma demonstrates the potential for adoptive T cell therapies (ACTs) in solid tumors. However, the paucity of tumor-associated targets without expression in normal tissues remains a major bottleneck, especially in rare cancer subtypes. Methods We developed a comprehensive computational pipeline called SCAN-ACT that leverages single-cell RNA sequencing and multi-omics data from tumor and normal tissues to nominate and prioritize putative targets for both chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)- and TCR-T cells. For surface membrane targets, SCAN-ACT proposes monospecific targets and potential target pairs for bispecific Boolean logic-gated CAR T cells. For peptide-MHC targets, SCAN-ACT proposes intracellular peptides bound to a diverse set of human leukocyte antigens. Selected targets were validated experimentally by protein expression and for peptide-MHC binding. Results We applied the SCAN-ACT pipeline to soft tissue sarcoma (STS), analyzing 986,749 single cells to identify and prioritize 395 monospecific CAR-T targets, 14,192 bispecific CAR-T targets, and 5020 peptide-MHC targets for TCR-T cells. Proposed targets and target pairs reflected the mesenchymal, neuronal, and hematopoietic ontogeny of STS. We further validated SCAN-ACT in glioblastoma revealing its versatility. Conclusions This work provides a robust data repository along with a web-based and user-friendly set of analysis tools to accelerate ACT development for solid tumors ( https://scanact.stanford.edu/ ).

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01693-z.abstract: The role of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), such as exosomes, in cell-to-cell communication is increasingly recognized. Both during development and postnatally, sEVs have been shown to mediate a multitude of essential functions in the central nervous system. While abnormal sEV biogenesis has been observed in a number of neurodevelopmental disorders, a causal link has been largely lacking. We clinically evaluated five families in which newborns presented with a novel neonatal-onset encephalopathy. Positional mapping, exome sequencing, and trio exome sequencing were utilized to identify the underlying genetic variants. Additionally, we utilized Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants and performed cellular assays to evaluate ESCRT-II interaction, cellular localization, and sEV secretion and cargo capacities. The observed lethal encephalopathy is characterized by severe hypotonia, brain anomalies, and epilepsy. In families 1, 4, and 5 (multiplex consanguineous), we identified a novel homozygous missense variant in VPS25 as the likely candidate. Family 2 comprises a simplex case with two missense variants in trans in VPS25, one of which impacts the same residue as in the other three families. Family 3 also comprises a simplex case where we revealed a homozygous missense variant. VPS25 is an essential component of ESCRT-II, itself required for sEV biogenesis. We show that Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants recapitulate the developmental brain malformation observed in patients. We also show that mutant VPS25 is associated with abnormal ESCRT-II interaction, abnormal cellular localization, and highly abnormal sEVs. Specifically, mutant cells displayed engorged multivesicular bodies and were significantly defective in their capacity to secrete sEVs such as exosomes, while secreted sEVs contained altered cargo, lacking vital proteins for axon protection and maintenance. We report a novel neurodevelopmental disorder caused by biallelic hypomorphic variants in VPS25. The consistent impact of these variants on sEV biogenesis suggests a potential pathomechanism. While future cases will further delineate the phenotypic spectrum, these findings offer a new perspective on abnormal sEVs as drivers of human neurodevelopmental disorders.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01718-7.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remains a therapeutically challenging hematological malignancy with high relapse rates, especially in patients harboring mutations in the FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3) gene. FLT3, a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in hematopoietic cell proliferation and survival, is frequently mutated or overexpressed in AML, contributing to leukemic proliferation and poor prognosis. Although FLT3 inhibitors have demonstrated clinical benefit, resistance often develops, underscoring the need for alternative treatment strategies. In this study, we developed and evaluated allogeneic anti-FLT3 CAR T cells engineered by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated targeted integration into the T cell receptor α constant (TRAC) locus (TRAC-CAR T). This approach enables CAR expression under the endogenous TRAC promoter while simultaneously disrupting native TCR expression, thereby allowing the use of allogeneic T cells with reduced risk of graft-versus-host disease. TRAC-CAR T cells demonstrated efficient disruption of TCRαβ expression, robust surface CAR expression, and superior integration efficiency compared to safe harbor AAVS1-targeted and lentivirally transduced CAR T cells (LV-CAR T). Functionally, TRAC-CAR T cells exhibited potent and selective cytotoxicity against FLT3-positive AML cell lines in vitro, achieving comparable killing relative to LV-CAR T cells. In a xenograft AML mouse model, TRAC-CAR T cells effectively reduced leukemia burden and prolonged mouse survival, with efficacy matching that of LV-CAR T cells. Notably, TRAC-CAR T cells exhibited reduced exhaustion marker expression. Together, these results highlight TRAC-integrated anti-FLT3 CAR T cells as a promising off-the-shelf immunotherapy candidate, combining precise gene editing, efficient manufacturing, and potent anti-leukemic activity.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01720-z.abstract: Core genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) is a powerful method for bacterial strain genotyping. However, the size of the core genome decreases as the phylogenetic breadth of the target group increases, reducing discriminatory power. To overcome this discrimination/applicability tradeoff, here we developed a cumulative cgMLST approach, where sets of core loci conserved within nested phylogenetic entities are added. We illustrate this approach using the Klebsiella pneumoniae species complex (KpSC), for which a widely used cgMLST scheme (KpSC-cgMLST) comprises only 629 genes. We created non-redundant cgMLST schemes for the individual species K. pneumoniae sensu stricto (Kpn-cgMLST scheme), and its multidrug resistant sublineages (SLs) SL147 and SL307. To extract core genes, we used 37,874 genome assemblies originating from over 80 countries worldwide. A methodology was set to filter redundant loci before importing them into the genotyping tool BIGSdb, where they were combined into schemes together with preexisting loci conserved at higher phylogenetic levels. The performance of the cumulative cgMLST schemes was evaluated on previously published datasets and on novel data from an inter-hospital outbreak of SL307. The Kpn-cgMLST, SL147 and SL307 schemes comprise 2752, 852, and 947 additional loci, respectively. The mean allele call rate of the novel loci was > 99% in the validation datasets. Compared to the KpSC scheme used alone, pairwise allelic distances among isolates increased on average 5.6-fold using the Kpn scheme, and further by 1.2-fold and 1.3-fold using the SL147 and SL307 schemes, respectively. We demonstrated the added value of this increased discriminatory power for epidemiological analyses and observed a level of discrimination that approaches that of whole-genome single nucleotide polymorphism analysis. The cumulative cgMLST strategy combines broad phylogenetic applicability and nearly complete genotyping resolution, expanding the utility of this harmonized approach for genomic epidemiology.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01723-w.abstract: Pre-existing psychiatric disorders have been associated with the severity of acute respiratory infections, including COVID-19, particularly in hospitalized populations. However, the underlying mechanisms, especially in community-based populations, remain unknown, limiting preparedness for future pandemics. We investigated the role of genetic liability for psychiatric disorders and related traits in COVID-19 and other respiratory infection severity among individuals reporting SARS-CoV-2 testing and available respiratory symptom data. We included population-based cohort data from Denmark, Estonia, Iceland, Norway, and the United Kingdom (N = 78,507; 62% female; 41% SARS-CoV-2-positive; May 2020-March 2023). Respiratory infection severity was defined by self-reported days bedridden and an eleven-symptom composite score during the acute illness phase. Polygenic scores (PGSs) for eight psychiatric disorders and the personality trait neuroticism indexed genetic liability. Meta-analysed estimates from stepwise-adjusted regression analyses controlling for education, lifestyle, and psychiatric and somatic diagnosis history were used to assess associations between PGSs and acute respiratory infection severity, stratified by COVID-19 status. Higher genetic liability to insomnia, major depression (MD), and neuroticism was consistently associated with longer time bedridden (relative risk ratios per 1 SD change in PGS: 1.07-1.14, 95% confidence intervals [CIs]: 1.03-1.21) and more symptoms (incident rate ratios [IRRs]: 1.02-1.04, 95% CIs: 1.01-1.05) due to COVID-19. PGSs for insomnia, MD, neuroticism, anxiety disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia were also linked to higher non-COVID-19 symptom count (IRRs: 1.01-1.05, 95% CIs: 1.00-1.07). These associations remained robust after adjustment for lifestyle, education and medical comorbidities. Individuals in the highest MD PGS decile reported 20% more symptoms in non-COVID-19 illness and 10% more in COVID-19 compared with the bottom decile. No consistent associations were detected with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, alcohol dependence and post-traumatic stress disorder. No genetic link was observed with ischaemic heart disease or type 2 diabetes. Shared genetics may contribute to the link between psychiatric conditions and respiratory infection severity in community settings. Our results underscore the role of psychiatric genetic liability, beyond diagnosed psychiatric disorders, in contributing to both COVID-19 and other respiratory infection severity. These findings provide insights that may improve future risk stratification and public health strategies targeting respiratory viruses.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01725-8.abstract: Sequencing respiratory virus genomes is essential for public health surveillance and research. Although shotgun metagenomics is pathogen agnostic, its sensitivity is limited by abundant off-target host nucleic acids. Hybridization bait capture overcomes this limitation by selectively enriching viral sequences prior to sequencing. We evaluated three respiratory viral bait capture workflows (veSEQ, RVI-seq, and Illumina) to compare their performance and assess their suitability for scalable respiratory virus sequencing. Synthetic RNA controls and clinical samples containing SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, influenza B, human parainfluenza virus, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) were analysed. All three workflows demonstrated high efficiency, reproducibility and broadly comparable performance across respiratory viruses. Complete viral genomes were consistently recovered from samples containing 10,000 viral copies, while viral reads remained detectable at substantially lower viral loads, including approximately 100 copies. Workflow optimisation reduced reagent costs and enabled laboratory automation without compromising sequencing sensitivity. Hybridization bait capture provides an effective and scalable approach for respiratory virus genome sequencing. Cost reductions and automation can be implemented without compromising performance, supporting its use in routine genomic surveillance and public health preparedness.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01730-x.abstract: Fibroblast plasticity underlies a wide spectrum of pulmonary diseases, yet the molecular programs governing fibroblast state transitions in non-malignant contexts remain poorly understood. We integrated 1,470,730 single-cell transcriptomes across three non-cancer lung diseases to construct a comprehensive fibroblast atlas. Integrated clustering and regulon analyses were used to delineate fibroblast subtypes, disease-associated transcriptional programs, and state transitions. ANTXR1, identified as a representative regulator, was validated by tissue immunohistochemistry and siRNA knockdown in primary lung fibroblasts under TGF-β stimulation. Compared with malignancy, fibroblasts in non-cancer lungs exhibited relatively modest transcriptional alterations but maintained distinct disease-associated phenotypes. We further identified a set of fibroblast-specific genes unique to non-malignant contexts, defining molecular features that distinguish fibrotic remodeling from tumor-associated stromal activation. Analysis of fibroblast subtype- and disease-specific regulons revealed 76 gene signatures that were significantly inversely correlated with lung function and distinguished chronic from acute fibrotic fibroblast states. Functional validation demonstrated that ANTXR1 knockdown markedly reduced COL1A1 expression, underscoring its role in fibroblast activation. This work establishes a comprehensive single-cell fibroblast atlas of non-cancer lung diseases, uncovering disease- and subtype-specific regulatory programs and highlighting potential therapeutic targets for fibrotic remodeling.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01732-9.abstract: Chronic pain is a major global health burden with a substantial but incompletely understood genetic basis. Although genome-wide association studies have identified multiple common-variant loci for pain-related traits, the contribution of rare coding variants to chronic pain susceptibility, biological mechanisms, and shared architecture across pain phenotypes remains unclear. We performed an exome-wide association study across ten chronic pain phenotypes using whole-exome sequencing data from 327,642 European participants in the UK Biobank. Variant-level and gene-level association analyses were conducted to identify common and rare coding signals. Downstream analyses included conditional analysis, statistical fine-mapping, validation in non-European populations, replication in independent cohorts, cross-trait meta-analysis, colocalization, pathway and tissue enrichment, single-cell enrichment, summary-data-based Mendelian randomization, and estimation of heritability and genetic correlation from common and rare variants. We identified 286 significant variant-level associations arising from 235 unique variants mapped to 117 genes, including 13 novel lead variants and 44 independent lead signals. Gene-level analyses identified ten significant genes driven predominantly by rare functional variants: ADAMTSL5, ANKRD12, ARID5A, DPP7, GMCL1, HCK, KIF20B, SLC13A1, UBR2, and ZNF558. Functional analyses implicated pathways related to nervous system development, axonogenesis, and synaptic organization, with enrichment in brain tissues and hTRPM8-expressing dorsal root ganglion neurons. Mendelian randomization analyses highlighted convergent regulatory effects across neural and immune-related tissues. Heritability analyses showed that rare coding variants explained a modest proportion of variance relative to common variants but exhibited larger average effects in the most damaging functional classes, particularly high-confidence loss-of-function variants. Genetic correlation analyses revealed shared genetic components among chronic pain conditions and positive correlations with selected psychiatric and nervous system disorders. These findings provide a comprehensive map of coding variation underlying chronic pain and show that both common and rare coding variants contribute to its genetic architecture. Rare coding variants explain only a limited fraction of heritability but offer strong mechanistic insight by implicating discrete genes and pathways related to neuronal development, neuroimmune signaling, and tissue homeostasis. This work advances understanding of chronic pain biology and provides a foundation for future multi-ancestry studies and functional validation.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01734-7.abstract: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) is a leading cause of anovulatory infertility. Although follicular developmental arrest is a defining feature of PMOS, the cell-type-specific mechanisms linking genetic susceptibility, endocrine imbalance and follicular microenvironmental dysfunction remain incompletely understood, particularly across clinical subtypes. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing of preovulatory follicular-fluid cells from healthy controls and women with uncomplicated PMOS, hyperandrogenic PMOS and metformin-treated insulin-resistant PMOS. We integrated these data with GWAS-derived disease relevance scores and ovarian chromatin-accessibility annotations to map genetic risk to follicular cell populations and regulatory programmes. Ligand-receptor analyses were used to infer intercellular communication networks. Transcriptomic metabolic findings were further assessed by follicular-fluid metabolic and steroid-hormone measurements, DHT-treated granulosa-cell functional assays, and reanalysis of a DHEA-induced mouse PMOS-like ovarian dataset. We generated a single-cell atlas of the PMOS follicular microenvironment comprising 220,983 high-quality cells. Granulosa cells showed the strongest enrichment of PMOS-related genetic risk, with regulatory-genetic support from ovarian snATAC-seq integration. Among granulosa cell states, a GC2_CYP19A1⁺ population was preferentially associated with hyperandrogenic PMOS and displayed a transcriptional programme characterized by steroidogenic remodelling coupled to reduced energy-metabolic activity. Biochemical profiling supported this endocrine-metabolic imbalance, showing increased follicular-fluid androstenedione (ASD) and estrone, reduced estradiol and E2/ASD ratio, decreased ATP, citrate and fumarate hydratase activity, and increased lactate and β-hydroxybutyrate. Prolonged DHT exposure impaired granulosa-cell mitochondrial respiration, ATP production and mitochondrial membrane potential. In parallel, PMOS subtypes showed immune remodelling and altered ligand-receptor signalling, with hyperandrogenic PMOS associated with increased inflammatory signalling and reduced homeostatic or tissue-repair pathways. Reanalysis of a DHEA-induced mouse ovarian dataset provided supportive evidence for androgen-associated steroidogenic pathway perturbation. This study provides a cell-resolved framework linking PMOS genetic susceptibility to endocrine-metabolic and immune remodelling in the preovulatory follicular microenvironment. The identification of a hyperandrogen-associated GC2_CYP19A1⁺ state highlights a candidate cellular programme in which steroidogenic imbalance is coupled to impaired granulosa-cell bioenergetics. These findings provide a resource for future validation and may inform microenvironment-guided stratification of PMOS and the development of strategies aimed at restoring follicular function.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01735-6.abstract: Ovarian cancer (OC) remains highly lethal due to frequent late-stage diagnosis and the challenge of distinguishing malignant from benign adnexal masses (BAM) preoperatively. Reliable non-invasive diagnostic biomarkers remain an unmet clinical need. This multi-center study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic potential of plasma circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA (ccf-mtDNA) fragmentomics for improving OC management. We developed two machine learning models based on ccf-mtDNA features: an OC Detection (OD) model to distinguishing OC from healthy controls (HC), and a Benign vs. Malignant Differential diagnosis (BMD) model to discriminate OC from BAM. The OD model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.987 in the training cohort and maintained high performance (AUC above 0.979) in internal and external validation cohorts, with 91.67% sensitivity for Stage I OC at 95% specificity. The BMD model demonstrated strong discriminatory power (AUC = 0.982) and generalizability (AUC ranging from 0.961 to 0.980 in four validation cohorts), significantly outperforming serum biomarkers. Remarkably, both models performed robustly in the Chinese minority cohort. These findings establish ccf-mtDNA fragmentomics as a powerful liquid biopsy approach for the early and accurate detection of OC, with significant potential for clinical translation in high-risk populations and differential diagnosis of benign vs. malignant adnexal masses.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01738-3.abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a X-linked disease affecting skeletal and cardiac muscle and is caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene (DMD). Patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) serve as reliable in vitro disease models. Their genetic correction by CRISPR/Cas9 allows the generation of isogenic controls and holds promises for gene therapy. However, restoring full-length dystrophin, especially when deletions involve multiple exons, constitutes a technological challenge. This study aimed to fully repair the dystrophin gene from a DMD iPSC line carrying the deletion of exons 49-50 and to characterize the rescue of the cardiac phenotype. We developed an innovative CRISPR/Cas9-based approach involving the insertion of coding sequences of the deleted region, at the 3' of exon 48, thereby generating a single continuous coding sequence encompassing exons 48-49-50. Subsequently, iPSCs were differentiated into cardiomyocytes and cardiac fibroblasts. Cardiac phenotypes were analysed by western blot, immunofluorescence, ELISA, FACS, Ionoptix, 3D engineered heart tissue (EHT) and single-nuclei RNA-seq. The correction of a two-exons DMD gene deletion in Duchenne iPSCs, using CRISPR/Cas9, enabled the re-expression of a stable and functional full-length dystrophin in cardiomyocytes resulting in the rescue of cardiac pathological phenotypes. Edited cardiomyocytes showed improved morphology, reduced release of the cardiomyocytes damage marker troponin I, and decreased ROS production. Moreover, dystrophin restoration enhanced contractility and ameliorated the Ca2+ kinetics. Notably, edited iPSC derived fibroblasts showed reduced pro-fibrotic stimuli response. In parallel, we also observed enhanced functioning of a 3D engineered heart tissue and profound change in the transcriptomic profile in both cardiomyocytes and fibroblasts after the re-expression of full-length dystrophin. We developed an innovative approach that enabled the re-expression of full-length dystrophin in a DMD iPSC line with consequent complete rescue of in vitro DMD cardiac phenotypes. On the long term, these results could lay a foundation for future applications of cell therapy or in vivo CRISPR/Cas9-based intervention to treat DMD.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01747-2.abstract: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a major cause of hospital-associated infections globally. In the Capital Region of Denmark, VREfm ST80 emerged as the dominant vanA-positive clone but declined significantly over the following decade. To investigate the genomic mechanisms underlying this epidemiological shift, we assembled and performed whole-genome sequencing and phylogenomic analysis of 334 ST80 isolates collected from colonisation (83%) and infection (17%) cases across nine hospitals in the region between 2012 and 2020. Two major clusters (Clusters 1 and 2) and nine sub-clusters (1.A-G and 2.H-I) were identified. Sub-cluster-1.A (169/334) was the dominant lineage, accounting for 72% of isolates from 2012-2015. Isolates from 2016-2020 were distributed across all sub-clusters, indicating increasing diversification over time. Genetic variation was driven by accumulation of mutations, recombination and gain/loss of accessory genes and plasmids. Eight recombination hotspots were identified in core genes involved in cell wall synthesis, phosphotransferase systems, amino-acid biosynthesis, and several transporters. Accessory genome comparisons revealed sub-cluster-specific enrichment of resistance genes, including ermG (89% in 1.B), tet(S) (85% in 1.A), and tet(M) (88% in sub-cluster-1.B). Additionally, genes associated with biofilm formation, ABC transporters, and biosynthesis of polysaccharides, terpenoids, and aspartate were differentially enriched across the clusters. These genomic signatures may have contributed to niche adaptation and intra-clonal diversification. Plasmidome analysis showed increased diversity in later years, with the decline of Inc18 family plasmids (from 80 to 38%) and the rise of two new plasmids, coinciding with reduced clonal stability. Long-read hybrid assemblies uncovered mosaic phage-like plasmids harboring the vanA operon alongside ermB, aadE, and aph(3')-IIIa suggesting a unique mechanism for co-mobilization of antimicrobial resistance via transduction or conjugation. Despite the observed diversity, a continuous and sustained intra- and inter-hospital transmission and dissemination of this clone was evidenced by the small SNP difference (≤ 15 SNPs) between strains. This study showed the continuous hospital transmission and intra-clonal diversity of VREfm ST80. The dissemination, transmission and persistence dynamics of the vanA ST80 clone in Denmark may have been shaped by recombination events and gain/loss of genes involved in general metabolism, antibiotic resistance and virulence, and inter-clonal competition.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01757-0.abstract: While the association between gut microbiota and cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) has been explored, existing research has been limited to bacterial components. The alterations in non-bacterial members (fungi, archaea, and viruses) and their functional characteristics in CCA remain unclear. This study aimed to comprehensively characterize the multi-kingdom gut microbiota and functional profiles in CCA patients and develop a non-invasive diagnostic model. We performed metagenomic sequencing on 700 fecal samples collected from three distinct regions in China, comprising 289 CCA patients, 312 healthy controls, and 99 hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients. Multi-kingdom microbial composition and functional profiles were analyzed. We integrated multiple machine learning algorithms to generate 117 distinct modeling schemes for constructing and screening the optimal CCA diagnostic model. The model was validated across three independent cohorts and tested for specificity against HCC. We also benchmarked the model against established diagnostic approaches by reviewing 15 CCA clinical practice guidelines/consensus statements and their cited evidence and by evaluating model detection in CA19-9-positive and CA19-9-negative patients. Extensive alterations were identified in CCA patients across multi-kingdom and functional layers, including 198 archaeal, 154 bacterial, 78 fungal, and 120 viral species, as well as 278 genes, 99 pathways, and 151 carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes). A panel of 21 multi-kingdom and functional markers demonstrated superior diagnostic accuracy with an average AUC of 91% across three validation cohorts, outperforming any single-kingdom model. The model exhibited high specificity in distinguishing CCA from HCC, achieving an AUC of 99.74% with a false positive rate of 11.11%. Benchmarking supported a complementary role as a noninvasive screening aid, the model showed pooled sensitivity and specificity of 96.2%, and 78.5%, respectively, and detected 97.6% of CA19-9-negative CCA cases. This study represents the first comprehensive characterization of multi-kingdom gut microbiome and functional markers in cholangiocarcinoma. Gut multi-kingdom and functional microbial signatures represent a promising noninvasive tool that may aid the screening and early identification of cholangiocarcinoma in high-risk populations, complementing existing diagnostic approaches.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01765-0.abstract: Abstract Background Prolonged fasting may improve metabolic health, but controlled data in healthy adults with longer follow-up and multi-omics profiling are limited. We investigated the immediate and 12-week follow-up effects of a 5-day fasting intervention on body composition, gut microbiome, and circulating and fecal metabolites, and assessed whether baseline characteristics predict individual weight-loss response. Methods In a randomized, waitlist-controlled trial, 38 healthy adults completed a 5-day fasting intervention with 12-week follow-up (LEANER study). Outcomes included body mass index and body composition, gut microbiome composition, and plasma and fecal metabolites. Changes over time and between groups were evaluated using regression-based models and paired non-parametric tests, as appropriate. Additionally, permutation-based multivariate testing was performed on microbiome and metabolome data. Twelve-week body weight response was predicted using data-driven machine learning with cross-validation, followed by external validation in three independent cohorts undergoing prolonged fasting protocols. Results Fasting reduced body mass index acutely, predominantly driven by loss of fat mass, and these improvements partially persisted at 12 weeks. Fasting induced marked shifts in gut microbiome composition and in plasma and fecal metabolites. Post-fasting and longer-term changes in microbial diversity were associated with baseline microbiome diversity. A model combining baseline microbiome and clinical variables predicted body mass index response at 12 weeks; prominent predictors included an unclassified Faecalibacterium species, Oscillibacter sp. 50_27, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and systolic blood pressure. The model generalized to three independent cohorts, including individuals with metabolic syndrome, patients with multiple sclerosis exposed to repeated fasting, and healthy volunteers fasting for 6–12 days. Conclusions In healthy adults, a 5-day prolonged fasting intervention produces robust short-term metabolic changes with partial persistence and consistent remodeling of the gut microbiome and metabolite profiles. Baseline microbiome and clinical characteristics can help stratify expected longer-term responses, supporting the development of individualized fasting-based interventions. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04452916. Prospectively registered on June 29, 2020.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01770-3.abstract: Environmental exposures such as air pollution may influence human health partly through microbiome, but statistical modeling is challenged by spatial dependence across regions and ecological correlations among taxa. We propose SpaMixed, a novel spatial mixed modeling framework for microbiome count data that incorporates both sources of dependence using conditional autoregressive priors. In simulations, SpaMixed achieved high feature selection power while maintaining low false positive rates and reduced estimation error relative to existing methods. Applied to two real studies with fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposures, SpaMixed identified biologically plausible PM2.5-associated taxa, supporting its utility for environmental microbiome research.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01772-1.abstract: Abstract Background Genetic mosaicism is a well-recognized consequence of CRISPR–Cas9 genome editing, yet its characterization remains challenging, especially when it involves low-frequency structural variants. A comprehensive analysis of mosaicism requires deep and unbiased sequencing of the target loci, with accurate single-molecule reads. Methods We performed amplification-free PureTarget PacBio sequencing to investigate CRISPR-Cas9 outcomes at on-target and off-target sites in genome edited zebrafish and their offspring. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing was performed by micro-injection in fertilized eggs at the single-cell stage. Results Thirty samples from pooled larvae and individual zebrafish were successfully sequenced, resulting in > 1100x average target coverage. The PacBio reads reached an exceptional accuracy (QV39) over the target regions, with every read originating from a unique DNA molecule. The two haplotypes of the target loci displayed a balanced depth of coverage, while long-range PCR of the same samples resulted in skewed data. Further analysis of the PureTarget data revealed widespread genetic mosaicism in individual founder (F0) fish, with up to 18 distinct on-target events and 11 off-target events present in a single adult founder. Several CRISPR-Cas9 editing outcomes, including large structural variants and off-target mutations, were inherited to the F1 generation. Notably, as many as seven unique editing events were found among sibling F1 juvenile offspring derived from a single founder pair, thereby confirming the presence of genetic mosaicism in germ cells of founder zebrafish. This implies that some consequences of CRISPR-Cas9 editing may emerge only in the second generation. We also analyzed DNA methylation signals in the PureTarget data but did not observe altered 5mC CpG levels in genome edited samples. Conclusions PureTarget enables efficient, accurate, and unbiased profiling of genetic mosaicism and DNA methylation at pre-defined genomic regions. Our results show that CRISPR–Cas9–induced mosaicism is widespread and represents an important factor to consider in genome editing experiments.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01776-x.abstract: Developing peripheral blood-based diagnostic models for idiopathic Parkinson's disease (iPD), particularly those leveraging the T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire, has long been considered infeasible because patient-derived TCRs appear to lack convergent sequence motifs. We reasoned that this apparent absence of shared TCR features likely reflects both insufficient sample sizes and unaccounted immune heterogeneity within the iPD population. We reconstructed TCR repertoires from the two largest iPD cohorts currently available, anchoring them with three mechanistically distinct mouse models to stratify patients into model-anchored informed subtypes. Within these data-driven subtypes, we trained subtype-specific, multimodal multi-instance classifiers. We demonstrated that iPD patients can be successfully stratified into model-anchored informed subtypes. Furthermore, the trained subtype-specific, multimodal multi-instance classifiers achieved an Area Under Curve (AUC) exceeding 0.8 for both subtypes. Our findings underscore the critical role of disease stratification in enabling TCR repertoire-based modeling in neurodegenerative diseases.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01785-w.abstract: Abstract Background Ciprofloxacin resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is common or emerging in many geographies, and knowledge of local resistance rates is important for empirical therapy. While K. pneumoniae ciprofloxacin resistance determinants are known, there is a lack of systematic data on the effect of these determinants, alone and in combination, and there are no publicly accessible tools for predicting ciprofloxacin resistance from whole genome sequence data. Methods The KlebNET-GSP AMR Genotype-Phenotype Group aggregated a matched genotype-phenotype dataset of n = 12,167 K. pneumoniae species complex ( Kp SC) isolates from 27 countries between 2001 and 2021. We developed a rule-based classifier to predict ciprofloxacin resistance by categorizing the number of mutations in the quinolone resistance determining regions of gyrA and parC and the number of plasmid-mediated quinolone resistance genes, including the presence/absence of aac(6 ' )-Ib-cr (which can acetylate ciprofloxacin). Predictive performance was assessed using the discovery dataset, with the reassessment of discrepant and concordant isolates; and validated using externally contributed datasets ( n = 7,030 Kp SC isolates). Results The rule-based classifier predicted R vs S/I with categorical agreement, sensitivity, and specificity > 96%, and major/very major error rates < 4%. Performance was similar across diverse Kp SC sources (human, animal, other), species, and intra-species lineages. External validation of the classifier yielded overall 90.18% categorical agreement [95% confidence interval (CI), 89.49–90.88%], 8.74% major errors [95% CI, 7.41–10.06%], 4.19% very major errors [95% CI, 3.60–4.77%], and 10.14% minor errors [95% CI, 9.44–10.85%]. We implemented the classifier in Kleborate, a command-line tool that is integrated into the Pathogenwatch web platform. Using this to assess the global distribution of ciprofloxacin resistance determinants in Kp SC genomes available in Pathogenwatch ( n = 31,319, from 109 countries between years 2000–2023), we observed a significant positive association between national quinolone consumption rates and predicted ciprofloxacin resistance (R 2 = 0.20, p = 0.004). Conclusion Ciprofloxacin resistance phenotypes can be reasonably predicted from genotype, which is sufficient for informing surveillance. However, unexplained resistance remains and accuracy is insufficient for clinical applications. We demonstrate the value of aggregating genotype-phenotype data to explore resistance mechanisms and develop predictors, but highlight complexities in combining phenotype data from different assays and standards.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01792-x.abstract: As whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is increasingly used in clinical and public health contexts, clearer expectations regarding the amount of variation present in the "average" human genome are required to contextualise findings. We analysed WGS data from two large population cohorts: 490,541 individuals in UK Biobank (UKB) and 414,830 individuals in All of Us. Following variant and genotype QC, we aimed to assess the range of neutral and disease-associated variation across six genetically-inferred ancestry groups. The "average" genome contains ~4.3-5.3 million variants, of which ~1.5% are rare (within-cohort allele frequency 10,000 basepairs per genome, and rare autosomal copy number variants > 1 Mb present in ~ 1 in 41 (2.5%) individuals. On average, ~32-42% of variants per person are homozygous and individuals have ~4 unique runs of homozygosity > 1.5 Mb, with marked variation observed across ancestry groups. Of the ~21- 26,000 SNVs/indels per person in coding exons of MANE Select transcripts, ~48% are predicted to alter the protein, of which ~0.8% are high-confidence loss-of-function and ~0.1% have REVEL score > 0.7 suggestive of pathogenicity. Depending upon parental age, the average genome contains ~63 de novo variants, of which ~75-80% are paternal in origin. Considering only rare variants in GenCC-curated monogenic disease-associated genes, the average genome contains ~1-3 ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants, ~2-5 high-confidence loss-of-function variants, and ~50 ClinVar variants of uncertain significance. Most ClinVar pathogenic variants are heterozygous in recessive disease genes, consistent with carrier status, and have multiple ClinVar submitters. Finally, applying polygenic scores (PGS) for 28 common diseases within UKB, we estimate that the average person is in the top 10% for ~3 conditions, and around 1 in 5 people are in the top 1% for at least one PGS. The ubiquity of genetic variation in individuals has important implications for policy-makers considering genomic screening and clinicians counselling families. The continued underrepresentation of many global populations reflects a broader limitation of contemporary genomic research, underscoring the need for more inclusive datasets worldwide in order to enable equitable precision medicine.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01797-6.abstract: Abstract Background SpliceAI is a deep learning algorithm that predicts whether genetic variants are likely to affect splicing. Precomputed SpliceAI predictions for all theoretical SNVs and small indels were released in 2019, and are used by variant annotation tools such as VEP and dbNSFP to batch annotate large numbers of variants quickly. While the use of precomputed scores vastly reduces the computational cost of retrieving SpliceAI predictions, several limitations to their utility have emerged, for which the impact on the prioritisation of likely splice-altering variants in cohort studies has not been established. Methods We identify transcript annotation and genome version inconsistencies impacting the precomputed SpliceAI scores by comparing the original gene annotation file with MANE v1.0 Select transcripts. To quantify the impact that these factors may have in variant prioritisation pipelines for diagnostic purposes, we re-analysed variants in 660 genes linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD), identified in 7,221 participants with NDD from the Genomics England 100,000 Genomes Project (100kGP). Results We find outdated gene annotations and genome version inconsistencies impact 8.34% of theoretical SNVs included in the SpliceAI precomputed scores, and affect the accuracy of SpliceAI predictions in 34.98% of disease-associated panelApp green genes. In 7,221 Genomics England participants, re-running SpliceAI with updated annotations and parameters results in an increase of 18.2% predicted splice-altering variants compared with variants identified using precomputed scores alone. These variants constitute a diagnostic increase of 11.7% versus the precomputed scores, assessed retrospectively using confirmed diagnoses in 100kGP. To mitigate issues with the precomputed scores we provide ‘SpliceAI-splint’- a command-line tool to allow users to identify variants within a VCF file whose potential splice-altering effects would be missed by the precomputed scores. Conclusions: Although the precomputed scores continue to represent a useful resource in the annotation of variants in cohorts with genetic disorders, we find key limitations that can lead to their missing clinically relevant splice-altering variants, and provide a command-line tool to mitigate these issues.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01801-z.abstract: Abstract Background Primary mitochondrial diseases affect 1 in 4300 livebirths and cause early death or lifelong disability but our understanding of their impact on survival and causes of death is limited. There is conflicting evidence about whether they cause an increased incidence of cancer. We aimed to determine survival, causes of death and risk of developing cancer in people with mitochondrial disease by linking genetic results with routinely collected healthcare data at a national scale. Methods Individuals with mitochondrial diseases were identified in England (population 60.2 million) by National Health Service diagnostic laboratories and Genomics England. A curated cohort was assembled. Individual consent was not required because the National Disease Registration Service has legal permission to collect patient data. We used national datasets to find out the vital status, cause of death and any cancer diagnoses for each individual. Kaplan-Meier survival, Cox regression model and standardised cancer incidence ratio were analysed. Results 1266 unique individuals were identified, with 1164 having a known region in England. Following clinical review, 1107 were included (527 males, 580 females, median age 48 years, age range from infancy to 90 years). 74% had a mitochondrial DNA diagnosis and 26% had nuclear genetic diagnosis. 170 were deceased. 159 were diagnosed during childhood (14.3%). Most childhood deaths were due to the underlying mitochondrial disorder. Common causes of death in adults included cardiac, cancers, and pneumonia. Survival after diagnosis varied by genetic diagnosis and by age at diagnosis with poorer survival for people diagnosed during childhood (hazard ratio 2.11, p < 0.001) or older age (2.83, p < 0.001) and those with recessive POLG disease (hazard ratio 3.06, p < 0.001). For the whole cohort, survival at 10 years after genetic diagnosis was 80.3% (95% confidence interval 76.9% to 83.7%) and survival at 20 years after diagnosis was 58.9% (95% confidence interval 49.6% to 70.0%). Standardised cancer incidence ratios did not show a difference in cancer incidence compared to the general population. Conclusions Survival was much longer than anticipated, with differences due to the precise genetic diagnosis and age at onset. Despite prior contradictory evidence, there was no increased cancer risk in this large cohort.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01803-x.abstract: Abstract Background Sonic hedgehog (SHH) medulloblastoma (MB) accounts for approximately one-third of all MB cases, the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Despite therapy, SHH MB relapse is frequent and has a dismal prognosis. New treatments for recurrent SHH MB are needed; however, the molecular drivers of relapse are poorly understood. Methods We profiled 22 SHH MB specimens (16 primary and 6 recurrent), including four primary–recurrent patient pairs, using overlapping single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq; n = 16), single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (snATAC-seq; n = 13), and spatial transcriptomic ( n = 6) cohorts. We integrated these data with exome-derived variant calls from 25 specimens, including seven patients with primary and recurrent samples. Bulk RNA-seq data from 48 specimens representing 24 primary–recurrent pairs were used for validation. Results Our analyses show evidence of positive selection for nonsynonymous tumor mutations, including TP53 mutations involving its DNA-binding and tetramerization domains. TP53 mutations were associated with reduced base-excision repair (BER) gene expression and accessibility of linked cis-regulatory regions. Recurrent tumors showed increased tumor mutational burden (TMB) and an endoplasmic-reticulum (ER) stress expression program associated with poorer survival. Angiogenic gene expression and inferred immunosuppressive myeloid signaling were increased in recurrent disease. Conclusions These data define recurrence-associated cellular and regulatory programs, nominate candidate therapeutic targets and prognostic markers, and provide a single-cell and spatial atlas of SHH MB.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01815-7.abstract: Abstract Background Timely and comprehensive molecular classification is essential for therapeutic decision-making in pediatric oncology, yet current diagnostic workflows rely on multi-step, time- and resource-intensive testing strategies. We present a standardized whole-genome sequencing approach with adaptive sampling (AS-WGS) using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) optimized for pediatric cancers, that enables rapid and comprehensive molecular profiling in a single assay. Methods We designed an AS-WGS panel comprising 380 clinically relevant loci that we applied to the sequencing of 36 pediatric cancer and control samples. To support real-time interpretation, we developed an open-source bioinformatic pipeline (nf-core-oncoseq) enabling on-the-fly analysis during sequencing. We compared the AS-WGS results to those obtained by standard clinical assays, including exome and transcriptome sequencing. Results AS-WGS achieved somatic-grade coverage (mean 172X) in target regions while maintaining pan-genomic coverage (18X), thus supporting genome-wide copy number and methylation analyses. AS-WGS reliably detected all classes of clinically actionable alterations including fusion genes (20/20), small variants (SNVs and indels, in 58/59 mutated genes) and large CNVs (20/21). SNVs were robustly captured down to a 5% allelic frequency, similar to clinical exome sequencing. The PCR-free workflow supported methylation-based tumor classification, providing orthogonal confirmation of hematological and solid tumor subtypes in 9/11 acute lymphoblastic leukemias and in 8/12 solid tumors. All clonal alterations were identified with >5 supporting reads from data generated in the first 24 hours of sequencing (20/20 fusions and 47/47 SNVs with allelic frequencies > 25%), with some, such as large CNVs and methylation predictions, detected within the first hour. Conclusions Our results show that applying AS-WGS to pediatric hematological and solid tumors supports the rapid identification of all classes of genomic alterations and enables methylation-based classification in a single assay. Future efforts aimed at clinical translation will establish its position within the current multi-assay diagnostic landscape.

doi:10.1186/s13073-026-01818-4.abstract: Abstract Background Given the growing use of cancer screening, colorectal tumors are increasingly diagnosed before metastasizing to distant organs. However, up to 25% of patients with early-stage colorectal cancer later develop metachronous metastases – often years after primary tumor resection. When limited to the liver, they remain potentially curable by surgery, but outcomes following curative-intent resection vary substantially: some patients remain durably disease-free, whereas others relapse within months. Clinico-genomic determinants of this heterogeneity are not well understood, and genomic markers to personalize surgical decisions in patients with metachronous liver metastases are lacking. Methods We assembled a deeply annotated cohort of 41 colorectal cancer patients undergoing resection of metachronous liver metastases – with whole-exome and transcriptome sequencing of metastases and matched primary tumors (where available) and structured annotations of their longitudinal clinical trajectories, including a median follow-up of 66.4 months, relapse after metastatic surgery, adjuvant therapies, radiologic assessments, and blood-based markers. We further dissected relapse-associated genomic features in five independent datasets. Results Early relapse (< 12 months) correlated with a larger number of metachronous liver metastases and a characteristic copy-number pattern involving loss of arms 3p and 5q. Metastases with late/no relapse were characterized by multi-hit APC mutations. These genomic features also correlated with significant differences in relapse-free survival after metastatic surgery, and they were consistent between patients with and without adjuvant therapy for their primary and metastatic tumors. Early-relapsing metastases typically harbored an accumulation of multiple relapse-associated genomic changes. Moreover, metachronous metastases differed in genomic characteristics from synchronous metastases in an independent cohort, exhibiting a higher frequency of 5q loss and a higher burden of copy-number alterations relative to their matched primaries, suggesting continued evolution after primary-tumor resection. Transcriptomically, relapse-associated copy-number changes correlated with gene-dosage effects on the respective arms and differential expression of genes related to proliferation and metabolism. They also correlated with advanced disease and shorter survival in two independent datasets. Conclusions Our study characterizes the clinico-genomic basis of early relapse in metachronous liver metastases. Ultimately, these features could help identify patients with a high propensity to relapse after surgery and personalize the management of colorectal cancer patients with metachronous liver metastases.

doi:10.1186/s40164-026-00831-y.abstract: Patient-derived tumor organoids (PDTOs) are strongly influenced by culture medium. We compared OncoPro™ (OP) Tumoroid Culture medium with conventional Wnt/R-spondin/noggin (Wnt) medium. This recently developed OP medium offers a standardized, serum-free alternative to Wnt-based formulations. We compared OP and Wnt media across 36 PDTO lines from various malignancies (colorectal, pancreatic, breast, lung, gastric, gastroesophageal junction, biliary head and neck and unknown primary), assessing establishment success. Selected PDTO models were subjected to downstream characterization, including morphological assessment and bulk transcriptomic profiling with comparison to public single-cell RNA sequencing reference datasets (n = 11), whole-exome sequencing (WES) (n = 9), and pharmacological response profiling to a 33-drug panel (n = 3). Adaptation from Wnt medium to OP succeeded in 83.3% (15/18), whereas de novo establishment favored Wnt (33.3% vs 11.1%). Key oncogenic driver alterations were retained across matched organoid cultures, supporting preservation of tumor-relevant genomic features. Transcriptomic profiling confirmed preserved tumor-identity across media, while revealing different epithelial state programs: Wnt upregulated proliferation/stemness-associated genes (e.g. LGR5) and OP enriched adhesion-associated genes and inflammatory/TGF-β programs. In scRNA databases OP signatures preferentially mapped to malignant epithelial compartments in pancreatic cancer, whereas Wnt signatures were linked to non-malignant epithelium. Similarly, in colon cancer OP signature mapped predominantly to the malignant epithelial compartments. Drug (n = 33) screening in pancreatic- and colorectal cancer PDTOs (n = 3) demonstrated consistent medium-dependent shifts: Wnt-grown PDTOs were globally more sensitive in the screened subset, particularly to MAPK-axis inhibitors and apoptosis-sensitizers, while OP-grown PDTOs exhibited relative resistance. Culture medium composition is a key determinant of PDTO phenotype, transcriptome and drug sensitivity. Wnt medium was associated with drug-sensitive states, whereas OP medium was associated with adhesion- and inflammatory-related programs, relative resistance in the screened subset of 33 drugs and closer alignment with malignant epithelial programs in the analyzed pancreatic / colorectal cancer single-cell atlases.

doi:10.1186/s40164-026-00832-x.abstract: High-risk myelodysplastic syndromes (HR-MDS) are associated with poor survival despite standard therapy with hypomethylating agents (HMAs). Although the VERONA trial did not meet its primary endpoint, a granular interpretation of these results alongside real-life data may help identify patient subsets that could potentially benefit. At the 2025 American Society of Hematology (ASH) Meeting and at the 2026 European Hematology Association Congress (EHA), several studies reported updated data on venetoclax-based combinations in HR-MDS across clinical and biological subgroups. The randomized phase III VERONA study evaluated venetoclax plus azacitidine (VEN/HMA) versus azacitidine alone in the frontline setting, while additional phase I/II and real-life studies explored oral hypomethylating backbones, therapy-related disease, and molecularly defined subsets. Collectively, these data suggest that venetoclax enhances response rates in HR-MDS, although survival benefits remain heterogeneous, with a potential benefit observed when used as a bridge to transplantation. Given the lack of randomized data in transplant-eligible patients, this Correspondence provides a narrative, non-systematic review of the available evidence based mostly on abstracts and not peer reviewed publications. Additionally, we summarize the most clinically relevant findings and discuss their implications for future treatment strategies.

doi:10.1186/s40164-026-00839-4.abstract: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is one of the most aggressive thyroid cancers characterized by rapid progression and high resistance to conventional therapies. Although mutations in the BRAF gene are common in thyroid cancer, targeted therapies against this mutation show limited clinical benefit. This study investigated whether inhibition of downstream signaling pathways using the selected MEK inhibitor cobimetinib provides advantages over direct BRAF inhibition. Genomic and expression analyses of thyroid cancer datasets confirmed frequent BRAF alterations and activation of MAPK-pathway-associated signaling. Functional studies using thyroid cancer cell lines demonstrated that cobimetinib more effectively reduced MAPK pathway activity specifically reducing ERK1/2 phosphorylation compared to direct BRAF inhibition. This pathway suppression was associated with decreased tumor cell invasion, migration, and expression of epithelial-mesenchymal transition markers, alongside increased induction of late apoptosis. Furthermore, cobimetinib altered immune-related features of tumor cells by reducing expression of immune inhibitory molecules and cytokine secretion, while simultaneously enhancing expression of molecules involved in antigen presentation, such as HLA-ABC. Co-culture experiments with human fibroblasts showed that cobimetinib modulates tumor-fibroblast communication and fibroblast phenotype composition. Cobimetinib reduced the formation of specific immune-suppressive fibroblast subtypes, whereas exposure to interleukin-8 promoted their development and increased tumor cell migration. Secretome profiling confirmed that cobimetinib markedly depleted pro-tumorigenic cytokines, particularly reducing IL-8 secretion. While data provide preclinical evidence that downstream MEK inhibition alters tumor cell signaling and IL-8-associated tumor-fibroblast communication in ATC-centered models, they do not establish cobimetinib monotherapy as a replacement for clinically established BRAF/MEK combination therapies. Instead, these data support the broader therapeutic potential of MEK inhibitors as a strategy to target both tumor progression and immune evasion in aggressive endocrine malignancies.

doi:10.1186/s40164-026-00840-x.abstract: The intratumoral microbiome critically influences immunotherapy efficacy by modulating the host immune microenvironment and epigenetic landscape through its metabolites. Microbial derived metabolites such as short chain fatty acids, secondary bile acids, trimethylamine N oxide, and tryptophan derivatives reprogram host cell epigenetics via DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs, thereby shaping anti-tumor immunity and driving either immune activation or resistance. In turn, the hypoxic, acidic, and nutrient deprived tumor microenvironment reshapes microbial composition and metabolism, forming a vicious cycle that further affects therapeutic outcomes. Given these pivotal roles, targeting the intratumoral microbiota has emerged as a promising strategy. Advances in synthetic biology have enabled the development of engineered bacteria as programmable living therapeutics. These engineered strains achieve tumor specific colonization, controlled drug release, and multimodal functions such as cytokine secretion, immune checkpoint blockade, STING pathway activation, and metabolic reprogramming. By enhancing immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy and synergizing with cell therapies, engineered bacterial therapy represents a highly promising approach to improve immunotherapy efficiency. Despite challenges in clinical translation including heterogeneity, anti-vector immunity, and manufacturing complexity, this strategy offers a new paradigm for precision cancer treatment.

doi:10.1186/s40164-026-00843-8.abstract: Cancer metabolism-associated immune suppression remains a major barrier to durable therapeutic responses. Indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase 1 has been pursued as a therapeutic target, but incomplete pathway suppression has limited clinical success. As the aryl hydrocarbon receptor is a ligand-activated transcription factor and downstream effector of tryptophan metabolism, we investigated how myeloid-cell aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling shapes the tumor immune microenvironment and whether its inhibition can restore antitumor immunity. Conditional aryl hydrocarbon receptor knockout mice targeting dendritic cells or macrophages were used to evaluate the effects of genetic aryl hydrocarbon receptor ablation. Pharmacologic inhibition was assessed using DA-4505 across syngeneic lung, colorectal, and breast cancer models and an immune checkpoint inhibitor-refractory humanized patient-derived xenograft model. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated alone or in combination with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 therapy, chemotherapy, or surgery. Tumor growth, survival, metastasis, and immune remodeling were analyzed by flow cytometry, multiplex immunohistochemistry, single-cell RNA sequencing, cytokine profiling, and human tumor datasets. Conditional aryl hydrocarbon receptor depletion in macrophages and dendritic cells enhanced innate and adaptive immune activation, increased interferon-γ-producing T cells, and strengthened antitumor immunity. In mouse tumor models, pharmacologic aryl hydrocarbon receptor blockade enhanced macrophage chemotaxis and activation programs, promoted M1-like macrophage polarization, increased interferon-γ-producing CD8⁺ T cells, and reduced regulatory T cells and polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells. These changes promoted robust T-cell activation and durable tumor control. Aryl hydrocarbon receptor inhibition further synergized with chemotherapy, surgery, and immune checkpoint blockade, leading to expansion of effector and memory T-cell populations and sustained antitumor responses. In a humanized lung cancer model, aryl hydrocarbon receptor blockade increased intratumoral CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and cytotoxic-memory programs while reducing regulatory T-cell enrichment. In human tumor datasets, aryl hydrocarbon receptor-positive macrophages correlated with FOXP3⁺ T-cell infiltration, and higher aryl hydrocarbon receptor inhibition-associated T-cell signatures were associated with improved patient survival.

doi:10.1186/s40164-026-00848-3.abstract: Cancer remains a formidable challenge in global oncology, with conventional treatments often failing to achieve durable responses in advanced stages. Adoptive cell therapy (ACT), despite its revolutionary success in hematological malignancies, faces critical bottlenecks in solid tumors, including a hostile immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), restricted cellular trafficking, and the rapid onset of T-cell exhaustion. This review systematically explores the evolution of ACT platforms, ranging from foundational tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) to precision-engineered chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T and T-cell receptor (TCR)-T therapies. We highlight how innovative engineering strategies such as the integration of "armored" CARs, synthetic gene circuits, and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing have been employed to enhance the persistence and polyfunctionality of effector cells. Beyond T-cell-centric approaches, we examine the emerging landscape of diverse immune effector cells, including CAR-natural killer (NK) cells, and CAR-macrophages (CAR-M), which offer unique advantages in antigen recognition and safety profiles. Furthermore, we detail the synergistic potential of multimodal combination regimens, where ACT is paired with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), localized radiotherapy, or nanotechnology-based delivery systems to dismantle TME barriers and achieve systemic anti-tumor immunity. By tracing the journey of therapeutic cells from ex vivo expansion to intratumoral infiltration and cytotoxicity, this review illuminates the molecular mechanisms governing therapeutic efficacy. Finally, we discuss the current clinical trial landscape, manufacturing hurdles, and the regulatory pathways essential for transitioning these sophisticated cellular products from bench to bedside.

doi:10.1186/s40164-026-00849-2.abstract: Direct RAS targeting has progressed from pharmacologic proof of concept to routine treatment for selected KRAS G12C-mutant cancers. KRAS G12C inhibitors and KRAS G12C-EGFR combinations established allele- and lineage-specific treatment paradigms. More recently, the multiselective RAS(ON) inhibitor daraxonrasib became the first FDA-approved direct RAS-targeted therapy for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, while the KRAS G12D-directed degrader setidegrasib remains investigational. Target engagement alone, however, does not ensure durable disease control, and the same drug class can perform differently across tumor lineages. This Review develops an adaptive RAS signaling ecosystem model in which allele and isoform biology, membrane organization, feedback architecture, mutant-wild-type RAS crosstalk, co-mutation patterns, chromatin state, epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, metabolism, spatial heterogeneity, the tumor microenvironment and treatment delivery jointly determine pathway dependence and therapeutic escape. Comparisons among pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, lung adenocarcinoma and NRAS-mutant melanoma show how related oncogenic RAS nodes acquire different vulnerabilities in distinct tissue contexts. We integrate direct RAS inhibition with mechanism-guided vertical and horizontal strategies directed at feedback rebound, bypass signaling, cell-state persistence, stromal protection, metabolic adaptation and immune exclusion. We then translate this model into a biomarker-integrated development framework that links serial circulating tumor DNA, modality-matched pharmacodynamic assays, paired tissue sampling, spatial profiling and toxicity-aware scheduling to prespecified, falsifiable treatment hypotheses. RAS dependence is conditional rather than absolute. Durable control will require strategies that match the RAS allele and tumor lineage to the dominant adaptive circuitry, verify that target and pathway suppression persist over time, and maintain sufficient dose intensity to exert biologically effective pressure without disabling antitumor immunity or normal-tissue function.

doi:10.1186/s40164-026-00850-9.abstract: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) is a well-established oncogenic driver in multiple solid tumors, most prominently in breast and gastric cancers. Beyond gene amplification-driven signaling through canonical PI3K/AKT and RAS/MAPK pathways, emerging evidence reveals that HER2 functions within a highly dynamic and context-dependent tumor ecosystem. Interactions between HER2-positive tumor cells and immune and stromal compartments actively shape the tumor microenvironment, contributing to immune evasion, therapeutic resistance and disease progression. A central challenge in the clinical management of HER2-altered cancers is pronounced spatial and temporal heterogeneity, which undermines both diagnostic accuracy and the durability of targeted therapies. In response, advances in multi-omics profiling, liquid biopsy technologies and artificial intelligence-assisted analytics are redefining HER2 assessment, shifting it from static tissue-based classification towards dynamic, minimally invasive monitoring. In parallel, the therapeutic landscape has evolved from single-agent HER2 blockade to rational combination strategies. In particular, antibody-drug conjugates have emerged as a transformative modality, extending the therapeutic reach of HER2 targeting beyond traditional indications and offering new opportunities to overcome heterogeneity and drug resistance. This review synthesizes current insights into the molecular and microenvironmental biology of HER2-altered solid tumors and discusses how these advances are reshaping next-generation precision oncology.

doi:10.1186/s40164-026-00851-8.abstract: Timdarpacept (IMM01) is a recombinant signal regulatory protein α-IgG1 fusion protein that exerts antitumor activity by blocking the "don't eat me" signal while simultaneously activating the "eat me" signal, inducing robust antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis. We report the final phase II results of treatment-naïve higher risk chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) patients treated with IMM01 in combination with azacitidine. We assessed the safety and efficacy of IMM01 in combination with azacitidine (AZA) as first-line therapy for newly diagnosed CMML patients. IMM01 was administered intravenously at 2.0 mg/kg weekly, and AZA was administered subcutaneously at 75 mg/m² on days 1-7 of each 28-day cycle. As of the data cut-off on May 13, 2025, 24 patients were enrolled. Of 22 efficacy-evaluable patients, the overall response rate (ORR) was 72.7% (16/22; 95% CI 49.8-89.3), including 27.3% complete response (CR), 13.6% marrow CR (mCR) with hematologic improvement (HI), 4.5% HI alone, and 27.3% mCR alone. The median time to response was 1.8 months (range, 0.9-3.6), and the median duration of response was 16.9 months (95% CI 5.1-NE). Median overall survival and progression-free survival were 22.2 months (95% CI 9.0-NE) and 17.8 months (95% CI 5.3-NE), respectively. The most common grade ≥ 3 treatment-related adverse events (≥ 10%) were lymphopenia (66.7%), leukopenia (62.5%), neutropenia (62.5%), thrombocytopenia (58.3%), anemia (33.3%), and pneumonia (16.7%). IMM01 in combination with AZA was generally well tolerated and effective in treatment-naïve higher risk CMML patients. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov identiﬁer: NCT05140811.

doi:10.1186/s40164-026-00854-5.abstract: For more than a century after its initial description, glioblastoma (GBM) has remained one of the most therapeutically refractory human malignancies, resembling an almost impregnable fortress against modern oncology. Despite extensive molecular characterization and identification of numerous actionable targets, survival outcomes have improved only marginally. GBM is characterized by profound spatial and cellular heterogeneity, adaptive signaling rewiring, extensive phenotypic plasticity, an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, and major pharmacological constraints imposed by the blood-brain barrier. This review examines the resulting disconnect between biological rationale and clinical outcome through three interrelated translational principles that determine whether mechanistically compelling therapies can achieve meaningful clinical benefit in GBM. First, who is treated and what is biologically active: therapeutic efficacy depends on matching patients to functional pathway dependencies beyond static molecular alterations. Second, whether the drug reaches and modulates its intended target: candidate therapies must achieve sufficient intratumoral exposure and demonstrate target modulation. Third, how the tumor adapts under therapeutic pressure: durable efficacy requires accounting for receptor tyrosine kinase switching, phenotypic plasticity, immune adaptation, and spatial escape. By linking these principles to the molecular, spatial, and pharmacological organization of GBM, this review frames the disease as a dynamic tumor ecosystem and provides a framework for interpreting recurrent clinical failure and guiding more biologically informed therapeutic development.
