doi:10.1186/s40364-023-00540-2.abstract: Abstract While the field of precision oncology is rapidly expanding and more targeted options are revolutionizing cancer treatment paradigms, therapeutic resistance particularly to immunotherapy remains a pressing challenge. This can be largely attributed to the dynamic tumor-stroma interactions that continuously alter the microenvironment. While to date most advancements have been made through examining the clinical utility of tissue-based biomarkers, their invasive nature and lack of a holistic representation of the evolving disease in a real-time manner could result in suboptimal treatment decisions. Thus, using minimally-invasive approaches to identify biomarkers that predict and monitor treatment response as well as alert to the emergence of recurrences is of a critical need. Currently, research efforts are shifting towards developing liquid biopsy-based biomarkers obtained from patients over the course of disease. Liquid biopsy represents a unique opportunity to monitor intercellular communication within the tumor microenvironment which could occur through the exchange of extracellular vesicles (EVs). EVs are lipid bilayer membrane nanoscale vesicles which transfer a plethora of biomolecules that mediate intercellular crosstalk, shape the tumor microenvironment, and modify drug response. The capture of EVs using innovative approaches, such as microfluidics, magnetic beads, and aptamers, allow their analysis via high throughput multi-omics techniques and facilitate their use for biomarker discovery. Artificial intelligence, using machine and deep learning algorithms, is advancing multi-omics analyses to uncover candidate biomarkers and predictive signatures that are key for translation into clinical trials. With the increasing recognition of the role of EVs in mediating immune evasion and as a valuable biomarker source, these real-time snapshots of cellular communication are promising to become an important tool in the field of precision oncology and spur the recognition of strategies to block resistance to immunotherapy. In this review, we discuss the emerging role of EVs in biomarker research describing current advances in their isolation and analysis techniques as well as their function as mediators in the tumor microenvironment. We also highlight recent lung cancer and melanoma studies that point towards their application as predictive biomarkers for immunotherapy and their potential clinical use in precision immuno-oncology.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01000-3.abstract: Abstract Central nervous system (CNS) leukemia remains a major clinical challenge in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, largely due to the restrictive nature of the blood–brain barrier (BBB), which severely limits therapeutic delivery and contributes to high relapse rates and poor prognosis. Here, we report ALB-phage, a bioengineered a nti- l eukemia b ackpack–phage system designed for active BBB navigation and intracranial drug delivery. M13 bacteriophages were genetically engineered to display BBB-homing ligands, forming a high-aspect-ratio biological transport platform (BTP). A leukemia-targeting therapeutic backpack (L-Pak) was constructed by encapsulating methotrexate within lipid nanoparticles fused with leukemia cell membranes, enabling homotypic targeting. The L-Pak was conjugated to the BTP via a matrix metalloproteinase-responsive PLGVR linker, allowing selective cleavage within the cerebrospinal fluid. Owing to its filamentous morphology, ALB-phage achieved efficient BBB translocation predominantly through energy-dependent macropinocytosis with an additional contribution from clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Both in vitro and in vivo studies demonstrate that ALB-phage effectively penetrates the BBB and selectively eradicates leukemia blasts, resulting in marked tumor suppression and a significant extension of median survival from 29 to 40 days in cell-line-derived xenograft models. Collectively, this M13 bacteriophage-based all-in-one platform integrates targeted BBB penetration with homology-mediated cytotoxicity, offering a promising strategy for the treatment of CNS leukemia and other central nervous system malignancies.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01011-0.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy has achieved clinical progress in various malignancies, yet primary and acquired resistance limits its efficacy in solid tumors. Myeloid cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME), including tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs), and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), undergo metabolic reprogramming under hypoxia and nutrient stress. They impair effector T cell function and may contribute to exhaustion-associated states via nutrient competition, release of toxic metabolites, and formation of physical barriers, representing a critical resistance mechanism. This review summarizes the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of myeloid cells and the metabolic networks underlying their immunosuppressive phenotypes, focusing on dysregulated lipid and cholesterol metabolism, amino acid remodeling, the glycolytic switch, and subcellular stress responses. We analyze how metabolic dysregulation causes T cell dysfunction and, in defined contexts, contributes to exhaustion-associated transcriptional programs through nutrient competition, toxic metabolite accumulation, and upregulation of inhibitory receptor ligands, and summarize intervention strategies targeting myeloid recruitment, phenotypic remodeling, metabolic reprogramming, and pathological structures combined with ICB. We discuss challenges of efficacy heterogeneity and safety in clinical translation, and highlight the prospects of multi-omics and computational biology in guiding next-generation combination immunotherapy. Understanding myeloid metabolic plasticity may provide a basis for overcoming immunotherapy resistance and establishing precise synergistic strategies.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01016-9.abstract: Abstract Background Edematous malnutrition, aka kwashiorkor, is a phenotype of severe malnutrition whose pathophysiology remains poorly understood. Methods In this case-control study, we employed plasma lipidomics, metabolomics, and proteomics, urine metabolomics and gut microbiome profiling to delineate molecular features specific to kwashiorkor in 60 children aged 6–59 months from Niger compared to marasmus ( n = 60) and non-malnourished children (NAM) ( n = 60) matched by age, sex, and clinical triage score. Features were defined as kwashiorkor-specific if they also correlated with edema severity and normalized following nutritional rehabilitation. Results We identified a plasma proteomic factor featuring lumican, gelsolin, and tetranectin and a lipidomic factor enriched in sphingolipids. Both differed in kwashiorkor compared to marasmus and NAM, were associated with edema grade, and trended towards normalcy after nutritional treatment, which are consistent with ECM remodeling and sphingolipid dysregulation. In contrast, neither (plasma and urine) metabolomic profiles nor gut microbiome composition showed kwashiorkor-specific signatures, although our urine and gut microbiome analyses may be underpowered. Conclusion These findings advance understanding of kwashiorkor pathophysiology beyond nutrient deficiency and highlight ECM and sphingolipid features associated with its distinct clinical and molecular characteristics compared to marasmus.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01017-8.abstract: Attenuated oncolytic bacteria represent a promising targeted delivery platform for cancer therapy; however, the lack of non-invasive biomarkers to monitor their persistent intra-tumoral colonization severely limits clinical translation, efficacy assessment, and safety monitoring. Here, we identify the sustained elevation of peripheral blood CXCL1 as a dynamic, non-invasive biomarker for the persistent colonization of attenuated Salmonella in solid tumors. Across four orthotopic preclinical models (including lung, breast, and bladder cancers, as well as melanoma), effective bacterial colonization specifically drove prolonged systemic CXCL1 elevation. Focusing specifically on the melanoma model, rapid bacterial eradication via intratumoral antibiotics restored CXCL1 to baseline. Furthermore, comparisons with a colonization-deficient mutant strain confirmed that CXCL1 elevation strictly depends on intra-tumoral, rather than systemic, bacterial burden. Mechanistically, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) revealed that tumor-colonizing bacteria profoundly reshape the tumor microenvironment by directly activating and recruiting neutrophils, monocytes, and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), which act as the primary cellular sources of CXCL1 production and systemic leakage. These findings highlight peripheral blood CXCL1 as a robust and actionable biomarker for real-time monitoring of oncolytic bacterial colonization, providing crucial guidance for dosing optimization and biosafety evaluation in clinical applications.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01019-6.abstract: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) of histone H3 at lysine 9 (H3K9) contribute to chromatin homeostasis and transcriptional regulation and have been implicated in cancer progression. However, how distinct H3K9 modification states differ in function, compete for the same lysine residue, and dynamically respond to cellular context remains incompletely understood. This review summarizes the biochemical characteristics and enzymatic regulation of H3K9 methylation, acetylation, and non-acetyl acylations, including lactylation, β-hydroxybutyrylation, butyrylation, and crotonylation. We examine their roles in DNA replication, transcription, and DNA damage repair, as well as their interplay with other epigenetic regulatory mechanisms. We further discuss how H3K9-associated regulatory networks contribute to tumor proliferation, stemness maintenance, metabolic reprogramming, invasion and metastasis, immune microenvironment remodeling, therapeutic resistance, and programmed cell death, emphasizing their context-dependent and, in some settings, opposing biological effects. Finally, we evaluate preclinical and clinical advances in pharmacologically targeting H3K9-associated regulatory enzymes, distinguishing residue-specific mechanistic evidence from broader enzyme-level effects, and outline future directions for biomarker-guided epigenetic therapies in cancer.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01020-z.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are key regulators of tumor progression and immune suppression within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Emerging evidence identifies ubiquitination, a dynamic post-translational modification that regulates protein stability, localization, and signaling activity, as a critical determinant of TAM function. Ubiquitin signaling orchestrates macrophage inflammatory responses, metabolic reprogramming, and tumor cell-immune cell crosstalk through coordinated actions of ubiquitin-activating enzymes, ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes, ubiquitin-protein ligases (E3s), and deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs). Dysregulation of these ubiquitin networks fosters an immunosuppressive microenvironment, thereby promoting tumor growth, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. In this review, we summarize recent advances in the role of ubiquitination in TAM biology, focusing on key E3 ubiquitin ligases and DUBs in TAM immunity. We further discuss emerging ubiquitin-dependent signaling pathways that integrate metabolic and inflammatory cues within TAMs. Finally, we highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting ubiquitination machinery to reprogram TAMs and remodel the TME. Collectively, this review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding ubiquitin-mediated regulation of TAM function and offers novel perspectives for developing ubiquitination-based cancer immunotherapies.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01020-z.title: Ubiquitin signaling in tumor-associated macrophage reprogramming: mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities in cancers.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01021-y.abstract: Persistent CAR-T donor cells after CAR-T-bridged allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) may complicate hematopoietic recovery. When CAR-T and HSCT cells share the same donor, standard donor chimerism cannot distinguish their contributions. We report three patients with relapsed/refractory T-cell malignancies who received CAR-T and allo-HSCT from distinct donors, enabling three-party short tandem repeat (STR) analysis to resolve CAR-T donor, HSCT donor, and recipient compartments. Patient 2, with detectable residual CAR transgene at transplantation (240 copies/µg gDNA), developed mixed chimerism with cytopenia (MCC) and a CAR-T donor contribution of 47.72%. Patient 3, also with detectable residual CAR transgene (22,162 copies/µg gDNA), developed mixed chimerism, with a CAR-T donor contribution of 14.23%. In contrast, Patient 1, with undetectable CAR transgene at transplantation, showed stable complete donor chimerism (CDC) and hematopoietic recovery. Guided by the two-step reconstitution pattern observed in Patient 1, we administered CAR-target-knockout donor lymphocyte infusion (KO-DLI) as rescue treatment in Patient 2 and preemptive intervention in Patient 3. Both eventually became CAR-undetectable, with restoration of CDC and hematologic recovery, although the independent effect of KO-DLI could not be isolated. All three remain in complete remission (follow-up + 713, +335, + 201 days). Residual CAR transgene at transplantation may serve as an early risk signal for CAR-T donor cell persistence, and KO-DLI warrants prospective validation as a transplantation-sparing salvage approach.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01021-y.title: Persistent CAR-T donor cells contribute to mixed chimerism with cytopenia after CAR-T-bridged allo-HSCT: rescue by CAR-target-knockout DLI in three cases.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01023-w.abstract: Abstract Background The revision of the WHO classification of CNS tumours now distinguishes grade 4 diffuse gliomas by their molecular features, but tailored treatment is yet to be standardised. Glioblastoma (isocitrate dehydrogenase ( IDH ))-wildtype tumours harbouring an unmethylated O 6 -methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase “(u MGMT )” promoter are inherently resistant to temozolomide (TMZ). However, no standardised treatment recommendations are available for grade 4 astrocytoma IDH -mutant. We previously demonstrated that administration of bortezomib (BTZ) 48 h prior to TMZ depletes MGMT protein and sensitizes u MGMT glioma cells to TMZ. Based on these findings, a phase IB/II trial was initiated to evaluate the safety and clinical activity of sequential BTZ and TMZ. This interim analysis aimed to determine a futility safeguard, identify molecular and pharmacodynamic determinants of treatment response and failure in the first 15 patients consecutively treated. Methods Adult patients with recurrent grade 4 IDH- mutant astrocytoma or IDH- wildtype glioblastoma, u MGMT promoter, measurable disease, Karnofsky Performance Status ≥ 70, and disease progression ≥ 12 weeks after radiotherapy were enrolled. Patients received intravenous BTZ 1.3 mg/m² on days 1, 4, and 7 of each 28-day cycle, followed by oral TMZ 200 mg/m²/day for 5 consecutive days beginning on day 3. Targeted sequencing of glioma-associated genes and longitudinal plasma proteomic profiling using LC-MS/MS were performed before, during, and after treatment. Results Fifteen patients (median age 52 years) comprised 10 patients with IDH - wildtype glioblastoma and 5 patients with grade 4 IDH -mutant astrocytoma. Disease control (partial response and stable disease) was observed in 4/10 (40%) IDH - wildtype glioblastoma patients, comprising one PR and three cases of SD. In contrast, all five patients with grade 4 IDH -mutant astrocytoma experienced rapid progressive disease. Notably, non-responding IDH -wildtype glioblastomas and all IDH -mutant tumours harboured alterations affecting the CDKN2A/RB1 -cell-cycle regulatory axis, including CDKN2A and/or RB1 loss, with one IDH -mutant patient additionally harbouring PIK3CA gain. By comparison, responding IDH- wildtype glioblastomas were characterized by amplified EGFR , nuclear NF-κB (p65/RelA) activation, and absence of RB- pathway alterations. Longitudinal proteomic analyses demonstrated comparatively attenuated treatment-induced changes in proteins associated with invasion and extracellular matrix remodelling in responders, whereas proteins involved in damage clearance immune phenotype, platelet activation, aggregation, and degranulation were significantly altered during disease control. Conclusions Sequential BTZ and TMZ therapy was feasible with manageable hematologic and non-hematologic toxicities and met prespecified interim futility criteria, supporting continued recruitment to the phase II study. Disease control was restricted to a molecularly defined subset of IDH - wildtype glioblastoma characterized by EGFR amplification and NF-κB activation. In contrast, universal treatment failure among grade 4 IDH -mutant astrocytomas was associated with alterations of the CDKN2A/RB1 cell-cycle checkpoint pathway, suggesting that advanced molecular evolution and cell-cycle deregulation may override the survival advantage typically associated with IDH -mutant gliomas and limit the effectiveness of MGMT-targeted sensitization strategies. Registry ClinicalTrials.gov trial registration number: NCT03643549, date of registration: 2018-08-21.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01025-8.abstract: Solid tumors remain challenging for cellular immunotherapy, and CAR-T or CAR-M cells alone often have limited efficacy. Combining these approaches may improve therapeutic activity; however, our previous in vitro study observed increased IL-6, while extracellular matrix (ECM) barriers can restrict immune-cell access. We engineered IL6-CD147 CAR-M, a synthetic IL-6-responsive macrophage construct designed to couple an IL-6-binding scFv to a CD147-containing module. Following IL-6 stimulation, IL6-CD147 CAR-M showed increased MMP-2, MMP-9, MMP-11, and MMP-13 transcripts and proteins. A CD147-deletion control did not reproduce the enhanced MMP transcriptional response, and GM6001 reduced CAR-T cell migration through Matrigel toward IL6-CD147 CAR-M-conditioned medium. In defined 80:20 mixed-antigen tumor models, IL6-CD147 CAR-M plus CAR-T increased tumor killing and inflammatory/cytotoxic mediators while reducing detectable extracellular IL-6. In vivo, combined therapy reduced tumor burden, prolonged survival, increased immune-cell infiltration, altered immune composition, and was not associated with overt histopathological abnormalities in the examined major organs at the assessed time points. These findings support further evaluation of an IL-6-responsive, CD147-containing CAR-M strategy; proximal receptor signaling and the mechanism underlying reduced extracellular IL-6 remain unresolved.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01026-7.abstract: Familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (FHLH) is classically pediatric, but adult-onset disease is increasingly recognized. Whether adult-onset FHLH differs from pediatric/adolescent-onset disease remains incompletely defined. We aimed to characterize age-related differences in a nationwide multicenter cohort of patients with FHLH in China. We conducted a nationwide multicenter retrospective study of 223 patients with FHLH from 27 centers in China. Genetic architecture, central nervous system (CNS) involvement, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), and survival were compared by age at onset, with adult-onset disease defined as onset at age ≥ 18 years and pediatric/adolescent-onset disease as onset at < 18 years. In this cohort, adult-onset disease accounted for 54/223 cases (24.2%). In the PRF1/UNC13D subset (n = 192), higher non-truncating variant burden was associated with adult onset (unadjusted OR per additional recorded variant, 1.95; 95% CI, 1.17-3.39), although the association attenuated after adjustment for gene and zygosity (adjusted OR, 1.58; 95% CI, 0.94-2.75). Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was the predominant documented trigger in adults. CNS involvement was common across age groups (46.4%), with uncertain prognostic significance. Adults underwent allo-HSCT less frequently (49.1% vs. 70.2%) and were less often in complete response before transplantation (15.4% vs. 46.8%). Adult onset remained associated with poorer overall survival after multivariable adjustment including time-dependent allo-HSCT (HR, 3.74; 95% CI, 1.96-7.12). Post-HSCT survival was also poorer in adults. Adult-onset FHLH was associated with non-truncating variant enrichment and poorer overall and post-HSCT survival. These findings support considering inherited disease despite acquired triggers and careful assessment of disease control and transplant-related risks in adults with FHLH.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01026-7.title: Adult-onset familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis has distinct genetic architecture and outcomes: a nationwide multicenter cohort study in China.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01027-6.abstract: A recent population-based cohort study of Seoul residents in South Korea reported increased incidence of several cancers within one year of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination. We examined whether a short-term, population-level change in cancer incidence trends was detectable at the national vaccination rollout, using a design that does not compare vaccinated with unvaccinated individuals. We conducted an interrupted time series analysis of Korea National Health Insurance Service data for 36,024,394 individuals born between 1955 and 2004, covering February 2011 to September 2025 (176 months). The intervention point was August 2021, when cumulative first-dose coverage exceeded 50%. Monthly incidence of 13 cancer categories defined by ICD-10 code ranges and of four site-specific cancers (stomach, colorectum, lung and prostate) was compared with counterfactual forecasts from ARIMA/SARIMA models, and segmented regression estimated immediate level and trend changes (significance threshold P < 0.01). The placement of the intervention point was varied from 0 to 18 months, and the resulting estimates were compared with those obtained at 30 placebo points in the pre-pandemic period. Overall, 89.3% of the population received at least one dose. No immediate level change (relative risk 0.923-1.072) or trend change (0.995-1.005) reached significance for any of the 13 categories, and none reached significance for the four site-specific cancers. Across the lag grid, 2.0% of estimates met the threshold, compared with 4.1% at placebo points. The 99% confidence limits excluded immediate increases larger than 8.9% to 23.0% across the 13 categories and 8.1% to 23.4% across the four site-specific cancers. The national SARS-CoV-2 vaccination rollout in South Korea was not accompanied by a detectable short-term, population-level change in cancer incidence trends over the 50 months that followed. Not applicable.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01029-4.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a heterogeneous autoimmune disease for which selecting the most appropriate first targeted therapy remains challenging. We integrated ex vivo immune-cell functional assays, targeted proteomics, clinical outcomes, and a three-dimensional (3D) synovial model to identify treatment-associated molecular signatures and evaluate their relationship with subsequent response to Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKi) or tumour necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi). Peripheral blood mononuclear cells and neutrophils from 48 b/tsDMARDs-naïve RA patients were cultured with autologous serum and treated ex vivo with Baricitinib or Etanercept to assess proliferation, adhesion, NETosis, and 92 inflammation-related proteins. The resulting JAKi- and TNFi-modulated protein signatures were subsequently evaluated in pretreatment serum from four independent RA treatment cohorts (n = 223; naïve and non-naïve). Unsupervised clustering was used to identify molecular subgroups, which were related to longitudinal DAS28-CRP outcomes at 3, 6, and 12 months. Logistic regression, neural network, and random forest models were evaluated using repeated nested cross-validation in naïve patients to discriminate treatment-specific 6-month remission outcomes. In a subset of naïve remission achievers, paired baseline and 6-month sera were applied to a 3D synovial micromass model. Ex vivo JAKi and TNFi comparably modulated immune cell functions but induced distinct protein signatures with limited overlap. When evaluated in pretreatment baseline serum, these signatures stratified b/tsDMARD-naïve patients into clusters with different baseline inflammatory profiles and treatment-specific ΔDAS28-CRP. High baseline expression of a drug-specific signature was associated with remission with the corresponding therapy and failure to achieve remission with the alternative treatment. Under repeated nested cross-validation, logistic regression showed the highest mean discrimination among the models, with an AUC of 0.70 (SD, 0.03; empirical 2.5th-97.5th percentile, 0.65-0.75) for distinguishing treatment-specific remission outcomes in b/tsDMARD-naïve RA. In remission achievers, 6-month sera from either therapy significantly reduced synovial lining thickness in 3D micromasses versus baseline. Ex vivo-derived JAKi- and TNFi-associated immune-related protein signatures, integrated within a machine-learning framework, showed moderate discriminatory ability for treatment-specific remission patterns in b/tsDMARD-naïve RA and, together with complementary evidence of reduced synovial lining thickness in remission achievers, support further investigation of biomarker-informed selection between JAKi and TNFi as first targeted therapies.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01030-x.abstract: The immune checkpoints and their inhibitors are revolutionary advances in tumour immunotherapy. Immune checkpoints, however, have a broad spectrum effect. They not only contribute to tumour immune escape, but also are involved in the regulation of the pathopathological processes of numerous inflammatory illnesses, such as sepsis, autoimmune diseases, organ transplant rejection, and viral infections, among others. Today, a considerable gap in knowledge remains regarding immune checkpoints and immune checkpoint inhibitors in non-tumour inflammatory diseases, which remains largely unaddressed. At the same time, the emergence of immune-related adverse events and resistance challenges related to the clinical use of immune checkpoint inhibitors is becoming increasingly prominent, posing a significant obstacle to their application across various diseases. To overcome such issues, this narrative review establishes a systematic framework that links immune checkpoints to various inflammatory diseases and explores the associated therapeutic and clinical challenges. These diseases pose therapeutic and clinical challenges of immune checkpoint inhibitors, which we explore. The paper not only thoroughly describes the clinical picture, pathophysiology, and interventions in immunologic adverse events but also suggests a prospective strategy to confront the existing problems with immune checkpoint inhibitors in 3 dimensions: evaluation, management, and prevention. It will attempt to present a new conceptual framework for a comprehensive understanding of the dual role of immune checkpoints (in maintaining immune homeostasis and facilitating disease progression) and to provide a solid theoretical foundation for the development of safer and more effective cross-disease immunotherapy.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01031-w.abstract: Abstract Background T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive malignancy with poor prognosis, especially in relapsed/refractory patients. Aberrant PI3K/AKT/mTOR and NOTCH1 signaling converge on c-MYC to drive proliferation and ribosome biogenesis, but single-agent inhibitors targeting these pathways have shown limited clinical efficacy. Methods An FDA-approved drug library screen identified osimertinib as a candidate anti-T-ALL agent. Its efficacy and mechanism were evaluated in four T-ALL cell lines (MOLT-4, Jurkat, CCRF/CEM, and MOLT-3) with different TP53 statuses and in primary T-ALL blasts. Combination studies with selinexor, an exportin 1 (XPO1) inhibitor, were performed. Multi-omics, biochemical, and functional assays were used, and efficacy and toxicity were assessed in T-ALL xenograft models. Results Osimertinib suppressed leukemic progression in vivo by promoting proteasome-dependent degradation of c-MYC through a non-canonical, EGFR-independent pathway that cannot be fully explained by inhibition of PI3K/AKT/mTOR or NOTCH1 signaling alone. This c-MYC suppression impaired ribosome biogenesis, and combining osimertinib with selinexor further disrupted this process. The combination increased apoptosis at low concentrations (0.5-2 µM osimertinib plus 20 nM selinexor), with clear synergy at 2 µM in all four T-ALL cell lines. Mechanistically, the combination caused nuclear retention of RPS6, nuclear accumulation of RPL5/RPL11, nucleolar stress (fibrillarin dispersal), decreased MDM2 protein levels, p53 stabilization, BAX activation (6A7), cytochrome c release, c-MYC depletion, and translational suppression. In vivo, the combination improved survival and reduced leukemic burden with minimal toxicity to normal cells at low doses. Potential biomarkers include c-MYC dependency and TP53 status as candidate stratification factors, and treatment-induced c-MYC depletion and RPL5/RPL11 nuclear accumulation as candidate pharmacodynamic biomarkers. Conclusions Osimertinib plus selinexor depletes c-MYC, induces nucleolar stress, and suppresses translation, which together drive T-ALL cell apoptosis. This mechanism-driven combination shows preclinical efficacy with limited toxicity in the normal-cell and xenograft models tested. Further studies incorporating pharmacokinetic monitoring, PDX models, and prospective validation of candidate biomarkers such as c-MYC dependency, TP53 status, and RPL5/RPL11 nuclear accumulation are warranted before clinical translation.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01032-9.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has significantly influenced cancer therapy by enabling the targeting of traditionally undruggable oncogenic drivers such as transcription factors, chromatin remodelers, and mediators of protein-protein interactions, overcoming limitations of conventional inhibitors. This approach harnesses endogenous cellular machinery, specifically the ubiquitin-proteasome system and lysosomal pathways, to achieve precise and efficient elimination of pathogenic proteins. Currently, one degradation-based agent, vepdegestrant, has been approved by FDA, while most agents remain in Phase I or II evaluation, representing significant progress in addressing previously intractable targets in cancers. Nevertheless, a substantial number of disease-relevant proteins remain challenging to modulate effectively. This review focuses on undruggable targets in cancer and distinguishes three target categories: 1) Structurally undruggable targets; 2) Formerly undruggable, now inhibitor-accessible but degradation offers a mechanistic advantage; 3) Non-enzymatic targets. We highlight recent advances in the development of TPD strategies against these elusive targets to a cutoff of 30 September 2026, with the aim of providing a more systematic theoretical foundation for the broader application of the developing TPD in cancer therapeutics.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01036-5.abstract: Abstract Background Relapsed/refractory (R/R) lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remains a clinical challenge with limited therapies and poor prognosis. CAR‑NK cell therapy has shown promise in solid tumors, but its efficacy is limited by both the availability of effective targets and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. CD73 (NT5E), highly expressed across solid tumors, catalyzes adenosine production to drive immunosuppression, representing both a specific CAR‑NK target and a key leverage point to overcome tumor immune evasion. However, its systematic evaluation as a therapeutically actionable target for CAR‑NK cell therapy in R/R LUAD remains unexplored. Methods We first characterized CD73 expression through integrative analysis of public datasets, primary and relapsed clinical LUAD specimens, and LUAD cell lines derived from primary and metastatic tumors. We then constructed CD73‑CAR‑NK cells and assessed their in vitro cytotoxicity across LUAD cell lines of varying malignancy, as well as their effects on extracellular adenosine and resistance to adenosine‑mediated immunosuppression. Finally, we assessed their antitumor efficacy in a stepwise manner across a tiered panel of in vivo models, including cell line‑derived xenograft (CDX), metastasis, patient‑derived xenograft (PDX), and clinically relevant immune‑humanized PDX models. Results CD73 expression was elevated in metastasis-derived LUAD cell lines and R/R LUAD specimens. Accordingly, CD73-CAR-NK92 cells exhibited potent cytotoxicity against CD73-high LUAD cells, accompanied by an activated effector phenotype, reduced extracellular adenosine, partial resistance to adenosine-mediated suppression, and limited activity toward normal bronchial epithelial cells. Notably, this enhanced function was consistently observed across multiple NK cell sources including peripheral blood-derived NK (PBNK), umbilical cord blood‑derived NK (UBNK), and iPSC-derived NK (iNK). In vivo, CD73‑CAR‑NK92 cells significantly suppressed tumor growth and metastasis, with enhanced tumor‑site enrichment, prolonged retention, and elevated intratumoral levels of TNF‑α and IFN‑γ. Importantly, in an immune‑humanized PDX mouse model, CD73‑CAR‑NK92 cells significantly reduced the growth of R/R patient‑derived xenografts, accompanied by immune remodeling, without marked systemic inflammation during the observation period. Conclusions These findings provide preclinical evidence that CD73-CAR-NK cells exhibit potent antitumor efficacy for R/R LUAD through their dual functions of eliminating CD73-high tumor cells and resisting adenosine-mediated immunosuppressive signaling, supporting their therapeutic potential.

doi:10.1186/s40364-026-01036-5.title: CD73-targeted CAR-NK cell therapy displays potent antitumor activity and translational potential in relapsed/refractory lung adenocarcinoma.

doi:10.1200/po-25-00377.abstract: PURPOSE Updated analysis of phase I/II trials in recurrent/refractory (R/R) Ewing sarcoma (EwS) over the past 11 years. METHODS A systematic review was performed to identify phase I/II trials for R/R EwS in three databases (WHO, US National Library of Medicine, and European Clinical Trials Database) and/or published in PubMed/ASCO/European Society for Medical Oncology websites from 2014 to 2024. The search criteria included EwS OR bone sarcoma OR sarcoma AND Phase-I OR Phase-II. Eligibility and data extraction were performed independently by three reviewers, with priority given to trials with EwS specified data. Trials were categorized by therapeutic intervention, including targeted therapies, immunotherapy, chemotherapy, and combined therapies. RESULTS One hundred eight trials met inclusion criteria, predominantly academic (70%) and multicenter (81.5%), with significant US and European collaboration. Trial designs were mainly single-arm, with an increase in multiarm trials in the recent years and increased focus on the pediatric population. Trial modalities emphasized targeted therapies with tyrosine kinase, poly-ADP ribose polymerase, EWSR1::FLI1, and cell cycle inhibitors. Immunotherapy with monoclonal antibodies and CAR-T cells as primary agents is also under investigation. The COVID-19 pandemic coincided with a marked reduction in trial initiation in 2020. Among evaluable data, disease control rates averaged 44% and response rates 8%. CONCLUSION This review highlights evolving therapeutic directions in R/R EwS, with increased emphasis on targeted therapies and immunotherapies. Despite pandemic-related delays, trials have progressed in exploring novel targets, including EWSR1::FLI1 oncogenic fusion and DNA repair pathways. These findings underscore ongoing global efforts to address critical unmet needs in EwS treatment, offering a foundation for future trial designs, especially international, randomized phase‐II trials across all age ranges.

doi:10.1200/po-25-00642.abstract: PURPOSE High levels of DNA replication stress and defects in the DNA damage response (DDR) pathways are vulnerabilities of many poor prognosis childhood malignancies. Ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related protein (ATR) is a key regulator of these pathways and constitutes an attractive target, especially in combination. However, the malignancies where ATR inhibitors have maximum benefit and synergistic combinations differ between adults and children. DESIGN ACCELERATE convened a multistakeholder meeting and conducted review and analysis to propose the optimal pathway for the development of ATR inhibitors in pediatric malignancies. RESULTS Considering the lack of identified biomarkers, the initial evaluation of ATR inhibitors should focus on Ewing sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and neuroblastoma in view of their high levels of DNA replication stress and defects in DDR pathways. Early phase trials of ATR inhibitors should be iterative, based on a clear hypothesis with responders and nonresponders undergoing detailed molecular analysis and a revised new hypothesis generated. Trial designs should restrict monotherapy evaluation to a brief exposure in a small number of patients and progress rapidly to combinations. Highlighted combination partners are poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors and antibody drug conjugates with topoisomerase I inhibitor payloads. Combinations with ALK inhibitors (in ALK / MYCN -aberrant neuroblastoma) and aurora A kinase (in MYCN -amplified) are supported by robust mechanisms of action and preclinical data. Early interactions with regulators are crucial, and early phase clinical trials should be conducted in regulatory-approved, academic-sponsored, industry-supported, platform trials. CONCLUSION ATR inhibitors are a prototype for the development of medicinal products in a limited pediatric population. For the substantial potential of ATR inhibitors in children with malignancy to be realized, strategic planning between academia, industry, regulators, and patient advocates is vital.

doi:10.1200/po-25-01195.abstract: No curative options are available for medulloblastoma (MB) in the relapse setting. The tumor microenvironment (TME) influences progression and therapy response, presenting a promising target for therapeutic advances. Prior single-cell analyses have characterized the cellular components of the TME but lack spatial context. We hypothesize that spatial architecture, beyond cell composition, influences tumor progression and treatment outcomes. We performed spatial transcriptomic sequencing on 18 pediatric MB samples obtained at diagnosis, including two matched diagnosis-relapse pairs. Samples at diagnosis were stratified into high- and standard-risk groups. Spatial data were analyzed for spatial proximity to other cell types, cell-cell communication networks, and expression of cell cycle dormancy signatures. Findings were validated using immunohistochemistry in the same cohort. Our analyses revealed intertumoral and intratumoral heterogeneity within the TME, comprising tumor-associated astrocytes (TAAs), macrophages (TAMs), stromal components, and distinct subpopulations of MB cells at different stages of neuronal differentiation and cell cycle progression. We identified dense regions of quiescent progenitor-like MB cells enriched in patients with high-risk (HR) features and an increase in TAAs, TAMs, and dysregulated vascular endothelium following relapse. Our study presents novel insights into the spatial architecture and cellular landscape of the MB-TME, highlighting differential spatial patterns correlating with HR features. Future studies should evaluate their role in relapse and therapy resistance and may lead to uncovering novel therapeutic targets.

doi:10.1200/po-26-00300.abstract: Skin adnexal carcinomas (SACs) are rare and heterogeneous tumors with no established systemic treatment options and poor long-term survival rates in the advanced disease setting. Here, we aimed to characterize the genomic landscape and clinically actionable alterations across SAC subtypes. We analyzed next-generation sequencing data from SACs in the American Association for Cancer Research Project GENIE. Mutations, copy number alterations, and structural variants were annotated using OncoKB. Actionable alterations were defined as Level 1-2 alterations or tumor mutational burden (TMB) ≥10 mut/Mb. TMB was compared across subtypes and with melanoma, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), and basal cell carcinoma (BCC). A total of 224 SACs were analyzed (49% extramammary Paget disease [EMPD], 33% apocrine/eccrine, 17% sebaceous, 1% follicular). In EMPD, the most frequent actionable alterations were in PIK3CA (25.7%) and ERBB2 (22.9%). In sebaceous carcinoma, actionable alterations were mainly in KRAS (10.3%) and PIK3CA (10.3%). Apocrine/eccrine tumors also presented ERBB2 and PIK3CA alterations, but at lower frequencies (5.5% and 8.2%, respectively). TMB-high occurred in 10.1% of EMPD, 28.2% of sebaceous, and 21.9% of apocrine/eccrine tumors, lower than in melanoma (52.1%), CSCC (64.4%), and BCC (63.3%). SAC drivers showed important heterogeneity across subtypes. Overall, 48.2% of SACs harbored at least one potentially actionable alteration. SACs frequently harbor clinically actionable alterations in a histotype-dependent manner. The identification of lineage-specific genomic differences underscores the clinical and translational relevance of integrating histology with genomic profiling for guiding therapeutic decision making.

doi:10.1200/po-26-00390.abstract: BRCA1/2 mutation testing identifies patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) eligible for poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors; however, clinical outcomes remain heterogeneous within these genotypes. We evaluated whether plasma-derived genomic instability status (GIS) was associated with outcomes beyond BRCA1/2 and PALB2 mutation status in the phase II TRITON2 study. This retrospective biomarker analysis included TRITON2 patients with available baseline plasma profiled using Guardant360 Liquid. GIS is a probabilistic measure of homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) inferred from genome-wide copy number variants and somatic mutational signatures. Analyses were restricted to patients with baseline tumor fraction (TF) ≥ 25%. Radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) was analyzed using Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox models adjusted for age and baseline TF. Secondary end points included objective response rate (ORR), serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA50) declines, and overall survival (OS). Among 104 patients with TF ≥ 25%, 43 (41%) had GIS detected. Compared with GIS detected, absence of GIS was associated with shorter rPFS (hazard ratio [HR], 2.81 [95% CI, 1.61 to 4.93]; P <.001). Joint stratification demonstrated patients with both GIS detected and BRCA/PALB2 mutation experienced the longest rPFS, whereas absence of GIS was associated with shorter rPFS regardless of BRCA/PALB2 mutation status. In BRCA2-mutated patients, rPFS trended being longer in those with GIS detected (compared with those without GIS detected; HR, 2.02 [95% CI, 0.95 to 4.29]; P = .069), with numerically higher ORR (25.7% v 14.3%) and PSA50 response rate (65.7% v 42.9%). No statistically significant differences in OS were observed. Plasma-derived GIS was associated with improved rPFS and higher response rates in rucaparib-treated patients and further stratified outcomes within mutation-defined populations. These findings support genomic instability assessment as a complementary biomarker to mutation testing and warrant prospective validation.

doi:10.1200/po-26-00484.abstract: Immunotherapy with chemotherapy significantly improves progression-free survival in advanced endometrial cancer (EC), especially in microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) cases. Despite this, for recurrent EC in the postimmunotherapy setting, new treatment options are urgently needed. The PI3K pathway is frequently altered in gynecologic cancers, including EC, representing a potential treatment target. In a preplanned translational analysis of the MITO END-3, we retrospectively analyzed the genomic abnormalities of 107 patients with samples eligible for next-generation sequencing (NGS) analysis (FoundationOne CDx) with a focus on PIK3CA mutational status. In our analysis, the four most frequently mutated genes were TP53, PIK3CA, ARID1A, and PTEN. PIK3CA mutations were detected in 51.4% (55/107 patients) of tissue samples. A total of 68 different PIK3CA mutations were observed, of which 64 were considered pathogenic and four were classified as variants of unknown significance, with the co-occurrence of two different pathogenic mutations in 2 patients. The most frequent PIK3CA mutations were found in the kinase domain, most commonly H1047R (11/68) and H1047Y (3/68), and in the helical domain, including E545K (4/68) and E542K (3/68). Notably, 24 different PIK3CA mutations out of 68 reported in MITO END-3 are considered predictive of response to PI3K inhibition with alpelisib according to current literature in breast cancer. Interestingly, PIK3CA mutations were observed in all The Cancer Genome Atlas categories. In this post hoc analysis from the MITO END-3 trial, we confirmed the high frequency of PIK3CA mutations in EC, establishing this tumor as an ideal candidate for testing of PI3K inhibitors in clinical trials.

doi:10.1200/po-26-00601.abstract: Purpose The clinical utility of genomic profiling in gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (GEP-NENs) remains incompletely defined, particularly for clinically relevant annotated alterations and prognostic stratification. We performed a multi-institutional analysis to characterize genomic alterations across GEP-NEN subtypes, generate prevalence estimates to inform precision oncology efforts, and evaluate associations with clinical actionability and survival. Methods We performed a retrospective analysis of 1,691 GEP-NENs from the American Association for Cancer Research Project Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange database. Tumors were classified into neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) or neuroendocrine carcinomas (NECs) and stratified by primary site. Genomic alterations, including single-nucleotide variants, insertions/deletions, copy number alterations, and structural variants, were analyzed using a panel-adjusted approach. Alterations were annotated for clinical relevance using multiple knowledge bases. Overall survival was evaluated in a subset (n = 502) with available data. Results Genomic alterations were identified in 86.5% of patients. NETs were enriched for alterations in chromatin-remodeling genes ( MEN1, DAXX ) and mTOR pathway regulator TSC2 , whereas NECs were characterized by canonical drivers ( TP53, RB1, KRAS, APC , and BRAF ). Annotated alterations were identified in 34.1% of all patients, with higher rates in NECs compared with NETs (74.4% v 28.5%, P < .001). Notable annotated targets included BRAF V600E (2.2%; 14.8% of all colorectal NECs), KRAS -activating mutations (6.8%; 0.35% G12C), and NTRK fusions (0.2%). Annotation rates varied by primary site with the highest rates observed in colorectal, gastric, and esophageal NECs. In NETs, the presence of NEC-associated driver alterations was associated with worse overall survival (hazard ratio, 3.67 [95% CI, 2.49 to 5.42], P < .001). Conclusion Genomic profiling reveals meaningful differences in biomarker prevalence and prognosis across GEP-NEN subtypes. These findings support integrating genomic profiling with histologic classification to refine risk stratification and inform biomarker-driven clinical trials.

doi:10.1200/po-26-00691.abstract: Enfortumab vedotin and pembrolizumab (EVP) is the standard first-line treatment for locally advanced and metastatic urothelial cancer (la/mUC) although response biomarkers remain an unmet need. Tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has proven to be useful as a marker of response in a variety of cancers. We sought to explore whether ctDNA dynamics is associated with survival outcomes. This retrospective study included patients with la/mUC receiving first-line EVP, who had plasma ctDNA collected using the Signatera assay within 3 months after treatment initiation. Associations between ctDNA clearance and overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were assessed using multivariable time-dependent Cox proportional hazard (CPH) models and landmark analyses at 1, 2, and 3 months after EVP initiation. Longitudinal ctDNA trends were examined in a subpopulation with baseline ctDNA values collected. Fifty-eight patients were included. In multivariable time-dependent CPH models, ctDNA clearance was associated with both OS (hazard ratio [HR], 0.04 [95% CI, 0.01 to 0.24], P < .001) and PFS (HR, 0.09 [95% CI, 0.02 to 0.32], P < .001). In landmark analyses, ctDNA clearance was associated with longer OS and PFS at 2 months (log-rank test P = .003, P < .001, respectively). Among patients with baseline ctDNA (n = 42), 69% achieved ctDNA clearance after EVP initiation, whereas just 14% (n = 6) never had a decrease in ctDNA. The median time to clearance of ctDNA was 1.41 months (IQR, 0.85-1.94). While primarily hypothesis-generating, this study suggests that patients with la/mUC treated with first-line EVP frequently and rapidly clear ctDNA. Clearance of ctDNA in this population is associated with longer survival and merits further study.

doi:10.1200/po-26-00703.abstract: TAPUR is a phase II basket trial evaluating the antitumor activity of commercially available targeted agents in patients with advanced cancer and genomic alterations. Results of two cohorts of patients with advanced thyroid (TC) or biliary tract cancer (BTC) with BRAF V600E mutations treated with cobimetinib plus vemurafenib (C + V) are reported. Eligible patients had measurable disease (RECIST v1.1), Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-2, adequate organ function, and no standard treatment options. The primary end point was disease control (DC), defined as objective response (OR) or stable disease (SD) of at least 16+ weeks duration. Simon's two-stage design was based on a null DC rate of 15% versus 35% (power = 0.85; α = .10). Both cohorts expanded to stage II but closed before reaching the target sample size by pharmaceutical company request; inferences are based on thresholds set forth in the protocol to maintain the α level. Secondary end points included OR, progression-free survival, overall survival, duration of response, duration of SD, and safety. Patients with TC (N = 22; n = 16 evaluable) or BTC (N = 18; n = 15 evaluable) with BRAF V600E mutations were enrolled. In the TC cohort, the DC and OR rates were 94% (one-sided 90% CI, 78 to 100) and 63% (95% CI, 35 to 85), respectively. In the BTC cohort, the DC and OR rates were 67% (one-sided 90% CI, 47 to 100) and 53% (95% CI, 27 to 79), respectively. The null hypothesis of 15% DC rate was rejected for both cohorts (P < .0001). Twenty-one patients (53%) had ≥1 treatment-related grade 3 to 4 adverse event (AE) or serious AE. The combination of C + V met the prespecified criteria to declare a signal of activity in patients with TC and BTC with BRAF V600E mutations.

doi:10.1200/po.23.00555.abstract: PURPOSE Current guidelines for the management of metastatic non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) without driver mutations recommend checkpoint immunotherapy with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, either alone or in combination with chemotherapy. This approach fails to account for individual patient variability and host immune factors and often results in less-than-ideal outcomes. To address the limitations of the current guidelines, we developed and subsequently blindly validated a machine learning algorithm using pretreatment plasma proteomic profiles for personalized treatment decisions. PATIENTS AND METHODS We conducted a multicenter observational trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04056247 ) of patients undergoing PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor–based therapy (n = 540) and an additional patient cohort receiving chemotherapy (n = 85) who consented to pretreatment plasma and clinical data collection. Plasma proteome profiling was performed using SomaScan Assay v4.1. RESULTS Our test demonstrates a strong association between model output and clinical benefit (CB) from PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor–based treatments, evidenced by high concordance between predicted and observed CB ( R 2 = 0.98, P < .001). The test categorizes patients as either PROphet-positive or PROphet-negative and further stratifies patient outcomes beyond PD-L1 expression levels. The test successfully differentiates between PROphet-negative patients exhibiting high tumor PD-L1 levels (≥50%) who have enhanced overall survival when treated with a combination of immunotherapy and chemotherapy compared with immunotherapy alone (hazard ratio [HR], 0.23 [95% CI, 0.1 to 0.51], P = .0003). By contrast, PROphet-positive patients show comparable outcomes when treated with immunotherapy alone or in combination with chemotherapy (HR, 0.78 [95% CI, 0.42 to 1.44], P = .424). CONCLUSION Plasma proteome–based testing of individual patients, in combination with standard PD-L1 testing, distinguishes patient subsets with distinct differences in outcomes from PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor–based therapies. These data suggest that this approach can improve the precision of first-line treatment for metastatic NSCLC.

doi:10.1213/ane.0000000000008119.abstract: Simulation-based interdisciplinary training improves perinatal outcomes, but scalable and adaptable models for diverse labor and delivery (L&D) settings remain limited. The TeaM-L&DSim (Interdisciplinary Training for Patient Safety and Quality Care in Modern Labor & Delivery Simulation) program was developed by the No Pain Labor & Delivery-Global Health Initiative, combining nontechnical and technical simulation training, to enhance team functions, clinical decision-making, emergency preparedness, and complex care in resource-variable maternity care environments. We implemented TeaM-L&DSim using a mixed-methods quality improvement framework nationally at six training hubs in the first year, with obstetricians, anesthesiologists, neonatologists, midwives/nurses, and hospital administrators from 52 hospitals in China. The program emphasized three educational innovations: the Three Co(re) Domains (Collaboration, Cognition, and Competence), the 4P Strategy (Prevision, Prophylaxis, Preparedness, Prompt responses), and a cascading mentorship model for trainer development. Training included 27 standardized simulation modules delivered through hybrid virtual-physical formats. Evaluation was structured using the four levels of the Kirkpatrick model (reaction, learning, behavior, and results). Data sources included pre/post-training surveys, voluntary feedback, site-level implementation audits, and observational reports. Ninety-seven percent of participants reported that the training met or exceeded expectations. Self-reported outcomes included improved interdisciplinary communication (92.7%), greater emergency response confidence (88.2%), and clearer role understanding (90.5%). A one-year follow-up survey with 29% response rate indicated 72% of respondents reported changes in personal practice, while 43% reported institution-initiated protocol modifications. These changes saw greater impact in Level 3A hospitals. The program demonstrated feasibility across both urban academic and rural hospitals, with early reports noting enhanced team dynamics and emergency response times. TeaM-L&DSim is a scalable, interdisciplinary simulation program that improved team-based clinical competencies in L&D units, better effective in Level 3A facilities. More data are needed to understand adaptation to lower resource settings. This model holds promise for broader dissemination in global maternal safety initiatives.

doi:10.1213/ane.0000000000008219.abstract: Late motor responses, including F-waves and H-reflexes, are commonly recorded during electrophysiological diagnostic evaluation in awake patients. Although these responses could offer added value during intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, their use has not yet been widely adopted. This systematic review aims to assess current knowledge on how anesthetic and surgical factors influence the recording and monitoring of spinal late responses during surgery. The authors searched PubMed and EMBASE for relevant articles on studies of late response recording. Studies were considered eligible if the influence of one or more of the following parameters on late responses were assessed: (1) ventilation and metabolic parameters, (2) volatile agents, (3) intravenous agents, (4) neuromuscular blocking agents, (5) epidural or intrathecal agents, or (6) surgical factors. The QUADAS-2 tool was used to assess the risk of bias and concerns regarding applicability. Sixty-two studies were included. Respiratory conditions like hypercapnia reduced H-reflex amplitude, whereas hyperoxia and intermittent hypoxia had limited impact. Volatile agents, including isoflurane, sevoflurane, and nitrous oxide decreased late response amplitudes, with dose-dependent effects. Most intravenous anesthetics, particularly propofol, reduced H-reflex amplitude and F-wave persistence in a dose-dependent manner. Conversely, ketamine was found to increase H-reflex amplitude. During spinal and vascular surgeries, H-reflex monitoring proved feasible and provided valuable supplementary data to the conventional motor evoked potential (MEP) and somatosensory evoked potential (SSEP) modalities. This systematic review demonstrates that H-reflexes and F-waves are significantly influenced by anesthetic factors. The reviewed studies indicate that intravenous and volatile anesthetics significantly affect late responses, by reducing H-reflex and F-wave amplitudes, whereas latencies appear unaffected. The methodological quality varied significantly across the included studies and affects the interpretation of their conclusions. These findings support the potential integration of late response monitoring into intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring (IONM) protocols, provided that anesthetic management and surgical context are carefully considered.

doi:10.1213/ane.0000000000008309.abstract: Patients referred for postoperative care within enhanced care units in the United Kingdom are less likely to have their surgery canceled than those referred to critical care. Presently, it is unclear whether this association remains when examined at an individual hospital level, and whether specific structure and process features of enhanced care services influence cancelation rates within a facility. We conducted a nationwide, retrospective, observational study documenting clinical and organizational features of enhanced and critical care facilities in the United Kingdom. Features of interest included resource protections, staffing, and clinical scope. Sites with availability of both enhanced and critical care facilities, with >10 referrals to enhanced care during the study period, were selected for analysis. Cancelation rates of elective surgery within these facilities were quantified over a 3-month period between September 1, 2023, and November 30, 2023. Rates were defined as the number of elective cases canceled divided by the number of elective referrals to each facility. Multilevel regression was used to explore relationships between structure and process features of enhanced care units and surgical cancelation, using a two-level model with cases nested within hospitals to account for institutional confounding. Complete data were available for 65 sites, of which 28 had an enhanced care facility with sufficient activity for analysis, representing 4112 patients referred to enhanced or critical care. In most institutions, surgical cancelation rates were lower within their enhanced care facility than in critical care. Enhanced care units with beds reserved exclusively for elective cases (odds ratio [OR], 0.54 [0.39-0.76]; P < .001) and clinical care involving multiple specialities (OR, 0.48 [0.33-0.69]; P < .001) were associated with reduced odds of cancelation. On the other hand, enhanced care units that permitted admission of emergency cases (OR, 1.61 [1.06-2.43]; P = .024) were associated with a greater odds of cancelation. Structure and process features of enhanced care pathways are associated with cancelation rates among high-risk surgical patients in the United Kingdom. These findings may explain why cancelation rates in enhanced care are typically lower than within critical care and may have important policy implications.

doi:10.1213/ane.0000000000008327.abstract: Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain disorder frequently co-occurring with depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and insomnia, particularly in veterans, and safer nonpharmacological therapies are needed. Cranial electrotherapy stimulation, also referred to as cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES), may help with anxiety and sleep, but its effect on pain is unclear. This feasibility study evaluated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to identify neural correlates of pain and treatment response for CES effects on fibromyalgia pain in veterans. In a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial at a single US government hospital, veterans aged 20 to 60 with fibromyalgia were assigned to active or sham in-home CES, stratified by sex. Participants self-administered CES for 60 minutes daily over 12 weeks. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was acquired at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks with clinical outcomes, including the Defense and Veterans Pain Rating Scale (DVPRS), National Institutes of Health (NIH) Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) measures, and tests of physical function. Forty-eight participants were randomized (25 active, 23 sham) and 47 were analyzed. Both groups showed significant improvements in DVPRS pain (-1.88 ± 2.2) and pain interference with sleep (-2.25 ± 2.8), mood (-1.88 ± 2.6), activity (-1.83 ± 2.4) and stress (-1.77 ± 3.0) at 12 weeks versus baseline (P < .01), with significant between-group differences only in sleep (P = .04). Neuroimaging revealed significant increases in connectivity between the cerebellar 7b seed and the left occipital fusiform gyrus (0.079 ± 0.1) left lingual gyrus (0.063 ± 0.08), and right lingual gyrus (0.058 ± 0.08) for the CES group and decreases in the sham group (-0.088 ± 0.1; -0.121 ± 0.08; and -0.135 ± 0.1), respectively. No adverse events occurred. Both groups improved similarly in pain and function, though new analgesic usage was more prevalent in the sham group. Neuroimaging revealed differential changes in cerebellar-sensory-visual networks and baseline patterns distinguishing responders from nonresponders, supporting feasibility and design of larger, adequately powered CES trials in fibromyalgia.

doi:10.1213/ane.0000000000008332.abstract: Processed electroencephalogram (pEEG) monitors are commonly used in anesthesia practice. The relationship between the pEEG and clinical levels of sedation over anesthetic concentrations with and without opioids is not well understood. The purpose of this trial was to investigate the relationship between Bispectral IndexTM (BISTM), clinical measures of sedation, and inhaled anesthetics across a range of anesthetic concentrations and hypnotic states with and without intravenous opioids. This prospective, randomized trial enrolled 211 healthy volunteers. Participants were randomized to one of five anesthetic regimens: sevoflurane, sevoflurane with remifentanil, sevoflurane with fentanyl, desflurane, or isoflurane. Target anesthetic end-tidal concentrations were increased in a stepwise fashion until a BIS index of 30 to 40 was reached. Opioids were administered by target-controlled infusion and commenced before the inhaled agent began. At each targeted end-tidal concentration, responsiveness was assessed using the Modified Observer's Assessment of Alertness/Sedation (MOAA/S) score and the BIS index was recorded. The MOAA/S score was used to assess participant responsiveness, with a score ≤2 considered unresponsive and a score ≥3 considered responsive. The primary outcome measure was the BIS50 for each anesthetic regimen, representing the BIS index at which 50% of participants were unresponsive. Secondary outcomes included BIS95 (representing the BIS index at which 95% of participants were unresponsive) and evaluation of the BIS index as a predictor of responsiveness. BIS50 and BIS95 were estimated using random intercept logistic regression models, and the predictive performance of BIS indices was assessed by calculating the corresponding area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). One hundred and forty-three participants were randomized to a treatment group and completed the procedure with adequate data. Mean age was 26.5 ± 6.7 years (52% male). There were no reported device-related adverse events. Across treatment groups, BIS50 ranged from 67.5 (95% confidence interval [CI], 63.6-71.4) to 76.2 (73.5-78.8), and BIS95 ranged from 49.1 (42.9-55.4) to 63.3 (59.5-67.2). Compared to the sevoflurane and isoflurane groups, the desflurane group exhibited slightly lower BIS50 and BIS95 values. The addition of opioids to sevoflurane had minimal impact on BIS50 and BIS95. The BIS index alone was a strong predictor of the level of responsiveness, with AUCs consistently close to the ideal value of 1 (≥0.95) across all treatment groups. BIS indices were highly correlated with MOAA/S scores. These results describe the relationship between BIS levels and responsiveness for commonly used volatile anesthetics, with and without opioids, across a range of anesthetic concentrations. The results of this study should be interpreted in light of the study design which included young, healthy adult volunteers with no sustained, noxious stimulation. These findings may not be generalizable to other populations or clinical situations.

doi:10.1213/ane.0000000000008352.abstract: Although the interaction of sevoflurane, propofol, and opioids has been investigated regarding motor response to laryngoscopy, their hemodynamic impact during surgical stimulation remains unexplored. We therefore assessed the effect of sevoflurane, propofol, and remifentanil on the hemodynamic response to pneumoperitoneum and laparoscopic surgery. The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status I or II patients scheduled for elective laparoscopic surgery were randomly assigned to one of six groups with different combinations of sevoflurane-remifentanil, propofol-remifentanil, or sevoflurane-propofol-remifentanil, respectively. The Ce50 BARPP (pneumoperitoneum) for sevoflurane and propofol in combination with remifentanil was determined with the up-and-down method, and the interaction of the three drugs on mean arterial pressure (MAP) response was described with a linear-additive model. During surgery remifentanil was titrated to keep the MAP <100 mm Hg at fixed concentrations of sevoflurane (1 vol%), propofol (3 µg mL-1), or sevoflurane (0.5 vol%) plus propofol (1.5 µg mL-1). The relationship between remifentanil and MAP during surgery was described with a linear mixed-effects model. Data of 155 patients were analyzed. At remifentanil 5 ng mL-1 the Ce50 BARPP (95% CI) of sevoflurane was 1.56 (1.18-1.95) vol%, and of propofol 4.82 (4.29-5.36) µg mL-1. At remifentanil 3 ng/ml plus either propofol 1.8 µg mL-1 or sevoflurane 0.6 vol%, the values were 2.2 (2.0-2.4) vol% and 5.9 (5.7-6.0) µg mL-1. The drug interaction model revealed a propofol scaling factor (scaleSP) of 0.31 (0.19-0.44), representing the potency of propofol relative to sevoflurane, and a remifentanil constant kremi of 2.03 (0.82-3.24), representing the hypnotic-sparing effect of remifentanil. The median (interquartile range) of remifentanil during surgery was 6.4 (5.8-7.7), 4.9 (3.6-6.7), and 5.0 (3.7-6.0) ng mL-1 in groups SR, PR, and SPR, respectively. The MAP did not correlate with the remifentanil concentrations, demonstrating evidence for the drug titration paradox. The relative potency of sevoflurane to propofol in reducing the MAP response to pneumoperitoneum is similar to that for tolerance of laryngoscopy but differs from that for hypnotic endpoints. The effect of remifentanil on reducing the MAP response is similar whether it is combined with sevoflurane or propofol. Because titration to a dynamic clinical end point decouples the traditional relationship between drug input and clinical outcome, titration data cannot be used to validate pharmacodynamic models.

doi:10.1213/ane.0000000000008353.abstract: The Risk Assessment of Morbidity in Pediatric Surgery (RAMPS) score was developed by a tertiary care children's center to predict risk of noncardiac pediatric surgical morbidity using intrinsic surgical risk (ISR) and individual comorbidity. The score demonstrated good internal validity, discrimination, and generalizability. This study seeks to externally validate the score in a similar patient population at a different tertiary care children's hospital. Following institutional review board (IRB) approval, data for all noncardiac, nontrauma, and nontransplant pediatric surgeries performed at the external children's hospital in 2019 were collected via review of medical records. The RAMPS score for each patient was calculated. A composite morbidity score defined as transfer to intensive care unit (ICU), cardiac arrest, unplanned endotracheal intubation, or unplanned initiation of positive pressure ventilation (PPV) in the 72 hours following surgery was calculated. Discrimination was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, and calibration between predicted and observed risk of morbidity was assessed. Of 13,718 patients included, 409 (2.98%) experienced the composite morbidity outcome. The most common morbidity was postoperative PPV-361 (2.63%). Only 1.5% (n = 205) of the cohort was critically ill, though 14.1% (n = 1934) had at least three chronic conditions and 19.5% (n = 2668) of patients had a procedure in ISR quartiles 3 or 4. Each component of the RAMPS score was significantly associated with the outcome. The RAMPS score had very good discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] = 0.829; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.809-0.849) and good calibration between observed and predicted probabilities (Brier score = 0.03). The RAMPS score performed well in this external validation with overall less patient complexity and less morbidity than in the original cohort included for development and internal validation. The score moderately overestimated risk in the most complex patients, which does not diminish its utility in guiding resource allocation to manage or prevent perioperative adverse events. In summary, the RAMPs score is a simple, highly discriminant, well-calibrated, and externally validated tool clinicians and health systems can use to predict morbidity among pediatric surgery patients.

doi:10.1213/ane.0000000000008360.abstract: Preoperative anxiety affects 30% to 80 % of ambulatory surgery patients and is associated with increased anesthetic requirements, postoperative pain, and delayed recovery. Virtual reality (VR) is a promising nonpharmacological anxiolytic, but evidence remains limited in the ambulatory setting. The AMBLUMEEN (AMBulatory LUMEEN) trial is a single-center, randomized, open-label, superiority trial conducted in an adult ambulatory surgery unit. Patients with moderate-to-severe preoperative anxiety (State-Trait Anxiety Inventory Form Y-A [STAI-YA] > 45) were randomized 1:1 to standard care alone (control) or standard care and a single 20-minute preoperative VR session (immersive 360° natural contemplative scenes). The primary end point was the change in STAI-YA score from arrival in the ambulatory unit (baseline) to immediately before operating room transfer (presurgery), analyzed under the intention-to-treat principle with a linear mixed model. Secondary end points included preoperative benzodiazepine use, postoperative morphine requirement, unplanned overnight admission, patient satisfaction, and device acceptability. Of 106 randomized patients (53 per group) with a median [interquartile range] baseline STAI-YA of 49 [46-55] and 49 [46-58] respectively in the control and VR group, the VR group experienced a markedly greater reduction in state anxiety than controls. Adjusted mean between-group difference in STAI-YA change from baseline to presurgery was -18.7 95% confidence interval (CI) [-21.4 to -16.1] points in favor of VR. Although benzodiazepine requirement, postoperative pain, and unplanned overnight admission were comparable between groups, the morphine requirement in postanesthesia care unit was lower in the VR group (6/53 [11.3% 95% CI, 11.3 {4.3-23.0}] vs 0/53 [0.0%, 95% CI, {0.0-6.7}]; P = .027). Global perioperative satisfaction was high in both groups (median 8 [8-9] on 10). A single 20-minute session of medical-grade VR significantly reduced preoperative anxiety in ambulatory surgery patients, with high acceptability and an excellent safety profile.

doi:10.1213/ane.0000000000008364.abstract: Although carbon dioxide (CO2) is widely regarded as a driver for cerebral vasomodulation, often termed cerebrovascular CO2-reactivity, experimental evidence has shown that this response is primarily mediated through changes in pH rather than CO2. This complicates the management of cerebral blood flow (CBF) during the treatment of acid-base disorders with partial respiratory or metabolic compensation, when the CBF has normalized together with pH equilibration, despite persistent hyper- or hypercapnia. Although a pH-guided approach would therefore be preferred, no quantitative estimate of the relationship between pH and CBF has currently been reported in the literature. Therefore, this study aims to estimate the cerebrovascular sensitivity to pH and explore whether changes in CBF velocity (CBFV) are more closely related to arterial pH or CO2. In patients undergoing cardiac surgery, CBFV and continuous in-line arterial blood gas monitoring, incorporated in the cardiopulmonary bypass circuit, were analyzed. Mixed-effects models were constructed with percentage change in CBFV as response variable and arterial pH and/or CO2 as explanatory variable(s). Model fit of the explanatory variables was compared using marginal and conditional R2. Improvement of model fit and parsimony were assessed with the likelihood-ratio test (LRT) and change in Akaike information criterion (ΔAIC), respectively. Thirteen patients were included in the analysis with a total of 1960 datapoints. CBFV decreased by 30.6% per 0.1 increase in arterial pH (95% confidence interval [CI], 28.9-32.2; P < .0001), and increased by 1.95% per mm Hg increase in PaCO2 (95% CI, 1.76-2.14; P < .0001). Arterial pH explained a greater proportion of variance than PaCO2 (marginal R2: 0.444 vs 0.294; conditional R2: 0.744 vs 0.530). Furthermore, adding arterial pH to the null CO2-model considerably improved model fit (LRT = 616.4) and parsimony (ΔAIC = -615), whereas adding arterial CO2 to the pH-model barely improved model fit (LRT = 4.6) and parsimony (ΔAIC = -3). This exploratory study provides a quantitative estimate of the relationship between CBFV and pH, and suggests that changes in CBFV are more closely related to arterial pH than to CO2. This estimate of the cerebrovascular sensitivity to pH was used to describe a feasible pH-guided approach in the management of CBF during the treatment of partially compensated acid-base disorders.

doi:10.1213/ane.0000000000008377.abstract: While antiretroviral therapy has improved surgical safety for people living with HIV, comprehensive data on perioperative organ injury and its impact on patient safety remain limited. This study aimed to compare the incidence of perioperative organ injury, in-hospital mortality, hospital length of stay, and hospitalization costs between people living with HIV and HIV-negative individuals undergoing surgery in the United States. This retrospective cohort study used data from the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) from 2016 to 2021. The population-based sample included adult patients (age >18 years) identified via International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes. Of 41,622,004 eligible surgical admissions, 2,088,307 (5.0%) were people living with HIV and 39,533,697 were HIV-negative. Primary outcomes were perioperative organ injury incidence and associated mortality; secondary outcomes included hospital length of stay and total hospital charges. Adjusted models accounted for baseline characteristics and surgical complexity. Among the 41,622,004 surgical admissions, people living with HIV were found to be older and carried a significantly higher comorbidity burden, with a Charlson Comorbidity Index of 8 compared to 1 in the HIV-negative group. Perioperative organ injury occurred in 1,348,363 of 2,088,307 people living with HIV (64.6%) compared with 7,867,547 of 39,533,697 HIV-negative patients (19.9%). Acute myocardial infarction (33.5%) and acute kidney injury (22.0%) were the most common injuries among people living with HIV. In-hospital mortality occurred in 66,935 of 2,088,307 people living with HIV (3.2%) compared with 872,170 of 39,533,697 HIV-negative patients (2.2%). Hospital length of stay and hospital charges were also significantly higher. Adjusted analyses demonstrated that HIV status was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (odds ratio [OR], 1.66; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.54-1.78), longer hospital length of stay (β = 2.73 days; 95% CI, 2.56-2.90), a decreased likelihood of home discharge (hazard ratio [HR], 0.73; 95% CI, 0.72-0.73), and increased hospitalization costs (β = $18,423; 95% CI, 16,712-20,134). Sensitivity analyses demonstrated that elevated perioperative risk persisted among patients with asymptomatic HIV infection, although the greatest risk was observed among patients with symptomatic HIV disease/AIDS. People living with HIV incur a significantly higher risk of perioperative organ injury and worse surgical outcomes despite advances in antiretroviral therapy. HIV status was independently associated with adverse perioperative outcomes in adjusted models, supporting its inclusion as a risk stratification variable in surgical planning. Future research should incorporate immunologic markers, such as CD4 count and viral load, to further refine perioperative risk prediction and optimize outcomes for this population.
