doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1974418.abstract: Purpose Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) accounts for more than 75% of renal cell carcinomas and is characterized by high metastatic potential and resistance to therapy. Fibronectin 1 (FN1), a major extracellular matrix glycoprotein, is overexpressed in various cancers and promotes tumor progression; however, its precise molecular mechanisms in RCC remain unclear. Methods We analyzed the expression level of FN1 and its clinical relevance in ccRCC using TCGA database. Subsequently, FN1 was knocked down in ACHN cells, followed by functional assays, RNA sequencing, and Western blot validation. Furthermore, we integrated FN1-interacting proteins from the BioGRID and STRING databases and combined this information with differentially expressed genes to identify key downstream effectors of FN1. Results FN1 was significantly upregulated in ccRCC and strongly associated with lymph node metastasis, distant metastasis, and poor overall survival. FN1 knockdown markedly suppressed invasion of ACHN cells, induced transcriptomic alterations, and downregulated key oncogenes, including CSF2, SOX9, and LAMC2. Pathway analysis revealed significant inhibition of the PI3K–Akt signaling axis. Integrating FN1-interacting proteins with the DEGs identified YWHAZ—a known regulator of the PI3K–Akt pathway—as a critical downstream effector of FN1, whose expression was markedly reduced upon FN1 knockdown. Rescue experiments further showed that YWHAZ overexpression substantially restored FN1 knockdown-impaired invasion but only modestly and non-significantly affected Akt phosphorylation. Conclusion FN1 promotes invasion in RCC cells at least in part through YWHAZ-dependent mechanisms, with partial involvement of PI3K-Akt signaling and additional pathways likely contributing. These findings suggest that the FN1/YWHAZ axis may serve as a candidate prognostic marker and a potential target for future preclinical investigation in RCC.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1974528.abstract: The assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) in endometrial carcinoma is critical for optimizing the extent of surgical resection and formulating individualized therapies. This study aimed to investigate the associated factors of the LNM in endometrial carcinoma. 438 patients with endometrial carcinoma who underwent primary surgical staging between June 2014 and June 2025 were retrospectively analyzed. Clinicopathological data and immunohistochemical expression profiles of ER, PR, HER2, p53, Ki67, ERCC1, and GST-π were systematically collected. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify independent associated factors for LNM. The overall incidence of LNM in the study was 10.27% (45/438). Univariate analysis revealed that menopausal status, histological grade, Bokhman pathological subtype, depth of myometrial invasion, lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI), and the expression levels of ER, PR, Ki67, p53, and HER2 were significantly associated with LNM (all P < 0.05). Subsequent multivariate analysis identified each one-category increase in HER2 staining level was associated with higher odds of LNM (OR 3.859, 95% CI 2.314-6.436, P < 0.001), as was each one-category increase in p53 staining level (OR 1.932, 95% CI 1.212-3.082, P = 0.006). The presence of LVSI was also an independent associated factor for LNM. Higher p53 and HER2 staining levels and the presence of LVSI are independently associated with LNM in endometrial carcinoma.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1974982.abstract: Treatment resistance is usually attributed to genetic or adaptive changes within tumor cells. Here, we propose that, in some tumors, resistance also depends on specific interactions between malignant and non-malignant cells. We define relational resistance as a resistant phenotype that requires the functional organization of particular intercellular relationships. This concept is narrower than microenvironment-mediated resistance: the presence of stromal, immune, or vascular cells is not sufficient to establish relational resistance; a defined interaction must contribute functionally to treatment failure. We organize evidence along a five-step sequence: predicted edge, spatial support, functional edge, relational dependency, and therapeutic vulnerability. Genitourinary cancers illustrate different positions along this sequence: bladder cancer provides a predicted CD6-ALCAM edge with independent clinical association but without targeted perturbation; prostate cancer provides myeloid circuits with preclinical causal support and phase 1 proof-of-concept targetability; and renal cell carcinoma provides spatially organized multicellular programs with functional and preclinical perturbation support. We further propose relational memory as the hypothesis that a treatment-induced or treatment-selected interaction persists after therapy and influences response to a subsequent treatment. The framework therefore shifts the therapeutic question from which resistant cells are present to which relationships are required for resistance to persist.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1974982.title: Resistance in the edges: a relational framework for treatment resistance in genitourinary cancers.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1975159.abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is the most common histological subtype of lung cancer, with a dismal prognosis partly attributed to immune evasion mediated by T cell dysfunction within the tumor microenvironment. However, the molecular determinants governing CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocyte functional competence remain incompletely understood. Chloride intracellular channel 3 (CLIC3) has been implicated in cancer progression, but its role in T cell immunity within the LUAD TME is unknown. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing on tumor tissues from nine LUAD patients spanning three pathological stages (adenocarcinoma in situ [AIS], minimally invasive adenocarcinoma [MIA], and invasive adenocarcinoma [IAC]), integrated with spatial transcriptomics, TCGA-LUAD bulk RNA-seq analysis, and flow cytometric validation in an independent cohort of 32 LUAD patients. Functional module scoring and pseudotime trajectory analysis were applied to characterize CLIC3-associated CTL functional states. CLIC3 was predominantly expressed in CTLs and showed a stage-associated decline from AIS to MIA to IAC. CLIC3+ CTLs exhibited significantly higher module scores for cytotoxicity, cytoskeleton remodeling, interferon signaling, and chemotaxis compared to CLIC3- CTLs. Pseudotime trajectory analysis indicated that CLIC3+ cells were positioned at one end of the inferred transcriptional continuum, corresponding to a functionally active state, while CLIC3- cells were positioned at the other, corresponding to a dysfunctional state, accompanied by a decline in CD247, GZMB, PRF1, and TNF along the trajectory. High CLIC3 expression in TCGA-LUAD was associated with significantly longer overall survival. Flow cytometry showed a stage-associated decrease in CLIC3 expression on CD8+ T cells with increasing tumor invasiveness and poor differentiation. CLIC3 serves as a novel marker of CTL functional competence in LUAD, and its stage-associated downregulation reflects T cell dysfunction during tumor progression. CLIC3 expression in CD8+ T cells may represent a predictive biomarker for immunotherapeutic response and a potential target for restoring T cell function in LUAD.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1975159.title: Loss of CLIC3 in CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes is associated with immune dysfunction and poor prognosis in lung adenocarcinoma.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1975605.abstract: Cervical cancer is a common malignancy in women worldwide, with distant metastases frequently occurring in the lungs, liver, bones, and lymph nodes. However, this case report presents an extremely rare isolated metastasis to the left scapular region,specifically located between the supraspinatus and the trapezius muscles, in a patient with locally advanced cervical squamous cell carcinoma who developed this lesion during maintenance therapy with a programmed death receptor-1 (PD-1) inhibitor after completing concurrent chemoradiotherapy. The clinical presentation of this metastatic lesion was atypical and posed a significant diagnostic challenge; however, multimodal imaging (MRI, PET/CT) and histopathological examination ultimately confirmed the diagnosis of cervical cancer metastasis. This finding underscores the necessity of maintaining a high level of vigilance for metastases in atypical sites, even in the era of immunotherapy. To manage this rare presentation, a multidisciplinary team developed a comprehensive treatment strategy centered on surgical resection, followed by postoperative adjuvant radiotherapy administered concurrently with chemotherapy and anti-angiogenic therapy(Q3W) consisting of paclitaxel 135 mg/m², cisplatin 50 mg/m², and bevacizumab 10 mg/kg. The patient remained recurrence-free at 13 months, suggesting that a multimodal combined local and systemic strategy may be feasible for selected patients with solitary muscle metastasis. This case not only adds to the clinical understanding of rare metastases in cervical cancer but also demonstrates that tumors can still metastasize to atypical sites under immunotherapy. These findings highlight the need for vigilance regarding metastases at atypical sites during immunotherapy. Any underlying mechanism-including immune editing and clonal evolution-remains speculative in the absence of paired molecular data and requires further validation.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1975605.title: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma manifesting as a solitary metastasis to the skeletal muscle of the scapular region accompanied by invasion of the adjacent bone while on PD-1 inhibitor maintenance therapy: a case report.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1975694.abstract: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is a common skin malignancy in aging populations. Surgical resection and radiotherapy can result in significant morbidity, as well as functional and cosmetic impairments. PD-1 antibodies are promising treatments for locally advanced disease. Two elderly men (aged 71 and 73) with locoregionally advanced head and neck tumors received neoadjuvant treatment with cemiplimab (350 mg IV every 3 weeks). Both patients presented with neurologic symptoms concerning for nerve involvement; however, perineural spread could not be identified radiographically or by limited biopsies. Both patients achieved a significant clinical response after only four doses of cemiplimab. After 4 additional doses, both patients underwent elective treatment discontinuation and surgery and radiotherapy were omitted. With over 12-month follow-up, both patients remained free of recurrence. Treatment was well-tolerated with only Grade 1 pruritus. These observations are promising and suggest the feasibility of response-adapted management following cemiplimab therapy in selected patients with advanced squamous cell skin cancer with resolution of neurologic symptoms. This approach may allow for omission of surgery and radiotherapy in selected patients. Further investigation to define appropriate candidates for this approach appears warranted.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1975694.title: Case Report: Improvement in neurologic symptoms and remission following non-operative management of locally advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck following cemiplimab therapy: two cases.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1975884.abstract: Currently, whether surgical staging can confer a survival benefit in patients with cervical cancer remains controversial, and its efficacy is similarly uncertain across different subgroups. The primary aim of this study was to assess the efficacy of laparoscopic para-aortic and pelvic lymphadenectomy prior to chemoradiotherapy in patients with International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) stage IIB-IIIC cervical cancer. The secondary aim was to identify the main prognostic factors. A total of 396 patients were included in this retrospective study, 97 patients who underwent laparoscopic para-aortic and pelvic lymphadenectomy before chemoradiotherapy comprised the surgical staging group, and 299 patients who received chemoradiotherapy alone comprised the clinical staging group. Kaplan-Meier and log-rank methods were used to construct and compare progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) curves, respectively. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to identify independent prognostic factors. There were no statistically significant differences in PFS (p = 0.187) or OS (p = 0.490) between the two groups. The estimated 5-year PFS rates were 67.0% (95%CI, 56.9%-75.7%) in the surgical staging group and 73.6% (95%CI, 67.4%-78.7%) in the clinical staging group. The corresponding 5-year OS rates were 76.3% (95%CI, 66.0%-83.9%) and 78.6% (95%CI, 72.7%-83.2%), respectively. Subgroup analysis stratified by imaging lymph node status demonstrated comparable survival outcomes. Multivariate analysis identified adenocarcinoma, pelvic wall involvement, and imaging-positive lymph nodes as independent risk factors for PFS; adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, pelvic wall involvement, and imaging-positive lymph nodes were independent predictors of OS. Laparoscopic para-aortic and pelvic lymphadenectomy before chemoradiotherapy was not associated with improved PFS or OS in this retrospective cohort, Tumor histology, pelvic wall involvement, and imaging-positive lymph nodes were the main prognostic factors.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1975884.title: Laparoscopic para-aortic and pelvic lymphadenectomy before chemoradiotherapy was not associated with improved survival in patients with FIGO stage IIB-IIIC cervical cancer: a single-center retrospective study.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1975965.abstract: Transformed small cell lung cancer (T-SCLC) is most commonly observed in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma and represents an important mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs). Its reported clinical incidence is approximately 3%-10%. Patients with T-SCLC often experience rapid disease progression and poor overall prognosis, and no established standard treatment regimen is currently available. We report a case of advanced EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma with RB1 , TP53 , and BRCA2 co-mutations that underwent small-cell transformation during treatment. Small-cell transformation was detected through close surveillance and confirmed by repeat biopsy. The patient subsequently received individualized multimodal therapy, including chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and local radiotherapy, and remained alive 43 months after the initial diagnosis.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1975965.title: Prolonged survival after small-cell transformation of EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma: a case report

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1977660.abstract: Adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancer survivors have complex long-term survivorship needs beyond cancer recurrence surveillance. Although survivor concerns and healthcare provider perspectives have been reported separately, few studies have evaluated both within the same healthcare setting. We conducted complementary surveys of AYA cancer survivors and physicians to characterize survivorship concerns, barriers to long-term follow-up (LTFU), and telemedicine preferences. This single-center, cross-sectional study included questionnaire surveys of 98 AYA cancer survivors receiving outpatient follow-up after cancer treatment and 45 physicians involved in AYA survivorship care at the National Cancer Center Hospital, Japan. Survivors were surveyed regarding LTFU, survivorship concerns, and telemedicine preferences, and physicians regarding LTFU practices, referral barriers, and AYA-specific challenges. Associations between survivor characteristics and telemedicine preference were explored using univariable analyses. Among survivors, 84 of 98 (85.7%) considered LTFU necessary, and 51 (52.0%) reported difficulty attending follow-up because of school or work commitments. Of 91 survivors evaluable for telemedicine preference, 69 (75.8%) were likely or somewhat likely to use at least one telemedicine service. Among all 98 survivors, frequently selected telemedicine topics included disease information (45.9%), daily activities (31.6%), anxiety and worry (30.6% each), financial issues (29.6%), and work- or school-related concerns (27.6%). No demographic, clinical, treatment-related or healthcare utilization factors were significantly associated with telemedicine preference. Among physicians, 13 of 44 (29.5%) reported an established departmental LTFU policy. Follow-up at the treating cancer center was supported by 76.2% for survivors at high risk of recurrence but by only 21.4% for all AYA survivors. Major barriers to coordinated care included difficulty identifying hospitals providing cancer-specific LTFU (73.8%) or multidisciplinary care (71.4%). Physicians identified reproductive medicine and life events as major AYA-specific challenges and mental health, endocrine disorders, and sexual and reproductive health as areas requiring additional support. AYA cancer survivors reported substantial survivorship concerns, whereas physicians identified barriers to coordinated multidisciplinary care. Telemedicine was of interest to many survivors and warrants prospective evaluation as a potential component of multidisciplinary survivorship care.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1977660.title: Barriers to survivorship care for adolescent and young adult cancer survivors: perspectives of survivors and cancer specialists.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1977793.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) comprises a clinically and biologically heterogeneous group of breast cancers defined by the absence of estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor expression and the lack of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) overexpression or amplification. Although systemic treatment has expanded beyond chemotherapy to include immune checkpoint blockade, poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibition in selected patients with germline BRCA1/2 variants, and antibody-drug conjugates in advanced disease, therapeutic resistance and disease recurrence remain major challenges. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are abundant stromal cells that contribute to the organization and function of the TNBC microenvironment. Rather than representing a single uniformly tumor-promoting population, CAFs encompass transcriptionally and functionally diverse states that vary across tumors, spatial niches, and treatment contexts. Current evidence supports roles for selected CAF populations in extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, paracrine signaling, metabolic exchange, immune-cell positioning, and adaptation to therapeutic stress. Recent single-cell and spatial studies have further identified ECM-rich, inflammatory, hypoxia-associated, and progenitor-like fibroblast states that correlate with distinct immune landscapes and treatment responses. However, many proposed CAF markers are shared across states, nomenclature remains inconsistent among datasets, and most CAF-directed therapeutic strategies are supported primarily by preclinical evidence. This review summarizes the current understanding of CAF heterogeneity in TNBC, examines the mechanisms through which fibroblast states influence tumor progression and antitumor immunity, and critically evaluates their contribution to chemotherapy and immunotherapy resistance. Particular attention is given to the distinction between mechanistic evidence and associative transcriptomic findings, as well as to the translational challenges that must be addressed before CAF-based biomarkers or therapies can be incorporated into routine TNBC management.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1977793.title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts in triple-negative breast cancer: heterogeneity, tumor-stroma crosstalk, and therapeutic resistance.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1977843.abstract: Primary enteric-type adenocarcinoma of the renal parenchyma is an exceptionally rare malignancy, accounting for less than 1% of renal epithelial tumors. Due to its morphological and immunohistochemical overlap with metastatic gastrointestinal malignancy, establishing a primary renal origin presents a considerable diagnostic challenge. Radical nephroureterectomy has traditionally been the standard surgical treatment. We report a 47-year-old asymptomatic female with an incidental 68 mm cystic-solid left renal mass detected during a trauma evaluation. Imaging suggested Bosniak category IV on computed tomography and cystic teratoma on magnetic resonance imaging. Notably, the patient had bilateral renal malrotation. Serum tumor markers (CEA and CA19-9) were within normal limits. The patient underwent successful robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy with a warm ischemia time of 15 minutes. Histopathology revealed adenocarcinoma with an enteric immunophenotype: positive for CK20, CDX-2, SATB2, and Villin, with complete loss of PAX-8 and GATA-3. Postoperative gastrointestinal endoscopy and 18F-FDG PET-CT excluded primary gastrointestinal or distant occult malignancies, confirming a primary renal parenchymal origin. At one-month follow-up, the patient showed no evidence of recurrence without adjuvant therapy. This case represents the first reported association of primary enteric-type renal adenocarcinoma with bilateral renal malrotation and demonstrates that robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy can be a feasible nephron-sparing approach for selected patients with this aggressive tumor. A systematic diagnostic approach including surgical resection, immunohistochemical profiling, and exclusion of gastrointestinal metastasis is essential for accurate diagnosis and optimal management.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1977843.title: Primary enteric-type adenocarcinoma of the renal parenchyma in a patient with bilateral renal malrotation: a case report and review of the literature.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1978296.abstract: PD-1 inhibitors are widely used anticancer drugs and frequently trigger immune-related adverse events, with thyroid dysfunction as the most prevalent. Suspected isolated central hypothyroidism emerging during PD-1 inhibitor therapy has rarely been documented. A 56-year-old man received pembrolizumab for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Before treatment, he had pre-existing Hashimoto's thyroiditis with low TT4 and normal TSH. He developed painless thyroiditis manifesting as transient thyrotoxicosis followed by primary hypothyroidism. Shortly after hypothyroidism was pharmacologically controlled, TSH progressively declined to the lower limit of detection, accompanied by low TT4. Pituitary MRI showed pituitary gland thinning without focal structural abnormalities. Integrating the clinical course, central hypothyroidism was considered. Given altered upper gastrointestinal anatomy after esophagectomy, split-dose levothyroxine was administered, and the patient's FT4 levels remained stable. This rare sequential evolution of thyroid dysfunction may represent an uncommon endocrine immune-related adverse event of immune checkpoint inhibitors.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1978296.title: Pembrolizumab-associated primary hypothyroidism followed by central hypothyroidism: a case report.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1978519.abstract: Autologous breast reconstruction restores breast volume and contour after mastectomy, but reconstruction of the nipple-areola complex remains central to the perception of breast completeness. Traditionally, nipple reconstruction has been delayed until the reconstructed breast mound has stabilized, allowing the final nipple position and projection to be adjusted after soft-tissue settling and scar remodeling. However, in selected patients undergoing autologous reconstruction, simultaneous nipple reconstruction can be integrated into breast shaping, thereby reducing additional procedures, avoiding a second local incision and making use of redundant skin and soft tissue that would otherwise be discarded during flap tailoring. This strategy also allows surgeons to plan breast contour, nipple position, projection and symmetry as a single three-dimensional aesthetic unit. Nevertheless, accurate intraoperative positioning, reliable perfusion and durable long-term projection remain major technical challenges. In this case-based narrative review, we discuss the rationale, potential advantages, patient selection and limitations of immediate nipple reconstruction during autologous breast reconstruction. We further present three representative approaches from our center: a local flap, a pedicled perforator-based flap and a free perforator-based flap. These cases suggest that immediate nipple reconstruction should not be regarded as a single standardized operation, but as a flexible reconstructive strategy that should be tailored to tissue availability, vascular anatomy and aesthetic goals.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1979150.abstract: FOXM1, a forkhead-box transcription factor, is consistently overexpressed in breast cancer, particularly in the basal-like and triple-negative subtypes, in which high expression predicts poor survival. We propose, as a falsifiable hypothesis rather than an established mechanism, that FOXM1 may function as a dosage-integrating rheostat, in which convergent genomic, transcriptional, epitranscriptomic, translational, and post-translational inputs would determine discrete output states involving mitotic fidelity, chromosomal instability, metabolic rewiring, immune evasion, and stem-like plasticity. We further hypothesized that therapies directed elsewhere in the network are frequently buffered by the persistence or reactivation of FOXM1-associated outputs, while noting that resistance to direct FOXM1 inhibition proceeds instead through reversal of that output, which bounds the hypothesis rather than supporting it. Accordingly, we classified FOXM1-directed strategies, including direct inhibitors, degraders, condensate disruptors, upstream suppressors, and targeted delivery platforms, by their mechanism of engagement rather than by their chemical class. Existing evidence remains largely correlative and bulk-derived: available perturbation studies are categorical rather than graded, no study has titrated FOXM1 through intermediate levels or measured its outputs bidirectionally, and the few single-cell, time-resolved datasets resolve one output at a time. We identified these gaps, specified the components of an isoform-, localisation- and activation-resolved FOXM1 activity metric that would define dose in measurable terms, and proposed experiments to test threshold-dependent activation, discrete single-cell states, and history-dependent switching, grounding the last of these in the material properties and physical ageing of FOXM1 condensates rather than in an equilibrium phase boundary alone in order to distinguish dosage-dependent state selection from regulatory hub behavior.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1979150.title: FOXM1 as a candidate dosage rheostat and state selector in breast cancer: linking multilevel regulation to adaptive plasticity and therapy resistance.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1979803.abstract: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) is a rare malignancy characterized by indolent growth, frequent perineural invasion, and a propensity for locally advanced disease involving the skull base. High-dose radiation to complex target volumes must be balanced with minimizing exposure to adjacent organs at risk, making particle therapy attractive. Proton beam therapy (PBT) and carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) provide favorable dose distributions compared with photon-based radiotherapy, while CIRT offers additional theoretical radiobiologic advantages through its higher linear energy transfer and relative biological effectiveness. However, whether these properties translate into superior clinical outcomes remains uncertain. This perspective reviews physical and radiobiologic characteristics of PBT and CIRT and evaluates contemporary clinical evidence supporting their use in ACC. Available studies demonstrate favorable local control, overall survival, and toxicity outcomes with both modalities but have not established a clear clinical advantage of CIRT over modern PBT. Interpretation is limited by heterogeneous patient populations, treatment techniques, fractionation schedules, institutional practices, follow-up, and the absence of prospective data. Additionally, differences in infrastructure, cost, geographic availability, and reimbursement influence treatment selection and patient access. Current evidence supports PBT as an efficacious and broadly applicable treatment option for ACC, particularly for complex skull base and perineural target volumes. Future research should prioritize comparative dosimetry, refinement of biologic dose modeling, multicenter clinical outcomes, contemporary cost-effectiveness analyses, and patient selection. Expanding equitable access to particle therapy should remain a parallel objective. Current literature supports PBT in the treatment of ACC. Reported treatment outcomes are comparable to CIRT.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1980190.abstract: Therapeutic mRNA vaccines are a clinically validated cancer immunotherapy platform using in vitro transcribed mRNA encoding tumor antigens to induce durable anti-tumor immunity. Advances in mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery, and immunomodulatory combinations have propelled this approach from preclinical models to randomized trials with survival benefit. This review systematically examines vaccine efficacy through an antigen-delivery-immunomodulation tripartite framework. We trace the evolution from shared tumor-associated antigens to personalized neoantigens identified by computational pipelines, discuss ionizable lipid chemistry and LNP formulation for controlled tissue tropism and transfection, and analyze the bidirectional crosstalk between vaccine components and innate immune sensing that shapes adaptive T cell responses. Clinical evidence across melanoma, pancreatic cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, and other solid tumors is critically evaluated, alongside combination strategies-checkpoint blockade, oncolytic virotherapy, and adoptive cell therapy to overcome TME resistance. Persistent challenges include optimal neoantigen selection, standardized immune monitoring, and predictive biomarkers. We conclude that future research should prioritize systematic optimization of the tripartite design through multi-antigen targeting, tissue-specific delivery engineering, and rational combination immunotherapy, aiming to establish mRNA cancer vaccines as a standard-of-care modality.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1980560.abstract: Gastric cancer peritoneal metastasis (GCPM), particularly associated with diffuse and poorly cohesive cancers, in which tumour cells grow singly or in small, loosely associated groups, presents an anatomical and immunological treatment challenge. This review examines the peritoneal surface and surrounding fluid as an interacting immune compartment comprising tumour implants, malignant ascites, free tumour cells, stroma and immune populations. Human studies identify cytotoxic-cell depletion or exhaustion, macrophage-rich ascites and suppressive soluble mediators; experimental findings support complement-pathway involvement in immune-checkpoint ligand expression. These observations offer a biological explanation for impaired local immunity but do not establish clinical resistance to checkpoint inhibition. Systemic therapy remains the treatment backbone, yet pivotal trials rarely report the Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI), cytology, ascites response or peritoneal-specific progression. Early studies combine checkpoint blockade with pressurised intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy (PIPAC), repeated intraperitoneal paclitaxel or hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC); direct intraperitoneal antibodies, cytokines and cellular therapies are also under investigation. Feasibility and local pharmacodynamic changes do not establish synergistic benefit. Future trials should compare an added intraperitoneal treatment against an otherwise identical systemic regimen, collect matched blood, ascites and peritoneal tissue samples over time, and relate immune changes to cytological clearance, PCI, symptoms and survival. Operative consolidation requires a separate randomised assessment in prospectively defined responders. Treatment continuity, quality of life, nutrition and hospital-free survival are essential measures of net benefit.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1981680.abstract: Introduction Bilateral vestibulopathy (BVP) presents with oscillopsia, unsteadiness, and imbalance. Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is a rare and underrecognized cause of BVP, with direct infiltration of the vestibulocochlear nerves representing a potential mechanism of bilateral vestibular dysfunction. We report a case of LM-related BVP documented by quantitative video head impulse test (vHIT) of all six semicircular canals. Case report A 61-year-old man presented with a six-month history of dizziness, tinnitus, oscillopsia, imbalance, and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. vHIT showed reduced vestibulo-ocular reflex gain in all six semicircular canals. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed leptomeningeal enhancement and enhancement of both vestibulocochlear nerves. CSF showed elevated protein, lymphocytic pleocytosis, and malignant cells. Serum anti-AQP4 antibodies were positive (1:320), but no other paraneoplastic antibodies were identified. He was diagnosed with LM from lung adenocarcinoma causing secondary BVP via direct infiltration of the vestibulocochlear nerves. Dizziness improved with intrathecal chemotherapy. However, he died approximately one year after discharge. Conclusion BVP may be the initial presentation of LM. It underscores the necessity of considering rare etiologies in patients with unexplained BVP. Early recognition and targeted therapy may improve neurological outcomes, although overall prognosis remains limited in the setting of disseminated malignancy.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1981709.abstract: Experimental oncofertility remains fragmented across models of cancer biology, treatment-associated gonadotoxicity, fertility preservation, and reproductive recovery. We propose extending the Oncopig concept into a translational platform that reconnects these states within one genetically defined, cancer-bearing host. The Oncopig provides the oncologic backbone, combining programmable cancer in an immunocompetent large-animal host with clinically scaled intervention and longitudinal sampling. High-resolution porcine genomics, CRISPR-based genome engineering, somatic-cell nuclear transfer for line generation, comparative experimental pathology, and mature reproductive biotechnology extend this architecture toward reproductive endpoints. Here, programmability refers to deliberate specification of the cancer state-genotype, cell lineage or induction strategy, and timing-whereas the reproductive phenotype is measured longitudinally rather than programmed. Distant-cancer modules can test whether cancer status modifies gonadotoxicity, while reproductive-organ modules require disease-specific alleles, appropriate cell-of-origin targeting, and pathology-led validation. Because porcine and human reproduction align in several endocrine and gonadal processes but differ in cycle organization, implantation, placentation, and pregnancy, translation should emphasize process-level endpoints rather than numerical equivalence. The platform is particularly suited to unresolved questions involving targeted therapies and immunotherapies, preservation timing, and pediatric or prepubertal patients. Porcine reproductive biotechnology provides functional endpoints from gonadal tissue and gametes to embryos and offspring. Rather than replacing rodent or human-based models, the Oncopig framework adds an integrated translational layer for questions requiring clinically scaled intervention, longitudinal physiology, and functional reproductive recovery.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1982346.abstract: Cancer in children, adolescents, and young adults (AYA) remains a global health challenge, with disparities in survival and quality of life between high-resource and low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). These disparities arise across the cancer continuum, including delayed recognition, inadequate diagnostic capacity, fragmented referral pathways, treatment abandonment, limited supportive care, unequal access to molecular diagnostics, and insufficient survivorship services. Precision oncology provides an opportunity to address these challenges, but its equity potential extends beyond genomic sequencing and targeted therapies. This narrative review examines an integrated precision oncology continuum encompassing early recognition, diagnostic and pathological accuracy, molecular characterization, risk stratification, precision treatment, response monitoring, supportive care, and lifelong survivorship. Evidence from LMIC settings is used to illustrate diagnostic delay, referral barriers, treatment abandonment, health-system limitations, and outcome disparities without attempting an exhaustive country comparison. The review proposes a tiered, equity-centered framework in which foundational cancer services are strengthened alongside progressively accessible molecular and digital technologies. Regional referral networks, patient navigation, tele-oncology, pathology and laboratory networks, targeted molecular testing, multidisciplinary care, survivorship planning, and longitudinal cancer registries are emphasized as practical components. For AYA patients, fertility, reproductive health, mental health, education, employment, and transition between pediatric and adult services are incorporated into precision care. Ultimately, equitable precision oncology should connect biological precision with health-system precision, ensuring that every young person can receive timely diagnosis, appropriate treatment, continuous monitoring, and lifelong survivorship support.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1982346.title: From missed diagnosis to lifelong survivorship: a precision oncology roadmap for equity in pediatric and AYA cancer care.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1982354.abstract: Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) has undergone substantial epidemiological and clinical changes, with an increasing proportion of human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated tumours and declining tobacco exposure. We investigated temporal changes in patient characteristics, HPV/p16 status, treatment patterns, and survival among patients with OPSCC in Denmark. Patients with OPSCC were identified from the Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database (2000-2023) and the Danish National Patient Cancer Registry (DCR; 1980-2021). The Copenhagen database provided detailed clinical and pathological data, including HPV/p16 status, while the DCR enabled assessment of long-term survival trends. Temporal changes were evaluated across diagnostic periods. Overall survival, relative survival, and restricted mean survival time were estimated. Among 3,631 OPSCC patients in the Copenhagen database, median age at diagnosis increased from 59 years in 2000-2005 to 64 years in 2018-2023 (p<0.001). The proportion of HPV+/p16+ patients increased significantly from 43.5% in 2000-2005 to 62.8% in 2018-2023. The proportion of never smokers also increased from 0.5% to 23.5%, while ≥20 pack-years decreased from 73.2% to 52.1% (p<0.001). Treatment patterns changed substantially, with radiotherapy alone decreasing from 87.6% to 27.9% and chemoradiotherapy increasing from 1.6% to 46.3%. Among 9,379 patients in the DCR, five-year relative survival increased from 31.8% in 1980-1984 to 70.1% in 2015-2019. Among HPV+/p16+ patients, five-year overall survival increased from 63.1% in 2000-2005 to 83.7% in 2018-2023. In Denmark, OPSCC has undergone substantial epidemiological and therapeutic changes accompanied by marked improvements in survival, including among HPV+/p16+ patients.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1982354.title: Changing epidemiology and survival of HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer in Denmark: four decades of population-based data.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1983430.abstract: Hormone receptor–positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2–negative (HR+/HER2−) breast cancer accounts for the majority of breast cancers and remains highly dependent on endocrine therapy across both early and advanced disease settings. Although the incorporation of CDK4/6 inhibitors has substantially improved clinical outcomes, endocrine resistance, whether primary or secondary, ultimately limits durable disease control. Resistance arises through heterogeneous and evolving mechanisms, including ESR1 mutations and fusions, ER transcriptional reprogramming, activation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR and other bypass pathways, cell-cycle escape, epigenetic remodeling, and metabolic adaptation. These molecular insights are increasingly being translated into biomarker-guided therapeutic strategies, including next-generation oral selective estrogen receptor degraders, PROTAC ER degraders, and PI3K/AKT/mTOR inhibitors; antibody–drug conjugates are considered separately as antigen-directed options after endocrine resistance. Importantly, circulating tumor DNA monitoring of emerging ESR1 mutations provides an opportunity to identify molecular progression before radiographic progression and to support earlier treatment adaptation. This narrative review integrates recent mechanistic and clinical evidence on endocrine resistance in HR+/HER2− breast cancer, with emphasis on how resistance mechanisms and biomarkers can inform drug selection, treatment sequencing, and dynamic disease monitoring. A mechanism-guided approach may therefore help move clinical management from empiric treatment switching toward more individualized, biomarker-driven, whole-course care.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1983430.title: Endocrine resistance in HR+/HER2− breast cancer: molecular mechanisms and emerging therapeutic strategies

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1984066.abstract: Urothelial carcinoma is a common urinary malignancy with high incidence, recurrence, and mortality. Early diagnosis is pivotal for improving patient outcomes. Current standards have important limitations: cystoscopy, although the cornerstone of diagnosis and surveillance, is invasive and costly, while cytology has limited sensitivity for low-grade or early-stage lesions. Urine, as a liquid biopsy, offers a non-invasive and repeatable approach for sampling urogenital pathology, with the potential for longitudinal monitoring through serial collection. The review covers urinary multi-omics biomarkers, including cfDNA/methylation, miRNAs, extracellular vesicles (EVs), and proteomic/metabolomic signatures. We summarize their performance in early detection, staging, and postoperative monitoring. Integrated multi-analyte models, including true multi-omics assays and multiplex single-omics panels, generally outperform single biomarkers, with some panels achieving >90% sensitivity and >95% specificity in prospective cohorts. Despite progress, several challenges remain: standardization, large-scale prospective validation, and regulatory/reimbursement barriers. We conclude that urinary multi-omics diagnostics are promising complementary tools that may optimize surveillance and risk stratification. Still, limited prospective validation, lack of standardization, and the persistent risk of false-negative results constrain adoption. On current evidence, they are not positioned to replace cystoscopy, which remains the cornerstone of diagnosis and surveillance, particularly in non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). However, their most realistic and immediate clinical role is as a triage tool to optimize the selective use of cystoscopy-particularly for risk-stratifying patients with hematuria, adjudicating equivocal cytology, and potentially reducing the frequency of invasive surveillance in low-risk NMIBC patients.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1984365.abstract: Tumor budding (TB) is a histopathological marker of tumor aggressiveness and an established prognostic factor in colorectal cancer. In rectal cancer, however, TB is usually assessed on biopsy or resection material, and a reliable result may not be available when preoperative management is being considered. To develop and internally validate a radiomics model for preoperative discrimination of low-grade versus intermediate/high-grade TB in patients with rectal cancer who proceed to upfront surgery without neoadjuvant treatment. The primary model was selected according to the highest repeated cross-validation AUC, with alternative feature sets and algorithms evaluated exploratorily. This retrospective study included 139 patients with pathologically confirmed rectal cancer who had received no neoadjuvant treatment. TB was assessed on postoperative resection specimens. T1WI, T2WI, arterial-phase contrast-enhanced T1WI, and DWI were analyzed. Radiomics features were extracted from the tumor core, a combined tumor-plus-2-mm expansion, and an isolated external 2-mm ring. Seven feature sets and four machine-learning algorithms were evaluated; the primary model was selected according to the highest repeated cross-validation AUC. Feature filtering, imputation, selection, and scaling were performed within the training portion of every split. Model performance was estimated using stratified five-fold cross-validation repeated five times and patient-level out-of-fold (OOF) probabilities. The primary core-ROI Elastic Net model achieved a repeated cross-validation AUC of 0.825 (range 0.809-0.839 across repetitions), with PR-AUC 0.781, sensitivity 0.604, specificity 0.851, and Brier score 0.173. Its patient-level mean OOF AUC was 0.829 (2,000 paired bootstrap replicates; 95% CI, 0.755-0.896). At a probability threshold of 0.50, patient-level sensitivity was 0.607 and specificity was 0.867. In conditional paired bootstrap comparisons, the core model showed higher AUCs than the clinical, peritumoral-ring, clinical-plus-expanded, clinical-plus-core, and clinical-plus-core-plus-ring models (BH-adjusted P = 0.004-0.005). The difference versus the expanded ROI was smaller and did not reach statistical significance after adjustment (P = 0.052). Multiparametric MRI radiomics features from the tumor core showed promising internal discrimination of low-grade versus intermediate/high-grade TB among patients who underwent upfront surgery without neoadjuvant treatment. The model may support preoperative TB risk stratification in this population, but external validation is required before clinical use.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1984427.abstract: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) regulate multiple mechanisms associated with glioblastoma (GBM) therapy resistance, which remains a major challenge in GBM treatment. Some resistance mechanisms involve genetic heterogeneity, glioblastoma stem cells, the tumor microenvironment, autophagy, metabolic reprogramming, vascular adaptation, and altered transcriptional regulation. By regulating protein activity, stability, localization, interactions, and signaling, PTMs can influence several of these processes and affect treatment response. This review examines the roles of phosphorylation, ubiquitination and ubiquitin-like modifications, acetylation, methylation, and glycosylation in resistance to temozolomide, radiotherapy, and targeted therapies. We further discuss emerging PTMs, including lactylation, succinylation, and UFMylation, for which evidence linking individual modifications to therapeutic resistance ranges from direct resistance mechanisms to effects primarily associated with GBM biology. PTM crosstalk is also discussed in the context of DNA repair, redox homeostasis, metabolism, glioblastoma stem cell maintenance, and therapy response. Finally, we examine pharmacological targeting of PTM-regulating enzymes and pathways and the effects of natural bioactive compounds on PTM-dependent mechanisms.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1985943.abstract: Epigenetic therapies can reverse malignant transcriptional programs, but their activity is often constrained by adaptive stress responses that allow cancer cells to survive and recover. Autophagy is a central component of this adaptation. By sustaining metabolic homeostasis, mitochondrial fitness, proteostasis, and lysosomal recycling, autophagy can buffer the cellular injury produced by inhibitors of DNA methyltransferases, histone deacetylases, and bromodomain proteins. These observations provide a strong rationale for combining epigenetic therapies with autophagy inhibition. However, the field has too often equated autophagosome accumulation with increased autophagic flux and treatment-induced autophagy with a functional dependency. Moreover, the lysosomotropic agents used in early clinical studies incompletely inhibit autophagy and exert broader effects on lysosomal biology. Consequently, compelling preclinical activity has not translated into consistent clinical benefit. Here, we critically evaluate the mechanisms through which epigenetic therapies engage autophagy, distinguish correlative markers from causal evidence of resistance, and assess the preclinical and clinical data supporting combination strategies. We also define the major barriers to translation, including inadequate pharmacodynamic assays, a lack of predictive biomarkers, context-dependent effects on tumor and immune cells, and the limited potency and selectivity of current autophagy inhibitors. Defining when, where, and how autophagy becomes a targetable dependency will be essential to translate this compelling biology into an effective precision treatment.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1986814.abstract: Two randomized trials, CALGB 140503 and JCOG0802, established segmentectomy as an oncologically acceptable alternative to lobectomy for small, peripheral, clinically node-negative non-small cell lung cancer. Both reached that conclusion under a protocol-enforced condition that is rarely emphasized when their results are applied in practice: nodal status had to be verified intraoperatively against a defined anatomic standard. CALGB 140503 required frozen-section confirmation of N0 status at two mediastinal stations and one major hilar node before randomization, whereas JCOG0802 mandated systematic or selective dissection of N1 and N2 stations in both arms and explicitly disallowed sampling as a substitute. This review examines whether that nodal rigor is reproduced, or even reported, once segmentectomy leaves the trial setting. National data indicate that it is not. Segmentectomy accounts for 4.4% of resections for clinical stage I to IIA disease, and only 12.6% of segmentectomy cases met all three Commission on Cancer quality measures, with adherence concentrated in academic and higher-volume programs. Retrospective series consistently report lower nodal upstaging after segmentectomy than after lobectomy, but the difference is driven by N1 rather than N2 stations and tracks the smaller nodal footprint of the operation, so a lower upstaging rate cannot by itself distinguish less disease from less looking. Anatomic mapping data indicate that exhaustive intersegmental dissection is unnecessary, whereas reliable hilar and mediastinal sampling is not. Across the wider literature, adequate nodal evaluation is defined inconsistently and reported at a granularity too coarse for readers to verify compliance, a two-axis problem that we characterize here for the segmentectomy literature specifically. Robotic assistance increases the number of nodal stations harvested relative to video-assisted surgery but has not been shown to improve risk-adjusted detection of occult disease. We propose a seven-point minimum standard, anchored on station-based rather than count-based adequacy, for segmentectomy performed outside a clinical trial.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1988923.abstract: Recurrence remains common after curative-intent liver resection or thermal ablation for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). These interventions transiently remodel the hepatic and treatment-bed immune microenvironment through overlapping but distinct processes, including tissue injury, vascular and coagulation activation, neutrophil recruitment, and, particularly during resection, hepatic ischemia-reperfusion. We organize the evidence using a peri-interventional two-component heuristic: chronic liver disease and tumor-associated inflammation may shape baseline susceptibility, whereas acute treatment injury may trigger intervention-specific neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) accumulation. Experimental studies across liver-intervention and cross-cancer models link NETs to impaired CD8+ T-cell immunity, tumor-cell retention, extracellular-matrix remodeling, and metabolic adaptation. Patient-linked evidence remains limited and largely associative; much of the mechanistic framework therefore relies on colorectal liver metastasis and cross-cancer models. Translational studies should distinguish monitoring, pharmacodynamic, prognostic, and predictive applications and prioritize serial MPO-DNA as the best-supported circulating peri-interventional candidate, with NE-DNA or H3Cit-based measures as supportive assays and spatial validation where feasible. Candidate preclinical approaches include limiting NET formation, degrading established NET structures, and disrupting NET-target-cell signaling. NET-checkpoint combinations remain preclinical hypotheses, particularly because current phase III adjuvant ICI studies have not established postoperative HCC benefit. Because NET and neutrophil functions are context dependent, prospective studies should define intervention-specific NET kinetics, immune correlates, target engagement, recurrence phenotype, and safety.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1989686.abstract: Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) have revolutionized the management of high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC). Yet, current treatment decisions remain almost exclusively guided by static BRCA/homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) genotyping. This paradigm is increasingly challenged by a profound eligibility-benefit gap: real-world data show 93.4% of patients are PARPi-eligible, but only 22.0% achieve meaningful 2-year progression-free survival benefit, compounded by 10-30% HRD test failure rates, inability to capture dynamic resistance evolution, and negligible predictive value in the ~50% of HGSOC that are homologous recombination-proficient. This narrative review, based on literature up to June 2026, systematically evaluates functional biomarkers that complement BRCA/HRD testing by assessing real-time tumor biology. To our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate these biomarkers into a unified whole-disease-course framework accounting for evidence level, assay cost, and global resource setting. RAD51 immunohistochemistry directly visualizes homologous recombination repair capacity, achieving 95% accuracy in predicting PARPi response in preclinical patient-derived xenograft models and demonstrating robust predictive value in prospective clinical cohorts. The KELIM model, derived from early CA-125 kinetics and evaluated in >12,000 patients within prospective trial and registry datasets, provides a no-additional-assay-cost, tissue-independent readout of chemosensitivity with potential for broad, low-cost global deployment. Circulating tumor DNA enables noninvasive longitudinal monitoring of resistance, potentially preceding radiographic progression by weeks to months. Exploratory immune and artificial intelligence-based multimodal markers further refine response stratification. We propose deployment of these biomarkers at four critical clinical nodes-diagnosis, post-chemotherapy, maintenance, and progression-to guide therapy selection dynamically. By transitioning from static genotype-based eligibility to real-time functional phenotyping, this integrated strategy aims to close the eligibility-benefit gap and advance adaptive precision oncology for ovarian cancer globally. As a narrative review, this work aims to offer forward-looking conceptual frameworks and stimulate future research rather than to establish high-level clinical evidence or formal guidelines.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1990706.abstract: Ultra-high-dose-rate (UHDR) pulsed irradiation can deliver therapeutic doses within an extremely short time window, but UHDR is a physical delivery state, whereas the FLASH effect is a conditional comparative phenotype in which normal-tissue injury is reduced relative to a spatially dose-comparable conventional-dose-rate (CDR) irradiation comparator without loss of tumor control. This Review integrates evidence across four levels: physical exposure characterization, dosimetric measurement, biological comparison, and clinical translation. We examine the temporal structure and quality-assurance requirements of electron, very-high-energy electron, photon, proton, and heavy-ion UHDR platforms; synthesize positive, negative, and conditional findings across normal-tissue and tumor models; and integrate mechanistic studies spanning multiple time scales. Current evidence does not support 40 Gy/s, or any single average dose-rate metric, as either a sufficient or a necessary threshold for the FLASH effect. Effect magnitude and reproducibility are more likely determined jointly by dose per pulse, pulse structure, total delivery time, fractionation, irradiated volume, radiation quality, tissue-specific radiobiological characteristics, and biological state. Mechanistic data likewise favor multiscale coupling across time rather than a single explanatory pathway, although several causal links from early oxygen and radical dynamics to cellular and tissue outcomes still lack direct interventional validation. Human studies have established the feasibility of clinical UHDR delivery on selected electron and proton platforms and have provided preliminary safety data, but comparative clinical benefit over CDR irradiation has not yet been demonstrated. Further translation should therefore prioritize pulse-resolved traceable dosimetry, organ-specific normal-tissue dose-response relationships, late toxicity, comparable tumor control, and concurrent comparative clinical endpoints, with expansion guided by prespecified stage-gated translational criteria.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.2000409.abstract: Antigen-presenting cancer-associated fibroblasts (apCAFs), commonly defined by MHC class II molecules, CD74, and related transcriptional programs, exhibit divergent functions across gastrointestinal tumors. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, mesothelium-derived apCAFs promote regulatory T-cell differentiation and suppress effector responses, whereas their abundance in gastric cancer is associated with earlier-stage disease, longer survival, and improved immunotherapy responses. This paradox may reflect microenvironmental context and classifications that conflate transcriptional state, cellular origin, and immune function. apCAFs may therefore represent reversible, context-dependent states defined by origin, MHC class II-restricted antigen presentation, and co-stimulatory capacity. We propose a two-layer model that has not been validated in apCAFs. In this model, the chromatin accessibility of CIITA, CD40, CD80, and CD86 constructs a functional licensing range, while interferon - γ (IFN - γ), interleukin-1 (IL-1), and transforming growth factor - β (TGF - β) guide the formation of specific phenotypes within this range. Insufficient co-stimulation may favor immune tolerance; activation of co-stimulatory programs may support CD4 + T-cell help and CD8 + T-cell infiltration. Treatment-induced changes in CAF composition may reflect selective survival or genuine state transitions. Distinguishing these mechanisms requires lineage tracing, longitudinal single-cell transcriptomic and chromatin profiling, and patient-derived organoid–fibroblast co-cultures. Neoadjuvant therapy and serial endoscopic sampling provide feasible settings for capturing transient states. This framework supports replacing broad CAF depletion with temporally and state-informed functional reprogramming.

doi:10.3390/cancers18172880.abstract: Background and Aims: Until now, according to the EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of chronic hepatitis B (CHB), the relationship between steatotic liver disease (SLD) and the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in CHB patients still yields conflicting results, with some data suggesting an increased risk of HCC, while several cohort studies have indicated a reduced risk in CHB patients with SLD. Sex is a predominant factor in the development and severity of chronic liver diseases. We aimed to understand the effect modification by sex in this association using a large population-based cohort study with long-term follow-up of patients with CHB. Approach and Results: This population-based study from Taiwan’s National Health Insurance Research Database (2009–2022) comprised two cohorts of patients with CHB aged 40–75 years: (1) 53,888 patients treated with entecavir or tenofovir, and (2) 525,109 antiviral-naive patients. HCC was identified in 4245 and 9491 patients in the treated and untreated cohorts, respectively. After adjusting for competing risk of death and relevant covariates, SLD was associated with a lower risk of HCC in males but a higher risk in females, and this sex difference (p < 0.0001 for sex–SLD interaction) was identified in both treated (subdistribution hazard ratio [SHR] [95% CI]: 0.85 [0.74–0.96] in males and 1.42 [1.17–1.73] in females) and untreated (0.75 [0.67–0.84] in males and 1.34 [1.14–1.56] in females) patients. Using propensity score matching with stratification by sex, further accounting for differences in medication use between SLD and non-SLD groups, yielded consistent results. The excess risk of HCC with SLD among females was mainly in those aged≥55 years, and even existed in the presence of diabetes, whereas among males, SLD exhibited an inverse association with HCC, regardless of age or diabetes. Conclusions: There was a sex disparity in the association between SLD and CHB-related HCC. Future studies and management of SLD for CHB should consider the sex disparity.

doi:10.3390/cancers18193068.abstract: Importance: Urine drug test (UDT) can help screen and monitor aberrant controlled substance use among patients requiring opioid therapy for cancer pain. However, data on UDT utilization in patients with cancer pain remains limited. Objective: To determine the rate of UDT ordering and the factors associated with UDT order placement and the frequency and type of abnormal UDT findings. Methods: This retrospective study included adults (≥18 yrs) with a cancer diagnosis receiving prescription opioids for pain in an ambulatory pain clinic from November 2017 through April 2018. Descriptive statistics summarized patient characteristics and UDT findings. Logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with UDT ordering. Results: Five hundred fifty-eight patients were included in the study; the median age was 61 years, 52% were female, 74% were White, and 93% had active cancer. One hundred forty-one patients (25%) had UDT orders. On multivariate analysis, UDT ordering was associated with SOAPP-14 score ≥ 7 (OR, 2.03 95% CI 1.19-3.47 p = 0.009) and a history of substance use disorder (OR, 2.87 95% CI: 1.39-5.75 p = 0.004). Among those tested, 49 (35%) had abnormal results. A total of 80 abnormalities were identified, with some UDTs showing multiple findings; the most common was the absence of prescribed opioids (48%). Conclusions: Only one in four patients receiving opioids in an ambulatory cancer pain clinic received a UDT order, suggesting a more selective rather than routine use. UDT ordering was more common among patients with a SOAPP-14 score ≥ 7 and a history of substance use disorder. Among patients who underwent UDT, approximately one-third had abnormal results, with the absence of prescribed opioids or their expected metabolites being the most common finding. These findings suggest that UDT may provide important clinically relevant information as a component of comprehensive opioid monitoring. Further research is needed to establish evidence-based approaches to UDT implementation that promote consistent opioid safety practices.

doi:10.3390/cancers18193069.abstract: Background: Differentiating tumor recurrence from treatment-related changes in patients with glioma remains a major diagnostic challenge because conventional MRI has limited specificity. Amino acid positron emission tomography (PET) has emerged as a promising adjunctive imaging modality. Purpose: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of amino acid PET for distinguishing tumor recurrence from treatment-related changes in previously treated glioma patients. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted according to the PRISMA-DTA guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to March 2026. Studies evaluating clinically used amino acid PET tracers (MET, FET, or FDOPA) in previously treated glioma patients and reporting sufficient data to construct 2 × 2 contingency tables were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated using a bivariate random-effects model. The primary analysis was restricted to studies reporting patient-based data from non-overlapping cohorts. A post hoc sensitivity analysis, added in response to peer review, retained both potentially overlapping patient-based datasets. Lesion- and scan-based studies were excluded from quantitative synthesis because within-patient clustering could not be accounted for using the published aggregate data. Subgroup and meta-regression analyses explored sources of heterogeneity. Results: Sixteen studies met the inclusion criteria. The primary synthesis comprised 12 studies reporting patient-based data from non-overlapping cohorts (728 patients, one 2 × 2 table each). Amino acid PET demonstrated a pooled sensitivity of 0.87 (95% CI 0.83-0.90) and specificity of 0.78 (95% CI 0.72-0.83). The positive likelihood ratio was 3.91 (95% CI 3.04-5.02), the negative likelihood ratio was 0.17 (95% CI 0.13-0.23), and the diagnostic odds ratio was 22.8 (95% CI 14.6-35.7). At the pooled prevalence of recurrence of 68%, a positive scan corresponded to a post-test probability of 89% and a negative scan to 27%. Univariable I2 estimates were 10% for sensitivity and 0% for specificity, but these measures should not be interpreted as evidence of overall homogeneity. Estimates were essentially unchanged when both potentially overlapping datasets were retained (13 studies, 756 patients). Tracer type was nominally associated with the diagnostic odds ratio (p = 0.044), but tracer type was strongly confounded by study sample size and publication era, and the association was not robust in the sensitivity analysis. No statistically significant subgroup differences were identified; however, these analyses were limited by the small number of studies and methodological heterogeneity. Conclusions: Amino acid PET usefully but not decisively revises the probability of recurrence in patients under suspicion after treatment. At the pooled pre-test probability of 68%, a positive PET increased the post-test probability of recurrence to 89%, whereas a negative PET reduced it to 27%; therefore, a negative result does not exclude recurrence. Because positivity thresholds were largely derived post hoc and reference standards were composite, these estimates are likely to be optimistic. Apparent tracer-related differences observed in subgroup and meta-regression analyses were strongly confounded by publication era and study sample size and were not supported by head-to-head within-patient comparisons. Therefore, no superiority of MET, FET, or FDOPA can be inferred from the available evidence. The analysis was limited to MET, FET, and FDOPA, and the findings may therefore not be generalizable to other amino acid tracers.

doi:10.3390/cancers18193070.abstract: Metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) is biologically heterogeneous, resulting in variable outcomes despite similar disease burden and treatment. Although metastasectomy offers the only potentially curative option for selected patients, surgical selection remains largely anatomy based. Whether biological factors continue to influence outcomes after resection remains unclear. We retrospectively analysed 290 consecutive patients with stage IV colorectal adenocarcinoma treated at a Brazilian tertiary oncology centre (2003-2019). Tumour sidedness, RAS mutational status, and metastasectomy were evaluated for overall survival (OS) using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression in the overall cohort and the metastasectomy subgroup. Median OS was 40.2 months. Patients undergoing metastasectomy had significantly longer survival than those managed non-operatively (median 116.0 vs. 30.1 months; 5-year OS 63% vs. 14%; p 70 ys vs. ≤ 70 HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.37-0.92; p = 0.021) and metastatic presentation (synchronous vs. metachronous: HR 0.61 95% CI 0.39-0.95; p = 0.028). RAS status remained associated with survival in patients undergoing metastasectomy (HR 3.75, 95% CI 1.46-9.60; p = 0.006). Tumour biology remains a dominant determinant of survival in mCRC even after metastasectomy. These data challenge purely anatomy-based surgical paradigms and support integrating molecular and clinicopathological risk into post-resection management and treatment planning.

doi:10.3390/cancers18193071.abstract: Tebentafusp is a first-in-class bispecific fusion protein that redirects T cells toward gp100-expressing cells and represents the first systemic treatment shown to improve overall survival in patients with HLA-A*02:01-positive metastatic uveal melanoma. As gp100 is also expressed on normal cutaneous melanocytes, skin toxicity is one of the most common adverse effects of treatment, although it remains relatively underrecognized. This narrative review summarizes the available evidence regarding tebentafusp-related cutaneous toxicity from clinical trials and emerging real-world studies. Across published cohorts, cutaneous adverse events occur in most patients receiving tebentafusp. They typically manifest within hours of the initial infusions as diffuse, frequently photodistributed erythematous eruptions accompanied by pruritus, with both frequency and severity generally decreasing with subsequent treatment. Other reported manifestations include xerosis, edema, pigmentary and hair alterations, including vitiligo-like depigmentation and poliosis, as well as less common urticarial, bullous, and photosensitive reactions. Although the development of early cutaneous toxicity has repeatedly been linked to better survival outcomes, this relationship does not appear to be independent of established prognostic variables. Accordingly, rash should currently be interpreted as a potential indicator of immune activation rather than a validated surrogate for therapeutic efficacy. Most cutaneous reactions are mild and can be effectively managed with emollients, topical corticosteroids, and antihistamines, while permanent discontinuation of therapy is uncommon. With tebentafusp becoming increasingly integrated into routine clinical practice and other gp100-targeted and bispecific T-cell-engaging therapies entering development, recognition of this characteristic dermatologic toxicity profile and early involvement of dermatology will be important for effective supportive care and continuation of treatment. Further prospective studies using standardized terminology are warranted to better define the incidence, prognostic relevance, and optimal management of these cutaneous adverse events.

doi:10.3390/cancers18193072.abstract: The expanding molecular classification of renal neoplasia has created a growing need for biomarkers that translate biologic insights into practical diagnostic tools. This review focuses on recently introduced immunohistochemical (IHC) and RNA in situ hybridization (RNA-ISH) assays with potential relevance to routine kidney tumor pathology. Biomarkers were selected based on their applicability to conventional formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue; commercial accessibility and potential for cost-effective implementation; evaluation in substantial tumor cohorts; comparison with established or gold-standard methods; and, where available, validation in independent and/or multi-institutional studies. The reviewed biomarkers encompass markers of cellular lineage and differentiation (L1CAM, FOXI1, and LINC01187); markers of tumor identity, molecular alterations, and metabolic pathway dysregulation (GPNMB, AKR1B10, 2SC, VSTM2A, TRIM63, and Merlin); and prognostic or therapeutically relevant biomarkers (BAP1, HER2, ABCC2, and PD-L1). We critically evaluate their biologic rationale, diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive applications, technical limitations, and current level of validation. By distinguishing biomarkers supported for broader or selective clinical implementation from those requiring additional validation or remaining primarily relevant to defined therapeutic contexts, this review provides a practical framework for their integration into contemporary renal tumor pathology.

doi:10.3390/cancers18193073.abstract: Background: Germline pathogenic variants in BRCA1 and BRCA2 are established contributors to hereditary breast cancer, yet their separate prognostic effects in non-metastatic disease remain uncertain because they are frequently analyzed as a single group. Methods: We retrospectively evaluated 360 patients with stage I-III invasive breast cancer who underwent germline genetic testing. Patients were categorized as BRCA-negative (n = 281), BRCA1-positive (n = 43), or BRCA2-positive (n = 36). Disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox proportional hazards models with adjustment for molecular subtype and clinicopathological variables. Results: During follow-up, 76 DFS events and 27 deaths were observed. BRCA2 positivity was independently associated with worse DFS (hazard ratio [HR] 2.13, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.14-3.98; p = 0.017), whereas BRCA1 positivity showed an association with improved OS (HR 0.08, 95% CI 0.01-0.51; p = 0.007). The OS finding should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited number of death events and the risk of model instability. Conclusions: Germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants may have divergent prognostic implications in non-metastatic breast cancer and should not be treated as a single homogeneous prognostic entity. Separate evaluation of these variants may improve risk stratification and support more individualized patient management, although validation in larger cohorts is warranted.

doi:10.3390/cancers18193074.abstract: Background: Overexpression and increased activity of ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters, such as P-glycoprotein (ABCB1/P-gp), breast cancer resistance protein (ABCG2/BCRP), and multidrug resistance-associated proteins (ABCC/MRPs), are known to be among the major contributors to multidrug resistance (MDR) in tumors to structurally similar or even different chemotherapeutic agents, thereby decreasing treatment efficacy. Thus, there is an urgent need to develop novel, effective therapies that overcome MDR and increase chemotherapy response rates. Results: We showed here that receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (RTKIs) designed to inhibit the overactivated FGFR and/or VEGFR signaling pathways exert an "off-target" effect on MDR proteins in colorectal cancer (CRC), thereby sensitizing CRC to certain chemotherapies. In particular, Pemigatinib and Infigratinib ranked among the top eight tested selective and non-selective FGFR/VEGFR inhibitors that effectively resensitized all types of CRCs to the DNA topoisomerase II inhibitor Doxorubicin and, in fewer experimental settings, to the antimetabolite 5-Fluorouracil. This was evidenced by a significant increase in apoptosis in CRCs treated with the aforementioned chemotherapeutic drugs in combination with RTKIs. Of note, despite the CRCs exhibiting signs of FGFR and VEGFR activation, RTKIs alone exhibited only minor pro-apoptotic and anti-proliferative activities. The enhancement of pro-apoptotic activity of Doxorubicin when co-treated with Pemigatinib, Lucitanib, and Regorafenib in HCT116 cells was consistent with a decrease in proliferative activity in CRCs treated with these RTKIs alone. This was also revealed by high synergy scores (SC) between several RTKIs (e.g., Pemigatinib, Lucitanib, and Regorafenib) and Doxorubicin in CRCs. The aforementioned effects of RTKIs were due to the inhibition of MDR-related ABC transporter activity, particularly ABCB1 and ABCG2. Indeed, in HCT116 cells, Lucitanib and, to a lesser extent, Pemigatinib impaired the efflux of the intrinsically fluorescent Doxorubicin and Mitoxantrone. Similarly, the efflux of Calcein AM, an ABCB1 substrate, was significantly impaired in Lucitanib- and Pemigatinib-treated CRCs, thereby revealing ABCB1 as a molecular target for these RTKIs. Consistent with SC data, Infigratinib and Cabozatinib effectively impaired the efflux of Doxorubicin from Colon-26 cells. Similarly, ABCB1 protein was found to be a primary target for Infigratinib in Colon-26 cancer cells, which was evidenced by competitive assay data based on the combined use of selective ABCB1 and ABCG2 inhibitors (e.g., Tariquidar and Ko-143, respectively). Importantly, ABC-inhibitory effects of RTKIs in CRCs were mediated solely by the impaired efflux of chemotherapeutic agents from CRCs and were not due to the decreased expression of ABC transporters or their subcellular distribution. Lastly, in the small-cohort allograft study, we found Infigratinib to be an effective chemosensitizing agent for the Colon-26 murine colon carcinoma in vivo. This was evidenced by the reduced growth of Colon-26 allografts in the experimental group receiving the combined therapy of Infigratinib and Doxorubicin compared with the single-treated groups. Consistent with these findings, immunohistochemical (IHC) staining revealed a substantial increase in apoptotic cells (e.g., cleaved caspase-3-positive) and a decrease in proliferative cells (e.g., Ki-67-positive) in allografts from animals treated with a combination of Infigratinib and Doxorubicin. Conclusions: We show here for the first time that some FGFR inhibitors (e.g., Pemigatinib and Infigratinib) can effectively potentiate cytotoxic and anti-proliferative activity against CRCs overexpressing MDR-related ABC transporters, thereby suggesting potential therapeutic avenues for treating CRC that progresses despite standard conventional therapies.
