doi:10.3390/cancers18203270.abstract: Background/Objectives: Establishing biomarkers is crucial for early cancer detection. Structural biomarkers can be revealed by noninvasive X-ray diffraction. We applied this approach to human nails and observed structural changes in the major nail tissue component, keratin, which coincided with a cancer diagnosis. Methods: X-ray diffraction patterns were obtained from 230 nail samples (control/cancer split: 92/138) belonging to 133 patients (48/85) in wide (WAXS) and small (SAXS) ranges of scattering angles. For both ranges, we obtained one-dimensional scattering profiles in meridional and equatorial directions. We examined these profiles using machine-learning techniques such as logistic regression and linear discriminant analysis. Results: We obtained good classification metrics that allow us to distinguish participants with cancer from controls. The results are similar for both machine-learning methods. Combining all four profiles (WAXS meridional, WAXS equatorial, SAXS meridional, and SAXS equatorial) produced a sensitivity of 0.753 and a specificity of 0.771 for the Linear Discriminant Analysis at the Youden point. For the limited set of patients of the same age, we showed that the patterns can still be distinguished, supporting our hypothesis that the observed aberrations are cancer-induced. Conclusions: Our exploratory research demonstrated the feasibility of cancer detection using the X-ray diffraction of human nails.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203271.abstract: Cancer therapy-related cardiovascular toxicity (CTR-CVT) is associated with morbidity, mortality, and interruptions to cancer treatment. Current cardio-oncology clinical assessment tools generally rely on a limited range of clinical data; however, in the era of precision medicine, it may be possible to leverage multimodal data, including imaging and multi-omic inputs, to personalise CTR-CVT prediction and assessment. In this review, we examine the genotypic and phenotypic predictors of CTR-CVT and the evidence supporting their incorporation into multimodal risk models. Most research focuses on cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD). We identify a strong evidence base for multimodal imaging-guided prediction, particularly cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE)-derived global longitudinal strain measurements. Emerging evidence also supports the potential value of novel imaging parameters, including computed tomography (CT) and TTE-derived radiomic features. From the genomic and proteomic perspective, truncating titin variants and microRNA-126 may be informative predictors of cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD). At the same time, the literature also highlights potential epigenomic markers of CTR-CVT. Finally, we consider how these diverse data can be integrated into multimodal risk models and how digital innovation and advanced machine learning methods may further improve model predictive performance. However, a large implementation gap remains, with challenges such as data privacy and a lack of external validation studies preventing routine clinical implementation.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203272.abstract: Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) have a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer (CRC) compared with the general population. This increased risk is mainly related to chronic colonic inflammation and is influenced by factors such as disease duration, disease extent, family history of CRC, and the presence of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). Although the incidence of CRC in IBD has decreased over recent decades, it remains an important cause of disease-related morbidity and mortality. CRC prevention in IBD extends beyond colonoscopic surveillance and includes high-quality endoscopic surveillance, early detection and appropriate treatment of dysplasia, and long-term control of intestinal inflammation through a personalized approach. This review summarizes current evidence on IBD-associated colorectal carcinogenesis and strategies for CRC prevention, with emphasis on risk stratification, optimization of endoscopic surveillance, dysplasia management, treat-to-target strategies and multidisciplinary management.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203272.title: Colorectal Cancer in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: How to Minimize the Risk.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203273.abstract: Background: Microcystic adnexal carcinoma (MAC) is a rare cutaneous adnexal malignancy characterized by slow clinical growth but pronounced local aggressiveness, extensive subclinical infiltration, and a propensity for perineural invasion. Owing to its rarity and often inconspicuous clinical presentation, diagnosis and treatment remain challenging, particularly in the anatomically complex head and neck region. Methods: A narrative review of the literature was performed using PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase, covering publications available up to August 2026. Relevant studies addressing the clinical presentation, diagnostic work-up, histopathology, imaging, surgical and non-surgical treatment, recurrence, and follow-up of MAC were reviewed, with particular emphasis on MAC arising in the head and neck region. Results: Adequate deep biopsy extending into the subcutaneous tissue is essential for reliable diagnosis, as superficial sampling may result in misdiagnosis. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging may be considered when deep infiltration or clinically significant perineural spread is suspected, although MAC-specific imaging evidence is limited. Complete surgical excision with comprehensive microscopic margin assessment represents the cornerstone of treatment. Mohs micrographic surgery or staged excision with comprehensive peripheral and deep margin assessment may be favored when technically feasible; comparative evidence is retrospective and does not establish a survival advantage. More extensive oncological resection may be required for tumors involving deep structures or major nerves. Elective treatment of the clinically negative neck is generally not indicated because regional metastases are uncommon. Radiotherapy has a selective role in patients with high-risk features, unresectable disease, or inadequate surgical margins, but supporting evidence remains predominantly retrospective. Conclusions: Management of head and neck MAC should focus on accurate diagnosis and durable local and perineural disease control. Available evidence and expert guidance favor margin-controlled surgery, with radiotherapy considered selectively; the optimal treatment and surveillance strategies have not been prospectively established. Given the potential for late recurrence, prolonged clinical surveillance is warranted.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203273.title: Microcystic Adnexal Carcinoma of the Head and Neck: Diagnostic Work-Up and Contemporary Treatment Strategies-A Narrative Review.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203274.abstract: Background/Objectives:Pneumocystis jirovecii colonization induces persistent low-grade pulmonary inflammation, which may alter fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake in positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT). We aimed to evaluate whether asymptomatic infection influences the maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) or clinicopathological parameters of primary lung cancer. Methods: In this prospective single-center observational study, 107 consecutive patients undergoing surgical resection for primary lung cancer were enrolled. Preoperative FDG PET/CT scans were obtained within four weeks prior to surgery. Intraoperative respiratory secretions and lung tissue samples were analyzed for P. jirovecii, using nested polymerase chain reaction (nested-PCR) targeting the mitochondrial large subunit rRNA gene. Propensity score matching (PSM) adjusting for age, sex, and body mass index was performed across 1:1, 1:2, and 1:3 matching models. Results:Pneumocystis jirovecii colonization was confirmed in 12 of 107 patients (11.21%). In the unadjusted cohort, no significant differences in primary lesion SUVmax were identified between positive and negative patients (10.38 ± 6.50 vs. 8.86 ± 6.58, p = 0.411), nor across matched models (1:1: p = 0.555; 1:2: p = 0.951; 1:3: p = 0.926). Following PSM, patients without colonization exhibited significantly larger maximum tumor diameters in both 1:2 (30.71 ± 19.23 vs. 18.25 ± 6.63 mm, p = 0.035) and 1:3 matching models (29.08 ± 17.47 vs. 18.25 ± 6.63 mm, p = 0.035). Conclusions: We did not find any association between P. jirovecii colonization and preoperative metabolic tumor staging on FDG PET/CT. However, asymptomatic carriage was associated with smaller primary tumor dimensions following propensity adjustment in 1:2 and 1:3 matching models, warranting further exploration of host-fungal interactions within the pulmonary tumor microenvironment.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203274.title: Is PET/CT Useful in Detecting Pneumocystis jirovecii Colonization in Patients with Primary Lung Cancer?

doi:10.3390/cancers18203275.abstract: Background/Objectives: Surveillance of intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) provides a clinically relevant window in which biological changes associated with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) development may potentially be investigated before advanced disease occurs. Nanoparticle-enabled protein corona (PC) fingerprinting has shown analytical potential in PDAC, but the extent to which different nanoplatforms recover distinct information across the biologically proximate IPMN-PDAC spectrum remains unclear. This exploratory study compared three nanoplatform configurations to identify a candidate workflow for subsequent validation. Methods: Plasma from 22 patients with de novo PDAC (n = 11), IPMN (n = 6), or IPMN-derived PDAC (n = 5) was incubated with graphene oxide (GO) nanosheets, gold nanoparticles (AuNPs), or cationic DOTAP-DOPE liposomes. Wash-resistant PCs were analyzed by SDS-PAGE, quantified across predefined molecular weight (MW) regions, and evaluated using exploratory linear discriminant analysis with repeated stratified cross-validation. Results: The three nanoplatforms generated non-equivalent electrophoretic PC architectures. In this small exploratory cohort, GO showed the broadest pattern of nominal clinical-group-associated variation in relative MW-region contributions and yielded internal cross-validation AUC estimates of 0.955 for IPMN versus de novo PDAC, 0.767 for IPMN versus IPMN-derived PDAC, and 0.927 for IPMN-derived versus de novo PDAC. Corresponding AUCs were 0.606-0.700 for AuNPs and 0.621-0.691 for liposomes. Conclusions: GO provided the broadest group-associated variation and numerically highest internal discrimination estimates, supporting its prioritization for independent validation and prospective longitudinal evaluation in IPMN surveillance.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203276.abstract: Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is a rare and aggressive malignancy with recurrence rates of 54-70% following curative-intent resection, even after microscopically complete (R0) surgery. In this review, we summarize the current evidence for adjuvant mitotane, platinum-based chemotherapy, and radiation therapy in resected ACC, and discuss patient selection based on prognostic risk stratification. We also highlight the importance of multidisciplinary management at expert centers, remaining evidence gaps, and future directions including biomarker-driven treatment strategies.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203277.abstract: Dermoscopy improves the diagnosis of melanoma and keratinocyte carcinoma, but its value depends on the observer, the lesion mix, the anatomic site, and the action taken after the examination. Recent reviews have mainly focused on one modality or image-classification accuracy. This narrative review follows the clinical pathway and compares five linked areas: defined diagnostic criteria, sequential digital monitoring, site- and skin-tone-specific interpretation, multimodal imaging, and artificial intelligence (AI). Melanoma and keratinocyte carcinoma are discussed separately because their criteria, diagnostic problems, imaging needs, and management differ. Meta-analyses support dermoscopy over naked-eye examination, although accuracy remains closely related to clinician experience. A randomized trial of three-dimensional total-body photography with sequential dermoscopy led to more procedures and higher costs without finding more malignant tumors over two years. Reflectance confocal microscopy can improve specificity in selected equivocal lesions, while optical coherence technologies add architectural and depth information that is most relevant to keratinocyte carcinoma. AI has moved from retrospective benchmarks to prospective multicenter studies, but false-positive burden, dataset shift, underrepresentation of darker skin tones, limited explainability, and uncertain workflow effects remain. The review also considers foundation models, regulation, and patient-facing tools and uses a SWOT analysis to define research priorities. The field is at an inflection point in evidence, not image quality. Progress should be judged by effects on biopsy decisions, missed-cancer rates, timeliness, cost, access, and patient outcomes in defined populations.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203278.abstract: Modular megaprosthetic reconstruction is a central limb-salvage strategy after major skeletal resection, but long-term outcomes remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate patient and implant survival, complication burden, Henderson failure modes, and associated risk factors. We retrospectively analyzed 340 consecutive patients undergoing modular megaprosthetic reconstruction at a tertiary referral center from 2003 to 2024 for primary malignant bone tumors, metastatic disease, or complex revision- or trauma-related indications. Kaplan-Meier methods estimated patient, implant, and complication-free survival. Implant failure and first recorded Henderson failure modes were additionally assessed using competing-risk methods. Cox regression evaluated risk factors, with multivariable modelling focused on Type IV infection. Median follow-up was 5 years. Patient survival was 71.4% at 5 years and 61.3% at 10 years and was poorer in metastatic disease (p < 0.001). Implant survival was 78.0% and 70.3%, respectively. Complications occurred in 133 patients (39.1%). Type IV infection was the most frequent first failure mode (49, 14.4%), followed by Type I soft-tissue failure (40, 11.8%). The cumulative incidence of infection was 14.6% at 5 years and 15.3% at 10 years. Previous surgeries at the operative site (hazard ratio [HR] 2.30 per additional surgery, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.90-2.80), operative time (HR 1.005/min, 95% CI 1.002-1.008), and diabetes mellitus (HR 2.30, 95% CI 1.25-4.25) were independently associated with infection and remained significant after expanded adjustment. Implant survival remained 70.3% at 10 years, but complications were frequent. Infection was the dominant first failure mode, and prior local surgery, longer operative time, and diabetes identified higher-risk patients. These findings support individualized risk assessment, preventive planning, and long-term surveillance.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203279.abstract: Background/Aims: Mirabegron, a selective β3-adrenergic receptor agonist used to treat overactive bladder (OAB), can promote adipose tissue browning and alter systemic metabolism, raising interest in its potential relationship with cancer development. However, clinical evidence regarding cancer risk remains limited and inconsistent. We compared the risks of obesity-related and site-specific cancers between patients with OAB initiating mirabegron and those initiating antimuscarinic medications. Methods: We conducted a multicenter emulated target trial using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults aged ≥20 years with OAB or related symptoms who newly initiated mirabegron or an antimuscarinic medication were included using a new-user, active-comparator design. Patients with pre-existing malignancy were excluded. Propensity score matching was performed 1:1, and a 1-year lag period after treatment initiation was applied for cancer outcomes to reduce potential reverse causation from occult malignancy. Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) under an intention-to-treat analog. Results: A 365-day lag/landmark period was applied before propensity-score matching. Patients with a recorded neoplasm or death during this period, or without follow-up extending through day 366, were excluded. Subsequent 1:1 propensity-score matching yielded 106,500 patients in each treatment group. Mirabegron initiation was not associated with the composite of obesity-related neoplasms compared with antimuscarinic initiation (HR, 1.011; 95% CI, 0.954-1.071). The individual neoplasm outcomes also showed no significant between-group differences. However, among patients eligible for the 1-year landmark mortality analysis, mirabegron initiation was associated with higher subsequent all-cause mortality (HR, 1.083; 95% CI, 1.044-1.124). Exploratory negative-control analysis of Hodgkin lymphoma showed no significant association. Conclusions: Among patients with OAB, mirabegron initiation was not associated with a significant difference in overall obesity-related neoplasm risk compared with antimuscarinic initiation. The observed associations with all-cause mortality should be interpreted cautiously given the observational design, multiple comparisons, and potential residual confounding. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in prospective studies.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203280.abstract: Induction failure (IF) after standard induction chemotherapy is associated with poor outcomes in pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (pAML); however, whether established molecular markers such as FLT3-ITD retain prognostic significance across induction response states remains incompletely understood. We characterized the genomic landscape of IF and evaluated the prognostic significance of FLT3-ITD according to induction response. This multi-cohort study integrated a TARGET discovery cohort (n = 1979) and an independent cohort from the Children's Hospital of Chongqing Medical University (CHCMU; n = 98). Clinical characteristics, somatic mutations, fusion profiles, and gene-gene interaction patterns were compared between patients with and without IF. Multivariable logistic regression identified genomic factors associated with IF, and survival analyses evaluated the prognostic impact of FLT3-ITD according to induction response. IF was associated with inferior OS (overall survival) (pooled HR = 3.24, 95% CI: 2.66-3.95). FLT3 mutations were consistently enriched in IF patients, whereas KIT mutations and favorable core-binding factor fusions were more frequent among non-IF patients. NUP98-NSD1 fusion was strongly enriched in IF patients in the TARGET cohort. Gene interaction analyses revealed reduced recurrent co-mutation patterns among IF patients. FLT3 mutation independently and reproducibly associated with IF. Among patients achieving induction remission, FLT3-ITD remained associated with inferior OS (HR = 1.34, 95% CI: 1.06-1.69, p = 0.014), whereas no statistically significant additional prognostic effect was detected among patients with IF. This study characterizes the genomic landscape of IF in pAML and identifies FLT3 mutation as a reproducible marker of induction resistance. Achieving induction remission does not eliminate the adverse prognostic significance of FLT3-ITD, supporting the integration of molecular risk and treatment response in subsequent risk stratification.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203281.abstract: Pemetrexed, an antifolate, is a standard therapy for lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). Since folic acid is vital for nucleic acid metabolism, disrupting its pathway affects both tumor cells and regenerating healthy cells. The PemToxTrial examined the impact of pemetrexed on severe hematotoxicity and mortality. This retrospective analysis included 136 LUAD patients (UICC8 stage IVA/B) receiving palliative treatment. Ninety-two patients received pemetrexed-based therapy, while 44 received pemetrexed-free treatment (68 and 38 with immune-checkpoint inhibitors). Bone metastasis (BM) was present in 47 patients in the pemetrexed group and 22 in the comparison group. The primary endpoint was grade III-V hematotoxicity; secondary endpoints included mortality, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). Hematologic outcomes following a subsequent change in clinical practice were prospectively assessed in a post-implementation cohort of 15 patients with bone-metastatic LUAD receiving pemetrexed-free regimens. Median age was 66 years, 59.6% were male and median follow-up was 13.5 months. Grade III-V hematotoxicity was most frequent (81%) in patients with BM receiving pemetrexed (n = 47), significantly higher than in other subgroups (p < 0.0001). Mortality was also increased in this group (66% vs. 29%, p < 0.0001), with hematotoxicity directly contributing to death in 42% versus 11.5% of cases. PFS was significantly inferior (5.2 vs. 8.6 months). Multivariable analysis identified BM as the only independent predictor of severe hematotoxicity and mortality. Only a mutational burden of ≥4 potential driver alterations was associated with inferior PFS. Bone-derived total lesion glycolysis (TLG) on PET-CT strongly correlated with high-grade hematotoxicity (p < 0.0001). The PemToxTrial identified a strong association between pemetrexed exposure, bone metastases, and severe hematotoxicity, supporting further prospective evaluation of bone metastasis status as a potential clinical risk factor for treatment-associated hematotoxicity.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203282.abstract: We developed and internally validated the Bladder Risk Index using Clinical and Systemic biomarkers (BRICS), a preoperative prediction model designed to estimate the likelihood of high-grade (HG) disease and muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) in patients undergoing their first transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT). This retrospective single-center study included 161 patients with newly diagnosed urothelial bladder cancer. The BRICS-HG model included tumor size, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), and creatinine-to-hemoglobin ratio (CHR), while the BRICS-MIBC model was based on tumor size and NLR. Model performance was assessed in terms of discrimination, calibration, and Brier score, together with exploratory decision curve analysis. Internal validation was performed using 2000 bootstrap resamples. MIBC was identified in 20 patients (12.4%). BRICS-HG demonstrated limited discriminatory ability, with an apparent AUC of 0.649 and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.623 (95% bootstrap interval: 0.541-0.703). BRICS-MIBC achieved moderate discrimination, with an apparent AUC of 0.735 and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.709 (95% bootstrap interval: 0.588-0.826). Across the bootstrap resamples, the model combining tumor size and NLR was selected in 53.9% of cases, reflecting uncertainty in predictor selection. BRICS-HG should be regarded as an exploratory model, and its current performance does not support clinical application. BRICS-MIBC demonstrated moderate discrimination after internal validation; however, its performance should be interpreted cautiously given the small number of MIBC events. Validation in larger, independent cohorts, ideally across multiple centers, is necessary before the model can be considered for clinical implementation.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203283.abstract: This review investigated whether exposure to certain endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) increases skin cancer risk. We performed a comprehensive narrative review of in vitro, animal, and human studies examining the association of EDCs with melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC). Chemicals are classified as (i) established EDCs with evidence of skin carcinogenicity; (ii) chemicals that are carcinogenic with endocrine-related effects; and (iii) chemicals with limited or uncertain evidence. Proposed carcinogenic mechanisms include oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, immunosuppression, DNA repair inhibition, and epigenetic alterations; AhR likely mediates the carcinogenicity of dioxin (TCDD), dioxin-like PCBs, and PAHs. Epidemiological evidence linking PCBs with melanoma is inconsistent. High cumulative occupational exposure to PAH-containing mineral oils or tar/pitch increases skin cancer risk. Evidence for PFAS and skin cancer is limited and inconsistent. Increased melanoma incidence has been reported after chronic occupational exposure to certain pesticides, including carbaryl, parathion, and maneb/mancozeb. There is substantial evidence of a dose-response association between chronic arsenic exposure and NMSC risk. High chronic exposure to specific EDCs (especially arsenic, certain PAHs, and certain pesticides) may increase skin cancer risk. For several chemicals, evidence supports carcinogenicity with endocrine-related effects, but direct mechanistic evidence that endocrine disruption specifically mediates skin carcinogenesis is lacking.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203284.abstract: Pulmonary malignancies encompassing both primary lung cancer and metastatic lesions are a leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally. Percutaneous thermal ablation of primary and metastatic lung tumors using radiofrequency ablation, microwave ablation, or cryoablation has emerged as an established minimally invasive treatment modality for selected patients unsuitable for surgery or requiring lung preservation. Although most lung ablation complications are self-limiting, some adverse events may result in long-term morbidity or mortality. Post-ablation pneumothorax has the highest reported incidence, with pooled incidences of 37-44%, although rates may vary according to patient cohorts and study definitions. As indications for percutaneous thermal ablation of pulmonary lesions expand to include complex lesions or higher-risk patients, the prevention and management of procedure-related complications remain central to safe clinical practice. Although prior reviews have described the techniques, oncological outcomes, and complication profiles of image-guided lung ablation, less emphasis has been placed on integrating practical complication prevention and management strategies throughout the periprocedural workflow. This narrative review aims to synthesize various complication prevention and management strategies for percutaneous thermal ablation of both primary and metastatic pulmonary lesions. The review focuses on both common and rare complications, and various aspects of complication prevention such as patient/lesion selection, procedural planning, and anesthesia/respiratory control. A comprehensive understanding of complication profiles and mitigation strategies is essential to optimize procedural safety, guide patient selection, and establish ablative techniques as a pillar in multidisciplinary thoracic oncology care.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203285.abstract: Background: Pathologic fractures of the humerus due to metastatic disease cause severe pain, loss of function and reduced quality of life. Surgical treatment is predominantly palliative and aims to achieve rapid pain relief, early functional recovery and minimal treatment-related morbidity. The photodynamic bone stabilization system (IlluminOss®) is a minimally invasive, radiolucent, intramedullary device that may address these needs. Methods: This retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data from two centers included 51 patients with 52 pathologic humeral lesions (completed or impending fractures) treated with photodynamic intramedullary stabilization between 2013 and 2025. Baseline variables comprised demographics, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, comorbidities, pain (numeric rating scale, NRS) and function (Musculoskeletal Tumor Society Upper Extremity Score, MSTS-UE; Toronto Extremity Salvage Score, TESS). Lesion characteristics, operative details, in-hospital course, follow-up outcomes (TESS, patient satisfaction/quality of life) and long-term endpoints (survival, complications) were recorded. Results: The study cohort (25 women, 26 men; mean age 68.5 years) represented a highly palliative population with advanced, disseminated malignant disease. Of the 52 humeral lesions, 35 (67.3%) presented as pathological fractures, whereas 17 lesions (32.7%) were classified as impending fractures due to extensive osteolysis. Among the impending fractures, Mirels scores ranged from 8 to 10, with three lesions scoring 8, eight lesions scoring 9, and six lesions scoring 10. ECOG performance status was 0-2 in 75.0% and 3-4 in 25.0% of patients. Preoperative pain was high (mean NRS 7.1) and function markedly reduced (median MSTS-UE 9.5/30; median TESS 36.5/100). Postoperatively, pain improved significantly from NRS 7.1 to 2.0 (p < 0.001). MSTS-UE increased from a median of 9.5 to 20 (p < 0.001). Follow-up showed further functional improvement with an increased TESS of 36.5 to 61 (p < 0.001), high patient satisfaction and subjective improvement in quality of life. Kaplan-Meier analysis (n = 44) demonstrated a median survival of 6 months for ECOG 0-2 and 3 months for ECOG 3-4. Implant failure (Henderson type III) occurred four times (7.7%) and was successfully revised with plate and/or screw osteosynthesis or diaphyseal replacement. Conclusions: Photodynamic intramedullary stabilization provides effective treatment for selected pathologic humeral lesions with low implant failure rate, offering rapid pain relief, functional improvement and low perioperative morbidity. Implant failure in complex fracture morphologies highlights the need for morphology-adapted indication and consideration of supplemental fixation in high-risk cases.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203286.abstract: Background: Accumulating evidence suggests that vitamin D may influence cancer prognosis. We aimed to explore whether the TP53 codon 72 polymorphism (p.Pro72Arg; rs1042522) may be associated with differential effects of vitamin D supplementation on digestive tract cancer prognosis. Methods: This post hoc analysis of the AMATERASU randomized controlled trial included patients in whom both germline TP53 codon 72 genotype and p53 immunohistochemistry (IHC) assessment were available. Patients were stratified according to TP53 codon 72 genotype and p53 IHC expression. The association between vitamin D supplementation and relapse-free survival (RFS) was evaluated using Cox proportional hazards regression models within each subgroup. Results: A total of 333 participants (79.9%) out of 417 in the AMATERASU trial were included in the analysis. RFS was comparable between the vitamin D and placebo groups across the TP53 codon 72 genotype subgroups. The vitamin D group was significantly associated with more favorable RFS compared with the placebo group in patients with both the Arg/Arg genotype and high p53 IHC expression (HR, 0.32; 95% CI, 0.12-0.87; p = 0.03). However, with a fragility index of 2 and a non-significant three-way interaction among vitamin D supplementation, p53 IHC expression, and the Arg/Arg genotype (p for interaction = 0.09), these findings remain fragile despite reaching statistical significance, warranting careful interpretation. Conclusions: Vitamin D supplementation was associated with more favorable RFS among patients with digestive tract cancer who had both the Arg/Arg genotype and high p53 IHC expression. These exploratory findings warrant further investigation in prospective studies.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203287.abstract: Background/Objectives: Chronic kidney diseases are fatal disorders, and early treatment is crucial for reducing mortality. Segmenting kidneys, tumors, and cysts from computed tomography scans has a significant role in assessing these diseases' progression, determining their severity, and planning surgeries. However, accurate segmentation is challenging for many reasons. The objective of this study is to develop a hybrid network that can overcome these challenges. Methods: The proposed network was designed using (i) a patch-joining and swin transformer block to capture global features efficiently, (ii) a Dynamic Channel Attention block to emphasize significant feature locations with the help of channel-wise attention, (iii) a block to perform complementary fusion of features coming from different layers, (iv) an edge-detection block to improve the performance by paying extra attention to edge features, and (v) an efficient activation function to overcome dying neuron and bias-shifting problems caused by the commonly used rectified linear unit. Extensive experiments were conducted using images from KiTS-2023 and Kaggle databases. Also, state-of-the-art techniques were applied to identical datasets and evaluated using identical metrics for fair comparisons. In addition to the commonly used Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), the Normalized Surface Distance (NSD) was used for evaluation. Results: The proposed method yields DSC/NSD scores of 98.35 ± 0.65%/97.62 ± 0.55%, 94.88 ± 0.57%/93.84 ± 0.50%, and 81.99 ± 0.45%/80.93 ± 0.40% for kidneys, tumors, and cysts, respectively. Conclusions: The results indicate the superiority of the proposed approach in segmenting kidneys, tumors, and cysts. The proposed method has the potential to support medical experts by providing quantitative and objective segmentation results.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203288.abstract: Background: Breast cancer progression is strongly influenced by tumor cell interactions with the extracellular matrix (ECM). Three-dimensional (3D) cell culture models provide more relevant systems for studying aspects of the tumor microenvironment (TME), including tumor architecture, matrix remodeling and cell-ECM communication. Collagen type I (Col I), fibronectin (FN) and hyaluronan (HA) are key ECM components involved in breast cancer progression. At the same time, integrins act as major matrix-sensing receptors that translate ECM cues into cellular responses. In this study, we investigated how defined ECM contexts regulate functional cell properties in shERβ MDA-MB-231 and Hs578T advanced 3D breast cancer cell models. Methods: Cells were cultured in 2D and 3D systems under matrix-free conditions or in Col I, FN, and mixed Col I/FN environments, in the presence or absence of HA or sulfated HA (sHA). Spheroid growth, matrix-dependent spheroid organization and dissemination were evaluated. In parallel, selected collagen- and fibronectin-associated integrin subunits, together with HA-related molecules including HAS2, CD44, and RHAMM, were analyzed to assess receptor-mediated matrix- and HA-associated responses. Results: Matrix substrates strongly influenced breast cancer spheroid behavior. Col I promoted outward dissemination, whereas FN-containing environments favored compact organization and restricted spreading. HA supported spheroid-like organization in a matrix-dependent manner, whereas sHA disrupted organized spheroid assembly in ECM-rich conditions, resulting in looser structures or smaller cell colonies, depending on the matrix context. Gene expression analysis revealed model-dependent remodeling of matrix- and HA-associated programs, with broader adhesion-related responses in shERβ MDA-MB-231 cells and stronger dimensionality-driven regulation in Hs578T cells. Conclusions: Overall, these findings demonstrate that defined ECM contexts actively regulate breast cancer spheroid behavior and matrix-associated receptor programs. Col I, FN and mixed Col I/FN environments generated distinct 3D phenotypes, affecting spheroid growth, organization and dissemination, while HA/sHA further modified these matrix-dependent responses. This study supports sHA as a functional matrix molecule with anti-cancer relevance and highlights the value of 3D matrix-based models for investigating tumor-matrix communication in breast cancer.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203289.abstract: Ovarian cancer remains the most lethal gynecological malignancy, largely due to high recurrence rates and the development of therapy-resistant disease. Cancer stem cells (CSCs) contribute to treatment failure by promoting chemoresistance through signaling pathways such as Wnt/β-catenin, Hedgehog, and Notch, as well as through dynamic interactions with the tumor microenvironment (TME). Ovarian CSC (OCSC)-associated biomarkers, including CD44, CD24, CD133, and ALDH, have expanded opportunities for specific tumor characterization and biomarker identification. Effective targeting of OCSCs requires experimental models that preserve cellular plasticity and hierarchical organization. Development of synthetic matrices and chemically defined media has improved the reproducibility and scalability of three-dimensional (3D) organoid cultures for preclinical drug testing. CSC-derived organoids, established by enriching cells positive for CSC markers directly from patient tumor material, provide a 3D platform for studying OCSC-associated phenotypes and therapeutic responses. This review examines current understanding of ovarian CSC biology and the development of OCSC-derived 3D organoid models that can recapitulate cellular architecture and patient-specific drug responses. These 3D organoid models provide a guided platform for evaluating emerging therapeutics, such as micropeptides encoded by short open reading frames or engineered from functional tumor-suppressor protein domains selected to target OCSCs. Their small size enables modulation of intracellular signaling and highly specific protein-protein interactions. We further review micropeptide stabilization strategies and tumor-targeted delivery systems designed to enhance bioavailability. This review highlights how integrating patient-specific OCSC-derived organoid models with engineered micropeptides may accelerate the development of personalized treatment strategies for ovarian cancer while improving the preclinical evaluation of novel therapies.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203290.abstract: Rare cancers represent a substantial health burden, comprising 25% of cancer mortality. Early-phase oncology trials are essential for rare cancers, where limited patient numbers, biological heterogeneity, and the absence of established standards of care necessitate innovative approaches to drug development. Advances in trial design-including basket, umbrella, and adaptive platforms-have enabled efficient evaluation of molecularly defined subgroups and accelerated identification of clinically meaningful activity across rare tumor types. Early-phase studies have demonstrated the therapeutic potential of antibody-drug conjugates, immunotherapy, targeted agents, and cellular therapies, particularly when guided by predictive biomarkers and tumor-agnostic strategies. These approaches have expanded treatment options for patients with historically limited therapeutic opportunities. Persistent challenges remain, including restricted trial access, difficulties with patient accrual, variability in biomarker assessment, and uncertainty regarding generalizability of outcomes. Additional challenges persist after early-phase trial completion, as continued access to therapies demonstrating clinical benefit may remain limited when regulatory approval or broader clinical availability has not yet been established. Evolving regulatory and collaborative frameworks have partially mitigated these barriers by supporting multi-institutional enrollment and pathway-flexible approvals. Over the past decade, biomarker-driven strategies have been increasingly incorporated into modern clinical trial design, shifting the field away from traditional histology-based approaches. Continued innovation in trial design, biomarker integration, and collaborative infrastructure will be essential to sustaining progress and expanding durable clinical benefit for patients with rare cancers.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203292.abstract: Objective: To assess the long-term oncologic and survival outcomes of percutaneous cryoablation (PCA) for patients with solitary de novo T1a renal cell carcinoma (RCC). Methods: This retrospective study was conducted following the STROBE guidelines. We included patients with a single, biopsy-confirmed, treatment-naïve T1a RCC (<4 cm) who underwent PCA between January 2008 and December 2021. Patient demographics, tumor characteristics, and procedural details were collected. Survival analyses were performed using the Kaplan-Meier estimator. Results: Eighty-six patients (57 men and 29 women) with a median age of 69 years met the inclusion criteria. Fifty patients (58%) had a history of an additional non-renal malignancy. In total, 86 renal tumors were treated using PCA, with a median tumor diameter of 2.7 cm. Clear cell RCC accounted for 67.4% of the tumors. Procedural complications classified as Clavien-Dindo grade III or higher occurred in 4.6% of cases. Local tumor recurrence at the ablation site was observed in five patients (5.8%), and four patients (4.6%) developed new lesions elsewhere within the kidney. The estimated median overall survival was 10.34 years. The 10-year local recurrence-free and disease-free survival rates were 93.5% and 84.0%, respectively. Both metastasis-free survival and cancer-specific survival rates at 10 years were 100%. Conclusions: Percutaneous cryoablation provided durable local tumor control with low major morbidity and favorable long-term oncologic outcomes in this selected cohort of patients with solitary cT1a renal tumors.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203293.abstract: Objective: Our objective was to characterize the molecular–pathologic profile and recurrence patterns of endometrial cancer with pelvic lymph node isolated tumor cells (ITCs). Methods: A single-center retrospective study of patients with endometrial cancer and ITCs was conducted. Patients with concurrent lymph nodes or distant metastasis were excluded. Cases were reviewed by a gynecologic pathologist, and electronic medical records were reviewed. Descriptive statistics were performed using R 4.4.2. Results: A total of 43 patients were included, with a median follow-up time of 33 months. The majority were endometrioid carcinoma (91%) and stage I (72%). In total, 28 (65%) were MMR-proficient and p53-wild-type (MMRp p53wt), nine (21%) were MMR-deficient (MMRd), six (14%) were p53-abnormal (p53abn), and none were POLE-mutated (POLEmut). Additionally, 27 (96%) MMRp p53wt cases showed a microcystic, elongated, and fragmented (MELF) pattern of invasion. Adjuvant therapy was indicated in 38 (88%) patients; 32 (74%) received therapy and six (14%) declined. Four (9.3%) patients recurred, with a recurrence rate of 33% (2/6) for p53abn, 11% (1/9) for MMRd, and 4% (1/28) for MMRp p53wt. All recurrences were to distant sites. In the MMRp p53wt group, 16 (57%) had external beam radiation (EBRT) +/− vaginal brachytherapy (VBT), three (11%) had chemotherapy +/− radiation, and nine (32%) had no adjuvant treatment or VBT alone. Conclusions: Molecular profile is prognostically relevant in endometrial carcinoma with ITCs. ITCs in MMRp p53wt endometrioid carcinoma present a low risk of disease recurrence. As the majority of our cohort received adjuvant therapy, future work may explore de-escalating treatment in low-risk ITC cases.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203294.abstract: Background/Objectives: The incidence of small intestinal neuroendocrine tumors (SI-NETs) has increased in recent years, while effective therapeutic options remain limited. This study aimed to investigate the antitumor effects of orlistat on SI-NETs and elucidate the underlying mechanisms. Methods: The effects of orlistat were evaluated using STC-1 cells, patient-derived primary SI-NET cells, and xenograft models. Functional assays, RNA sequencing, lipidomic profiling, ATAC sequencing, and molecular analyses were performed to assess tumor-related phenotypes and investigate the underlying mechanisms. Results: Orlistat inhibited cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, induced G1-phase arrest and apoptosis, and suppressed tumor growth in vivo. Mechanistically, orlistat triggered endoplasmic reticulum stress, inhibited PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling, and upregulated activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3). Lipidomic profiling revealed alterations in lipid metabolism. Increased reactive oxygen species and lipid peroxidation, together with changes in ferroptosis-related proteins, indicated the involvement of ferroptosis-associated pathways. ATF3 overexpression reproduced the antitumor and ferroptosis-associated effects of orlistat. Integrated ATAC-seq and RNA-seq analyses identified CHAC1 as a potential downstream effector of ATF3. Conversely, ATF3 knockdown reduced CHAC1 expression and attenuated the effects of orlistat both in vitro and in vivo. Conclusions: Orlistat suppresses SI-NET progression and is associated with changes in endoplasmic reticulum stress, ATF3 expression, and ferroptosis-related responses, with CHAC1 identified as a potential downstream effector of ATF3. These findings support further investigation of orlistat as a potential therapeutic strategy for SI-NETs.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203295.abstract: Platinum-based chemotherapy remains a key treatment for epithelial ovarian cancer, but platinum resistance is a major cause of treatment failure and mortality. Traditionally, platinum resistance has been defined by the interval between the last platinum treatment and disease progression, with progression within six months generally classified as platinum-resistant. This six-month platinum-free interval has long provided a useful framework for treatment selection. However, growing preclinical and clinical evidence suggests that this interval should not be treated as a strict biological boundary. Platinum susceptibility can change as tumors evolve, with some tumors retaining residual sensitivity while others develop stable or potentially modifiable resistance mechanisms. These mechanisms include restoration of homologous recombination, altered DNA-damage tolerance, epigenetic regulation, changes in platinum transport and detoxification, adaptive survival signaling, and alterations in cell-death pathways. Some resistance mechanisms are relatively stable, whereas others may remain biologically plastic and potentially amenable to therapeutic modification. This distinction has important implications for platinum rechallenge. Responses to platinum reintroduction in selected patients previously classified as platinum-resistant indicate that the six-month interval does not fully capture the biology of platinum responsiveness. However, renewed clinical activity after rechallenge should not automatically be interpreted as biological resensitization. True resensitization requires evidence that a defined resistance mechanism has been modified and that this alteration increases platinum susceptibility. Preclinical studies have identified multiple strategies to modify platinum-resistance pathways, but clinical translation remains limited. This perspective therefore proposes that platinum resistance should be understood as a clinically defined phenotype encompassing biologically heterogeneous states, some of which may be stable and others potentially reversible. Recognizing this distinction has implications for biomarker development, treatment selection, trial design, and interpretation of platinum rechallenge. Prospective studies incorporating longitudinal tumor profiling and functional assessments of platinum susceptibility may ultimately identify patients in whom platinum activity can be therapeutically restored.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203296.abstract: Introduction: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA)-based molecular residual disease (MRD) testing is emerging as a tool to refine relapse risk and guide surveillance after curative-intent therapy for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Tissue-free (plasma-only) MRD assays may improve feasibility where tumor tissue is limited. Prospective and trial-embedded studies have established that ctDNA MRD detected after curative-intent therapy is prognostic for recurrence in NSCLC, but how tissue-free MRD testing is deployed in routine care in Asia-Pacific and the Middle East (AMEA) has not been described. We characterized ordering patterns and first-test positivity in an AMEA cohort. In this descriptive cohort (159 NSCLC patients; 257 samples), 40.9% of patients underwent more than one MRD test, with a median interval of 4.9 months between the first two tests; first-test MRD positivity was 15.7% (25/159; 95% CI 10.9-22.2) with rates of 0% (0/9; 95% CI 0.0-29.9), 8.8% (5/57; 95% CI 3.8-18.9), 21.5% (17/79; 95% CI 13.9-31.8) and 21.4% (3/14; 95% CI 7.6-47.6), respectively, across stages I, II, III, and oligometastatic stage IV disease. No hypothesis testing was performed, and the stage I and oligometastatic stage IV subgroups are small, so the confidence intervals overlap widely and apparent between-stage differences should not be interpreted as a stage effect. Case Presentation: Six illustrative cases involving patients with stage II-IVB describe the use of MRD testing in routine clinical care. The cases were selected purposively, not consecutively, to span the contexts in which the results were interpreted: a positive result shortly before radiographic nodal recurrence (Case 1); a positive result during long-term adjuvant osimertinib preceding isolated mediastinal relapse (Case 2); a transient positive result with subsequent clearance and radiographic regression (Case 3); a positive result that prompted PET-CT revealing occult metastatic disease (Case 4); serially negative results concordant with sustained radiographic remission (Case 5); and a positive result that prompted comprehensive genomic profiling identifying an actionable KRAS G12C alteration (Case 6). Conclusions: Across Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, tissue-free MRD testing in NSCLC was used primarily during surveillance and often serially; first-test positivity was 15.7% (95% CI 10.9-22.2) overall, with wide and mutually overlapping confidence intervals across stages. The cases illustrate that MRD results may prompt diagnostic evaluation when interpreted alongside imaging and other clinical findings, but they are purposively selected, and treatment changes that followed a result are reported as description, not as evidence of benefit. No assay performance characteristic is estimated. These findings are hypothesis-generating; prospective, MRD-directed trials with standardized timepoints, thresholds, confirmatory strategies and pre-specified clinical actions are needed before MRD results can guide treatment.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203297.abstract: Background/Objectives: Lutetium-177 prostate-specific membrane antigen radioligand therapy ([177Lu]Lu-PSMA-RLT) is an effective treatment for patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but no validated PSMA-PET/CT-based biomarker currently identifies patients at risk of early treatment failure. The aim of this study was to assess whether semi-quantitative PSMA-PET/CT parameters, in particular the fraction of PSMA-positive tumor volume with high uptake, are associated with early biochemical progression (EBP) and PSA50 response and secondarily with PSA-PFS and OS. Methods: Semiquantitative PSMA-PET parameters comprised reference lesion SUVmax (RL-SUVmax), SUVmean, total PSMA tumor volume (tPSMA-TV), tPSMA-TV above a fixed SUV threshold of 20 (tPSMA-TV20), the percentage of tPSMA-TV20 within tPSMA-TV (tPSMA-TV%), total lesion quotient (TLQ), TLQ20, and rTLQ%. The co-primary endpoints were EBP, defined as PSA progression according to the PCWG3 criteria within 4 months of the start of treatment, and PSA50 response, defined as a reduction in PSA of at least 50% compared with baseline. PSA-PFS (PCWG3-defined PSA progression or death from any cause) and OS were secondary endpoints. Results: 63 patients were retrospectively included (median follow-up, 20.9 months). In univariable analyses, higher baseline tPSMA-TV% was significantly associated with lower odds of EBP (OR per 10% increase, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.57-0.87; p = 0.001) and higher odds of PSA50 response (OR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.07-1.61; p = 0.009). It was associated with longer PSA-PFS (HR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.67-0.84; p < 0.001) and longer OS (HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.72-0.91; p < 0.001). Exploratory ROC analysis identified a tPSMA-TV% cut-off of 47.54% for EBP (AUC, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.57-0.86]; sensitivity, 0.61; specificity, 0.93), although this threshold requires external validation. In exploratory models including tPSMA-TV and SUVmean, tPSMA-TV% remained associated with PSA-PFS and OS but not with EBP or PSA50 response. Conclusions: Baseline tPSMA-TV% was associated with EBP, PSA50 response, PSA-PFS and OS in mCRPC patients undergoing [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-RLT, and these associations remained after adjustment for baseline PSA and metastatic presentation. tPSMA-TV% is a candidate prognostic imaging biomarker that requires external validation.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203298.abstract: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) are the most common malignant mesenchymal tumors that compose a heterogeneous group due to various molecular alterations. This study aimed to determine the molecular characteristics of patients with GIST treated between 2002 and 2017 and to follow their overall survival (OS) over 20 years. DNA was isolated from surgical biopsies of 490 patients with gut sarcomas and was analyzed using PCR and Sanger sequencing of hotspots of KIT, PDGFRA and BRAF genes. Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining was used to determine SDHB expression. 417 GIST patients, including 13 children, were included; females predominated (male-to-female ratio 0.65), median age of 55.4 years old. KIT and PDGFRA mutations were found in 288 GISTs (69.1%) and 52 (12.5%), respectively. A total of 25 KIT and 3 novel PDGFRA mutations were revealed in 30 GISTs. KIT/PDGFRA mutations were not detected in 77 (18.5%) GISTs; among them were 2 NF1 GISTs, 10 with BRAF mutation, 14 with SDHB deficiency, and 3 "pediatric" GISTs. The overall survival (OS) of 280 GIST patients over more than 20 years. Genetic changes have a certain prognostic value in addition to such factors as tumor size, mitotic index, and location. The OS of GIST patients with KIT mutations was lower than that of patients with PDGFRA mutation, BRAF mutation, or SDHB deficiency, but the difference was non-significant. Our study highlights the heterogeneous nature and molecular features of GISTs in Russian population. The precise molecular characterization of the tumor should be considered an integral part of modern personalized GIST treatment.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203299.abstract: Background: Ovarian cancer (OC) poses an escalating global health burden, with marked disparities in incidence, mortality, and survivorship. Social, psychological, and structural determinants, including deprivation, stigma, and access to specialist care, may influence outcomes but are not well-represented in existing models of cancer care. We introduce the Tumour, Macroenvironment and Resource (TMR) framework, a novel conceptual model exploring interactions among tumour biology, social determinants, and healthcare resources in OC survivorship and care. Methods: Framework development occurred in three phases. First, a narrative review identified factors influencing OC outcomes across tumour, macroenvironmental, and healthcare resource domains. Second, multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) was used to structure these factors within a preliminary framework and assign indicative domain weightings. Third, two cross-sectional expert opinion surveys were conducted to refine and validate the concept of the framework. The final model was then evaluated in a retrospective pilot cohort to assess the feasibility of collecting predefined TMR variables from routinely available clinical data. Results: The review identified limited evidence addressing broader determinants of health beyond biological prognostic factors. Available studies suggested interactions between tumour characteristics, social determinants, and healthcare infrastructure that may influence outcomes. A preliminary model allocated 50% weighting to tumour factors and 50% to combined macroenvironmental and healthcare resource factors. Expert surveys (n = 20 and n = 44) achieved consensus and informed development of the final TMR framework. Application to a UK pilot cohort of patients with OC (n = 42) demonstrated the feasibility of collecting variables across all TMR domains and identified multiple adverse factors across tumour, macroenvironmental, and resource domains. Conclusions: The TMR framework provides an integrative, hypothesis-generating model for exploring disparities in OC survivorship and care. Further retrospective and prospective validation are required before clinical or prognostic applications can be considered.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203300.abstract: Ethnic inequalities in cancer incidence and outcomes are widespread, although the evidence available for people in the UK is more limited than in some other countries. This narrative review details the current evidence relating to ethnicity and differences in primary care cancer diagnosis in the UK and possible contributing factors. In general, cancer rates are higher for White individuals than for Asian or Black individuals in the UK, but for some cancer sites, the inverse is true. There are also differences in stage at diagnosis by ethnic group for some cancer sites. The routes through which cancer inequalities emerge are complex and difficult to attribute to a single patient characteristic. A variety of social, demographic, genetic and health service factors interact to influence outcomes. There is a wide research base demonstrating that Asian and Black individuals in the UK can experience a range of obstacles when interacting with health care services, including cancer investigations. Future research evidence and health service planning needs to include a diverse range of stakeholders in order to decrease cancer inequalities.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203301.abstract: Cellular senescence is a stress-induced, stable proliferative arrest that acts as a potent barrier to tumorigenesis, yet the senescence-associated secretory phenotype that accompanies it can paradoxically fuel inflammation, angiogenesis and the phenotypic plasticity contributing to tumor heterogeneity, therapy resistance and cancer stem cell emergence. A largely unexplored molecular layer in the senescence program is alternative pre-mRNA splicing, which generates protein isoforms with functionally divergent effects on cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis and the secretory program. More than 90% of human multi-exon genes are alternatively spliced, so most of the nearly 1000 genes linked to senescence are expected to produce several isoforms, yet fewer than twenty have been examined at this level, and direct evidence is available for only about half of these. We review how alternative splicing, together with related mechanisms such as alternative promoter usage and alternative reading-frame selection, modulates distinct outputs of the senescence program, including commitment, persistence, escape and SASP composition, across gene groups such as the TP53/TP63/TP73 family, MDM2/MDM4 and the androgen receptor locus. This evidence ranges from direct causal manipulation to correlative or mechanistically adjacent findings, classified explicitly by evidence level. Direct causal evidence remains limited, making isoform-resolved functional validation a major unmet need in the field.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203302.abstract: Background: Accurate axillary response prediction is clinically relevant in clinically node-positive (cN+) breast cancer patients treated with neoadjuvant chemo-(immuno)therapy (NAC). This study evaluated the value of [18F]FDG PET/CT-derived metabolic characteristics and tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) to predict axillary pathologic complete response (pCR). Second, the association between [18F]FDG PET/CT-derived metabolic characteristics and TILs was evaluated. Methods: This retrospective study included cN+ breast cancer patients treated with NAC and axillary surgery from the prospective multicentre RISAS trial (NCT02800317). Baseline [18F]FDG PET/CT-derived metabolic activity of the breast tumour, axillary lymph node metastases (ALNMs), and spleen was assessed, together with TILs measured in the breast tumour and ALNMs. TILs were classified as low (<10%) versus high (≥10%). Associations were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results: Of 135 patients, 46 (34.1%) achieved axillary pCR. Higher liver mean tumour-to-background ratio (2.7 vs. 1.9, p = 0.042), trends towards higher breast and ALNM maximum standardised uptake value (SUVmax), lower splenic SUVmax and high breast tumour TILs were associated with axillary pCR. Multivariable logistic regression combining tumour grade, subtype, maximum spleen-to-liver ratio, and breast tumour TILs yielded an apparent area under the curve of 0.80 [95%CI 0.73-0.88]. Higher ALNM SUVmax and SUVmean (10.5 vs. 6.3, p = 0.024; 6.4 vs. 3.7, p = 0.015) and lower splenic SUVmean (2.6 vs. 3.1, p = 0.035) were associated with high breast tumour TILs. Conclusions: A model combining clinicopathological, metabolic, and immune-related characteristics may be informative for predicting axillary response to NAC but did not perform better than clinicopathological characteristics alone. Future studies should evaluate whether accurate prediction models can support safe axillary treatment de-escalation.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203303.abstract: Upfront allogeneic stem cell transplantation (allo-SCT) without pretransplant cytoreduction is an established concept in patients with myelodysplastic syndromes with increased blasts (MDS-IB), but the optimal conditioning strategy remains to be defined. While fludarabine and treosulfan (Flu/Treo) has become an established regimen for older patients based on its favorable ratio between toxicity and efficacy, its impact when used in the context of upfront transplant is less well described. Here, we retrospectively investigated Flu/Treo as the backbone for conditioning in 35 patients with MDS-IB (median blast count 13%) receiving upfront transplantation. Outcomes in this high-risk cohort (75% IPSS-M high or very high) were promising, with an estimated 2-year overall (OS), relapse-free survival (RFS) and non-relapse mortality (NRM) of 76%, 56% and 13%, respectively. Relapse was the major cause of treatment failure, reflected by a relapse incidence (CIR) of 31%. We identified the TP53 mutation status as the main driver of relapse (2-year RFS TP53 mutated 17% vs. 67%, p = 0.01; 2-year CIR 54% vs. 24%, p = 0.08) and an adverse prognostic factor, while the pretransplant blast count did not affect the post-transplant outcome. Intensification with the addition of melphalan (Mel, n = 18) to a sequential conditioning approach did not improve the outcome (Mel vs. Flu/Treo 2-year OS 62% vs. 87%, RFS 50% vs. 63%, CIR 37% vs. 24%, NRM 14% vs. 12%, all not significant). This pilot series shows that upfront transplantation using Flu/Treo conditioning in high-risk MDS patients facilitates promising post-transplant outcomes and may serve as a backbone to further improve these results through innovative peri-transplant interventions.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203304.abstract: Background: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as a potential marker of minimal residual disease (MRD) after resection of colorectal liver metastases (CRLM), but its prognostic value and possible role in guiding postoperative management remain uncertain. This systematic review evaluated the available evidence on ctDNA for predicting recurrence and survival after CRLM resection, with particular attention to perioperative and serial ctDNA measurements and their potential value in guiding adjuvant treatment. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 21 July 2026 for studies evaluating ctDNA in patients undergoing resection of CRLM. Prospective and retrospective cohort studies and relevant randomized trial sub-studies were eligible. The primary outcome was the association between ctDNA status and recurrence, while secondary outcomes included recurrence-free survival (RFS), disease-free survival (DFS), overall survival (OS), serial ctDNA dynamics, and the potential predictive value of ctDNA for adjuvant chemotherapy. Risk of bias was assessed using the QUIPS tool. Findings were synthesized narratively, with an additional exploratory random-effects meta-analysis of early postoperative tissue-informed ctDNA positivity and RFS/DFS. Unadjusted and adjusted HRs were pooled separately. Results: Twenty-eight studies published between 2018 and 2026 were included, representing 2079 unique patients after accounting for overlapping cohorts. In six studies, postoperative ctDNA positivity was associated with poorer RFS/DFS (pooled unadjusted HR 5.15, 95% CI 3.65-7.27; I2 = 0%). Five studies provided adjusted estimates (pooled HR 4.95, 95% CI 2.45-10.01; I2 = 60.5%). Serial monitoring provided additional prognostic information: persistent ctDNA positivity or conversion from negative to positive during follow-up was associated with poor outcomes, whereas ctDNA clearance was generally associated with a lower risk of recurrence. ctDNA could precede radiological recurrence by approximately 2.5 to >20 months, although detection was less reliable in patients with small-volume pulmonary recurrence. In contrast, the prognostic value of preoperative ctDNA was less consistent and appeared to depend on assay methodology, quantitative ctDNA burden, and previous systemic treatment. Observational studies reported associations between postoperative MRD status and outcomes following adjuvant chemotherapy, but non-randomized treatment allocation and potential time-related bias limit conclusions about treatment benefit. Considerable variation in assay platforms and postoperative sampling schedules remained across studies. Conclusions: Postoperative ctDNA positivity is associated with poorer recurrence-related outcomes after CRLM resection. However, the moderate-to-high risk of bias and differences between studies limit confidence in the evidence. The predictive value of ctDNA for adjuvant chemotherapy benefit remains unproven. Prospective randomized trials are needed to determine whether ctDNA-guided management improves patient outcomes.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203305.abstract: Background/objective: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a hematological malignancy characterized by the proliferation of clonal plasma cells. While [18F]FDG PET/CT is widely established for assessing disease extent, bone involvement, and treatment response in MM, novel molecular imaging targets like CXCR4 (e.g., using [68Ga]Ga-Pentixafor) have emerged to offer potentially superior sensitivity and theranostic applications. The aim of this manuscript is to systematically review and compare the diagnostic performance, expressed as detection rates, of CXCR4-targeted PET/CT versus [18F]FDG PET/CT in patients with MM. Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted across major databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library) for head-to-head comparative studies evaluating both [18F]FDG and [68Ga]Ga-Pentixafor PET/CT in MM patients. Risk of bias and study quality were assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. Results: Eleven studies were collected, amounting to a total of 347 patients. A patient-based analysis showed that [68Ga]Ga-Pentixafor had a higher detection rate than [18F]FDG PET/CT (86.3%, 95% CI: 80.3-92.3% vs 60.9%, 95% CI: 42.5-79.4%). In a descriptive analysis, mean lesion SUVmax values reported across individual studies were generally higher with [68Ga]Ga-Pentixafor PET/CT than with [18F]FDG PET/CT. Conclusions: [68Ga]Ga-Pentixafor PET/CT may serve as a robust alternative or complementary imaging modality to [18F]FDG PET/CT in MM. It could also be helpful for selection in CXCR4-directed theranostic pathways, but more high-quality studies are warranted.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203306.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among cancer survivors. Contemporary cardio-oncology frameworks emphasize baseline cardiovascular risk assessment before potentially cardiotoxic cancer therapies. Historical real world implementation of baseline electrocardiography (ECG), however, remains incompletely characterized. The objective of this study was to characterize historical baseline ECG ascertainment before cancer diagnosis and examine its association with documented cardiovascular diagnosis patterns in cancer survivors. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of 4592 adult cancer survivors within the Froedtert & Medical College of Wisconsin health system from 2000 to 2020. The analytic cohort was derived from a previously established longitudinal cancer survivor resource integrating demographic and cardiovascular clinical data, cancer treatment exposures, multimodality cardiac function ascertainment, and linked clinical, radiation oncology, and cancer registry information. Cardiac function ascertainment from an available cardiovascular imaging modality within three years before cancer diagnosis was one component of the analytic cohort definition. Patients were stratified by ascertainment of a 12-lead ECG within the same pre-diagnostic interval. Cardiovascular diagnoses documented before and after cancer diagnosis were characterized separately. For the newly documented diagnosis analyses, each cardiovascular outcome was evaluated among participants without a prior diagnosis of that same condition before cancer diagnosis. A multivariable logistic regression model evaluated the association between baseline ECG ascertainment and newly documented overall CVD diagnosis (including HF, AFIB, CAD, and stroke) while adjusting for age, sex, race, comorbidity count, and treatment count. Among 4592 individuals, 3726 (81%) had a baseline ECG. ECG ascertainment was associated with older age and greater pre-existing cardiovascular and cardiometabolic burden. The available follow up distributions were similar between patients without and with baseline ECG ascertainment (748 [Q1 258, Q3 1781] vs. 767 [Q1 219, Q3 1822] days; p > 0.9). In multivariable analysis, baseline ECG ascertainment was associated with lower odds of a newly documented overall CVD diagnosis (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.31-0.46); this odds ratio represents an association rather than a time-specific risk or protective effect. Baseline ECGs were commonly ascertainable within this longitudinal cancer survivor cohort and identified groups with different pre-existing cardiovascular burden and subsequent cardiovascular diagnosis patterns. These findings provide a historical benchmark for cardiovascular assessment in cancer care and support prospective patient-level studies integrating ECG findings with clinical and oncologic risk factors to refine cardiovascular surveillance strategies across cancer survivorship.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203307.abstract: Background/Objectives: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a major complication of cancer. The predictive performance of baseline D-dimer and factors influencing its levels among patients with cancer remain unclear. We aimed to identify predictors of subsequent VTE development and evaluate the cancer-specific predictive performance of baseline D-dimer. Methods: This retrospective study included 23,505 patients with any of 11 malignancies who underwent baseline D-dimer measurement at initial diagnosis at Gifu University Hospital between January 2015 and December 2025. Patients with pre-existing VTE were excluded. Predictors were identified using logistic regression analyses. Cancer-specific predictive performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analyses, with optimal cutoff values determined by the Youden index. Factors associated with baseline D-dimer were also assessed. Results: The median follow-up was 45.3 months (30.4-59.1 months), during which VTE occurred in 784 (3.3%) patients. Higher baseline D-dimer levels and distant metastasis were independent predictors of subsequent VTE. Cancer type was significantly associated with VTE overall, and breast cancer was associated with lower odds than esophageal cancer. D-dimer performance varied among cancer types, with optimal cutoff values of 0.55-2.35 μg/mL. Older age and higher platelet counts were independently associated with elevated baseline D-dimer levels, whereas a higher cholesterol level was inversely associated. Conclusions: Baseline D-dimer level is an independent predictor of subsequent VTE in patients with cancer. Its predictive performance and exploratory thresholds vary among cancers, suggesting that cancer type should be considered when interpreting baseline D-dimer levels. External validation is required before these cancer-specific thresholds can be applied clinically.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203308.abstract: The incidence of p16-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) is increasing, with improved prognosis compared to non-HPV-related cancers. Standard treatment of locally advanced OPSCC involves high-dose cisplatin (HDC) with radiation but is associated with significant toxicity. Low-dose cisplatin (LDC) administered weekly has shown comparable efficacy to HDC in prior studies. This study evaluates the real-world outcomes of LDC in p16-positive OPSCC in a regional centre. Patients treated with curative radiation and concurrent LDC (40 mg/m2 weekly) for p16-positive OPSCC from January 2015 to December 2021 were retrospectively analysed (n = 103). Primary endpoints included overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), with secondary endpoints being loco-regional and distant recurrence rates, and chemotherapy-related toxicity. Overall survival rates were 94%, 89%, and 84% at two, three, and five years, respectively. The progression-free survival rates were 90%, 83%, and 80% over the same periods. The low-risk group showed excellent outcomes with no loco-regional recurrences and low distant relapse rates (6% at 5 years). The intermediate-risk group had higher loco-regional recurrences (10% at 5 years) and a similar distant relapse rate (7% at 5 years). T4 or N3 disease patients had lower survival and higher distant relapse rates but excellent loco-regional control. The median cumulative cisplatin dose was 240 mg/m2, with no survival difference between those receiving ≥200 mg/m2 versus less. Toxicity led to dose reductions (8%), delays (13%), and early cessations (30%). LDC is effective for p16-positive OPSCC with manageable toxicity, showing outcomes comparable to outcomes previously reported in studies using HDC.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203309.abstract: Breast cancer exhibits marked molecular and phenotypic heterogeneity, with important implications for prognosis and therapeutic response. Although magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is widely used for detection and staging, its potential role as a prognostic biomarker across molecular subtypes remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to evaluate the association between MRI-defined tumor imaging phenotypes and disease-free survival (DFS) among different breast cancer molecular subtypes. This retrospective single-center study included 407 patients with invasive breast carcinoma of no special type who underwent pre-treatment breast MRI between October 2015 and May 2021. Tumors were classified into molecular subtypes and three MRI phenotypes based on lesion morphology and distribution. Associations between imaging phenotype, molecular subtype, and DFS were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards models. Type 3 was the most prevalent imaging phenotype overall (60%), followed by Type 2 (21.9%) and Type 1 (18.2%). Imaging phenotype distribution differed significantly among molecular subtypes. Over a median follow-up of 57 months, imaging phenotype was not associated with DFS in Luminal A, Luminal B, or HER2-overexpressed tumors. However, in the triple-negative/ER-low subgroup, imaging phenotype demonstrated an independent association with DFS. In multivariable analysis, patients with the Type 1 phenotype had an 8.16-fold higher risk of recurrence compared with those with the Type 2 phenotype (95% CI: 1.49-44.60; p = 0.015). Type 2 lesions showed the most favorable survival outcomes. In this exploratory analysis, MRI phenotype was associated with disease-free survival in triple-negative and ER-low breast cancers. Circumscribed, unifocal tumors are associated with improved survival, whereas spiculated or multifocal patterns are associated with worse outcomes. However, given the small number of events in this subgroup, these exploratory findings need to be confirmed in larger studies before MRI morphology can be considered a prognostic imaging biomarker in aggressive breast cancer subtypes.
