doi:10.3390/cancers18203310.abstract: Background: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is increasingly implemented for cytoreductive surgery (CRS) combined with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) for peritoneal surface malignancies (PSM). This systematic review and meta-analysis compared minimally invasive CRS/HIPEC (M-CRS/HIPEC) and open CRS/HIPEC (O-CRS/HIPEC) in terms of perioperative, postoperative, and long-term oncological outcomes. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched for comparative studies of M-CRS/HIPEC versus O-CRS/HIPEC in adult patients. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and RoB 2.0. Pooled relative risks (RR) for dichotomous outcomes and standardized mean differences (SMD) for continuous outcomes were calculated with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the potential influence of disease burden and primary tumor heterogeneity. Results: Twenty-one studies (1 randomized controlled trial and 20 retrospective cohorts) including 1184 patients (452 M-CRS/HIPEC and 732 O-CRS/HIPEC) were analyzed. Operative time did not differ between groups (SMD = 0.195; p = 0.667). Most cytoreductive procedures were comparable, although small bowel resections were less frequent with M-CRS/HIPEC (RR = 0.537; p = 0.018). The minimally invasive approach achieved higher CC0 rates (RR = 1.053; p = 0.045), with lower blood loss (SMD = -1.838; p < 0.001) and fewer transfusions (RR = 0.588; p = 0.002). Postoperative recovery favored M-CRS/HIPEC, with earlier return of bowel function and resumption of oral intake, shorter hospital stay, fewer readmissions, and earlier chemotherapy resumption (all p < 0.05). Overall and major morbidity were reduced, while postoperative mortality and 1-, 3-, and 5-year disease-free and overall survival did not differ significantly between groups. In the disease burden-restricted sensitivity analysis, differences in small bowel resection, CC0 rate, and 90-day readmission were no longer statistically significant, whereas the main perioperative and recovery benefits persisted. No significant differences in DFS or OS were identified in the additional sensitivity analyses at the evaluable time points. Conclusions: This meta-analysis supports a selective, expertise-driven use of M-CRS/HIPEC, offering perioperative and recovery advantages without significant differences in cytoreductive adequacy or long-term outcomes in appropriately selected patients.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203311.abstract: Real-world evidence describing the presentation, management, and outcomes of follicular lymphoma (FL) in Saudi Arabia remains limited, and the frequency and prognostic weight of progression of disease within 24 months of first-line therapy (POD24) have not been reported in this population. This study evaluated the clinicopathological characteristics, treatment patterns, POD24 incidence, and survival outcomes of patients with FL treated at two Saudi tertiary centres. This two-centre retrospective chart review included adults with histologically confirmed FL diagnosed between November 1999 and May 2025. Overall survival (OS) and first-line progression-free survival (PFS) were measured from the initiation of first-line treatment and estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. POD24 was defined as progression, relapse, or death from any cause within 24 months of first-line initiation among patients evaluable for that endpoint. Outcomes were additionally examined by calendar era of diagnosis. All group comparisons were unadjusted and exploratory. A total of 139 patients were included. The mean age at diagnosis was 54.7 years (range, 18-91), 61.9% were male, 79.1% had Ann Arbor stage III-IV disease, and 51.1% had an FLIPI score ≥ 3. Bendamustine plus rituximab was the most frequent first-line regimen (43.9%), followed by R-CHOP (30.2%). The overall response rate was 77.0% in the whole cohort and 82.4% among the 125 patients who received response-evaluable systemic first-line therapy. After a median follow-up of 71.0 months, 5-year OS was 92.5% (95% CI, 84.8-96.4) and 5-year PFS was 66.1% (95% CI, 54.9-75.0); the corresponding medians were 210.0 and 114.6 months but were estimated with few patients at risk and should be interpreted cautiously. Among 97 patients evaluable for POD24, the event occurred in 24 (24.7%; 95% CI, 17.2-34.2), and the incidence was stable across calendar eras (23.4% before 2018 versus 24.5% thereafter; p = 1.000). Primary refractory disease accounted for 14 of the 24 events (58.3%). POD24 was associated with poorer ECOG performance status (odds ratio [OR] 11.08; 95% CI, 3.85-31.86), older age (OR 5.27; 95% CI, 2.00-13.89), and higher FLIPI score (OR 3.09; 95% CI, 1.13-8.42). In the 24-month landmark analysis, OS was significantly shorter after POD24 (log-rank p = 0.008), and both documented histological transformations occurred in the POD24 group. Patients with FL in this two-centre Saudi cohort frequently presented with advanced-stage and high-risk disease, yet contemporary anti-CD20-based treatment was associated with favourable long-term survival. Approximately one quarter of evaluable patients experienced POD24, predominantly as primary refractory disease, and this event identified a subgroup with materially inferior subsequent survival. POD24 may help identify patients who warrant closer surveillance and consideration for clinical trials or novel therapies.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203312.abstract: Objective: To investigate the clinical characteristics and prognostic significance of distinct Ki-67 proliferation indices in patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM). Methods: A retrospective analysis of clinical data from 307 NDMM patients admitted to the Second Hospital of Shanxi Medical University from January 2015 to December 2023. Patients were stratified into two cohorts based on Ki-67 proliferation index: Ki-67 > 10% and Ki-67 ≤ 10%. Results: Among the 307 enrolled NDMM patients, 199 (64.82%, 199/307) were assigned to the Ki-67 ≤ 10% group. The median progression-free survival (mPFS) was 45.52 months (95% CI: 39.40-51.66) in the Ki-67 ≤ 10% group, compared with 25.81 months (95% CI: 20.61-31.00) in the Ki-67 > 10% group, with a statistically significant difference in PFS between the two cohorts (p 10% group, with a statistically significant difference in OS between the two cohorts (p 10% have a significantly worse prognosis than those with Ki-67 ≤ 10%. A high Ki-67 index (>10%) is identified as an independent adverse prognostic parameter for NDMM. Furthermore, the integration of Ki-67 proliferation index with ISS staging can substantially enhance the accuracy of prognostic risk stratification in patients with NDMM.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203313.abstract: Introduction: Despite their benefit, current anti-EGFR therapies are limited by narrow efficacy profiles due to dose-limiting toxicities. This phase 2 open-label study evaluated the efficacy and safety of ABT-806, an EGFR-targeting antibody that is tumor specific, in patients with advanced EGFR-expressing tumors including head and neck cancers (H&NC) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of other sites. Methods: Patients with advanced H&NC (cohort A) or SCC of other sites (cohort B) were enrolled in the study. ABT-806 was administered as monotherapy at a dose of 24 mg/kg intravenously using a twice weekly dosing schedule until unacceptable toxicity and/or evidence of disease progression. Adverse events (AEs) were graded using the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v4.0; tumor response was assessed using the Response Evaluation criteria in Solid Tumors v1.1. EGFR status was assessed with mAb806 and EGFRvIII immunohistochemistry and correlated with outcomes. Results: ABT-806 was well tolerated with no grade 3+ treatment-related AEs. Disease stabilization was observed in two patients (14%) and for a median duration of 19.5 weeks. This included one patient from cohort A and one patient from cohort B. Progression-free survival and overall survival was not significantly different between the two cohorts. Conclusions: Although clinical activity was limited in this small, heavily pre-treated, and biomarker-unselected population, ABT-806 demonstrated an excellent safety profile with minimal classical EGFR-related toxicity. These findings support the development of more tumor-specific EGFR antibodies for use, particularly in combinatorial regimens.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203315.abstract: Lipid mediators are small molecules, derived from lipid metabolism, that initiate cellular responses. In this review, the major classes of lipid mediators are considered with respect to their effects on prostate cancer cells. These classes are: sphingolipids (sphingosine 1-phosphate and ceramide), glycophospholipids (lysophosphatidic acid; LPA), eicosanoids (prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and leukotrienes), cannabinoids, and free fatty acids. Almost all of these mediators elicit effects by binding to druggable G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) to initiate cell proliferation, stimulate migration, and enhance survival. The exceptions are omega-3 fatty acids and endocannabinoids, which inhibit proliferation. The mediators and their receptors serve as potential targets for (1) enzyme inhibitors that block their synthesis, or (2) GPCR antagonists or agonists. These agents are in various stages of development. Progress in testing their translational potential varies between the mediator classes. Lipid mediators also show potential as diagnostic or prognostic biomarkers. Interesting mechanistic aspects have been identified in the course of studying lipid mediator responses in prostate cancer cells. These include positive cross-talk between LPA receptors and EGF receptors, and negative cross-talk between LPA receptors and free fatty acid (FFA) receptors. Together, these findings suggest new strategies for modulating prostate cancer growth and survival pathways in a therapeutic direction.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203316.abstract: To systematically review the literature on the impact of integrated molecular classification of endometrial cancer on diagnosis, prognostic stratification, and clinical management. A systematic search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane Library (January 2013-December 2025), following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. We included original studies, systematic reviews, clinical guidelines, and cost-effectiveness analyses applying TCGA molecular classification or its surrogate classifiers (ProMisE, TransPORTEC). Data were extracted on subtype distribution, survival outcomes, hazard ratios, stage migration, and therapeutic implications. Fifty studies were included. Of these, 13 provided data on molecular subtype distribution (comprising 3527 patients), 8 reported survival outcomes, and 7 reported hazard ratios. The weighted subtype distribution from the 13 studies was as follows: POLEmut 8.9%, MMRd 25.8%, p53abn 16.7%, and NSMP 48.2%. POLEmut was associated with an excellent prognosis (5-year overall survival >95%, hazard ratio 2.0). p53abn was the only independent risk factor for peritoneal (odds ratio 8.54) and vaginal (odds ratio 6.51) recurrence. Molecular classification modified risk group assignment in 6-33% of patients and improved prognostic discrimination of the 2023 FIGO staging system. Therapeutic implications include treatment de-escalation in POLEmut, immunotherapy in MMRd, and intensive chemotherapy in p53abn. Barriers to implementation include access to POLE sequencing and cost-effectiveness. Integrated molecular classification is an essential tool for prognostic stratification and treatment personalization in endometrial cancer. Molecular subtypes demonstrate clearly differentiated prognostic profiles and recurrence patterns, justifying their systematic incorporation into clinical practice and international guidelines.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203317.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary liver malignancy, and accurate tumour segmentation in contrast-enhanced computed tomography is essential for treatment planning, assessment of ablation margins, and post-treatment evaluation. Existing deep learning methods typically use fixed-intensity CT preprocessing, overlooking the adaptive windowing employed by radiologists to enhance tumour visibility. To address this limitation, we propose BCIW-Net, a boundary-conditioned intensity-windowed network that integrates spatially adaptive and differentiable intensity windowing into the segmentation process as a clinically motivated inductive bias. Methods: The proposed framework first generates complementary soft-tissue and tumour-enhancing intensity representations using differentiable sigmoid-based transformations. A primary encoder-decoder module predicts tumour guidance, boundary probabilities, and pixel-wise error proxy maps, which collectively guide the dynamic estimation of spatially varying window centre and width parameters. The resulting adaptively windowed features are selectively blended with fixed-intensity representations through an error-gated mechanism before final refinement in a secondary encoder-decoder network. A multi-task objective jointly optimises tumour segmentation, boundary prediction, error-proxy estimation, and adaptive window regularisation in an end-to-end manner. Results: Experiments on the primary liver cancer (PLC)-CECT dataset demonstrate that BCIW-Net achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 78.68% and an intersection over union (IoU) of 64.85% across five-fold patient-level cross-validation, outperforming the seven evaluated CNN-, Transformer-, and state-space baselines. Evaluation on LiTS2017 without dataset-specific fine-tuning yielded a tumour Dice score of 89.84%, providing preliminary evidence of cross-dataset generalisation. Conclusions: Qualitative feature visualisations show that adaptive windowing enhances tumour representation and boundary delineation, demonstrating the effectiveness and interpretability of BCIW-Net for HCC segmentation.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203318.abstract: Multiportal video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) was introduced in Japan in the 1990s, with uniportal VATS (U-VATS) and robot-assisted thoracic surgery (RATS) following in the 2010s. U-VATS gained significant traction after the 1st Fellowship of the Japanese Association for Chest Surgery (JACS; currently the Japanese Society for Thoracic Surgery, JSTS) in 2018, leading to the establishment of the Japanese Uniportal VATS Interest Group (JUVIG) in April 2018. JUVIG has since driven wider adoption through extensive activities, including educational programs, publications, and collaborative multicenter studies. As a result, expert surgeons now utilize U-VATS for complex procedures such as bronchoplasty, completion lobectomy, complex segmentectomy, and pediatric surgery. Concurrently, RATS gained insurance coverage in Japan in 2018 and has become more prevalent than U-VATS. Despite the significant costs associated with RATS, its adoption rate surpasses that of U-VATS due to institutional policies, perceived ease of implementation, branding, recruitment incentives, and recent national healthcare insurance reimbursement revisions (add-ons) introduced in 2026, which may create administrative pressure to prioritize robotic cases. Although reduced-port RATS is gaining popularity-blurring the lines with U-VATS-and newly emerging indigenous robotic platforms are expected to further accelerate RATS adoption, multiportal VATS (M-VATS) remains the dominant approach in many institutions. Furthermore, maintaining proficiency in VATS, U-VATS, and open thoracotomy remains indispensable for surgical education, economic viability, and acute intraoperative crisis management. Ultimately, while U-VATS represents a promising minimally invasive option, its widespread adoption for major and complex resections in Japan continues to be restricted by both educational and societal barriers.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203319.abstract: Locoregional therapies are used across the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treatment spectrum, including for curative treatment of small tumors, as bridging or downstaging therapy before liver transplant, for treatment of intermediate-stage disease, and as part of combination treatment with systemic therapy in selected patients. This narrative review summarizes recent developments in transarterial radioembolization (TARE), transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), and percutaneous ablation techniques and separates established clinical advances from early investigational work. The strongest evidence supports personalized TARE dosimetry and radiation segmentectomy, selective TACE with reassessment before repeat treatment, and image-guided thermal ablation with objective margin assessment. Phase 3 trials of TACE combined with antiangiogenic and immune checkpoint therapy demonstrated improved progression-free survival in selected patients with unresectable, nonmetastatic HCC, although the survival benefit of these combinations so far extends only to progression-free survival, and the best treatment sequence remains to be defined. Histotripsy, pulsed electric-field ablation, electrochemotherapy, cryoablation, high-intensity focused ultrasound, imageable or alternative radioembolic microspheres, new embolic agents, robotics, and artificial intelligence remain at different stages of clinical development. Most supporting data are derived from single-arm studies, retrospective cohort studies, trials in mixed liver-tumor populations, or studies in preclinical models. Treatment selection should account for tumor burden and location, liver function, portal hypertension, vascular invasion, transplant candidacy, available alternatives, local expertise, and patient preferences. Future studies should focus on durable local control, preservation of liver function, quality of life, transplant eligibility, overall survival, and cost.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203320.abstract: To compare the efficacy, survival benefits, and safety of whole-brain radiotherapy (WBRT) alone versus WBRT combined with simultaneous integrated boost (WBRT+SIB) for patients with brain metastases. A total of 100 patients treated from 2017 to 2022 were retrospectively analyzed. Tumor response was assessed per RECIST 1.1. Survival differences were compared using the Kaplan-Meier method and log-rank test. Multivariate Cox regression and subgroup analyses were performed to evaluate the prognostic value and stability of WBRT+SIB. The WBRT+SIB group exhibited numerically higher objective response and disease control rates without statistical significance. With a median follow-up of 31.0 months, WBRT+SIB significantly prolonged median overall survival (11.0 vs. 8.0 months, p = 0.011) and improved 1-, 2-, and 3-year survival rates. After adjusting for multiple confounders, WBRT+SIB independently reduced mortality risk (HR = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.27-0.97, p = 0.039). Subgroup analyses were exploratory; therefore, consistent survival advantages across strata cannot be confirmed. No significant differences in acute, subacute, or late neurotoxicity, including radiation-induced brain necrosis, were found between the two groups. WBRT+SIB was associated with longer overall survival compared with WBRT alone, without a significant increase in the incidence of radiotherapy-related adverse events. Although ORR and DCR were numerically higher in the WBRT+SIB group, these differences were not statistically significant. Given the limitations of this exploratory study, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require validation in prospective randomized trials.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203321.abstract: Background/Objectives: The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition subdivides node-positive periampullary adenocarcinoma into N1 and N2 by the number of positive nodes. We quantified how much this subdivision and the lymph node ratio (LNR) each add to nodal positivity, and how the nodal yield affects the comparison. Methods: This retrospective cohort comprised 147 consecutive pancreatoduodenectomies for pancreatic head (n = 49), distal bile duct (n = 63), ampullary (n = 31) or duodenal (n = 4) adenocarcinoma. In covariate-adjusted Cox models stratified by origin, the N1/N2 subdivision and the LNR were tested over nodal positivity and over each other with nested likelihood-ratio tests, overall, with the examined-node count in the model and by the period of resection. Results: The median nodal yield was 17 (10 in 2013-2016, 19 in 2017-2024). Beyond nodal positivity, the N1/N2 subdivision added χ2 0.25 (p = 0.61; adjusted N2-versus-N1 hazard ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.59-2.45) and the LNR added χ2 9.60 (p = 0.002; hazard ratio 1.41 per 0.1, 95% CI 1.22-1.62). The LNR added to the N category (p = 0.002; optimism-corrected C-index gain 0.020, 95% CI 0.002-0.041), whereas the N category did not add detectably to the LNR (p = 0.54). With the examined-node count in the model, the LNR increment was attenuated (p = 0.045) and the subdivision's increment rose (χ2 3.65, p = 0.056). From 2017 onward (n = 113), the LNR and the positive-node count were nearly collinear among the node-positive patients (ρ 0.90 versus -0.02 before 2017), and neither the subdivision (p = 0.49) nor the LNR (p = 0.17) added significantly to positivity. Conclusions: The N1/N2 subdivision added little beyond nodal positivity, although imprecisely estimated, and its increment rose when the examined-node count was in the model. The LNR added prognostic information mainly when the yield was low or variable; where the yield was higher and more uniform, the ratio and the count-based category conveyed nearly the same information, and no additional value of the ratio was demonstrated.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203321.title: Incremental Prognostic Information Beyond Nodal Positivity: The AJCC 8th Edition N1/N2 Subdivision and the Lymph Node Ratio in Resected Periampullary Adenocarcinoma.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203322.abstract: Background/Objectives: The HER2-low classification has redefined therapeutic strategies, but its prognostic significance remains uncertain. We compared overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) across HER2 categories (HER2-low, HER2-negative, HER2-positive) in a real-world cohort. Methods: This was a single-center retrospective cohort study conducted at a high-complexity cancer center in Colombia; it included 373 patients with invasive breast cancer classified as HER2-positive (IHC 3+ or ISH+), HER2-low (IHC 1+ or 2+/ISH-), or HER2-negative (IHC 0). Survival was estimated by Kaplan-Meier. Multivariable Cox models were adjusted for age, clinical stage, histological grade, and hormone receptor status, and PFS was additionally analyzed separately in stage I-III and stage IV disease. Results: The cohort included HER2-low (38.3%), HER2-negative (39.7%), and HER2-positive (22.0%) tumors. HER2-low tumors showed lower grade and higher hormone receptor expression (p < 0.001), without better survival. Three-year OS (81.8%, 76.5%, 62.8%; p = 0.178) and PFS (p = 0.227) did not differ. Advanced stage remained the main determinant of mortality, whereas the association with high grade was attenuated. HER2-low was not independently associated with OS (HR 0.67; 95% CI 0.31-1.45) or PFS (HR 0.77; 95% CI 0.40-1.49). Hormone receptor positivity was associated with lower mortality (HR 0.43; 95% CI 0.21-0.88). PFS did not differ across HER2 categories in stage I-III (p = 0.307) or stage IV disease (p = 0.068). Conclusions: HER2-low status was not independently associated with survival. Its more favorable clinicopathological profile was largely explained by higher hormone receptor expression, which was itself associated with survival once included in the models.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203323.abstract: Background/Objectives: This is the first study in Eastern Europe to integrate skin and iris phenotypic characteristics with selected polymorphisms in genes related to skin aging, melanogenesis and skin pigmentation, and inflammatory regulation in relation to cutaneous melanoma (CM) risk. Methods: This case-control study included 180 patients with primary CM identified from the Hospital of the LSMU Kauno klinikos database and 181 controls without a personal history of skin cancer selected from a population-based study in Kaunas. All participants underwent dermatological and ophthalmological examinations and completed questionnaires assessing sun-exposure habits, including severe sunburn history, and Fitzpatrick skin phototype. The total-body number of common melanocytic nevi (CMN) >2 mm in diameter and the number of iris freckles were evaluated using standardized protocols. Five selected genetic polymorphisms, including TYR rs1126809, SLC45A2 rs26722, SLC45A2 rs16891982, IL6 rs1800795, and TNF-α rs1800629, were genotyped. Associations with CM were assessed using multivariable logistic regression. Results: We identified three phenotypical factors independently associated with increased odds of CM (OR; 95% CI): a total-body CMN count >15 (7.89; 4.29-14.53), ≥4 iris freckles (3.70; 2.04-6.74), and a history of severe sunburn (2.76; 1.50-5.07). Compared with Fitzpatrick skin phototype IV, phototypes II (0.35; 0.15-0.82) and III (0.28; 0.11-0.70) were associated with decreased CM odds. In the multivariable model the heterozygous SLC45A2 rs16891982 genotype was associated with increased CM odds (6.64; 1.48-29.83), while the IL6 rs1800795 Mono G genotype revealed an inverse association with CM (0.39; 0.16-0.97). Conclusions: A total-body CMN count >15, ≥4 iris freckles, and severe sunburn history revealed strong independent associations with increased CM risk. However, associations involving SLC45A2 rs16891982 and IL6 rs1800795 in this Lithuanian case-control study were model-dependent. These findings highlight the potential value of integrating selected genetic markers with phenotypic characteristics and sun-exposure history in the development of personalized CM risk prediction models; however, validation in larger populations is required.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203324.abstract: Observation is generally recommended for asymptomatic meningiomas, but evidence from incidental meningiomas is derived largely from heterogeneous intracranial locations and may not directly apply to tumors involving the anterior visual pathway. We investigated whether preoperative visual status remained associated with postoperative visual function after adjustment for baseline clinical and anatomical differences in this location-specific subgroup. We retrospectively reviewed 146 patients who underwent resection of skull base meningiomas contacting or compressing the optic nerve and/or chiasm. Preoperative visual status was categorized by comprehensive ophthalmologic evaluation as normal visual function or visual dysfunction. The primary outcome was postoperative normal visual function, defined as preservation of normal vision in patients with normal preoperative visual function and complete recovery in those with preoperative visual dysfunction. Multivariable logistic regression was performed, and propensity score matching was conducted using age, sex, tumor volume, tumor laterality, and optic canal involvement. Propensity score matching yielded 48 matched pairs with adequate balance across all measured covariates (all standardized mean differences < 0.1). Postoperative normal visual function was preserved or achieved in 95.8% of patients with normal preoperative visual function versus 31.3% of those with preoperative visual dysfunction (exact McNemar p < 0.001). Favorable visual outcome occurred in 95.8% versus 77.1%, respectively (p = 0.0225). Among surgically treated patients, normal preoperative visual function remained strongly associated with postoperative normal visual function after adjustment for measured clinical and anatomical differences. These findings do not establish that earlier surgery improves visual outcomes or define an optimal surgical timing strategy, but suggest that preoperative visual status and tumor anatomy should be considered in individualized management decisions.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203325.abstract: Melanoma is the most aggressive and rapidly metastasizing malignant neoplasm of the skin and mucous membranes, arising from melanocytes of neuroectodermal origin. Despite substantial advances in immune checkpoint inhibitors and targeted therapy, a significant proportion of patients develop primary or acquired resistance, which is largely attributable to the complex interactions between tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment (TME). This review presents a comprehensive analysis of the cellular and molecular components of the melanoma TME and their contribution to immunosuppression, tumor progression, and therapeutic resistance. The role of keratinocytes as the primary niche-forming cells in the epidermis is examined, including their reprogramming during melanomagenesis and their involvement in drug resistance. Particular attention is given to cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), which orchestrate stromal remodeling, promote immune exclusion, and limit the efficacy of immunotherapy. The phenotypic and functional heterogeneity of innate and adaptive immune cells-macrophages, granulocytes, natural killer cells, dendritic cells, T and B lymphocytes-is discussed in the context of their dual role in antitumor immunity and immune escape. A detailed analysis of immune editing mechanisms, including defective antigen recognition, resistance to apoptosis, and the establishment of an immunosuppressive microenvironment, is provided. The review further summarizes the current landscape of cellular immunotherapy for melanoma. Clinically established approaches, including tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and CAR-T cells, are discussed with reference to completed phase II-III clinical trials, whereas emerging strategies such as CAR-macrophages and dendritic cell vaccines are presented as largely preclinical or early-phase investigational platforms. It is concluded that the melanoma TME functions as a unified immunosuppressive network rather than a collection of individual cell populations. Based on currently available comparative clinical evidence, reprogramming this network through the combination of cellular platforms with immune checkpoint inhibitors, stromal modulators, and macrophage-repolarizing agents, supported by personalized assessment of TME composition, represents a rational and actively investigated therapeutic direction.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203326.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the incremental predictive value of pretreatment tri-modal ultrasound deep learning integrating two-dimensional ultrasound (2DUS), color Doppler flow imaging (CDFI), and contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) for predicting breast pathologic complete response (bpCR) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC), and to assess performance stability across independent centers. Methods: This retrospective multicenter study included 1089 patients with primary invasive breast cancer. Center 1 provided the training cohort (n = 572) and internal validation cohort (n = 246), whereas centers 2 (n = 160) and 3 (n = 111) served as independent external validation cohorts. Using pretreatment 2DUS, CDFI, and CEUS within a standardized intratumoral and 10-mm peritumoral framework, single-modality, all three dual-modality combinations, and tri-modal models were developed. The best-performing dual-modality model was identified and locked during training as the primary imaging comparator. A Tri-modal + Clinical model further integrated pretreatment clinical and biomarker variables. Performance was assessed using AUC, Brier score, calibration, decision curve analysis, and ablation experiments. Results: Overall, 383 patients (35.2%) achieved bpCR. CEUS was the strongest single modality, and 2DUS + CEUS was the best-performing dual-modality model. Compared with 2DUS + CEUS, the tri-modal model increased the AUC from 0.895 to 0.919 in the combined external cohort (ΔAUC, +0.023; 95% CI, +0.010 to +0.038; p = 0.001), with corresponding improvements in Brier score (0.124 to 0.105) and F1 score (0.747 to 0.786). The AUC point estimate increased in both external centers, although the 95% CI for the incremental AUC included zero in external validation cohort 2. Despite modest standalone discrimination, CDFI provided measurable incremental information when added to 2DUS + CEUS. Further integration of pretreatment clinical and biomarker variables increased the combined external AUC to 0.935. Reduced-input retraining showed performance decreases after omission of any modality, with the largest reduction after CEUS omission. Conclusions: Pretreatment tri-modal ultrasound deep learning provided incremental predictive value for bpCR beyond the best dual-modality model, with a consistent direction of benefit across two independent external centers. Clinical and biomarker integration provided additional predictive information, supporting further evaluation of this multimodal framework for individualized pretreatment bpCR prediction.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203328.abstract: Cancer remains a major global health challenge and a leading cause of mortality worldwide. As incidence continues to rise, early detection remains one of the most effective strategies for improving survival and reducing disease burden. Urine is an attractive source of biomarkers due to its non-invasive collection, ease of repeated sampling, and rich molecular composition. This scoping review evaluates the current landscape of urinary biomarkers for the early detection of cancer and their potential for clinical translation. A detailed literature search was conducted using PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science to identify studies investigating urinary biomarkers for cancer detection. Biomarkers were categorised by analyte class, and diagnostic performance, validation status, and clinical applicability were assessed. Urinary biomarkers demonstrated diagnostic potential across multiple malignancies, including lung, breast, pancreatic, hepatobiliary, colorectal, renal and ovarian cancers, while several urinary assays are already clinically available for bladder and prostate cancers. Promising diagnostic accuracy was reported for multiple biomarker classes, particularly multimarker panels integrating metabolites, proteins, nucleic acids, and epigenetic signatures. However, most studies were exploratory, involving small cohorts, methodological heterogeneity, and limited independent validation. Urinary biomarkers represent a promising and rapidly evolving approach to non-invasive cancer detection. Despite encouraging diagnostic performance, few candidates have progressed to clinical implementation. Large prospective multicentre studies, rigorous validation, and assay standardisation are essential to establish urinary biomarkers as reliable tools for cancer screening, early diagnosis, and risk stratification.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203329.abstract: Background/Objectives: Pathological response after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is an established prognostic factor in locally advanced gastric cancer, but it does not fully reflect the biological heterogeneity of residual disease. The immune microenvironment may provide additional prognostic information. We therefore investigated the relationship between post-neoadjuvant Immunoscore, pathological findings, and disease-free survival in patients with microsatellite-stable locally advanced gastric cancer. Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included patients with locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma who received four cycles of neoadjuvant FLOT followed by curative-intent gastrectomy between November 2023 and May 2025. Immunoscore was determined in post-neoadjuvant resection specimens based on CD3+ and CD8+ T-cell infiltration in the tumor center and invasive margin. Immunoscore assessments were performed by two pathologists blinded to clinical and outcome data, with final evaluations established through consensus review. Associations between Immunoscore and clinicopathological features were examined, including exploratory multivariable analyses adjusting for baseline clinical T stage and histological subtype. Disease-free survival was analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method and Cox proportional hazards regression. Results: The final analysis included 48 patients. Compared with the low-Immunoscore group, the high-Immunoscore group had lower rates of ypT4 disease (37.5% vs. 75.0%; p = 0.014), ypN3 disease (21.9% vs. 68.8%; p = 0.002), and perineural invasion (43.8% vs. 75.0%; p = 0.041). The association between low Immunoscore and ypN3 disease persisted after adjustment for baseline clinical T stage and histological subtype (adjusted OR 5.89, 95% CI 1.32-26.23; p = 0.020). Tumor regression grade did not differ significantly between the groups (p = 0.211). During a median follow-up of 18.0 months, 17 patients developed recurrence. Disease-free survival was numerically longer in the high-Immunoscore group. The difference was not significant by the log-rank test (p = 0.100), whereas an exploratory Breslow analysis showed a difference between the survival distributions (p = 0.025). However, Cox regression did not demonstrate a statistically significant association with disease-free survival (HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.18-1.21; p = 0.117). Conclusions: A higher post-neoadjuvant Immunoscore was associated with less advanced residual tumor and nodal disease and less frequent perineural invasion, without a statistically significant association with tumor regression grade or disease-free survival in the primary analyses. Immunoscore may therefore complement conventional pathological assessment after neoadjuvant FLOT. These findings require validation in larger prospective cohorts.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203330.abstract: Distinction of melanoma from less aggressive melanocytic neoplasms is essential to avoid over- or undertreatment. Melanocytic neoplasms can harbor a broad spectrum of molecular drivers, including mutations, amplifications, and fusions, associated with an array of morphologies and biologic behavior. This molecular complexity creates challenges for classification and diagnosis of malignancy. Here, we review current knowledge to present a molecular framework for classifying melanocytic neoplasia and describe current molecular testing modalities useful for informing accurate diagnosis in challenging cases.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203331.abstract: Background: Evidence regarding EUS-guided intratumoral phosphorus-32 (P-32) microparticle implantation for locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC) remains limited. This prospective pilot study evaluated its technical feasibility, preliminary safety, and early disease-control outcomes when administered in combination with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel. Methods: Seventeen patients with unresectable LAPC underwent EUS-guided intratumoral P-32 microparticle implantation through a 22-gauge fine-needle aspiration needle during the fourth week of systemic chemotherapy. Intratumoral distribution was assessed using Bremsstrahlung SPECT/CT. Tumour response was evaluated according to RECIST version 1.1, and treatment-emergent adverse events were graded according to CTCAE version 4.0. The main secondary endpoint was local disease control rate at approximately 16 weeks (LDCR16w). All analyses were descriptive. Results: Implantation was technically successful in all 17 patients (100.0%; exact 95% CI, 80.5-100.0%), and SPECT/CT confirmed intratumoral distribution in every case. No implantation-related procedural complications were recorded (0/17; exact 95% CI, 0.0-19.5%). At approximately 16 weeks, CT assessment was available for 16 patients: seven had a partial response and nine had stable disease. The LDCR16w was 16/16 among evaluable patients (100.0%; exact 95% CI, 79.4-100.0%) and 16/17 in the all-treated analysis (94.1%; exact 95% CI, 71.3-99.9%). A reduction in CA19-9 of at least 50% was observed in 13/16 evaluable patients. Four patients underwent subsequent R0 resection (4/17, 23.5%; exact 95% CI, 6.8-49.9%). Adverse events were predominantly grade 1-2; one grade 3 abdominal pain event and no grade 4-5 events were recorded. Only three deaths occurred during a median OS follow-up of 15.6 months, making survival estimates exploratory and statistically immature. Conclusions: In this small, single-center pilot cohort of highly selected patients, EUS-guided intratumoral P-32 microparticle implantation combined with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel was technically feasible and provided preliminary safety information. Because of the absence of a chemotherapy-only comparator, the small sample size, and the limited follow-up, the radiographic, biomarker, resection, and survival outcomes cannot be attributed specifically to P-32 implantation and should be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Larger controlled studies with longer follow-up are required to determine clinical efficacy.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203332.abstract: Gastric cancer remains a leading cause of cancer mortality. However, earlier detection has increased the number of cases suitable for organ-preserving treatment. Sentinel node navigation surgery has been proposed as an alternative to standard gastrectomy for early gastric cancer. The safety of this procedure hinges on how accurately sentinel node mapping predicts nodal status. This systematic review synthesizes its diagnostic accuracy and outcome data. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, the Web of Science Core Collection, and Scopus from inception without date limits, along with two trial registries; screening was restricted to English-language reports. Estimates and exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) 95% confidence intervals were recalculated from each study's reported contingency counts using a consistent statistical method. Each included cohort was appraised using QUADAS-2. Eight cohorts contributed per-patient accuracy data, and three contributed per-node molecular comparisons. Detection rates were 97.1% or higher in every cohort entry, with the exception of the naked-eye dye arm of a within-cohort comparison and the smallest feasibility series. Sensitivity was 93.0% (53/57; 95% CI, 83.0-98.1) in the single adequately powered treatment-naive cohort, compared to 69.6% (16/23; 47.1-86.8) in the single prospective trial conducted after non-curative endoscopic resection. Sensitivity also depended on the thoroughness of sentinel node examination: within one cohort, the same patients yielded a sensitivity of 53.6% with single-plane frozen section versus 85.7% with multiple paraffin sections. Therefore, estimates were not pooled. No appraised cohort demonstrated a low risk of bias across all four QUADAS-2 domains. Stomach preservation guided by sentinel node mapping may be a reasonable approach for treatment-naive disease in experienced centers. However, it is not supported after non-curative endoscopic resection.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203333.abstract: Prognostic PET biomarkers in glioblastoma remain mostly as a single tracer and poorly characterized at recurrence. We investigated whether paired [18F]FDOPA/[18F]FDG PET captures complementary metabolic information associated with survival in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma. Sixty-five consecutive patients underwent paired [18F]FDOPA/[18F]FDG PET/MR at baseline and/or recurrence. Survival was analyzed from baseline PET/MR (OS1, n = 36) and recurrence PET/MR (OS2, n = 55); longitudinal analyses used the paired subgroup (n = 26). FDOPA and FDG tumor masks were independently segmented within a FLAIR-derived tumor box, and metrics were extracted from tracer-specific masks, their intersection, and their union. Metrics significant in Kaplan-Meier or univariable Cox analyses were tested in adjusted Cox models. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was used as a sensitivity analysis for the continuous Cox screening tests. In exploratory screening, prognostic associations were sparse at baseline and more prominent at recurrence. At OS2, three metrics remained independently associated with survival after adjustment: the FDOPA/FDG union-domain SUVmeanunion ratio (HR, 1.50; p = 0.0168), MTVinter (HR, 1.63; p = 0.0154), and MTVDOPA (HR, 1.58; p = 0.0191). The SUVmeanunion ratio and MTVDOPA showed limited correlation, suggesting complementary information. Their integration into IR-MTVDOPA, defined as FDOPA/FDG SUVmeanunion ratio × log(MTVDOPA), showed higher apparent OS2 discrimination (HR, 1.73; log-rank p = 0.0001; C-index, 0.730; bootstrap .632-corrected C-index, 0.684; 12-month AUC, 0.863). In this exploratory single-center cohort, paired [18F]FDOPA/[18F]FDG PET showed prognostic associations at recurrence. Inter-tracer intensity balance and metabolic tumor burden provided partially complementary survival information, and their exploratory integration showed higher apparent discrimination. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203334.abstract: Background/Objectives: Histological subtype and resection completeness are established prognostic factors in retroperitoneal liposarcoma, but evidence often derives from resected primary disease. We characterized management and post-referral survival in a referral cohort. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 61 patients managed from May 2015 to September 2025. Overall survival (OS) was measured from first presentation at our center. Kaplan–Meier and exploratory Cox analyses were performed, allowing the association between tumor diameter and mortality to vary over time. Results: Forty-two patients had primary disease, and 19 had recurrent disease; 12 had well-differentiated liposarcoma (WDLPS), and 49 had dedifferentiated liposarcoma (DDLPS). Among 24 patients who underwent surgery, 21 had macroscopically complete (R0/R1) resection. Twenty-five patients died. No deaths occurred in WDLPS; median OS was 29.8 months in DDLPS (p = 0.008). In DDLPS, recurrent versus primary disease was not associated with OS (hazard ratio [HR], 0.99; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.41–2.38). Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status ≥ 2 (n = 6 in the entire cohort) was associated with poorer OS (adjusted HR, 8.03; 95% CI, 2.20–29.36), and the association between tumor diameter and mortality varied over time (adjusted interaction HR, 1.44; 95% CI, 1.07–1.95). Conclusions: Observed post-referral survival differed by histological subtype. Among patients with DDLPS, no survival difference between primary and recurrent disease was demonstrated, but the wide CI and referral-related survivor selection preclude an inference of equivalence. Associations involving performance status and time-varying tumor diameter were exploratory and require external validation.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203335.abstract: Background/Objectives: Liver transplantation may provide prolonged survival in fibrolamellar carcinoma (FLC), but the frequency and timing of post-transplant recurrence, and the basis for patient selection, remain poorly defined. We described the course from listing through long-term follow-up and tested whether routine pretransplant measurements distinguished the recurrence risk. Methods: Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients data identified separate listing and first-transplant cohorts during 2002-2025. Competing-risk analyses assessed waiting-list outcomes and reported recurrence of the pretransplant tumour. Exploratory recurrence models were internally validated with 500 patient bootstrap samples, with performance assessed only in omitted recipients. Recorded explant tumour extent was examined in the registry's liver explant file. Results: This study included 61 listed candidates and 51 first-transplant recipients; 42 recipients had a pathology-supported discharge diagnosis of FLC. One-year incidence of transplantation was 76.5% (95% CI 65.9-86.6). After a median potential follow-up of 8.1 years, five-year post-transplant survival was 63.3% (95% CI 46.4-76.2). Seventeen recurrences were reported and the three-year cumulative incidence was 26.1% (95% CI 13.9-39.1). Malignancy was the recorded primary cause in 13 of 23 deaths. Laboratory-component and compact clinical models had mean three-year validation areas under the curve of 0.571 and 0.507, and neither reduced prediction error relative to its matched cohort-average prediction. Conclusions: Transplantation was followed by prolonged survival in selected patients with FLC, although reported recurrence was common and sometimes late. Routine pretransplant variables did not identify reproducible recurrence-risk groups. With 51 recipients and 17 recurrences, these estimates are imprecise and the prediction analyses are exploratory; selection should remain multidisciplinary while tumour extent, treatment response and biological markers are evaluated prospectively.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203336.abstract: Background: Maternal embryonic leucine zipper kinase (MELK) is a cell cycle-regulated serine/threonine kinase frequently overexpressed in human malignancies, and represents a promising anticancer drug target. Discovery of structurally novel, highly selective MELK inhibitors remains an unmet need. Methods: In the study, we implemented an integrated computational pipeline combining four machine learning regressors (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM), hierarchical Glide docking (HTVS to SP to XP), MM/GBSA rescoring, ADMET prediction, and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations to screen a ~15.58 million-compound commercial library, yielding 12 prioritized candidates. Three commercially available compounds (CPD4, CPD6, CPD10) were evaluated in an antiproliferative panel. Results: CPD6 was identified as the most active hit, with IC50 values of 1.44 μM in MDA-MB-468 and 1.66 μM in H1299, modestly exceeding the reference compound MELK-8a under the same assay conditions (2.48 and 2.51 μM, respectively). Cellular thermal shift assay in cell lysates provided biochemical evidence of MELK engagement, and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations supported a computationally predicted binding mode in the MELK kinase domain. Additional substrate phosphorylation and MELK overexpression rescue assays further supported MELK-dependent inhibitory activity. Colony formation, EdU incorporation, and cell cycle analyses demonstrated dose-dependent antiproliferative effects and G2/M arrest, with concomitant downregulation of CDC25C, CDK1, and Cyclin B1. Discussion: CPD6 is a structurally novel MELK lead distinct from reported inhibitors. While our data support MELK target engagement, kinome selectivity profiling remains required, and this ML pipeline demonstrates the utility of AI-driven large-scale anticancer lead screening. Conclusions: Using the integrated machine-learning virtual screening pipeline established in this work, we identified CPD6 as a structurally novel MELK-targeted lead that engages MELK, induces G2/M arrest, and exerts low-micromolar antiproliferative activity in triple-negative breast cancer and lung adenocarcinoma models.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203338.abstract: Oligometastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is defined anatomically by a threshold of five or fewer metastatic lesions across three or fewer organs. That definition is a proxy for a biological question it cannot answer: whether the metastatic process has been arrested at a stage where eradication of all detectable disease is curative. Randomized phase II trials of local consolidative therapy have shown median progression-free survival gains of 6.2 and 8.0 months and, in one trial, a median overall survival of 41.2 months vs. 17.0 months, yet median progression-free survival with local therapy did not exceed 14.2 months, and the phase II/III NRG-LU002 trial found no significant survival benefit from adding local therapy to maintenance therapy. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) measures molecular disease burden. In resectable NSCLC, preoperative ctDNA detection is associated with a higher risk of relapse; in oligometastatic disease, the baseline sample is instead the quantitative reference for response. ctDNA kinetics during induction therapy track systemic response before any operation, although no response threshold has been validated, and postoperative molecular residual disease anticipates radiological relapse by a median of approximately 5 months. This review synthesizes the evidence linking liquid biopsy to surgical decision-making and proposes, as a hypothesis for prospective testing, a dynamic risk stratification framework anchored on five plasma sampling points. We separate established prognostic evidence from untested hypotheses, address oncogene-driven and other oligometastatic states, and define the assay requirements, confounders and trial designs needed before ctDNA can select patients for or against thoracic resection.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203339.abstract: Neoadjuvant treatment for early-stage triple-negative breast cancer has been widely used, and the KEYNOTE-522 (KN522) regimen has become a standard of care for early-stage TNBC, with alternative treatment options including a dose-dense anthracycline/taxane-based regimen for patients without access to neoadjuvant immunotherapy. Nevertheless, real-world evidence in Chinese populations, especially high-risk cohorts such as older populations and those with substantial nodal burden, is limited regarding both efficacy and tolerability. This study describes the outcomes associated with neoadjuvant systemic therapy in a Hong Kong Chinese cohort. This study aimed to describe the feasibility, treatment delivery, tolerability and safety of the KN522 regimen in stage I-III TNBC in a Chinese cohort in Hong Kong. Another cohort treated with dose-dense neoadjuvant chemotherapy, which is also a standard-of-care treatment alternative, is presented to provide context of local treatment practice. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of 59 patients with stage I-III TNBC who received neoadjuvant systemic treatment prior to breast surgery at a tertiary centre in Hong Kong between February 2022 and June 2025. The primary cohort received the KN522 regimen (n = 30). A contextual reference cohort received dose-dense epirubicin/cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel (n = 29) to describe local treatment patterns. Descriptive outcomes included pathological complete response (pCR), treatment delivery, adverse events, surgery completion, and exploratory event-free survival (EFS). Analyses were primarily descriptive; between-cohort comparisons were exploratory in nature. Fifty-nine patients were included overall: 30 treated with the KN522 regimen and 29 treated with dose-dense neoadjuvant chemotherapy. In the KN522 cohort, the median age was 56 years, 80.0% of patients were postmenopausal, and 33.3% had N3 disease. Pathological complete response occurred in 13 of 30 patients (43.3%; exact 95% CI 25.5-62.6%). Grade ≥3 chemotherapy-related adverse events occurred in 15 patients (50.0%), immune-related adverse events occurred in 11 patients (36.6%), and Grade 3 or higher immune-related adverse events occurred in four patients (13.3%). Pembrolizumab was suspended in six patients (20.0%), while all 30 patients proceeded to definitive surgery. In the dose-dense chemotherapy cohort, the pCR rate was 31.0%, with a grade ≥3 chemotherapy-related adverse event rate of 20.7%, and all patients proceeded to definitive surgery. In this descriptive real-world single-centre Hong Kong study, the neoadjuvant KN522 regimen was feasible in Chinese patients with early TNBC, although treatment-related toxicity and treatment modification were common. The observed pCR rate was lower than that reported in the original KN522 trial, possibly reflecting differences in patient selection and real-world treatment delivery patterns. Larger multi-centre studies are needed to evaluate outcomes in Chinese and other Asian populations.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203340.abstract: Sleeve lobectomy serves as a parenchyma-sparing alternative to pneumonectomy for central non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This study describes and compares early postoperative outcomes and overall survival between sleeve lobectomy and pneumonectomy and explores factors associated with survival. A retrospective cohort analysis was conducted on 97 consecutive patients with central NSCLC operated at the Marius Nasta National Institute of Pneumophthisiology between September 2021 and December 2022, with follow-up through 1 March 2025. Patients were divided into two groups: sleeve lobectomy (n = 41) and pneumonectomy (n = 56). Early morbidity, mortality, and overall survival were evaluated using univariate analysis and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression. After multivariable adjustment, surgical procedure was not significantly associated with overall survival. A low rate of major anastomotic complications was observed in the sleeve lobectomy group, with one case of early partial anastomotic leak (2.44%) requiring surgical reinforcement. In an exploratory multivariable model, pathological nodal involvement and the number of involved lymph nodes were associated with mortality. In appropriately selected patients where an R0 parenchyma-sparing resection is technically feasible, sleeve lobectomy is associated with acceptable morbidity and survival. After adjustment, the surgical procedure was not significantly associated with overall survival. Nodal disease burden was the factor most strongly associated with survival in this cohort.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203341.abstract: Background: Kidney tumors comprise a biologically diverse and diagnostically challenging group of neoplasms. Many entities share overlapping morphologic features despite having distinct molecular profiles. Although histomorphology remains the cornerstone of diagnosis, molecular biomarker testing has become increasingly important for accurate classification, recognition of emerging entities, identification of hereditary cancer syndromes, and therapeutic decision-making. Focus of the Review: This narrative review provides a practical, pathology-oriented framework for molecular biomarker testing in kidney tumors. It integrates immunohistochemistry, fluorescence in situ hybridization, polymerase chain reaction-based methods, and next-generation sequencing with morphologic assessment. Particular attention is given to diagnostically relevant alterations involving VHL, TFE3, TFEB, MET, FH, ELOC, and ALK, genes encoding SDH subunits, and components of the mTOR signaling pathway, together with commonly used immunohistochemical surrogates. The prognostic and predictive roles of selected biomarkers, including their potential value in hereditary risk assessment and treatment selection, are also discussed. Practical limitations, such as limited biopsy material, intratumoral heterogeneity, and technical variability, are considered. Conclusions: Molecular biomarker testing is reshaping kidney tumor pathology by supporting an integrated diagnostic approach that complements, rather than replaces, careful morphologic evaluation. Its appropriate use can improve diagnostic accuracy, refine clinical stratification, and facilitate the recognition of emerging renal tumor entities with hereditary or therapeutic relevance. Future developments are expected to include methylation profiling, transcriptomic classifiers, liquid biopsy platforms, and artificial intelligence-assisted interpretation.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203342.abstract: Cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) can compromise cardiovascular health and the delivery of anticancer treatment. Echocardiography and cardiac biomarkers remain the first-line surveillance tools; cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) provides complementary assessment of ventricular function and myocardial tissue when findings are inconclusive or additional characterization may change management. This narrative review examines multiparametric CMR across seven anticancer treatment groups and proposes a risk-adapted approach to its clinical use. Cine imaging, T1 and T2 mapping, extracellular volume fraction (ECV), late gadolinium enhancement, and feature-tracking strain provide different, partly overlapping information. Serial interpretation requires attention to local reference ranges, measurement reproducibility, hematocrit, and acquisition and analysis consistency. An absolute ECV increase of at least 3 percentage points is discussed as an observational risk signal, not proof of collagen deposition or a validated treatment threshold. The guideline threshold of a greater than 15% relative decline in global longitudinal strain derives from echocardiography and should not be assumed to apply directly to CMR feature tracking. We distinguish guideline-supported practice, randomized evidence, observational evidence, and mechanistic extrapolation from the authors' proposed surveillance and rechallenge framework. Suspected immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis requires urgent clinical evaluation even when CMR is negative. Prospective trials are needed to establish whether CMR-informed management improves cardiovascular outcomes, treatment completion, or survival.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203343.abstract: Background/Objectives: Arterial coupling in microsurgery remains technically challenging despite widespread venous coupler adoption. We developed a novel everter device to facilitate arterial anastomosis using mechanical couplers and evaluated its feasibility and potential efficiency in abdominal-based breast reconstruction. Methods: Five pigs underwent paired superior epigastric artery flap reconstruction with everter-assisted and hand-sewn arterial anastomoses, analyzed using a paired t-test. A retrospective clinical series included 12 patients, 22 reconstructed breasts, 14 coupling attempts, and 8 primary hand-sewn recipient arterial anastomoses. The primary clinical outcome was successful coupling without revision or conversion. Clinical timing comparisons were descriptive. Results: All five porcine arterial couplings were successful. Mean arterial time was 8.47 ± 2.83 min versus 20.26 ± 3.32 min for hand-sewn controls, a paired reduction of 11.79 min (95% CI, 5.86 to 17.72; p = 0.005). Clinical coupling succeeded in 9 of 14 attempts (64.3%). Five attempts required conversion (35.7%), including three thrombotic and two technical failures. All were converted intraoperatively, with no flap loss. Mean arterial times were 9.2 ± 4.2 min for successful coupling (n = 8) and 20.2 ± 8.0 min for primary hand-sewn anastomosis (n = 6), an approximately 55% difference. Conclusions: Everter-assisted arterial coupling demonstrated clinical feasibility and shorter mean arterial times when successfully completed. These findings support further refinement and evaluation of the technique to establish safety and overall procedural efficiency.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203344.abstract: Background: This exploratory study assessed whether qualitative dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) time-intensity curves (TICs) differentiate non-progressive treatment-related changes (NPTRC) from tumor progression after stereotactic radiotherapy for brain metastases. Methods: Thirty-two patients with 51 treated lesions underwent DCE-MRI. Five neuroradiologists independently delineated a volume of interest and classified the resulting TIC as Type A-D. Longitudinal clinical and MRI follow-up provided the reference outcome, which was recorded before the TIC framework was finalized. An A/B versus C/D grouping was evaluated as a secondary exploratory analysis. Results: Thirty-five lesions were classified as NPTRC and 16 as tumor progression. All 17 Type A lesions were NPTRC, whereas all 13 Type C/D lesions showed progression. Type B was observed in 21 of 51 lesions (41.2%), including 18 NPTRC and 3 progressive lesions, representing a substantial indeterminate subgroup. The exploratory A/B versus C/D grouping yielded 81.3% sensitivity and 100% specificity. The ordinal TIC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.952. Interobserver agreement was high within the present reader group (Fleiss' κ = 0.889). Conclusions: Type A was associated with NPTRC, Types C/D were associated with progression, and Type B represented an indeterminate pattern. These descriptive findings require independent validation before clinical use.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203346.abstract: Background/Objectives: During radiofrequency ablation (RFA) for the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), electrodes are generally inserted into the center of the tumor through the hepatic parenchyma under image guidance, including ultrasound or computed tomography (CT) guidance. However, tumors located just below the hepatic capsule require special puncture techniques. This retrospective study aimed to analyze the efficacy and outcomes of RFA for HCC located just below the subcapsular region of the liver. Methods: A total of 81 patients with 81 subcapsular HCC tumors underwent RFA. Baseline patient characteristics, treatment results, and adverse events were investigated. Factors associated with local recurrence were also examined. Results: Among the 81 patients, 59 (73%) were male, the median age was 74 years (range, 46-93 years), and 68 (84%) were classified as Child-Pugh class A. The median tumor size was 1.5 cm (range, 0.5-3.7 cm), and 56 of 81 tumors (69%) were <2.0 cm in diameter. 53 tumors were located in the right lobe of the liver (65%). Monopolar RFA was performed in 55 patients (68%), and no-touch multi-bipolar RFA was performed in 26 patients (32%). Treatment success was achieved in 75 tumors (93%), with inadequate ablative margins observed in 6 tumors (7%). Of these six tumors, five (83%) were treated with monopolar RFA; however, differences between the RFA devices were not statistically significant (p = 0.368). Local tumor progression (LTP) was observed in 19 patients (24%), with cumulative LTP rates of 13%, 29%, 33%, and 33% at 1, 3, 5, and 10 years, respectively. Multivariate analysis using a COX proportional hazards model identified insufficient ablative margins as a significant factor associated with LTP (hazard ratio, 4.64; 95% confidence interval, 1.14-14.9; p = 0.031). Adverse events occurred in 17 patients (21%), all of whom recovered with conservative treatment. Tumor seeding occurred in only one patient (1%). Conclusions: In the present study, achieving an adequate ablative margin using either monopolar or multi-bipolar RFA systems was associated with a reduced risk of local tumor recurrence in patients with subcapsular HCC.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203347.abstract: The imaging-defined peritumoral region may contain quantitative imaging information beyond that captured by the tumor core, but its radiomic deviation from normal-appearing breast parenchyma remains insufficiently characterized. This retrospective single-center study investigated whether peritumoral-to-normal radiomic distances exceed the within-patient bilateral normal-appearing parenchymal reference distance. Fifty-six patients with histopathologically confirmed breast cancer and preoperative bilateral dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI were included. Single-slice radiomic analysis was performed for four predefined regions: tumor core (T), peritumoral microenvironment (M), remote ipsilateral normal-appearing parenchyma (I), and contralateral normal-appearing parenchyma (C). After quality control, 101 radiomic features were standardized and analyzed using standardized Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine, and Ledoit-Wolf Mahalanobis distances. Peritumoral-to-ipsilateral (dMI) and peritumoral-to-contralateral (dMC) distances were compared with the within-patient bilateral normal-appearing parenchymal distance (dIC). Across all four metrics, both dMI and dMC exceeded dIC, and all eight primary paired Wilcoxon comparisons remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q≤1.07×10-6), with matched-pairs rank-biserial correlations ranging from 0.749 to 0.989. The principal pattern was broadly preserved across alternative Mahalanobis covariance formulations, reduced-dimensional PCA analyses, particularly when three or four principal components were retained, exclusion of all 13 retained shape features, separate radiomic feature-family analyses, and replacement of selected non-normalized non-uniformity features with normalized counterparts. These findings show that, in the present cohort, peritumoral-to-normal radiomic distances exceeded the within-patient bilateral normal-appearing parenchymal reference distance. Because the four analyzed regions differed in size, shape, and sampling geometry, the reported distances should be interpreted as region-level radiomic differences under the present ROI definitions rather than as geometry-independent tissue properties. Larger multi-institutional studies using full-volume three-dimensional radiomics and standardized imaging and preprocessing strategies are needed to assess reproducibility, clarify the biological correlates of this radiomic pattern, and evaluate its potential clinical relevance.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203348.abstract: Stage III/N2 non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) can often be treated with either surgery-based multimodality therapy or definitive chemoradiotherapy. Historical randomized trials showed that surgery improved local control without demonstrating an overall-survival benefit; neither platform demonstrated superiority, although none was designed to establish equivalence. In the immunotherapy era, both pathways have improved through separate evidence streams: perioperative trials compared immunotherapy with chemotherapy-based surgical controls, and PACIFIC compared durvalumab with placebo after chemoradiotherapy. Neither stream determines which complete modern pathway is better for a patient eligible for both, and cross-trial comparisons are confounded by differences in populations, randomization points, and endpoint definitions. This review distinguishes three questions that are often conflated: whether direct comparative evidence exists, how large any relative treatment effect may be, and whether sufficient clinical equipoise exists to justify randomization. Technical resectability, physiological operability, and irradiability define eligibility for a platform, not comparative benefit, and no current biomarker has been shown to modify the relative effect of the two platforms. Comparative uncertainty is most visible in multistation, bulky, or anatomically complex N2 disease, the most practicable starting point for randomization; superiority of either platform, however, has not been demonstrated at either end of the N2 spectrum. A staged randomized comparison of the complete modern pathways, with prespecified analyses of candidate treatment-effect modifiers, is proposed as a reasoned research strategy.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203349.abstract: Liquid biopsy is an emerging approach for the molecular characterization of hepatopancreatobiliary (HPB) malignancies through the analysis of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), circulating tumor cells (CTCs), and extracellular vesicles (EVs). These biomarkers may complement conventional imaging and serum markers by providing additional information on tumor biology and disease evolution. This narrative review examines the available evidence concerning the potential applications of liquid biopsy in HPB surgical practice, with particular emphasis on preoperative prognostic assessment, postoperative molecular residual disease detection, recurrence monitoring, and treatment adaptation. Among the different circulating biomarkers, ctDNA currently has the most developed perioperative evidence base. Studies involving pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and biliary tract cancers have demonstrated associations between ctDNA detection and unfavorable oncological outcomes, particularly postoperative recurrence. Nevertheless, the available evidence remains predominantly observational, with considerable heterogeneity in patient populations, sampling protocols, analytical platforms, and outcome definitions. Although the integration of circulating biomarkers with conventional anatomical criteria has generated interest in the concept of "biological resectability", this framework remains hypothetical and has not been prospectively validated for surgical treatment selection. Similarly, ctDNA-guided modifications of neoadjuvant therapy, adjuvant treatment, or postoperative surveillance have not yet demonstrated clinical benefit in HPB malignancies. Liquid biopsy should therefore currently be regarded as a promising investigational prognostic tool rather than an established determinant of surgical or oncological management. Standardized methodologies and prospective interventional trials are required before its routine clinical implementation.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203350.abstract: Neoadjuvant treatment has become an integral component of multidisciplinary management for resectable esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Over recent decades, treatment has evolved from surgery alone to postoperative chemotherapy, neoadjuvant chemotherapy, intensified systemic therapy, neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, and, more recently, the incorporation of immune checkpoint inhibitors into curative-intent treatment. This evolution has been driven by persistent challenges including systemic recurrence, locoregional failure, treatment-related toxicity, and heterogeneous treatment response. This review traces the evolution of neoadjuvant treatment for resectable ESCC through landmark clinical trials that have shaped current practice. We discuss the transition from postoperative to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, the development of intensified chemotherapy and neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, and the emergence of immunotherapy, distinguishing the established role of adjuvant nivolumab from the emerging role of neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy. We then examine the unresolved relative roles of these strategies and the challenges in treatment selection. Finally, we discuss future directions centered on accurate response assessment, circulating tumor DNA-based molecular residual disease assessment, and response-adapted treatment, with particular emphasis on organ-preserving strategies after a clinical complete response. Although active surveillance has emerged as a potential alternative to immediate surgery in carefully selected patients, accurate identification of residual disease and appropriate surveillance remain essential. Future advances may therefore shift the focus from treatment intensification alone toward response-adapted strategies that can maintain oncological safety while potentially enabling organ preservation.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203351.abstract: Platinum-based chemotherapy remains a standard-of-care treatment for non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet its efficacy is influenced by multiple factors, such as the functionality of DNA damage response pathways. DNA-damaging agents, like cisplatin, contribute to the generation of an "inflamed" tumor microenvironment (TME), which in turn correlates with an active antitumor immune response. MicroRNAs (miRNAs), a family of small, non-coding RNAs, have emerged as critical post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression, playing vital roles in modulating DNA Damage Repair (DDR) pathways and sensitivity to cisplatin. Their functional involvement in these mechanisms underscores their potential as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers in lung cancer. In this study, we investigated the diagnostic and prognostic value of a previously validated six-miRNA signature (hsa-miR-26a, hsa-miR-29c, hsa-miR-34a, hsa-miR-30-5p, hsa-miR-30e-3p and hsa-miR-497) in paired tumor and healthy tissue samples from surgically treated NSCLC patients (n = 76), who later received platinum-based therapy. To explore the translational applicability of this signature, we also compared miRNA expression levels between matched tumor tissue and plasma samples (n = 36). We further examined the presence of an "inflamed" TME and its association with the miRNA signature by examining the mRNA levels of TIGIT, CD8A, FOXP3, CXCL10 and PD-L1, and performing correlation analysis. All selected miRNAs were significantly downregulated in NSCLC tumor tissue compared to healthy samples. Moreover, miRNA expression was differentially regulated in plasma samples, supporting their potential clinical relevance as minimally invasive biomarkers. The complete six-miRNA signature demonstrated good discriminatory ability between tumor and matched non-malignant tissue (AUC = 0.786, 95% CI: 0.713-0.860; p < 0.001), with 72% sensitivity and 77.3% specificity. A significant correlation with relapse-free survival (RFS) (p = 0.039) was also observed. Distinct immune-related transcriptional alterations were observed in tumor tissue, including increased expression of immune checkpoint-associated genes (TIGIT and PD-L1) and reduced CD8A expression. Tumor PD-L1 expression showed modest positive correlations with miR-26a (p = 0.046) and miR-30e-3p (p = 0.031). Our findings underscore the potential value of this novel six-miRNA signature both as a prognostic and diagnostic biomarker in NSCLC. Its correlation with immune microenvironment characteristics supports its relevance in guiding personalized therapeutic strategies. This signature warrants further clinical validation and may serve as a valuable tool for patient stratification and outcome prediction for patients treated with platinum-based chemotherapy.
