doi:10.3390/cancers18203392.abstract: Background/Objectives: Distant metastasis to the infratemporal fossa (ITF) is rare and can mimic primary skull-base tumors. We systematically reviewed reported distant ITF metastases. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420261422546), PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through 12 June 2026, for reports of ITF metastasis from a distant primary tumor; direct extension from adjacent tumors was excluded. Data were summarized descriptively, and reports were appraised with the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Case Reports. Results: Seventeen reports (17 patients) were included (median age 59 years). The lung was the most frequent primary site (n = 4), followed by the kidney, colorectum, and thyroid (n = 3 each); adenocarcinoma was the most common histology (n = 7). Facial pain (n = 9) and numbness (n = 6) predominated. Bone destruction was reported in 12 patients, and the maxillary sinus (n = 7), orbit (n = 6), pterygopalatine fossa (n = 5), middle cranial fossa (n = 5), and cavernous sinus (n = 4) were involved. The median reported interval to ITF metastasis was 36 months; 11 metastases were metachronous, and 11 patients had other metastatic disease during the reported course. Five patients underwent regional resection or debulking; radiotherapy was reported in eight, radioiodine in three, and systemic drug treatment in nine. At last follow-up, 11 patients were alive, four had died, and status was unknown in two. Conclusions: Distant ITF metastases may present with facial pain and cranial neuropathies. Prognosis is insufficiently characterized, and management should be individualized within a multidisciplinary team. The evidence is limited to case reports with incomplete reporting. No external funding was received.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203393.abstract: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy worldwide and remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality among women. Despite advances in screening, molecular classification, and systemic therapies, treatment of advanced and metastatic disease remains challenging because of tumor heterogeneity, multidrug resistance, systemic toxicity, limited drug selectivity, and inadequate penetration into the tumor microenvironment. This review aims to critically evaluate advanced drug delivery systems (DDSs) for breast cancer therapy, emphasizing the relationship between carrier design, tumor biology, therapeutic performance, and clinical translation. The recent literature on DDSs for breast cancer treatment was comprehensively reviewed, covering liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles and micelles, dendrimers, nanogels, lipid- and inorganic-based nanoparticles, extracellular vesicles, biomimetic platforms, and stimuli-responsive systems. Particular attention was given to active and passive targeting, controlled drug release, strategies for overcoming multidrug resistance and biological barriers, and combination approaches integrating chemotherapy with immunotherapy, gene therapy, and phototherapy. Clinically approved and clinical-stage nanomedicines were also considered. Advanced DDSs can improve drug stability, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, tumor accumulation, cellular uptake, and controlled release, potentially enhancing therapeutic efficacy while reducing systemic toxicity. Targeted, biomimetic, and stimuli-responsive platforms provide additional opportunities to address tumor heterogeneity, the tumor microenvironment, and therapeutic resistance. Several DDS-based nanomedicines have reached clinical use or advanced clinical development, demonstrating their translational potential. However, manufacturing scalability, reproducibility, long-term safety, regulatory requirements, and patient heterogeneity remain important barriers. Advanced DDSs represent promising tools for improving the precision and efficacy of breast cancer treatment. Future progress will require biologically informed carrier design, reproducible manufacturing, rigorous clinical validation, and patient stratification. Integrating nanomedicine with precision oncology may accelerate the clinical translation of next-generation DDSs and support more effective personalized therapeutic strategies.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203394.abstract: Background: Conventional measures such as p-values and hazard ratios (HRs) do not directly quantify the sensitivity of time-to-event outcomes to small changes in individual outcomes. The Survival-Inferred Fragility Index (SIFI) evaluates the minimum number of survival-outcome changes required to reverse trial conclusions and provides complementary information on result robustness. Methods: This systematic review (PROSPERO: CRD420251182325) identified phase III colorectal cancer randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published from 2015 to 2025 via PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane. SIFI was calculated using Bomze’s framework with the “flip best” strategy. The fragility quotient (FQ) and the relationship between SIFI and withdrawals or losses to follow-up (WCLFU) were assessed. Analyses used R version 4.5.1. Results: SIFI was calculated for 50 phase III colorectal cancer RCTs, including 9 three-arm trials, resulting in 59 pairwise comparisons. Among positive results, median SIFI values for colorectal, colon, and rectal cancer were 6.0 (interquartile range [IQR]: 2.0 to 11.0), 19.0 (IQR: 15.5 to 22.5), and 4.0 (IQR: 4.0 to 4.0). Higher SIFI was observed in trials with HR < 0.75 than in those with HR 0.75–0.94 (median SIFI: 9.0 vs. 1.0; p = 0.035) and in trials with power > 85% than in those with power ≤ 85% (median SIFI: 8.5 vs. 2.0; p = 0.028). For negative results, median SIFI values were −4.5 (IQR: −7.2 to −3.0), −30.5 (IQR: −43.5 to −18.0), and −10.5 (IQR: −11.0 to −5.5). Greater absolute SIFI values were associated with adjuvant therapy, sample size ≥ 500, disease-free survival as the primary endpoint, and HR ≥ 0.95 (all p ≤ 0.005). Overall, 44.07% of pairwise comparisons had an absolute SIFI < 5. Conclusions: SIFI shows some phase III colorectal cancer RCT conclusions were sensitive to small outcome changes. It complements conventional statistics by illuminating result robustness.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203395.abstract: Background/Objectives: Episodic memory impairment is common in patients with intracranial tumors and has significant implications for clinical management. Memory is often treated as a unitary construct, and parameter-specific patterns and perioperative changes remain poorly understood. This study aimed to examine different memory parameters, their temporal dynamics, and clinical predictors of impairment. Methods: This observational study included 76 patients undergoing resection of supratentorial tumors, assessed preoperatively and at one week and three months postoperatively. Episodic memory was evaluated using a standardized word-list learning paradigm, yielding measures of immediate recall, delayed recall, and recognition. Performance was classified using age-adjusted z-scores, and relevant intraindividual changes were examined. Risk factors for impairment were analyzed using logistic regression. Results: Long-term memory measures were more frequently impaired than immediate recall across all time points. Impairment rates increased markedly one week after surgery to as high as 46.5% but returned to baseline levels at three months; however, individual trajectories were heterogeneous. Preoperative impairment was associated with lower functional status. Postoperative memory deficits were strongly associated with preoperative impairment, with older age being additionally associated with transient deficits. Conclusions: Memory impairment after brain tumor surgery is dynamic and parameter-specific, with long-term memory particularly vulnerable. Predictor findings are exploratory given limited event numbers and substantial cohort heterogeneity. Although deficits are often transient, high interindividual variability exists, underscoring the need for individualized risk stratification and neuropsychological care. Increased attention should be paid to the vulnerable acute postoperative period, as intact short-term memory may mask impairments.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203396.abstract: Background: Metabolic adaptation and stemness-associated programs contribute to bladder cancer growth. This study investigated the regulatory and functional relationships among specificity protein 4 (SP4), nuclear protein 1 (NUPR1), and selenoprotein M (SELM). Methods: TCGA-BLCA analyses were combined with silencing, overexpression, and rescue experiments in 5637 and T24 cells. Viability, migration, invasion, colony formation, glucose uptake, lactate production, extracellular acidification, oxygen consumption, and OCT4/SOX2 expression were assessed. Protein interactions and promoter-associated regulation were examined using co-immunoprecipitation, immunofluorescence, chromatin immunoprecipitation, and reporter assays. Xenograft experiments in female BALB/c nude mice evaluated NUPR1 depletion with or without SP4 overexpression. Results: Higher NUPR1 expression was associated with higher glycolysis- and stemness-associated transcriptional scores in TCGA-BLCA tumors. NUPR1 depletion reduced viability, glycolytic activity, glucose uptake, lactate production, and OCT4/SOX2 expression while increasing oxygen consumption. SP4 interacted with NUPR1 and showed enrichment at the NUPR1 promoter region. NUPR1 promoted SELM expression and reporter activity, with enrichment detected at the SELM promoter region. SP4 or SELM overexpression partially rescued the effects of NUPR1 depletion. SELM silencing attenuated NUPR1-associated increases in viability, migration, invasion, and colony formation. NUPR1 depletion suppressed xenograft growth, which was partially rescued by SP4 overexpression. Conclusions: These findings support functional relationships among SP4, NUPR1, and SELM that connect glycolytic activity with stemness-associated phenotypes in bladder cancer models. The results provide a basis for further investigation of this regulatory network in cancer metabolism.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203396.title: The SP4-NUPR1-SELM Axis Promotes Glycolytic Reprogramming and Stemness-Associated Phenotypes in Bladder Cancer.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203397.abstract: BCR::ABL1 negative myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) are driven predominantly by somatic mutations in JAK2, CALR, and MPL, which underpin diagnosis, prognostication, and measurable residual disease (MRD) monitoring. Advances in molecular assays have improved sensitivity for detecting canonical drivers and additional mutations across the MPN spectrum. In this review we evaluate current and emerging molecular methodologies for polycythemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythemia (ET), and primary myelofibrosis (PMF). We review the utility of PCR-based approaches, including allele-specific PCR, real-time quantitative PCR, and droplet digital PCR (ddPCR). Advances in ddPCR demonstrate precision and lower limits of detection for JAK2 V617F, CALR, and non-driver mutations, thus supporting the expanding role of ddPCR in MRD monitoring and relapse prediction. Recent advances in NGS techniques provide targeted profiling, enabling identification of possible co-occurring driver mutations and additional mutations associated with disease progression, treatment resistance, and leukemic transformation. Collectively, emerging workflows complement established gold-standard methodologies, while offering enhanced analytical performance and deeper pathological insight across the MPN spectrum. Optimal method selection requires balancing assay sensitivity, cost, and clinical utility. Advances in ddPCR and NGS methodologies have applicability for MRD monitoring in MPN and are powerful tools for detection of heterogenous and co-occurrent mutations across the MPN spectrum.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203397.title: Measurable Residual Disease (MRD) Monitoring in Myeloproliferative Neoplasms.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203398.abstract: Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) is characterized by the proliferation of blood cell clones that possess acquired genetic modifications. While therapy-related CH refers to CH detected in the setting of prior or current treatment in cancer populations, therapy-selected CH demands demonstration that treatment preferentially expanded or maintained an extant clone; therapy-induced CH requires evidence of de novo treatment-associated mutation supported by serial sampling and mutational-signature analyses. To map evidence distinguishing therapy-related, therapy-selected and therapy-induced CH across cancer treatment, including clonal dynamics, genomic features, clinical outcomes and surveillance gaps. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidance, PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane Library and Google Scholar were searched from inception through 1 June 2026, and updated on 15 September 2026. Primary evidence mapping was limited to original human studies. Reviews and conceptual sources were used only for context or reference tracking and were ineligible for the primary evidence map. Narrative synthesis was employed as critical variation existed in sequencing platforms, variant allele frequency thresholds, timepoints of sampling, filtering strategies, and outcome definitions. Of 684 records identified, 213 duplicates were removed and 471 records were screened. Across both pathways, 121 full texts were assessed, 87 excluded and 34 primary reports mapped; contextual citations were outside the included set. Contextual references were used for definitions and interpretation and were excluded from the included-report count. Six domains were deductively established and inductively refined during charting: terminology; therapy-associated mechanisms of clonal selection/expansion; genomic architecture; longitudinal clonal dynamics; clinical consequences; and study design and methodological heterogeneity. Treatment-associated selection or expansion of pre-existing TP53 and PPM1D clones was the most consistently reported mechanism of therapy-related CH, while CHEK2 was inconsistently detected. Pediatric cohorts and mutational-signature analyses also supported de novo mutagenesis with therapy in select contexts. Progression to therapy-related myeloid neoplasm was the most consistent outcome across studies; however, cytopenia, CAR-T-therapy-associated toxicity, cardiovascular events and mortality were inconsistently reported. Current evidence supports a spectrum of mechanisms ranging from selection of pre-existing clones to therapy-induced de novo mutation. Existing literature cannot support universal CH screening recommendations or guide treatment decisions. Prospective serial analyses harmonized on definition, employing sensitive baseline assays with paired germline controls and tumor-contamination checks, are needed to justify clinical implementation and assessment of fixed outcomes.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203398.title: Clonal Hematopoiesis Across the Cancer Treatment Continuum: A Scoping Review of Clonal Selection, Evolution, and Clinical Outcomes.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203399.abstract: Background/Objectives: Locoregionally recurrent or persistent head and neck cancer (rpHNC) after prior radiotherapy carries a poor prognosis, and optimal salvage strategies remain uncertain. We evaluated survival, patterns of failure, and 90-day postoperative complications after salvage surgery combined with intraoperative electron radiation therapy (IOERT). Methods: We retrospectively identified 127 previously irradiated patients treated with salvage surgery and IOERT between 1999 and 2023. Overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS) were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and locoregional failure (LRF) and distant failure were estimated using Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence with death as a competing event. Associations were evaluated one predictor at a time in age- and sex-adjusted Cox (OS, DFS) and Fine-Gray (LRF) models without multiplicity adjustment, and they are exploratory. Results: With a median follow-up of 70 months, median overall survival (OS) was 20.5 months (95% CI, 14.6-40.2), with 1-, 2-, and 3-year OS rates of 63%, 48%, and 43%, respectively. Median disease-free survival (DFS) was 8.8 months. Positive surgical margins and extranodal extension (ENE) were associated with worse OS in separate age- and sex-adjusted models. The 1-, 2-, and 3-year cumulative incidences of LRF were 34.3%, 44.7%, and 49.8%, respectively. The corresponding cumulative incidences of distant failure were 21.6%, 24.0%, and 26.7%, respectively. Thirty-seven patients had a documented distant failure, of whom 27 (73%) experienced distant failure within one year. Available records documented three deaths within 90 days (3/127, 2.4%). Conclusions: Among rpHNC patients treated with this IOERT-containing multimodality salvage strategy, median OS was 20.5 months. Because the study lacked a salvage-surgery-only comparator, postoperative treatments were selectively administered, and complication reporting was incomplete, neither the efficacy nor the comparative safety of IOERT can be determined from these data.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203399.title: Salvage Surgery with Intraoperative Electron Radiation Therapy for Recurrent or Persistent Head and Neck Cancer After Prior Radiotherapy.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203400.abstract: Peripheral T-cell lymphomas (PTCL) comprise a biologically diverse and clinically aggressive family of mature T/NK-cell neoplasms, for which outcomes remain poor in the majority of patients treated with conventional anthracycline-based frontline regimens. Contemporary classifications (WHO-HAEM5 and ICC) increasingly incorporate immunophenotypic and molecular information, underscoring that "PTCL-NOS" is not a single disease but rather a diagnostic umbrella that includes biologically distinct entities and molecular subgroups. Among these are the TBX21- and GATA3-driven PTCL-NOS subsets, the latter associated with inferior survival and a distinctive cytokine/microenvironmental program. These advances, many of which were shaped by long-standing contributions from the Bologna group, support a rational shift from empiric chemotherapy toward mechanism-based and immune-based interventions. CAR-engineered cellular therapies have revolutionized the care of B-cell malignancies, yet translation to PTCL has been delayed by lineage-specific barriers: (i) fratricide during manufacturing when targeting shared T-cell antigens (e.g., CD5, CD7), (ii) the risk of profound and prolonged T-cell aplasia (a markedly less "replaceable" toxicity than B-cell aplasia), and (iii) product contamination by malignant T-cells in autologous platforms. Recent progress in genome editing (CRISPR/Cas9 and base editing), intracellular antigen "blocking" strategies, and alternative effectors (allogeneic "universal" CAR-T, CAR-NK, and iPSC-derived platforms) has begun to address these obstacles at the manufacturing level, while their downstream clinical consequences (e.g., prolonged cytopenias, infectious risk and delayed immune reconstitution) remain incompletely resolved. Early-phase clinical trials now demonstrate clinically meaningful responses for select targets, particularly CD7, CD5, TRBC1 and CD30, for the pan-T targets. However, the strongest efficacy data remain largely derived from T-cell lymphoblastic malignancies (T-ALL/T-LBL), whereas evidence in mature PTCL remains limited and at an earlier stage, with target-specific differences in safety, immune reconstitution and relapse patterns. This review synthesizes the biological rationale for antigen selection in PTCL, the emerging clinical evidence for leading CAR targets, and the engineering strategies most likely to improve the therapeutic index. It also proposes an integrated hematology perspective on how CAR-based therapies might be positioned relative to transplant and evolving targeted agents in relapsed/refractory PTCL.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203401.abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCCs) are challenging pathologies to treat with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), as only a minority of patients achieve durable clinical benefit. The highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), the frequent loss of antigen presentation, the marked spatial heterogeneity, and the anatomical proximity of tumors to critical structures limit the efficacy and safety of current immunotherapeutic approaches. Immune cell engagers (ICEs) have emerged as promising strategies to redirect endogenous immune cells toward tumor targets. While conventional surface-antigen-directed engagers can bypass major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-restricted antigen presentation, peptide-HLA-directed constructs remain dependent on antigen processing, peptide presentation, and the appropriate HLA allele. More recently, tumor-restricted activation technologies, collectively referred to as "masking immunotherapy", have been developed to preferentially restore target and/or immune-cell engagement under TME-associated conditions, such as increased protease activity. These approaches have demonstrated enhanced tumor-preferential activity and/or improved tolerability in preclinical models; however, the extent to which these properties translate into clinically meaningful tumor selectivity and an improved therapeutic index remains under investigation. In this review, based on the authors' comprehensive literature knowledge and targeted searches, we critically examine the biological rationale, the engineering principles, the current preclinical evidence, and the early clinical development of ICEs with particular emphasis on their potential application in HNSCC. While early clinical studies have demonstrated acceptable safety profiles, clinical activity has generally been poor. We discuss the major barriers that limit clinical translation and we highlight emerging strategies aimed at overcoming these limitations. We believe that successful clinical development of ICEs in HNSCC will likely depend not only on the identification of optimal target antigens, but also on spatially controlled immune activation, integration with TME-modulating approaches, and incorporation of dynamic biomarkers into future clinical trial design.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203403.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is characterised by the absence of expression of oestrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2). Compared with other breast cancer subtypes, TNBC is generally associated with a more aggressive clinical course, in part because of its marked molecular heterogeneity. Consequently, the availability of effective targeted therapies remains limited. Chemotherapy continues to be a major component of treatment, although its clinical benefit may be constrained by toxicity and the development of drug resistance. This review examines the principal clinical challenges in TNBC, evaluates currently available therapeutic approaches and their limitations, and discusses important areas that remain insufficiently addressed. Particular emphasis is placed on recent advances in emerging treatment strategies. Together, these developments may improve our understanding of TNBC and support future research towards more precise and personalised therapeutic approaches.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203404.abstract: Background: Identification of high-risk patients with endometrial cancer (EC) remains challenging despite advances in molecular profiling. Methods: We comprehensively analyzed the RNA expression of 18 amino acid transporters (AATs) in 373 EC samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). Results: Our clustering analysis based on AAT expression identified a patient group with a significantly worse prognosis. Sideroflexin family (SFXN1, SFXN5), glutamine (SLC38A1, SLC38A3), glycine (SLC6A9) transporters, and the heavy-chain subunit of heteromeric AATs (SLC3A2) were elevated in poorly differentiated tumors. In contrast, the transporter of small neutral amino acids (SLC1A4) and proline/imino-acid transporter (SLC6A20) were enriched in lower-grade disease. SFXN1 and SLC38A1 were also higher in advanced (III/IV) FIGO stages. AAT expression differed across molecular subtypes, with SFXN5, SLC38A1, SLC38A3, and SLC3A2 associated with the copy-number-high profile. In survival analysis, we demonstrated that SLC38A3, SFXN4, and SLC3A2 were associated with shorter disease-free survival, and SLC38A1, SLC38A3, and SFXN1 with worse overall survival, whereas SLC1A4, SLC6A20, and the taurine transporter (SLC6A6) were related to favorable outcomes. Conclusions: These findings highlight AAT expression as a potential marker of EC aggressiveness and prognosis and suggest that integrating metabolic features with molecular classification may improve risk stratification and identify potential therapeutic targets.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203404.title: Prognostic Significance of Amino Acid Transporters in Endometrial Cancer.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203405.abstract: Optic nerve sheath meningioma (ONSM) is a rare orbital tumor that can pose a significant threat to visual function due to its close relationship with the optic nerve and surrounding vascular structures. Early and accurate diagnosis is essential to preserve vision and guide individualized management. The objective of this narrative review is to provide a comprehensive overview of the current evidence on the clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, imaging characteristics, and management of ONSM, with a particular focus on recent advances in imaging techniques and their implications for clinical decision-making. This review synthesizes current knowledge on clinical presentation, diagnostic workup, and evolving treatment strategies for ONSM, with particular emphasis on advanced imaging modalities. Magnetic resonance imaging remains the cornerstone of diagnosis, yet functional imaging, especially somatostatin receptor--based techniques such as 68GaDOTATATE PET/CT have shown potential as a useful adjunct in the diagnostic evaluation of ONSM, especially for assessing tumor characteristics, extent, and treatment planning in selected cases. We discuss the emerging role of DOTATATE imaging in differentiating ONSM from other optic nerve and orbital pathologies, as well as its potential application in monitoring therapeutic response. We also highlight contemporary management approaches, including fractionated radiotherapy and the selective role of surgical intervention, underscoring the importance of multidisciplinary decision-making in optimizing visual outcomes. Emerging molecular insights from meningioma research may inform future therapeutic strategies for ONSM; however, clinical evidence specific to ONSM remains limited.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203406.abstract: Although immune activation can occur in both papillary thyroid carcinoma (TC) and nodular goitre (NG), the transcriptional programmes distinguishing malignant from non-malignant immune-rich thyroid tissue remain poorly understood. In this pilot study, bulk RNA sequencing of 19 specimens (10 TC, 9 NG) allowed classification into four tumour microenvironment (TME) subgroups. Immune deconvolution showed that TC Immune-Enriched tumours were characterised by cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) enrichment rather than predominant lymphocytic infiltration. Differential expression analysis identified only nine genes distinguishing TC Immune-Enriched from NG Immune-High tissue, suggesting transcriptomic similarity between malignant and benign immune-activated states in this small cohort. To identify tumour-associated stromal programmes, we identified genes shared between immune-enriched versus immune-depleted comparisons in papillary TC and nodular goitre. This yielded a 441-gene candidate tumour-associated stromal programme enriched for collagen-containing extracellular matrix organisation and TGFβ-associated ECM-remodelling pathways, supported by WGCNA and protein-protein interaction analyses. In 456 TCGA-THCA carcinomas, stromal enrichment correlated inversely with thyroid differentiation and was highest in BRAF-like tumours and the tall-cell histological variant. These findings suggest that transcriptomic convergence largely reflects shared inflammatory programmes, whereas stromal remodelling identifies a candidate tumour-associated stromal programme.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203407.abstract: Inflammation is suggested to play a central role in cancer-related appetite loss, yet the available evidence remains limited. This study analyzed data from a prospective, longitudinal, multicenter study of patients with metastatic cancer followed for one year. The longitudinal associations between appetite loss and both clinical characteristics and inflammatory markers were examined. Logistic generalized equation model (GEE) was used. Among 526 patients, 299 (57%) experienced appetite loss at baseline. During longitudinal observation appetite loss was associated with older age (OR 1.19, CI 1.01-1.39 as per 10-year years increase), poorer performance status (OR 0.85, CI 0.77-0.94), recent weight loss (OR 2.74, CI 2.11-3.56), and symptoms including constipation, nausea, fatigue, and lower emotional functioning. Corticosteroid use was associated with lower risk of appetite loss (OR 0.69, CI 0.53-0.90). Several inflammatory markers were also associated with appetite loss, including IL-8, IP-10, IL-6, CRP, eotaxin, albumin. Appetite loss in metastatic cancer is linked to clinical factors, symptom burden, and inflammatory markers. Optimizing symptom management and targeting inflammation might have a positive impact.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203408.abstract: Background/Objectives: Burkitt lymphoma (BL) is an aggressive germinal center B-cell (gcBC) malignancy driven by MYC deregulation and cooperating molecular alterations. A mouse model combining constitutive MYC and PI3K activity in gcBC closely recapitulates key features of human BL, but its epigenetic similarity to the human disease has not been investigated in detail. Here, we compared genome-wide DNA methylation patterns between human sporadic EBV-negative BL and this murine model. Methods: DNA methylation profiles of 37 human BL samples and 20 gcBC controls were compared with those of 8 murine tumors from the MYC/PI3K driven mouse model and 11 murine gcBC controls using Illumina methylation arrays. Differentially methylated CpGs were identified using linear modeling, and chromatin-state enrichment, cross-species gene overlap, protein interaction, and pathway enrichment analyses were performed. Results: BL showed global DNA hypomethylation in both species and distinct methylation profiles from gcBCs. CpGs hypomethylated in BL were enriched at enhancers, whereas hypermethylated CpGs were strongly enriched at poised promoters. We identified 695 genes with shared hypermethylation and 512 with shared hypomethylation between human and murine BL. Restricting the analysis to regulatory regions identified 86 genes consistently hypomethylated in both species. These genes were significantly enriched for regulation of intracellular signal transduction and sphingolipid signaling. Included are regulators of GTPase and kinase signaling, such as GNA13, RASA3, RASAL1, SPRED2, PIK3R2, PRKCA, PRKCE, and FYN. The conserved set also contained genes with established roles in germinal center B-cell biology, including FOXO1, BACH2, and NR3C1. Conclusions: Human and murine BL share conserved regulatory DNA methylation features, supporting the MYC/PI3K mouse model as a system to study epigenetic mechanisms of BL.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203408.title: Conserved Regulatory DNA Methylation in Human and MYC/PI3K-Driven Murine EBV-Negative Burkitt Lymphoma.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203409.abstract: Background: In postmastectomy radiotherapy, radiation reaches an already-reconstructed breast, and implant-based reconstruction remains feasible in selected patients. Far less studied is reconstruction within a previously irradiated field: after breast-conserving therapy, ipsilateral breast tumor recurrence (IBTR), and salvage mastectomy. We compared implant-based and autologous reconstruction in this setting and propose a hypothesis-generating treatment algorithm. Methods: From 2219 consecutive breast reconstructions (2012-2026), we cross-matched implant-removal, radiotherapy, and local-recurrence registries to identify all immediate total reconstructions of a previously irradiated breast after salvage mastectomy for IBTR (n = 13; 8 implant-based [all stand-alone, without vascularized flap coverage], 5 autologous [all latissimus dorsi-based]). The primary endpoint was reconstruction failure, defined in a modality-neutral manner as definitive loss or abandonment of the reconstruction; implant-based reconstructions of breasts not previously irradiated at the time of reconstruction (n = 689) served as a descriptive institutional reference cohort. Results: Seven of eight implants (87.5%) were removed at 3 to 51 months; the single retained implant has a persistent wound; none achieved complication-free success. Failure modes comprised early envelope necrosis, periprosthetic infection, and late attritional failure; chronic retained-capsule seroma followed removal without capsulectomy. All five autologous reconstructions healed without failure or unplanned reoperation (reconstruction failure, 7/8 [87.5%; 95% CI, 47.3-99.7%] vs. 0/5 [0%; 95% CI, 0-52.2%], p = 0.005; log-rank p = 0.039; median follow-up, 32.0 vs. 10.9 months; failure or major complication, 8/8 vs. 0/5, p = 0.0008). The implant-removal rate also exceeded that of the institutional reference cohort (87.5% vs. 11.2%; unadjusted, descriptive comparison). Conclusions: In this small consecutive series, stand-alone implant-based reconstruction of the previously irradiated breast was associated with a very high failure rate, whereas reconstruction importing well-vascularized autologous tissue healed in every case, a pattern biologically consistent with chronic radiation injury. These findings constitute a strong cautionary signal rather than definitive evidence. Our findings support an autologous-first approach after salvage mastectomy of the irradiated breast; stand-alone implant-based reconstruction should be offered only to carefully selected, fully counseled patients, and the proposed algorithm requires external validation.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203409.title: Implant-Based Versus Autologous Reconstruction After Salvage Mastectomy for Ipsilateral Breast Tumor Recurrence in the Previously Irradiated Breast: A Consecutive Institutional Series and a Proposed Autologous-First Algorithm.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203410.abstract: Background/Objectives: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) comprises distinct cellular states characterized by different differentiation programs and therapeutic responses. How a cell-surface receptor adapts its function across these states remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether the spatial organization and functional output of CD44 vary across PDAC cellular states. Methods: CD44 expression and spatial distribution were examined in human PDAC tissues and PDAC cell models representing different differentiation states. The functional roles of CD44 were investigated using genetic depletion, transcriptomic analysis, migration and invasion assays, and xenograft and orthotopic models. Hyaluronan (HA) responsiveness and downstream signaling were assessed following exogenous HA stimulation, and the therapeutic effects of HA synthesis inhibition with 4-methylumbelliferone (4-MU) were evaluated alone or in combination with gemcitabine. Results: In differentiated PDAC tissues and classical PDAC models, CD44 was predominantly localized to the basolateral membrane and spatially segregated from E-cadherin at cell-cell junctions, consistent with a role in epithelial organization and cell-matrix interactions. In contrast, poorly differentiated PDAC tissues and basal-like models exhibited increased CD44 abundance, E-cadherin loss, and redistribution of CD44 along the cell periphery. Genetic depletion of CD44 preferentially impaired malignant phenotypes in basal-like models. Mechanistically, basal-like cells exhibited enhanced CD44-dependent responsiveness to extracellular HA, accompanied by activation of EMT-associated signaling and destabilization of E-cadherin. Inhibition of HA synthesis with 4-MU preferentially suppressed basal-like PDAC models and enhanced gemcitabine sensitivity, with these effects further supported in orthotopic models. Conclusions: These findings suggest that the functional output of CD44 in PDAC is influenced not only by its expression level but also by cellular context and spatial organization. The context-dependent responsiveness of the HA-CD44 axis may contribute to functional heterogeneity among PDAC states and represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability of basal-like PDAC.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203410.title: Context-Dependent Spatial and Functional Roles of CD44 Across Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma States.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203411.abstract: Background/Hypothesis: Therapeutic resistance and recurrence remain major barriers to durable cancer control because conventional therapies may eliminate proliferating tumor cells while allowing dormant, stem-like, senescence-like, or polyploid populations to persist. This review examines polyploid giant cancer cells (PGCCs) as therapy-tolerant states and evaluates whether their adaptive survival mechanisms create vulnerabilities that could be targeted through ferroptosis-oriented nanomedicine. Methods: We investigated recent evidence (PubMed) linking PGCC persistence with redox buffering, glutathione/GPX4 activity, iron regulation, lipid remodeling, autophagy, mitochondrial adaptation, and metabolic plasticity, in addition to nanomedicine potential to target these pathways. Results and Findings: Emerging studies provide direct proof-of-concept that PGCCs can exhibit ferroptosis susceptibility, while nanomedicine offers potential strategies to improve therapeutic localization and coordinate iron delivery, reactive oxygen species amplification, glutathione depletion, GPX4 inhibition, and combination therapy. However, PGCC-selective nanoparticle efficacy remains largely untested, and important barriers include heterogeneous tumor penetration, off-target toxicity, model limitations, and biomarker uncertainty. Conclusions and Perspective: The specific contribution of this review is to integrate PGCC biology, therapy-tolerant cancer states, ferroptosis, and nanomedicine into a unified framework for targeting residual disease. This perspective is timely as direct evidence of PGCC ferroptosis sensitivity and new characterization of treatment-resistant PGCC states are emerging. By identifying the mechanistic overlap among these fields, this review highlights testable opportunities for eliminating persistent cancer cells that may otherwise contribute to recurrence.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203411.title: Targeting Polyploid Giant Cancer Cells (PGCCs) to Prevent Cancer Recurrence: Opportunities for Nanomedicine.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203412.abstract: Background/Objectives: Cutaneous melanoma spreads preferentially through the lymphatic system, and sentinel lymph node status is among the strongest prognostic factors. Whether tumour angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis add prognostic information beyond conventional histopathology has been examined in many immunohistochemical studies, with heterogeneous results. We conducted a systematic review, reported according to PRISMA 2020 and not registered, of blood microvascular density (MVD), lymphatic vessel density (LVD) in the intratumoral and peritumoral compartments, proliferating (Ki-67-positive) lymphatic vessels and lymphatic invasion (LI) as prognostic markers in primary cutaneous melanoma. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE was searched to 10 September 2026, supplemented by a Web of Science export and by citation tracking of the reference meta-analysis by Pastushenko et al. (2014). Twenty-one cutaneous study units (25 reports) and four ocular studies providing indirect evidence were included, and risk of bias was rated with the QUIPS tool. Results: In the reference meta-analysis, peritumoral LVD and LI, but not MVD or intratumoral LVD, were associated with metastasis. The newer cohorts confirmed this pattern and provided adjusted effect sizes: peritumoral LVD predicted disease-free (HR 2.14) and melanoma-specific survival (HR of 2.74; 95% CI 1.31 to 5.73), immunohistochemically detected LI predicted sentinel node metastasis (33% vs. 11% positive nodes) and overall survival, and a Ki-67-positive lymphatic endothelium predicted melanoma-specific mortality (adjusted HR of 2.03; 95% CI 1.33 to 3.10) in 264 patients. Blood MVD and blood endothelial proliferation were not prognostic. Heterogeneity of markers, counting methods and effect measures precluded re-pooling. Conclusions: Peritumoral LVD, LI and proliferating lymphatics are promising adjunct biomarkers for selecting patients for sentinel node biopsy, adjuvant therapy and closer follow-up, pending standardised, digital-pathology-based quantification.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203412.title: Lymphatic Microvascular Density, Lymphatic Invasion and Endothelial Cell Proliferation as Prognostic Biomarkers in Cutaneous Melanoma: A Systematic Review and Evidence Map.

doi:10.3390/cancers18213427.abstract: Background: Pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (PNENs) represent a rare, heterogeneous group of tumors with highly variable clinical outcomes. While standard clinicopathological parameters like World Health Organization (WHO) grading and TNM staging provide critical prognostic data, they do not fully explain the survival disparities observed in patients with similar tumor characteristics. This narrative review evaluates the clinical and prognostic significance of the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR)—a widely accessible marker of systemic inflammation—in patients with PNENs. Methods: A comprehensive literature review was conducted to synthesize current evidence regarding the prognostic utility of peripheral NLR levels. Results: Studies conducted specifically in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs) suggest that elevated peripheral blood NLR is associated with adverse clinicopathological features and, in several cohorts, with shorter overall survival (OS) and recurrence-free survival (RFS). However, the strength and independence of these associations vary across studies. Evidence from mixed gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasm (GEP-NEN) cohorts undergoing systemic treatment or peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) provides complementary insights into the predictive capacity of NLR regarding treatment response, though it remains indirect evidence for PNETs, particularly when pancreatic-specific subgroup results are unavailable. Differences in tumor differentiation, grade, stage, treatment setting, and NLR cut-off values limit direct comparisons across studies. Conclusions: NLR is an accessible, candidate adjunctive prognostic biomarker in PNETs, particularly in surgically treated populations. However, the evidence remains highly heterogeneous, and its clinical utility and standardized thresholds remain unvalidated. Proposed applications in treatment selection or surveillance intensity should be strictly regarded as investigational and hypothesis-generating, rather than validated clinical strategies. NLR should complement, rather than replace, established clinicopathological prognostic factors

doi:10.3390/cancers18213427.title: Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte Ratio as a Prognostic Biomarker in Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Neoplasms

doi:10.3390/cancers18213448.abstract: Background/Objectives: Previous studies of ABO blood group and breast cancer prognosis have yielded inconsistent results, mainly evaluating blood group itself as a prognostic factor. We investigated whether the prognostic associations of clinicopathological factors differ according to ABO blood group in stage II–III breast cancer. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 1540 patients with stage II–III breast cancer who underwent curative resection between 2010 and 2019. Blood group-specific prognostic analyses of breast cancer-specific survival (BCSS) were performed, with continuous variables analyzed without dichotomization. Based on the observed patterns, an exploratory interaction between blood group B and pathological nodal status was tested, and its robustness was assessed using a permutation test and sensitivity analyses. Results: ABO blood group was not associated with BCSS overall (p = 0.641). In blood group-stratified multivariable analyses, ≥4 lymph node metastases was an independent adverse prognostic factor in blood groups A, O, and AB, but not in blood group B. A significant interaction was observed between blood group B and pathological nodal status (0–3 vs. ≥4 nodes) (p for interaction < 0.001; permutation-adjusted p = 0.004). Among patients with 0–3 lymph node metastases, blood group B was independently associated with worse BCSS (hazard ratio, 2.04; 95% confidence interval, 1.25–3.32; p = 0.004), consistently across sensitivity analyses; this association was more evident among patients who received neoadjuvant chemotherapy. In this subgroup, blood group B was also associated with more distant and visceral recurrence (all p < 0.05). Conclusions: The prognostic association of nodal burden in stage II–III breast cancer may differ according to ABO blood group. The exploratory findings in patients with limited nodal involvement suggest that blood group B may identify a subgroup characterized by worse BCSS and increased distant and visceral recurrence. Given the small number of events in blood group B with ≥4 nodes and possible differences according to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, these findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant independent validation.

doi:10.34133/cancomm.0051.abstract: Squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) develop from the stratified epithelia of the esophagus, head and neck, lung, and skin, providing a tractable model to investigate how altered epithelial fields progress toward invasive cancer. Across SCC subtypes, evolution often begins before overt malignancy, with age- and exposure-associated mutant clones expanding within histologically normal epithelia. As lesions advance, early driver selection becomes coupled to copy number alterations, chromosomal instability, and epigenetic remodeling, whereas later stages are shaped by branching diversification, cellular plasticity, and regionally constrained selection. Despite tissue-specific differences, several recurrent principles emerge, including clonal expansion within mutated normal fields, transition bottlenecks marked by genome-scale instability, and the spatial organization of subclonal architecture and invasive-front states. In this review, we synthesize recent progress in the temporal ordering and spatial patterning of SCC evolution and discuss how genetic alterations, epigenetic remodeling, and tissue ecology jointly drive disease progression. We further highlight the implications for early interception, biomarker development, immune evasion, and evolution-informed prevention and therapy.

doi:10.34133/cancomm.0052.abstract: Over the past 5 decades, small cell lung cancer (SCLC) has persisted as one of the most formidable malignancies, largely attributed to its aggressive early metastasis, limited therapeutic arsenal in both first-line and subsequent treatments, and rapid onset of treatment resistance. The dawn of a new era in the treatment of SCLC appeared in 2018, with the introduction of first-line chemotherapy combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors, as well as tarlatamab for later-line treatment. However, the improvements in survival, although tangible, were still unsatisfactory. Therefore, this review focuses on unraveling the mechanisms underlying cancer initiation, progression, and particularly metastasis, as well as emerging advances in molecular subtyping and drug resistance from the epigenetic perspective. Simultaneously, we outline their hallmark characteristics—high plasticity, heterogeneity, redundancy, and ambiguity driven by intercellular crosstalk under spatiotemporal dependency. Furthermore, we highlight the evolving progress of various successful drugs or therapeutic strategies and molecular biomarkers in clinical practice for SCLC, as well as promising agents under investigation. Finally, we also discuss how to leverage artificial intelligence and innovative biomedical technologies, as well as learn from various challenges in order to improve the therapeutic landscape of SCLC.

doi:10.34133/cancomm.0056.abstract: Background: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC) is the second most common primary liver cancer. Macrophages are crucial components of the tumor microenvironment (TME). Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2-positive (TREM2 + ) macrophages have recently emerged as potent pro-tumor progress players in several cancers. However, the heterogeneity and tumor-promoting mechanisms of macrophages especially TREM2 + macrophages in ICC remain systematically unexplored. Therefore, this study aimed to systematically elucidate the heterogeneity of macrophages in ICC, with a specific focus on the pro-tumor role of TREM2 + macrophages. Methods: We collected tumor tissues, adjacent nontumor tissues, and tumor-adjacent border tissues from 16 ICC patients. These samples were subjected to single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic sequencing, followed by comprehensive analysis. The findings were further validated through flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, multiplex immunofluorescence, and in vitro cellular assays. Furthermore, we established an ICC model using genetically engineered ( Trem2 −/− ) mice as a validation cohort to corroborate the discoveries from human samples. Results: Macrophages are important prognostic factors in ICC, with functional heterogeneity. TREM2 + macrophages in tumor tissues promote immune suppression by exhausting CD8 + T cells and inducing the generation of regulatory T cells to produce. At the tumor border region, TREM2 + macrophages enhance ICC invasion via the urokinase-type plasminogen activator–urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor axis and induce hepatic stellate cell conversion to myofibroblastic cancer-associated fibroblast, forming a physical immune barrier that impedes CD8 + T cell infiltration in tumor tissues. TIMD4 + macrophages in adjacent tissues also suppress CD8 + T cell function. Combining anti-Trem2 and anti-Timd4 with anti-Pd-1 antibodies significantly improved treatment outcomes in the ICC mice. Conclusions: TREM2 + and TIMD4 + macrophages are key regulators of the immunosuppressive TME in ICC. Targeting Trem2 and Timd4 enhances the effectiveness of anti-Pd-1 therapy in ICC mouse models.

doi:10.34133/cancomm.0060.abstract: Background: Bacteria-mediated cancer therapy is emerging as a promising approach due to its low cost, scalability, and sustained efficacy. While bacterial immunomodulation has been extensively studied, the role of bacterial metabolic competition, particularly for glucose, in tumor suppression remains unclear. We aimed to investigate how engineered Salmonella strains exploit metabolic competition to trigger antitumor immunity and improve therapeutic outcomes in bladder cancer models. Methods: Using genetic screening, we generated a gluconeogenesis-deficient Salmonella strain, the AISIH strain with the glpX gene knocked out (GLA1), with enhanced glucose uptake. In vitro and in vivo assays were performed to assess tumor cell glucose deprivation, mitochondrial stress, cytosolic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release, and activation of the cGAS/STING pathway. An engineered strain, GLA2, was generated from the AISIH strain by knockout of the glpX gene and was subsequently further engineered to locally deliver an anti-tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) nanobody under quorum-sensing control. Efficacy was evaluated in subcutaneous and orthotopic bladder cancer models, with analysis of tumor-infiltrating immune cells, dendritic cell (DC) maturation, and T cell priming. Results: GLA1 competitively depleted glucose in the bladder tumor microenvironment, inducing energy stress, mitochondrial damage, and mtDNA release, which noncanonically activated the STING pathway. This promoted type I interferon production, DC maturation, and antitumor immune responses. However, TNF-α-mediated vascular abnormalities limited efficacy. GLA2 normalized tumor vasculature via local anti-TNF-α delivery, enhancing nutrient competition and immune activation. Both strains markedly suppressed tumor growth, with GLA2 showing superior efficacy due to synergistic metabolic and immune reprogramming. Conclusions: This study demonstrates that bacterial competition for glucose is a pivotal mechanism of antitumor activity in bladder cancer, linking metabolic stress to STING-dependent immune activation. Engineered Salmonella strains that combine enhanced glucose uptake with local vascular normalization offer a robust platform for bladder cancer. These findings highlight a novel strategy to integrate microbial metabolic engineering with immune modulation, providing a foundation for precision bacteriotherapy in oncology.

doi:10.6004/jnccn.2026.7004.abstract: Immunotherapies have recently changed the treatment landscape of multiple myeloma (MM). CAR T cells and T-cell–redirecting bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) yield impressive responses and extend survival in patients with relapsed/refractory MM. There are now 2 BCMA-directed CAR T-cell products and 4 BsAbs (3 targeting BCMA, 1 targeting GPRC5D) currently approved by the FDA for relapsed/refractory MM, in which they demonstrated considerable efficacy. These drugs are now being evaluated in early treatment settings, including as part of frontline regimens for newly diagnosed MM. Importantly, administration of CAR T-cell therapy and BsAbs necessitate careful attention to unique toxicities, including cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome, cytopenias, and heightened infection risk. This review summarizes the current landscape of immunotherapy in MM, including perspectives on sequencing CAR T-cell therapy and BsAbs. It also discusses ongoing clinical trials evaluating immunotherapy in new combinations and treatment contexts. Immunotherapies have become a key component of the MM therapeutic armamentarium and are poised to assume an even larger role in the coming years.

doi:10.6004/jnccn.2026.7035.abstract: Background: Fatigue is a prevalent and debilitating symptom among patients with cancer. Physical activity (PA) may help reduce fatigue and improve quality of life (QoL). This study evaluated longitudinal associations between PA, fatigue, and QoL across the cancer care continuum. Methods: Data were analyzed from 1,718 participants in a prospective multicenter cohort. Self-reported PA was assessed at baseline and up to 24 months post-diagnosis using a questionnaire based on the International PA Questionnaire (IPAQ). Metabolic equivalent task (MET)–minutes per week were calculated for walking, moderate, vigorous, and total physical activity. Fatigue and QoL were measured using the EORTC Quality of Life Questionnaire-Core 30 (QLQ-C30). Mixed-effects models evaluated associations between PA and outcomes. Lagged fluctuation models examined temporal relationships, separating between-person and within-person effects. Results: PA levels increased steadily from diagnosis through 24 months, coinciding with reduced fatigue and improved QoL. Higher PA was consistently linked to better fatigue and QoL outcomes. Walking was associated with lower odds of severe fatigue at 6 months (odds ratio [OR], 0.78; 95% CI, 0.62–0.98; P =.031) and 12 months (OR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.59–0.94; P =.014), with higher odds of better QoL at all follow-up points. Vigorous activity showed the strongest protective effect against fatigue at 24 months (OR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.45–0.94; P =.023). In patients with nonmetastatic disease, protective associations were observed across all activity types and time points. Lagged models indicated that higher average vigorous activity predicted lower future fatigue ( P <.001). Conclusions: Greater PA, particularly walking, was associated with lower fatigue and improved QoL, especially in patients with early-stage disease. The posttreatment period (approximately 1 year post-diagnosis) may represent an important window for behavioral intervention. Findings support stage- and recovery phase–specific guidance and highlight walking as a scalable, low-risk target for survivorship care.

doi:10.6004/jnccn.2026.7048.abstract: Background: Treatment for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) lasts >2 years and can impact families. The Children’s Oncology Group multicenter therapeutic trial AALL0932 randomized patients with NCI standard-risk, average-risk B-ALL (NCI-SR AR B-ALL) to receive maintenance vincristine/dexamethasone every 4 or 12 weeks (VCR/DEX4 or VCR/DEX12, respectively). Embedded in AALL0932, this study aimed to (1) longitudinally measure adverse family outcomes overall, and (2) determine whether patients on the VCR/DEX4 regimen (vs VCR/DEX12) had fewer adverse family outcomes. Methods: Patients with NCI-SR AR B-ALL who were offered enrollment on the multicenter randomized-controlled therapeutic trial AALL0932 were aged ≥4 years with an English-speaking parent. Parent-reported surveys were administered at T1–T5 (approximately 2, 9, 18, 26, and 38 months after diagnosis, respectively; T5 was assessed only in boys) and assessed household changes since leukemia diagnosis, leukemia-related household expenses in the past 4 weeks, unhealthy family functioning (Family Assessment Device score >2), and parents’ perceived child vulnerability (Child Vulnerability Scale ≥10). Postrandomization outcomes at T3 and T4 were compared between treatment groups using generalized linear mixed models and multivariable logistic regression models, as appropriate, adjusting for race and ethnicity. Results: Among 555 participants with completed evaluations, 420 were randomized (mean [SD] age, 6.0 [1.6] years; 45.7% female). At T1, 56.2% of randomized participants reported household changes since diagnosis (81.2% by T4), 88.6% reported ≥$100 in leukemia-related household expenses in the past 4 weeks (61.5% at T4), 19.0% had unhealthy family functioning (23.9% at T4), and 55.8% perceived their child as vulnerable (62.5% at T4). In multivariable models, VCR/DEX4 (vs VCR/DEX12) had an increased likelihood of reporting ≥$100 in leukemia-related expenses in the past 4 weeks (odds ratio, 1.73; 95% CI, 1.03–2.91), but other outcomes were similar between treatment arms. Conclusions: B-ALL family burdens develop early. Reducing maintenance VCR/DEX frequency may decrease expenses but not other outcomes. Interventions are needed to support families early and throughout ALL therapy.

doi:10.6004/jnccn.2026.7051.abstract: Background: Prehabilitation is recommended to reduce surgery-related functional decline but is not routinely integrated into presurgical breast cancer care, often resulting in rehabilitation being delayed until after surgery. We conducted a retrospective comparative effectiveness study evaluating outcomes associated with real-world prehabilitation versus delayed rehabilitation care models. Methods: Women who began rehabilitation before (prehabilitation; n=416) or after breast cancer surgery (delayed rehabilitation; n=232) were identified from the electronic medical record. Upper extremity function and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) outcomes were extracted presurgery, postsurgery, and at final evaluation. Adjusted linear mixed-effect models examined change over time and between-group differences, and logistic regression estimated likelihood of achieving normal limits. Analyses were conducted overall and stratified by surgery type. Rehabilitation utilization and recovery to baseline levels among patients who received prehabilitation were summarized descriptively. Results: Prehabilitation was associated with superior postsurgery function and HRQoL, as well as higher odds of achieving normal limits, compared with delayed rehabilitation. Both groups improved during postoperative rehabilitation; however, functional outcomes and strength remained superior among patients who received prehabilitation at final evaluation. Benefits of prehabilitation were most pronounced among women undergoing mastectomy or bilateral mastectomy, although meaningful benefits were also observed following lumpectomy. All patients who received prehabilitation recovered to baseline levels on at least one outcome. Across the perioperative period, patients who received prehabilitation attended fewer visits than those who received delayed rehabilitation (median, 5 vs 7; P =.008). Conclusions: Both prehabilitation and delayed rehabilitation supported recovery of upper extremity functioning and HRQoL following breast cancer surgery. However, prehabilitation may represent a more effective and efficient care model—particularly for women undergoing more extensive surgical procedures—achieving comparable or better outcomes with fewer visits. These findings support integration of prehabilitation into breast cancer surgical care pathways.

doi:10.6004/jnccn.2026.7054.abstract: Background: Only 3%–5% of patients with cancer nationwide enroll in clinical trials. Although participation among patients with solid tumors has been well studied, data in the hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) setting remain limited. We sought to (1) describe clinical trial participation rates by HSCT type; (2) examine associations between patient, disease, and transplant characteristics and trial participation; and (3) explore the association between trial participation and overall survival (OS). Methods: We conducted a retrospective study using Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplant Research (CIBMTR) data from US adults aged 18–75 years who underwent autologous or allogeneic HSCT between 2013 and 2019 (N=84,151; autologous: n=51,133; allogeneic: n=33,018). Logistic regression models assessed predictors of participation, while Cox models evaluated associations with OS. Results: Trial participation was 2.0% among patients undergoing autologous HSCT and 11.1% among those undergoing allogeneic HSCT. Among autologous recipients, greater comorbidity burden was associated with lower odds of participation. Patients with multiple myeloma had higher odds than those with non-Hodgkin lymphoma (odds ratio [OR], 1.25; P =.01). Among allogeneic recipients, older adults had higher odds of participation (eg, OR, 2.19 for age ≥70 vs 18–19 years; P <.0001), as did non-Hispanic Black patients compared with non-Hispanic White patients (OR, 1.35; P =.0002). Participation was higher with cord blood grafts, mismatched unrelated donors, and certain diagnoses (eg, sickle cell disease). Lower participation was observed for severe aplastic anemia and haploidentical or peripheral blood grafts. Trial participation was not associated with OS in either group. Conclusions: Clinical trial participation remains low, particularly among autologous HSCT recipients, younger adults, and patients with specific diagnoses. Findings highlight the need to broaden trial eligibility, enhance outreach, and ensure equity in trial access to promote generalizable, patient-centered evidence in HSCT.

doi:10.6004/jnccn.2026.7055.abstract: Background: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are common toxicities of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but their prognostic implications in older adults remain uncertain. Patients and Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using SEER–Medicare (2010–2019). We included patients aged ≥66 years with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC who initiated ICI monotherapy or chemoimmunotherapy from 2015–2017. Follow-up began at treatment initiation and continued until death, Medicare disenrollment, or December 31, 2019. The primary exposure was a clinically meaningful irAE, defined as an irAE diagnosis with evidence of systemic immunosuppressant use and/or treatment delay, or discontinuation. In secondary analyses, we categorized patients as having no irAE, an irAE managed without hospitalization, or an irAE requiring hospitalization. The primary outcome was overall survival. We estimated adjusted survival differences and restricted mean survival time using doubly robust causal inference methods. Results: The cohort included 5,304 patients (mean age, 75 years; 52.7% female; 81.9% White). Clinically meaningful irAEs occurred in 1,807 (34.1%) patients, with a median onset of 3.8 months (IQR, 1.1–9.4). Death occurred in 65.1% of patients with irAEs and 78.7% without irAEs, corresponding to an adjusted absolute survival benefit of 6.6% (95% CI, 5.3%–8.0%) and a 6.5-month gain in restricted mean survival time (95% CI, 5.6–7.4). In secondary analyses, irAEs managed without hospitalization showed the greatest benefit (odds ratio [OR], 0.44; 95% CI, 0.35–0.54), whereas irAE hospitalization was associated with attenuated benefit (OR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.89–0.99). Conclusions: Among older adults with advanced NSCLC receiving ICIs, clinically meaningful irAEs were associated with improved overall survival, particularly when managed without hospitalization. These findings highlight the clinical importance of early recognition of immune-related toxicities; irAE-related hospitalization may identify a higher-risk group warranting closer monitoring and supportive care.

doi:10.6004/jnccn.2026.7056.abstract: Background: Patients with cancer often require hospital-level care to address urgent needs and symptom concerns. However, little research has sought to identify patient factors, particularly rural-urban residence, associated with care outcomes in this population. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study including adult patients with cancer admitted to the University of Oklahoma Medical Center from January 2017 through December 2022. We extracted patients’ sociodemographic (ie, age, sex, race, ethnicity, rural-urban residence [Rural-Urban Continuum Codes]) and clinical (ie, Charlson comorbidity index [CCI] score, cancer type, metastatic disease status) information from the electronic health record. We used multivariable models to explore associations of patient factors with clinical outcomes (time to hospital discharge for length of stay [LOS], time to first readmission, and time to death [overall survival]). Results: We identified 20,683 patients in our cohort (mean [SD] age, 62.6 [15.4] years; 52% female sex, 40% with a CCI score ≥3, 41% with metastatic cancer, 31% with nonmetropolitan residence). Median hospital LOS was 4.0 days, with 30- and 90-day readmission rates of 15% and 23%, and median survival was 5.0 years. Older age (hazard ratio [HR], 0.93; P <.001), male sex (HR, 0.94; P <.001), higher comorbidity (CCI score ≥3: HR, 0.70; P <.001), and metastatic disease (HR, 0.88; P <.001) were associated with longer LOS. Higher comorbidity (CCI score ≥3: HR, 2.70; P <.001) was associated with a greater risk of readmission. Older age (HR, 1.50; P <.001), CCI score ≥3 (HR, 1.68; P <.001), and nonmetropolitan residence (HR, 1.08; P =.007) were associated with worse survival. Conclusions: In this cohort of hospitalized patients with cancer, we identified associations of patients’ sociodemographic and clinical factors with their hospital LOS, risk of readmission, and survival. Findings from this work could help inform targeted efforts to enhance care delivery and outcomes for this population.

doi:10.6004/jnccn.2026.7070.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have changed the treatment landscape of pleural mesothelioma (PM) over the past decade. This review summarizes the history of immunotherapy in PM, covering studies of single-agent immunotherapy, combination checkpoint blockade, the integration of ICIs into frontline therapeutic strategies, and ICI-VEGF combinations. Also discussed are the emerging role of biomarkers in guiding first-line therapy selection for patients with PM and novel therapeutic approaches. Dual checkpoint blockade targeting PD-1 and CTLA-4 demonstrated clinical efficacy in early-phase studies and led to the pivotal phase III CheckMate 743 trial, which established nivolumab and ipilimumab as a standard first-line systemic therapy for PM, particularly in patients with nonepithelioid histology. Since that time, other combination therapy approaches have been explored. For example, chemoimmunotherapy studies have evaluated ICIs, including pembrolizumab and durvalumab, in combination with platinum chemotherapy, with pembrolizumab plus platinum-doublet chemotherapy expanding the approved frontline treatment options for PM. VEGF inhibition, validated in the phase III MAPS study, provided a biologic rationale for combining antiangiogenic agents with ICIs. This prompted investigation of bevacizumab in combination with atezolizumab and chemotherapy in the BEAT-meso study. Unfortunately, this combination did not provide meaningful benefit in this setting. Optimal patient selection and treatment sequencing remain undefined. Although robust data support the use of second-line immunotherapy after first-line chemotherapy, there is a paucity of evidence regarding the efficacy of chemotherapy following frontline ICI. Despite advancements in therapeutic options in PM, biomarker-driven treatment selection remains limited at this time. Future large clinical studies must incorporate validated and standardized biomarker subanalyses, including approaches such as circulating tumor DNA and multiomics, for biomarkers to become clinically relevant in this heterogeneous malignancy. Finally, novel therapeutic strategies, including bispecific antibodies, targeted therapies, perioperative immunotherapy, vaccines, and cellular therapies, are under active investigation and may further expand treatment options for patients with PM.
